Dutch exports to US plummet 25% as tariffs bite
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Exports from the Netherlands to the United States fell by 25% in the first half of this year, knocking the US out of the top five destinations for Dutch goods.
Dutch companies sold €13 billion worth of goods to the US between January and June, €4.3 billion less than in the same period last year, figures from national statistics office CBS show. The decline began after the Trump administration imposed a general import tariff of 15% on goods from the EU in August last year.
Almost every type of product was affected. Machinery and transport equipment, the biggest category of Dutch exports to the US, accounted for nearly half the fall. Sales of medicines and other chemical products dropped by more than 30%, and manufactured goods such as medical instruments fell by almost a quarter.
As a result, the US now takes 4% of Dutch goods exports, down from 5.5% a year earlier. Italy has overtaken it as the fifth-biggest market, with Spain also catching up. Exports to Belgium, Germany, France, Spain and Italy all rose over the same period.
Trade in the other direction has grown – imports from the US were up 19% to €27.6 billion, although most of that increase was oil and other fuels, which have become more expensive because of the conflict in the Middle East. Other kinds of imports rose by 6.7%.
The tariffs have been costly for the US as well. The country’s Supreme Court ruled in February that most of the levies Donald Trump introduced last year were illegal, and Dutch companies are now claiming back more than €1 billion in duties.
Philips has already received €186 million, and Heineken and Ahold Delhaize are expected to recover hundreds of millions between them.
In 2024, before the tariffs were introduced, the Netherlands exported more than €38 billion worth of goods to the US, nearly 6% of all its exports.

The European Commissioner for Agriculture, Christophe Hansen, tells Euronews this has been “a very challenging summer” for farmers, with many “losing their harvests” due to extreme climate conditions.
Europe is recovering after a summer of heatwaves and droughts that have devastated crops and left many farmers facing huge financial losses. To help farmers cope, the European Commission is urging member states to make use of "flexibilities" in the EU's farm subsidy programme.
But Hansen admits no new money will be available for farmers. Instead, he asks for the “solidarity” of consumers and advises against expecting “a certain quality” of produce this year.

Unknown

CDU politician and German MP Günter Krings calls the Saxony-Anhalt election results “devastating”, saying the situation is “even worse than expected” after the far-right AfD won 43.8% of the vote.
It would not be “responsible” for the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) to talk about "changing the Chancellor" just one day after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) swept to electoral victory in Saxony-Anhalt, CDU politician and German MP Günter Krings has told Euronews.
He says his party should focus its energy on addressing its “low” credibility, and also points the finger at the European Union, saying that “a significant part of the anger of the voters comes from the EU’s decisions”.
AfD won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern German state on Sunday, more than double its showing five years ago.
That was well ahead of Merz’s Christian Democratic Union, which polled 17.2%, losing about half of its support. It's putting mounting pressure on the Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose popularity has fallen to record low levels in opinion polls.

IED master of arts graduates deploy design against the loss of common goods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:30:46 UTC
16:30:46 KST

IED MASTERS of arts EVOLVE PRACTICE THROUGH DESIGN X COMMONS
Marking an evolution in how design intervenes within contemporary society, the Master of Arts programs at Istituto Europeo di Design (IED)treat the discipline as a mediator between communities and common goods. Grounded in the understanding of commons as the material and immaterial resources that multiple communities engage with as the collective heritage of humanity, the overarching theme of Design X Commons elevates these graduate thesis projects past formal styling exercises and traditional product development. Combining research alongside speculative design strategies, the emerging designers confront climate vulnerability, urban privatization, labor exploitation, and spatial inequality to reshape collective urban futures.
IED Master of Arts Exhibition | all images courtesy of Istituto Europeo di Design (IED)
POSITIONING DESIGNERS AS AGENTS OF SOCIAL EQUALITY
IED structures its two-year Master of Arts programs to foster independent critical thinking in response to systemic global issues. Central to this educational model is the concept of common goods, encompassing both natural resources such as water, land, and air, as well as immaterial assets like cultural knowledge, open data, and public spaces. The institute positions the management of these resources, known as commoning, as a fundamental design practice. Through research, material testing, and participatory methods, graduates learn to challenge traditional industrial habits and build regenerative models that support both human and environmental ecosystems.
IED’s Master of Arts graduates present their thesis projects under the umbrella ‘Design X Commons’
GRADUATE PROJECTS SPOTLIGHT ECOLOGICAL REGENERATION AND SOCIAL equality
This design approach materializes in graduate work that targets specific local vulnerabilities while developing frameworks adaptable to global conditions. At IED Milano, Michele Martelloni addresses coastal erosion along the Apuan shoreline with ‘Systemic Reef’. The project transforms the industrial tetrapod into a porous, modular structure designed to dissipate wave energy and encourage marine life colonisation. The designer integrates waste marble powder from local quarries into a structural mixture, establishing a five step protocol for systemic coastal management.
‘Systemic Reef’ operates at the intersection of territorial knowledge, material research, and ecological urgency
In the Visual Communication program, Ana Sofia Camacho created ‘En la Olla. Narratives of Joyful Subversion’, a project that explores cultural identity. She focuses on everyday Latin American expressions, showing how creative play acts as a form of resistance against long standing social challenges. Camacho organizes these visual symbols into a series of objects that function as a collection and a manifesto, elevating local traditions and street culture into recognized, valuable contributions to modern creative practice.
the project reinterprets structural violence while challenging the dehumanizing legacy of colonization
At the intersection of spatial politics and climate adaptation, Olga Matsiuk developed ‘Where did water go? Urban bathing as a Common Practice Responding to an Ecosocial Emergency in Milan’ to address urban water accessibility. Framing water access as a basic human right, the project centers on a temporary public bathing festival around an underused fountain in Piazza Kaisserlian. The installation brings community members together to enjoy shared space while advocating for the reopening of nearby closed public swimming facilities.
framing public water access, the thesis acts as a political gesture of resistance against urban privatization
At IED Roma, Elena Bicocchi targets neighborhood revitalisation through ‘Strada domestica’, a project created for the Tuscolano district in collaboration with local authorities. The design reclaims Via Valesio from automobile traffic, expanding the comfortable qualities of domestic space into the street. Opening connected residential courtyards to community activities and adding flexible public structures called habitats, Bicocchi turns a vacant roadway into a resident-managed civic center.
through community-focused design, the ‘Strada domestica’ revitalizes a marginalized urban area
In the Textile Design program at IED Firenze, Ruby Berryman developed ‘Invisible Hands’ to examine human rights within Tuscany’s luxury fashion supply chain. The research highlights labor conditions affecting immigrant workers behind the Made in Italy label. To address these issues directly, Berryman created Mani Visibili, an online platform offering legal guidance, union resources, and a secure space for worker organizing.
the project ‘Invisible Hands’ reveals the complex social dynamics shaping contemporary fashion manufacturing
Focusing on geographic migration, Anna Leccese created ‘Punto di Ritorno’ within the IED Torino Interaction Design program to explore youth movement between southern and northern Italy. The project examines young people from Puglia who moved away for study or work and are considering moving back. The platform addresses the complex process shaped by personal desires, uncertainties, and career expectations, guiding individuals through well informed transitions back to their home region.
‘Punto di Ritorno’ examines the spatial and social conditions that enable displaced youth to return to their hometown
Virginia Urro responds to the urban housing crisis with ‘COHO MUNITY’, an interior design project based at IED Torino. The proposal converts the disused Manifattura di Moncalieri industrial site into an accessible, flexible cohousing ecosystem. Retrofitting existing building stock instead of constructing new facilities, Urro integrates shared domestic spaces and modular living units designed to reduce urban isolation and lower environmental impact.
transforming a disused industrial building into a housing scheme, ‘COHO MUNITY’ prioritizes shared spaces
from historic monuments to independent galleries and temporary spaces, discover the exhibitions, installations, and design events shaping paris design week 2026.

16:29:16 KST

COLOMBO, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka has marked 10 years since being certified malaria-free by the World Health Organization (WHO), maintaining elimination of indigenous transmission of all human malaria parasites in the country.
The WHO South-East Asia Region recognized Sri Lanka for sustaining its malaria-free status since certification in 2016, citing continued national commitment and surveillance efforts aimed at preventing the re-establishment of the disease.
Sri Lanka was among several countries recognized on Tuesday during the 79th Session of the WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia.
The country was also among nine regional members recognized for sustaining the elimination of maternal and neonatal tetanus for a decade following validation.
WHO said the achievements reflected sustained national commitment, effective health systems, surveillance and community engagement across the South-East Asia Region. ■

Kristian Pärt: Interior security not a poor relative of national defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:29:00 UTC
16:29:00 KST

Kristian Pärt: Interior security not a poor relative of national defense
Alongside military defense, it is equally necessary to significantly and visibly strengthen the protection of the country's internal security, because threats do not begin only in a crisis or wartime, nor are they carried out solely by military means, writes Kristjan Pärt.
The three saboteurs who set out to torch defense industry company Milrem Robotics on the night of August 15 were already sitting in Latvian police detention cells as suspects just a couple of days later. How was it possible to catch them so quickly? Perhaps cadets at the Estonian Academy of Security Sciences will hear the answer in a surveillance course — but even then, only 10 or more years from now.
The investigation is ongoing. We will determine whether the sabotage against Estonia was carried out in the interests of a state or organization and, if so, which one. But at this point, one's thoughts inevitably turn to Hando Runnel's poem "Jälle" ("Again"):
"Again the winds are howling, again the tempests roar.
Again from the east come herds of elk and bears."
Estonia's strength lies in its open society, democratic system of government and rule of law. Those strengths, however, can also present a window of opportunity to those who see our way of life as a thorn in their side.
Because of Estonia's geopolitical location, our internal security — and the country's overall security situation — is most strongly affected by external factors and developments, whether political, socioeconomic or technological, as well as by external threats, hostile foreign states and non-state organizations operating across borders.
Among hostile foreign states, Russia is the principal threat to European security, along with, indirectly, the regimes that support it. Other threats include violent extremist and terrorist groups, as well as international criminal organizations and networks. Each uses covert, nonmilitary methods to achieve its objectives, seeking to exploit the vulnerabilities of open societies and democratic ways of life — or the limited capabilities of security and law enforcement agencies.
The security of the state and society is threatened both by direct hostile activity and by harmful effects or external dependencies that materialize as a result of our own vulnerabilities.
If a hostile foreign state can gather intelligence on our territory without risk, influence our society or specific target groups and prepare positions that can be used to provoke a crisis or support a military operation, the conditions have been created for further escalation.
When strategic vulnerabilities are left unaddressed, the damaging effects on security can also emerge gradually and insidiously.
Depending on the specific risks and the area affected, the consequences may include damage to the state's internal sovereignty or to Estonia's status as a nation-state, the fragmentation of society, the spread of radicalization and violent extremism, growing anti-state attitudes among certain groups in society or deepening economic or energy dependence on high-risk countries. These are all threats that military defense capabilities can neither mitigate nor repel.
Russia carries out its nonmilitary hostile activities even before a crisis becomes perceptible or aggression becomes visible — in other words, during what we understand as peacetime. Damaging and weakening other countries and societies through nonmilitary and hybrid methods is part of Russia's foreign policy doctrine, with its aggressive intelligence and security services playing an integral role.
Russia's primary objective is not to seize territory, but to create a situation in which another country's ability to make decisions and resist has already been weakened before a crisis begins or in which that country has surrendered a significant part of its self-determination. A strong defense force alone is not enough to counter such a strategy. The state must also be capable of mitigating risks and detecting and preventing threatening activities at an early stage.
In short, ensuring national security requires both strategic risk mitigation and sufficient operational capabilities. The first of these involves reducing vulnerabilities in society and its institutions. This requires consistent policy measures with a broad, society-wide and nationwide impact that must also mitigate so-called creeping threats to our security and sovereignty.
A strategy for reducing vulnerabilities means assessing risks, developing policy and engaging society in ways that increase resilience to attacks of any kind, harmful influences on society and external dependencies.
Resilient societies are characterized by shared fundamental values, trust within the country, citizens' voluntary contributions and the ability to cope with and recover from different crises.
Examples of decisions aimed at reducing Estonia's vulnerabilities include the transition to Estonian-language education, visa restrictions and restrictions on real estate purchases by citizens of aggressor states, as well as the introduction of up-to-date continuity and security requirements for the country's vital services and digital service providers.
In the long term, many measures aimed at reducing the country's vulnerabilities directly support internal security and the principle of domestic peace enshrined in our Constitution.
The second prerequisite for maintaining security is the ability to detect and prevent hostile activity at any time, in both military and nonmilitary domains. This is where the strategic role of internal security begins: protecting the continued existence and functioning of the state.
The task of internal security agencies is to ensure that hostile states, their intelligence and security services or extremist groups cannot operate in Estonia in ways that threaten our constitutional order or the security of society as a whole. The primary responsibility for this rests with the Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS) and the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA).
Interior Ministry Secretary General Tarmo Miilits recently wrote about freedom, which resonates with those who can hear it. He rightly emphasized that the internal security services, which work around the clock to counter threats that have already reached Estonia, are the country's final line of defense for safety and security before the Defense Forces have to leave their training grounds and actually go into battle.
Counterintelligence, border security and migration monitoring and the prevention and disruption of hostile influence operations, terrorism and sabotage are proactive measures for ensuring national security. Their purpose is to respond effectively to offenses that have already been committed but, even more importantly, to detect and counter activities threatening Estonia's security before they develop into a broader crisis. Maintaining these capabilities, however, requires up-to-date legal powers, technological capabilities and sufficient resources.
These two main lines of action — reducing vulnerabilities and maintaining readiness to prevent or counter various attacks — complement one another and create an environment in which acting against Estonia becomes difficult, costly and ineffective for those who threaten us.
The Milrem Robotics sabotage case is a good illustration of why maintaining internal security requires a physical presence and the ability to respond at the scene, but also, of course, the capacity to collect, process and lawfully use information necessary for security purposes.
In today's digital societies, detecting and proving many such crimes increasingly depends on technological capabilities and the use of digital footprints. In its first internal security advisory submitted to the interior minister, the ISS described this as striking a balance between preventing threats and ensuring access to data.
"Security and law enforcement agencies must have effective tools to protect security in today's digital society and to detect and prove crimes that have been committed using digital evidence," the ISS wrote in its advisory. Of course, that means access to data, but it also means ensuring that the use of data and oversight are proportionate.
A legal framework that reflects the threats we face and enables action is a critical part of the capacity to ensure internal security. If the state can identify threats in time and respond to them, it can preserve public safety while also safeguarding people's freedoms and the functioning of the democratic system. A democratic state becomes stronger when it is able to prevent threats lawfully and proportionately.
Believe it or not, keeping the capabilities of Estonia's internal security agencies up to date is not a narrow institutional interest of the interior ministry, the ISS or the PPA, just as developing national defense is not a narrow institutional interest of the Ministry of Defense or the Defense Forces. All of this is a strategic investment in the continued existence of the Estonian state and in our sovereignty.
Like military national defense, the development of internal security capabilities requires stable and predictable funding. This makes it possible to pursue developments that meet contemporary requirements and reflect the current threat landscape, recruit highly capable people, provide continuous staff training, invest in forward-looking technologies and much more.
Military national defense and internal security are not competitors, but partners that complement one another. One prepares the country for a military crisis; the other helps do everything possible to prevent hostile activity within the country from escalating into a crisis. A strong defense force without robust internal security leaves an adversary free to act against us in areas where weapons are not used. Likewise, strengthening internal security alone is not enough without credible military deterrence and defense capabilities. Estonia needs both.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

AmCham Shanghai report shows sharp rebound in business confidence among member companies
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:28:45 CST
16:28:45 KST

SHANGHAI, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 China Business Report, released on Thursday by the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai (AmCham Shanghai), revealed a significant rebound in business confidence among its surveyed member companies operating in China.
Business confidence bounced back markedly, as 58 percent of respondents expressed optimism about China's five-year business outlook, up 17 percentage points year on year, the report said.
Profitability rebounded to its highest level since 2019, with 78 percent of respondents profitable in 2025, an increase of 7 percentage points from the 2024 level, according to the report.
As business confidence rebounded and more companies reported profits, investment confidence in China also strengthened, resulting in 28 percent of respondents increasing investment in China last year, the highest level in four years.
Improved market sentiment is also reflected in a positive assessment of China's business environment. Fifty-five percent of surveyed companies said the business environment in China is transparent, up 7 percentage points year on year.
"Members have clearly noticed government efforts to improve the regulatory environment, and this year those gains are reinforced by steadier U.S.-China relations," said Jeffrey Lehman, chair of AmCham Shanghai. "We urge both countries to build on the momentum of recent engagement and lock in a stable, transparent framework that is conducive to cross-border trade and investment."
Eric Zheng, president of AmCham Shanghai, emphasized the great importance of the Chinese market, mainly from two dimensions.
China remains one of the most efficient manufacturing bases in the world and continues to be a highly strategic market for members' products and services, Zheng said. "That underpins the positive sentiment," he added.
Chinese operations also contributed to the global and domestic business performance of U.S. companies, the survey showed.
Among members with U.S. operations, three-quarters confirmed that their China presence benefits their U.S. operations in some way, with one-third emphasizing that their China presence enhances the global competitiveness of their U.S. operations.
A notable strategic shift is also emerging, with more surveyed companies adopting a global-oriented strategy. The "in China for the world" strategy has become the top business priority for 29 percent of surveyed companies in 2026, surpassing the "in China for China" model chosen by 24 percent.
More respondents are also betting on China-based innovation, the report said. Half of surveyed members with China-based research and development (R&D) facilities plan to increase R&D spending this year, up sharply from one-third in 2025.
The report is based on AmCham Shanghai's 2026 China Business Survey of 262 member companies.
In a vote of confidence in the Chinese market, General Motors (GM) in August announced a 20-year extension of its joint venture partnership with Chinese automaker SAIC Motor, with it now running to 2047.
"We will continue to strengthen our performance here in China by developing products and technologies in China, for China, and bringing them to market faster," said John Roth, GM senior vice president & president of GM China. The joint venture plans to launch at least 30 new energy vehicle models by 2030.
"We see meaningful opportunities to grow beyond China. SAIC-GM has strong local capabilities across engineering, manufacturing and quality, and we can apply those strengths in select international markets, including the Middle East, Africa, South America, Mexico and Asia-Pacific," Roth said.
"Foreign companies continue to value the Chinese market for its scale and dynamism and, increasingly, as a base for serving the world," noted Jeff Yuan, head of tax at PwC China, adding that China remains a critical part of their global strategy for innovation, production and sourcing. ■

Andrea Renda, Director of Research at the Centre for European Policy Studies, believes the main issue is that “we don't know enough” about what is actually happening inside AI development companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

Study finds earliest evidence of habitual drug use
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
15:28:34 CST
16:28:34 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists have uncovered what may be the earliest evidence of habitual drug use, dating "betel nut" use among early human foragers to as early as 25,000 years ago, tens of thousands of years before agriculture.
A team led by Australia's Griffith University archaeologists found evidence that humans were using mind-altering substances much earlier in time than previously supposed, according to a university statement released Thursday.
The team, working with Indonesian archaeologists, combined biochemical and archaeological evidence to trace the prehistoric roots of betel nut, one of the world's most popular addictive stimulants and an ancient drug used throughout much of the Asia-Pacific region.
The study, published in Science Advances, reports the discovery of extremely rare skeletal remains of two early human foragers from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, one dating to 25,000-16,000 years ago, the other to 7,600-6,300 years ago.
Both hunter-gatherers display highly unusual deep, rounded tooth grooves, a marker the researchers established was caused by a previously unknown drug-use behavior: habitual sucking of whole betel nuts, researchers said.
Biochemical analyses also detected arecoline in the foragers' dental tissues, providing strong evidence for betel nut ingestion, they said, adding that experiments showed that sucking intact betel nuts can release enough arecoline to have a physiological effect and alter brain function.
Betel nut use was previously thought to have emerged around the Neolithic or Bronze Age, about 3,500 years ago.
The findings suggest habitual psychoactive substance use existed among hunter-gatherers tens of thousands of years before farming, and betel nut-sucking may represent the earliest evidence of drug use yet recorded. ■

A fire burned overnight on a passenger ferry off the western Philippines, leaving dozens of people missing Thursday and killing at least five. So far, more than 40 people have been rescued, coast guard spokeswoman Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said.
The blaze broke out on the M/V June Aster Wednesday evening about 2.2 km offshore, the coast guard said, adding that five casualties had been brought ashore.

Passengers were helped into smaller boats taking them to shallow water, and body bags were laid out at what looked like a port. The ferry had sailed from the capital Manila and was near its destination of Coron in Palawan province when the fire started on Wednesday. Bad weather and big waves challenged rescuers.
Coast Guard rescued more than 40 people
Hundreds of people, desperate for news about the incident, have left comments on the Coron town mayor's Facebook page, searching for relatives, friends and even a dog.
"Based on the data we have right now on rescued (42) and the casualties, we still have 86 people who are unaccounted for," coast guard spokeswoman Noemie Cayabyab told a local radio station on Thursday.
She said 134 people were on board, 117 of them passengers and 17 crew. There was no information about any foreigners on board.
In January, a triple-decker ferry carrying more than 340 people sank off the southern Philippines, killing at least 52 people.
The M/V Trisha Kerstin 3 sank along nearly the same route where 31 people died in 2023 after a fire broke out aboard the Lady Mary Joy 3 ferry.

New B-21 hangar heads to Missouri’s Whiteman Air Force Base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:26:50 UTC
16:26:50 KST

- The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers awarded Conti Federal Services a $74.8 million contract to build a B-21 radio frequency hangar at Whiteman Air Force Base.
- Whiteman, which currently hosts the Air Force's entire B-2 fleet, is set to become the B-21 program's second main operating base after Ellsworth.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has awarded Conti Federal Services a $74.8 million contract to build a new radio frequency and measurements hangar for the B-21 Raider stealth bomber at Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri.
The facility will include space for one B-21 aircraft, along with supporting workshops, material storage, and administrative offices. Three companies bid on the project, which the Corps solicited online. Work is expected to be finished by September 25, 2029. The Army Corps’ Kansas City district is managing the contract, funded through fiscal 2026 military construction dollars.
The B-21 is the aircraft the Air Force is counting on to anchor its bomber fleet for decades to come. Built by Northrop Grumman as a nuclear-capable stealth bomber, it first flew in November 2023 and remains in low-rate initial production, with the Air Force and Northrop Grumman announcing an agreement in February 2026 to expand production capacity and speed up deliveries. The Air Force has said the B-21 is designed to penetrate the kind of heavily defended airspace that older bombers can no longer survive in, and the service confirmed in July 2026 that the aircraft will fly with a two-person crew. The program has continued hitting test milestones through 2026, including an aerial refueling demonstration with a KC-135 tanker in April.
Whiteman is set to become the B-21’s second main operating base, after the Air Force picked the installation over Dyess Air Force Base in Texas. Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota became the program’s first main operating base in 2021 and currently serves as the B-21’s formal training site; Air Force leadership visited Ellsworth in July 2026 to mark what the service called a historic milestone in that base’s B-21 facilities work. Whiteman already hosts the Air Force’s entire fleet of B-2 Spirit stealth bombers, 19 aircraft in total, two of which have been lost in crashes over the years.
The B-21 is being built to gradually replace both the B-2 and the older B-1 Lancer, which the Air Force expects to begin retiring around 2031 and 2032 as it moves toward a two-bomber fleet alongside the B-52.
A radio frequency and measurements hangar is used to test an aircraft’s radar signature and electronic systems in a controlled environment, work that matters for a stealth bomber designed to evade enemy radar. Conti Federal has built several other B-21 support facilities at Ellsworth, including a $31.7 million fuel cell maintenance hangar awarded in October 2024, part of what the company has described as a broader, multi-year construction effort tied to the bomber’s rollout.

U.S. Air Force signs $149M deal to keep its bunker busters in production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:22:22 UTC
16:22:22 KST

- The U.S. Air Force awarded four manufacturers a combined $149 million in contracts to build large penetrator warhead cases for bunker-busting bombs.
- The Eglin Air Force Base-run competition drew four offers, with work expected to run through September 2033 if a contract option is exercised.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded four manufacturers a combined $149 million to build metal cases for large bunker-busting bombs, splitting the work across small forging and machining shops rather than a single prime contractor.
Superior Forge and Steel of Lima, Ohio; Ellwood National Forge of Irvine, Pennsylvania; Faxon Machining LLC of Cincinnati, Ohio; and Grand Valley Manufacturing of Titusville, Pennsylvania each received a firm-fixed-price, cost-type indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract for what the Air Force calls large penetrator warhead case assembly production. The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Attack Weapons Branch at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, ran the competition and received four offers before making the awards.
The contracts cover manufacturing of the warhead cases and their components, including both full-scale and subscale versions used for testing. Work at all four companies is expected to wrap up by September 7, 2033, if the Air Force exercises an option to extend the deal. The Air Force obligated just $10,000 in fiscal 2026 research and development funding at the time of the award, a placeholder amount typical for IDIQ contracts where the government orders and pays for specific quantities of work over time rather than committing the full ceiling value upfront.
A large penetrator warhead case is the hardened metal shell built to survive the impact of slamming into a hardened target, like a bunker or tunnel complex, before the explosive charge inside detonates.
The Air Force’s existing weapon in this category is the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, a 13,600 kg (30,000-pound) bomb built by Boeing that carries a roughly 2,700 kg (6,000-pound) warhead and is dropped from B-2 and B-52 bombers. The Pentagon used GBU-57 bombs against Iran’s Fordow nuclear facility in June 2025.
The Air Force is also developing a successor weapon, the Next Generation Penetrator, after awarding Applied Research Associates a two-year design and prototyping contract in September 2025. Boeing is partnered with ARA on that program, building the new weapon’s tail kit. The Air Force notice announcing this week’s case-assembly awards did not specify which penetrator program, or programs, the contracts will supply.

====================================================================================================

Trump's Iran campaign echoes the post-9/11 'forever wars' - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:22:04 UTC
16:22:04 KST

When Donald Trump campaigned for a second term in the White House, he promised to be a “president of peace” who would stop foreign wars, not start them.
Now, a quarter-century after the September 11, 2001, attacks that triggered America’s global “war on terror,” he is entangled in an unpopular conflict of his own making that analysts say risks becoming his version of a “forever war."
With the 9/11 anniversary at hand, Trump’s war against Iran is drawing comparisons in foreign policy circles to the long, divisive conflicts in Afghanistan and Iraq that preceded it. It is also prompting questions about whether the US has again failed to learn the lessons of past conflicts or prepare a clear exit strategy.
“Trump has broken an important post-Iraq and Afghanistan constraint in Washington against launching another major, open-ended war in the Middle East,” said Sina Toossi of the Center for International Policy, a Washington think tank. “That could leave his successor inheriting ... an entrenched US-Iran confrontation.”
Administration officials have said the war against Iran is nothing like the protracted post-9/11 engagements.
During the conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan, the US removed hostile governments, committed thousands of ground troops who took and held territory, suffered and inflicted much higher casualties, and struggled to instill Western-style governance.
US mired in war of attrition
This time, the US is relying mainly on air and naval power, operations that have damaged Iran militarily and economically but have not defeated it or spurred Iranians to overthrow their rulers as Trump initially urged.
But after six months of war, the United States is mired in a battle of attrition punctuated by bursts of hostilities - exemplified by this week's exchange of attacks on oil tankers - while Trump tries to tighten the economic noose around Tehran.
Analysts warn it is likely to drag on well past the US midterm elections in November, when voters' opposition to the war could threaten Trump's Republican Party's chances of keeping control of Congress.
And, much like those earlier conflicts, there is no obvious exit even as the economic costs weigh on US consumers.
Tehran’s disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has pushed US gasoline prices higher. The war has weakened Trump’s approval ratings and undermined Washington’s international standing, which was also one of the repercussions from the Iraq and Afghan wars.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said Trump alone had “possessed the courage” to confront Iran over its nuclear program, that he had achieved all of his objectives, and that Iran's economy was being crippled by stepped-up sanctions and a US maritime blockade.
She did not respond directly to Reuters' questions on how the Iran conflict fits into America’s legacy of post-9/11 wars.
Lessons ignored?
Analysts say Trump has failed to heed the central lessons of the post-9/11 era, which began after al-Qaeda militants crashed planes into New York’s World Trade Center and the Pentagon outside Washington, killing nearly 3,000 people.
Those include the steep political downsides of long wars and the dangers posed by an entrenched foe fighting for its survival.
The attacks led to decades of conflict, starting with the invasion of Afghanistan, where al-Qaeda leaders were sheltering, and followed by the 2003 invasion of Iraq, based on what turned out to be faulty intelligence that it was developing weapons of mass destruction.
The twin wars undertaken by President George W. Bush overstretched the US military and destabilized the Middle East.
The resulting US public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, and he won a second term in 2024, vowing to avoid military adventurism and focus on Americans’ economic concerns.
But similar to how the Bush administration underestimated the insurgencies the US would face in Iraq and Afghanistan, Trump and his aides have miscalculated Iran’s resiliency and ability to throttle a fifth of the world’s energy shipments, analysts say.
Notably, Trump’s "Operation Epic Fury" launched alongside Israel on February 28 was not precipitated by a 9/11-type national trauma but was deemed by critics to be a war of choice. Experts have disputed Trump’s claims that Tehran’s nuclear program posed an imminent threat to the US
Iran may be taking a page from Afghanistan’s Taliban, who returned to power five years ago after a chaotic US withdrawal, that a determined foe can outlast Washington’s superior firepower while domestic pressure erodes its resolve.
The Iran conflict has also illustrated the cost of going to war with few allies on board.
Bush secured significant international support before launching his Iraq and Afghan campaigns, though that backing waned over time.
By contrast, Trump attacked Iran with little prior consultation or explanation and has found European and Asian leaders mostly resistant to his demands for assistance.
Relations with Trump had already been strained by his threat to seize Greenland, his questioning of NATO’s utility, his reduction of weapons supplies to Ukraine and his sweeping tariffs on trade partners.
High cost for allies
The conflict has also mirrored the Iraq invasion in terms of a regional spillover that seemed to catch Washington off-guard, in this case Tehran’s retaliation against US Gulf allies.
With Iran’s neighbors quietly seeking to de-escalate a conflict they never wanted, a Gulf official lamented that the administration might be making some of the same errors of the post-9/11 wars.
“What was the (US) strategy here?” asked the official, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Saudi analyst Aziz Alghashian described "a sense of limitation and helplessness in the Gulf about the wars that are taking place due to the whims of the United States."
While the Iraq and Afghan wars ended as unpopular conflicts, both started with solid support at home.
Trump’s war enjoyed no such honeymoon in public opinion.
Most Americans were against it from the outset, and he has even drawn criticism from prominent figures associated with his “America First” movement.
Trump had initially expected to replicate his quick win from a January 3 raid that captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro.
But the Iran campaign instead has hardened into an uneasy stalemate that has not achieved most of Trump’s shifting objectives, including shutting down its nuclear program, and has depleted the Pentagon's missile stockpiles.
Still, Trump is not without defenders.
Mark Dubowitz, head of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an anti-Iran think tank in Washington, denied Trump had plunged the US into an endless war and insisted he had scored successes that would eventually bring victory.
“It’s been a 47-year war waged by the Islamic Republic against America,” Dubowitz said. “And now we’ve struck back.”

NATO allies foil Russian subsea cable sabotage plot in Arctic waters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:22:04 UTC
16:22:04 KST

Deep in Arctic waters near the remote Svalbard archipelago this spring, NATO allies caught Russian subs training to unleash a secret weapon designed to disable critical undersea cables without leaving any fingerprints.
The clandestine Russian operation, described to Reuters by two Western officials, was carried out by Moscow's GUGI undersea warfare directorate, which used deep-sea submersibles to simulate the deployment of the sophisticated and destructive technology.
A joint operation involving Britain, Norway and the United States tracked and confronted the Russian vessels at sea, said the two officials, speaking on condition of anonymity. The vessels were prevented from completing their exercise and eventually left the area.
Britain and Norway disclosed in April that they had uncovered a covert Russian operation in Arctic waters. But the discovery of the new weapon, the location of the operation and the US involvement have not been reported.
The deep-sea face-off comes at a time when some Western intelligence officials fear the Kremlin is ramping up sabotage operations in Europe and preparing for a conflict with NATO.
Some US intelligence analysts are increasingly concerned Russia may test NATO's mutual defense pact, known as Article 5, three US officials said. If it does, destroying subsea cables could be a critical part of that effort, the Western officials said.
Cables no thicker than a garden hose, lying on the seabed or buried just below, are critical to global internet connectivity and financial transactions. Their economic and strategic importance has made them targets in past conflicts, including in the First and Second World Wars, when they were critical to delivering orders by telegraph or telephone.
Two 1,400 km subsea fiber-optic cables linking Svalbard to mainland Norway lie as deep as 2,700 meters below the sea's surface. They carry vast amounts of satellite data downloaded at the SvalSat satellite ground station, the world's largest and part of NASA's Near Space Network.
Russia's Defence Ministry didn't respond to a request for comment on the incident. The Kremlin consistently denies conducting sabotage operations in NATO countries or plotting any confrontation.
Some Western officials argue that Moscow's targeting of European states has increased in recent months as the front line in Ukraine has become largely static.
Countries including Poland, Lithuania, and Romania have confirmed various violations. Most recently, an attempted drone attack on the Leipzig/Halle Airport in August triggered a series of responses from Germany, including the closure of a Russian consulate in Bonn and a cultural center in Berlin.
In August, Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe visited intelligence counterparts in Moscow, in part to warn Russia against escalating sabotage operations in Europe, said two people familiar with the matter.
Reuters couldn't determine if Ratcliffe raised Russia's covert subsea operations. The Kremlin declined to say what had been discussed or to provide any further details.
Arctic exercise
At the same time as the confrontations at sea, British and Norwegian officials took their findings to Moscow to show they were aware of the new technology – hoping it might make Russia hesitate to use it, the two Western officials said.
Russia didn't damage any cables. The exercise focused on simulating the deployment of the technology in the event of a conflict with NATO, the officials said. They declined to detail how the technology works.
Asked for comment, NATO referred Reuters to Norwegian and UK authorities.
"Through our joint operation, we sent a clear message to Russia that they cannot operate covertly," Norway's Defence Minister Tore Sandvik said in a statement.
"We have made it unequivocally clear to Russian authorities that any attempt to target our critical infrastructure will be detected and met with consequences," he said. "It is in no one's interest to escalate tensions in the High North."
Britain's Defense Ministry pointed to April 9 statements acknowledging attempted covert activities in and near Norwegian and British waters by Russia's Main Directorate of Deep-Sea Research, known by its Russian acronym GUGI. Washington and London have both imposed sanctions on the secretive directorate.
The White House didn't respond to a comment request. The CIA declined to comment.
Any escalation between Russia and NATO could quickly underscore the strategic importance of an icy expanse of water between the southern tip of the Svalbard archipelago and mainland Norway known as the Bear Gap, one of the Western officials said.
To reach the Atlantic, Russian nuclear submarines based in the Kola Peninsula would cross the 400-mile-wide stretch of water before passing Norway's remote volcanic island Jan Mayen.
Britain said this week it deployed forces to Jan Mayen in August alongside Norwegian and US allies for an exercise to demonstrate NATO's ability to operate jointly in the High North.
Norway plans to have new fiber-optic cable linking Svalbard and Jan Mayen to the mainland by 2028.
'Burgeoning Russian threat'
NATO allies have focused on subsea infrastructure security since the 2022 destruction of three of the four Nord Stream subsea pipelines supplying Germany with Russian gas. German prosecutors have indicted a Ukrainian man who was a special forces officer at the time of the attack. Ukraine denies any role in the sabotage.
And since 2023, more ships have sailed slowly over or near sensitive subsea infrastructure, including pipelines, power cables and telecoms cables, to map their location, an activity known as drifting.
Last year, drifting in the North Sea rose 52% to 13,079 vessels from the previous year, data from maritime risk analytics firm Windward showed, while activity in the South China Sea region jumped 88% to 18,401 vessels.
It's not illegal to survey infrastructure in international waters, but security experts see such extensive mapping as preparation for sabotage.
The activity and suspected interference with some cables prompted new initiatives launched in January last year, including NATO's Baltic Sentry monitoring system and the UK-led Nordic Warden, bringing navies together for increased patrols of critical infrastructure.
In the Baltic Sea – one focus area for monitoring – 2025 drifting activity was down 5% to 526 vessels from a year earlier, Windward data showed. It said at least 11 subsea cables had been damaged or cut in the Baltic from October 2023 through the end of last year.
"The current thinking is that Russia and China are probably the most active and critical underwater threats," said Windward Chief Executive Ami Daniel.
The global network of power and telecoms cables running across seabeds is expanding each year, supported by increases in demand for data and electricity, partly driven by artificial intelligence, and some analysts say Europe remains vulnerable.
"In the last 25 years, Europe did two things simultaneously. It dramatically expanded the extent to which it relies on seabed infrastructure, and it dramatically shrunk its capacity to protect that infrastructure," said Bruce Jones, a senior fellow with the Brookings Institution. "It's belatedly rebuilding now, in the face of a burgeoning Russian threat."

A US grant program for organizations pursuing Trump administration priorities in Europe will exclude French groups because of sensitivities over allegations of foreign interference ahead of next year's presidential election, according to two sources.
The decision has already been communicated to French officials, one of the sources said. It reflects a recognition in Washington that funding MAGA-aligned organizations in France could jeopardize extensive economic ties between both countries.
US President Donald Trump's administration has sought to support far-right parties across Europe, accusing the continent's centrist leaders of overseeing "civilizational erasure" and "the subversion of democratic processes."
The US State Department's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor (DRL) grant program offers between $1 million and $3 million to organizations seeking "to strengthen and develop democratic resilience, rule of law, freedom of speech and freedom of the press, and the defense of human rights in Europe," according to DRL's July 13 funding guidelines.
Eligible groups may also focus on "national sovereignty, migration, censorship, and lawfare challenges."
French concerns over election interference rise
France, which faces a presidential election next April-May that could hand power to Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally (RN), has grown increasingly worried about potential US interference in the vote. The RN has pledged a constitutional reform to ramp up deportations, restrict birthright citizenship and give French nationals priority access to public services.
In July, just days after DRL published its funding announcement, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot reacted angrily on X, writing: "France and the Europeans will not tolerate any attempt at foreign interference in their electoral processes, regardless of where it comes from."
One French applicant, who declined to be named, said they had sought $1 million for their organization's work on anti-censorship and freedom of speech initiatives. They were recently informed that French groups would be excluded because of concerns over foreign interference.
According to the source, US officials were particularly concerned that US-funded activities could conflict with a proposed French law that would strengthen penalties for online disinformation and foreign interference in democratic processes. The fast-tracked, government-backed bill is currently before the Senate.
Although DRL's August deadline has now passed, the source said they may relocate their organization, potentially to Brussels, to qualify for future funding opportunities.
A State Department spokesperson declined to answer whether French groups were now excluded, saying "programs are still in active deliberation," and adding "we do not comment on private diplomatic discussions."
France's foreign ministry did not respond.
Franco-American relations strained
Although several senior MAGA officials within the State Department have sought a tougher line on France over freedom of speech and tech regulation, sources say they have faced pushback from other US officials who fret about negative repercussions for US companies with significant operations in France.
The United States is France's top foreign investor, with $107.9 billion invested in the French economy in 2024, while the two nations traded $160.9 billion in goods and services that year, according to US government data.
Still, diplomatic relations are at a low ebb.
On top of lingering issues over tariffs, the Iran war and threats to European sovereignty, Washington has yet to accredit France's next US ambassador following public French criticism of the United States' human rights record.
French officials have been irked by US Ambassador to Paris Charles Kushner, whose son Jared is married to Trump's daughter Ivanka. He has twice failed to respond to summonses in Paris following diplomatic incidents.
They were also upset when DRL officials traveled to Paris last year to support Le Pen after a court barred her from office as part of a drive against alleged "lawfare" against conservatives.

"Harming a teacher or any staff member is an attack on the heart of the educational system, and we will not tolerate it. Violence is not a way to resolve disputes, is not legitimate under any circumstances, and will not be part of the agenda," it added.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

====================================================================================================

Iran dodges sanctions using barter system to buy billions of dollars of Chinese goods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:21:42 UTC
16:21:42 KST

Iran has used a barter-like arrangement to bypass sanctions on its oil sales and buy billions of dollars’ worth of goods from China, including military gear, two senior Iranian sources and three other people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The secretive trade mechanism, in which Iranian oil is exchanged for credits for Chinese imports, has provided a financial lifeline for Tehran in recent years as the United States stepped up economic and military pressure over its nuclear program, according to the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
It has also helped China, the world’s biggest crude importer, retain access to discounted Iranian oil while shielding banks and companies that export to the Islamic Republic from international scrutiny or penalties, they said.
The US has imposed sanctions on some smaller Chinese entities that buy or facilitate shipments of Iranian oil but has stopped short of the most punishing measures that could have repercussions on the global economy.
Washington has intensified the pressure as it tries to resolve its war with Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. In August, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned countries to cut business ties with Iran or risk being forced out of the dollar-based financial system.
Reuters could not determine the impact on the barter-like arrangement of the US naval blockade imposed on Iran as part of the six-month war. No Iranian crude cargoes have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz to China since the blockade was reinstated on July 14, the news agency reported last week.
China and Iran have repeatedly denounced what they regard as illegal unilateral Western sanctions and have vowed to protect their interests. The countries are longstanding economic and political partners but have said little publicly about how they keep trade flowing despite international restrictions.
Iran has used the arrangement to buy medicines, vehicles and communication equipment from China, all the sources said. The manufacturers were not dealing directly with Iran, and there is no indication they were in breach of sanctions.
The mechanism was also used at least once in the past year in connection with contracts to supply Iran with air defense equipment worth millions of dollars, the sources said.
They did not provide details about any of the alleged transactions with Chinese manufacturers, and Reuters could not independently verify that they took place.
A UN embargo on the export of most major conventional weapons to Iran was reinstated with other sanctions in September 2025 after the US withdrew from a 2015 nuclear accord between Iran and world powers during President Donald Trump’s first term, and Tehran stopped complying with some of its provisions.
Iran and China said the move by European countries to automatically restore the sanctions through a “snapback” mechanism was “legally and procedurally flawed.”
Responding to Reuters questions about the barter-like trade, China’s foreign ministry said it was “not familiar with the situation you describe.”
“China has consistently opposed unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law and have not been authorized by the United Nations Security Council,” it said.
Iran’s UN missions in New York and Geneva did not respond to requests for comment.
In response to questions to the White House, a US official said the Trump administration works with economic partners including the European Union to “deprive Iran of the material means of furthering its nuclear ambitions.” The official did not comment on the arrangement described to Reuters.
Avoiding international banking channels
Decades of US sanctions have left Iran with few oil customers. China is the main buyer, accounting for more than 80% of Iran’s shipped oil in 2025, or an average 1.4 million barrels per day, according to commodities data and analytics firm Kpler.
In 2021, the two countries signed a 25-year strategic partnership accord covering sectors such as energy and infrastructure, but public details remain scarce.
The arrangement described to Reuters is one of a number of mechanisms through which Iran purchases goods and services from China without paying Chinese companies directly through international banking channels, three of the sources said.
A Western official and two other people familiar with the matter said a buyer acting on behalf of Chinese state-owned oil trader Zhuhai Zhenrong was at least until this year depositing hundreds of millions of dollars a month with an obscure, China-based financial entity known as ChuXin.
The deposits covered purchases agreed with a Hong Kong-registered company linked to Iran’s national oil company, the people said, citing material gathered by intelligence agencies. ChuXin would then send funds to Chinese exporters and companies that build infrastructure in Iran, likely via other Chinese financial institutions.
Roughly 70% of the Iranian oil proceeds handled by ChuXin are allocated to infrastructure projects, the three sources said, an arrangement first reported by the Wall Street Journal last October. The rest go into accounts belonging to a special purpose vehicle (SPV) used to pay companies that supply goods to Iran.
The Iranian sources, who are close to the country’s decision-making circle, confirmed the existence of the SPV, which has not previously been reported.
All five sources said funds in the SPV are managed by two entities: a firm acting on behalf of China's Ministry of Commerce and one linked to Iran’s central bank. The Iran-linked firm notifies the Chinese one when Iran’s central bank authorizes importers to access funds in the SPV so payments can be sent to the suppliers, three said.
Reuters could find no record of a financial institution called ChuXin in Chinese company registries or of the firms said to be acting on behalf of China’s commerce ministry and Iran’s central bank. One source said ChuXin might only exist on a spreadsheet.
Companies with the same names as those said to be acting on behalf of the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) and Zhuhai Zhenrong are listed in the Hong Kong companies registry, but Reuters could find no public records of their ownership structure or business dealings. Neither responded to questions delivered to their registered addresses, which are in offices belonging to secretarial services companies.
Plausible deniability
Zhuhai Zhenrong has been a target of US sanctions over its alleged dealings with Iran. One source shared what appeared to be a July 22, 2025, letter from NIOC to the Chinese oil trader requesting confirmation of an outstanding balance – evidence, the person said, of a business relationship.
Reuters could not independently authenticate the document. NIOC and Zhuhai Zhenrong did not respond to questions about it or their alleged roles in the trade mechanism.
Iran’s central bank and China’s commerce ministry also did not respond to requests for comment.
The mechanism described to Reuters has been in place since at least 2021 and was first used to supply medicines and COVID-19 vaccines to Iran, three sources said.
As Washington has stepped up pressure on companies that do business with Iran, it has become increasingly important for trade, they said. They estimated that between $2 billion and $2.5 billion flowed through the SPV over the last year.
China is using such arrangements to push back against the US and show it cannot be coerced with the threat of secondary sanctions, said Andrea Ghiselli, an international politics lecturer at the University of Exeter who studies Beijing’s relations with the Middle East.
But he said China’s leaders do not want their banks or companies excluded from the international financial system.
“They want plausible deniability.”

In total, 32 properties were damaged across the region,” Tkachenko said, noting this included two industrial or warehouse facilities.

Too late? Palestinians cautiously welcome settlement sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:18:39 UTC
16:18:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Palestinians in occupied West Bank cautiously welcome sanctions on Israeli settlements, but is it too late?
Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank have met the announcement by 12 Western countries that they intend to restrict trade in Israeli settlement products with a mixture of relief, scepticism and a familiar question: will anything actually change?
For decades, Palestinians have watched Israeli settlements expand across their land, while Israeli settler attacks, military incursions and land confiscations have become an increasingly routine part of life.
On Tuesday, Britain, France, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden announced plans to restrict trade in goods produced in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, or to support similar measures at the European level.
The move marks a shift from diplomatic criticism towards economic action, potentially opening the door to measures that could place a direct cost on businesses and entities involved in the settlement enterprise.
Yet in the occupied West Bank, where Palestinians have seen years of international condemnations produce little change on the ground, the announcement has also prompted a more pressing question: will these measures actually be enforced?
"At least it is a good step, even if it is belated," Ahmed Nubani, 47, from Nablus, told The New Arab.
"We [in the West Bank] had spent years hearing Western governments condemn Israeli settlements while watching them continue to grow," he said.
"We have waited many years for Western nations to move from condemning settlements to taking economic action," he added.
Yet he does not believe restricting settlement products alone can stop the expansion.
"We see the settlements growing right before our eyes," Nubani continued. "So, when we hear about a ban on settlement products, we ask: Will this actually lead to a halt in construction and confiscation?"
For him, meaningful pressure would have to reach deeper into the economic system supporting settlements.
"If they truly want to help the Palestinians, they must stop the flow of funds and investments into the settlements and punish those who attack Palestinians, rather than simply banning a few products," he explained.
From statements to enforcement
Fatima Al-Arouri, 31, from Ramallah, is even more cautious. She has heard too many international statements over the years, she said, while settlement construction continued.
"What matters isn't just 12 countries saying they will impose restrictions, but actually seeing those restrictions enforced," she told TNA.
"Will they block these products from their markets? Will they take action against companies dealing with the settlements? And will there be real sanctions?" she asked.
Without clear enforcement mechanisms, Al-Arouri fears the announcement could become another diplomatic statement with little impact on Palestinians' daily lives.
The Palestinian presidency welcomed the move, describing it as an important shift towards practical measures.
In a press statement, it called on the signatory countries, the European Union, and the wider international community to go further by adopting binding measures, including banning trade and dealings with settlements and imposing sanctions on settlers and those who support them.
The PLO's Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission similarly described the announcement as significant, but stressed that the measures remain insufficient to protect Palestinians.
"Targeting settlement trade strikes at part of the economic infrastructure that enables settlements to survive and expand," the commission said in a press statement.
But warned against portraying settlement expansion as solely the work of settlers.
It urged that the Israeli government provide the political and institutional backing that allows the settlement enterprise to continue.
Ramallah-based Palestinian political analyst Abdel Majid Sweilem told TNA that the shift should not be dismissed simply because it came late.
"Moving from expressing concern and condemnation to taking economic measures" represents an important development because the settlement project cannot be challenged through political statements alone," he said.
"The real test lies in the scope of these measures and the extent of the countries' commitment to implementing them," he added.
He argued that restrictions on settlement products could mark the beginning of a broader process if they are followed by measures targeting companies, institutions, and other entities that support settlements.
The economic value of settlement exports, however, is relatively small.
Settlement exports are estimated at around US$34 million annually, compared with US$44 billion in total Israeli exports of goods and services, according to figures cited by Yedioth Ahronoth from Roey Fischer, director of the Foreign Trade Administration at Israel's Ministry of Economy.
But the newspaper reported that Israel's concern is less about the value of settlement exports themselves than the possibility that restrictions could eventually spread to a much broader range of Israeli exports.
For Sweilem, this potential expansion is the most important part of the story.
The question, therefore, is not simply whether Israel loses revenue from settlement goods, but whether the restrictions establish a precedent for treating the wider settlement economy as something that carries an international cost.
'Not enough'
Adnan Samara, another Ramallah-based political analyst, cautioned against attaching too much significance to the announcement before details of its implementation become clear.
"The problem lies not in the announcement, but in the implementation," he told TNA. "Israel has faced decades of international opposition to its settlement policy, but such positions have done little to prevent settlement expansion."
Limited trade restrictions, he argued, are unlikely to alter Israeli policy on their own, particularly while Israel continues to receive extensive political and military support from the United States.
"Any serious attempt to confront settlement expansion must therefore go beyond individual products and target the companies, banks and institutions involved in financing and implementing settlement projects," he said.
"If the matter remains limited to banning certain goods, the political message may well outweigh the economic impact," Samara added. "However, if these measures evolve into a comprehensive policy, the situation will be different."
Esmat Mansour, a Ramallah-based political analyst, also sees the announcement as politically important, but believes its significance will ultimately depend on what follows.
"The 12 nations are seizing a political moment when the cost of settlements is becoming increasingly apparent on the international stage," he told TNA.
"But limited economic measures will not change the reality on the ground unless they are accompanied by sustained political pressure and stronger legal and economic consequences," Mansour added.
"The deeper question," he said, "is whether the international community is willing to stop treating settlement expansion as merely a political file and instead confront it as an organised system that must carry a cost."

Taiwan Cabinet says premier salary freeze violates constitutional interpretation

07:18:10 UTC
16:18:10 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Cabinet said Thursday that freezing Premier Cho Jung-tai’s (卓榮泰) salary violates Constitutional Interpretation No. 601 and exceeds the legislature’s authority.
CNA reported that the legislature passed the 2026 central government budget on Aug. 14 and froze Cho’s salary for the final four months of the year. Lawmakers also removed funding for the salaries of political appointees at the Ill-gotten Party Assets Settlement Committee.
Cabinet Spokesperson Michelle Lee (李慧芝) said the premiership is established by law and protected under the Constitution. She said the premier’s salary is a legally required government expense paid under public-sector compensation rules.
Lee said freezing Cho’s salary through the annual budget process interferes with his ability to perform his constitutional duties. She said the move violates Constitutional Interpretation No. 601 and breaches the separation of powers by exceeding the legislature’s authority.
The Cabinet also said the salary freeze conflicts with the proviso in Article 52 of the Budget Act. The provision allows lawmakers to attach conditions or deadlines to approved spending unless doing so is prohibited by law.
Lee said about three and a half months remain in the year, but the approved budget has not yet been sent to the Cabinet. She said the government will review the issue after receiving the budget.

Taiwan population falls for 32nd straight month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:18:03 UTC
16:18:03 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s population declined for the 32nd consecutive month in August, as the number of births fell 11.5% from a year earlier amid the country’s continuing demographic decline, according to the Ministry of the Interior.
Household registration data showed a population of 23,224,721 at the end of August, down 103,622 from a year earlier, per ETtoday. Compared with July, the population decreased by 10,281.
Taiwan recorded 7,492 births in August, or roughly one birth every six minutes, for an annualized crude birth rate of 3.80 per 1,000 people. The number was down 972 from a year earlier and 414 from July.
Lienchiang County had the highest crude birth rate at 6.05 per 1,000 people, followed by Taitung County at 6.01 and Hsinchu County at 4.98, ETtoday reported. Keelung had the lowest rate at 1.87, followed by Chiayi County at 2.96 and Tainan at 3.21.
There were 16,470 deaths in August, or roughly one every 2.7 minutes, resulting in an annualized crude death rate of 8.35 per 1,000 people. Deaths increased by 1,244 from a year earlier but fell by 649 from July.
Taitung County recorded the highest crude death rate at 11.79 per 1,000 people, followed by Pingtung County at 11.78 and Hualien County at 11.44, according to ETtoday. Lienchiang had the lowest rate at 2.59, followed by Kinmen County at 5.83 and Taoyuan at 6.49.
By age group, 2,616,236 people, or 11.26% of the population, were aged 0 to 14 at the end of August, while 15,818,414, or 68.11%, were aged 15 to 64, per Newtalk. People aged 65 and older numbered 4,790,071, or 20.62% of the population, while those aged 20 and older numbered 19,640,702, or 84.57%.
In August, 66,399 people moved into Taiwan’s household registration system, down 8,248 from July, while 67,702 moved out, down 6,295, per CNA. Taiwan recorded net out-migration of 1,303 people.
In the first eight months of this year, Taiwan recorded 61,742 births and 132,098 deaths. There were more than twice as many deaths as births, resulting in a natural population decrease of 70,356.

Trump's passivity gives Beijing room around Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:17:16 UTC
16:17:16 KST

Ahead of the scheduled Sept. 24 Trump-Xi summit at the White House, China has broadened coast guard patrols and checks from waters near Kinmen off China’s coast to open waters east of Taiwan, while the Trump administration has downplayed China’s intensifying gray-zone tactics as “routine activities” in a move to appease Chinese leader Xi Jinping ahead of their meeting.
Since June, China’s coast guard has intercepted nearly 200 commercial ships passing Taiwan’s east coast. While the increase in patrols around Taiwan-administered islands in the Taiwan Strait is already disturbing, US dismissal of China’s “law enforcement” patrols east of Taiwan, in international waters of the western Pacific, will only further enable Beijing to expand its baseless territorial and legal claims.
From the Persian Gulf to the Taiwan Strait, the US has traditionally been a guarantor of freedom of navigation. Since the end of World War II, US armed forces have actively protected global trade lanes, ensuring the free flow of goods under international law.
Following Trump’s return to the White House in 2025, the reliability of US naval commitments has faced intense scrutiny from allies and partners as Washington pivots toward a more transactional foreign policy.
On the other side of the globe, Trump has also allowed similar tactics by Iran around the Strait of Hormuz. This has allowed the totalitarian regime in Tehran to patrol critical Middle Eastern waterways, resulting in economic shockwaves for traditional US allies thousands of miles away.
Iranian patrols aimed at asserting Tehran’s “legal” claims have halted vital energy shipments to import-dependent Japan and South Korea. Trump’s inaction has sown doubt over US support for such staunch traditional allies, leaving room for exploitation by authoritarian regimes such as China, Russia, and Iran.
Normalizing coercion
As Trump yields to authoritarian leaders by dismissing a new wave of hostile naval action carried out in the name of “law enforcement,” he gives such regimes a green light to create a new normal of intruding upon and controlling other states’ sovereign territory while deepening public mistrust toward the US.
Although turning a blind eye to such aggression could help Trump gain short-term trade concessions, such complacency is detrimental to long-term US national interests and trade security.
China is exploiting this inaction by turning military drills into permanent unilateral “law enforcement” patrols in Taiwan’s eastern exclusive economic zone. Continued US passivity could help authoritarian actors such as China and Iran expand territorial claims by asserting administrative jurisdiction in international waters.
In Taiwan, this bolsters Beijing’s false, defeatist narrative. Routine and permanent coercion could signal to Taiwanese that Beijing can readily blockade the nation, while fueling distrust of the government by suggesting it has conceded maritime sovereignty.
Given that Taiwan is already “ground zero” for Chinese disinformation campaigns, US inaction provides ready-made ammunition for fueling skepticism among voters about US commitment and reliability in Taiwan’s defense.
Pro-China politicians have been selling the “US abandonment” narrative for decades. Such inaction will only prove their point.
It could create a vacuum for Chinese proxies and propel China-friendly political parties to electoral victories, weaken Taiwan’s deterrence and resolve in defending national sovereignty, and eventually push Taiwan’s government to concede to Chinese demands.
Make no mistake: China’s eventual end game is to effectively annex and control Taiwan.
Energy vulnerability
Beyond the political consequences, US passivity toward Chinese coast guard “lawfare” encroachments on Taiwan’s eastern flank creates deep economic vulnerabilities for Taiwan and its trade partners.
With more than 90% of the world’s advanced chips produced in Taiwan, an energy crisis here could significantly disrupt almost every corner of the globe.
Taiwan relies heavily on foreign energy imports, with a hyper-vulnerable safety margin of seven to 10 days of liquefied natural gas (LNG) reserves.
A sudden conversion of routine Chinese patrols into an energy blockade could delay, divert, or turn back LNG carriers without an armed invasion. This could grind Taiwan’s manufacturing to a halt through nationwide power grid disruption in little more than a week.
Taiwan’s defense capabilities would face severe disruption, while global semiconductor production could also grind to a halt. The immediate economic paralysis would not only affect Taiwan, but directly harm US national and economic interests.
It is imperative that Trump consider the near-term implications of his silence rather than prioritize short-term gains ahead of his meeting with Xi.
Regional fallout
Beyond Taiwan, Trump is also handing China free propaganda in other Pacific theaters.
On Aug. 16, Trump ordered a sudden and substantial reduction of joint US-South Korea military exercises. The order came the night before the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield joint drills were to begin.
Similar to his attempts to build rapport with Xi, Trump cited preserving a “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un as one of his reasons for the cut.
The reduction shortened Ulchi Freedom Shield to just five days, eliminating critical live-fire field exercises that synchronize modern warfare involving drones, GPS disruption, and coordinated cyber warfare — all areas in which China is rapidly building capabilities.
Trump even canceled scheduled large-scale September joint drills with South Korea.
Military analysts have raised alarms over these sudden reductions. They have also generated concerns in Japan, the US’ staunchest Pacific ally.
Critics have warned that the reductions could erode readiness at a time when authoritarian actors in North Korea and China are expanding their offensive capabilities beyond their borders.
As Taiwanese voters take note of US inaction and reduced US security support, all eyes will be on what Trump discusses with Xi at the White House in late September.
Chinese disinformation campaigns have already hyped the US “retreat” narrative around Trump’s delay on arms sales to Taiwan. Regardless of the actual impact on the region’s security balance, US passivity will only exacerbate that narrative.
Although overall US support for Taiwan appears unchanged, any Trump concessions to Xi at the White House summit will have far-reaching global implications.
