NEW DELHI: DMK president MK Stalin on Thursday hit back at Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay over his recent remarks in the state assembly, accusing him of attempting to demean the party and its leaders while recalling his arrest and alleged custodial torture during the Emergency.Responding to Vijay’s criticism of the DMK, Stalin said the party’s history and its ideological struggle could not be changed by political attacks.“Thambi Vijay, what you said is true. It is not a lie. During the Emergency, opposing it, leader Kalaignar organized a huge gathering at the Marina beach and severely criticized the MISA Act,” Stalin said in a video message shared on X.
His remarks came after Vijay launched a strong attack on the DMK in the assembly on Wednesday, accusing previous governments of corruption and referring to the Sarkaria Commission as well as Enforcement Directorate documents concerning alleged corruption during the 2021-26 regime.Stalin recalled that the Union government dismissed the DMK government on January 31, 1976, during the Emergency imposed by the Indira Gandhi government.“The very next second after dismissing the government, police came to the Gopalapuram house to arrest me under the MISA Act,” Stalin said, recounting how his father and former chief minister M Karunanidhi told police that his son was away campaigning and would return the next day.
Stalin said that after he returned, Karunanidhi himself called the police and asked them to arrest him.Recalling his time in prison, Stalin alleged that he was subjected to severe physical abuse and was kept with other prisoners in a small room where leprosy patients had earlier been housed.“In prison, many atrocities happened to me. We were taken and locked up in a place where leprosy patients were kept. Ten people were locked inside a small room. Inside that same room, in a single pot, all of us had to urinate,” he said.Stalin alleged that police beat prisoners with lathis at night, kicked them with boots and that other inmates also assaulted them. He recalled the death of DMK leader and former MP Chitti Babu, whom he said died in jail following the beatings.“Due to their beating, my dear brother, Member of Parliament Chitti Babu, died inside the jail itself. Due to their beating, my jawbone was broken,” Stalin said.The DMK has condemned Vijay’s remarks and announced a statewide protest on September 12, accusing the chief minister of making “scurrilous remarks” against Stalin, Karunanidhi and other party leaders.Law minister R Nirmal Kumar, however, has disputed Stalin’s account, saying there was no official record to indicate that his detention during the Emergency was under MISA. The minister said Stalin was arrested following remarks concerning Indira Gandhi and her 20-point programme.
Stalin also rejected Vijay’s allegations relating to the Sarkaria Commission and corruption charges against Karunanidhi, arguing that successive governments would have acted if the allegations had been established.Turning to Vijay’s conduct in the Assembly, Stalin urged him to maintain the dignity expected of a chief minister and focus on governance rather than political controversies.“The Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly has dignity and respect. It is a place sculpted by many great leaders, great men. That responsibility is now with you,” Stalin said.

U.S. Army awards NG $4.8B for helicopter missile defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:16:08 UTC
16:16:08 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Northrop Grumman a contract worth up to $4.84 billion for full-rate production of its CIRCM laser-based helicopter missile defense system.
- CIRCM protects aircraft including the AH-64 Apache and UH-60 Black Hawk from heat-seeking missiles that have downed numerous helicopters in Ukraine since 2022.
Helicopters have carried flares to dodge heat-seeking missiles since the late 1960s. The U.S. Army just committed nearly $4.84 billion to replace that decades-old defense with a laser that jams the missile itself.
The Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, awarded Northrop Grumman the firm-fixed-price, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract on September 8 for full-rate production of the Common Infrared Countermeasures system, known as CIRCM. Only Northrop Grumman bid on the work. The contract runs through September 30, 2035, though the Pentagon’s notice did not specify how many units it covers or how funding breaks down year to year.
CIRCM mounts on helicopters and some small fixed-wing aircraft to counter MANPADS, the shoulder-fired, heat-seeking missiles that have proven lethal against low-flying aircraft in recent conflicts. In Ukraine, MANPADS supplied by the U.S., UK and Poland have downed numerous Russian helicopters since 2022, underscoring just how vulnerable rotary-wing aircraft remain to this class of weapon.
Instead of dumping flares and hoping a missile’s seeker gets confused, CIRCM detects an incoming missile using warning sensors already on the aircraft, then fires a laser directly at the missile’s infrared seeker, distorting its view of the target and steering it off course. The company says the whole sequence takes only a few seconds. At the core of the system is a quantum cascade laser, a solid-state laser technology the Army selected in part because it can jam multiple incoming missiles at once and continues working in poor weather, unlike earlier infrared jammers that struggled in cloud cover or rain.
The Army launched the program to meet a Tri-Service requirement, meaning the Army, Navy and Air Force all agreed on a common specification so the same system could go on multiple services’ aircraft rather than each branch developing its own jammer. Northrop Grumman won the engineering and manufacturing development contract in 2015, beating out BAE Systems after both companies had spent several years in an earlier technology-maturation phase. The Army took delivery of its first CIRCM systems in 2016, and the system replaced the older Advanced Threat Infrared Countermeasures suite that had been in service since the 1990s.
CIRCM has since gone on the Army’s AH-64 Apache, CH-47 Chinook and UH-60 Black Hawk helicopters. Northrop Grumman has said the system reached its 500th delivered shipset within two years of entering full-rate production.
As of this year, the company says nearly 700 CIRCM systems have been installed on rotary-wing aircraft worldwide, logging more than 70,000 operational flight hours. In March 2026, Northrop Grumman reached a separate agreement to supply CIRCM for Germany’s new CH-47 Chinook fleet, extending the system to at least one allied air force beyond the United States.
The system’s open architecture is designed to let the Army swap in new hardware or software as missile threats evolve, without redesigning the aircraft’s survivability suite from scratch.

'Enemy of the people': Writer Kati Marton on Budapest return after Orbán's regime rejection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:16:07 UTC
16:16:07 KST

The American-Hungarian writer, a Peabody Award winner, has avoided Budapest for years but she's now returned to because her novel about her parents, "Enemies of the People", has been adapted for the stage.
A monodrama based on the novel about the family of Kati Marton, a US journalist and author of Hungarian origin, has recently premiered at the Central European University's Budapest building.
Marton's book "Enemies of the People: My Family's Journey to America", has been adapted for the stage with Erika Marozsán in the lead role.
The story follows the fate of Marton's parents. Both were journalists, reporting for American news agencies from communist Hungary. While researching her parents background, it emerged that their nanny had in fact been an informant, filing reports on the family.
When her parents were imprisoned, she and her sister were first taken to their grandparents. However, the grandparents were given passports to Australia so they could emigrate to relatives there. The state took away their flat in Buda, as it did with so many others.
According to Marton, this too formed part of the psychological pressure the state devised against people it had branded "enemies". Prison officials told her parents that the two small children had been left without adult supervision; it was with this "cruel choreography" that people were broken, she recalled.
Later, Kati and her sister Juli were placed with temporary foster parents somewhere in the outskirts of Budapest. She remembers how frightened people were; they did not dare speak even about those who had disappeared, including her own parents. Former friends of the family did not come to visit the two little girls.
Learning the truth
The drama of her parents' lives also includes the fact that her Jewish grandparents were murdered in Auschwitz, something that was never discussed at home. She herself was brought up as a Catholic and only decades later learned the truth about her family's origins.
"The communists branded my parents enemies of the people because they were well-off. When I began to reconstruct my family's story, I discovered, while reading through the thousands of pages of surveillance reports, that they probably had the thickest file in the archive. I really am talking about several thousand pages," said Marton. "Because I can read Hungarian, I was able to use this material for my book, 'Enemies of the People', and it is the play based on that book that has brought me to Budapest. On every single page my parents are referred to as enemies of the people. For a time I too was given that label by the Orbán regime."
The Budapest premiere was all the more special because Kati Marton had stayed away from Hungary for years after the Orbán regime branded her "an enemy of the people", just as her parents had been branded by the communist regime.
The play based on the novel by Peabody Award-winning journalist and bestselling author was directed by János Mohácsi and has also been staged in the United States.
Kati Marton is also known for bestsellers such as "The Great Escape - Nine Jews Who Fled Hitler and Changed the World" and "Merkel", about the former German chancellor Angela Merkel (original title: "The Chancellor - The Remarkable Odyssey of Angela Merkel").

Spanish archaeologists find 4,400-year-old tomb in Egypt with original colours intact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:15:38 UTC
16:15:38 KST

A Spanish-Egyptian archaeological team has found in Saqqara an outstanding late Fifth Dynasty tomb with two chapels and colourful reliefs of farming and offering processions.
A Spanish-Egyptian archaeological mission, led by Spanish Egyptologist Josep Cervelló, has uncovered a "striking and beautiful" tomb dating from the late Fifth Dynasty of Egypt's Old Kingdom (2494-2345 BC) in the Saqqara necropolis, southwest of Cairo.
The find was made during this summer's excavations, led by the Autonomous University of Barcelona (UAB) and Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities. It is an exceptional mastaba with two funerary chapels, commissioned by Yunmen, a senior official under Pharaoh Djedkare Isesi, who also ordered that his father, Iti, a lower-ranking official, be buried there.
Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities confirmed that the tomb dates from the end of the Fifth Dynasty, during the reign of Djedkare Isesi, and is located in the Mariette necropolis, north of Saqqara. According to the statement, it contains "two funerary chapels belonging to two high-ranking officials, Younmin and his father, Ity".
According to the UAB, the tomb has made it possible to identify figures of great historical, social and cultural interest. For the archaeological team, the discovery has also been a surprise because of the richness and beauty of the monument.
Among the most notable features are a high-quality architrave and funerary texts adapted to the figure and offices of their owner. The Egyptian ministry also highlights the exceptional state of preservation of the scenes and reliefs, which show "agricultural activities and processions with offerings", and notes that many of them "have retained their original colours".
The decoration also includes depictions of donkeys and other animals. According to the Egyptian authorities, the discovery "provides new and valuable data on the architecture, art and administrative life of ancient Egypt at the end of the Fifth Dynasty".
The excavation reveals daily life in the Saqqara necropolis
As well as its historical and scientific value, the mastaba stands out for its beauty. Archaeologists believe that the double tomb may reflect the social ascent of Yunmen, the son of a provincial official who rose to a senior position in the central administration and wanted to share his funerary destiny with his father.
The area has been known since the excavations carried out by Auguste Mariette in the 19th century, but it had never been studied and documented in depth. The research aimed to reconstruct the topography of Saqqara and to understand the necropolis as a living space, where ancient Egyptians brought offerings and worked continuously on the construction of funerary monuments.
The aim is to understand how the necropolis was organised and operated, from its streets and squares to the movement of people and the cult rituals. The analysis of maps and the reconstruction of the layout led the team to a previously unknown mastaba and to indications of two more nearby, which they hope to excavate in future seasons.

Primark will offer home delivery in Britain for the first time, as the fast-fashion retailer prepares to spin off from its owner Associated British Foods (ABF).
The clothing chain, which already offers a click and collect service in the UK, has long avoided home delivery, arguing that its low prices made it too difficult to absorb the cost of packing and shipping orders.
However, the company disclosed on Thursday that it had acquired an automated fulfilment facility in Sheffield and would offer home delivery “in the future”.
“Primark’s digital maturity, including the success of click and collect, and online market developments, mean there is now the opportunity for profitable growth through the home delivery channel,” it said in a statement.
The news comes as Primark prepares to split from its parent company ABF, the owner of Twinings tea and Kingsmill bread. The demerger, which is likely to complete in December 2027, is expected to create two new FTSE 100 companies, with analysts predicting that Primark could be valued at as much as £9bn, and the food business £4bn.
The company told investors in an update on Thursday morning that it expected Primark’s sales to drop 3% in its quarter ended on 12 September, with the UK and Ireland up 0.4% but continental Europe down 4.3%.
George Weston, the chief executive of ABF, said Primark’s trading in Europe “remained challenging”, but the initial customer reaction to its “iconic value” campaign – in which it cut prices across hundreds of autumn and winter products – had been encouraging.
Weston, a member of the billionaire family that controls ABF and who is the long-term chief executive of the group, is to lead the food business after the demerger.
Eoin Tonge, an experienced former ABF, Marks & Spencer and Greencore finance director, will remain as chief executive of Primark.
The fashion chain, which was founded by Arthur Ryan under its Irish brand name, Penneys, in Dublin in 1969, opened its first shop in Britain in 1974, in Derby. It employs more than 80,000 people around the world.

Russia slams U.N. watchdog for reporting on North Korean nuclear facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:10:40 UTC
16:10:40 KST

IAEA can’t verify DPRK’s nuclear program, Moscow argued, after agency identified another enrichment facility in Yongbyon
		
		
Russia has brushed off a U.N. nuclear watchdog’s report on North Korea’s nuclear program that included findings on a newly built uranium enrichment facility, citing insufficient evidence attributed to the agency’s lack of access to the country.
A Russian representative to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in a statement in Vienna on Wednesday noted the watchdog had not conducted inspections in the DPRK since 2009, arguing that it was “unable to draw any reliable conclusions regarding the state of the country’s nuclear infrastructure.”
“The Secretariat’s assessments, based solely on satellite imagery and information from open sources, have no added value, create a misleading impression and give rise to additional risks,” the representative said, while calling on the IAEA to stop issuing reports on North Korea’s nuclear program.
The remarks followed an Aug. 28 report by IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi titled “Application of Safeguards in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea,” which detailed recent developments in the country’s nuclear program.
The report included updates on a new uranium enrichment facility completed between Dec. 2024 and March 2026 at Yongbyon, a nuclear complex about 50 miles north of Pyongyang. Grossi previously linked the new “nuclear material production plant” to DPRK leader Kim Jong Un’s June 3 visit and expressed serious concern over its operations.
		 
The August report identified the site Kim visited as a new two-story building at Yongbyon by comparing state media photographs with commercially available satellite imagery taken during construction. The agency referred to the site as Yongbyon Uranium Enrichment Facility 2 (Yongbyon UEF2).
“The photographs from the visit indicate that gas centrifuge cascades are installed on both the upper and lower floors of the main building,” the report said. “This building could accommodate up to 28 of the cascades depicted in the photographs.”
The capacity estimate is consistent with an earlier assessment by nonproliferation expert Jeffrey Lewis, who assessed that the building could house 28 cascades, or roughly 4,600 centrifuges.
The IAEA report said the centrifuges visible in the state media photographs appeared to be of the same type as those at Kangson and Yongbyon’s older enrichment facility, which the agency referred to as Yongbyon UEF1. 
“Installation of at least one of the cascades depicted in the photographs was incomplete,” the report said, noting that “at least one of the cascades” seen in the state media images appeared to “have a different configuration from the cascades comprised of 344 centrifuges shown in the earlier photographs of Kangson UEF and Yongbyon UEF1.”
The report described the continued development of North Korea’s nuclear program as “deeply troubling” while providing updates on other facilities.
The IAEA noted signs of ongoing activity at the Kangson uranium enrichment facility a few miles southwest of  Pyongyang, where an annex was added in 2024.
“Beginning in Jan. 2026, there were also indications that operations had commenced within its annex,” the report said. The agency also observed indications of continuous operation at Yongbyon UEF1.
Cooling-water discharges and other indicators suggested that Yongbyon’s 5 MW(e) Experimental Nuclear Power Plant “continued to operate in its seventh operational cycle throughout the reporting period,” with “occasional shutdowns of one or two days’ duration.”
The agency also reported indications that Yongbyon’s Light Water Reactor (LWR) was in stable operation from early Dec. 2025 to mid-March, followed by a shutdown until the end of April. It then operated through the end of the reporting period, apart from a shutdown lasting a few days in mid-May.
“Overall, the Agency has observed that the LWR was operating for approximately two-thirds of the reporting period,” the report said.
Grossi’s report pointed to the apparent completion of a campaign at Yongbyon’s Radiochemical Laboratory to reprocess irradiated fuel from the 5 MW(e) reactor’s sixth operating cycle, with intermittent operation of its supporting steam plant between April and July suggesting subsequent waste treatment or maintenance.
The report noted “expanded mining, milling and concentration activities at the Pyongsan Uranium Mine and the Pyongsan Uranium Concentrate Plant” and “ongoing activity at the Wolbisan Uranium Mine.”
The IAEA did not observe “indications of significant activity” at the nuclear test site at Punggye-ri but stressed that the facility “remains capable of supporting a nuclear test.”
North Korea has conducted six nuclear tests, most recently on Sept. 3, 2017.
The IAEA “continues to maintain readiness to carry out its verification role should it regain access to North Korea’s nuclear facilities, which halted after the DPRK ceased cooperation,” the report concluded.

Trump delivered the extraordinary overture during a primetime speech that lasted nearly two hours and firmly placed him at the center of the midterm campaign at a time when his sagging approval ratings could weigh on Republicans' chances.
Vice President JD Vance will give the keynote address on Thursday night, though Trump is scheduled to make closing remarks to bring the made-for-television two-day event in Dallas to an end.
With Trump constitutionally barred from seeking a third term, Vance's speech could serve as an early audition for the 2028 presidential election and offer clues about how he would lead a party reshaped by Trump.
It was not immediately clear how the $5,000 payments would work or whether they would be legal. The proposal would likely cost more than $1 trillion, with approximately 270 million U.S. adults, and could require the approval of Congress.
The convention's focus on Trump – some Republicans have dubbed it "Trumpapalooza" – amounts to a risky bet that he can mobilize the voters who carried him to the presidency two years ago, despite opinion polls showing his popularity is at an all-time low.
But it remains to be seen whether his campaign-style speech will appeal to the critical swing voters who have drifted away from Trump's party amid growing dissatisfaction with the cost of living and the war on Iran.
'PRETEND THAT I'M ON THE BALLOT'

Fetterman said he would always "reject the extremes in socialism," a comment that is likely to bolster Republican attacks on Democrats as too left-wing. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his fellow Democrats, has nevertheless rejected speculation that he might leave the party.

Researchers to probe found cavities in Vilnius Cathedral in search of grand duke’s remains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:04:00 UTC
16:04:00 KST

Researchers studying the walls and underground spaces of Vilnius Cathedral say they have identified about 20 previously unexplored and undocumented cavities, including one that will be examined in October to test a controversial theory that the remains of Lithuania’s Grand Duke Vytautas may have been secretly reburied there.
Researchers from the Lithuanian Institute of History have been examining the cathedral’s masonry since the beginning of the year and say there could be more undiscovered spaces.
The first cavity to be investigated is in the western wall of the mausoleum of the Chapel of Saint Casimir. Researchers plan to drill a small hole from the outside, which they say is the safest approach. Microbiologists will first examine the space, followed by an attempt to inspect it with a camera.
“We will technically drill a hole about 5 to 10 centimetres in diameter, microbiologists will conduct their research, and then we will try to scan the room with a camera,” said Saulius Sarcevičius, an archaeologist with the Institute of History.
The investigation is intended to test a hypothesis put forward by restorer and historical artifact researcher Saulius Poderis, who believes the remains of Vytautas the Great, Lithuania’s 15th-century ruler, may have been secretly reburied in the cavity during the interwar period.
The government has allocated more than 33,000 euros for the investigation.
Poderis said he believes the remains may be visible in a photograph held in a Polish archive. He theorises that Vytautas’ remains could have been discovered during reconstruction of the cathedral in the interwar period, alongside the remains of Lithuanian and Polish rulers Alexander, Elizabeth of Austria and Barbara Radziwiłł.
Poderis stressed that the theory still needs to be tested.
“There is such a possibility. We should not get ahead of ourselves and assume that they are definitely there. It needs to be checked,” he said.
Art historian Birutė Rūta Vitkauskienė criticised the project, saying the research team initially lacked a historian and that the case for investigating the cavity was based largely on Poderis’ hypothesis.
“The whole project really lacks a scientific, historical approach,” Vitkauskienė said. She also questioned Poderis’ qualifications to interpret and publicly recount historical documents.
Researchers said historians will be involved in the broader work. Sarcevičius said the decision to begin with the cavity identified by Poderis was driven by public interest.
“For us researchers, it made no difference which cavity to investigate,” Sarcevičius said. “After Saulius Poderis expressed his opinion, part of the public supported it, and some even said that we were hiding something.”
Poderis is not part of the research team. The Institute of History said he was excluded because he is not an institute employee. He has previously been convicted for dealing in illegally excavated archaeological artifacts.
The search for Vytautas’ remains began about a century ago. A special sarcophagus was cast in the 1930s to mark the 500th anniversary of the ruler’s death.
With the 600th anniversary approaching, the government has allocated 7.5 million euros for comprehensive scientific research at Vilnius Cathedral.

Melting Swiss glacier reveals debris from 1963 plane crash
Around 250 kilograms of debris from an aeroplane that crashed in 1963 have been recovered from the Hüfifirn Glacier in canton Uri in central Switzerland. A mountaineer had informed the Uri cantonal police about the exposed wreckage.
Investigations carried out in conjunction with the Swiss Transportation Safety Investigation Board (Sust) revealed that it is “highly likely” that the wreckage is from an aircraft that crashed in 1963. The recovered wreckage will now be disposed of properly by a recycling company.
The fact that the wreckage was not recovered after the crash more than 60 years ago is not unusual, given the limited technical capabilities at the time, the cantonal police wrote. The remains only became visible again as the glacier melted.
+ Glaciers of the world – local melting and global impactsExternal link
The recovery operation took place on Thursday September 3 and was organised by Sust. In addition to the Uri Cantonal Police, a private helicopter company, another private transport firm and the Swiss Air Force’s mountain detachment were also involved, the police statement added.
More
Cold cases: Swiss glaciers reveal grisly surprises
Several aviation accidents in May 1963
In May 1963, several aviation accidents occurred on the Hüfifirn Glacier near the Clariden Pass between Uri and Glarus, as shown in the Sust’s report database. First, on May 9, a pilot and a passenger crashed in a Champion light aircraft. They were unharmed.
The following day, a recovery attempt led to another crash involving a Piper Super Cub, again with no injuries. On May 21 and 22, further attempts were made to recover the two aircraft with the aid of a helicopter.
While the wreckage of the Champion aircraft arrived at Mollis airfield on May 22, 1963, the attempt to recover the Piper aircraft was unsuccessful. On May 21, the first attempt failed because the wreckage became stuck in the snow, rolled over and struck the helicopter with its right wing. The following day, the operation failed after the load began to swing violently during take-off. The pilot decided to unhook the wreckage, and it fell hundreds of metres to the ground.

August sets new global heat record as climate extremes intensify
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:00:14 UTC
16:00:14 KST

The EU’s climate monitor said on Thursday that August was the hottest month ever recorded globally, with ocean temperatures also reaching unprecedented highs as Western Europe capped its warmest summer.
Responding to the assessment by the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the UN warned that until humanity weaned itself off fossil fuels, the planet would only be pushed deeper into uncharted territory.
Copernicus observations go back to 1940, but other evidence, such as ice cores, tree rings and coral skeletons, allows scientists to place today’s climate within a much longer historical context.
“Humans haven’t seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years,” Samantha Burgess of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, told AFP.
Global average air temperatures in August reached 16.96°C, Copernicus said, surpassing by 0.01°C the previous all-time monthly record set in July 2023. Given the narrow difference, Copernicus said it considered the two months jointly the hottest on record.
Scientists say the burning of fuels such as coal, oil and gas has warmed the planet by roughly 1.4°C since pre-industrial times and increased the severity and likelihood of extreme weather.
Yet heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions rose to new highs in 2025.
“The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiralling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fuelling,” UN climate chief Simon Stiell said of the Copernicus report.
More heat ahead
Global sea surface temperatures also set a new daily high and tied the record for the hottest August, extending a three-month streak of record-breaking warmth across the world’s oceans.
More than 90 per cent of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gas emissions has been absorbed by the oceans, sparing the land from further warming but at a severe cost to marine life, reefs and coastal communities.
Records tumbled in overheated basins such as the Atlantic and Mediterranean, as well as in the tropical Pacific, where the strongest El Nino weather pattern of the modern era is rapidly gaining strength.
El Nino events are marked by unusually warm Pacific waters but raise the likelihood of extreme weather thousands of miles away, from floods in Peru and droughts in Africa to wildfires in Australia.
As the warmer phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino episodes usually deliver a temporary spike in global temperatures already elevated by long-term warming.
Scientists expect records to keep falling in the months ahead as this “super” El Nino approaches peak intensity around December. They expect 2027, and possibly even 2026, to become the hottest years ever recorded.
“Climate change makes every El Nino hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil and gas, these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming,” said Friederike Otto, a climate scientist at Imperial College London.
Sizzling summer
Copernicus also said August “marked the end of Western Europe’s warmest summer”, surpassing the long-standing record set in 2003.
The June-to-August season was defined by severe, back-to-back heatwaves that shut schools, dried up rivers and primed the land for devastating wildfires.
Between mid-July and mid-August, Europe recorded more than 32,000 excess deaths, according to estimates from the continent’s EuroMomo monitoring platform.
Scientists from the World Weather Attribution network concluded that a particularly intense heatwave in June would have been “virtually impossible” without the influence of climate change.
But extraordinary heat was felt around the globe.
On Wednesday, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said the contiguous United States had endured its hottest summer on record.
Regions home to around 900 million people also experienced the hottest July ever recorded, according to an AFP analysis of Copernicus data.
“We’ve had an exceptional summer, not only in Europe, but in other parts of the world where records that have existed for close to a century have fallen,” said Burgess, an ocean scientist and strategic lead at ECMWF.
The climate would “continue to get more extreme unless we turn off the tap to global emissions”, she added.

Mainland Chinese shoppers lose trusted Hong Kong veggie tag as customs revamp hits shelves
Change sparks concern among consumers, with the Hong Kong label having long served as a selling point for high quality
The removal stems from new rules by the General Administration of Customs. From September 1, registration will no longer be required for growing farms, and only food-processing firms need to register.
This means vegetables grown on the same farms that supply Hong Kong can no longer carry the Hong Kong-bound label when sold in mainland supermarkets.
“Before, I just looked for the Hong Kong-bound label,” said a female consumer in a post this week on Chinese social media platform RedNote. “Now I must check the details myself, and that’s the change.”
Hong Kong-bound labelled lettuce was once a bestseller at Walmart-owned Sam’s Club on the mainland, drawing middle-class shoppers who trusted its quality.
Given its high popularity, the retailer added a tag on the product to explain the new customs rule. The 600-gram pack, still priced at 12.90 yuan (US$1.90), uses the same packaging and supplier from China’s northwestern Ningxia Hui autonomous region, distinguished only by the new “Dali lettuce” label.

Education minister says teacher pay rise unaffordable in current budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Education minister says teacher pay rise unaffordable in current budget
The Education Ministry told unions it has no room in the state budget for a teacher pay raise, saying any increase would require cuts elsewhere. The Education Workers' Union warned that teachers are prepared to stage work stoppages.
In the current economic situation it is practically impossible to add any increases to the state budget, because revenue from economic growth only covers previously indexed expenses, such as pensions and defense spending, said Minister of Education Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200).
This means that finding additional money for the education sector is extremely difficult. "We can plan a salary increase for teachers only if we cut somewhere. We would have to move money from somewhere else, take it away from someone, so that we could make a salary increase for teachers," Kallas said.
The minister does not consider the union's demand to raise next year's minimum salary to the Estonian average — €2,312 — to be realistic.
"I certainly don't consider it realistic that the minimum salary for teachers is the Estonian average salary, because most people in Estonia do not earn the average salary. In an ideal world, every education minister would say that a teacher actually deserves such a salary. Absolutely, this work brings very strong returns to society in the future. But simply, money is a finite quantity, and in reality we just do not have it in the state budget today," the minister noted.
In addition to salary issues, Kallas says the growing workload of teachers also needs to be addressed, a burden amplified by the increasing number of children with special needs.
Kallas pointed to fresh PISA results, which show that Estonia has the lowest student‑teacher ratio in Europe and a very large number of small high schools that consume a significant share of education funding. Due to demographic changes, the number of children entering school will begin to fall by 3,000 starting in 2028, reducing the per‑capita funding that municipalities use to pay teachers' salaries.
Teachers want long‑term security
Reemo Voltri, representative of the Education Workers' Union emphasized that the difficult state budget situation must not lead to compromises in education quality. According to him, teachers' minimum expectation is a €2,300 minimum salary or fulfillment of the pre‑election promise to keep teachers' calculated average salary at 120 percent of the national average.
"If teachers' salaries continue to fall compared to the national average — which they have done under this government — then this is a very ominous message for current teachers and future teachers," Voltri warned.
"This shows that we do not value the teaching profession, and as a result there is a high likelihood that the quality of our education will begin to decline, as highlighted in the OECD PISA analysis," he added.
Teachers are ready for compromises and would accept a smaller increase than requested, provided that the state budget strategy offers long‑term certainty for fulfilling promises in the coming years, Voltri said. However, they are not willing to accept a relative decline in salary.
"What teachers definitely will not accept is being told that salaries will not rise at all — meaning we immediately fall five or six percentage points behind average wage growth. That cannot be accepted," he added.
He recalled that during the previous strike, a €71 increase was achieved even in a situation where a raise was considered impossible, and added that on 14 September there will be a demonstration by education workers in front of the Riigikogu. If necessary, Voltri does not rule out new work stoppages.
Municipalities face difficult choices
Randar Lohu, head of the financial service of Saku municipality in Harju County, noted that a strong increase in the national minimum salary for teachers puts local governments in a difficult position when paying other employees. According to Lohu, teachers in Saku already earn €2,400–€2,500 gross, which is higher than the Estonian average, but constant national pressure requires additional resources.
"Of course there is hobby education, other teachers, and all sorts of other municipal institutions, and we may not be able to raise the salaries of those employees to the same extent if schoolteachers' salaries rise by ten‑plus percent," Lohu explained.
"Then all the other people are left without a salary increase, but we have about 650 people to whom we pay salaries every month," Lohu said.
According to Lohu, municipalities are currently waiting for more precise numbers from the state budget negotiations, which should become clear later this month.
Education workers, state representatives, and municipal specialists will meet again in two weeks to discuss the minimum salary for teachers.

Triangle of confusion: the government, the President's Office and parliament enter a new political season
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
10:00:00 EEST
16:00:00 KST

Triangle of confusion: the government, the President's Office and parliament enter a new political season
On 1 September Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, set another record by opening its 16th session since it was convened in July 2019.
The Rada's agenda was very revealing, and the results of the votes in the first sitting days of autumn were even more so. The MPs began their work by considering bills that have been listed as benchmarks in various international support programmes.
The fact that parliament started off with this particular set of bills points to Ukraine's main problem: its huge budget deficit.
Over the past few weeks, the new Cabinet of Ministers has been actively lobbying for these bills, holding endless meetings and consultations with MPs, including some from the president's own Servant of the People faction.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy got involved as well. A few weeks earlier, at a meeting of the National Security and Defence Council (NSDC) where one of the main items on the agenda was funding for the armed forces, the new prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, informed Zelenskyy of the real state of the budget deficit. NSDC members say the president was stunned – so much so that while the meeting was still going on, he telephoned the MPs responsible for the votes on the EU- and IMF-related legislation and started shouting and reprimanding them.
Yet even with that pressure from the very top, it still proved impossible to drum up more than 190 votes for the much-delayed bills.
This was a vivid illustration of the state of affairs within the authorities. The president's team is brilliant at putting on a show of unity and optimism at set-piece events such as prayer breakfasts with officials, celebrities and foreign guests, and National Legend ceremonies honouring soldiers, artists and Ukraine's international supporters. But it is going into the new political season with a President's Office and a president knocked off balance, a fragmented Rada, and a Cabinet still finding its feet.
In other words, all three of the centres that usually form Ukraine's triangle of power are entering the new season with serious problems of their own – or, figuratively speaking, their own dead ends.
As everyone knows, there are no dead ends in Euclidean geometry. But the formula of Ukrainian politics has long been reduced to calculating the sum of all the dead ends in which the authorities find themselves – and towards which they are leading the country.
The President and Office of suspicions
The topmost corner of Ukraine's triangle of power – and the one that has long been trying to widen its own angle of influence as far as possible – is President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his Office. There is some irony here: in geometry, a very large angle is called obtuse.
On 1 September, Zelenskyy made his anger plain after MPs failed to pass several bills needed to unlock international funding.
"MPs also bear some of the responsibility to the people of Ukraine: around US$15 billion depends on their share of the work which has to be done… The Verkhovna Rada has failed to pass three bills that could have brought Ukraine more than US$4 billion. Another two bills – which have also failed – were part of the IMF programme. This is not money for the government or the opposition," the president thundered at MPs.
At first glance the situation might seem odd. After all, it's the president's own single-party majority that is officially responsible for everything in the Rada. People close to Zelenskyy, such as Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People faction, have spent years convincing everyone of their virtuoso ability to play parliament like a piano.
But actually Zelenskyy's anger is not so much odd as symptomatic. The president now resembles a cart driver who's got stuck in the mud and is flogging his horse in the hope that a little more brutality will force a few final surges of energy out of it. The problem is that he drove the cart into the mire himself.
The fact is that the foreign policy and military situation around Ukraine is developing in a way that could hardly be further from what the president expected just a few months ago.
Since the summer, Zelenskyy himself has done everything he could to raise public expectations – and with them the expectations of the political class – to heights unseen since 2023 and the first counteroffensive.
The phrase "elections in November", which Zelenskyy first dropped casually into a conversation with his faction before the summer strikes on Crimea and then discussed seriously with his inner circle at a state residence near Kyiv, began to look entirely realistic in the upbeat media atmosphere whipped up by the President's Office.
Those expectations, among both the public and the political establishment, were further fuelled by much-trumpeted promises of "40 days to force Russia into peace" and the like.
But Ukraine is entering autumn in a very different military reality.
Across much of the country, back-to-school ceremonies on 1 September took place either in shelters or entirely remotely, with children joining online from different homes and cities.
Kyiv, Odesa, Kharkiv and other cities are enduring almost constant air-raid warnings and regular ballistic missile attacks which Ukraine simply does not have the resources to protect them from.
People can see the contrast between promises to "end the war by November" and rehearsals for the apocalypse in September, and between the government's regime of austerity for the country and the brazen attempt to launder UAH 150 million (about US$3.3 million) to get yet another government official released from pre-trial detention.
Previously, Zelenskyy has always managed to channel public discontent elsewhere. But after July's "cardboard Maidan" protests and yet another anti-corruption case – Forrest Gump – the accumulated negativity began to fall squarely on the president himself.
The protests in July and August and the controversy over the dismissal of Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister have been near-disastrous for Zelenskyy politically. Firstly, a highly promising competitor has appeared in a vacant political niche. Secondly, the president himself is no longer even one of Ukraine's three most trusted politicians.
In first-round presidential polling, respondents still name Zelenskyy as the favourite. But no one can really calculate how many of them genuinely support the incumbent, and how many are naming him out of caution – "just in case, God forbid".
The modelling of second-round voting, where Zelenskyy clearly loses to Valerii Zaluzhnyi, Kyrylo Budanov and Mykhailo Fedorov, suggests there are quite a few people in the latter camp. If this trend continues, we could reach the point where even Petro Poroshenko could allow himself to dream of at least a faint chance of revenge for 2019.
And all these setbacks have a single root cause – Zelenskyy has finally lost the moral high ground he used to have over the former embezzlers and oligarchs. His party campaigned under the slogan "Let's get them together", but were Zelenskyy to resurrect that slogan now, he and most of his team would probably find themselves among the "THEM".
The situation in the President's Office is the clearest illustration of this point. Soon the only officials there untouched by criminal allegations may be the foreign policy people.
The case involving Iryna Mudra, deputy head of the President's Office, at the end of August was particularly telling. According to the version of events that investigators set out in the case materials, UAH 150 million (US$3.4 million) was laundered so that bail could be posted for former energy and justice minister Herman Halushchenko.
Kyrylo Budanov's name hasn't come up so far, and no procedural actions have been taken against the head of the President's Office.
But people who know how such decisions are made inside the Office point to Mudra's particularly close relationship with Budanov. It was he who persuaded her to stay at Bankova instead of taking up the position of justice minister in the government.
That is why many people within the system find it hard to imagine that Mudra could have got involved in such a sensitive matter independently, without at least tacit approval from the leader.
But it seems equally implausible that getting the long-forgotten Halushchenko out of pre-trial detention could have been an initiative of Budanov's.
According to media reports, Halushchenko had begun to show a willingness to cooperate with the anti-corruption agencies, and therefore potentially to reveal who the Energoatom money was actually being collected for, who the high-end Dynasty houses were being built for, and who "Vova" is on the tapes.
But Budanov has not been implicated in the schemes surrounding Energoatom and did not own a Dynasty property. Moreover, from a purely political perspective, it may even have benefited him if Halushchenko had named his patrons, as that could potentially clear the way for Budanov in future elections.
And so, in this and many other criminal allegations, one's gaze is inevitably directed over Budanov's head and comes to rest on a single point: the office on the fourth floor – the presidential floor.
And however hard Zelenskyy tries to persuade journalists off the record that he only finds out about corruption in the President's Office when he reads the news, even as accomplished an actor as he is can't really convince us that he believes that.
Every story like the one about Mudra makes the political vertical harder to control. People within the system are gradually realising that it's better not to carry out an illegal order and lose their job than to carry it out and lose their freedom.
Zelenskyy can bang his fist on the table at NSDC meetings, make angry calls to MPs and ministers and rant in his evening addresses all he likes.
But this is looking less and less like a demonstration of strength and an ability to investigate, punish or force someone to make the required decision, and more like the exact opposite of that.
Gradually, the entire toolkit that Zelenskyy still uses to have his decisions put into practice and legitimise his own will is shifting from the realm of political compromise into plain old coercion and control.
This is the origin of Bankova's obsession with maintaining influence over the Security Service of Ukraine, the State Bureau of Investigation and the Prosecutor General's Office.
When political tools become scarce, the value of coercive tools automatically goes up.
Government scare tactics
The second corner of the classic triangle of power is the Cabinet of Ministers.
At the moment it's still in the process of finding its real place within the new configuration.
Clearly, Zelenskyy still wants to be able to influence the government and shape its agenda unchallenged.
But the Cabinet's leadership understood right from the start that the president's wishes alone – as was the case under former prime minister Oleksii Honcharuk or the early days of Denys Shmyhal – would not be enough for successful governance.
That is why the new prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, is making every effort to strengthen cooperation with MPs, encourage ministers to maintain constant communication with parliament, take part in government question times, attend committee meetings and get involved in other routine parliamentary work.
Unlike Yuliia Svyrydenko, who had been part of the ruling team almost from the outset, Koretskyi is a complete newcomer to the system.
And his arrival has already resulted in certain changes in the way the upper echelons of power operate.
First and foremost, these changes are noticeable even on a purely human level.
"Koretskyi is probably the most unemotional prime minister in all of Zelenskyy's presidency. Even Shmyhal sometimes looks like an excitable teenager next to him," one Servant of the People MP who frequently works with the PM says with a smile.
According to MPs, Koretskyi is extremely polite and constructive with everyone. But at the same time, he is equally cold and distant. Whether because he can't or won't, he does not try to build warm personal relationships.
He is a person who sets tasks and sees that they are carried out, and who apparently still does not fully understand why MPs can't be handled in that way.
According to Ukrainska Pravda's sources in the Servant of the People party, after taking charge of the country in mid-July, the prime minister immediately set about figuring out exactly what he would have to manage, what resources were at his disposal, and what needs he had to address.
"And it wasn't long before he was seriously shocked. What's more, Koretskyi didn't hide his shock and started laying out the truth to our MPs without pulling any punches. They're not used to that; the last time someone frightened them like that was Honcharuk at the start of the Covid-19 epidemic," one senior Servant of the People MP recalls of the events of August.
All through the last month of the summer, Koretskyi kept going to meetings at the President's Office and parliament, explaining things and presenting tables and charts. And those meetings left indelible impressions on a lot of MPs.
Ahead of a major NSDC meeting in mid-August, the prime minister prepared a highly revealing presentation for the president as well.
His slides vividly demonstrated the terrifying financial gap between the resources Ukraine currently has and the expenditure the state needs to cover by the end of the year: a shortfall measured in tens of billions of dollars.
Previously, the usually kind and smiling Yuliia Svyrydenko had tried not to stress people out too much and would explain complex financial problems as gently as possible. Koretskyi's presentation was a wake-up call for many in the government.
The new prime minister was banking on the idea that demonstrating the scale of the problem would convince parliament to take a constructive approach. In parallel with his "shock therapy", over the previous few weeks he had been persistently urging MPs to support bills furthering European integration and other legislation that would unlock international funding. The Verkhovna Rada put some of these bills to the vote as early as 1 September – and rejected almost all of them that same day.
As a result, Ukraine found itself facing the threat of losing a "quick" US$4-5 billion without any idea of how to make up the shortfall.
To the ministers and prime minister, the failure to pass the bills appears to be, if not outright sabotage, then at the very least acting against the interests of the government itself and the state. For Koretskyi, however, it could prove to be a very useful experience and his first hard lesson in an accelerated course in public administration.
The government can show MPs as many terrifying slides about holes in the budget as it likes, but it's parliament that ultimately votes on the legislation. And sometimes, whether you like it or not, you have to "listen to everyone" – especially when a crisis could be brewing, ready to hit this autumn.
The last grey eminence
The Verkhovna Rada is now operating with one eye on the new, and apparently the last, grey eminence in Volodymyr Zelenskyy's orbit.
Davyd Arakhamiia has become an indispensable figure in parliament, thanks to his ability to broker situational or relatively long-lasting coalitions there – especially after Andrii Yermak was pushed out of public politics after being named as a suspect by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), together with the associated protests and the negativity that had built up around him over the years.
Meanwhile, over the past month, Ukrainska Pravda has heard various iterations of the same story dozens of times in the corridors of parliament, government, the President's Office and law enforcement agencies: that Arakhamiia himself may soon be added to the anti-corruption bodies' list of suspects.
Arakhamiia himself is evidently relying on his ever-dependable negotiating abilities.
In particular, he is trying to maintain communication with people close to the anti-corruption agencies and secure the support of those who, though unlikely to be able to persuade the agencies to abandon procedural action against him, could at least convince them to delay it.
The argument is simple: the Verkhovna Rada must not be destabilised this autumn, when the situation in the country is already extraordinarily difficult.
It is also worth bearing in mind that Arakhamiia has a tacit agreement with Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, who plays a key role in the procedure for bringing MPs to criminal prosecution. [In late 2025, Kravchenko reportedly refused to sign treason charges against Arakhamiia and several other MPs, earning himself powerful allies in parliament in return – ed.]
But either way, the political class is already looking, with certain reservations, at the prospect of Arakhamiia continuing to remain the undisputed leader and the main driving force behind the parliamentary process.
Because if Arakhamiia were to drop out of the equation for some reason, the Verkhovna Rada could, at least in the short term, descend into serious disarray.
There is simply no one else who has the authority and the communication skills to simultaneously hold together the remnants of the former Opposition Platform – For Life party, various parliamentary groups, single-mandate MPs, and the fundamentally opposing factions within Servant of the People itself.
Theoretically, if Arakhamiia were to run into trouble, as things stand today, the only person who could try to help stabilise parliament would be the speaker, Ruslan Stefanchuk.
The speaker may not command much authority in the current parliamentary set-up, but at least he has no outright antagonists, and he is the only one capable of making surprise moves such as dropping into Poroshenko's party office.
How comfortable Stefanchuk – a hermit-like lawmaker who has always tried to distance himself from the political bargaining, behind-the-scenes deals and horse-trading that go on – would feel being at the very epicentre of these processes, and how capable he would be of handling it, is another question.
There is no answer to this question yet, nor will there be until Stefanchuk actually finds himself in that situation. If, of course, it comes to that.
***
Meanwhile, the Rada continues its low-level sabotage of European integration legislation and unpopular bills on VAT on parcels or taxes for sole traders, in the hope of carving out some degree of quasi-autonomy in its dealings with the President's Office, while also trying to keep the government in line.
But all the parliamentary groups that are rebelling against what they call "external governance", "the anti-corruption dictatorship", or some other phenomenon from the book of political fears and superstitions, will sooner or later hit the ceiling of what such resistance can achieve.
Because the fact is that what they call "external governance" became part of Ukraine's domestic political reality long ago.
More than half of the budget is financed by international partners and donors. Their ability to influence the procedures for overseeing how these frankly phenomenal amounts of financial aid is spent is simply a matter of exercising operational control over their investments.
Without this money, Ukraine will clearly be unable either to fight the war or to function properly as a state. The new prime minister is a good person to ask about this – he's figured it out exceptionally well.
Ukraine will have to honour its international commitments, however unpleasant that may be for conservatives from the Yuliia Tymoshenko Bloc or single-mandate Servant of the People MPs from eastern and southern regions. Not for the sake of the weakened President's Office with its unelectable candidate, the government terrified by the scale of the problems, or the "evil Brussels bureaucracy", but for Ukraine.
Because tomorrow the government will put up another slide showing a budget shortfall of tens of billions of dollars. And the question about the limits of "sovereign democracy" will turn into the eternal Ukrainian question: where do we get the money from?
Roman Romaniuk, Ukrainska Pravda

Parfümerie at the Biennale: Zurich’s underground club scene lives on in Venice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Parfümerie at the Biennale: Zurich’s underground club scene lives on in Venice
With a tribute to one of Zurich’s most important underground clubs, the ‘Parfümerie’, the performance duo Clarissa Herbst and Dominique Rust bring the spirit of a cultural movement back to life.
The underground club and music scene was in full swing at night in Zurich during the late 1980s. DJs, activists, female artists and musicians came together for music, performances and readings. Their illegal, ad hoc parties took place in disused factory spaces, shop premises or cellars. Among those present was Koyo Kouoh, the former chief curator of the Venice Art Biennale.
A tribute to the ‘Parfümerie’
In her younger years, Kouoh was part of this movement, which also had a significant influence on her own development as a cultural manager and curator. At the Biennale, Kouoh wanted to pay tribute to one of the key clubs of that era, the so-called “Parfümerie”.
Kouoh died last year at the age of 57. The Parfümerie concept will be retained following her death and carried forward by a team of female curators. It is being realised by the Zurich-based performance duo Clarissa Herbst (graphic designer, costume designer) and Dominique Rust (actor), two of the co-founders of the legendary club.
More
Koyo Kouoh: Art is in the cracks, not in the polish
A melting pot of scenes
Kouoh met the pair back then at the Parfümerie in Zurich and invited them to the Biennale in 2024. For the Parfümerie project, the curator planned to spread events across the entire Biennale – just as the club, true to its name, had dispersed “perfume” across the city of Zurich in the late 1980s and early 1990s.
For Kouoh, it was a very personal project and her time in Zurich was a very important one for her, says Herbst. “It was such a melting pot of very different scenes, and that fascinated her. The fact that such a community emerged from the underground scene.”
Beams of light in the garden shed
For Kouoh, this spontaneous social organisation was also intended to serve as a model for the present day. “She wanted to encourage people to claim their own spaces now, in their own cities or wherever they live,” Herbst continues.
The Parfümerie itself has no comprehensive archive: only leaflets and blurred photographs have survived. At the 2026 Biennale d’Arte, the club is now taking over the Casetta Scaffali, a striking historic exhibition building in the rear garden area of the Arsenale in Venice.
Here, Clarissa Herbst and Dominique Rust explore the concept of Parfümerie on a sensory level, presenting a multimedia installation at the Arsenale: a cone of light invites visitors to dance, surrounded by light projections, videos and Parfümerie leaflets from back then.
A soundtrack by Martin Schütz, a cellist and improviser from the city of Biel/Bienne, gently envelops the space. To accompany the Parfümerie project, a music album dedicated to Kouoh is also being released, featuring further sounds by Schütz and the Berlin-based electronic music pioneer Frank Bretschneider.
The Parfümerie tribute thus establishes a strong musical and visual Swiss presence at the major art exhibition in Venice: the Zurich underground scene lives on.
Parfümerie can be experienced until the end of the Venice Biennale (November 22). A lecture and a performance will also take place during the final month.

How a Swiss aid operation helped former SS members reach Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:00:00 KST

How a Swiss aid operation helped former SS members reach Brazil
New research reveals how former Waffen-SS members were included in one of Switzerland’s largest post-war humanitarian projects and ended up living freely in the South American country.
Crossing the Atlantic on a journey of around 10,000 kilometres to Brazil was long, expensive and difficult. But for around 2,500 people known as the Danube Swabians, it became an opportunity for a new beginning. Of German origin and language, these people had lived for generations in what was then Yugoslavia but, after the Second World War, faced reprisals, expropriations and expulsions after part of the community had collaborated with the Nazi regime.
Among those who chose to leave Europe for Brazil, however, were at least 16 former members of the Waffen-SS, the paramilitary branch of the Nazi Party, whose units were involved in war crimes and crimes against humanity. These men did not arrive in the South American country on their own. They came as beneficiaries of a Swiss humanitarian operation that mobilised the Catholic Church, NGOs and Swiss government funds to establish a new colony in the southern Brazilian state of Paraná.
“It was known that Nazi war criminals were leaving Europe through the so-called ratlines, and it was evident that men there [within the project] were Nazis and members of the SS. But even so, nobody asked questions,” says Peter Hug, a Swiss historian specialising in Switzerland’s relations with Nazi Germany and author of Humanitäre Hilfe der Schweiz für SS-Kriegsverbrecher (Swiss humanitarian aid for SS war criminals), the book that reveals the story.
Published in May 2026, his research documents the presence of at least 16 former Waffen-SS members among the settlers sent to Brazil and reconstructs how Swiss humanitarian organisations and authorities helped make their resettlement possible.
“For Switzerland and the Vatican, this population became an opportunity to present themselves as defenders of refugees, after Switzerland had been very close to the German regime and the Church had never formally protested against Nazi crimes. The fact that there were criminals among them ended up being considered less important,” he adds.
The establishment of the colony, called Entre Rios, also affected populations who already lived and worked on the farms allocated to the Europeans. They ended up marginalised within the new social structure, amid an attempt by the settlement’s leaders to preserve a supposed German cultural superiority.
An operation involving several actors
The operation that brought former Waffen-SS members to Brazil began to take shape in the years immediately after the war, through an articulation between representatives of the Catholic Church in Austria and the Vatican and a group of Danube Swabians linked to the former Ustasha state in Croatia, a fascist puppet state that existed from 1941 to 1945.
“The idea came from Croatian priests close to the Germans and from Andreas Rohracher,” says Hug, referring to the then Archbishop of Salzburg and one of the most influential figures in the Austrian Catholic Church, who, according to Hug, was close to Austrofascism, the authoritarian Catholic-conservative regime that ruled Austria from 1934 to 1938.
“From 1945, they wanted to create closed settlements for the Danube Swabians, where the idea of German cultural superiority could be preserved even after the defeat in the war,” he says.
The project gained momentum with the involvement of Caritas, the Catholic humanitarian non-profit organisation based in Lucerne. According to Hug, the organisation had a fundamental advantage: it was part of a Catholic network with a global presence and capable of opening doors in different countries.
“It was a huge operation which needed to be coordinated globally on two continents,” he says.
The scale of the undertaking, however, eventually exceeded Caritas’s capacity. From 1950 onwards, the project passed into the hands of the Schweizer Europahilfe, or Swiss European Aid, an organisation close to the government. With it came Swiss diplomacy, resources and more direct involvement by the country’s authorities in the operation that would eventually choose the interior of the Brazilian state of Paraná as its destination.
The change was not merely administrative. In Hug’s assessment, the project became an operation combining Switzerland’s humanitarian, diplomatic and economic interests. “The project started within the Catholic Church. Then they had big problems, and then it was the Swiss government and these NGOs around the Swiss government who took it over,” Hug says.
At the centre of the operation was the Agrária Cooperative, created in 1951 to organise the new settlement. Its first president, Michael Moor, had held leadership positions in economic organisations of the German community in the Ustasha State of Croatia, an ally of the Nazis, and had influence over the choice of land and the first groups sent to Brazil.
The colony and its collective memory
“These families lived as refugees and stateless people in Europe after having actively participated in the Second World War on Germany’s side. The main difference, which we must emphasise, is the fact that some of the adult men sent with their families to Entre Rios had fought in the war as members of the Waffen-SS. This did not prevent them from entering Brazil,” says Méri Frotscher, a history professor at the State University of the Midwest (Unicentro) and a researcher on German immigration.
In Brazil, the Swabians arrived at a time when the country was reopening to European immigration and were presented to the authorities as refugees and skilled farmers, a profile that suited the country’s colonisation policy.
A past that challenges Swiss neutrality
For Hug, more than revealing failures in a specific humanitarian operation, the Entre Rios case challenges the way Switzerland has constructed and preserved its own memory of the Second World War.
“We are neutral. We are humanitarian. And we are the best in the world,” Hug says ironically, describing this narrative. “The island of peace in a world of chaos. And this is wrong.”
More than seven decades later, this reassessment is beginning to reach the Swiss organisations involved in the operation, as well as the impact that initiatives such as the creation of the Entre Rios colony had in Switzerland and on local populations.
SWISSAID acknowledges that the perspective of local populations remains largely unexplored and says it is seeking out their descendants to learn their side of the story. “We are currently in the process of establishing contact with the descendants of the communities affected at the time,” the organisation said in a statement to Swissinfo.
SWISSAID argues that this historical reassessment should not be restricted to humanitarian organisations. “It remains to be seen how the story can be told from a Southern perspective. Perhaps, and hopefully, the [Swiss government] will take an interest in coming to terms with this part of history”.
Caritas Switzerland also now acknowledges serious failures in the operation. The organisation says there was no individual vetting of the backgrounds of the selected settlers and regrets that funds intended for humanitarian purposes benefited members of the Waffen-SS.
“We deeply regret that, through this project, funds intended for humanitarian purposes benefited people who were members of the Waffen-SS,” the organisation said in a statement.
Caritas also offers a critical assessment of the impact on the population already living in the region, saying their rights and needs were not considered in the planning. For Caritas, the creation of a closed European settler colony was rooted in a colonial logic and today serves as an example of how humanitarian aid can produce the opposite of its intended effect.
“The approach taken and the establishment of a closed settler colony in Brazil after the Second World War can serve today as a warning of how aid can turn into its opposite,” the organisation said in a statement.
The Agrária Cooperative did not respond to requests for comment.

That is the plan laid out by researchers from the Shenyang Aircraft Design & Research Institute, a top Chinese military aircraft design organisation, in a paper last month.
The lead researcher is chief flight-control designer Zhang Dong at the institute, and his team’s paper – rare for its public details – was published in a peer-reviewed journal Aircraft Design in August.
China’s next-generation stealth fighter programmes were undergoing a “leapfrog transformation from being able to fly steadily to being able to win in combat”, wrote Zhang and his colleagues.
Zhang’s study presents a future of pilots handing over control during periods of extreme workload or incapacitation, quantum navigation technologies supporting operations in satellite-denied environments and crewed fighters coordinating attack, reconnaissance and protection missions with reconfigurable wingman drones.

Syria welcomes IAEA consensus decision closing outstanding nuclear file issues

Ikrame Imane Kouachi
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Syria welcomed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Board of Governors’ consensus adoption of a resolution closing outstanding issues related to the country’s nuclear file and removing the matter from the board’s agenda.
In a statement late Wednesday, the Foreign Ministry said the decision “closes a chapter that has lasted for years” and opens “new prospects” for Syria to cooperate internationally on the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and technology.
The ministry described the resolution as an “important diplomatic and legal achievement for Syria,” saying it reflected the country’s “success in building consensus within the IAEA Board of Governors.”
It said Damascus had adopted “transparency, cooperation and respect for international obligations as a consistent approach since the country’s liberation,” in an effort to address the legacy left by the government of former President Bashar al-Assad.
On Wednesday, the IAEA Board of Governors decided to end the noncompliance finding on Syria’s nuclear obligations after the completion of technical and legal requirements, according to the Syrian state television Alikhbariah.  
Verification of former regime’s nuclear activities 
In August, the head of Syrian Atomic Energy Commission Mudar al-Akaleh said Syria was moving toward closing the noncompliance file and expanding peaceful nuclear applications.
He said the commission, in coordination with the Foreign Ministry, had worked in recent months to provide all technical requirements needed to assess nuclear materials and waste linked to the former regime, in accordance with international safeguards and the IAEA’s legal framework.
Speaking in Damascus on Aug. 18, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi announced the presence of “several tons of nuclear materials” remaining from the Assad era in Deir ez-Zor province, adding that inspectors had been granted access to the site.
An IAEA report circulated to member states and leaked to the media said agency inspectors conducted verification and investigative work at various sites in Syria in August.
The report said the site visits revealed that the Assad regime had failed to declare nuclear materials, facilities and types of activities that should have been reported under Syria’s comprehensive safeguards agreement with the NPT.
On Monday, opening a meeting of the IAEA Board of Governors in Vienna, Grossi said the agency made a “historic breakthrough” after Syria’s new administration provided required information and allowed access to the Deir ez-Zor facility and other sites.
