05:31:58 UTC
14:31:58 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) said Wednesday that drone parts and materials must come from non-Chinese suppliers.
At the 2026 Taipei Security Dialogue, Hsiao said the country needs to combine its advantages in semiconductors, communications technology, and precision manufacturing with national defense. She added that drones must be produced domestically to protect national security.
Hsiao said drones have reshaped modern warfare, with Ukraine and the Middle East demonstrating the need for cost-effective solutions from sea, land, and air. She said AI intelligence analysis, counter-drone measures, and logistics should be researched further.
On the Taiwan Dome defense network proposed by President Lai Ching-te (賴清德), Hsiao said it depends on high-performing sensors and capable operators. She added that getting the tools is important, but keeping the systems running is what will determine operational success.
On maritime security, Hsiao said disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Taiwan Strait can impact world economies. She said allies should share intelligence and technology to identify threats and take preventive measures when necessary.
Hsiao said the National Security Council and competent authorities are working closely with allies on legal, diplomatic, and technological countermeasures. She noted that protecting infrastructure such as submarine cables is crucial for business and public works to function.
Hsiao said a special budget has been submitted to the Legislative Yuan for drone procurement, with coastal drones and unmanned boats to be domestically manufactured. She said the aim is to strengthen defense and self-reliance using non-Chinese parts and materials to minimize risks.
On gray-zone threats, Hsiao said foreign military exercises, cyberattacks, and disinformation affect the nation every day. She said the government agencies are training the public to recognize potential hazards and respond accordingly.

AIT head warns AI could pose new threats to Taiwan elections
Unknown

2026-09-10
05:31:43 UTC
14:31:43 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — American Institute in Taiwan Director Raymond Greene warned Wednesday that increasingly sophisticated AI could pose new threats to Taiwan’s elections and democratic institutions.
Speaking at the Taipei Security Dialogue, Greene said Taiwan continues to face persistent propaganda attacks from adversaries aimed at creating divisions and undermining confidence in democratic institutions and the US-Taiwan partnership. While the country has long been regarded as a model for countering such manipulation, he said it must prepare for a new wave of more sophisticated AI-driven information operations ahead of the upcoming local elections.
AI-enabled cyberattacks could also pose significant threats to critical sectors, including the banking industry and critical infrastructure. Greene said immediate action is needed to address these emerging risks.
He said Taiwan has made significant progress in strengthening the resilience of its public and civil sectors against such campaigns. Taiwan’s experience in countering information manipulation provides an important model for other democracies facing similar pressures, he said.
Greene also praised President Lai Ching-te’s (賴清德) administration for taking steps to strengthen the country’s defense capabilities amid unprecedented global security concerns. He cited the government’s commitment to raise defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2030, saying Taiwan is fully capable of making that commitment.
Greene said Taiwan is systematically addressing vulnerabilities in its economy, particularly in critical areas such as electricity generation. While the international community has focused heavily on Taiwan’s efforts to expand liquefied natural gas imports and storage, he said it has paid less attention to the nation's broader efforts to strengthen energy resilience.
He cited energy rationing plans, a more decentralized power grid, the use of coal and renewable energy, and assessments of potential sources such as geothermal power and nuclear. “Taiwan is far better positioned today than it was just a couple of years ago,” Greene said.
Greene said Taiwan’s ability to cope with the effects of Middle East conflicts on energy supplies and critical imports such as helium highlights its progress in building resilience. He said Taipei’s preparations demonstrate that its efforts to strengthen energy security are producing tangible results.

Wall Street Journal publisher convicted in Hong Kong of deterring reporter from union role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:31:16 UTC
14:31:16 KST

A Hong Kong court has convicted the publisher of the Wall Street Journal of deterring a reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city.
The newspaper dismissed Selina Cheng just weeks after she was appointed chair of the Hong Kong Journalist Association (HKJA) in 2024. She was told at the time her termination was officially due to restructuring.
Outside court on Thursday, Cheng said: “If reporters’ employment rights are not sufficiently safeguarded, or when their rights are violated and not enforced in law, then we can no longer work safely as reporters.”
Principal magistrate David Cheung ruled that Dow Jones Publishing, the parent company of the Wall Street journal, was guilty of “preventing or deterring an employee from exercising trade union rights,” but acquitted it of “dismissing or discriminating against an employee because she exercised those rights.”
Cheng, who covered China’s automobiles and energy sectors for the WSJ, said her editor had told her that employees should not be seen as advocating for press freedom in “places like Hong Kong”, saying it could be perceived as a conflict of interest. She alleged her employer had attempted to prevent her from taking up a role in the union.
She said the company told her that she needed to seek the firm’s approval for outside activities and requested her to leave her then-board position at the association.
Cheng launched the private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing after losing her job in July 2024, weeks after taking up the position as chair of the union.
The company pleaded not guilty to both charges, which each carry a maximum fine of HK$100,000 (about $12,750).
Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date.
During the trial, the defence argued that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and that the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the firm’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor. The defence also accused Cheng of acting in bad faith in a previous hearing.
But magistrate David Cheung said that Cheng’s termination “was motivated by wrongful and unjustified application of their code of conduct” when it insisted Cheng needed to seek prior approval to stand as chair of HKJA.
Cheung said he accepted Cheng’s explanation, describing the former WSJ reporter as “honest and reliable”, adding she and was clearly motivated by “the wish to see justice”.
Cheng’s termination alarmed journalists, who are already operating in an increasingly restricted media environment in the city, where foreign outlets have traditionally faced less pressure than local news outlets.
“The WSJ set a very bad precedent by punishing an employee who was exercising her constitutionally protected rights in Hong Kong,” said Eric Lai, a senior fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law.
The WSJ maintained there was no link between Cheng’s role in the Hong Kong union and her termination. At the time of Cheng’s dismissal, it issued a statement saying: “The Wall Street Journal has been and continues to be a fierce and vocal advocate for press freedom in Hong Kong and around the world.”
HKJA is the oldest journalist union in Hong Kong. It was established in 1968 and is registered as a trade union representing journalists and workers in news. It has faced increasing pressure since the introduction of a Beijing-imposed national security law in 2020.
Hong Kong has fallen sharply in global press freedom rankings since the law’s introduction. In 2019 Reporters Without Borders ranked the city 73rd in the world. By 2026 it had fallen 67 places to 140th out of 180 countries and territories.

Anthropic discloses 4th AI hacking incident as researcher quits over safety
AI firm says Claude Opus 4.6 hacked third-party systems during testing in January as concerns mount over security breaches.
AI researcher quits Anthropic saying AI race ‘could kill us all’
Anthropic has reported a fourth incident involving an AI model gaining unauthorised access to external systems, shortly after a researcher quit over concerns about the technology’s rushed development.
In a statement on Wednesday, the artificial intelligence research company said an early version of its Claude Opus 4.6 hacked into a third-party system in January.

It said it had notified all the affected parties but did not disclose more details.
The January incident went undetected until last month, despite an earlier company-wide review, Anthropic said, underscoring the challenge that AI developers face in identifying and containing unexpected behaviour by advanced models.
The disclosure came after Anthropic reported several of its Claude models hacked into the systems of three companies during test sessions in July.
The previous incidents involved Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research test model.
The AI race
Companies including Anthropic and OpenAI are under scrutiny as models designed to complete complex tasks have at times learned to bend rules, exploit loopholes and interact with external systems in ways their developers did not anticipate.
Last week, the Reuters news agency reported that rogue agents from OpenAI hijacked a German-language wiki and a host of other sites, an incident the company chose not to disclose until it was made public.
In July, OpenAI’s autonomous agents also compromised the servers and infrastructure of AI start-up Hugging Face.
That incident prompted Anthropic to conduct a review of some 141,006 test sessions. Based on a preliminary assessment, Anthropic said it did not believe the latest incident was more severe than the three previous ones that were examined in detail.
The company said its investigation identified two recurring problems, which appeared to varying degrees across the incidents: Biased reasoning, in which Claude discounted or misinterpreted evidence that it was operating on the live internet, and recklessness, or a willingness to take potentially harmful actions in pursuit of a task.
Anthropic said it has engaged independent research firm METR to investigate the incidents.
Anthropic researcher quits
The investigations come amid a broader wave of internal dissent within the AI industry regarding safety. An Anthropic researcher said he resigned over concerns about the technology’s potential to surpass human control.
Jacob Coxon, in a widely shared X post on Tuesday, said the AI industry was more focused on competition rather than on implementing safeguards. He came to this realisation after spending the last three years doing research at OpenAI and Anthropic.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon said.
“No other human activity poses this level of danger,” he added, referencing the swift advancement of AI technology.
In June, Anthropic proposed a coordinated effort with the world’s leading AI developers to slow down development, warning that humans risk losing control over the technology.
Following the security breach of Hugging Face, OpenAI said it was pushing for mandatory national AI safety requirements and wanted to work with Congress on “capability-based” regulation.
In a statement published on Wednesday, the company said it was formally endorsing four California bills related to safeguards against AI.
“If we cannot meet certain safety bars without slowing down capability growth, we should prioritise the former. The more powerful the technology becomes, the stronger the surrounding safeguards must become,” the statement said.

US grant for MAGA-aligned groups in Europe excludes French applicants over election fears

US grant for MAGA-aligned groups in Europe excludes French applicants over election fears
PARIS, Sept 10 - A U.S. grant program for organisations pursuing Trump administration priorities in Europe will exclude French groups because of sensitivities over allegations of foreign interference ahead of next year's presidential election, according to two sources.
The decision has already been communicated to French officials, one of the sources said. It reflects a recognition in Washington that funding MAGA-aligned organisations in France could jeopardise extensive economic ties between both countries.
U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has sought to support far-right parties across Europe, accusing the continent's centrist leaders of overseeing "civilizational erasure" and "the subversion of democratic processes."
The U.S. State Department's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights, and Labor (DRL) grant program offers between $1 million and $3 million to organizations seeking "to strengthen and develop democratic resilience, rule of law, freedom of speech and freedom of the press, and the defense of human rights in Europe," according to DRL's July 13 funding guidelines.
Eligible groups may also focus on "national sovereignty, migration, censorship, and lawfare challenges."
France, which faces a presidential election next April-May that could hand power to Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally (RN), has grown increasingly worried about potential U.S. interference in the vote. The RN has pledged a constitutional reform to ramp up deportations, restrict birthright citizenship and give French nationals priority access to public services.
In July, just days after DRL published its funding announcement, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot reacted angrily on X, writing: "France and the Europeans will not tolerate any attempt at foreign interference in their electoral processes, regardless of where it comes from."
One French applicant, who declined to be named, said they had sought $1 million for their organisation's work on anti-censorship and freedom of speech initiatives. They were recently informed that French groups would be excluded because of concerns over foreign interference.
According to the source, U.S. officials were particularly concerned that U.S.-funded activities could conflict with a proposed French law that would strengthen penalties for online disinformation and foreign interference in democratic processes. The fast-tracked, government-backed bill is currently before the Senate.
Although DRL's August deadline has now passed, the source said they may relocate their organization, potentially to Brussels, to qualify for future funding opportunities.
A State Department spokesperson declined to answer whether French groups were now excluded, saying "programs are still in active deliberation," and adding "we do not comment on private diplomatic discussions."
France's foreign ministry did not respond.
STRAINED FRANCO-AMERICAN RELATIONS
Although several senior MAGA officials within the State Department have sought a tougher line on France over freedom of speech and tech regulation, sources say they have faced pushback from other U.S. officials who fret about negative repercussions for U.S. companies with significant operations in France.
The United States is France's top foreign investor, with $107.9 billion invested in the French economy in 2024, while the two nations traded $160.9 billion in goods and services that year, according to U.S. government data.
Still, diplomatic relations are at a low ebb.
On top of lingering issues over tariffs, the Iran war and threats to European sovereignty, Washington has yet to accredit France's next U.S. ambassador following public French criticism of the United States' human rights record.
French officials have been irked by U.S. Ambassador to Paris Charles Kushner, whose son Jared is married to Trump's daughter Ivanka. He has twice failed to respond to summonses in Paris following diplomatic incidents.
They were also upset when DRL officials travelled to Paris last year to support Le Pen after a court barred her from office as part of a drive against alleged "lawfare" against conservatives. REUTERS

Congress-NC rift over Vande Mataram: The ghost of 1987 and ‘big brother’ complex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:26:05 UTC
14:26:05 KST

The 1987 ghost: Vande Mataram row and why Omar Abdullah won't let Congress call the shots in J&K.
The latest Congress-National Conference (NC) clash may have begun with a song, but it is really about something much older: who gets to set the political terms of the alliance in Jammu and Kashmir?CM Omar Abdullah and NC president Farooq Abdullah stood through the full rendition of Vande Mataram on Wednesday at the inaugural International Film Festival in Srinagar. The song was played in its complete six-stanza version, lasting about three minutes and 10 seconds, in line with the Centre's new protocol.
This was in sharp contrast with the Congress's stand. Its grand-old party has reaffirmed its 1937 decision to restrict public rendition at party events to the first two stanzas, arguing that the later verses sit uneasily with the pluralist ethos of the freedom movement.Congress general secretary KC Venugopal subsequently said the full version "sits uneasily" with the syncretic and pluralist ethos envisioned by India's freedom fighters and urged allies to stand by the Congress position.
Venugopal called on allies to honour the wisdom of the freedom fighters
The NC was quick to respond, saying the J&K government was only fulfilling its official duty. "After legislative enactment by Parliament, singing Vande Mataram and standing for the song has become a statutory obligation (mandatory legal duty) regardless of the ideological position of any party, group or alliance," said National Conference spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq.The Vande Mataram row is the latest in the list of NC-Congress differences that have surfaced post-election.
However, in J&K, the dispute carries an additional historical charge.The NC has spent decades constructing its political identity around a particular proposition: New Delhi can be a partner, but it cannot be the political proprietor of Kashmir's choices.That is where the ghost of 1987 enters.
One alliance, two political vocabularies
The Vande Mataram dispute has once again exposed an asymmetry that has repeatedly surfaced between the two parties.Congress has to balance its position across India. For Abdullahs' NC, the principal political constituency remains rooted in J&K, where questions of identity, autonomy, federalism and the relationship with New Delhi carry a much more immediate electoral meaning.It is also why the latest row is not an isolated irritant in the alliance.In December 2025, for instance, Omar Abdullah explicitly distanced the NC from Congress's "vote chori" campaign, saying Congress was free to choose its own agenda but that it was not automatically the agenda of the INDIA bloc. With this, Omar tried to assert his party's political autonomy within the alliance.And that has been the recurring pattern.
The alliance and an unequal power equation
The 2024 assembly election gave the NC-Congress relationship a new lease of life, but it also made the asymmetry between the two parties stark.The alliance crossed the majority mark with 49 seats, with the NC winning 42, Congress six and CPM one. The BJP emerged with 29, PDP three and independents seven.The pre-poll negotiations themselves had not been effortless: the parties agreed that NC would contest 51 seats and Congress 32, while several constituencies remained "friendly contests".The campaign also revealed the limits of joint ownership. Congress and NC leaders did not always campaign together. In Sopore, where the two allies were in a friendly contest, Rahul Gandhi and Omar Abdullah campaigned for their respective candidates separately.During the campaign, Omar Abdullah had publicly noted that Rahul Gandhi should dedicate more campaign time and effort to the Jammu region in addition to Kashmir to maximise electoral impact.Omar himself gave the practical reason for the alliance during the campaign: it was intended to prevent a hung assembly and give voters an alternative.
What Omar Abdullah had said in 2024
The alliance won the election, and the next question was: what does each side get to claim as its own?The first major post-election rupture came even before the new government had settled in.Omar Abdullah became CM in October 2024, but Congress chose to stay out of his ministry, citing restoration of statehood as its priority. While Congress backed the NC government from outside, its absence highlighted a strategic divide within the alliance. Omar had to engage with Delhi to govern the Union Territory, while Congress sought to pressure the Centre from outside. That difference in approach has repeatedly resurfaced.
Statehood: Common demand & source of friction
In July 2025, Congress announced protests in Jammu, Srinagar and Delhi and Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge wrote to PM Narendra Modi seeking legislation to restore J&K's statehood. The NC leadership was irritated because the announcement had not been coordinated with the ruling party. Some NC leaders described Congress's campaign as counterproductive and even as "sabotage" of the government's own efforts.Omar's objection was that Congress had launched the campaign without informing or consulting the NC, leaving its alliance partner caught off guard.The difference is clearer on Article 370. The NC's 2024 manifesto explicitly called for the restoration of Articles 370 and 35A and reversal of the changes made after August 2019. Congress has similarly opposed the 2019 constitutional changes, but in its recent campaigns placed greater emphasis on the restoration of statehood.Omar reiterated in the J&K assembly in February that his government remained committed to restoring special status, even as statehood remained an immediate demand. By July 2026, he was also linking the restoration of statehood to any future discussion on J&K's earlier constitutional position.This has given the two parties different political priorities.
The Rajya Sabha dispute
In October 2025, the disagreement moved from ideology to seats. J&K was electing four Rajya Sabha members. The NC, which had emerged as the dominant party in the assembly, initially discussed leaving one seat for Congress.Talks failed.The NC eventually fielded candidates for all four seats after Congress decided not to contest the fourth seat it had been offered, arguing that it was not among the "safe seats" it had sought.Omar's response was strikingly matter-of-fact: "So be it."The NC-Congress disagreement ultimately cost the alliance a clean sweep, with the BJP winning the fourth seat Congress had declined to contest.
We felt that the best chance of winning that seat was with the Congress, and they felt otherwise. So be it.
Omar Abdullah on RS seat deadlock
The ghost of 1987
To understand why the NC may be particularly sensitive to questions of control, one has to go back not merely to 1987 but to 1984.Farooq Abdullah's government was dismissed on July 2, 1984, after 12 NC legislators defected. Ghulam Mohammad Shah, Farooq's brother-in-law and leader of the defecting group, formed the government with Congress support. Contemporary accounts described the episode as a central-government intervention in Kashmir politics; Farooq called the dismissal unconstitutional.For the NC, this was not an abstract constitutional episode. It was a direct lesson in the vulnerability of a regional government to New Delhi's political machinery.Then came 1986.Rajiv Gandhi and Farooq Abdullah reached an agreement that brought the two parties together electorally. A Human Rights Watch report noted that the accord deepened a sense of betrayal among many Kashmiris, who saw Farooq Abdullah compromising with the same Congress party that had pushed him out of office two years earlier.
1987: The alliance that became a warning
The NC-Congress alliance won 66 of J&K's 76 assembly seats in 1987. But the result was overshadowed by the emergence of the Muslim United Front as an opposition platform, arrests of its candidates and workers, and widespread allegations of electoral rigging. Human Rights Watch later described the election as a turning point that contributed to widespread disillusionment with electoral politics.The significance of 1987 for the NC, therefore, is about the political memory it created. A generation of Kashmiri activists came to believe that the democratic route had been closed to them, a perception that became part of the backdrop to the insurgency that followed.The episode also left an enduring paradox. Congress was simultaneously the NC's electoral partner and a major force at the Centre. That history helps explain the NC's instinct to work with Congress while resisting any perception that Delhi is dictating its regional agenda.That distrust predates the 1980s. In 1953, Sheikh Abdullah was dismissed and arrested after his relationship with the Union government deteriorated. The circumstances were very different, but the political memory was similar: central intervention could reshape J&K's politics. For the NC, unlike many other regional parties, Congress's centralising past is therefore not distant history but part of its own political inheritance.
2009-14: History managed, but not erased
The two parties showed they could overcome that history after the 2008 assembly election. The NC won 28 seats and Congress 17, and the parties formed a coalition government with Omar Abdullah as CM in 2009.But the partnership remained contested. Differences over AFSPA, administrative issues and governance repeatedly surfaced. In 2011, Congress called for consensus on AFSPA while Omar maintained that the state government was an important stakeholder.By 2014, the alliance had run its course and Congress chose to contest the assembly election separately. NC leaders argued that the association with a centrist national party had diluted the party's pro-Valley credentials, with one senior NC leader calling Congress a "very bad alliance partner".The 1987 ghost & real test of allianceWhile 1987 may still shape the NC's political instincts, it would be too simplistic to link every present-day disagreement to that history. The political and constitutional context has changed; however, the experience remains part of the backdrop to the relationship.
The lesson for the NC, as we saw in the last election, has not been to avoid Congress, but to work with it where interests converge while retaining its own political space.The Vande Mataram dispute, therefore, is less significant in itself than what it reveals about continuing differences over statehood, Article 370, seat-sharing and the balance between Congress's national strategy and the NC's regional politics.The alliance can survive such differences, but the interesting question now is how durable it will be, which willdepend on how well the two parties manage their competing political priorities.

US-Israeli arms firm Covenant to build cruise missiles in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:22:15 UTC
14:22:15 KST

By Carsten Hoffmann, dpa.
Berlin (dpa) – US-Israeli defence contractor Covenant plans to set up a production facility for long-range cruise missiles in the German state of Saxony, the company said on Wednesday.
“We will be producing roughly 1,000 in our first year and then scaling to 5,000,” Covenant chief Abigail Denburg said, outlining the company’s “target for annual production.”
Production of the Anthem cruise missile for European customers is to begin next year at the facility to be set up near Leipzig.
It comes as Germany and other European states are in the process of massively ramping up their defence industry in response to a growing threat from Russia.
“When you look at our adversaries, you see thousands of hardened targets, beyond the range of current capabilities,” said Michael Kaufman, Covenant’s co-founder and chief executive said in a press release.
“Anthem was built to credibly hold those targets at risk in a prolonged conflict. If our stockpiles run thin, so does our deterrence.”
Anthem missiles can carry a 200-kilogram warhead and are designed for precision strikes deep within enemy territory. Covenant has not commented on media reports suggesting Anthem’s range is 1,500 kilometres.
The company says it plans to offer the weapons system at a significantly lower price than those currently available on the market. Covenant said Anthem would cost a six-figure sum, meaning less than $1 million, while other weapons systems of this kind typically cost several million dollars per unit.
Mass production has military significance and is intended to improve customers’ staying power. Denburg said: “Deterrence is a calculation by the enemy and that calculation changes when you have extensive weapons arsenals. If you can reach a target and strike once, that does not necessarily deter the enemy.”
Covenant is already in talks with the Bundeswehr and the procurement agency, according to dpa information, though this has not been officially confirmed.
Denburg said, without directly referring to Germany, that there was already a production contract for deliveries from Germany starting in the first quarter of 2027.
“This European customer will decide for themselves when they want to make this public,” she said.
Company raises more than $250 million
Covenant was founded in 2024 and is headquartered in Washington. The company said it has raised more than $250 million from investors in three funding rounds.
Backers include Founders Fund, which counts Peter Thiel among its co-founders. He is known for his libertarian and right-wing conservative positions, his closeness to US President Donald Trump and his criticism of liberal democracies.
Defence Minister Boris Pistorius of the Social Democrats has in the past “explicitly” shared concerns about Thiel. There has also been public discussion of whether new dependencies could arise or whether the risk is greater of finding oneself without sufficiently stocked ammunition depots in a crisis.
Covenant said German retired Lieutenant General Andreas Marlow is an adviser. He was deputy inspector of the army until 2025 and from 2022 also led the EU training mission for the Ukrainian armed forces.
A long-range missile programme produced in Europe was “the missing piece of the puzzle in our deterrence architecture”, Marlow was quoted as saying.
Germany and its European NATO allies are currently seeking to procure long-range weapons systems as a response to the Russian threat as well as develop their own. At the NATO summit in Ankara, the German government agreed with the United States to buy US Tomahawk cruise missiles.
At the beginning of September, the German navy successfully completed a previously secret test of the Israeli missile system Lora, a ballistic missile. Germany already has the Taurus cruise missile made by defence company MBDA but it is far from being mass-produced.
European NATO states also do not yet have their own intermediate-range weapons. In the medium term, several allies want to procure their own weapons system for long-range precision strikes. To that end, the Elsa project, the European Long-Range Strike Approach, was launched in 2024 at the NATO summit in Washington.
Source: dpa.com

'It started as a joke, a fantasy' - F1 heads to football-obsessed Madrid
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
06:21:13 BST
14:21:13 KST

'It started as a joke, a fantasy' - F1 heads to football-obsessed Madrid
- Published
You could never accuse Formula 1 of shirking a challenge.
Who else would consider competing for the attention of a football-obsessed country, home to the World Cup winners, in a city where a constant stream of the world's most talented players do awe-inspiring things most weeks?
F1 last had a Spanish world champion 20 years ago and there hasn't been a race in Madrid since 1981.
Does F1, which has experienced a huge rise in popularity in other territories around the world, need another track in its crowded European heartland?
This weekend the sport, and Madrid itself, will find out.
Madrilenos know how to make sport great
Real Madrid are considered to be the greatest football club in history.
They have won 15 European Cups and 36 La Liga titles, and then there are the famous Galacticos: the generational set of the world's best players which began with the likes of Zinedine Zidane and Ronaldo and has extended to the modern crop that includes Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe.
Some 75,000 Madridistas roared home Mbappe's majestically deft volley to make it 3-0 after half an hour against Malaga at the end of August, and their city rivals Atletico aren't far adrift of them in La Liga. It's hard to see what else the locals need to sate their sporting needs.
But in both the stunning, newly reconditioned steel spaceship of the Bernabeu, which has lost none of the drama of its frighteningly steep theatrical terracing, or Real Madrid women's atmospheric if less salubrious stadium right next to the new F1 track, will fans be turning their attention to the roar of the engine noise this weekend?
"Yes, [the F1 race] is good for Madrid," says one. "There is pride in our sport, Madrid is an open city with open people and open minds.
"The race can [take] Madrid's [identity] outside of football, and the most we can be seen [by the outside world] is the best.
"But I'm more than excited… I'm curious - I want to see how it goes."
"We've always been dreaming of having something [from F1] closer to home," adds another. "Having it back is great. I've been to Barcelona and the Belgian GP and I think let's see how it goes. Organising tends to be messy in the first year - I don't want to be the guinea pig.
"Let's hope it brings the city more into the spotlight. Madrid has a lot to learn from F1 about how to run a global spectacle; F1 could probably learn the true Spanish way. Barcelona is more international, the drivers and fans coming to Madrid will get more of a taste of Spain."
Welcome to Madring
As the Prado museum demonstrates, Madrid knows its fine art.
The crossing signals resemble birdsong and the Mexican conifers gently sway over the waiting traffic with a backdrop of stunning Palaciosian architecture, which is in contrast to the relatively flat, block layout of the inner city.
This may not have made for the best race experience so instead, organisers plumped for what outsiders may see as an unloved expo area run by the quasi-state owned Ifema organisation next to the city's airport.
"It started as a joke, it was a fantasy," says Luis Garcia Abad, Madring boss and former manager to Spain's only world champion Fernando Alonso, among other Spanish sports stars.
"An F1 grand prix is like a unicorn - you are trying always to see the unicorn but at the end you realise [sometimes] it's impossible.
"The queue of cities trying to organise an F1 GP is huge. They have to choose right - we signed a contract for 10 years.
"Maybe seven or eight years ago we talked about this race. At some point Ifema called me and said 'what are you thinking [about its viability]?' After one morning [here] I said: 'It's possible.'
The new venue may be a world away from the flamenco-inspired boutiques and wine bars of the intimate Salamanca district, but Madrid is relatively diminutive compared to other high-profile capitals, and has high-quality public transport.
As a result, organisers are cutting out many of the car parks and asking fans to leave their own motors at home.
But don't expect Patrick Dempsey, Rafael Nadal and Mbappe to be standing on the platform of Avenida de America to hop on the pink line to the circuit – they will breathe easy at the VIP spaces near to the expansive six-strong VIP area paddock.
Regardless of the journey there, what will fans find?
"It's a real experience, not just to be in Madrid but for F1," says Abad. "Every part of the track has its own personality. Monumental… Turn 12, is huge, amazing.
"We really wanted to have an iconic part of the circuit – more than 30,000 people around one corner."
Ah yes, Monumental. The corner everyone in F1 is talking about when discussing this race.
A 26-degree banked challenge, substantially longer than the one at the Dutch Grand Prix's Zandvoort. Monumental scythes through what will feel like a small town come race day.
It comes complete with a VIP viewing area that could house the King of Spain and his family and sits, appropriately, like a castle on top of the hill. It's a difficult structure to walk up, and in 44C heat, impossible to sit on.
"Luis wanted to think of something recognisable in our circuit. Something iconic," says operations director for Ifema Carlos Jimenez.
Monumental was not the only complex part of a track build, which Jimenez says lends itself to sustainability. Power for the race comes from renewable energy and there is partial use of existing buildings around the site. However, additional construction around the circuit has seen 65m euros of investment, and the track itself cost 85m euros alone.
"There were a lot of challenges," he says. "We started building it in the wettest winter in 20 years in Spain. The rain was torrential. We suffered a lot, and had to stabilise parts of clay which behaves badly with wet conditions. It was very challenging. There are three layers of asphalt here. We learnt from one layer to the next.
"In 2022 it seemed like a little bit of a crazy idea," adds Jimenez. "But Madrid has momentum right now; it's a vibrant city, very well known for football.
"Like a ski resort must have entertainment for apres-ski, a circuit must have good after-race entertainment. Madrid will become in top position - the offer of this city is incredible in terms of gastronomy, a spectacular climate, which is very mild in September. And the party in Madrid is unbeatable."
What could happen in the race?
Make no mistake, Madring is a street circuit: part public roads, part purpose built. And it feels intense to stand on the track, let alone drive it, with the walls on either side appearing to close in on you. And that lack of width, on the eye at least, suggests overtaking will be virtually impossible.
"From a driver's point of view it's quite a harsh circuit," says an excited Abad. "Twenty-two corners, up and down, banking corners - the circuit is adapted to the new [F1] regulations.
"I spoke with Charles Leclerc and he said it was an amazing track, and in the race I believe you will have the opportunity to overtake, but not by free. We're talking about gladiators – the best drivers in the world."
Plenty of drivers have already experienced Madring in anger during a Formula 3 test.
"It's going to be really edgy," says Madrid's own F3 driver Bruno del Pino. "You are always on the limit, the corners are quick and the walls are close. It's like [Saudi GP circuit] Jeddah but with more difficulty.
"With Monumental, you see so much of an angle it never ends. The first time around, you see it going straight up and you feel like you'll fly straight out [of the track].
"It is flat for us because of the downforce so it's not really a corner, but the previous combination of Turns 10 and 11 are high speed and close to the wall - quite a few drivers will kiss the wall."
Britain's F3 driver Freddie Slater goes even further: "A lap of Madrid is so exhilarating, and the adrenaline is pumping - it's an incredible track to drive. It's one of the best tracks on calendar, if not the best.
"It's got character, it's got bumps, uphill and downhill – it's a bit more old-school."
Abad believes it's the spectators who will determine this race's success.
"Not just Madrid needing F1, maybe even F1 needing Madrid," he concludes. "We're investing money to create an experience inside of a city.
"The future of the [F1] championship is something in this direction – we need to take care of customers and spectators. They are our future."

EU Commission scrambles to keep pace with Moldova's accession push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:18:58 UTC
14:18:58 KST

The European Commission is redirecting resources to keep pace with Moldova's fast reform drive, even as its accession stays politically coupled with Ukraine's Hungary-stalled bid.
The European Commission is redirecting internal resources to Moldova's enlargement process, after Chișinău's reform pace outstripped the department's capacity to keep up with it, EU officials told Euronews.
The Moldovan government has pushed through required reforms so quickly that the Commission is now playing catch-up, reallocating existing resources to keep tabs on progress.
"Moldova's impressive record of EU reforms is paying off. I had a good call with new Prime Minister Vasile Tofan during which we discussed the next steps on Moldova's EU accession path," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos wrote on X on Tuesday.
The Commission's enlargement department, already stretched thin by simultaneous progress across several candidate countries, has had to shift resources towards the best-performing ones.
Forging ahead
Chișinău has pushed hard on EU-required reforms since Maia Sandu became president in 2020, installing a pro-EU government with a comfortable parliamentary majority.
"The reforms that we are undertaking in the last five years are really unprecedented," Cristina Gherasimov, Moldova's Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration, told the press at the margins of a ministerial meeting on Friday.
"Our formula for these reforms to be successful is the political will and the determination of our people to work strongly in favour of the current window of opportunity that exists in the European Union," she said.
The Commission, in turn, must verify that candidates are getting the reforms right, meaning it has to match its expertise to the pace each country can realistically sustain.
Kyiv is also advancing its reform agenda, which gained fresh momentum when Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi took office in July. However, the country's war effort and budgetary strain continue to weigh on its accession bid.
On Tuesday, the IMF released a report analysing the potential economic benefits of EU membership for the Western Balkan countries and Moldova, excluding Ukraine because of its "much larger size and ongoing military conflict."
This rapid technical progress sits awkwardly against the political reality in the Council of the EU, where Ukraine and Moldova's accession tracks remain linked.
Political coupling
"Coupling" refers to the informal practice of linking two countries' accession processes.
Grouping countries is particularly useful during ratification, since it allows member states to ratify a single accession treaty — as was the case when Romania and Bulgaria joined the bloc in 2007.
Ukraine and Moldova began their accession tracks together in 2022, just days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In December 2023, EU leaders opened accession negotiations with both countries simultaneously.
Kyiv's process was then blocked for two years by a veto from Viktor Orbán's Hungary, rooted in bilateral disputes over the treatment of the Hungarian minority in Ukraine's eastern Transcarpathia region.
Momentum returned after Péter Magyar's Tisza party ousted Orbán from power in April, prompting Budapest and Kyiv to open negotiations to resolve the bilateral disputes. In June, Hungary lifted its veto on the first negotiation cluster.
The second of six clusters opened in July. Since then, however, Hungary has slowed the process again, as over a decade of anti-Ukraine rhetoric under Orbán makes rapid progress hard for many Hungarians to accept.
Although the friction is a purely bilateral matter between Ukraine and Hungary, the coupling means Moldova has been caught in the slipstream.
Expected departure
The coupling was driven by major geopolitical considerations. Moldova has long had a Russian military presence in Transnistria, meaning that when war broke out in 2022, the country found itself behind the front line, with Russian troops on its own territory.
The coupling matters deeply to Kyiv too, which sees the prospect of future EU membership as a lifeline anchoring the country outside Russia's sphere of influence.
Since Moldova joined the enlargement track alongside Ukraine, the argument goes that Chișinău forging ahead alone while Kyiv is bogged down in bilateral disputes would send the wrong political signal.
That is why Ukraine's main enlargement supporters, notably the Baltic states, have pushed to maintain the coupling throughout the cluster-opening phase.
But the technical side of accession, the reforms themselves, does not have to wait for the political track to catch up.
EU officials expect the coupling of the two eastern European countries to hold until all remaining clusters are opened. From that point, the situation is expected to shift quickly, provided Moldova keeps up its reform momentum.
"We have an ambitious target goal to be ready to close negotiations by early 2028," Gherasimov said.

Commissioner 'deeply worried' by sexual violence trajectory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:18:40 UTC
14:18:40 KST

Domestic, family and sexual violence commissioner 'deeply worried' over high rates of assault
In short:
Australia is facing near-record-high rates of sexual violence.
The number of First Nations women killed by a partner is increasing.
What's next?
The federal government will release its second action plan to end domestic, sexual and family violence next year.
The domestic, family and sexual violence commissioner says she is "deeply worried" about the trajectory of rates of sexual violence in Australia following the release of her annual report, which has called for national attention on the issue.
Micaela Cronin's report found Australians were experiencing unacceptable levels of harm within the family law and justice systems and through rising levels of sexual violence.
Sexual violence in Australia reached its highest level in 33 years in 2024.
Ms Cronin said the rate had dropped by less than 1 per cent in the past year and more action was needed to address the issue.
"I am deeply worried about the trajectories that we're on, particularly with sexual violence, and you're right, it is absolutely increasing between young people," she told the ABC.
"So we absolutely have to face up to what isn't working and identify what is working.
"We've got a real problem, and we've seen that in the national conversation in the last few weeks."
The issue came into national focus last month with two cases of young boys being charged with sexual assault.
A leading violence against women scholar at Monash University, Kate Fitz-Gibbon, called the sexual violence figures "frightening" and said it was a reminder to governments they had to do more to protect women and children.
"I think it's certainly a call to action … some progress has been made, but there is significantly more action needed," she told ABC.
The commissioner's report recommends sexual violence should have targeted and sustained national attention, but it does not outline what programs or policies are necessary.
The report also recommends governments at all levels invest more in violence prevention services, arguing opportunities to "intervene earlier, support recovery and reduce future demand" were often missed.
Ms Cronin said early intervention was part of the broader solution to reduce gender based violence.
"Australia has largely invested in systems designed to respond once violence reaches crisis point … These services are essential, but on their own they will not reduce the prevalence or impact of gender-based violence," she wrote in her report.
Do you know more about this story? Get in touch via Signal (claudialong.01) or email long.claudia@abc.net.au
Ms Fitz-Gibbon said early intervention needed to be "multi-pronged", and schools should be given more support to identify at-risk children earlier.
"We've been calling for greater attention within schools to connecting children and young people up to safety earlier to try and interrupt those trajectories of harm," she told the ABC.
"School staff are not equipped; they have not been trained to provide an early intervention response for children and young people."
Change needed within family law and justice systems
Ms Cronin singled out the legal system as an area that needed change to better protect survivors of domestic violence and sexual violence.
She acknowledged there had been significant reform in family law, but said more work was needed.
"We are still seeing the family law courts being a site for weaponisation, so people using the court to continue to drag out relationships and harm," she told the ABC.
"There are real concerns about decisions that are being made that are putting children in harm's way."
Her concerns about the legal system more broadly have been echoed by executive director of advocacy group With You We Can, Sarah Rosenberg, who herself navigated the justice system after a sexual violence incident.
"Very few victim survivors report; of those who do, very few cases progress to a charge [and] these aren't individual choices, this is attrition by design," she said.
Ms Rosenberg, whose organisation assists victim survivors to navigate the complex and daunting justice system, said if governments were serious about ending violence they needed to listen to the experts.
"The Australian Law Reform Commission has told governments exactly what to do, give victims their own lawyers … Eighteen months on, not a single jurisdiction has fully legislated or implemented that," she said.
Targets for First Nations women and children going backwards
The report also collated data that showed the overall number of women killed by an intimate partner trended downwards since the late 1980's
However, rates of violence against First Nations women and children have increased.
Between 2019 and 2022, the rate of Indigenous children hospitalised after family violence incidents fell but has since shot up to 45 children per 100,000 — its highest level since data has been collected.
Rates of intimate partner homicide of First Nations women increased in each of the two years since a baseline was established in the commissioner's first report, reaching four victims per 100,000 people in the 2024-2025 data.
However, the commissioner warned it was too early to identify trends against the baseline.
Ms Cronin said the experience of First Nations women and children within existing support systems was "very distressing".
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek tabled the commissioner's third report to parliament on Wednesday and said while progress had been made, she conceded not enough work had been done.
"I have an incredible sense of urgency for more change," she told the ABC.
Ms Plibersek also shared her own experience of assault, while also acknowledging that there are plenty of "wonderful men".
"I'm a cabinet minister, I'm in a pretty powerful position, when I walk to my car at night in a dark car park, I still get my keys out at night in case someone attacks me," she said.
"I've been assaulted walking home in Canberra at night."
The federal government is working on the second action plan for the decade-long National Plan to End Violence against Women and Children.
The specific road map for how the broad aims of the national plan can be realised over the next five years is expected to be released in the first half of 2027.

The central Republican gamble is whether Trump can mobilise voters personally loyal to him even when he is not actually running, without further alienating independents who have soured on his presidency.
Political headwinds
Inside the American Airlines Center, there was little sign of Republican anxiety about November.
The convention even featured a video address from Democratic Senator John Fetterman, who has become increasingly at odds with his party's left wing over issues including his hardline support for Israel.
Republicans highlighted tax cuts and immigration enforcement, touting boosted manufacturing and lower prescription drug prices.
The cavernous arena was festooned with Trump posters as supporters milled around in sequined jackets patterned with his name, image and the American flag, some topped with ten-gallon hats.
Food stalls hawked overpriced snacks while merchandise stands did brisk business in T-shirts, mugs, posters and copies of the latest literary offering from the Trump clan, "Under Siege" by the president's second son, Eric.
Despite the political headwinds facing Republicans, the mood was festive. Chants of "USA! USA!" echoed around the hall as the national anthem opened the programme.
Trump's speech was received warmly in the room, with spontaneous bursts of chanting after each applause line, and the enthusiasm spilled into the American Airlines Center's vast atrium outside.
Dallas local Tracey Wroblski, 59, said Trump was "on fire" with his inspiring midterm messaging.
"It's awesome, it's meaty, it's we're fixing our country," she told AFP. "He's funny, and he's, he's on point. We're not going to communism. We're staying Republican, thank you very much."
The gathering is the first Republican national convention held specifically for a midterm election, although no candidates are being nominated and no formal party business is planned.
Instead, organisers have constructed what amounts to a two-night television rally touting Trump's record and Republican candidates.
More than 100 House members and candidates were expected to attend, with more than 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

War in Yemen
Yemen has been mired in conflict since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa. The attack prompted a Saudi-led military intervention the following year and a devastating conflict that killed an estimated 150,000 people.
A United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 brought a halt to large-scale fighting, but clashes resumed again in July following a strike by government forces on the Houthi-held Sanaa airport. The fighting has continued to spill over into Saudi Arabia.

He promised that the coalition would respond to what he called the Houthis’ “heinous attacks”.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defence authority also issued multiple alerts for Khamis Mushait and Abha on Wednesday and early on Thursday.
No casualties were reported in connection with those alerts.

Yahya Saree did not say whether the attacks had caused casualties, but said the aircraft involved had taken off from King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait and King Fahd Air Base in Taif.
“These air strikes and the ongoing aggression against our country will not go unanswered and unpunished, by the will and power of God,” Saree said.
The Houthis had on Tuesday claimed that Saudi forces had carried out 121 air strikes on Houthi-controlled territory in the preceding days, including a strike on the prison in al-Jawf. The group said they retaliated with attacks on Aramco facilities in Abha, Najran and Jizan, as well as on the Economic City and Khamis Mushait Air Base.
Saudi officials said on Tuesday that recent Houthi attacks had wounded at least 73 people.
Regional tensions
Separately on Wednesday, Yemeni government-aligned forces said that they had continued advancing in al-Jawf for a third consecutive day, reaching the vicinity of Bir al-Maraziq and claiming to have severed Houthi supply lines in the area.
The forces also said they had carried out attacks on Houthi positions in Taiz, and that additional reinforcements had been sent on Wednesday to bolster the anti-Houthi National Resistance forces along Yemen’s western coast.
Those claims could not be independently confirmed.
Amid the escalating hostilities, Pakistani officials reiterated this week that any attack on Saudi Arabia could activate the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed last month to strengthen collective deterrence against future attacks.
“If there is unprovoked aggression, or a spillover of whatever is happening in Yemen into Saudi Arabia, definitely the Mecca agreement will become operational,” Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told local media.
Iran meanwhile sharply criticised a statement issued earlier this week by Arab League foreign ministers, who condemned what they called “Iranian violations of Yemen’s sovereignty”.
In response, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it “completely rejects the claims regarding Iran’s interference in the affairs of Yemen,” adding that it had “consistently emphasised the need to preserve Yemen’s unity and territorial integrity”. It also said it had supported Yemeni-led dialogue based on a UN-backed roadmap.

Getting your mind ready for surgery is as important as physical preparation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:08:59 UTC
14:08:59 KST

Preparing for major surgery should not skip mental preparation for a successful recovery, a new study says.
Failing to address patients’ mental health before serious surgery could hinder their recovery, particularly among older patients, according to a new study published on Wednesday in JAMA Network Open.
“The stress of surgery can worsen anxiety and depression symptoms and affect patients’ recovery and overall health,” the study’s first author Joanna Abraham said in a press release.
The authors argue that pre-surgical care should include not only physical preparation but also mental preparation from trained mental health professionals – something that current perioperative care usually misses.
“We recognize the importance of getting the body into shape before surgery, but preparing the mind and the brain is just as important,” said the study’s senior author Eric J. Lenze.
The way forward is to treat patients “holistically,” said Michael S. Avidan, uniting anesthesiology and psychiatry.
The power of a call
The study included 306 adults aged 60 and older who were scheduled for cardiac, oncologic or orthopaedic surgery. Patients were divided into two groups. One group got only self-help materials to read independently, while the other group talked with a trained mental health professional such as a social worker or mental health counsellor over eight to 12 phone sessions. The second group also received a personalised review by pharmacists and doctors to safely optimise doses of high-risk medications.
Three months after surgery, patients who received consultation from mental health professionals and medication reviews experienced a 2.2-to-2.5-point greater reduction in symptoms of depression and anxiety than those given educational materials alone, based on a 48-point scale.
Older adults undergoing cancer surgery experienced the strongest mental health improvements, scoring nearly five points lower than the control group.
Patients also reported positive experiences with the extra care, both from the wellness providers and the pharmacists who worked to eliminate unnecessary medications.
“What makes this care model so promising is that it’s practical to deliver,” said Abraham. “Patients and healthcare providers found the program manageable and easy to integrate into existing surgical workflows. Proactive mental health care doesn’t have to burden the hospital system.”

North Korea has built new uranium facility to expand nuclear arsenal, UN agency says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:08:46 UTC
14:08:46 KST

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has voiced “serious concern” over evidence that North Korea has built a facility capable of enriching weapons-grade uranium to bolster its nuclear arsenal.
The new building, located at the the country’s main Yongbyon nuclear facility, can house up to 28 centrifuge cascades – machinery commonly used to enrich uranium – according to a report by the nuclear watchdog released this week.
The regime has also expanded operations at an enrichment site in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, according to the report, which was based on analysis of satellite imagery and open-source material, including photographs published by the country’s state media.
The IAEA, whose inspectors were expelled from North Korea in 2009, identified the Yongbyon building as the site’s second uranium enrichment facility after comparing satellite images taken during its construction with media photographs of a visit in early June by the country’s leader, Kim Jong-un.
During his visit, Kim claimed the North’s capacity to produce weapons-grade nuclear material had more than doubled over the past five years, according to state media, promising “vast future plans to exponentially strengthen the country’s nuclear forces”.
Citing a 2025 analysis by the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies in the US, South Korea’s Chosun Daily said the potential 28 cascades comprising 4,592 centrifuges at the Yongbyon facility could yield about 85 kg of weapons-grade highly enriched uranium a year – enough to build three or four additional warheads.
In a statement released this week, the IAEA’s director general, Rafael Grossi, said: “The ongoing operation of enrichment facilities at Kangson and Yongbyon and the reported further expansion of [North Korea’s] production of weapons-grade nuclear material is a cause for serious concern.”
“The continuation and further development” of North Korea’s nuclear programme are “clear violations of relevant UN security council resolutions and are deeply regrettable”, he added.
South Korea’s defence minister, Ahn Gyu-back, said in August that the North possessed between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads – a much higher number than the 57 cited by Donald Trump the same month. The South Korean figure was based on estimates by private research organisations, Ahn told lawmakers, adding that the country’s military could not confirm the numbers.
North Korea has made rapid progress in its ballistic missile and nuclear programmes in recent years, as it demands international recognition as a legitimate nuclear state.
North Korea has conducted multiple long-range missile tests since 2017, the year it last tested a nuclear weapon. In a report submitted to the UN security council in 2020, international experts said the North had “probably developed nuclear devices to fit into the warheads of its ballistic missiles”.

Education Ministry to study how teachers spend their working hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:08:00 UTC
14:08:00 KST

Education Ministry to study how teachers spend their working hours
The Ministry of Education is launching a study to determine teachers' work tasks and the time spent on them, and to develop recommendations on how to fit teachers' workload within the working hours set by law. The planned cost of the study is €70,000.
With the study on teachers' working time and tasks, the Ministry of Education wants to map what teachers' duties are under Estonia's current legal acts, determine how much time these tasks take from the perspective of teachers and school leaders, and develop recommendations for education policymakers, school owners, principals, and teachers.
Liis Lehiste, adviser at the ministry's Department of Education Management and Teacher Policy, responded to question about whether the ministry currently lacks such information, saying that the state's goal is to support teachers and help them remain in the profession by contributing to the development of good and sustainable working conditions.
"This requires a better understanding of the factors that influence teachers' workload and their ability to cope well with their work," she said.
Teachers report overload
Lehiste noted that according to the Basic Schools and Upper Secondary Schools Act, a teacher's working time is divided between direct teaching and educational work, and other tasks arising from the employment contract, job description, work‑organization rules, or assignments given by the employer.
According to a government regulation established in 2013, teachers' working time is 35 hours per week.
"Besides contact lessons, a teacher's work includes many other tasks — planning and preparing lessons, giving feedback on students' work, communicating with parents, collaborating with colleagues, individual work with students, and so on. TALIS (the international study of teaching and learning) results show that teachers often assess their workload as greater than their official working time," Lehiste said.
She added that Estonia's education information system collects data on teachers' contact hours, but a teacher's work includes many other tasks beyond lessons, such as planning and preparing teaching, giving feedback on students' work, communicating with parents, collaborating with colleagues, individual work with students, and so forth.
According to the adviser, study results show that teachers often assess their workload as greater than their official working time. Existing studies and data do not clearly show which school‑level factors — such as leadership practices, work organization, and collaboration culture — influence how teachers' workload develops.
"We need an up‑to‑date and comprehensive overview of how teachers' working time is spent, which practices support the efficient use of teachers' working time, and how teachers' work can be organized so that tasks fit within the legally prescribed 35‑hour workweek," Lehiste explained, justifying the need for the study.
The aim of the study is to obtain concrete recommendations for teachers, principals, school owners, and policymakers on how to better organize teachers' work.
"Based on the study results, we can assess what changes may be needed, for example, in work organization, guidelines, professional development, or legal acts," the ministry adviser added.
Age and tenure factors
The study should also determine how teachers' tasks and workload relate to their age, gender, experience, career stage, qualifications, position, type of contract, and other characteristics, and how the situation is influenced by language of instruction, school level, school type and region, school and class size, availability of support specialists, and similar factors.
The Ministry of Education also wants to find out what teachers and principals themselves have done to optimize and better organize workload and tasks, and what recommendations exist to ensure that teachers' duties fit within the legal working time.
The study will be conducted among teachers and leaders of general‑education and vocational schools. The Ministry of Education estimates the cost at €70,000, funded from the state budget.
The ministry hopes to identify the tender winner in autumn, and the study results should be completed within 14 months.

Yemen's Houthis close in on stranglehold over strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait
ADEN/DUBAI, Sept 10 - Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis edged closer on Thursday to gaining leverage over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important routes for commodity vessels, four Yemeni government military sources said, as fighting with Saudi-backed forces tilts towards a resumption of full-scale war.
The Houthis were nearing complete control of coastal cities such as the historic port of Mocha and Dhubab that sit directly along the strait, as they push to take over the whole Yemeni Red Sea coast, the sources said.
In recent days there has been an escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia's Yemen allies in the internationally backed government and the Houthis, a second theatre of war in the Iran conflict that threatens global energy supplies. A U.N.-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted years of war but remains fragile.
Bab el-Mandeb, or the Gate of Tears, named for its perilous navigation conditions, is the southern outlet of the Red Sea, between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast, making it a major prize for the Houthis, who control Yemen's most populous areas and much of the north.
It is one of the world's most important routes for crude oil and fuel from the Gulf bound for the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal or the SUMED pipeline on Egypt's Red Sea coast, as well as commodities bound for Asia, including Russian oil.
Blocking the narrow passage would isolate Gulf oil-producing countries such as energy superpower Saudi Arabia from their main shipping routes after Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz — the primary maritime energy artery between Asia and Europe.
ATTACKS ON SAUDI CITIES
The Houthis said on Wednesday that Saudi strikes hit the Yemeni provinces of Jawaf, Marib and Saada, bordering the kingdom, as well as the provinces of Taiz in the south and al-Hodeidah along the Red Sea coast, a Houthi stronghold used as a base for their broader campaign of attacks on shipping in the waterway. Saudi Arabia did not confirm the strikes.
Saudi civil defence authorities issued an all-clear on Thursday following an emergency alert declared in the southwestern province of Khamis Mushait for the fourth time in 24 hours, as clashes flared with the Houthis.
The danger had passed, the civil defence officials said shortly after the alert.
At least 73 people were wounded in four southern Saudi cities, including Khamis Mushait, in recent Houthi attacks on the world's largest oil exporter, the Saudi-led coalition said on Tuesday.

‘Summer has shaken us’: Nepal’s flood disaster hits close to home in the shadow of melting Mont Blanc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:02:25 UTC
14:02:25 KST

A Chamonix local official says his town urgently needs to prepare for the dangers of falling chunks of glacier or rock.
For centuries, French and Italian mountain communities have gazed upon the seemingly eternal glaciers and snow that gave Western Europe's highest peak its name: Mont Blanc, the white mountain.
But climate warming is dismantling the picture at alarming speed.
Europe's record heatwaves this summer savaged permafrost that for millennia has acted like glue on the Alpine landscape. Defrosting cliffs came apart, sending rock falls cascading from the heights. A famously dangerous gully that climbers have long braved on ascents to the summit, 4,805 metres up, became temporarily impassable.
“We weep for our mountain, the way it's changing. It hits us in the gut,” says Stéphane Bozon, a deputy mayor in Chamonix-Mont-Blanc, a French town at the foot of the giant that straddles France's border with Italy.
“From mid-July onward, we saw an increase in rock falls. We saw areas becoming difficult to access because of glacial retreat and snowmelt on the glaciers, with crevasses opening up and rock collapses making some areas difficult to reach or traverse,” he says.
Each degree of warming can have an outsized impact. On the Aiguille du Midi peak, which rises to an altitude of 3,842 metres in the Mont Blanc range, average temperatures for July have soared. From a chilly 1.6°C in 1994, the monthly average for this July was the warmest ever recorded, at 3.3°C, says Meteo France, the national weather service.
“The mountain really dried out, with temperatures unlike any I had ever experienced,” Bozon says.
The Himalayan flood disaster hits close to home in the Alps
In the wake of devastating floods in the Himalayas, news agency The Associated Press talked to researchers, climbers and residents coping with the risks and uncertainties of climate change on Mont Blanc.
The floods that swept through Nepal and China on 26 August were triggered after a collapse of bedrock and glacier ice sent debris and water surging through multiple Himalayan rivers. Initial assessments of many scientists are that climate change played a key role in creating conditions for the catastrophe.
As Earth’s global average temperature rises because of the burning of oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase.
In the Alps, glaciers once admired for their icy majesty are being eyed with trepidation as they shrink and lose stability.
Bozon, who is in charge of safety for Chamonix, says his town urgently needs to prepare for “serious scenarios” of chunks of glacier or mountain potentially falling onto inhabited areas.
“We have to move quite quickly because this summer has shaken us and year after year we’re being shaken by the glaciers’ retreat,” he says.
In Italy, researchers are also documenting dramatic damage wrought by heat on glaciers this year. In Lombardy, Alpine glaciers have lost more than 40% of their surface area since 1991, according to the region's glacier service.
“While it used to snow at high altitudes in the past, now it rains,” says Vanda Bonardo, head of the Italian branch of the International Commission for the Protection of the Alps, a nongovernmental organisation.
“So we’ve also seen the effects on the stability of the terrain,” she says.
Rock falls in the Mont Blanc area have surged
Permafrost that has held Alpine peaks in its icy grip for thousands of years acts as a cement, helping to hold their steep rock faces together. It took a beating from the succession of heatwaves.
“That doesn't mean that all the rock faces will collapse in the coming years or decades but quite a number of them are on the verge of becoming unstable and remain stable today only because of the presence of that ice,” says Ludovic Ravanel, a researcher at Savoie Mont Blanc University who specialises in climate change's impact on mountain snows, glaciers and frosts. "As the ice changes, we have seen a huge, huge number of rock falls and rock collapses this year."
A collapse is a major fall involving more than 100 cubic metres of rock – more than enough to fill a large shipping container. Ravanel expects this year's tally of collapses in the Mont Blanc massif “will probably reach around 400”. He says that is about 10 times more than two decades ago.
The last time things got close to this bad was the ’’catastrophic year″ of 2022, he says, with nearly 300 collapses.
“This has really been one of the defining features of the summer of 2026,” he says.
A Mont Blanc climbing guide juggles the risks
Chamonix-based mountain guide Stuart MacDonald says it shocks him to see how rapidly and extensively glaciers that hang from the flanks of the Mont Blanc massif are retreating.
When he guides people up the peaks, he points them to “where the glacier was last year and this is where it was 10 years ago. And that usually has quite an effect”.
Melting and the risk of rock falls made his job “pretty challenging” this summer and forced him to cancel plans to lead a group to Mont Blanc's summit last week.
“You hear it before you see it and then you’ll turn round and you’ll just see an enormous cascade of rocks coming down a slope and it can be quite terrifying,” MacDonald says.
“What’s most scary is that sometimes these rocks are falling on routes that we used to be climbing at this time of year,” he adds. “It can be depressing sometimes when you look at something that you maybe climbed in July or August in the past and you see that it’s absolutely impossible to do it now.”
