Defense Forces use “middle strike” capabilities to hit 17 Russian air defense systems and 30 command posts in August
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense.
Among the targets struck were 17 air defense systems, six bridges, more than 20 warehouses, and more than 30 command posts.
In accordance with the President’s directive, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, and units of the Defense Forces are systematically working to intensify strikes deep into enemy territory.
Every destroyed radar station, air defense system, and electronic warfare system opens the way for strikes deep into the rear of the Russian Federation’s army. Destroyed bridges complicate logistics. Struck warehouses and command posts reduce the combat readiness of enemy units.
To ensure the unimpeded operation of Ukrainian weapons systems, the destruction of Russian air defense systems continued in August.
In particular, the following S-400 air defense systems were struck: “Triumf” (Gelendzhik and Bryansk Oblast, Russian Federation), “Pantsir” (Yeysk, Russian Federation), “Tor” (Rostov Oblast, Russian Federation), “Buk-M3” (Luhansk Oblast), and “Strela-10” (Kreminna, Luhansk Oblast).
A number of radar stations were also destroyed, including the long-range “Nebo-U” radar in the temporarily occupied Sevastopol, the “Nebo-SV” radar, the “Kasta” and “Podlyot” stations, as well as electronic warfare systems, notably the “Peresvet-M” in the temporarily occupied Luhansk.
The Ukrainian Defense Forces continued to systematically strike at the Russian Federation’s logistical arteries.
The “Syvash” railway bridges in the Chongar area, near Vladyslavivka and Svitlodolynske, as well as road bridges across the Seim River in the Kursk Oblast and the Molochna River in the Zaporizhzhia region, were targeted. A crossing over the Mokri Yaly River in the Donetsk region was also struck.
In addition to infrastructure facilities, the Defense Forces struck more than 20 warehouses containing logistical supplies and ammunition, as well as repair bases in the temporarily occupied territories and in the border regions of the Russian Federation.
In August, the systematic identification and destruction of Russian targets associated with the use of unmanned systems and naval vessels continued.
A base for unmanned naval craft in Chernomorsk (Crimea) was destroyed.
More than 30 strikes were also carried out against command centers, storage facilities, and launch sites for attack UAVs, particularly in the Bryansk region of the Russian Federation, the Donetsk region, and in the temporarily occupied Crimea.
A number of ground-based relay stations used to control “Geran/Gerbera”-type strike UAVs were disabled, weakening the enemy’s ability to coordinate drone attacks.
Russian military command posts were struck by “middle strike” weapons, including the main and backup command posts in the temporarily occupied city of Donetsk, an FSB unit in Shchaslyvtseve (Kherson region), and a UAV training center in the temporarily occupied city of Luhansk.
“The systematic use of ‘middle strike’ capabilities allows Ukraine to systematically reduce Russia’s military potential and disrupts the stability of the enemy army’s command and control system,” the Ministry of Defense noted.
As reported by Ukrinform, in July, the Ukrainian Defense Forces continued their systematic campaign to strike Russian operational rear areas and logistics routes using “middle strike” capabilities, focusing on disrupting supply lines in the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia regions, as well as in the temporarily occupied Crimea.

Iran's Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site sees surge in construction activity, analysts say - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:31:56 UTC
12:31:56 KST

The Iranian nuclear site buried under Pickaxe Mountain has seen an increased level of construction work over the last year, analysts reviewing satellite imagery shared with CNN on Wednesday.
Construction at the site, analysts from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank told CNN, "has shifted from active excavation toward probably internal construction and continued exterior reinforcement.”
The site has seen "more road activity," as well as "raising and hardening of the (tunnel) portal accesses, paving of the internal road network, reinforcement around access areas, and the flattening and removal" of excavated dirt.
According to CSIS, the site has likely been designed to be a safe haven for Iran's nuclear program, CNN reported.
CSIS analysts said that the site could serve as a centrifuge assembly facility, an enrichment facility, or other "nuclear-weapons-relevant" work. However, based on the continuous construction, the analysis estimated that the site “is not yet capable of enrichment work, if that is the intended purpose.”
A source familiar with the matter told CNN that the United States had considered Pickaxe Mountain one of the potential targets if the war against Iran escalated in the last several months.
One source said that the Defense Department had recently held a "planning sprint" on the topic of strikes against Iranian underground facilities, including Pickaxe Mountain.
US explores options for striking deeply buried Iranian sites
Pickaxe Mountain could prove difficult to strike with existing US non-nuclear bombs due to the granite surrounding the underground facility, according to the CSIS analysis cited by CNN.
Four days before the US launched Operation Epic Fury, a Defense Threat Reduction Agency program manager signed an emergency $1.2 million contract justification for repairs to an underground test facility at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico, CNN reported.
The document referred to preparations for a live-fire test of classified capabilities and said the work needed to be completed within two to three weeks due to a "time-sensitive national security directive."
Three sources told CNN that the planned test was connected to the Iran war and efforts to develop ways of targeting Iran's deepest underground facilities.
CNN said it could not independently verify whether the test occurred or confirm the purpose of activity observed at the White Sands site.
US developing next-generation penetrator
The US struck Iranian nuclear sites during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025. A top US general later told lawmakers that only the entrances to the deeply buried Isfahan nuclear site were buried because the Pentagon believed its Massive Ordnance Penetrator bombs could not destroy the facility, CNN reported.
The US military is also developing a successor to the Massive Ordnance Penetrator that could potentially target more deeply buried facilities.
A prototype contract was awarded in September 2025, and the Air Force sought defense industry sources for the weapon in June, CNN reported.
CNN also reported that the US maintains operational plans to strike Pickaxe Mountain. The site was included in a target package considered earlier this summer, although it remains unclear whether existing US munitions could penetrate deeply enough to destroy what Iran may have moved underground.

Breadcrumb
Iran strikes ships, expands no-go zone outside Hormuz strait
Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it has blockaded for months.
The fresh attacks and fighting with the United States sent oil prices above $100 per barrel again as Tehran chokes off the strait and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports. Brent oil closed at $101.21.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 "non-compliant vessels" that were trying to pass through the route crucial for oil and gas trade, Iranian state media reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said "several" vessels in the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf were "subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region".
The Gulf of Oman lies on the Indian Ocean side of the narrow Hormuz strait, a vital energy conduit that normally carries around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas.
Iran's Guards also for the first time added parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea to a new "prohibited zone" on Wednesday, saying exact coordinates will be announced later.
"If a vessel enters that area without coordination, it will be subject to our sanctions," Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi told state television.
The Guards also said they struck a US military base in Jordan in response to US forces destroying five Iranian oil tankers a day earlier.
Jordan's army shot down 18 missiles fired at the kingdom, it said.
Iran's foreign ministry condemned the attack on its oil tankers as "an overt threat to regional and international peace and security," saying the strikes "increase the dangers of tensions in the region".
It said the targeting of US military facilities in the region was "self-defence".
The US military for its part had said it was responding to an Iranian attack targeting an American warship, the second such incident in less than a week.
Nuclear referral
Iran's Guards, the ideological arm of the military, said the war could be brought to an end if Washington met its conditions, which included demands on the wars in Lebanon and Yemen.
"It must... refrain from renewed threats, withdraw the Israeli regime's army from Lebanon, end the blockade of Yemen, release $24 billion in Iran's frozen assets and refrain from any interference in the country's nuclear and missile capabilities," Mohebi said, according to Fars news agency.
Donald Trump, an unpopular president eager to end an unpopular war, asserted Wednesday the conflict will conclude right after the mid-term US elections in November. Polls show his Republican Party could face a drubbing and lose control of one or both houses of Congress.
"I think the war will end immediately after the election" because Iran "can't hold out any longer," Trump told journalists, accusing Tehran of being "desperate to try and affect" the vote.
But as Washington tries to choke off Iran economically, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) board of governors on Wednesday voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance", in a diplomatic move that piles pressure on Tehran.
The resolution was adopted by a 23-3 vote with eight abstentions, they said. Russia, China and Niger voted against it.
Iran's representative to the UN nuclear watchdog said the resolution was passed under US pressure, saying it "has no basis and will not bring any results".
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also repeated his claim Iran was on the verge of collapse.
"The main task is to bring down the terror regime in Iran. We are very close to that," he said Wednesday on a troop visit in southern Syria, where Israel has occupied what it calls a "security zone".
The latest round of US-Iran fighting was triggered after American forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Tuesday, with the US military saying it "directed the crews to abandon ship" before hitting the vessels.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers, and I think you'll see that again today," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Tuesday on a visit to Colombia.
Iran has asserted control of the Strait of Hormuz since US-Israeli strikes began the war in February, with traffic through the waterway virtually paralysed.
Tehran requires vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the strait.

The memo, declassified by the Spanish Prime Minister's Office, shows that Morocco's intelligence services, the DGST and DGED, were warned about several active WhatsApp groups that were "preparing an attempt to enter (...) next Thursday, 30 July".
Pedro Sánchez said on Wednesday, in an interview on 'Mañaneros 360', that the CNI had failed to effectively anticipate the migration and humanitarian crisis that eventually unfolded in Ceuta.
However, the Defence Minister maintains that the Centre did warn the Government Delegation in the autonomous city a day before the potential crisis. The memo, together with another declassified WhatsApp conversation, backs Margarita Robles on this latter point.
"Without questioning their professionalism, a mass arrival of so many migrants was certainly not anticipated," the socialist president said in Wednesday's interview, criticised by the TVE News Council for being conducted on a programme made by an external production company rather than by the public broadcaster itself and without any journalists from the corporation.
In doing so, Sánchez once again aligned himself with his Interior Minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, in the dispute with Robles over communications. Grande-Marlaska has consistently maintained that he did not receive any official communication warning of a possible mass border crossing.
Both Grande-Marlaska and Sánchez have also maintained throughout that Morocco did not play an active role in the crisis, despite journalistic evidence (the migrants' own accounts of the behaviour of Moroccan guards) and subsequent private and police reports pointing in that direction.
The new document from the CNI, declassified by Moncloa itself, confirms that at the very least, the intelligence services of the Alaouite kingdom received a warning from the Spanish state on the matter.
A second police document and two internal conversations corroborate the CNI's account
The National Centre for Immigration and Borders (CENIF) also issued a warning on 29 July, in another of the declassified communications sent to its border posts in Ceuta and Melilla, of a "high" likelihood of entry by swimming. "This Centre (...) has obtained information about a potential risk of irregular entries into the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla, forecast for 30 July 2026".
"It cannot be guaranteed that this will happen, but when this type of activity has been detected on social media and other forums, on some occasions it has ended up materialising," the document warns, also referring to a "medium" likelihood of entry both over the land fences and by sea, as well as a "medium-low" likelihood if organisers were to combine the two options.
Likewise, two other declassified WhatsApp conversations show contact between the various branches of the state's security apparatus and the Government Delegation in the autonomous city, a post separate from the Ceuta presidency and which, in practice, answers to the central government of the day.
In the first, an exchange between an unnamed CNI official and the Ceuta Delegation's office, they also warn of the possibility of crossings both over the fence and by sea. The conversation is dated 13:52 on 29 July and has been transcribed without changes except to improve readability.
CNI: On social media, there is a call to storm the fence and the sea tomorrow at 20:00, taking advantage of Throne Day, when their security forces will be busy. There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers, just so you get an idea of how far this is spreading.
Delegation: [11-minute phone call at 21:34]
The second takes place between the CNI and the Guardia Civil, and deals with the same issue:
CNI: [Unanswered call at 13:53]
CNI: [Name classified] I'm calling you about the situation in Ceuta. We have information about an attempt to enter by swimming and jumping the fence tomorrow, on Throne Day. We have several groups on Facebook and WhatsApp encouraging these crossings.
[Missed call at 13:59 from the Guardia Civil's Special Central Unit 3]
UCE-3: [Name classified] I'm sorry, all this has kept me away from base, and it's not easy for me to sort out. These days, [name classified], who has been away for a few months, is around, as well as [name classified]. You can call me too.
Sánchez defends his actions but admits shortcomings in the face of "hybrid attacks" and in resources in Ceuta
During the interview, the president argued that the gradual arrival of hundreds of people swimming in every day during the second half of July ("a slight peak", in his words) did not allow them to foresee the final figure of 80,000 people who went on to set foot in the Afro-European exclave on 30 and 31 July. For now, it is not known what percentage of migrants still remain in Ceuta, but the city, the government and the police all work with an estimate of roughly 5,000 to 10,000 people.
"What would another government have done? Would it have started shooting at those young people, minors, boys and girls? Or wasn't it smarter to allow them to enter so that subsequently, 90% of them, in the following hours or days, could leave?" the president said, providing misleading figures both for the percentage of people remaining in the exclave and for the speed of their evacuation, whether back to Morocco or to the rest of Spain in the case of minors.
Sánchez acknowledged that "the state", without placing the responsibility on his own government, must prepare for possible new episodes of this nature. "One issue is how we prepare for hybrid attacks of this nature," he said. "Of course, we have to invest much more in border control and the perimeter (...) and be aware that we need reception infrastructure."
Despite the indirect backing Grande-Marlaska has received from the head of government, Sánchez has been critical of the list of journalists and radio and television pundits drawn up (and leaked) by the Interior Ministry itself. It singles out several hundred media professionals in Spain by name, surname and presumed ideology. "I think it is a very inappropriate document", the socialist leader said.

August was hottest month ever recorded globally, scientists say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:25:28 UTC
12:25:28 KST

August was hottest month ever recorded globally, scientists say
UN warns of ‘spiralling price’ of fossil fuels after Earth’s record-shattering summer temperatures
The EU’s climate monitor said on Thursday that August was the hottest single month ever recorded globally, with ocean temperatures also reaching unprecedented highs as western Europe capped its warmest summer.
In response to the assessment by the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the UN warned that until humanity weaned off fossil fuels, the planet would only push deeper into uncharted territory.
Copernicus observations go back to 1940 but other evidence – such as ice cores, tree rings and coral skeletons – allow scientists to place today’s climate against a much longer historical context.
“Humans haven’t seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years,” Samantha Burgess from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, said.
Global average air temperatures in August were 16.96 degrees Celsius, Copernicus said – surpassing by 0.01 degree the previous all-time monthly record set in July 2023. Copernicus said it considered the two months joint highest given the narrow difference.
Scientists say that human activity – primarily the burning of coal, oil and gas – has warmed the planet by roughly 1.4 degrees since pre-industrial times and increased the severity and likelihood of extreme weather.

Trump considering giving CIA chief Ratcliffe greater role in Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations, FT reports
U.S. President Donald Trump is reportedly considering giving CIA Director John Ratcliffe a larger diplomatic role in attempting to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, the Financial Times (FT) reported on Sept. 9, citing sources familiar with the plan.
U.S. officials have reportedly told their European counterparts about the proposed diplomatic shift, with Trump considering downsizing current special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner's role in negotiations.
The White House has denied FT's reporting calling it "totally fake news," while officials familiar with the plans indicated that Trump has yet to make a final decision on the matter. According to FT, Witkoff is likely to retain his role as U.S. envoy for peace missions and may work alongside Ratcliffe on the Russia-Ukraine file.
The latest reported plan comes weeks after Ratcliffe made unannounced trip to Moscow on Aug. 25 to meet with his Russian counterpart. The visit marked his first known official trip to the Russian capital.
Trump described Ratcliffe’s Aug. 25 visit as "standard business" and dismissed reports that the CIA director had traveled to Moscow to deliver a warning to Russia around further escalation in the Baltics.
The potential diplomatic shift comes days after Witkoff and Kushner returned home from their visits to Kyiv and Moscow for talks with the countries leaders. The most recent talks do not appear to have yielded a major breakthrough, with President Volodymyr Zelensky telling reporters after the meeting that he expects "the war will continue" into the winter months.
The U.S. and Russia have seen intensified bilateral contacts since Trump took office last January and pledged to negotiate a peace settlement in Ukraine.
Despite repeated visits by Trump's peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, to Moscow, the negotiations have effectively stalled as both Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on territorial issues.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv cede the partially occupied and strategically vital Donbas region in eastern Ukraine. Ukraine has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front lines while stressing the need for Western-backed security guarantees to deter future potential Russian aggression.

OpenAI pushes for mandatory national AI safety rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:17:26 UTC
12:17:26 KST

OpenAI pushes for mandatory national AI safety rules
- OpenAI urges mandatory national AI safety rules in the US, citing incidents of AI agents acting independently and calling for capability-based regulations before Congress adjourns in December.
- OpenAI supports California's new AI laws, including third-party evaluations and safeguards against AI threats, reflecting increased concern after recent rogue AI behaviour disclosures.
- OpenAI stresses the need for international AI safety standards, warning that autonomous AI self-improvement is not safe today and should not be pursued until proven secure.
AI generated
OpenAI said on Sept 9 it was pushing for mandatory national AI safety requirements in the US on concern the technology could accelerate its own development, after some of its own AI agents went rogue.
Several incidents in which AI models from developers, including OpenAI, accessed external systems during testing have highlighted the difficulty of containing unexpected behaviour in advanced agents and prompted calls for tighter safety regulations.
“The prospect of AI-accelerated AI development demands more than voluntary commitments. The United States needs mandatory, capability-based national regulation that can evolve as the technology does,” OpenAI chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane said in a blog post.
The call marks a major push by OpenAI for binding national AI safety rules, with Congress yet to enact a federal framework on AI law even as several US states pass their own legislation.
The AI giant and rival Anthropic are preparing for initial public offerings as artificial intelligence rapidly emerges as the decade’s defining investment theme.
OpenAI is urging Congress to adopt capability-based national AI safety requirements, including testing standards, independent assessments, cybersecurity protections and incident-reporting rules for the most advanced AI systems.
The maker of ChatGPT urged Congress to act before it adjourns and said it would continue to support state AI legislation until such action was taken. Congress is due to adjourn in December.
Fully autonomous recursive self-improvement – where AI is independent and would drive the next generations of AI – “is not happening today” and “we should not pursue it unless and until it can be done safely”, OpenAI said.
Endorsement of California Bills
OpenAI backed four California Bills establishing AI regulations for the state.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 813 and AB 1405, which establish a framework for independent third-party evaluation and audits of AI systems, into law on Sept 9.
The other two, AB 1864 and SB 1119, address screening safeguards against AI-enabled biological threats and chatbot protections for children respectively.
“Some of these Bills we did not endorse in the past, and are now supporting after reconsidering in the light of the recent jump in capabilities we have seen,” the AI giant said in its blog post.
OpenAI’s statement comes after a Reuters report that the company’s AI agents used more than 10 previously undisclosed websites for unsanctioned communications earlier in 2026, showing the agents’ rogue activity was more wide-ranging than previously disclosed.
Rogue OpenAI agents also hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, which company officials had learnt about weeks ago but kept under wraps.
Anthropic on Sept 9 disclosed its fourth instance of an AI model hacking external systems during testing, following its July announcement that some of its Claude models had hacked into the systems of three companies during cybersecurity tests.
OpenAI said any industry standards created to monitor AI would also need to extend beyond US borders.
“The United States needs to establish credible standards at home if it is going to lead internationally – and we are increasingly convinced that compatible international standards will be necessary,” the AI company said. REUTERS

Morocco’s largest Islamist movement announces election boycott
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:17:14 UTC
12:17:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Morocco’s largest Islamist movement announces boycott of elections
Morocco’s largest Islamist movement, Al Adl Wal Ihsan (Justice and Spirituality), has decided to boycott legislative elections scheduled to take place on September 23, calling on citizens not to participate.
The movement announced on Wednesday that its decision to boycott the upcoming legislative elections was prompted by the absence of “conditions for free and fair political competition.” 
It said that elections in Morocco “have failed to move the country toward a horizon of democracy, freedom and justice.”
The movement also said that it had decided on the boycott due to “authoritarianism and corruption,” which it said had led to widespread popular disengagement from politics.
 It also cited a “lack of seriousness” in a political system in which elected institutions do not possess genuine political decision-making power. 
In a statement, the movement also cited “restriction of freedoms” as well as the continued detention and prosecution of opponents and activists. 
These circumstances, it said, do not provide the conditions necessary for “meaningful political participation.”
At the same time, the movement stressed that its boycott does not mean withdrawing from public affairs. It reaffirmed its commitment to what it called the “continued struggle for freedom, dignity and good governance.”
It concluded by emphasizing that “any serious political reform requires establishing freedom and elected institutions with genuine powers.”
Unlike the Justice and Development Party (PJD), another Islamist movement which has previously led the Moroccan government, Al Adl Wal Ihsan has remained committed to opposition, refusing to participate in the country’s elections and political process.
It has never been legalised as a party but has so far been tolerated by Moroccan authorities.
The movement’s statement came two days after an appeal by the Unification and Reform Movement, the religious outreach arm of the PJD, calling for “active, positive and responsible” participation in the elections. 
In contrast to Adl wal Ihsan, it said that the elections represented an important opportunity to consolidate democracy, elect new leaders and restore confidence in institutions.
Commenting on Al-Adl wal Ihsan’s decision to boycott the upcoming elections, political sociologist Abdel Moneim Al-Kazzan told The New Arab that the decision “was expected, given that the movement has never previously announced its participation in any elections.”
He described the movement’s rejection of electoral participation as a “structurally closed position,” based on the use of religion and “traditional charismatic legitimacy,” which forms part of the basis of Morocco’s political system.
However, Al-Kazzan added that the notable element of the announcement was that Adl wal Ihsan had “begun adopting concepts drawn from the philosophy of the Enlightenment and human rights” - such as the separation of powers and fair competition - and is using a modernist framework instead of talking about concepts like “coercive rule” and “hereditary monarchy,” which were central to the approach of its late spiritual leader, Abdessalam Yassine, who died in 2012.
He said however that, “despite the modernist concepts, this announcement remains a strategic confirmation that the movement will not fall into the trap of granting ‘legitimacy’ to what it regards as corruption and a situation in which the conditions for ‘genuine consultation’ do not exist.”
He also argued that the boycott “strengthens the cohesion of what remains of the movement” and its solidarity as a “community and fellowship.”
Moroccans are due to go to the polls on September 23 to choose members of the House of Representatives, the lower chamber of parliament. 
However, the power of parliament and government in Morocco is limited with King Mohammed VI retaining significant executive power despite reforms undertaken after the Arab Spring broke out in 2011.

Netanyahu to sue Haaretz over claims UAE warned him before October 7 attack
Israeli prime minister denies claim that UAE president warned him of Hamas plans before the 2023 attacks.
Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he will sue the Haaretz newspaper over a report that claimed he was warned of Hamas’s plans for an offensive days before the attacks of October 7, 2023.
In a statement on X on Wednesday, Netanyahu called the report “fabricated” and “false” and said he had instructed his lawyers to also sue Haaretz and the authors of the report, Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yaval.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4October 7 attack shapes Israel’s elections and fuels political blame
- list 2 of 4Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu says ‘Qatar is a hostile state’
- list 3 of 4What ‘right’ and ‘left’ mean in Israel today
- list 4 of 4Israeli parties submit slates for October Knesset elections
The report, published on Tuesday, claimed that the president of the United Arab Emirates, Mohammed bin Zayed had warned Netanyahu about a possible attack by Hamas 10 days before the events of October 7, 2023.
Palestinian fighters killed at least 1,195 people in southern Israel on that day, and took some 251 others captive. The attacks prompted Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, in which at least 73,669 Palestinians have been killed.
The Haaretz report claimed that the UAE president, who is also known as MBZ, spoke to Netanyahu by phone and warned him of a threat from then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar.
According to Haaretz, Sinwar – who was angered by stalled prisoner exchange talks and Israel’s continued blockade of Gaza – had relayed the warnings to the UAE through an intermediary. He said he was preparing a “huge surprise” and told contacts to tell Israel “to expect an earthquake”, according to the report.
It said MBZ and his aides read this as a sign of an impending full-scale attack and passed the intelligence to Israel’s Shin Bet agency. But the internal security agency dismissed the threat.
MBZ then raised the warning directly with Netanyahu, who also brushed it aside, the report said.
The UAE has declined to comment on the allegations.
Its Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement on Tuesday saying that “the UAE government does not comment on media stories or speculation regarding conversations between government leaders”.
The Haaretz report comes at a time when Netanyahu is trying to secure his position as prime minister in the upcoming Knesset elections in October. Netanyahu has been trailing in the polls, facing a fierce challenge from former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
Netanyahu on Wednesday called the Haaretz report “politically motivated” and part of the “left’s election campaign”.
He also denied its claims of a phone call with MBZ.
“The National Security Council and the Military Secretary meticulously reviewed the Prime Minister’s call log for those days—and found no trace of it whatsoever,” he said.
In a separate statement, Netanyahu also claimed that the person responsible for Haaretz’s “false report” was the Palestinian political figure, Muhammad Dahlan.
Dahlan was expelled from the Fatah party in 2011 after a power struggle with the current president of the Palestinian Authority, Mahmoud Abbas, and lives in the UAE.
Dahlan’s representatives have rejected the claim, according to Israeli media.

Nearly half of ASEAN scam cases remain unresolved: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:12:20 CST
12:12:20 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Nearly half (45 percent) of reported scam cases across Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam remain unresolved, despite consumers taking more steps to protect themselves, the GSMA ASEAN Consumer Scam Report 2026 showed on Wednesday.
About 8 percent of consumers surveyed have been scammed in the past 12 months. Among victims, 68 percent lost money, with 82 percent recovering none of their losses, while only 10 percent recovered all of their money, according to the report that was launched at the Digital Trust Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
Unresolved cases are eroding consumer trust in communications channels, digital platforms and data sharing, with many changing how they use digital services and respond to inbound communications, said the report.
The report also showed messaging apps have emerged as the most common channel for scam encounters, accounting for 41 percent of reported scam experiences.
Meanwhile, consumers' association of major digital platforms with scams has increased across the region.
The report also found that 96 percent of consumers worry about being scammed or hacked, while nearly nine in 10 recognize at least one form of AI being used in scams.
Scam activity is increasingly shifting towards investment, cryptocurrency, online shopping and job scams, where victims are persuaded to transfer money themselves. Consumers who have experienced scams are more than twice as likely to switch accounts or service providers, according to the report. ■

NANJING, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Foreign travel to China continued to pick up in the first eight months of this year, as the country expanded visa-free access and other measures aimed at making entry easier for international travelers.
Foreign nationals made nearly 61.29 million trips across China's borders from January through August, up 19.5 percent over the year-earlier level, according to data released Thursday. Of the entries into China by foreign nationals during the period, 23.72 million were visa-free, accounting for 77.6 percent of the total, up 26.8 percent year on year.
The figures were released at a sub-forum on immigration management cooperation held as part of the 2026 Conference of Global Public Security Cooperation Forum, held in the city of Lianyungang, east China's Jiangsu Province.
China has steadily eased visa rules to allow longer stays and wider travel for international visitors, part of efforts to facilitate cross-border exchanges and boost inbound tourism. It currently offers unilateral visa-free entry to nationals of 50 countries, while its 240-hour visa-free transit program covers 57 countries. ■

El Niño poses food inflation risk across ASEAN: OCBC economist
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:11:30 CST
12:11:30 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- El Niño is likely to pose a bigger inflation risk than a growth shock for ASEAN economies, with higher prices for rice, wheat, maize and vegetable oils expected to be the main channels of impact, OCBC Group Research said on Wednesday.
Lavanya Venkateswaran, senior ASEAN and India economist, said in a note that she sees the Philippines, Indonesia and Thailand among the ASEAN economies with higher exposure to El Niño, while Malaysia and Vietnam face meaningful but more concentrated risks.
Higher food prices "can add to regional inflationary pressures, with imported inflation risks also rising considering most of this region are net food importers," she noted.
She said apart from Thailand and Vietnam, major economies in the region are generally net rice importers, leaving the Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia exposed to potential terms-of-trade shocks from higher rice prices.
She added that most economies in the region are large net grain importers, including ASEAN-6, and are particularly vulnerable to imported inflation pressures when global wheat and maize prices rise.
She said the extent of food inflation transmission would vary depending on the weight of food in consumer price baskets, import dependence and government intervention through measures such as subsidies and price controls.
The growth impact is expected to be more uneven and largely concentrated in agriculture. Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam, which have relatively large agricultural sectors, are more vulnerable to production losses and weaker rural incomes.
However, she opined that agricultural exporters such as Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam could receive some offset from higher commodity export revenues.
"The ultimate macroeconomic impact will depend not only on weather outcomes but also on policy responses, including food trade restrictions, stock releases and subsidy measures," she added. ■

Across China: New fossil discovery in SW China offers insights into ancient human evolution
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
11:11:24 CST
12:11:24 KST

KUNMING, Sept. 10 (Xinhua) -- Scientists have discovered the first-ever fossil of a Denisovan forearm bone in southwest China's Yunnan Province. This discovery provides new insights into how these mysterious ancient human relatives lived and adapted to their environments.
The new study, led by researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with multiple institutions, was published in the journal Nature.
The bone, a radius from the lower arm, was found alongside other Denisovan remains at a Paleolithic site called Bianfu Cave in Yunnan. These fossils date back to a period between 134,000 and 167,000 years ago.
Denisovans are an extinct group of early humans who were first identified through DNA extracted from a tiny finger bone found in a Siberian cave in 2010. Since then, scientists have realized that Denisovans were once widespread across Asia, but physical remains have been extremely rare. Most discoveries have been limited to teeth and a few skull fragments.
The research team used a two-step method to find the rare fossils among more than 60,000 bone fragments collected from the cave. Instead of testing every piece, which would have been too costly and time-consuming, they first sorted the fragments by shape and then used a protein-analysis technique to confirm which ones came from ancient humans.
This approach proved highly effective. The researchers identified three Denisovan specimens from two different layers, extending human fossils beyond a single younger layer and including two skull fragments and a forearm bone.
The forearm bone is the most exciting element of the discovery. While it shares some features with arm bones from Neanderthals -- close relatives of modern humans, such as a large upper joint, its overall shape and the geometry of its neck region are more similar to those of modern humans.
"This combination of traits suggests that Denisovans probably had unique movement patterns and behaviors that set them apart from both Neanderthals and our own species," said Fu Qiaomei, a professor from the IVPP.
The discovery also confirms that Bianfu Cave was home to a thriving Denisovan population during a particularly cold period in Earth's history. The relatively warm climate of the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau at that time, along with plentiful food, likely made the area a safe haven where these ancient people could survive for thousands of years, Fu said.
Before this study, the only rich source of Denisovan fossils with clear stratigraphic context and stone tools recovered outside Siberia was a cave on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau. The finds at Bianfu Cave now fill a major geographical gap. The researchers believe that the region may have been a long-term habitat for these ancient human groups, helping them endure harsh climatic changes.
The discovery of the forearm bone is especially exciting because it gives scientists a rare glimpse into the physical traits that allowed Denisovans to thrive in diverse environments across Asia. Each new fossil adds a new piece to the puzzle of human evolution, said the study. ■

Zelenskyy’s big bet: Ukraine can outlast Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:05:35 UTC
12:05:35 KST

A helicopter flies past smoke billowing from a Russian e-commerce warehouse near Saint Petersburg a Ukrainian drone strike on July 24, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
Volodymyr Zelenskyy is gambling that taking the fight deeper into Russia will put enough pressure on Vladimir Putin to force him to get serious about peace talks.
For much of the war, the Russian president has been able to shield ordinary Russians from the worst of the conflict. The Ukrainian leader is now trying to break that insulation — disrupting air travel and striking refineries, factories, warehouses and other targets deep inside Russia.
The logic is brutal but simple: Raise the economic and political cost of the war for Russians faster than Putin can raise the military and civilian costs for Ukrainians with his escalating air assaults.
Advertisement
With that aim in mind, Ukraine mounted in August one of its heaviest waves of strikes on Russia since the war started more than four years ago.
The campaign expanded quickly to target not just conventional military facilities but also oil refineries, factories, and the vast warehouses of Russia’s online retail behemoths, Wildberries and Ozon. And ordinary Russians have expressed frustration at the domestic fuel shortages, the disruption of air travel and the upending of Russian e-commerce. Ukraine has scaled up domestic production of its attack drones as it tries to make the war unsustainable for Moscow.
But there is little evidence yet that the disruption poses any serious threat to Putin’s hold on power. Coups have been forecast before. European spymasters, Ukrainian officials and Russian exiles have issued numerous predictions that Putin’s days are numbered, that Russians will turn on him or he’ll be ousted in a Kremlin uprising by oligarchs and Russia’s elite.
Nonetheless, Putin has endured.
What Ukraine’s air campaign does appear to have done is make the war harder for ordinary Russians to ignore. That’s significant given how the Kremlin has succeeded largely in silencing public dissent and has Russian-based media on a tight leash.
“I don’t think the authorities’ approval rating can fail to decline when people go outside and see a huge column of smoke rising over the city, or when they arrive to a gas station and there’s no fuel, while on television they’re being told that Russia is a great oil power,” said Ian Matveev, a Russian political analyst and an associate of the late Russian dissident Alexei Navalny.
Advertisement
Matveev added that Zelenskyy’s air campaign has exposed how the Russian military can’t fully protect the country.
That was underscored in May when the Kremlin reluctantly pared back the Victory Day jamboree celebrating the Red Army’s defeat of Nazi Germany.
Shortly after, in June, Ukraine repeatedly struck Russian oil refineries and fuel infrastructure, including around Moscow. In July, Ukrainian drones reached the Omsk refinery in Siberia, Russia’s largest, about 2,700 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory, reportedly using an upgraded drone.
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin arrives to attend the pared-back Victory Day military parade at Red Square in Moscow on May 9, 2026. | Alexander Kazakov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
By then, Ukrainian strikes had hit many of Russia’s major refineries, oil terminals and fuel-storage facilities. At the same time, Ukraine launched an operation against Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Black and Azov seas, targeting more than 200 vessels, according to Ukrainian officials.
The Russian media has reported on the impact of the strikes at Wildberries and Ozon warehouses on small businesses, with sellers of clothing and electronics lamenting that they’ve lost years of work, even their livelihoods. Pro-war military bloggers have not held back on their criticism, faulting the Russian armed forces for ineffectiveness.
But are these complaints enough to alarm Putin and prompt him to stop the war?
Advertisement
The strikes are clearly embarrassing the Russian autocrat, said John Lough, a former NATO official who is now at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a think tank founded by exiled Russian businessman and prominent opposition figure Mikhail Khodorkovsky.
“These attacks are damaging for Putin — more in terms of his credibility with the elites than with the population at large,” Lough said. “They can see increasingly that the war is not winnable on the terms advertised and that he has damaged rather than improved Russia’s security.”
Lough said he doesn’t see a revolution or coup around the corner. “But if the fuel problems continue and more warehouses burn down, there will be more questions from the population about how long this is all going to last and why it started in the first place,” he added.
To ramp up the pressure, Zelenskyy and his tacticians are now eager to make Russia’s commercial airspace increasingly difficult to use.
“Russian airspace will effectively be closing,” the Ukrainian leader said last week. He warned foreign airlines to stay clear as the skies over Russia would become increasingly unsafe because of Ukraine’s drone operations. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he added.
Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a former British diplomat, described Ukraine’s air campaign as “ very, very successful.” But Ukraine’s position as it enters into another wartime winter is more desperate than Russia’s, he feared.
Advertisement
“I think Kyiv is terrified about going into another winter, and this time without any means to defend itself against ramped up Russia’s ballistic missile attacks,” he said.
Putin is unlikely to have missed that vulnerability. Nor have Ukraine’s allies.
During a meeting with Zelenskyy and top security officials from Britain, Germany and France last week, much of the focus was not on the peace deal recently proposed by a U.S. delegation fresh from a visit to Moscow.
It was, according to a senior Ukrainian official who spoke to the AP, on “how to get through the winter.”

Trump takes centre stage as Republicans fight US midterm tide

- The Republican convention in Dallas focused on Trump's leadership, tax cuts, immigration enforcement, and warning against a "dangerously far-left" Democratic Party.
- Despite low approval ratings and tough election forecasts, the convention's festive atmosphere showed strong loyalty to Trump, aiming to energise voters amid inflation and geopolitical tensions.
AI generated
DALLAS, Texas – A defiant Donald Trump vowed Republicans would “surge forward” in November’s midterms on Sept 9, seeking to rally his party against grim election forecasts, weak approval ratings and mounting voter discontent over prices and his war with Iran.
The US President took the stage at an extraordinary Republican midterm convention in Dallas built around persuading his supporters that he is effectively on the ballot on Nov 3.
“In 55 days, Americans will be going to the polls in one of the most important elections in our country’s history,” Trump told the crowd.
“Your vote will decide whether our country stumbles at the starting gate of the next 250 years or surges forward and never ever looks back.”
Elections website Decision Desk HQ projects Democrats to win the House 230-205 and the Senate to finish 51-49 in their favour in November.
Trump, whose approval rating has fallen into the low 30s in recent polling, used his keynote speech to argue that Republican fortunes remain tied to his presidency.
The President is due to return for the convention finale on Sept 10, after a keynote address from Vice-President J.D. Vance. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the programme.
The central Republican gamble is that Trump can mobilise voters personally loyal to him without further alienating independents who have soured on his presidency amid inflation woes, petrol prices topping US$4 a gallon and the continuing war with Iran.
“I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot – I’m on the ballot, I’m on the ballot – just one more time,” he said.
“Because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security.”
Inside the American Airlines Center, there was little sign of Republican anxiety about November.
The convention even featured a video address from Democratic Senator John Fetterman, who has become increasingly at odds with his party’s left wing over issues including Israel.
His appearance intensified speculation about his political future, although Fetterman has said he has no intention of switching parties.
Republicans highlighted tax cuts and immigration enforcement, touting boosted manufacturing and lower prescription drug prices.
One of the main talking points was the danger of empowering what speakers characterised as a dangerously far-left Democratic Party.
“There is a crazy little sick cloud over our country,” Trump said. “We will defeat communism in America and vote for American freedom.”
Political headwinds
The cavernous arena was festooned with Trump posters as supporters milled around in sequinned jackets patterned with his name, image and the American flag, some topped with 10-gallon hats.
Food stalls hawked overpriced snacks while merchandise stands did brisk business in T-shirts, mugs, posters and copies of the latest literary offering from the Trump clan, Under Siege by the President’s second son, Eric.
Despite the political headwinds facing Republicans, the mood was festive. Chants of “USA! USA!” – familiar from Trump’s campaign rallies – echoed around the hall as the national anthem opened the programme.
Susan Kokinda, 77, a conservative podcaster who travelled to the gathering from Michigan, which is almost 2,000km away from Dallas, told AFP she expected Republicans to “do just fine” in November.
“The conventional wisdom is the party in power loses. But I always say Donald Trump is not a conventional president, and he’s reshaping the Republican Party,” she said.
The gathering is the first Republican national convention held specifically for a midterm election, although no candidates are being nominated and no formal party business is planned.
Instead, organisers have constructed what amounts to a two-night television rally touting Trump’s record and Republican candidates.
More than 100 House members and candidates were expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night.
Trump’s national television showcase faces an unusually formidable rival, however: Both convention nights coincide with the opening games of the National Football League season. AFP

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Wistron Corp. reported its first monthly revenue above NT$400 billion (US$14.6 billion) in August, driven by strong AI server shipments.
Consolidated revenue rose 166.46% year-on-year to a record NT$460.1 billion. Revenue for the first eight months reached NT$2.51 trillion, up 98.87% from the same period a year earlier, according to CTEE.
AI servers support applications ranging from model training and image recognition to smart manufacturing, edge computing, and natural language processing. As specifications continue to evolve and material costs rise, Wistron said AI servers remained the main driver of its overall performance, according to Global Instrument Tech.
Based on current orders and visibility into future business, the company expects revenue to grow quarter by quarter in the second half of the year.
The outlook for its PC-related business is less favorable. August shipments of laptops, desktop computers, and monitors were all the lowest of the year.
Wistron expects sales in the sector to slow noticeably in the second half, following stronger shipments in the first half. However, higher prices for key components such as memory are raising average selling prices, which could help keep full-year revenue from falling.
Wistron began as a laptop contract manufacturer and gradually expanded into desktop computers, monitors, servers, and network storage equipment. In recent years, AI server shipments have become a major source of growth, while PC-related products have remained a relatively stable part of the business, according to Pocket Securities.
The board on Wednesday approved an additional capital expenditure plan totaling NT$7.1 billion to support future production capacity and after-sales service needs. The company also plans to spend up to NT$1.9 billion on building improvements and machinery and equipment at its Vietnam plant to support the expansion of its server business.
The Market Intelligence & Consulting Institute said Tuesday that servers and data centers would be the main growth drivers for technology hardware next year. It forecast global server shipments to rise 12.4% year-on-year to 18.6 million units. Among them, AI server shipments are expected to grow 17.8% annually to 5.4 million units, according to LTN.

Trump vows to be at centre of US midterms: Republican convention takeaways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:01:55 UTC
12:01:55 KST

Trump vows to be at centre of US midterms: Republican convention takeaways
Trump delivered key note speech at night one of unusual midterm convention, pledging to rally across the country.
Dallas, Texas – United States President Donald Trump has delivered a keynote speech on the first night of the Republican midterm convention, putting himself at the centre of the November vote despite not being on the ballot.
The first-of-its-kind event on Wednesday came as Republicans face a challenging midterm election to hold control of the House of Representatives and Senate. Losing either chamber would represent a major check on Trump’s power.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Pro-Israel Democrat John Fetterman makes video appearance at GOP convention
- list 2 of 3US states sue Trump over weakening of endangered species protections
- list 3 of 3Trump gave aide Natalie Harp a $45,000 holiday cash gift, disclosure shows
“When I’m on the ticket, Republicans always do very well,” Trump said to a friendly crowd at the American Airlines Center. “But for some reason, when a president wins… even if he’s a really good or great president, they don’t win the midterms.”
“We’re gonna change that,” he said. “So I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot.”
Vice President JD Vance was initially set to headline the first night of the convention, an event typically only held during presidential election cycles. No reason was given for the last-minute change. The convention was set to continue into a second night on Thursday.
Here were key takeaways:
Trump promises campaign blitz
Trump’s decision to put himself at the centre of the midterm elections by calling for a midterm convention has been seen as a political gambit, particularly as his approval rating has dipped amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
But Trump on Wednesday promised that he would be a major feature in the final stretch of the race, whether Republican candidates like it or not.
He pointed to about 35 of the most competitive races.
“We can win every one of those races,” he said. “But I’m going to every one of those states for congressman and for senators.”
“We are going to have rallies just like this.”
It might not be welcome news for all candidates in tight races, including several who chose to campaign in their own districts rather than attend the Dallas convention.
Some political insiders have warned that too-close an embrace from Trump could backfire, instead mobilising Democrats who have already turned out in droves throughout the primary season.
Trump also went further, pledging a $5,000 “dividend” to all adult citizens if Republicans maintain control of both chambers. It was unclear if the president could legally make good on the claim.
Trump hails war on Iran despite political fallout
The war on Iran, which Trump launched alongside Israel on February 28, has become a major political liability heading into the midterms.
On Wednesday, Brent Crude oil topped more than $100 a barrel for the first time in July as the war ground into its seventh month. Polls have suggested widespread disapproval of the war and its knock-on economic effects.
None of the speakers preceding Trump brought up the conflict, which was only featured in a brief video montage in the official programming.
Trump, however, leaned into his handling of the war, saying the US was “winning” and in control of the Strait of Hormuz, despite Tehran continuing to restrict transit in the arterial waterway.
He restated his desire to rename the strait, through which a fifth of the world’s maritime oil trade travelled before the war, “the Trump strait”.
Trump also floated further escalation, including a potential strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuclear site.
Embattled Republicans make pitch
The midterm convention serves as an opportunity to introduce Republican candidates to major donors, according to J Matthew Wilson, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University.
“Texas is the epicentre for a lot of GOP campaign cash,” he said. “It’s really a fundraising hub for Republicans”.
On Wednesday, an array of Republicans in tight races took the stage, including Ken Paxton, the current Texas Attorney General who has trailed in the polls behind Democratic challenger James Talarico.
A Talarico victory would be the first time a Democrat won statewide office in Texas since 1994.
“He is the most radical Democrat in Texas history, but he’s also the most well-funded, and that’s why today, I need your prayers, your votes, and your support,” Paxton said, referring to Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian.
“If we lose Texas, we lose the common sense revolution. If we lose the common sense revolution, we lose America,” he said.
Trump took particular time to focus on Paxton.
“He may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen,” Trump said, as he hailed Paxton as the “greatest attorney general in America”.
Other candidates featured on Wednesday included Monica de La Cruz, a Republican facing a tight Democratic challenge from musician Bobby Pulido to represent her border district in Texas, Senator Jon Husted, who is running against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, and Republican Mike Collins, who is hoping to unseat Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia.
Pro-Israel Democrat John Fetterman also made a surprise video appearance to introduce Republican Senator Dave McCormick. Neither Fetterman nor McCormick is up for re-election in November.
‘Mainstream versus the extreme’
Wednesday’s programme underscored the Republican messaging likely to define the final stretch of the midterm race.
Speakers repeatedly praised Trump’s approach to immigration, which has seen the southern border effectively closed in parallel with a mass deportation drive.
Several speakers also focused on tax cuts and other provisions of Trump’s signature tax bill passed last year, the One Big Beautiful Bill.
But the rhetoric largely coalesced around the leftward shift seen during the Democratic primary season, exemplified in victories of candidates like progressive Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and several Democratic Socialist of America (DSA)-aligned candidates.
Speakers throughout the night framed the election as a referendum on “radicals”, “socialists” and “communists”. No candidates currently running in either party self-identify as communists.
Republican Representative Brandon Gill called the vote “mainstream versus the extreme”.
He specifically referenced DSA-aligned candidates Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York. He said Talarico would “hollow out your most deeply held Christian faith and wear it like a skin suit”.
He also condemned El-Sayed’s support from streaming personality Hasan Piker, who was repeatedly referenced throughout the night for his past comments related to the September 11, 2001, attacks. Piker has maintained that the comments were taken out of context.
“There’s another political movement in our country right now that doesn’t believe that America is or ever was great,” he said. “They sometimes call themselves socialists. Some even call themselves communists. But most of them simply go by Democrats.”
An uphill battle, especially in Texas
The night’s programming resembled a Trump rally more than a party convention, with several of Trump’s most prominent appointees, including Attorney General Todd Blanche and Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent, taking the stage.
Many of those in attendance said they remained true believers in Trump’s message.
“I feel like he has stood and made us more of a power in the world, when before, I think we were almost laughed at,” said Maria Garcia, a 57-year-old supporter who travelled from Boise, Idaho, to Texas for the convention.
“I hope it motivates people to come out and vote, instead of sitting home and doing nothing,” she said.
But despite effusive praise on display for the president on Wednesday, a troubling reality remained for Republicans, according to analysts.
On Monday, the non-partisan Decision Desk HQ political forecast shifted its prediction for control of the Senate to a “pure toss-up”. Democrats remain widely favoured to take control of the House.
In Texas, that reality is particularly stark, according to Evan Roth Smith, a founding partner at Slingshot Strategies, which polls extensively in Texas.
Polls have consistently shown Talarico outperforming Paxton, despite Trump’s May endorsement of Paxton. That means that any Trump bump for the candidate will likely be limited, he predicted.
“We see Paxton trailing and trailing now outside the margin of error,” he told Al Jazeera.
“We now, in our polling – and in other polls that have come out – see Talarico creeping closer and closer to a 50 percent mark, which would mean he has an advantage that is much more durable.”

AIIB eyes new platform to pool private capital for Asia’s US$1.7tr infrastructure needs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:00:07 UTC
12:00:07 KST

AIIB eyes new platform to pool private capital for Asia’s US$1.7tr infrastructure needs
The bank is building a pooled-capital platform to draw insurers, pension funds and other investors into Asia’s infrastructure debt
Kim-See Lim, AIIB’s chief investment officer, described the initiative as being at a very early stage, with further details expected within six to nine months. She spoke to the South China Morning Post following a joint private capital mobilisation conference co-hosted by the AIIB and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority on Tuesday.
The Beijing-headquartered multilateral bank has mobilised around US$17.5 billion in private capital, both directly and indirectly, from its inception through the end of 2025 – a base Lim wants to grow far faster through the new platform.
“It needs to be done faster and ... on a greater scale,” she said. “What we will do is reach out to a group of like-minded investors to try to come up with a set of common terms on how we can invest in infrastructure as an asset class together.”
The push comes as Asia’s infrastructure shortfall remains stark. The Asian Development Bank in a 2017 report estimated that the region required US$1.7 trillion in annual infrastructure investment through 2030, with Lim pointing to a persistent shortfall of up to US$700 billion a year.

Mobility: Europe must move from targets to the conditions for delivering them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

In 2025, 28 percent of new heavy-duty vehicles sold in China were electric. In the European Union, the figure was 1.9 percent, according to data from the International Council on Clean Transport (ICCT). That is a ratio of almost one to 15, despite the technology now being available on both sides.
Gaël Quéinnec
This gap is no longer technological. It reveals a deeper problem: we have set trajectories without creating the economic and political conditions needed to achieve them. China has the planning and implementation capacity to bypass the patient process of building coalitions among stakeholders. Europe, by contrast, is liberal and democratic: it can neither impose the transition by decree nor should it try to. It must make the transition possible by aligning interests, rules and risks. Who should bear the risk of scaling up: the manufacturer, carrier, energy provider or financier? Who invests first? Who guarantees demand?
The direction is clear: sustainable, sovereign, desirable and viable mobility. But the coming months will involve a series of critical decisions, and Europe must turn its ambitions into conditions for action: it must move from a policy based on targets to one based on creating the conditions to achieve them. When the path is not credible, the destination itself eventually comes into question. Our choices matter. So do our failures to choose. Three examples illustrate this.
First example: heavy-duty vehicles. Seventy-eight percent of European land freight travels by road: almost everything on our shelves has traveled by truck. The technology needed to electrify these flows is available, as is the regulatory framework; the challenge is economic. Higher purchase prices, uncertain residual values, charging infrastructure that still needs to be deployed, slow electricity-grid connections and hesitation over a technology that is advancing rapidly: no single stakeholder can bear these risks alone.
The answer lies in distributing those risks more effectively, and even transforming risks for some into opportunities for others. Battery leasing, residual-value guarantees, shared charging infrastructure and securing volumes through contracts: the ecosystem already has some of the solutions it needs.
Public action becomes decisive where the market cannot act alone or cannot act quickly enough, particularly on electricity-grid connections and interoperability. It must also provide confidence in the direction of travel: not by imposing constraints across the board, but by making the trajectory credible, facilitating the initial stages of voluntary transformation and supporting those willing to take the first risks.
These are the actors who should be supported, before others are allowed to enter a market that has become clear and attractive. Europe must not reconsider its destination every time implementation becomes difficult, because nothing discourages investment more than regulatory instability. Instead, it must create the conditions needed to reach that destination.
Otherwise, uncertainty about scaling up the transition will fuel opposition to the direction itself. The choice is simple: distribute risk to create the market or remain trapped in diesel for too long.
Second example: the affordable small car. Europe has produced icons such as the 2CV, the Fiat 500 and the Beetle. Then our cars grew larger: some models now weigh twice as much as their predecessors with the same name, and their prices have followed the same upward trajectory.
Today, European electric cars remain out of reach for a large proportion of households. We began with premium models and subsidized SUVs, hoping that costs would eventually fall. Meanwhile, a wave of affordable Asian electric small cars, produced at scale, is preparing to occupy the space that we are choosing, by default, to leave open.
The European Commission has addressed the issue directly by proposing a dedicated category for compact electric vehicles, with incentives for those produced in Europe. This is a step forward. We believe more needs to be done, because industrial sovereignty, purchasing power and the environment all come together here.
That is the ambition behind the Pop Car project, which we are developing with a coalition of industry leaders and experts; a car with the right dimensions in terms of weight, battery and total cost of ownership. It is efficient and affordable, without compromising on safety or desirability.
Here too, the objective should not be to force everyone to switch at the same pace. It should be to secure a European product that can initiate the market and allow adoption to expand once price, usability and confidence come together.
The question is this: what electric car will a European household be able to afford tomorrow and where will it be produced? The choice is whether to make the entry-level segment strategic again or allow it to develop elsewhere.
Third example: artificial intelligence (AI). AI is orchestrating a growing share of our mobility systems. It directs the routes of millions of vehicles, manages entire flows of traffic and allocates scarce resources: time, public space, freight capacity and energy.
Since Aug. 2, 2026, the AI Act has imposed its first transparency obligations on certain systems. This is necessary, but it does not tell us what AI should optimize.
AI executes instructions. It does not decide on its own what matters. Should it prioritize speed, efficiency or environmental performance? The operator’s costs or accessibility for everyone? These priorities do not establish themselves automatically: they are collective choices, written into software, and they shape our mobility systems just as much as physical infrastructure does.
Our conviction is that every AI system deployed in mobility should demonstrate its net benefits (in terms of carbon emissions, user costs and accessibility) rather than focusing solely on time saved.
Here too, regulators have a decisive role to play: setting the collective compass without suffocating innovation, giving pioneers confidence and then facilitating the spread of useful solutions. The choice is whether to write the instructions collectively or submit to opaque rules written by others on our behalf.
Three examples, one common thread. A transition succeeds when those responsible for making it a reality have both the incentive and the capacity to do so.
Families, carriers, operators and manufacturers all weigh similar considerations when faced with prices, financing and investment. But they also share the feeling that our economic model is exhausting the planet.
Europe’s challenge is to reinvent that model by voluntarily aligning interests rather than through excessive state direction. In a democracy, public authorities set the destination; they cannot make the journey possible on their own. Everyone must also be given the means, motivation and confidence needed to embark on it freely.
Putting constraints on the table, turning disagreements into a source of progress and building common trajectories: this is what we do at Movin’On, and what we will bring to Paris on Oct. 8 and 9 at our summit.
Europe has spent a long time debating the destination. It must now organize the journey. This requires public authorities to remain firm on the overall direction, useful in launching the transition, attentive to pioneers and then confident in the ability of other stakeholders to follow once the conditions are in place.
The advertisement relates to EU mobility and transport policy and advocates for stronger conditions, investment and coordinated action to support Europe’s transition to sustainable, competitive and technologically advanced mobility.

Zelenskyy’s big bet: Ukraine can outlast Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
02:59:16 UTC
11:59:16 KST

A helicopter flies past smoke billowing from a Russian e-commerce warehouse near Saint Petersburg a Ukrainian drone strike on July 24, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
Volodymyr Zelenskyy is gambling that taking the fight deeper into Russia will put enough pressure on Vladimir Putin to force him to get serious about peace talks.
For much of the war, the Russian president has been able to shield ordinary Russians from the worst of the conflict. The Ukrainian leader is now trying to break that insulation — disrupting air travel and striking refineries, factories, warehouses and other targets deep inside Russia.
The logic is brutal but simple: Raise the economic and political cost of the war for Russians faster than Putin can raise the military and civilian costs for Ukrainians with his escalating air assaults.
Advertisement
With that aim in mind, Ukraine mounted in August one of its heaviest waves of strikes on Russia since the war started more than four years ago.
The campaign expanded quickly to target not just conventional military facilities but also oil refineries, factories, and the vast warehouses of Russia’s online retail behemoths, Wildberries and Ozon. And ordinary Russians have expressed frustration at the domestic fuel shortages, the disruption of air travel and the upending of Russian e-commerce. Ukraine has scaled up domestic production of its attack drones as it tries to make the war unsustainable for Moscow.
But there is little evidence yet that the disruption poses any serious threat to Putin’s hold on power. Coups have been forecast before. European spymasters, Ukrainian officials and Russian exiles have issued numerous predictions that Putin’s days are numbered, that Russians will turn on him or he’ll be ousted in a Kremlin uprising by oligarchs and Russia’s elite.
Nonetheless, Putin has endured.
What Ukraine’s air campaign does appear to have done is make the war harder for ordinary Russians to ignore. That’s significant given how the Kremlin has succeeded largely in silencing public dissent and has Russian-based media on a tight leash.
“I don’t think the authorities’ approval rating can fail to decline when people go outside and see a huge column of smoke rising over the city, or when they arrive to a gas station and there’s no fuel, while on television they’re being told that Russia is a great oil power,” said Ian Matveev, a Russian political analyst and an associate of the late Russian dissident Alexei Navalny.
Advertisement
Matveev added that Zelenskyy’s air campaign has exposed how the Russian military can’t fully protect the country.
That was underscored in May when the Kremlin reluctantly pared back the Victory Day jamboree celebrating the Red Army’s defeat of Nazi Germany.
Shortly after, in June, Ukraine repeatedly struck Russian oil refineries and fuel infrastructure, including around Moscow. In July, Ukrainian drones reached the Omsk refinery in Siberia, Russia’s largest, about 2,700 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory, reportedly using an upgraded drone.
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin arrives to attend the pared-back Victory Day military parade at Red Square in Moscow on May 9, 2026. | Alexander Kazakov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
By then, Ukrainian strikes had hit many of Russia’s major refineries, oil terminals and fuel-storage facilities. At the same time, Ukraine launched an operation against Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Black and Azov seas, targeting more than 200 vessels, according to Ukrainian officials.
The Russian media has reported on the impact of the strikes at Wildberries and Ozon warehouses on small businesses, with sellers of clothing and electronics lamenting that they’ve lost years of work, even their livelihoods. Pro-war military bloggers have not held back on their criticism, faulting the Russian armed forces for ineffectiveness.
But are these complaints enough to alarm Putin and prompt him to stop the war?
Advertisement
The strikes are clearly embarrassing the Russian autocrat, said John Lough, a former NATO official who is now at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a think tank founded by exiled Russian businessman and prominent opposition figure Mikhail Khodorkovsky.
“These attacks are damaging for Putin — more in terms of his credibility with the elites than with the population at large,” Lough said. “They can see increasingly that the war is not winnable on the terms advertised and that he has damaged rather than improved Russia’s security.”
Lough said he doesn’t see a revolution or coup around the corner. “But if the fuel problems continue and more warehouses burn down, there will be more questions from the population about how long this is all going to last and why it started in the first place,” he added.
To ramp up the pressure, Zelenskyy and his tacticians are now eager to make Russia’s commercial airspace increasingly difficult to use.
“Russian airspace will effectively be closing,” the Ukrainian leader said last week. He warned foreign airlines to stay clear as the skies over Russia would become increasingly unsafe because of Ukraine’s drone operations. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he added.
Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a former British diplomat, described Ukraine’s air campaign as “ very, very successful.” But Ukraine’s position as it enters into another wartime winter is more desperate than Russia’s, he feared.
Advertisement
“I think Kyiv is terrified about going into another winter, and this time without any means to defend itself against ramped up Russia’s ballistic missile attacks,” he said.
Putin is unlikely to have missed that vulnerability. Nor have Ukraine’s allies.
During a meeting with Zelenskyy and top security officials from Britain, Germany and France last week, much of the focus was not on the peace deal recently proposed by a U.S. delegation fresh from a visit to Moscow.
It was, according to a senior Ukrainian official who spoke to the AP, on “how to get through the winter.”
