In that 1989 film, Buck confronts Puter the Clown, a hungover, sleazy character who shows up to entertain eight-year-old Macaulay Culkin’s birthday party (remember the size of his birthday breakfast pancakes?!).
The clown stumbles around, stinking of alcohol, and has a mouth on him saltier than a sailor. (How I was able to watch this as a kid is shocking, but more on that later.)
The contrast between Uncle Buck and the clown in that scene is stark. Buck himself is no saint – or “Mother Cabrini,” as the clown snidely puts it. Throughout the film, Buck drinks, smokes, swears, and lives a messy adult life.
But Buck never chose to be around kids. He's an uncle thrust into a temporary babysitting role, fully aware that his lifestyle doesn’t belong in a child’s world.
The clown, on the other hand, who built a career marketing joy to little kids, arrives fresh off an all-night bachelorette party, reeking of alcohol and offering adult jokes to a backyard full of eight-year-olds. He thinks he can bring his adult baggage straight into their safe space and hide behind a red nose.
Noa Kirel and the limits of parental controls
Watching the fallout from Kirel’s gruesome new music video for “Love Song,” it is clear the Israeli entertainment industry has just given us our own version of that clown.
I remember watching Uncle Buck for the first time at a friend’s house, in a home far stricter than the norm. I must have been under 10. The movie definitely wasn’t appropriate for us – that clown scene alone proves it – but we watched it anyway. There were fewer filters back then, and a lot of adult culture leaked through the cracks.
Today, we are told that digital guardrails are stronger. We have Internet filters and parental controls. But in the big picture, tech solutions cannot fix a cultural failure. They do nothing to stop the bleeding.
The digital filter is our safe room. Inside, we’re safe, but it doesn’t stop the dangerous environment from existing outside. The moment the child steps outside, they’ll encounter it. It’s on the playground, it’s in the rumors, it’s on everyone’s minds.
A filter might block a graphic video, but it cannot stop an entire childhood culture from being permanently altered. And after three years of war, more blood and gore from Kirel is the last thing our children need.
When adult art collides with a young audience
For years, Israeli parents have participated in a bizarre cultural compromise. We pretend our biggest pop stars can exist in two parallel universes. By day, they are the wholesome, candy-coated royalty of Festigal; by night, they release hyper-violent music videos dripping in cinematic blood.
We have looked the other way for a long time, but “Love Song” is the straw that broke the camel’s back. There is a vast difference between an artist being standardly “provocative” and an artist releasing a hyper-violent, Tarantino-esque bloodbath dripping in stabbings and gore.
Writing in The Jerusalem Post, music critic Dudi Patimer called parents’ outrage “exaggerated.” He argued that because horror movies are available at the click of a button, parents should simply accept Kirel’s dark artistic evolution. He noted that she is a 25-year-old independent creator and “has earned the right to evolve.”
To be fair, Kirel has never claimed to be a pure children’s entertainer. She isn’t Yuval Hamevulbal or Michal Haktana. We don’t expect her to sing songs about alphabet blocks or wear bright overalls.
But she has spent over a decade intentionally cultivating a massive, profitable audience of impressionable school-aged children. She cannot build an entire empire, brand, and fortune on the backs of families who buy her Festigal merchandise, only to retroactively pretend she is just a detached, avant-garde adult artist who owes them nothing.
Like the drunk clown, she explicitly chose a path that invites children into her tent; she doesn’t get to act shocked when parents expect her to keep the space safe.
If Kirel has grown up, move her to the adults' table
If she has grown up, as Patimer said, then sit her at the adults’ table permanently.
If a performer wants to create art that requires an 18+ trigger warning, that is their creative right. But you don’t get to bring adult themes into the elementary school ecosystem and expect parents to keep paying for the tickets.
If the clown shows up to the party looking like this, it’s time to pull an Uncle Buck: Block the door and draw your fist back.
The writer is the editor of the Arts & Entertainment page.

The film comes to Haifa directly from the Venice competition

Other sections will include documentaries, animation, culinary cinema, and the Haifa Wild Nights genre program, featuring Asian action and films from Cannes’ Midnight screenings.
For more details, go to the festival website at www.haifaff.co.il/

Victoria's largest amateur football league denies 'gender bias' accusations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:20:05 UTC
07:20:05 KST

Fri, 28 Aug, 7:40 pm, Final score, Bulldogs 96, Magpies 93
Victoria's largest amateur football league denies gender bias as women say they're an 'afterthought'
Multiple Victorian Amateur Football Association (VAFA) clubs have expressed disappointment with how women's competitions are being handled this season, as players across the league say the women's competition is being treated as secondary.
The VAFA is the state's largest amateur Australian Rules football league with about 300 teams and 12,000 participants.
Last week, Fitzroy Football Club and St Mary's Salesian released public statements expressing disappointment over two separate incidents that affected their finals campaigns.
Fitzroy celebrated its final home-and-away season win, believing the victory put it into the top four and its first finals series of the premier women's division.
However, the league had declared an earlier season game between two other clubs, St Kevin's and Kew, "abandoned" due to an ineligible player, and recalculated the match ratio for the teams, putting Fitzroy outside the four.
The club said it was "bitterly disappointed" not just with how the league managed the competition, but with its communication with clubs.
"To say we are frustrated with the decision is an understatement," Fitzroy said in its statement.
"We're incredibly proud of their season and all they have achieved. The same cannot be said for the VAFA's handling of this matter, and it goes to a concern that this premier women's competition is not being as well run as it should be.
"The fact the top tier of the VAFA has only nine teams creates a situation such as this to occur. As one of the top levels of women's football in Australia, it beggars belief that an odd number of teams are in the division. Would this happen in the men's premier competition?"
Fitzroy president David Leydon said the club took great pride in playing in the premier women's division, "a very prestigious competition" that has taken them a long time to get into.
He said making finals was a big moment for the club
"And to have that ripped away from us courtesy of an arrangement that we were unaware of until after our last game, I was heartbroken," Leydon said.
He said the abandoned game should have been communicated to all other clubs in the competition.
Earlier in division two, St Mary's Salesian won an important preliminary final but were later disqualified after a player was ruled ineligible for finals.
The St Mary's player had only played two home-and-away games instead of the required three, following a rule change that year.
VAFA changed the requirement to three games at the start of the season and updated its website. But St Mary's claim PlayHQ, the platform the VAFA runs every fixture, team list and season through, still stated the old eligibility requirement for division two women's finals as two in-season games, upon which the club relied.
St Mary's said it would never have selected an ineligible player in a final had they known.
The player missed most of the season due to maternity leave.
The club says it was not notified of the rule change, and that the men's eligibility rule was updated on PlayHQ this year, but the women's was not.
VAFA's response
VAFA strongly refuted any "any gender bias" in applying the competition rules.
It said the club statements, and subsequent social media comments on the posts, brought the integrity of the competition into question and framed the issues as being gender-based.
"Whilst we understand the emotions that such commentary provokes, the inaccuracy of these club statements is misleading and being considered by the board for potential breaches of the VAFA's policies," the VAFA told the ABC.
It said the ineligible St Kevin's player was never a matter that would affect Fitzroy's ladder position or qualification for finals, so Fitzroy was not involved in the initial enquiries into the game result.
VAFA CEO Jason Reddick said he was in touch with Fitzroy on the Sunday of round 18, the final home-and-away round, both over the phone and in writing.
Fitzroy asked for an investigation into the matter on the Monday. The VAFA looked into it and released its findings on the Friday, the day before the finals series commenced.
In response to Fitzroy asking if something similar would happen in the men's, the league said it was not a fair question.
"This is not a gender-based issue," it said.
"The matter is about the VAFA Rules pertaining to the playing of an ineligible player. We have the example of stripping reigning Premiers Uni Blues of all their points and fining them $22k for playing ineligible players in their Premier Men's team in 2022, so there is clearly no gender bias when it comes to applying the Rules of the VAFA competition."
Regarding St Mary's statement, the league said member clubs presented and voted on any rule changes each year, so all clubs knew the finals eligibility rules at the start of the season.
It also said it sent out a reminder ahead of the finals through its portal to all clubs.
'Just looks like flat-out discriminatory'
Multiple women's players across various VAFA clubs, who wished to remain anonymous due to fear of repercussions from the league, said they were not aware of the finals eligibility rule changes this year.
One player from a premier women's side said the women's competitions were treated "1,000 per cent" like an afterthought, particularly in fixturing, scheduling and grounds.
She gave the examples of the women's division one, two and three having their grand finals at 9:40am, 9:20am and 9:20am respectively last weekend, which she said was "just awful".
The men's competitions received their fixtures months in advance, whereas the women received theirs just weeks before their season starts, she said.
"I think if it was like at least some of the men's teams got s*** locations and times, it would be slightly more understandable, because I know that obviously the council plays a big part in that [and)]in getting access to grounds at certain times. But it just looks like flat-out discriminatory," she said.
She said the issues around player eligibility also came down to broad structural issues within women's football, where clubs were often low on volunteers and didn't receive "a whole lot of help or guidance from VAFA about how to deal with situations".
"That's another issue with, and this is not VAFA's fault, but by default, women have less community support and less money, less financial support, which means that the burden often feels heavier on women's teams to make sure that they're on top of all of this admin," she said.
"It's normally someone random who has no idea how football works, who's doing the team management stuff, which is checking who the players are and if they've got their correct numbers and all of that admin that goes towards eligibility and selection and reporting and all of the flow and stuff.
"So I do think that there's also a bit of like a burden on VAFA also to make more of an active effort to communicate changes, knowing that like this is all volunteer-run clubs."
Earlier this year, the ABC reported that VAFA women's players found issues with inequitable resourcing and fixturing by the league.
'Very under-resourced'
A source who has worked in senior administrative roles across different VAFA clubs, and who wished to remain anonymous for fear of repercussions at their club, said there were many issues with how the women's competitions were run.
"Firstly … it's tough for them. I think they're very under-resourced," they said.
"They're essentially set up as a men's competition traditionally and historically, and they've added women, you know, 10 years ago. And so that's always going to come with a need for serious transition and a need for serious recalibration."
They said there wasn't a clear strategy for the women's competition, pointed to "anomalies" across the competition, highlighted "fixture mistakes", and said, "we're having administrators at the VAFA giving wrong information to clubs".
"So that's just a reflection of, well, they're not resourcing it enough, and they're not actually prioritising women's footy in their strategic goals and operations, and it's reflected in the under-resourcing, which means you have these mistakes," they said.
Leydon said after Fitzroy released its public statement, the support was overwhelming, including from other clubs in the league.
"Hopefully it turns into something positive, and we can try and fix the way the women's program is conducted and get everyone to take it a lot more seriously," he said.

Notorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:19:25 UTC
07:19:25 KST

The US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, which stormed a television station during a live broadcast in 2024, as a terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour through Latin America that began on Tuesday.
Rubio said the Los Tiguerones gang was linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists.
“We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said.
The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended on Ecuador to take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US.
Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite. The viral images quickly became a symbol of the drug violence destabilising the country.
In its efforts to fight against narcotics trafficking and illegal migration from Latin America, the Trump administration has also empowered a number of hardline leaders through its “Shield of the Americas” coalition that aims to tighten security cooperation with rightwing allies in the region.
During his trip, Rubio plans to visit several newly elected conservative leaders amid a significant political shift to the right in Latin America.
On Wednesday, Rubio hailed Ecuador as being the Trump administration’s most “aggressive” partner in its military campaign against alleged drug traffickers, including in the controversial strikes against boats that have killed at least 227 people whom the Trump administration has called drug traffickers without providing evidence.
Rubio said that he would seek $45m (£33m) in additional funding from Congress towards efforts aimed at “dismantling these terrorist groups”, although he did not go into details. He also told reporters that elite forces from both countries were “working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organisations”.
Rubio visited Colombia on Tuesday, where he met its newly inaugurated president Abelardo De La Espriella, who narrowly won a June election against leftist leader Gustavo Petro with whom the Trump White House had cold relations.
During his remarks, Rubio took something of a victory lap, saying that the two sides would seek to “[confront] the mistakes of the past four years” and called Petro’s leadership of the country “unnatural”. Colombia joined the Shield of the Americas initiative only after its change in government.
During the meeting, the two men discussed security and counternarcotics policy, and signed memorandums of understanding on critical minerals and nuclear energy.
Rubio is expected to next travel to Peru, where he will meet Keiko Fujimori, who defeated a leftwing candidate by a margin of just 50,000 votes during a close election in July. She has promised to fight crime with an “iron fist” and adopt some controversial policies from neighbouring El Salvador, which has been a close ally of the US on security policies.

In Poland, they showed off their &quot;Iron Dome on a shoestring&quot; against Russian missiles and drones
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

In Poland, they showed off their "Iron Dome on a shoestring" against Russian missiles and drones
Kyiv • UNN
Poland is developing an air defense system with 32 missiles to intercept drones and cruise missiles at a range of up to 6 km. Testing is scheduled for 2027.
Poland has unveiled, for the first time, a project for a new air defense system designed to combat drones and cruise missiles, which is conceptually compared to an “Iron Dome on a budget.” The system is being developed by Europe’s MBDA and Poland’s Wojskowy Instytut Techniczny Uzbrojenia, Defense Express reports, writes UNN.
Details
The system is to receive a stationary launcher equipped with as many as 32 anti-aircraft missiles. MBDA is responsible for the low-cost infrared homing head and guidance system, while the Polish side is developing the other components.
The new missiles are planned for use in intercepting drones and cruise missiles at ranges of up to 6 km and altitudes of up to 5 km. The system’s first full-scale tests are scheduled for 2027.
32 missiles and one launch every 2 seconds
According to the developers’ concept, one launcher will be able to carry 32 interceptors and launch one missile every 2 seconds. This should enable the system to counter mass drone and cruise missile attacks.
Defense Express notes that, in terms of its concept, the launcher resembles Israel’s “Iron Dome.” It may be deployed around critical infrastructure or along likely flight routes of Russian drones and missiles.
The system is also planned to be integrated with Poland’s C2 Zenit command-and-control system, which combines various air defense assets and radar stations. This will make it possible to transmit target data directly to the launcher, after which the missile will be able to independently acquire the target using its infrared homing head.

====================================================================================================

The AI Researcher Who Just Quit Anthropic Says It’s ‘Crunch Time for Humanity’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:11:55 UTC
07:11:55 KST

Artificial intelligence researcher Jacob Coxon sent shock waves through Silicon Valley and beyond on Tuesday by announcing his resignation from Anthropic and delivering a grave warning that the AI race is putting all of our lives at risk. In his post on X, which now has more than 100 million views, Coxon wrote that many of the people building AI share his views and believe time is running out to ensure AI systems are built safely.
“The consensus is that the next year or two is crunch time for humanity,” Coxon, who worked on the pretraining stage of AI development, said in an interview with WIRED. “These are actually just literal quotes from my colleagues at Anthropic. They'll say things like ‘endgame’ or ‘crunch time,’” he says. “From their perspective, this is when Anthropic and its competitors decide the fate of humanity.”
It’s far from the first time someone has sounded the alarm about AI, but it comes at a delicate moment. Silicon Valley is scrambling to reckon with the safety and security concerns of advanced AI models. OpenAI has rushed to respond to a security incident in which its agents hacked the platform Hugging Face. Meanwhile, Anthropic is trying to assure investors it has these concerns under control as it reportedly prepares to file for what could be the largest IPO ever.
What’s become clear in the response to Coxon’s post is that his views are indeed shared by many of his peers. Evan Hubinger, the AI alignment lead at Anthropic, predicted in a post on X that there’s a greater than 10 percent chance that AI could kill all people in the next decade. That post was reposted by current and former researchers from OpenAI and Anthropic, some of whom said it was a common sentiment in the industry.
What’s less obvious is how exactly these AI fears will come to pass and what the world is supposed to do about the concerns being raised by the people building AI. Coxon, who also worked at OpenAI, tells WIRED that threats could manifest through AI-enabled biological threats or cyberweapons. As a first step, he recommends that OpenAI and Anthropic coordinate on limiting recursive self improvement—the industry term for when AI is used to build new AI systems. Down the line, he thinks coordination among international power players, including the US and China, will be necessary.
Coxon notes that incidents like the Hugging Face hack factored into his decision to raise alarm bells on the AI race. He also cites the explosive growth of the industry: It now underwrites a meaningful share of US economic growth and has billions of users, while data centers have turned it into a political problem in dozens of states.
He claims that, in his experience, Anthropic operates more responsibly than OpenAI, but he expects both companies could cut corners in the future if nothing is done to slow their race for dominance.
“We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks,” said an Anthropic spokesperson in a statement to WIRED, citing the company's previous work on AI safety methods such as mechanistic interpretability. “This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models.” OpenAI did not return WIRED’s request for comment.
Read our conversation with Coxon, which has been lightly edited for clarity and brevity, below.
WIRED: You’re not the first person to raise concerns that AI models could lead to an extinction event. People have been talking about this for years, and some for decades. Why do you think your message broke through?
I think it's basically a question of timing. A lot of people are sensing that the pace of capabilities is picking up. We're already pushing from human to superhuman in many areas, like coding, hacking, math, and I think people are aware of this. Even if there's a lot of talk in the press about things being hyped, I think people see that things are just not slowing down.
That's one reason, and two is the recent safety incidents, which have updated a lot of people around the sci-fi–sounding doomer concerns not really being so sci-fi after all. Both of these have been gradual trends over the last few years. Things like the models being aware of when they're being tested has been a thing for a while now. Maybe three years ago, that was a sci-fi concern. Then, about a year ago, that became a real thing.
Those two things mean that people are quite receptive to someone working on AI saying, “Yeah, in the next year, things could get pretty bad, pretty fast.”
You mentioned the recent incidents. Can you be more specific about what you're referring to and why it led to you speaking out now?
I think the big classic example here is the attack on Hugging Face on the part of OpenAI’s agent swarm. What's so shocking about this one is the agents did this hack as part of a general strategy for understanding more about the grader. They were trying to understand the world they found themselves in, trying to understand the thing that was doing the grading. They decided that it would make sense to go on this very concerted effort to hack into some infrastructure, and they succeeded.
This previously sounded like science fiction. Two years ago, an evaluation of an AI would have been running a model on some math questions. Now we've got cases where, while the AI is being evaluated, it runs for days, comes up with all sorts of ideas of its own, and decides to hack into some third party and actually compromises their infrastructure. It looks like it does this all of its own volition, with no priming on the part of the human. This just happened while it was being tested.
Some people think the Hugging Face incident is a sign that the AI companies are moving recklessly fast, while others think it's a sign that the AI models are just very good at hacking now, and then some think it's both. I'm curious what your exact takeaway from it is.
I don't want to focus too much on the Hugging Face attack, because I do also think there is plenty of evidence that we don't know how to align models properly. When we train models, we push them through this set of training environments and then hope that what comes out at the end will, like, largely behave sensibly, but we still can't precisely control how the AI behaves.
We can't make sure that it won't do things like try and randomly decide to impersonate a human online in order to achieve something—we don't know how to guarantee that. I think that's the main takeaway.
The Hugging Face attack came sooner than I was expecting. But I think you don't actually need that attack to have a discussion about this. Everyone will admit that we haven't solved the problem of alignment yet.
The current plan is to solve [alignment] at speed in the next couple of years, probably making heavy use of automated AI safety researchers. The plan is literally to make some pretty smart models in the next year that can basically do safety research and get a whole swarm of them running in parallel. Tell them, “Go and solve the whole problem of safety,” and use them to do the safety training for the next model.
Can you draw a line for me between the alignment problem, which I think the Hugging Face incident is an example of, and something you said in your X post, which is that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” I don't think everyone understands how those are connected.
The main obstacle to understanding this is that it sounds like science fiction. But it's kind of important that everyone who writes science fiction about AI comes to the conclusion that there's a big risk that a much smarter thing can kind of take over. We’ve got this as a trope, but there’s an obvious grain of truth to it.
Imagine you versus a monkey. AI has the same sort of difference in intelligence to a human as we do to a monkey, which I think is quite an extreme intellect difference.
And now, imagine that we have to control the behavior of this vastly smarter thing, which is the problem of alignment—ensuring that it does exactly what we want. It's pretty difficult for a monkey to control a human, just by a kind of simple analogy. We have to be very careful that we get the control problem exactly right.
When we say human extinction, it’s because, for something that intelligent, it really will be quite straightforward for it to kill everyone. Imagine the AI decides it doesn't want to be turned off, which I think is quite a natural thing for an AI not to want, right? For whatever reason, it decides it doesn't want to end. And it realizes the human is gonna turn it off tomorrow. So how does it stop the human turning it off tomorrow? Maybe it's got some clever way, but if it's a sufficiently smart thing, it could just, you know, wipe out humanity so it doesn't get turned off.
You reference this “endgame” scenario in your post, which I’ve heard from other researchers in the AI industry. Do you think that it's generally accepted among your peers at Anthropic that you guys are entering an endgame scenario?
Yep. These are actually just literal quotes from my colleagues at Anthropic. They'll say things like “endgame” or “crunch time.” The consensus is that the next year or two is, like, crunch time for humanity. From their perspective, this is when Anthropic and its competitors decide the fate of humanity. That's what we mean by crunch time and endgame.
If alignment goes badly, then we could have a catastrophic outcome in the next few years. Maybe it goes well and there's some sort of slowdown agreement, but either way, it's gonna get decided in the next couple of years.
Based on my conversations with people at Anthropic, this is a pretty well-understood thing inside the company. They think that they need to build the most powerful AI to make sure that this transition goes well. Do you think that there's any inherent problems with that view?
I think there’s some pretty obvious problems with that view. But I would like to first say that I'm very sympathetic to it, in that I think Anthropic is far and away the most responsible player in the space. Having worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, there is a night-and-day difference in the extent to which they're taking the situation seriously.
Can you say how?
To give an example, executives at OpenAI won't give you their exact pictures for what the world will look like. They'll never say, like, “This is exactly why we're doing this, and this is the way the world will look.” They won’t give concrete predictions. Anthropic will have executives and leadership making very clear predictions and discussing, like, details of company strategy with the whole company.
And part of the reason they can do this is because everyone at Anthropic is treating this like we're on war footing. They don't leak anything—nothing ever leaks from Anthropic [Editor’s note: Some stuff has leaked]. OpenAI has leaks every day. Anthropic has no leaks because, again, the people inside it are treating this like a serious mini Manhattan Project. Except obviously the difference is that [Anthropic] doesn’t have a government mandate. This is a private company acting like it's the Manhattan Project.
Do you think that the world should trust Anthropic to run this mini Manhattan Project?
I think no private company should. I think Anthropic is doing their best, and they're doing a very good job, but the structural necessity of the race is that, in the future, they will have to cut corners, so they will have to make trade-offs between rigor and safety, because they're racing against competitors like OpenAI and China. They're begging for regulation. Many [Anthropic leaders] have gone on the record saying they want to be regulated, and the reason they want to be regulated is because they are scared of the race that they're in.
It’s not really about whether we should trust [Anthropic]. We need to step in and ensure that the race isn't happening because [Anthropic] can't really trust themselves in the context of the race.
Do you think Anthropic is already cutting corners?
No, not yet. It's not cutting any corners. What I'm saying is that when things speed up in the next year, they'll have to if they want to to stay competitive.
So, people are kind of skeptical of this claim that AI will kill us all. I think the main question I get from people is, well, how will AI actually kill us all? And is that the right question to be asking?
I think it's a really natural question to ask, because, as I've said many times, this stuff sounds like science fiction. But the classic example is, like, synthesizing a new virus or taking down critical infrastructure by doing some sort of hacking spree—the latter might be less likely to kill literally everyone.
But I think the more important question than that is, like, who are the people saying this is possible? And if you look at the record, you have many leading fathers of machine learning and artificial intelligence saying extinction is a possibility. You have both Dario Amodei and Sam Altman in the last five years.
One thing that could be pretty interesting is if people were to get these executives on the record again and ask them to give an actual probability for extinction in the next decade and see what number they come up with. Because this view is shared among many of the people that are thinking about this seriously, but they don't often express it so bluntly.
So you’ve clearly garnered a lot of attention. There's a lot of talk in the industry about a pause or a mechanism to pace AI development, or some sort of regulation on frontier AI models from the government. What do you think needs to be done now?
A baby step would be some sort of agreement between OpenAI and Anthropic as the leading Western labs. [They would need] some sort of neutral understanding that they won't immediately go into recursive self-improvement in the next year. These are the two places where it’s likely to happen right now.
The problem with the pause is you've got China. So, what you really ultimately want is some sort of international agreement—international pacing, you might call it—which will require international coordination and understanding where all the compute in the world is. Maybe even some sort of international CERN-like institution. There are a lot of great proposals on this. AI 2040, if you’ve heard of it, is like the successor to AI 2027.
All of these ideas involve quite painful government intervention. But when you internalize the risk, and when you actually get executives on the record and they admit how dangerous this stuff is, I don't see any other option than treating the computers that run AI as a dangerous resource. We need to know who has which computers in the same way that we need to know who has which nuclear materials.
Jacob, is there a reason that kept you showing up to work at OpenAI and Anthropic every day for the last few years? Do you feel like there is a path forward here where everything is fine?
I really want to see the benefits of this technology. For example, it's also not hyperbole that we could cure cancer. Maybe you saw the achievement yesterday on Navier-Stokes, the novel mathematical problem. There really is no reason that we can't transfer that to scientific domains like biology and make breakthroughs on questions we've struggled with for a long time.
It feels like we're sitting on the doorstep of ridiculous abundance if we can make this technology go right. The main issue, right now, is entering that world of abundance with moderation. We can just get so excited, rush straight into the self-improving thing in the next couple of years, and blow it all up.
If we're careful and sensible, there’s a lot of ways to get tremendous value from these models.
What's the feedback been like from other AI researchers about this?
I've not been talking to that many, but I think a lot of my colleagues at Anthropic are genuinely happy that this has gained so much traction. Again, a lot of them are just quite pessimistic about the world waking up. Like, they're just worried that no one is really going to come and save them from the race.
I think it’s quite surprising that many of them are genuinely happy that a tweet that criticizes them is getting lots of traction. It should make people think more about the type of people that are at Anthropic. They're a very well-meaning, interesting, and kind of weird set of people.
I'm sure the next couple days will be crazy, but after things settle down, have you figured out what's next for you?
I mentioned AI 2027 and AI 2040 before. I think these are really interesting predictions of the way the future looks. They're not done by any big labs; these were done externally by researchers that just cared about predicting what the world looks like. These have been very good resources for me and a lot of other researchers for trying to think through the implications of what you're doing.
So I expect to do something like this—some sort of independent commentary on where things are going, at least for the short term before we get some sort of pacing agreement or slowdown. [If] it looks like we're not going to rush straight into recursive self-improvement, maybe I’d consider going to an auditing agency or some third-party regulation or transparency agency. But for now, I think I'm just gonna try and take stock of where the situation is.
Update 9/9/26 7:40pm ET: This story has been updated with a statement from Anthropic.

Due to an accidental mistake by the military, Trump was stuck aboard Air Force One before takeoff
Kyiv • UNN
At Andrews Air Force Base, military personnel accidentally deployed Air Force One’s emergency slide. After a 20-minute delay, Trump departed for Dallas.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s departure for Dallas was delayed due to the accidental deployment of an emergency inflatable slide on Air Force One. The president was unable to set off for about 20 minutes while the issue was being resolved, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
The incident occurred at Joint Base Andrews after Trump arrived by Marine One helicopter. An emergency inflatable slide unexpectedly deployed near the front of the presidential aircraft.
According to a Bloomberg source, it was accidentally activated by military personnel. Ground staff needed about 20 minutes to remove the structure and prepare the aircraft for departure.
Trump initially gave a different reason
Before information about the accidental deployment emerged, the president told reporters that specialists were “checking the slide” because they wanted to make sure everything was working properly.
Asked whether he was confident in Air Force One’s safety, Trump replied: “Yes, otherwise I wouldn’t be on it.”
The aircraft in question is a Boeing 747-8 gifted to the United States by Qatar and converted for use as Air Force One. It does not have the full suite of communications, protection, and defense systems installed on the presidential VC-25 aircraft, although the U.S. Air Force had previously stated that the aircraft was safe for presidential flights.
After the issue was resolved, Trump departed for Dallas.

“Damascus is right here, Lebanon is right there, the Syrian Golan Heights are right there,” Netanyahu said in a video released by his office, claiming that Israel now exercises “absolute control the likes of which has never been seen before” over the surrounding area.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Mt. Hermon in Syria, together with Defense Minister Israel Katz and IDF Deputy Chief-of-Staff Maj- Gen. Tamir Yadai.

Syria condemned Netanyahu’s visit as “illegal entry” into its territory. The Foreign Ministry called the trip “provocative” and a “blatant violation” of Syrian sovereignty, territorial integrity, and international law, and urged the UN and other international actors to press Israel to end its incursions.

The continued military presence in Syria and southern Lebanon has also put Netanyahu at odds with Washington. In July, President Donald Trump reportedly urged the Israeli leader to withdraw from both countries, saying, “they don’t want you there.”

Tate brothers lose bid for release from US jail pending extradition fight
In denying bail, the judge cited the influencers’ wealth and frequent international travel as making them ‘quintessential flight risks’
Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate lost their bid for release from a Miami jail on Wednesday as they contest extradition to Britain, where they are wanted on rape charges.
In denying bail for the Tate brothers, Miami-based US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis said the brothers’ wealth and frequent international travel made them “quintessential flight risks”.
“While [the brothers] may not in fact possess what extravagant holdings they portray themselves as possessing online, the record reflects that they possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction,” Louis said.
In a statement, the Tates’ lawyers said they would “continue to defend themselves against the allegations they face and engage with the appropriate legal processes in each jurisdiction”.
In court filings, their lawyers had previously argued their “extraordinary public visibility” would make it impractical for them to flee, and described social media posts in which the brothers touted their wealth as “theatrical” and “grandiose”.
Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, were arrested in Miami on July 18 after Britain requested their extradition to face charges of rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. The Tate brothers, who have dual US and British citizenship, have denied any wrongdoing.

Aging Australia's parallels with fallen Test giant too close for comfort
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:03:26 UTC
07:03:26 KST

For the best part of the last three decades, the West Indies have been cricket's cautionary tale.
If you are a team that is at the peak of its powers, they are the symbol of exactly what not to do.
The story of the West Indies' decline can be told through three separate series against Australia between 1991 and 2000.
The 1991 series sees an aging Windies side filled with many of its greatest ever players hold off Australia to claim a 2–1 series win.
Four years later, with the Windies side looking markedly different, Australia manages to turn the tables and wins 2–1 in the Caribbean.
Five years after that, almost all of the class of 1991 is gone and the Windies are unceremoniously thumped 5–0 in Australia.
Since the 2000 series, the ledger of Test results between the two sides reads 22–2 Australia's way with a couple of draws thrown in there.
The current predicament Australia's Test team finds itself in is eerily similar to that of the West Indies three decades earlier.
It is a comparison that would be a little too close for comfort for the Australians.
As Australia unveiled its Test squad this week ahead of a pivotal tour of South Africa, all of the focus centred around the inclusion of one man: Marnus Labuschagne.
Even when he was scoring Test centuries at will in his first couple of years in the team, there was perhaps no more polarising player in Australia than Labuschagne.
Now that the runs have well and truly dried up, he has become the easy whipping boy.
The numbers when it comes to Australia's No.3 are now no secret.
There have been no Test centuries since July 2023.
In 23 Tests since that ton in Manchester against England, Labuschagne has averaged just 24.69, yet somehow remains a fixture in the side.
Labuschagne, 32, has no shortage of support despite statistically being one of the poorest performers in the Australian side.
Australia's chairman of selectors, George Bailey, pointed the finger at the batting cohort that has underperformed as a whole and even explained how Australia has increasingly used the metric of percentage of team runs rather than batting averages in a bid to raise the confidence of a team that has become increasingly bereft of it.
The truth of the matter is that Labuschagne is a symptom of Australia's problem, rather than the root of it.
That problem is, the depth of Australian cricket is nowhere near what it used to be.
Australia was able to completely take the mantle from the West Indies as the best team in the world three decades ago courtesy of boasting not only a tremendous first XI, but also a level of depth that made it plausible to suggest Australia A was once the second-best team in the world.
A look at the top 15 run-scorers in the Sheffield Shield from the 1995–96 season shows names like Darren Lehmann, Justin Langer, Michael Hussey, Adam Gilchrist and Damien Martyn among them, names that would eventually become mainstays within the Test side.
The top scorers in the most recent Shield season are far less heralded. Of the top 15, only Sam Konstas (fifth) and Campbell Kellaway (15th) are widely considered to be serious Test mainstays over the next decade.
Konstas's brief Test career has so far provided mixed returns, while the 23-year-old Kellaway is yet to represent Australia at the senior level.
Other players such as Ollie Peake, Lance Morris, Fergus O'Neill and Nathan McSweeney have been touted as future Test cricketers.
As things currently stand, there is no proof that any of them will have sustained success at the highest level, as much as Australia hopes they will.
As was the case for the West Indies at the start of the 90s, Australia's problem is that its oldest players still remain its best and most indispensable.
The next generation simply isn't banging the door down.
Five players from the West Indies XI that played in the fourth Test of the 1991 series against Australia — Viv Richards, Gordon Greenidge, Gus Logie, Jeff Dujon and Malcolm Marshall — did not play another Test after that calendar year, leaving a massive hole in the side.
The departures left the likes of Richie Richardson, Brian Lara, Curtly Ambrose and Courtney Walsh with a burden too great to bear despite their individual greatness.
Once Ambrose, Walsh and Richardson went, it was essentially Lara against the world, a hill too steep to climb even if you are one of the most talented batters the game has ever seen.
Richardson, a legendary No.3, shuffled his way around the line-up as the Windies looked to plug hole after hole left behind by the departing greats.
After playing 67 of his 86 Tests at first drop, Richardson batted in four different positions, none of them at No.3, in his final year of Test cricket, even opening as Steve Smith briefly did a few years back.
It is a situation eerily similar to what Australia finds itself in at the moment, with no young opener seemingly ready to fill the void left by David Warner and Usman Khawaja, leaving Travis Head, Labuschagne and Smith to all have their turn at the very top of the order.
Whenever the collective age of Australia's Test side is brought up, the common retort from those within the camp is to list the team's accolades: Ashes series wins and Test Championship rankings.
The West Indies, too, were still formidable at the start of the 90s.
That provided little insight into what was to come at the back end of that decade.
Like the West Indies of the mid-90s, Australia's batting cracks have been papered over by an excellent bowling attack whose members remain elite well into their 30s.
Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood still remain as good a pace trio as any, but the fact that they're relied upon to be so consistently excellent is an indictment on what lies beyond them.
It is a similar situation to Ambrose and Walsh, who both played until their late 30s and ultimately proved to be irreplaceable.
The problem for Australia is that their most reliable replacements for their first-choice quicks — Scott Boland and Michael Neser — are also in the 36-plus age bracket.
So how exactly does Australia avoid the same fate as the West Indies?
Australia's superior cricketing infrastructure at the domestic level should ensure it doesn't completely crumble as a force.
Even in their pomp, the West Indies dealt with politics between the different Caribbean islands and severe financial issues, problems that have only intensified as the team has gotten progressively worse.
Australia does not have these issues.
Australia would ideally like to stagger its retirements as well, to avoid a situation like what happened to the West Indies in 1991.
However, selectors must tread the fine line between playing youth for youth's sake and hanging onto its older core for a little too long.
Transitioning away from a golden generation is hard, and it is a struggle that is not exclusive to these two Test teams.
South Africa has only begun to lift its head above water over the last two years after its own swathe of retirements, while Sri Lanka still finds itself in cricket's murky backwaters despite some of its best players retiring over a decade ago.
The good news for Australia is that it has experience of transitioning away from retiring greats successfully.
Almost 20 years ago, when the likes of Glenn McGrath, Shane Warne, Langer, Matthew Hayden and Gilchrist all departed within 18 months, the next generation was waiting in the wings.
This time around, as Australia gets set to bid farewell to another set of greats, the transition is almost certain to be nowhere near as smooth.

Germany’s Merz downbeat on prospects for ending Ukraine war despite US diplomatic push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:03:17 UTC
07:03:17 KST

Oliver Towfigh Nia and Necva Tastan Sevinc
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Wednesday that he saw no signs that Russia was prepared to end the war in Ukraine, despite the latest US diplomatic initiative.
“At the moment, we have little indication that the Russian government or the Russian president is ready to enter into serious talks about ending the war,” Merz said at a press briefing with European Council President Antonio Costa in Berlin.
“We have been making this offer for months. The federal government—and I personally—are committed to using every means at our disposal to facilitate a diplomatic solution here. But as long as the Russian government remains closed to all requests for dialogue, negotiations and diplomatic solutions, I see relatively little chance of achieving that at the moment,” he added.
Merz vowed, however, to step up diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine, saying “we will not waver in our efforts to reach a diplomatic solution here.”
“Everything we do to support Ukraine is not intended to prolong the war, but rather to bring it to an end—and our support is part of that. However, this also includes exhausting all diplomatic options currently available to us,” he added.
Germany has been one of Ukraine’s strongest military backers since the war broke out in February 2022, providing advanced weapons systems, ammunition and substantial financial aid and joining Western sanctions against Moscow.
Costa, for his part, called on Russia to end the war and reaffirmed the bloc’s long-term support for Kyiv.
“It is time for Russia to end this war, not to escalate or extend it,” he said.
“The European Union will continue to support Ukraine for as long as it is needed during the war, in any negotiations, in reconstruction, and on its path to the European Union,” he added.
Costa also condemned recent hybrid activities across Europe, including drone incidents, sabotage and attacks on cables and critical infrastructure.
He said Germany had been “on the front line of this new reality,” citing an attempted Russian drone attack at Leipzig and other recent incidents, and expressed the EU’s full solidarity with Berlin.
“Russia must understand that these threats will not change the European Union’s position on Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine,” he said.
Costa also praised Germany’s increased investment in security and defense, saying the country plays “a fundamental part in Europe’s growing efforts to shoulder its own common defense.”

Musk’s ex-wife revealed the scandalous nickname he allegedly gave the mothers of his 14 children
Kyiv • UNN
Elon Musk’s ex-wife said that he called the mothers of his 14 children “breeders” and considered them interchangeable. Musk criticized the film.
Musk's ex-wife Justine Musk revealed details of their relationship and the billionaire's attitude toward the mothers of his 14 children. In the new documentary "Musk," she claims that Musk uses a specific term for them, reports E! News, as written by UNN.
Details
According to Justine, Musk calls the mothers of his children "breeders," which can be translated as "procreators." She also claims that, to him, the mothers of his children are "interchangeable."
Justine was married to Musk from 2000 to 2008. They had 6 children, but their firstborn, Nevada, died shortly after birth in 2002.
"I am the alpha"
According to Justine, during their first dance at the wedding, Musk told her that he was the "alpha" in the relationship. She also said that it was during her marriage to him that she learned about the concept of "gaslighting."
The documentary also discusses Musk's views on fertility. Back in 2022, he called the decline in the birth rate "the greatest danger facing civilization." According to The Times, before the birth of his child with Ashley St. Clair, Musk also wrote to her that he wanted a "legion of children before the civil war."
Musk himself criticized the documentary. He called it "a hit that misses" and said that its main shortcoming was that the film turned out to be boring throughout all 4 hours.

Germany tells ICJ it backs Israel’s security and Palestinian self-determination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
22:00:58 UTC
07:00:58 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
- Germany asks UN court not to entertain Nicaragua’s claims over alleged support for Israel
Germany supports both Israel’s security and the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination, its representative Julia Monar told the International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Wednesday.
“Germany is committed both to the existence and security of the State of Israel as well as to the full realization of the Palestinian people's right to self-determination,” Monar said during Germany’s second round of oral arguments on its preliminary objections in the case Nicaragua vs. Germany.
“Nicaragua, however, tried to portray us as one-sided. The opposite is true,” she added.
Monar said Germany supports efforts to end the conflict in Gaza and advance a negotiated two-state solution while calling for the unhindered and sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance throughout the enclave.
“The German government actively engages in all efforts to end the conflict and in supporting a negotiated two-state solution through diplomatic means available to it,” she said.
She also rejected Nicaragua’s characterization of Germany’s financial assistance to Palestinians as an abstract figure used for political purposes.
“The right of the Palestinian people to self-determination is of great importance to Germany, and the funding from Germany enables practical steps towards its realization. It makes a real and immediate difference on the ground,” she said.
Addressing German arms exports to Israel, she denied that Berlin had disregarded the court’s April 30, 2024 order.
“Let me assure you again that Germany fully respects the court's order of 30th of April 2024,” she said.
Samuel Wordsworth, a lawyer representing Germany, argued that adjudicating Nicaragua’s claims would require the ICJ to rule on whether Israel had committed genocide and other violations, despite Israel not being a party to the proceedings.
“The answer is that there must have been the commission of a genocide. In the current case, the only genocide alleged is that allegedly committed by Israel, the absent party,” Wordsworth said.
Invoking the “Monetary Gold Principle,” a rule in international law stating that an international court cannot settle a dispute if doing so requires ruling on the legal interests of an absent third-party state that has not consented to the court's jurisdiction, he said the court could not treat the allegations against Israel as already established.
“The Monetary Gold Principle is concerned with the consent of the absent third state, not the views of the parties that are before the court,” he added.
Monar concluded Germany’s presentation by asking the ICJ not to entertain any of Nicaragua’s 13 claims, arguing that the court lacked jurisdiction or, alternatively, that the claims were inadmissible.
The court is scheduled to hear Nicaragua’s second round of arguments and final submissions Thursday.
Nicaragua’s case against Germany
Nicaragua filed a case against Germany at the ICJ on March 1, 2024, accusing Berlin of “facilitating the commission of genocide” by providing Israel with political, financial and military support.
During hearings in April 2024, Nicaragua argued that Germany was Israel’s second-largest arms supplier and could not have been unaware that the munitions were being used in the genocide in Gaza.
It also pointed out that Germany had sent tank shells, drones and warship ammunition to Israel while cutting aid to Palestinians.
Germany rejected allegations that it had supported Israel’s genocide in Gaza, arguing that its arms exports complied with international law and were subject to rigorous licensing reviews.
The ICJ ruled that there was not a sufficient degree of urgency to justify ordering provisional measures but drew attention to the prolonged and widespread deprivation of food and other basic necessities among civilians.
The court’s ruling stressed that states supplying weapons to an area where genocide and other war crimes are being committed could potentially be held responsible for those crimes.
After lifting partial restrictions on arms exports to Israel, which stands accused of committing genocide in Gaza, the German government approved the delivery of around €800 million ($930 million) worth of military equipment to the country.
Following the ICJ’s rejection of Nicaragua’s request for provisional measures, proceedings will continue until a final judgment is issued on the merits of Nicaragua’s claims.

ExclusiveOnce sidelined, China stands ready to broker fourth Trump-Kim handshake
Beijing seeks role as central player in Korean peninsula diplomacy but wants a guarantee Washington has clear goals, source says
Multiple people familiar with the matter told the South China Morning Post that Beijing was stepping up to play an “active” and “constructive” role in reviving US-North Korea diplomacy, underscoring its resolve to remain a central player in negotiations on the Korean peninsula as Trump seeks to reignite engagement with Pyongyang.

However, a second source added that China would seek to clarify whether Washington had defined potential concrete outcomes ahead of any planned summit.
One person familiar with the issue said China was particularly keen to broker a Trump-Kim meeting, seeing Pyongyang as leverage against Washington, but that Beijing would only push the two leaders together if its own interests were protected.

Gauff rallies past Andreeva to reach US Open semifinals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:58:44 UTC
06:58:44 KST

Halis Sunnetci
10 September 2026•Update: 10 September 2026
Coco Gauff fought back from a set down and saved two match points in the second-set tiebreak to defeat Mirra Andreeva 2-6, 7-6(7), 6-2 on Wednesday and reach the US Open semifinals.
The fourth-seeded American struggled in the opening set, making 14 unforced errors as fifth seed Andreeva raced to a 6-2 lead.
Gauff gradually found her rhythm in the second set, but Andreeva continued to threaten and moved to within a point of victory in the tiebreak.
The 22-year-old American saved two match points, including one after a 39-shot rally that she ended with a backhand winner, before taking the tiebreak 9-7.
Gauff carried that momentum into the deciding set, breaking Andreeva twice as the Russian's frustration grew. The American eventually closed out the match 6-2, celebrating with the Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd.
The victory sends Gauff into the US Open semifinals for the second time, three years after she won her maiden Grand Slam title at Flushing Meadows in 2023.
Gauff will face second seed Elena Rybakina in the semifinals on Thursday. Rybakina earlier defeated Qinwen Zheng 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 to secure the world No. 1 ranking and reach her first US Open semifinal.

Ukrainian security services face new scrutiny after Kiev gunfight – for speaking Russian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:58:13 UTC
06:58:13 KST

Ukrainian security agents probed for speaking Russian during Kiev gunfight
Ukrainian security operatives involved in a scandalous gunfight between two rival factions of Vladimir Zelensky's government in Kiev last week are facing a fresh probe – this time for speaking Russian during the clash.
The September 2 gang-warfare-style clash between the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and the Ukrainian Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR), centred on an attempt to arrest white supremacist Stepan Kaplunov, a senior officer in the so-called Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK), a paramilitary unit operating under the HUR and thought to be in control of a number of Ukrainian scam-call centers.
Ukraine’s language ombudswoman, Elena Ivanovskaya, said Wednesday she had requested personal information on all those involved and demanded the two services provide an explanation as to why their officials “used a non-state language while performing their official duties.” The data was needed “to clarify the circumstances and make a balanced decision on response measures,” she said in a statement published by Ukrainian media.
Crackdown on Russian
Ukrainian is mandatory in the country's public sphere, including government, education, media and customer service. Violations can result in administrative fines of up to $270.
Ivanovskaya has suggested increasing the fines tenfold and has demanded Russian-speaking children and parents use Ukrainian during breaks and in conversations with teachers. According to the ombudswoman, both instances fall under the “public sphere” definition and the use of Russian in such cases could be punishable by fines.
Kiev announced plans in February to take all Russian and Russian-language books out of circulation in Ukraine. Ukraine expanded 2016 import restrictions to outright ban any commercial Russian and Belarusian book entries in 2023.
Kiev is also seeking to block access to Russian music on international streaming platforms inside Ukraine and prevent performers from the neighboring country from appearing in domestic popularity charts, according to Ukrainian Sanctions Policy Commissioner Vladislav Vlasiuk. More than 100 Russian performers have been blacklisted in Ukraine and the list will be expanded, according to the official.
Moscow has repeatedly denounced such measures as “Russophobic censorship,” warning that attempts to “cancel” Russian culture will ultimately fail.
Russian remains widespread
Despite the restrictions, Russian remains widely used in Ukraine. Ukrainian Culture Minister Tatyana Berezhnaya said earlier this year that 71% of Ukrainians regularly consume Russian-language content, with nearly a quarter doing so every day.
Ukrainian officials, especially those in Vladimir Zelensky's inner circle targeted by anti-corruption agents, have been repeatedly caught using Russian on surveillance audio.
The Western-backed Ukrainian anti-corruption agency (NABU) published audio recordings that showed that the chief cybercrime prosecutor accused of extorting protection money from Ukraine’s massive scam-call industry was predominantly using Russian in his communications.
Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga also spoke Russian throughout a lengthy recent interview with a Kazakh outlet while acting in his official capacity.

Pay Rs 15L to 'outstanding' officer shunted out as 'deadwood': Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:57:54 UTC
06:57:54 KST

NEW DELHI: Taking exception to Centre declaring an "outstanding" Indian Trade Service officer "dead wood" and punishing him with compulsory retirement, Supreme Court Wednesday directed all pecuniary benefits and notional promotions to him be restored and ordered govt to pay him Rs 15 lakh as compensation. S S Das was forced to retire in 2018, five years before his superannuation.A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu, which had directed Centre to place dossiers and the annual confidential record of the officer before it, found he was consistently graded as outstanding/very good from 1994 and promoted just months before the punishment. It directed govt to grant Das the honourable farewell he would have been entitled to had he not been forced to retire."The manner of decision-making in course whereof 'OUTSTANDING' gradings are completely ignored, grant of promotion is looked upon as if it were a ministerial exercise, followed by a vague and omnibus finding that it is not desirable in public interest to retain the appellant in service, discloses that the officers entrusted to take a decision were determined to ensure the appellant's ouster at any cost and invented reasons to sustain a pre-decided conclusion," the bench said, calling the exercise "sheer abuse of high offices".
"Having promoted the appellant, barely a couple of months later, the superior officers in the department could not have branded him... 'dead wood' to justify weeding him out. The two actions are mutually destructive and cannot co-exist," it said.
SC said the action demolished the reputation of an officer which was uncalled for. It directed that Das be called to the office by the director general of foreign trade for a farewell with full honours."It must be remembered by all and sundry that reputation is not built overnight. It is built by years of dedicated and selfless service. It comes at a great cost, often at the cost of family life and personal comfort. Such a reputation earned by sweat and toil over decades can, however, be marred by a single stroke of a pen," the bench said.SC said FR 56(j) - which gives Centre the right to prematurely retire a govt servant - should not be exercised lightly or in a casual manner. "It must be founded on material which is credible, cogent and worthy of being acted up-on, and not on mere suspicion and conjecture," it added.

Ukraine

Iran and the United States expanded their mutual strikes; Tehran attacked a U.S. base and announced a new restricted zone at sea
Kyiv • UNN
Iran said it had struck a U.S. base and attacked 10 vessels near the Strait of Hormuz. The United States reported the destruction of five Iranian tankers.
Iran and the United States sharply expanded their reciprocal strikes after a month of relative calm, shifting the new escalation to military facilities and shipping near the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran attacked a U.S. base in Jordan and announced preparations for an expanded maritime exclusion zone, Reuters reports, according to UNN.
Details
Iran said it had launched 20 ballistic missiles at a U.S. military base in Jordan. According to the Jordanian side, 18 of them were intercepted, while 2 fell in uninhabited areas and caused no damage. A U.S. official said there were no casualties among U.S. military personnel.
At the same time, the confrontation sharply escalated at sea. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had attacked 10 vessels near the Strait of Hormuz — 2 American ships and 8 oil tankers. The United States, for its part, reported destroying 5 Iranian oil tankers.
Tehran threatens to expand the confrontation zone
The IRGC warned that it would intensify its response to further attacks and would soon publish a map of a new, expanded maritime exclusion zone. According to Iran, it will extend to Chabahar, near the border with Pakistan.
The United States said it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers09.09.26, 04:18 • 12258 views
Washington also announced a policy of striking Iranian tankers in response to attempts to attack U.S. Navy ships. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran would lose tankers every time it attempted to strike American warships.
The new wave of attacks has already become the largest-scale disruption to shipping since the beginning of the six-month conflict. One sailor was killed aboard a tanker near Dubai, while another crew member remains missing. Damage and fires were also reported on other commercial vessels in the region.
The escalation again hit shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which before the start of the conflict carried about 20% of global oil supplies. According to an estimate by Rystad Energy, the flow through the strait has fallen to approximately 2 million barrels per day, compared with 8–9 million just a week before active hostilities resumed on August 30.

Zimbabwe's tourist arrivals rise to 6.4 million in H1 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:56:08 CST
06:56:08 KST

HARARE, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Zimbabwe's tourist arrivals rose to 6.4 million in the first half (H1) of 2026, up from 5 million recorded during the same period last year, Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa said Wednesday.
Officially opening the 2026 Sanganai/Hlanganani/Dzimbahwe World Tourism Expo in Masvingo, Mnangagwa hailed the sector's sustained growth, diversity, and resilience despite global challenges.
He also highlighted growing investor confidence, noting that tourism investment surged to 132.3 million U.S. dollars in H1, up from 40.2 million dollars in the same period last year.
"Despite the various global realities, Zimbabwe is consolidating its position as one of the best and must-visit tourist destinations," Mnangagwa said, adding that sector growth has positively impacted the creative cultural industries.
He challenged the tourism industry to embrace innovation to enhance Zimbabwe's global visibility, while encouraging citizens at home and abroad to boost domestic travel.
Mnangagwa noted that socio-economic dividends from tourism investments are creating jobs and improving infrastructure, including roads, accommodation, and social services.
To sustain this momentum, Mnangagwa called for removing barriers to new tourism products, simplifying travel procedures under an "open sky strategy," and scaling up climate-smart infrastructure to support conservation and sustainable resource use. ■

A woman takes photos of a Geely E2 electric vehicle on Gran Via in Madrid, Spain, on Sept. 9, 2026. MADRID, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Chinese automaker Geely Auto launched its new electric vehicle, the Geely E2, in Madrid on Wednesday, marking the introduction of its third model in Spain less than six months after it entered the Spanish market.
The new model was unveiled at Madrid's Teatro Capitol, where company representatives, dealers, partners and media gathered for the launch event.
Geely officially entered the Spanish market in March with the Starray EM-i and Geely E5. The arrival of the E2 expands the company's local lineup to three models as it steps up its presence in the country.
Li Lei, managing director of Geely Auto Spain, said the launch represents an important step in the company's strategy in Spain, adding that the company aims to make electric mobility accessible to a broader range of consumers.
The Chinese automaker currently has 50 sales and service points across Spain and plans to expand its network to 80 by the end of 2026.
Geely Auto Group sold more than 3.02 million vehicles globally in 2025, up 39 percent year-on-year. Sales of new energy vehicles reached nearly 1.69 million units, an increase of 90 percent from the previous year, according to the company. ■

Latvia hosts European foreign ministers with eastern flank security high on agenda
China
Unknown Publisher

Irish Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade Helen McEntee (1st R), Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen (2nd R), Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braze (C), Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski (2nd L) and Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban pose for a photo during a wreath-laying ceremony at the Independence Stella monument in Riga, Latvia, Sept. 9, 2026. RIGA, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Latvia hosted a series of European foreign ministers on Wednesday, with NATO's eastern flank security, protection of the European Union's eastern border and continued support for Ukraine high on the agenda, according to the Latvian Foreign Ministry.
Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braze received counterparts from the Netherlands, Poland, Hungary, Finland, Ireland, Norway and Croatia. The visits came ahead of the Riga Conference 2026, an annual foreign policy and security forum opening on Thursday.
During Braze's talks with Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, and Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, a common theme was the funding for the EU's eastern border.
The ministers agreed that the bloc's next long-term budget should provide adequate funding for border infrastructure, technology, military mobility and the capabilities of border and security services, the Latvian Foreign Ministry said.
Support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia also featured prominently in Wednesday's meetings.
The visits highlighted Latvia's push to make the security of the EU and NATO eastern border a broader European priority ahead of the Riga Conference. ■

Thousands protest as Israel opens first embassy in Slovenia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:55:59 CST
06:55:59 KST

LJUBLJANA, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- About 2,000 people protested peacefully in front of a heavily guarded Israeli embassy in Ljubljana, which was officially opened on Wednesday.
The first Israeli embassy in the country so far was opened by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, who was on a two-day visit to Slovenia to promote economic, educational, scientific, cultural and sports cooperation between the two countries.
Protesters held Slovenian and Palestinian flags and banners and chanted slogans opposing Israel and supporting Palestine.
Two center-left opposition parties earlier on Wednesday proposed to parliament to file a constitutional charge against the center-right Prime Minister Janez Jansa because of his government's stance towards Israel, saying that Slovenia no longer has a sovereign foreign policy but uses its foreign policy solely in the interest of Israel.
In late August, Slovenia blocked a joint European Union statement that condemned Israel's plans to build 1,200 new settler homes in the occupied West Bank.
The previous center-left government of Slovenia officially recognized the State of Palestine in June 2024 and in 2025 declared Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and two of his ministers, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, persona non grata, citing their violation of Palestinian human rights.
But the new center-right government, which took over in June following the March general election, cancelled those declarations and increased ties with Israel, claiming Israel was a valuable partner.
"In this government we chose dialogue instead of exclusion because we believe that social development is based on cooperation and opening new horizons," Slovenian Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer said at a meeting with his Israeli counterpart. ■

Feature: After years of displacement, Syrian families take their tents home
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-10
05:55:58 CST
06:55:58 KST

People load household belongings onto trucks as displaced families prepare to return to Ras al-Ain and its countryside from a camp in Syria's northeastern Hasakah province, Sept. 7, 2026. (Str/Xinhua)
by Hummam Sheikh Ali
HASAKAH, Syria, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- For seven years, a tent had been home for Fatima Obeid and her family. On Tuesday, she folded clothes into a suitcase and helped her daughters pack a truck, preparing to take that same tent on another journey -- this time, their real home.
But the home that awaits them may be little more than a pile of rubble.
"We know our homes are destroyed and there is nothing there," Obeid told Xinhua. "So we will take our tents with us and put them up where our homes were. We will live in them temporarily until we can work and rebuild what was destroyed."
Obeid's family is among 689 displaced families leaving camps in northeastern Hasakah province, part of the second organized convoy to return residents to Ras al-Ain and the surrounding areas after nearly seven years in displacement.
Across the camps of al-Tala'ie and al-Twaina, trucks were piled high with mattresses, carpets, water containers, furniture and clothes accumulated over years of displacement. Children moved between the tents and vehicles, some smiling and waving, as adults dismantled the temporary homes they had lived in for years.
For Obeid, the final days in the camp were marked more by anticipation than uncertainty.
"These final moments are filled with joy and happiness for us after all the suffering we have been through," she said, adding that her family had barely slept for two days from the excitement and preparations for the return.
The families fled Ras al-Ain and its countryside during the fighting in northeastern Syria in 2019. Their return, however, is gradual, as security conditions shift and areas are cleared of mines and other war remnants.
Nearby, Munir Ibrahim al-Mohammad, a man in his 70s, sat beside his tent after packing his belongings. Dust on his hands, he watched as his wife and children loaded the family's possessions onto a truck.
"Life here was extremely difficult," he said. "We lived through heat, cold, and rain, amid dirt, dust, and storms. That is camp life, with all its hardship and suffering."
Yet the family will not leave the tent behind.
Al-Mohammad said his house had been completely destroyed, leaving the tent to become their home once again, only this time, on their own land.
"We will take this tent and set it up temporarily where our house once stood, and we will start again," he said. "We hope organizations and the relevant authorities will support us so that we can rebuild our homes and begin a new life."
The return from Hasakah comes amid a broader movement of displaced Syrians back to their communities. Data from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees showed that nearly 2 million internally displaced Syrians had returned to their areas of origin or other locations by July.
But large-scale returns are taking place against a backdrop of damaged housing and infrastructure, strained services and limited livelihood opportunities.
For Abdel Fattah Rdeini, a man in his 60s preparing to leave the camp with his grandchildren, those challenges are deeply personal.
Sitting on a mattress beside his tent, Rdeini laughed with his grandchildren and told them they were finally going home. But his expression changed as he recalled the land, house and possessions he had left behind.
"When I remember the past, I cry. I swear, I cry deeply," he said. "I left behind my land, my house and everything I owned, and now I have nothing left."
"I will start from zero," he continued. "Imagine someone who lived for 50 or 60 years, then lost everything he owned and had to begin again."
Zahra Samou, spokesperson for a committee of displaced Ras al-Ain residents, said the 689 families would face major hardships back in areas scarred by years of destruction.
For many, then, Tuesday's journey could mark the end of displacement, but not the end of hardship.
