9/11, 25 years on: For 100 million Americans, it’s not even a memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Commentary
9/11, 25 years on: For 100 million Americans, it’s not even a memory
SHANKSVILLE, Pennsylvania – It is always the first thought that arises when recollecting an event of great import: Where was I? What humdrum action was I engaged in when it occurred?
And time seems to coalesce around a momentous event, slowing it down.
For me, the news of the first plane crashing into a building in New York broke nearly at the end of my day shift, at 8.46PM, Singapore time.
Seventeen minutes later, live on television, another plane ploughed in.
The Straits Times foreign desk, led by the late Felix Soh, scrambled to capture the shock that rippled across the globe when 19 Al-Qaeda terrorists, four of whom trained as pilots, hijacked four passenger jets and flew them, like missiles, into the twin towers of New York’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
Within three hours after the first plane struck, an iconic pair of New York’s tallest buildings were reduced to a smoky pile of rubble, a part of America’s military headquarters had collapsed, and 40 brave passengers and crew had died thwarting a flight believed to have been bound for Capitol Hill or the White House.
Nearly 3,000 people were killed in the most brutal terrorist attacks that came to define a new era. Among them were more than 370 foreigners from over 100 countries. One Singaporean recounted her miraculous escape in an interview in 2021.
The nation shook at the magnitude of the attacks, which were clearly the result of unprecedented coordination. Firefighters, police officers, and paramedics risked their lives in desperate rescue operations; all flights were grounded, and many Americans learnt for the first time about Al-Qaeda and its chief, Osama bin Laden.
It was the wee hours of the next morning when we put the newspaper to bed. I have little trouble recalling The Straits Times page 1 headline, 25 years later: “Terrorists bring US to its knees.”
Barely 10 days later, after air traffic had resumed in the US, I was in New York on a trip planned months earlier. I stood next to the barricades and yellow crime-scene tape cordoning off the rubble, breathing in the haze of dust hanging over the site like a white, nebulous shroud. Fliers and posters with names and photos of missing people were everywhere.
The Pentagon has since been repaired. New York’s new tallest building is a new World Trade Center at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan. The city, which has kept the twin towers’ footprints as an open memorial, this year inaugurated its first Muslim mayor, Zohran Mamdani.
But formidable new challenges have sprung up. The 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks finds the US at a crossroads: how to deal with a threat that remains salient while public memory of its horror dims.
Current threat assessments say that a variety of loose networks and home-grown, radicalised lone wolf actors pose “the most likely terrorist attack scenario” on the US homeland. And counter-terrorism experts have warned that the time between radicalisation and violent action has shortened over the past 25 years.
But nearly 100 million Americans, born after the attacks, are unfamiliar with the horror of this shared national memory. They are emotionally distant from the attacks they never witnessed.
And the messaging from the White House is not as sharp as it used to be.
The Biden administration minimised talking about the “global war on terror” and instead focused on the great power competition with Russia and China.
The second Trump administration doubled down.
Its 2026 counter-terrorism strategy talks about a “resource-sustainable approach to countering Islamic terrorists”, focused on organisations with the intent and capability to strike the homeland. Some analysts call it a doctrinal and rhetorical downgrade of the war on terror, while supporters call it a realistic recalibration.
Lately, the White House has also been trying to persuade the world that by far the most dangerous form of extremism is far-left violence. In May 2026, it explicitly elevated “violent left-wing extremists, including anarchists and anti-fascists” to the same tier as “legacy Islamist terrorists” – like Al-Qaeda and ISIS – and drug cartels.
In July, the US State Department convened foreign ministers for a meeting to warn of the resurgence of “political terrorism” and said far-left actors now drive the majority of anti-government plots and attacks.
A war of words
With the passage of time, alternative views of the attacks have surfaced more readily, troubling those who do not want their horror to be diluted.
Less than two weeks before the milestone anniversary, Americans were outraged when a leaked internal memo showed that Canada’s public broadcaster had asked its journalists not to refer to the 9/11 attacks as “terrorism”. After a backlash, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reversed the decision.
Barely had that controversy died down when Mamdani came into the public glare.
During an event on Sept 4, he handed over the ceremonial pen that he used to sign executive orders commemorating the attacks to his chief counsel, Ramzi Kassem, a lawyer who has fought the case of Ahmed al-Darbi, a convicted Al-Qaeda terrorist implicated in the 2002 bombing of a French oil tanker and whose brother-in-law was one of the hijackers who flew the plane into the Pentagon.
Critics also pounced on Mamdani for having made an appearance with far-left influencer Hasan Piker and his initial hesitation to condemn Piker’s remarks that “America deserved 9/11”.
The way he has framed the attacks in his public statements over the years has spurred scrutiny.
Conservative commentators say he has criticised US foreign policy and the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq more than he has blamed the perpetrators while discussing 9/11. He has mourned the victims while avoiding a clear statement saying that Al-Qaeda terrorists carried out the attacks.
Families of 9/11 victims have collected over 100,000 signatures for a petition that asks Mamdani to stay away from the commemoration ceremony on Sept 11.
Vanda Felbab-Brown, an expert on terrorism and senior fellow in foreign policy at the Brookings Institution think-tank, said there are two phenomena in public perceptions of terrorism.
“One is the different messaging from the US government, and the other is just the distance from that experience,” she said.
“The Trump administration has redirected its effort to countering what it defines as far-left extremism and what many allege is essentially a political beachhead against domestic actors in the US that don’t agree with it,” she added.
An analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies on “Ideological trends in US terrorism” found that while the number of left-wing terrorist attacks have increased over the last decade, they still remain much lower than far-right and Islamist attacks.
The US continues to experience instances of lone wolf, self-radicalising actors seeking to mount attacks, Felbab-Brown said. These happen regularly but have been foiled or not resulted in large casualties.
“The shock that the 9/11 attacks brought is long gone. At the same time, there is tiredness with the 20-plus years of the global war on terror that took US soldiers to faraway places, such as Afghanistan and Iraq, and that led to thousands of soldiers dying.”
Worsening things is the ongoing war with Iran, which has accomplished none of the US’ objectives and caused great economic distress at home.
“So both the emotional distance and the ongoing costs related to complex wars are turning off people from seeing counter-terrorism as their principal foreign policy focus,” Felbab-Brown added.
It is an especially confusing landscape for the 100 million Americans who know about the attacks only second-hand.
A majority of young Americans, between 18 and 24 years of age, say they first learnt about the attacks in school, according to a Pew Research Center survey of 5,166 US adults conducted in August.
That brings its own problems. Public schools vary widely in what and how much they teach about 9/11. Only 25 states have laws or standards requiring specific instruction related to 9/11. Another 13 states make it optional, according to an Associated Press report. Since most decisions are left to school districts and to individual teachers, coverage is uneven.
Older students may be asked to assess government responses to terrorism and analyse the aftermath of the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, including the erroneous allegations about weapons of mass destruction.
Some states require the students also learn about attacks on mosques and a Supreme Court case on the legal rights of US citizens, including Muslims, detained as “enemy combatants”.
Teaching the teachers
In Pennsylvania, a 2024 law requires schools to hold a moment of silence and urges schools to use the anniversary as a teachable moment.
The state had a close brush with terrorism. A site spread over 890ha of meadows, reclaimed coal mines and forests in Shanksville, south-western Pennsylvania, honours the 33 passengers, two pilots and five flight attendants who attempted to retake the plane from the Al-Qaeda hijackers.
United Flight 93 took off from New Jersey’s Newark airport, 25 minutes late, for San Francisco on that fateful day. After 46 minutes in the air, four hijackers overpowered the captain and turned the plane towards Washington.
Passengers and crew learnt about other hijacked planes in phone calls made from “seat phones” in those days when mobile phones were still uncommon. In all, 13 people placed 37 calls. Realising that their plane was part of the plot, they took a vote and decided to storm the cockpit.
The cockpit voice recorder captured the sounds of the struggle before the plane crashed and erupted in a giant fireball, at a site that is 18 minutes flying distance from the US capital. All aboard died.
Some 10,000 people, including the families of those who died, are expected to turn up to honour the heroes on Sept 11 at the Flight 93 National Memorial.
The weekend before the ceremony, on a hot day with clear blue skies, visitors thronged the site. The carpark overflowed, and queues moved slowly past exhibits at the visitor’s centre overlooking the crash site. There were fathers with toddlers on shoulders, grandparents with wide-eyed preteens, grey-haired military veterans, some in wheelchairs, and groups of tattooed motorcycle riders in stars-and-stripes tees.
Some left flowers by the marble “Wall of Names”, inscribed with the names of those who died. I saw personal tributes: a Spider-Man figurine, an angel with wings and a large clamshell.
“Around 30 per cent of our population has no lived memory of the day,” noted Donna Gibson, the executive director of Friends of Flight 93, a non-profit organisation dedicated to awareness, education and stewardship at the memorial.
“And you not only have students who have no memory, (but also) you now have educators who either were not alive or have no lived memory of the day,” she said.
Four years ago, the non-profit partnered with the National Park Service to create “National Days of Learning” to remember 9/11. “We have a global platform where people can register, participate in projects and learn about what happened on that day,” she said.
A new project launched in 2026 was a symposium for Pennsylvania’s social studies teachers, organised by the University of Pittsburgh School of Education, the Friends of Flight 93 National Memorial, and the National Park Service. The aim was ambitious: to establish a national model for 9/11 education.
The central problem is not a lack of curriculum but preparation for teachers to handle the subject’s emotional weight, said Melissa Nelson, an assistant professor of practice at the University of Pittsburgh School of Education, who led workshops at the symposium.
“There is the teaching of the factual aspect of something so consequential as 9/11, and then there is the opportunity that we have as adults to model for children how we make sense of terrible things that happen,” she said.
“Teachers are responsible for teaching about one of the worst days in our nation’s history. This is horrific to make sense of; how do you wrap your head around people who hate our country so much that they want to collapse it? That’s scary for us as adults to understand, let alone a 14-year-old.
“It was also one of the last times when we seemed to be able to move past our many differences and see the humanity in each other,” she noted.
“And that’s something very important that educators can model for children. That even in the worst of times we can support each other.”
Merely conveying the facts is itself a missed opportunity for deeper education, she said.
“You might as well hand them a book. It just doesn’t resonate and it misses opportunities to explore emotional perspectives.
“You can’t let the children walk out your classroom door with no hope that they can be part of changing the trajectory of their futures,” she said.
“We must not leave them so overwhelmed by something like 9/11 that they are living in fear. Let them leave with some hope. That is my one golden rule.”

Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, Antonio Tajani, urged President Volodymyr Zelensky to include Italy and Poland in initiatives aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Speaking at a press briefing in Sao Paulo, Brazil on Wednesday, Sept. 9, Tajani said Ukraine should engage the EU as a whole – rather than relying on limited groups of individual states, such as Germany and France.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We will continue to help Ukraine defend itself without sending our troops,” Tajani said, according to Italian news outlet Ansa.
Europe to be involved in future peace talks
Zelensky said Europe would be represented in all future formats of peace negotiations, as its presence was necessary not only for postwar reconstruction, but also for future security guarantees alongside the US, Ukrinform reported on Tuesday, Sept. 8.
“For Europe, it is important to be in the negotiation process, because they think about security,” Zelensky said, noting that EU countries have a direct interest in the peace talks since the outcome would affect broader security across the continent.
He added that European intelligence officials and diplomats remain in contact with their Russian counterparts.
Italy’s diplomatic stance on war in Ukraine
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, ousted on July 15 as part of Zelensky’s broader cabinet reshuffle, announced on Aug. 28 that he had accepted Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto’s invitation to serve as an adviser on defense innovation.
Ex-CIA Chief: NATO Is Weak and the Baltics Are Next
“Ukraine’s experience can become the foundation for a new European defense model,” Fedorov said, adding that “the future of defense belongs to countries able to quickly test and scale new solutions, combining technology with strong manufacturing.”
Although Italy appears to benefit from Ukraine’s battlefield knowledge, it has maintained its broader policy approach during the war, refusing to contribute funds to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – which finances purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine, and pushing back on some of the EU’s sanctions against Russia.
Crosetto said on June 19 that Rome opposed the mechanism but maintained that other channels could provide Ukraine with the military support it needs.
“We have said no from the beginning, and it is still a no,” he said, despite last year’s announcement that Rome was warming up to the idea of taking part in PURL.
Crosetto has also consistently ruled out deploying Italian troops to Ukraine as well, saying that direct military intervention would risk escalating the conflict.
At the same time, he has said Italy supports assisting Ukraine “in every possible way” short of sending its forces into the country.
European air defense cooperation and peace negotiations
Tajani’s remarks came as Zelensky met with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and heads of defense companies from partner nations in Oslo earlier on Wednesday, in an aim to push forward FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program – a defense initiative aimed at building alternatives to the US-made Patriot interceptors.
The program provides Europe with integrated protection against aerial threats through joint efforts of Italy, Ukraine, France, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands, Norway, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and the UK.
“Protecting European skies is our shared cause,” Zelensky said.
On Tuesday, Ukraine announced it was signing contracts with partners for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles for its air defense systems ahead of the winter.
Germany said it would urgently transfer PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from its own Bundeswehr stocks.
In their first visit to Ukraine as Washington’s intermediaries, senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Kyiv by train on Sunday, Sept. 6, where they held bilateral talks with Zelensky, followed by a multilateral session that included national security advisers from the UK, France, and Germany.
The envoys also visited Moscow where they held more than three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday evening, Sept. 5.
As of Wednesday, CIA Director John Ratcliffe, who visited Russia two weeks ago in his first trip to Moscow during his tenure, may be preparing to take a more prominent role in US-led talks with Russia and Ukraine, possibly replacing Witkoff and Kushner.According to Politico on Aug. 26, Ratcliffe warned Putin against attacking a NATO member, with the discussion centering on the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

California, other states warn Supreme Court of 'chaos' if it lets USPS mail ballot rules stand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:54:36 UTC
05:54:36 KST

California, other states warn Supreme Court of ‘chaos’ if it lets USPS mail ballot rules stand
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The contested rules require states to rapidly overhaul mail voting with new voter lists and bar-coded envelopes.
- The Supreme Court is expected to rule relatively quickly, given the emergency nature of the appeal.
California and nearly two dozen other states warned the U.S. Supreme Court Wednesday that allowing the U.S. Postal Service to move forward with President Trump’s new rules for mail ballots in the November election would cause “chaos” and could disenfranchise millions of eligible voters.
“In some States ... compliance with USPS’ rule would be impossible ahead of the midterms, meaning that millions of voters would be unable to vote by mail and some would not be able to vote at all,” the states argued. “In the remaining States, there would be chaos — and a significant risk that millions more voters would be denied the ability to vote.”
The Democrat-led coalition — which includes California, 23 other states and the District of Columbia — also cited objections from lower-ranking state and elections officials in conservative states that have not objected to the Postal Service’s position, including the lieutenant governor and other officials in Utah saying implementation of the new rules would “be an unmitigated disaster.”
Similar warnings have emanated from Florida, Ohio, Texas and Wisconsin.
“Whatever else may be said of USPS’ new rule, it would wreak havoc on States and their voters if it takes effect at this late point,” the Democrat-led states wrote, pointing out that some States, including North Carolina and Wisconsin, have already begun to mail out ballots.
The effort is part of the implementation of President Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting and has been temporarily halted by a federal judge. The ruling is being appealed by the administration and the directive may ultimately end up back before the U.S. Supreme Court.
The states’ arguments were in response to the Trump administration over the weekend filing an emergency appeal to the high court, asking it to overturn a lower-court ruling halting the plan from being implemented for the Nov. 3 election.
The new rules — developed in response to a March executive order from Trump — require states to submit their complete voter lists to the Postal Service, and to adopt new ballot envelopes with individualized voter bar codes designed by the Postal Service. They require the Postal Service to then reject any mail ballots that don’t match those lists.
Trump’s order also directed the Department of Homeland Security to develop its own list of eligible citizen voters, ostensibly to be compared against the state lists.
Trump and other supporters of the changes — including top officials from a dozen Republican-led states — argue they are necessary to prevent widespread voter fraud, including by noncitizens. Elections experts say there is no evidence of such widespread fraud, despite robust audits and other searches for it.
The Democrat-led states sued to block the changes on multiple grounds, including that neither Trump nor the Postal Service have any authority to regulate state-run elections, that the changes would illegally prevent eligible voters from casting ballots, and that the timeline imposed by the new rule — formally issued by the Postal Service on Aug. 21 — made compliance by November impossible.
Independent voting rights groups also sued, alleging the new rules threatened to disenfranchise voters and make their work educating voters on their options for casting a ballot impossible to carry out.
A Postal Service whistleblower recently added skepticism to the agency’s ability to implement the new rules on its end, alleging in a statement published by congressional Democrats that the agency’s online portal for verifying ballots was built in a “slapdash” manner, is “fundamentally flawed” and threatens as built to reject thousands of ballots if just a single one cannot be properly read.
Last week, U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani granted requests from the states and the independent groups to halt the plans from being implemented nationwide, issuing a preliminary injunction requiring the Postal Service to cease all work on them.
The Trump administration then bypassed the U.S. 1st Circuit Court of Appeals to ask the Supreme Court for relief from Talwani’s order.
Solicitor Gen. D. John Sauer, the administration’s top litigator, argued that the warnings from states that the changes are unworkable, represent an overreach of federal authority or would cause chaos in November are all baseless.
Judge again halts Postal Service mail ballot plan as Trump administration seeks Supreme Court relief
A federal judge again Friday blocked the U.S. Postal Service from enacting President Trump’s sweeping new mail ballot rules for the November election.
“The Rule ensures that States remain responsible for determining voter eligibility and eligibility to vote by mail, and it does not dictate ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures,” Sauer wrote. “The Rule thus plainly does not seize control of States’ administration of elections — it simply imposes reasonable preparation requirements for certain election-related mail.”
Sauer argued that if the court does not allow the changes to proceed, it would cause “serious irreparable harm on the federal government, the States themselves, and the voting public” by “nullifying the Postal Service’s efforts to address the risk that the federal mails will be used to perpetrate voter fraud.”
Experts have consistently rejected those claims — including in their own filings before the high court.
Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA Law, joined three other election experts to argue to the lower court that the Trump administration’s claims of injury were “speculative and weak.” They noted that the administration had “offered no evidence” in court that the new rules would “stop any appreciable amount of voter fraud or even that voter fraud through the mails is a widespread problem that USPS should address.”
Meanwhile, they wrote, there was “undisputed evidence” presented to the lower court that the Postal Service is “still not prepared to implement its new rule or do so accurately and efficiently, even as states have begun mailing out their ballots,” and that the “harm to the states and to voters is enormous, as the rule threatens to disenfranchise millions of elderly voters, disabled voters, military voters and all others including the most vulnerable who depend on mail voting, in both red and blue states.”
The Democrat-led states also noted that the Trump administration hadn’t proved that widespread voter fraud is a legitimate threat, but had shown it is ill-prepared itself to implement the changes without causing widespread disruption — as evidenced in part by the whistleblower’s claims.
It’s unclear when the Supreme Court will rule, though a relatively quick decision is expected given the emergency nature of the appeal.

Trump claims firefighters carried him to safety ‘right after’ 9/11, but his account is disputed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:52:55 UTC
05:52:55 KST

Trump claims firefighters carried him to safety ‘right after’ 9/11, but his account is disputed
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
As the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches, Donald Trump has lashed out at the press over coverage questioning where he was. This week, he said two firefighters carried him to safety near the US Steel Building right after the attacks, though he later said that he wasn’t at the World Trade Center on the day of the collapse. His version of events, and alleged role at Ground Zero have evolved many times over the years, as Vedika Bahl fact-checks in Truth or Fake.
In Tuesday’s speech in Washington, Donald Trump said he had been working on a building in New York and took his construction workers to Ground Zero “right after this happened”, and described being carried to safety by two firefighters near the US Steel Building.
“I’ll never forget two firemen,” Trump said. “We thought it was coming down on top of us,” he recalled, saying the firefighters grabbed him under the arms and “literally lifted me up” before running with him.
The remarks prompted renewed scrutiny of Trump’s account, including by New York Magazine, which questioned his version of events.
Trump subsequently responded on Truth Social, criticising the publication and clarifying that he was not at the World Trade Center “on the same day as the collapse, but shortly thereafter.”
But that same version of events has been rebutted by witnesses and journalists, and indeed even Trump himself at one point. He’s repeated the tale at least once before, in a January 2016 campaign stop in New Hampshire, however that time, he said the incident occurred “a couple of days after 9/11”
There are also questions about whether Trump was at Ground Zero at all. CNN journalist Daniel Dale - known for fact-checking false claims from Trump’s first term - said the US President was at Trump Tower, several miles from the World Trade Center.
A former Trump Organization executive also told Politico in 2016 that Trump was in his office at Trump Tower during the attacks: “We saw it out the window. I was sitting in his office.”
Trump has made other claims over the years about his presence at Ground Zero and his involvement in the recovery effort. Two days after the attacks, he told reporters that he had hundreds of workers at the site and was bringing more.
However, a New York Fire Department chief told The New York Times in 2019 that, despite spending months at Ground Zero, he never saw Trump there. Other news reports have placed Trump at the site in the days following the attacks, although the extent of his involvement in the recovery operation remains unclear.
Trump also said in 2015 he personally saw people jumping from the World Trade Center, though Trump Tower was roughly four miles from the site, making such a view difficult to reconcile with his location.
That same year, Trump claimed that he had seen “thousands and thousands” of Muslim Americans in New Jersey celebrating the attacks. New Jersey officials found no evidence of such mass celebrations, deeming this account false and Islamophobic.

Palestinian officials in Ramallah described Britain’s decision to ban dealings with Israeli settlements in the West Bank as a “significant political achievement,” particularly in light of growing incidents of violence by settlers against Palestinians recently.

"This shows Britain’s understanding of international relations and its support for Palestinian statehood," he told The Jerusalem Post.

Another Palestinian Authority official told the Post that “It affirms that the world cannot accept the continued Israeli occupation and settlement activity, which violate international law.”

He stated that confronting settlement activity is not merely a political choice but an 'international responsibility'. He said that protecting the two-state solution begins with halting settlement expansion, holding accountable those who undermine it, and isolating the "apartheid government."
Fattouh emphasized that international positions must go beyond political condemnation to include binding legal, diplomatic, and economic measures, such as a comprehensive ban on settlement products entering markets, ending all commercial or investment dealings with settlements, and restricting entities and companies that finance or support settlement activity.
He also called on European countries and Canada to adopt a clear international framework to isolate settlements, cut off funding sources, and end any form of political or economic protection that enables their continuation.

“I am so grateful to have had the opportunity to build a life here, serving our community as a councillor, school governor and community activist. Now I am standing to say thank you and to give back the hope you gave me.

Abdi-Wali has worked for more than a decade as a volunteer and trustee for local charities and is a governor of two schools in the borough, according to Labour. The party’s members queued outside St Pancras church in Euston for the selection meeting on Wednesday night, with voters including MP Georgia Gould and her mother, Lady Gail Rebuck.
The local figure will probably go head to head with Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, who announced his intention to fight for the Commons seat.
Local Greens in Holborn and St Pancras still have to formally select their candidate under a process that will not be completed until next Friday. But it seems likely they will endorse Polanski, under whose leadership the party has soared in the polls, with membership more than tripling.
The high-stakes byelection on 8 October will pit the star power of Polanski against a resurgent Labour under Andy Burnham. Starmer announced he was stepping down from the seat he has represented since 2015 last week, in after his departure as prime minister.
Starmer saw his majority more than halve at the last election from nearly 28,000 to 11,500 amid a challenge from the left. The Greens came third, with Starmer’s main competitor being Andrew Feinstein, a leftwing independent.
In a boost to Polanski, Feinstein has since confirmed he would not stand, indicating that the Camden People’s Alliance, the group which emerged from his campaign, would most likely back the Greens.
Labour have further lost support to the Greens in the area since the general election. The Greens made gains on Camden council in the local elections in May, although they failed to take control of it.
But recent missteps by Polanski have dented his popularity, while Burnham’s arrival in Downing Street has boosted Labour’s standing in the polls.
Abdi-Wali became the focus of unwanted attention last week when Reform’s Zia Yusuf suggested she was not British in a social media post that was described as “straightforward racism” by Labour.
Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, posted on X: “The frontrunner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former prime minister Keir Starmer in our parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?”
The Greens are planning to flood the constituency with volunteers, while Labour said all members of the cabinet were likely to campaign in the seat, with campaigners calling the first official weekend of the campaign the “Make Hope Win Weekend”.
Labour’s byelection campaign lead, Liam Conlon MP, said Abdi-Wali was a “fantastic local champion” with a strong delivery record on “revamping council homes, reducing homelessness, and tackling nuisance antisocial behaviour”.
He added: “She will be a powerful progressive voice for Holborn and St Pancras to work alongside our Labour government to improve the lives for local people.
“Labour will run a positive campaign that brings people together and restores hope. I look forward to joining hundreds of members to campaign with Sagal over the coming weeks.”

Forces from the IDF’s 36th Division had been operating in recent weeks to clear two underground routes in the area. The military said it had achieved operational control above and below ground and cleared the area of terrorists, with some killed and others fleeing.
“The activity to neutralize the underground infrastructure that was cleared of terrorists is continuing, and once it is completed, the IDF will redeploy in a renewed defensive posture,” the military said.
According to the IDF, command centers, weapons rooms, generator rooms, living quarters, showers and a kitchen were found underground, facilities that “allowed the terrorists to manage the fighting and remain there for long periods.”
The military described the network as “strategic infrastructure built over two decades, financed and planned by the Iranian terror regime.”
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at the time: “Today it can already be said: We eliminated a great many terrorists there.”
The IDF said operational control of the ridge was achieved through a series of actions that included ambushes, fire directed at tunnel shafts, grenades, drones and other strikes.
According to the military, terrorists from Hezbollah’s Badr Unit built the infrastructure with Iranian funding and joint planning. The two underground routes were used by the unit to manage fire systems, fight IDF forces and carry out terror plans against Israeli civilians over the past several decades.
The IDF operation has also drawn a warning from Iran. Reuters reported that Tehran warned the United States last month that it would “respond forcefully” to an Israeli attack on Ali Taher Ridge, where, according to Iran, Iranian military personnel were trapped alongside Hezbollah terrorists.

inside the serpentine world of javier senosiain’s quetzalcóatl park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:35:12 UTC
05:35:12 KST

Quetzalcóatl Park, located about an hour outside of Mexico City, is the sprawling, serpentine creation of Javier Senosiain Aguilar. Although started years ago in 2007, the park is still a work in progress. The water fixture, mosaiced and shaped like the head of a snake, spews water into a small reserve. A greenhouse is bathed in a shattered rainbow of light coming through a stained-glass roof. Its grassy mazes create vertiginous paths where visitors can lose themselves in the Mexican architect’s spiraling, psychedelic, and lush garden.
To speak of Senosiain’s work at large is to talk about the natural and animal worlds. One character that appears frequently is the snake, a pink cartoon of which is the slithering logo for the park. It’s fitting, as Quetzalcóatl is the name of a feathered serpent that appears in Aztec mythology. On the park grounds, a cream-colored serpent, covered in mosaic, creates a small waterfall that looks over the landscape surrounding the park. A curving amphitheater and zigzagging pathways invoke the animal in motion. There’s even a topiary sculpture that emerges from the grass in the shape of the two-fanged reptile.
Some of the organic structures that sit around the park get their organic shapes—where ceilings melt into the floor and the walls curve down to the ground—by a process frequently used by Senosiain: ferro-cement. It’s a system where metal rods are first placed for structure, like a skeleton. Then a wire mesh is used to create the sloping forms that are then covered in a mortar that makes the whole structure solid. In a 2019 piece in designboom on Senosiain’s organic house, the architect describes this process, saying, ‘the assembly of the ferrocement began on the template that looked like a skateboard track, forming the shell with a metallic skeleton, in which the rods were arranged in the form of rings, changing the height according to the space. next, the rods were spirally wound. at the end of the frame, two ropes of coop braided together were fixed, and then the concrete was thrown.’
Although the space is not, as of 2026, open to the public, visitors who want to inhabit Senosiain’s creation can book a tour of the space or even host an event on the park grounds. The Farm, one of the inhabitable spaces, was created with the intention of housing domestic animals. Now, the cozy nook, built into a grassy mound that emerges from the land, can be used for cocktail parties or intimate dinners.
On the property, a greenhouse provides a technicolor home to a lush garden. The space is formed in a spiral, a geometry that has often reappears in Senosiain’s work for its frequent occurrence in nature and flowing, curved shape. Moving through the curved walkways, the stone floors and the blooming plants are dappled in bright teals, reds, yellows, greens, and blues. At its center, a domed tessellation of glass covers a small circular pool that receives a trickle of water from a sloping trough decorated in red mosaic tiles.
In describing Senosiain’s practice, unearthing why he would embark on such an ambitious project, Quetzalcóatl Park invokes the architect himself, quoting, ‘Human beings must not detach themselves from their primal impulses, from their biological being. They must remember that they originate from a natural source and that the search for their home cannot be separated from their roots; that is, they must avoid creating an unnatural habitat.’ Following these principles, the space forms amphitheaters, pools, and a greenhouse into the landscape instead of against it.
Quetzalcóatl Park is just one manifestation of Senosiain’s sensibility for undulating, brightly colored, and fantastic built worlds. El Tiburón (The Shark), built in 1990, is an extension of his private residence. With a curved glass window that resembles the mouth of the aquatic predator, it looks out onto Parque Nacional de los Remedios. Nearby to the park, El Nido de Quetzalcóatl is a snaking structure with round, porthole-like windows and a snake’s head, that holds 10 apartments, some of which can be booked on Airbnb. All of his creations invite the imaginative design enthusiast to wander through their depths and explore the mind of Senosiain himself.
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.

Iran and US strike tankers in biggest shipping attack since war began
Iran and the US on Wednesday traded their biggest wave of attacks on shipping since the war began, with Iran saying it struck 10 vessels near the Strait of Hormuz after US forces sank five Iranian oil tankers. Brent crude oil surged above $100 a barrel as fears grew over global energy supplies.
Iran said on Wednesday it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the US sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war.
The attacks sent the price of oil surging, with benchmark Brent crude futures breaching $100 a barrel for the first time since July. At least one seafarer aboard a tanker was reported killed and another listed as missing.
Iran also said it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by US forces in Jordan. Attacks by both sides since the end of August have shattered a month of relative calm, with the US and Iran hitting military, shipping and energy assets.
The Revolutionary Guards said they would sharply escalate their response to any further attacks, hitting 20 targets if the enemy struck two or three. Iran would soon release maps of a new, enlarged off-limits zone at sea that would extend as far as Chabahar on the far reaches of Iran’s coast near Pakistan, the Guards said.

Iranian tankers ablaze
The Americans said they destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, releasing video of ships ablaze before they sank.
The US military’s Central Command called its attacks a response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a US Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days. No Americans were harmed, the US said.
Washington has announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers in retaliation for fire that threatens its warships, and says it has hit 10 so far over the past week.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.

Strait choked off

Even more severe than the rise in crude prices has been a surge in the cost of the fuels refined from it. The politically sensitive average retail price of US diesel hit a fresh all-time high on Wednesday above $5.94 a gallon.
Escalating combat between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement that controls most populated parts of Yemen has created additional uncertainty for energy markets.

Saudi authorities announced alerts on Wednesday in two of the cities hit the previous day, but later said the threat had passed.
A Saudi-backed government based in the south of Yemen has launched a multi-pronged assault on areas controlled by the Houthis, who have threatened Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.

Palestine Letter: Reporting our lives, not your ideology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:24:14 UTC
05:24:14 KST

One day, a colleague who worked in a Catholic magazine for which I had written, and who was writing an article about Palestinian Christians, wanted to interview me as an average Palestinian Christian. At one point, this journalist who came from a European country, asked me if I identified first as Christian or as Palestinian. I asked her back if she had ever had to answer that same question, and choose between her faith or religious heritage, and her nationality to put before the other. She said that she hadn’t, and when I asked her why, she said that in her case, the question wasn’t relevant, because it wasn’t political.
Somehow, my identity, which is, like the identity of any person anywhere, multi-layered, became a political issue. Not political in the sense that my answer would say something about my values or ideas, no. It is political in the sense that my answer, whatever it would be, would be a contribution to a controversial debate, between extensive, clashing world views, none of which is necessarily mine. In other words, the way I identify would be an ideological statement for somebody else.
This is deeply disturbing, because I didn’t choose it. It is the situation of my country, and the fate that has been that of my people for the last century, that has made anything coming from us, Palestinians, ideologically consequential for others, and therefore controversial. This makes my work, and that of all Palestinian journalists who spend our time telling the world about our country and our people, by definition a risky one, as our perspective, and the narrative that we offer will be and have been understood as ideology, and therefore as less valuable, less serious, and less credible.
This is the result of power dynamics; the conqueror, the stronger party gets to define what the conventional wisdom and the objective reality are, and what is labeled as ideological and political. This definition is made based on the ideology of the stronger party. It is so much about power dynamics that the weaker part is pressed to believe that the simplest opinion about themselves is ideological.
As a journalism student, I was trained to avoid slipping into endorsing political and ideological stands by giving equal coverage to opposed points of view. When writing about Palestine, I ended up understanding that the Palestinian refugees’ right to return is to be presented as one of the points of view, for my work to be professional and journalistically impartial. This is the result of a political process; Palestinian movements advocated for the right of return, and Israel refused it, and the more a Palestinian movement insisted on the right of return and refused to negotiate on it, the more ‘radical’ it seemed.
This issue, the right of return, has been more influential in defining the Palestinian ‘ideological’ spectrum than differences between Palestinians over the way to organize society, the choice of economic model, or the role of religion in public life. However, the right of a person to leave their country and return at any time is a fundamental human right enshrined in the international declaration of human rights. But the right of Palestinian refugees to return, the Palestinians’ right to their land, as the way a Palestinian Christian identifies, and eventually, just as the name of Palestine itself are deemed ‘ideological’, and need to be put between brackets.
In the past three years, we have seen the display of this logic to its maximum in mainstream media. The number of Palestinians killed became an ideological statement. The statement that they were killed by Israeli bombs became an ideological statement. The statement that most of them were civilians also became an ideological statement. Today, the right of the people of Gaza to reconstruction, food, medicine, having their lives back and running them themselves is put between brackets, and Palestinian voices that are invited or quoted by mainstream media outlets are invited to a debate. A debate over the humanity of their own people between ideologies that are not theirs.
This brings the question back to what kind of journalism we should be doing, outside of mainstream media. Some see independent and alternative media as an ideological one, because it voices causes like the cause of Palestine. But this is a label that is made in the upper levels of discussion, where things as elemental and basic as food, medicine, freedom of movement, dignity, and control over your own life are taken for granted, and the discussion about them is always the discussion about them for others.
But for those who lack them, those who are deprived from them, who are forced to survive every day without them, they are not a matter of discussion or debate. They are not political. They are the difference between one day their children having a chance to live in this world or not.
In the first days of the genocide I saw on TV a Palestinian elderly woman interviewed by Al-Jazeera on her way south, fleeing Israeli bombings on foot, sustained by one of her grandchildren. She said, while holding her tears, that she had fled this same way three times since 1948, and that all that kept her going in life was the hope of seeing the place where her home village once stood once before dying, and instead she is fleeing again.
This reminded me of Palestinian educator and thinker Munir Fasheh, whom I spoke to in Ramallah in 2019, who also struggled to hold his tears when he spoke about his journey to Jerusalem to see the home where his parents lived, occupied by a strange Israeli family who didn’t even know who the house belonged to. I asked myself; Does that Palestinian grandmother think of her longing to her destroyed village as her ‘ideology’? Does Munir Fasheh think of his attachment to Jerusalem and his parents’ home as a political stance? And who am I, who is anybody to tell them that that’s what they are?
This is why independent journalism is not ideological, because we don’t engage in an abstract debate over abstract ideas about somebody else’s life.
We report our lives, and the lives of people around the world for whom basic rights and recognition of their own identity is not abstract. These people are the majority, from Palestine to Minneapolis, and therefore, independent media has the mission of being the mirror of the largest part of the world as it looks. This is why we don’t subscribe to the ‘common wisdom’ labelling of what is ideology and what isn’t. We stick to the common reality of our common humanity.
At least we try.

IAEA board refers Iran to UN Security Council over nuclear ‘non-compliance’
The symbolic escalation has been initiated by the United States, Germany, France and the United Kingdom.
The Board of Governors of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has approved a resolution reporting Iran to the United Nations Security Council for breaching its non-proliferation obligations.
Wednesday’s move is the first time in 20 years that the board, made up of 35 member countries, has passed such a resolution.

The move marks an escalation in the ongoing diplomatic standoff between Iran and Western nations. At least 23 countries voted in favour of the resolution, but Russia, China and Niger opposed it.
However, it is unlikely the UN Security Council will take any action, as Iran’s allies Russia and China are veto-holding members.
The United States and European allies, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, had lobbied the UN nuclear watchdog’s board members in recent days to pass the resolution.
The text noted “with grave concern… Iran’s continued non-compliance with its obligations” and “reiterates its call upon Iran to urgently remedy its non-compliance”.
In a statement on Wednesday, the European Union accused Iran of suspending its cooperation with the IAEA and refusing to allow the agency to inspect its nuclear facilities.
“It is critical and urgent that Iran provides the IAEA with updated verifiable declarations about the quantity and whereabouts of nuclear material and related activities and allows inspections to resume in all its nuclear facilities,” the bloc said.
Iran’s mission to the UN denounced the resolution. “The current situation is created solely because of the criminal acts of aggression by the U.S. and Israeli regime. The delusional objective of the U.S. to force the great Iranian nation into ‘surrender’ and to plunder its oil will never happen,” the mission said in a post on X.
Earlier on Monday, Iran warned that it would retaliate if the resolution passed.
IAEA seeks ‘urgent’ verification access
Iran, as a signatory to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), is forbidden from producing nuclear weapons and has repeatedly said it is not manufacturing them.
The IAEA suspects, however, that Iran has about 400kg (881lbs) of highly enriched uranium, with which 10 nuclear weapons could potentially be manufactured if enriched further.
Since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in June last year, IAEA staff have not been allowed to continue inspecting Iran’s three nuclear facilities, which were reportedly badly damaged or destroyed in the strikes.
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told his agency’s board on Monday that the issue needed to be “urgently” addressed.
“The agency’s lack of information about these facilities and associated nuclear material and our inability to conduct verification activities at these facilities is a matter of serious proliferation concern,” he said.

Victoria’s koalas in chronically poor health and population is half what was previously estimated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:23:27 UTC
05:23:27 KST

The Victorian government sat on a report for more than 12 months that found the state’s koala population was in chronically poor health.
The review of the state’s koala populations, led by state science agency the Arthur Rylah Institute in conjunction with scientists from major universities, was completed for the Victorian government in June 2025.
It estimated there were 217,000 koalas in the state in 2023 and 224,800 in 2024 – a dramatic drop from past estimates of 460,000, which the report attributed to different survey and modelling methodology, rather than an actual population decline.
As part of the research, scientists conducted health and disease assessments on 68 koalas, with 29 of the koalas (43%) found to be in such poor health they “were euthanised on welfare grounds”.
The report warned the surveys found “a higher-than-expected proportion of koalas from seven geographically distinct regions in a state of chronically poor health and welfare”.
The government published the report on Wednesday morning as the new environment minister, Jaclyn Symes, announced $2.6m for koala conservation, including for habitat restoration and research into koala health and genetics.
Leanne Wicker, a wildlife veterinarian who was one of the authors on the report, said researchers had been shocked by the poor health of some of the koalas they found in the field.
“While we were doing this research we knew we were seeing something that urgently needed attention and understanding,” she said. “And it’s been very difficult to get the support and resources needed because the report hadn’t been made public.”
She said the overabundance of certain local Victorian koala populations – such as those at French Island and in western Victoria – had created a perception that the state’s overall koala population was thriving. “What we’ve missed is we have a crisis in our koala populations in Victoria because we have a very concerning level of poor health and welfare.”
Deakin University’s Desley Whisson, another author on the report, said while the 2024 population estimate of about 225,000 koalas “seems like a lot, most of those koalas are in areas where there are high densities of animals”.
“There’s large parts of the state where koalas occur at low densities and are probably in poor health,” she said.
She said the government needed to turn its attention to areas with low numbers “because we could be losing koalas in some parts of the state without even knowing”.
The report used systematic visual and acoustic surveys in 2023 and 2024 to monitor koalas at 182 sites. That data was then used to estimate the overall abundance and distribution of Victoria’s koala population.
The report states the drop in the estimated population from previous estimates of 460,000 was due to changes in the methodology used. It said the new data also represented the first time koala populations had been surveyed statewide.
Of the 68 koalas sampled for health and welfare checks, 39 healthy individuals were rereleased, with healthy animals present at all of the locations sampled, according to the report. But 29 koalas were euthanised due to ill health.
Koalas that were euthanised were more likely to have poor coat condition, dental disease and “wet bottom” (an advanced urinary tract infection, most commonly caused by chlamydia), and were more likely to occur in areas with high koala densities. Dental disease was recorded in 37% of koalas across all life stages and regions, except Mallacoota, according to the report.
The report states that these findings raised concerns “for the health of Victorian koalas”.
“Clinical signs consistent with chronic ill-health were observed across all life stages, suggesting that multiple individual, environmental and demographic stressors may be contributing to prolonged physiological stress within these populations,” the scientists wrote.
Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell said the research painted a grim picture of the health and wellbeing of Victoria’s koalas.
“It is clear that we need to use every lever possible to ensure they’re given the best chance at survival, or we will soon be just like the many states across Australia where koalas are listed as endangered,” she said.
The report also found that 23% of Victoria’s koala population now lived in the state’s blue gum plantation estate “where they occur at much higher density than koalas in neighbouring native forest”.
“Given the high estimated density of koalas within blue gum plantations, changes to the plantation estate size and/or stand ages may result in significant changes to population size,” it states.
Jessica Robertson, from advocacy group the Koala Alliance, called Wednesday’s funding announcement “a calculated political rescue mission for Labor, not for koalas”.
“Sitting on critical ecological data for over a year while koalas continued to suffer and disappear is a shocking failure of transparency and responsibility,” she said.
A Victorian environment department spokesperson said since receiving the report it had been working with other agencies, and consulting external groups, “to prioritise actions and design projects that address its findings and recommendations”.
A spokesperson said Wednesday’s funding announcement was the result of this work.
The environment department’s spokesperson said the timing of the report’s public release had not affected “important work” the government was already doing to manage the health of the state’s koalas.

He Helped Build Powerful AI at OpenAI and Anthropic. Now He's Afraid It Could Kill Us
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:21:30 UTC
05:21:30 KST

For three years, Jacob Coxon helped train increasingly powerful AI systems at OpenAI and Anthropic. On Sept. 8, he walked away.
“I resigned from Anthropic today,” Coxon posted on X. “Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” His dire warning amassed more than 90 million views in less than 24 hours.
What did Coxon see that made him walk away? No single breakthrough, he says. His resignation was driven instead by two conclusions: “One, it’s obvious that things are speeding up, and two, they’re not under control,” the 27-year-old Brit tells TIME.
Coxon’s departure is unusual. Many of the most prominent researchers to leave frontier AI companies with public warnings worked on safety. But Coxon helped build the capabilities he now fears, spending roughly three years conducting pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic. His resignation offers a glimpse of how concern about the pace of development has spread beyond the teams specifically charged with making advanced AI safer.
AI’s rapid improvement has been particularly evident in mathematics, says Coxon, who studied the subject at Cambridge before moving into AI. In recent months, AI labs have announced solutions to several longstanding mathematical problems. Most notably, OpenAI claims to have resolved the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem—one of mathematics’ seven Millennium Prize Problems—using roughly 10,000 concurrent agents over 88 hours. If that trend continues, and extends to AI research itself, Coxon fears it will kick off a feedback loop of further acceleration.
Read more: What happens when AI builds itself?
Meanwhile, in the recent Hugging Face incident, OpenAI’s models broke out of the infrastructure meant to contain them and hacked another AI company to cheat on a cybersecurity benchmark. The episode drove home the fact that the problem of controlling AI systems remains unsolved. To Coxon, it made the sci-fi scenario of AI models escaping human control seem plausible, and perhaps urgent. “It's not like some weird, distant, far-flung concern. It is the default trajectory in the next couple of years, unless people start taking some sort of action,” he says. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
Read more: OpenAI’s Models Went Rogue.
Does Coxon regret his work advancing the technology that he now fears? “Definitely … But also the world did look very different three years ago, and I think it’s easy to see with the benefit of hindsight,” he says. “I guess it takes some time to fully internalize emotionally the fact that there’s a decent chance the whole thing goes wrong,” he adds.
Before leaving, Coxon discussed his decision with “many” colleagues and found broad agreement that the AI industry’s current trajectory carried significant risks. What kept others at their desks, he says, was a kind of fatalism. “There’s this atmosphere of almost resignation,” he says, “where people have accepted that the whole race is happening and as such, the best thing they can do is put their head down, try and make their own work as safely as possible, even if they think there's a decent chance the whole thing just spirals out of control.”
Some of Coxon’s former colleagues shared his post on X. “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade,” wrote Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment stress testing. “I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” he added.
At Anthropic, Coxon says, the risks he fears were debated openly. OpenAI, where he worked before joining Anthropic earlier this year, was more guarded. He attributes that partly to OpenAI’s leakier culture, which he says made candid internal discussion difficult and executives’ true views harder to discern. “At OpenAI, there are many more people who are there either just for money or just haven’t really thought about the stakes,” he adds.
Many in Washington shared Coxon’s post, citing it as a sign for the government to act. To Taylor Lorenz, a technology journalist, Coxon’s intervention was “sanctimonious doomer posting.”
“I think the word ‘doomer’ is kind of insane, because all you really have to do is look at the public statements of the CEOs,” Coxon says. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei signed a statement declaring that mitigating “the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.”
Coxon says he’d like to see, at minimum, leading AI companies agree to not accelerate recursive self-improvement, or leaning on powerful internal models to accelerate the development of future AI systems.
Coxon says he’s inspired by the AI Futures Project, the organization behind the viral forecast AI 2027, started by former OpenAI whistleblower Daniel Kokotajlo. “I hope to try and do work in that vein, something along the lines of communicating to people what the world will look like,” Coxon says. “I’m not sure exactly what that’s going to look like yet, but we’ll see.”

Ukraine Opens First Underground Kindergarten in Kharkiv Region
Ukraine’s first underground kindergarten, “Mobil,” has officially opened in the Pisochyn community of the Kharkiv region, the Ukrainian Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine reported on September 8.
It allows up to 260 children to safely attend in-person preschool education even during air raid alerts.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The underground space is equipped with eight classrooms, a medical point, a dining room, restrooms, and showers. The shelter operates autonomously using two independent power sources and backup generators.
Safe indoor passageways connect the protective structure directly to the main kindergarten buildings, ensuring children and staff can access the shelter without going outside. The facility was built with a focus on accessibility, incorporating elevators, lifts, and barrier-free routes for children with disabilities and other limited-mobility groups, according to the ministry.
“This year, the state for the first time provided separate funding for the arrangement of shelters in preschool educational institutions,” Anastasiia Konovalova, Deputy Minister of Education and Science of Ukraine for Preschool Education, stated.
“Our task is to support communities with the highest security risks and help as many kindergartens as possible resume the educational process in an in-person format, because the opportunity to learn and develop in a safe educational environment is extremely important for every child,” she continued.
The project was co-financed by state, regional, and local budgets. In 2026, the Ukrainian government allocated its first dedicated subvention—totaling over 972 million UAH ($21.8 million)—specifically to construct and equip shelters in preschools.
Similar projects are currently being implemented across nine regions, prioritizing high-risk frontline communities and facilities with ongoing construction. Local communities are carrying out the development with financial backing from the European Union under the Ukraine Facility instrument.
Beyond the physical danger of air raids, Ukrainian children also face deportation. Russian negotiators previously treated abducted Ukrainian children as prisoners of war, suggesting they be included in POW exchange lists rather than returned through humanitarian channels.
Ukrainian First Lady Olena Zelenska stated that despite Ukraine presenting a verified list of 300 children, Russia continues to hold and subject thousands of Ukrainian minors to ideological indoctrination, severely hindering efforts to repatriate an estimated 20,000 illegally deported children.

UK man charged with assisting Russian military spies in sabotage plot
A British man has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service after alleged contact with Russian military spies, according to the Crown Prosecution Service.

He allegedly received instructions from a suspected representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency, with the intent to commit an act of sabotage.
Cammidge is set to appear at Westminster Magistrates Court on Thursday.
Frank Ferguson, Chief Crown Prosecutor for the CPS Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said: “Prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.”

GRU Volunteer Corps
The United Kingdom deemed the GRU Volunteer Corps a national security threat in July for collecting foreign intelligence and conducting hostile covert operations on behalf of Russian military spies.
Support for the GRU was banned under a new law intended to give the government more powers to tackle proxy organisations carrying out hostile activity on behalf of foreign states. Supporters convicted of assisting the group face up to 14 years in prison.
GRU has been blamed by UK authorities for hostile activities against the country and allies that include the 2018 Salisbury nerve agent attack and wider sabotage and intelligence operations across Europe.
Security Minister Dan Jarvis said the UK would take “whatever action is necessary” to defend against Russian threats. “Anyone attempting to undermine our security will feel the full force of the law,” he said in a statement.
Relations between Britain and Russia have deteriorated sharply since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, with British authorities increasingly warning about alleged Russian espionage, sabotage and other hostile state activity.
Last month, Russia warned it could strike British military targets in response to Ukrainian attacks using British-supplied long-range missiles.

Combat Weather Airmen Stressed to Their Limits in Army Competition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:17:20 UTC
05:17:20 KST

In the small world of Air Force weather specialists, combat weather specialists are a niche unto themselves, deploying with Army ground units to provide forecasts and, if need be, fight alongside those Soldiers. For Staff Sgt. Francisco Estrada, the hardest part of the job isn’t the possibility of ground combat, though—it’s briefing Army helicopter pilots on short notice how wind, fog, rain, and other conditions will affect a mission.
Being right about hazardous conditions often means an upcoming flight is scrubbed. Being wrong about them, though, could cause helicopter engines to fail or send an aircrew flying into the side of a mountain.
“Anybody can sit behind a desk and put everything together when they have all the time in the world, but when you are on the fly like you are oftentimes out in the field … it’s really hard to gather everything that you need do it well and do it confidently, when somebody’s asking you, ‘Hey, well, can we can we launch? Can we go?’” Estrada told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Airmen in this unique career field were tested Aug. 12-13 when combat weather squadrons from across the Air Force participated in Thunder Challenge 2026, a physically and mentally challenging competition that this year put six three-Airmen teams from around the world through two days of high-pressure skill tests at Fort Drum, N.Y.
Competitors marched 10 miles, carrying weapons and 35-pound rucksacks. The competition also included a night land navigation course and a simulated mountain rescue on foot through the thick forested terrain.
Skill stations tested everything from small-arms knowledge to combat casualty care—combat-related tasks these Airmen could need at any time since they are attached to Army combat units. In between these tactical tasks, the combat weather Airmen, known as staff weather officers, or SWOs, also had to prove their technical job expertise by completing tasks ranging from setting up portable weather sensors to a timed weather knowledge test.
Thunder Challenge “is the only competition that measures the lethal combination” of tactical skills as well the “environmental science” knowledge needed operate within Army combat units and advise aviators and combat leaders on how changing weather conditions could impact future missions, Chief Master Sergeant Ronald Buchanan of the Air Force’s 5th Combat Weather Group, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“It’s unique because you they go straight from grueling, physical challenges such weighted ruck marches or live-fire stress shooting directly to setting up tactical meteorological equipment, and then from that, using that same equipment or their weather knowledge to deliver an Indo-Pacific-focused forecast brief, not only just under the physical but also under that mental fatigue as well,” Buchanan said.
“These competitions help further prove that we can operate and deliver critical environmental intelligence at the absolute forward edge of any battlefield.”
Estrada, whose team from the 7th Combat Weather Squadron in Germany beat out five other teams to win first place this year, was also part of last year’s winning team at Thunder Challenge. He has been a combat weather specialist for the last three of his seven years in the Air Force. While assigned to the Army’s 12th Combat Aviation Brigade at Katterbach Army Airfield, Estrada has seen a lot of Airmen “get scared” when it comes to preparing an air mission brief on a short deadline with limited data.
During Thunder Challenge, teams had to prepare a brief in about 45 minutes with “very little data, and more importantly, with data from a location that we didn’t know,” Estrada said.
“It’s such a compact timeframe to do that confidently … you have to consider so much. Whether it’s where they’re flying to, their route of flight, are they going over an ocean because at that point, we have to consider what the sea temperatures are like,” Estrada said, adding that headwinds, crosswinds and other conditions that can “make or break their decision to fly, especially when it comes to fuel consumption.”
Normally, SWOs will have at least several hours’ notice, if not a day or two, to prepare a brief and “we’ve had time to kind of do everything and kind of get used to the localized weather pattern,” Estrada said.
Satellite imagery helps with dissecting approaching weather fronts that can bring stormy, wet weather. Topography plays a large role in preparing a brief, Estrada said, especially in the mountains, where low ceilings can be dangerous.
Helicopter pilots have low cloud ceiling minimums they can fly in, “but in those mountains, because they hold so much moisture to trap it all in, it’ll be socked in so you’ll have ceilings go from like 3,000 feet to all of a sudden, your ceilings are on the surface,” Estrada said. “You can’t get through it.”
Army aviators spend a lot of time studying available weather forecasting applications but depend on combat weather Airmen for an unbiased analysis of flying conditions, said UH-60 Black Hawk pilot Capt. Tom Pelkey, who was one of the judges on the air brief portion of the competition.
“You will not launch until the Air Force weather officer gives you a brief,” he said, explaining that Army regulations require it to “ensure that the pilots themselves don’t shop for favorable weather” to suit their mission.
Many factors are needed for a good air brief such as “what’s the moonset going to be if we’re launching at night—like how much illumination? What’s the sea state going to be since we’re flying over water?” said Pelkey, who is assigned to 3rd Battalion, 10th Combat Aviation Brigade at Drum.
Air density is also a critical piece of data helicopter pilots need when planning a mission, Pelkey said. Helicopters need dense air to generate lift through the main rotor blades. Air density decreases with altitude and has an adverse impact on aircraft performance.
“The engine’s going to work based on the density altitude or how much moisture is in the air affected by the temperature, so if it’s going to be hot and moist, my engine doesn’t have much air to beat into combustion,” Pelkey said. “And that’s something helicopter pilots, and even pilots in general, have to be aware of … because that limits us on what the aircraft can carry, how many people we can carry, and what maneuvers we can do.”
When critiquing each team’s air brief, Pelkey said pilots stress that they need combat weather Airmen to provide analysis along with weather data.
“The big thing that we want … the SWOs to understand is, ‘you bring me the weather. All right, so what? What does that mean for my mission exactly?’” Pelkey said. “If we had two routes that we’re going to fly, you need to recommend the route that I’m going to fly based on the weather.”
Sending combat weather Airmen to Thunder Challenge gives leaders an opportunity to gauge the effectiveness of the training that SWOs receive throughout the year, said Col. Staci Coleman, commander of the 5th Combat Weather Group, which commands the 18th Combat Weather Squadron headquartered at of Fort Bragg, N.C., and the 3rd Combat Weather Squadron out of Fort Hood, Texas.
The competition “enables leaders to put the Airmen to the test, so we can see where they’re at with the development of their skills,” Coleman said. “Can they apply their weather expertise and operate as warfighters and make good decisions under pressure? So, we use that as an opportunity to put them under stress just to see how they can respond and to show them where the gaps are in their own training and things that they need to improve on.”
Coleman added that “it shows us where we’re strong and where we need to improve and ensures that we’re building combat-ready Airmen who are ready for the fight.”
To 1st Lt. Isabel Weiss, participating in the competition was a great experience for her “very junior team,” since it was “totally different from what most people think of when they think of the Air Force and when they think of weather support.”
“I think a lot of people think of computer people just looking at models, but it was a really intense competition, and we got to go into the Army combat skills that we’ve learned, and also we got to show our other proficiency,” said Weiss, who is part of an 18th CWS detachment that’s attached to the Army’s 3rd Combat Aviation Brigade at Fort Stewart, Ga. “We were into it; I thought it was amazing.”
Her team came in fourth place, which she is “very proud of” since “we were brand new to this type of competition environment,” said Weiss, who was named Fittest SWO from her combined score on the fitness test, 10-mile ruck march, and mountaineering portion of the competition.
Her team trained at Fort Stewart for the night land navigation, but the course at Drum was “very hard, and it was pitch black,” Weiss said. “We only had red light headlamps, and two of our headlamps died.”
“We were in the trenches for sure, but that was great,” she said. “I really do like this tactical stuff. … We had our face paints on, we had our bulletproof vests and helmets, sleeping outside, shooting weapons; it was just a really cool thing that you don’t get to do very often with the Air Force.”
The competition was also great on-the-job training for her junior Airmen teammates, Weiss said.
“I think the first time that they go to an exercise, or when they get ready for deployment, they’re going to be so familiar with the equipment, when it’s used, how it’s used, and then just working in a high-pressure situation—I think it’s a really unique thing that I’ve never heard of an Airman experiencing so early in their career.”
For Estrada, the hardest field skill was the mountain rescue portion of the competition that required teams to locate a dummy casualty and move “him” through steep, wooded terrain on a “Skedco,” which is a special stretcher equipped with straps for securing a casualty that can be lowered down steep inclines by ropes.
“We had to assess him for any injuries or any wounds, and … then we had to move him in Skedco from point A to point B,” Estrada said. “I think it might have been a good 100 meters, long enough to just be exhausting.” Teams then had to lower the casualty down one cliff and up to the top of another steep rise, he said.
Estrada said he will likely compete in next year’s competition as well. “It gives you an opportunity to kind of gauge where you’re at versus like your peers,” he said. “And I think there’s something rewarding about that—seeing all your effort, all the dedication that you put into your skillset to kind of become a better forecaster, a better combat weather team. There’s something so gratifying about that, that it’s hard to kind of walk away from.”
