New record set: Ukrainian drones strike Russian gas facility over 3,000 km away in Siberia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:57:42 UTC
04:57:42 KST

New record set: Ukrainian drones strike Russian gas facility over 3,000 km away in Siberia
Ukraine's Special Operations Forces (SSO) carried out Kyiv's deepest strike into Russia so far in the full-scale war, attacking a natural gas facility 3,200 kilometers (1,988 miles) from the Ukrainian border on Sept. 9, the military said. 
Ukraine's General Staff announced a successful strike on the Novy Urengoy Gas Condensate Treatment Plant (GCTP) in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug. 
Novy Urengoy is located in northwestern Siberia, over 3,000 kilometers from Ukraine's border. The attack marks the first time Ukrainian forces have struck Russia's Yamalo-Nenets region.
"Until today, this area was considered completely safe territory for the aggressor," the SSO wrote on Telegram.
The GCTP facility processes 19.5 million tons of crude oil and natural gas annually and produces diesel fuel and other petroleum products for Russia's military. The record-breaking strike also targeted the nearby Purovsky Gas Condensate Processing Plant.
Ukrainian weapons manufacturer Fire Point, producer of the Flamingo missile, said that its FP-1 drone model was used to carry out the strike.
Fires and smoke billowing from the plant were visible in footage shot by residents of Novy Urengoy. Monitoring channel Exilenova-Plus posted footage of the facility releasing excess gas through flare stacks to prevent explosions.
The attack was confirmed by Dmitry Artyukhov, governor of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug.
The strike on the GCTP facility was 600 kilometers (about 372 miles) from a major Russian liquefied national gas (LNG) site: the Yamal LNG project, located on Russia's Arctic Yamal Peninsula.
Yamal LNG is one of the country's largest LNG projects, accounting for over 60% of its total LNG exports — most of which flow to the European Union.
Alexander Kirk, sanctions campaigner at the German environmental and human rights organization Urgewald, said Ukraine's attack should serve as a wake-up call to Europe.
"The war has reached Russia's Arctic gas heartland, close to Yamal LNG, just days before this weekend's European Arctic Summit," Kirk said in a statement.
"The EU needs to get a grip. It should use the upcoming 22nd sanctions package to sanction all 14 Arc7 tankers sustaining Yamal LNG and close the sanctions gap around the European maritime and maintenance services keeping them operational."
Kirk urged EU countries to impose economic penalties against Russian LNG "before potential kinetic sanctions are applied to the Russian gas infrastructure supplying the European market."
The Yamalo-Nenets strikes demonstrate how Ukraine has increasingly extended the range of its unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in a campaign against Russia's energy infrastructure. 
In one of its previous farthest-reaching strikes, Ukrainian forces struck an oil refinery in Omsk, nearly 2,500 kilometers (around 1,550 miles) from Ukraine's border, the General Staff said on July 6. Ukrainian long-range drones also recently targeted oil refineries in Russia's Perm Oblast, located more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine, on Sept. 7.
Emphasizing Ukraine's success with long-range UAVs, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines, insurers, and foreign governments that Russian airspace "will be de facto closed" because of Ukrainian drone strikes.

An organized crime group member wanted on an Interpol Red Notice over attacks targeting a cafe and the Iraqi Consulate General in Istanbul was arrested while entering Türkiye from Georgia, prosecutors said on Wednesday.
Muhammed Ali Cinar was detained at the Turkgozu Border Gate in the northeastern province of Ardahan after being released from a prison in Georgia, according to a statement by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office.
The prosecutor's office said Cinar was identified as a suspect in attacks targeting a cafe in Istanbul's Bahcelievler district on Nov. 30, 2024, and the Iraqi Consulate General in the city's Sisli district on March 21, 2025.
An Interpol Red Notice was issued for his arrest as part of an investigation by the Organized Crime Investigation Bureau.
Authorities learned that Cinar had been released from prison in Georgia, and was detained as he entered Türkiye through the Turkgozu Border Gate.
Investigation also revealed that Cinar is standing trial on charges of membership in a criminal organization before Istanbul's 31st High Criminal Court.
He was formally arrested by a court following legal procedures.

'Passengers or pilots?' Europe looks to challenge US dominance in space sector with €10 billion plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

'Passengers or pilots?' Europe looks to challenge US dominance in space sector with €10 billion plan
Key figures from Europe’s space industry and other international players have converged on Paris to discuss how to advance the continent’s ambitions in a global market dominated by the United States.
The two-day International Space Summit that started Wednesday gathers officials, astronauts, researchers and industry leaders from about 120 countries to discuss the future of the space industry and pursue potential business deals.
“Europe is taking its destiny into its own hands, including in space,” French President Emmanuel Macron said in a message posted on X. He called for innovation and investment “to build a powerful Europe, independent even in space”.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Macron’s space summit underlines his push to reduce Europe’s reliance on the US for vital tech services, which extends to space launches as well as satellites for communications and reconnaissance.
The chief of the European Space Agency (ESA), Josef Aschbacher, on Wednesday called for a €10-billion ($11.6-billion) investment over 10 years for Europe to achieve independence in the space sector.
"Will we be passengers or pilots?" Aschbacher asked European ministers during a closed meeting Wednesday evening.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
He pointed to the rapid development in space technology by countries around the world from satellite development to the exploration of the Moon and Mars.
"In this emerging context, Europe must position itself as an indispensable partner, with its own capabilities," he said, according to a copy of his speech given to AFP.
If Europe commits to the path of furthering space exploration, Aschbacher estimated it would require an investment of around one billion euros per year for the next decade.
Without it, Europe would remain dependent on other players in the space industry, which also comes at a cost.
Read moreFrench astronaut Sophie Adenot completes second ISS mission spacewalk
"Buying flights for European astronauts from foreign providers would cost 5 billion euro over 10 years, with the majority of that money going into foreign industry and will require permission to fly beyond Europe's control," he explained.
"Alternatively, we can invest in capabilities that remain in Europe, create European jobs, strengthen European autonomy, inspire our youth and future workforce, and secure a stronger hand in international negotiations," he said.
Earlier at the summit, French astronaut Thomas Pesquet told AFP that Europe cannot stay on the sidelines in the space industry.
"We're leaders in technology, we have universities, labs, companies, space agencies – we need to take matters into our own hands," he said.
ESA member states could decide on how to move forward on Aschbacher's call for greater autonomy in the sector at a ministerial meeting in December.
Europe's push to compete in space
European nations have sought to build up their sovereign space capabilities since 2022 and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which highlighted how Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications service has become both a critical partner for Kyiv and a potential vulnerability.
Immediately after the war erupted, there were initial doubts about whether the billionaire would continue to fund Starlink services in Ukraine. Reports said Musk refused to let Starlink to be used to support an attack on a Russian naval base in 2022.
The European Union is working on a “sovereign satellite” constellation called Iris2 that is designed to rival Starlink by providing secure communications and connectivity to the 27-nation bloc’s citizens. However, it’s not expected to be fully operational until 2030.
Another inflection point came this year after the Iran war broke out and US satellite imaging companies Planet Labs and Vantor started withholding images of the conflict region in the Middle East, apparently to prevent adversaries from attacking the US and allies.
The US remains the global leader in the space sector, with NASA conducting major exploration missions and overseeing the Artemis program, which aims to establish a human presence on the moon.
Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX, has transformed the commercial launch industry by making reusable rockets operational, lowering costs and increasing the frequency of launches.
Read moreNASA launches Roman telescope to map 'a new atlas of the universe'
Meanwhile, Amazon launched its first internet satellites in 2025. The company plans to deploy more than 3,200 satellites to provide broadband service around the world. Amazon's founder Jeff Bezos also established the rocket company Blue Origin.
SpaceX and Blue Origin canceled plans to attend the Paris summit, the French government said. News outlet Politico reported that the White House had urged US space companies not to attend because it could appear to support European Union policies.
“There can be tensions, as well as technological competition between major powers, particularly the United States and China,” a French presidential official said, speaking anonymously in keeping with the presidency’s customary practices. “We do have strengths, but we can see that things are accelerating and that much more money is needed.”
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and AP)

AI may have solved one of math’s biggest puzzles, raising controversy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:55:57 UTC
04:55:57 KST

The motion of fluids seems simple, but the equations behind it are the subject of one of the most famous puzzles in mathematics. That puzzle now appears solved, thanks to AI, even as the feat came with a flood of controversy.
OpenAI announced September 8 a solution to the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem, which is so monumental that a $1 million prize has been offered for its resolution. “It’s one of the guiding problems for the field. It is a huge deal to know the answer,” says mathematician Dallas Albritton of the University of Wisconsin–Madison, who was not involved with the new work.
The day before, a pair of mathematicians had reported an advance on a closely related problem. To do so, Tristan Buckmaster of New York University and Levent Alpöge of the AI company Anthropic relied on assistance from various AI models, including OpenAI’s. The relationship between the two advances — and whether OpenAI had access to the duo’s progress — has been subject to intense speculation.
The Navier-Stokes equations describe the relationships between pressure, density and velocity of a fluid as they change over time. The equations are a foundation of science and engineering, relevant for weather forecasting, studying ocean currents and designing aircraft, pumps, turbines and more. “It’s an incredibly important, ubiquitous set of equations,” Albritton says.
Despite dating to the 19th century, the equations are not fully understood — in particular, whether they are always well-behaved has not been clear. There might be situations in which the equations break down, producing physically impossible situations like fluid flowing at infinite speed, known as “blowups.” Determining whether the equations are naughty or nice is one of seven challenges selected in 2000 by the Clay Mathematics Institute as the Millenium Prize Problems, each of which has a $1 million bounty.
Buckmaster and Alpöge focused on a set of equations called the Euler (pronounced like “oiler”) equations. While the Navier-Stokes equations include viscosity — a term describing a fluid’s resistance to flow — the Euler equations don’t, making them a stepping stone to the more famous Navier-Stokes problem. The pair found a blowup when an outside force pushes on the fluid, solving what’s called the forced Euler problem.
As the pair were finessing their results, rumors began flying about their work. Spurred by these vague rumors, OpenAI researchers started tackling the various Millenium Prize Problems, and quickly focused on Navier-Stokes, using around 10,000 AI agents at a time.
The agents discovered a solution to the forced version of the Navier-Stokes problem: a vortex that gets skinnier and faster until its speed goes to infinity. That means that the Navier-Stokes equations are not always well-behaved, answering the longstanding question. The feat of running so many AI agents cost millions of dollars, OpenAI researchers estimated. (OpenAI stated in a blog post that they will not claim the Millenium Prize.)
OpenAI’s solution has been confirmed by Lean, a tool that allows for the verification of complicated mathematical proofs. But, as the paper reporting the result is 166 pages long, mathematicians are still digesting its contents. “I don’t think anyone has completely verified the proof yet, certainly not on the human side,” says mathematical physicist Gregory Eyink of Johns Hopkins University.
The new achievements are part of a wave of AI results deluging mathematics. In the past year, AI has enabled major leaps, leaving mathematicians grappling with rapid changes to their field. The new result, on one of mathematics’ most important problems, is “the spectacular culmination of the arc we have seen over the last 12 months,” OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck said during a September 8 news conference.
In a statement published on his website on September 7 along with the forced Euler solution, Buckmaster said that his team’s results mark a “Deep Blue-Kasparov moment,” referencing the 1990’s milestone when a supercomputer beat the best human chess player. “The community needs to have serious and unhurried discussion about where to go from here,” he said.
Mathematicians are certainly taking notice. Albritton got wind of Buckmaster and Alpöge’s result around 1 a.m., awake with his newborn baby. He stayed up until 6 a.m. discussing it with colleagues.
Despite the problem’s mathematical clout, its solution won’t have significant practical implications, Eyink says. The Navier-Stokes equations describe fluid as a continuum, but real-world fluids are made of individual molecules and atoms, so it’s already known that there’s a cutoff where the equations no longer apply. It’s more about prestige, Eyink says. “There’s a huge mathematical celebrity associated with these equations.”
That also raises concerns about how credit for a discovery is doled out. After initial rumors began circulating, Buckmaster says he had a series of discussions with OpenAI researchers about how to present the two results. Those discussions, he alleged, involved a request to exclude his coauthor Alpöge, who works for OpenAI competitor Anthropic. Buckmaster’s narrative also raised questions about whether the AI agents had access to Buckmaster and Alpöge’s progress. OpenAI denies that its AI agents had direct access, but says, “while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.”
The biggest implication of the advance may be the issues it raises regarding the difficulty of attributing credit when AI is involved, Eyink says. “This is, for me, the really serious ongoing problem and issue that has to be resolved.”

Boeing, Anduril team moves ahead in race for new interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:54:15 UTC
04:54:15 KST

- Boeing and Anduril advanced to Phase 2 of the U.S. Army's competition to build a second interceptor for its IFPC Increment 2 air defense system.
- The interceptor is designed to counter cruise missiles and militarized drones, complementing the AIM-9X missile already used in the Army's Enduring Shield system.
Boeing has moved into the next phase of competition to build the U.S. Army’s second interceptor for its Integrated Fires Protection Capability, or IFPC, air defense system, the company announced September 9. Boeing is developing the missile with Anduril Industries, which will supply the solid rocket motor.
The interceptor is meant to defend fixed and forward operating bases against cruise missiles and militarized drones. It fills a gap in the Army’s layered air defense between shorter-range systems and longer-range defenses like Patriot, giving commanders another option specifically built for low-flying, midrange threats.
The Army’s current IFPC Increment 2 system, called Enduring Shield, already fields one interceptor: the AIM-9X Sidewinder missile, built by RTX and fired from launchers built by Leidos subsidiary Dynetics. The Army began looking for a second, more capable interceptor to complement the AIM-9X more than two years ago, after concluding that emerging cruise missile and drone threats exceeded what the existing system could handle.
Boeing’s design uses a modular open systems architecture, meaning individual components like the seeker, avionics or software can be swapped out and upgraded without redesigning the entire missile. The company says this approach is meant to keep the interceptor affordable and allow more rounds to fit in each magazine, since a smaller, more efficient missile lets base defenders carry more shots against a wave of incoming threats.
“Our scalable production approach is designed to provide a reliable, affordable layer of defense against a range of aerial threats to protect the warfighter with practical, dependable capability when it matters most,” said Bob Ciesla, vice president of Boeing Precision Engagement Systems.
“We welcome the opportunity to continue in this competition,” said Jim Bryan, executive director of Boeing Integrated Air and Missile Defense. “By combining proven seeker expertise with a purpose-built interceptor, we are delivering thoughtful, effective advances in air and missile defense that meet mission needs.”
Boeing and Anduril first partnered on the program in December 2025, after Boeing received an Other Transaction Authority award to begin developing the interceptor. In Phase 1 of the competition, Boeing and Anduril’s team competed against proposals from Lockheed Martin and Rafael Systems Global Sustainment, the U.S. arm of Israel’s Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, whose entry is based on the Tamir missile used in Israel’s Iron Dome system. Boeing’s September 9 announcement confirms its own advancement to Phase 2, which will include detailed design work, system development, integration and a competitive demonstration to test the missile against Army requirements; the company did not say whether Lockheed or Rafael also advanced.

SRINAGAR: J&K chief secretary Atal Dulloo Wednesday rolled out a three-year scheme to rehabilitate drug addicts under treatment at govt-run or aided de-addiction centres and institutions, prevent relapse, and aid their reintegration into society.The scheme will initially be introduced in the districts of Jammu, Srinagar, Kathua and Budgam and later extended to others, officials said.Under the scheme, a structured rehabilitation cycle will be established for drug abusers to ensure a seamless transition from “detoxification to socio-economic stabilisation” to reduce relapse rates and prevent premature exit from treatment, Dulloo said.The first six months will cover intake, assessment, treatment, stabilisation and rehabilitation planning under Phase I. The next six to 24 months will involve reintegration and livelihood activation under Phase II. The following 24-36 months will revolve around sustained monitoring and social inclusion.J&K home department will facilitate tracing and support for individuals requiring intervention. The health and medical education department will provide continuing mental health services, counselling, psychiatric care, de-addiction treatment and relapse-prevention support.
The education department will aid educational reintegration, academic continuity, re-enrolment, bridge learning and access to student support services, officials said.The labour and employment department will facilitate vocational training, skill development, employment placement and entrepreneurship development. The rural development and Panchayati Raj department will support community participation, family engagement, livelihood inclusion, social support networks and local-level rehabilitation and reintegration initiatives. The social welfare department will serve as the nodal department for implementation of the policy, officials said.On April 11, 2026, J&K Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha launched a 100-day anti-drug campaign under the “Nasha Mukt Abhiyaan”, which involved large-scale awareness programmes by the civil administration and police, destruction of poppy cultivation, random urine testing of drivers and intensified crackdowns on drug networks.
Over 32,500 drug abuse cases have been registered across J&K since 2022, with the highest number of patients reported from Srinagar and Jammu districts, govt data revealed. A 2022 study by Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences Kashmir estimated about 67,468 people in 10 Kashmir districts as “substance-dependent”.

'Sickening' racist remarks and calls for a coup: French police under investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:49:12 UTC
04:49:12 KST

A newspaper has released a video filmed in 2025 by police during a night patrol. The officer behind most of the extremist comments is a former paratrooper with close ties to the far-right National Rally party.
Six hours of footage and a torrent of racist, misogynistic and conspiratorial remarks. The local newspaper Midi Libre has published video from a night-time patrol by Carcassonne's municipal police, recorded on 6 November 2025.
Captured inadvertently by one officer's body camera, which they thought was switched off, it contains, according to the daily, comments described as "of exceptional violence".
According to Midi Libre, a preliminary investigation has been under way since January 2026, when the footage is said to have been passed to the Carcassonne public prosecutor's office.
Following the video's publication by the newspaper, the prosecutor's office confirmed to AFP that it had already opened an investigation, without specifying when.
'These wogs drive fast'
The evening is quiet: the municipal police officers are called out to just one incident. But inside their vehicle, the remarks keep coming. From inside the police car, one of the officers insults a passer-by, calling him a "wog who stinks of kebab". On two occasions, Black people are also compared to "monkeys".
Between remarks targeting foreigners and non-white French people, the patrol also discusses women: "Back in the days of the caves, those stupid bitches, if they weren't with their bloke, they'd get bumped off outside," and about politics: "We've been eaten alive, we let everyone in, we've had 40 years of crap from the left, lefty scum."
Beyond the racist remarks, the officers' exchanges also feature rhetoric commonly associated with far-right circles, according to Midi Libre, particularly from the patrol leader. He expresses concern about what he describes as a "civilisational replacement": "We became Christian under Clovis; we're going to become Muslim under Macron," he says.
Towards the end of their shift, the team even discusses a coup, with one officer expressing surprise that it has not already happened. "What we're missing is a general with some real balls. A little coup, a little dictatorship in France wouldn't do any harm," another says.
The patrol leader also admits to having found a weapon for someone close to him.
Officers suspended over remarks
In response to the controversy, Carcassonne city council initially issued a statement describing the remarks in the video as "unacceptable" and blaming the previous municipal administration's management of the police service. A few hours later, the mayor described the remarks as "sickening" and told reporters that "all those involved have been suspended".
Later in the evening, the Carcassonne public prosecutor's office issued a statement confirming that the municipal police officers involved had been suspended and their authorisations withdrawn, saying they "no longer meet the standards of integrity required for their duties".
A member of the RN's security team
The patrol leader, identified by the initials C.R. in Midi Libre's investigation, was responsible for nearly 90% of the hateful remarks made during the evening.
The 50-year-old is a former paratrooper and reportedly volunteered with the Protection and Security Department, the internal security service of France's far-right National Rally (RN). According to Midi Libre, "no declaration of additional activity was filed with Carcassonne city hall".
After the videos were circulated internally in late 2025, the officer was on sick leave between January and March 2026. On 16 March, the day after the victory of Christophe Barthès, Carcassonne's newly elected RN mayor, C.R. returned to the night shift. No disciplinary action had been taken against him at that point.
Potentially severe disciplinary sanctions
According to Benjamin Cottet-Emard, a lawyer with the Lyon Bar, insults of this kind do not constitute a criminal offence when they are not made publicly, for example in the media. Instead, they are considered a fifth-class offence, punishable by a fine of up to €1,500.
However, "non-public racist insults constitute, for a public official, a disciplinary offence separate from any criminal classification" and can result in permanent dismissal from public service, the lawyer told Euronews.
He said the remarks that emerged were "clearly unworthy of a public official and seriously undermine human dignity".
"The Council of State has already ruled that remarks made by a police officer in a WhatsApp group, including 'racist and discriminatory remarks on four occasions', as well as his failure to condemn 'racist, antisemitic and sexist messages shared by his colleagues', justified dismissal," he added.
Given the "repeated and particularly serious" nature of the conduct revealed by Midi Libre, Cottet-Emard concluded that it "should logically lead to the same sanction".

19:46:28 UTC

A US judge denied the bail request of the controversial social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate on Wednesday, ordering the brothers to remain behind bars as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom.
The Tate brothers, prominent figures in the so-called “manosphere”, were arrested in Miami on 18 July after British prosecutors filed new charges against them and sought their extradition to the UK. Those charges included criminal charges of rape and sex trafficking. British prosecutors previously charged the brothers with rape, human trafficking and sexual assault. The Tates, who are dual British-US citizens, have repeatedly denied the accusations against them.
The brothers have been held at the federal detention center in Miami since their arrest while they contest their extradition.
In a 30-page order issued on Wednesday, the US magistrate judge Lauren Louis wrote that the brothers “failed to meet their burden to demonstrate that they do not present a risk of flight or danger to the community, or that special circumstances warrant their release”.
“Respondents have failed to demonstrate that special circumstances here warrant relief, whether their proposed special circumstances are considered singly or together,” Louis said.
Louis also said the brothers “possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction”.
A lawyer for the brothers, Joesph McBride, criticized the ruling. “Detention first. Evidence later, maybe,” he wrote in a statement on X. “Andrew and Tristan Tate have been in federal detention since July 18 on a foreign accusation the United Kingdom has not yet been required to support with a single piece of evidence.”
“Every burden in that courtroom falls on Andrew and Tristan,” he continued. “None of it falls on the government that wants Andrew and Tristan handed over. Two American citizens, on American soil, ordered to prove a negative against a case that does not yet exist on paper.”
“September 16 is coming,” he said. “God bless.”
According to court documents, the UK government has until 16 September to provide information supporting its extradition request and the allegations against the brothers.

SRINAGAR: National Conference fired a political broadside at ally Congress Wednesday, defending full renditions of Vande Mataram at govt functions in J&K as a “constitutional” duty.Congress objected after all six stanzas of the national song was played at the inauguration of J&K’s first international film festival in Srinagar attended by CM Omar Abdullah and NC president Farooq Abdullah on Sept 7. As at other official functions, Omar stood at attention throughout.J&K Congress president Tariq Hamid Karra said NC and Congress should respect how the song’s place in India’s national life evolved through both the freedom movement and constitutional journey. “National symbols, songs and traditions occupy a special place in the heart of every Indian. Their true strength lies in their ability to bind together a nation as diverse as ours,” he said, calling it a concern that alliance partners had chosen to sing the full version.NC countered, asking Congress to look at CMs of states governed by the party, including Telangana and Karnataka, who have participated in full renditions.NC chief spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq shared on X a video featuring Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar at an event where the unabridged song was sung. When Parliament has adopted it, playing Vande Mataram becomes a statutory obligation and that is what govt did,” Sadiq said.

In Aug, the President cleared Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, which puts Vande Mataram on a par with the national anthem, making disrespect/disruption a punishable offence. The amended law did not change the stanzas, but people are now obligated to respect Vande Mataram as a constitutional duty.NC spokesperson Imran Nabi Dar said: “This is a constitutional obligation, and every one holding a constitutional office has to accept it, whether it is the CM, an MP or anyone else,” he said, adding the full version is now regularly played at govt functions across J&K.
Dar acknowledged the objection among Muslims. “Though religiously it is not acceptable to Muslims, it is a constitutional obligation that has to be fulfilled,” he said.The freedom movement broadly adopted first two stanzas of Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s 1875 poem, while the full song has six containing religious imagery that has drawn objections from Muslims. Congress general secretary GA Mir said freedom fighters had shaped the version used by the movement with inclusivity in mind.(inputs from PTI)

Returning to Tel Aviv: First United Airlines flight since February lands at Ben-Gurion Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:43:59 UTC
04:43:59 KST

The first flight of a United Airlines passenger plane from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Tel Aviv’s Ben-Gurion Airport (TLV) landed in Israel on Wednesday.
The plane, a Boeing 787-10 Dreamliner, took off to fly the return route back to Newark later on Wednesday.
The airline has not operated the route since before Operation Roaring Lion in February. Several airlines canceled their operations to the Middle East, including Israel, due to the then-regular Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks across the region.
Currently, it is operating two round trips between its main hub in Newark and Tel Aviv every day, with a third slated to be added from November, The Jerusalem Post learned.
Airline to resume direct flights between Tel Aviv, Chicago, Washington, San Francisco
Meanwhile, the airline has also planned to resume direct flights from Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD), and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) from October. Additionally, United is slated to resume flights from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) starting in March 2027, the Post previously reported.
The San Francisco flights, in particular, will boast the “highest frequency of business class seats between the two cities of any airline,” United claimed in August.
Delta also resumes flights, raising competition on the Israel-US route
Delta Air Lines also returned to Israel on Monday, landing at Ben-Gurion over 40 minutes ahead of schedule, the airline said at the time.
Delta’s Airbus A330-900neo left New York’s JFK Airport on Sunday, making it the first flight the airline operated since before Operation Roaring Lion.
Aaron Glick contributed to this report.

Sheba Medical Center held an appreciation ceremony for Turpaz Industries CEO and controlling shareholder Karen Cohen Khazon and her family following their donation of company shares worth approximately NIS 70 million to three major Israeli hospitals.
The donation, announced in July 2025, consisted of 1% of Turpaz Industries shares from the personal holdings of Cohen Khazon and her husband, Shay Khazon. It was designated for medical initiatives at Sheba Medical Center, Rabin Medical Center-Beilinson Hospital and Soroka Medical Center.
During the ceremony, Sheba inaugurated its Institute for Obstetric and Gynecologic Imaging in memory of Cohen Khazon’s late parents, Nediva (Gisèle) and Moshe (Musa) Cohen.
The event, held at Sheba’s Institute for Gynecological and Obstetric Ultrasound, included formal remarks and a ribbon-cutting ceremony. Prof. Yitshak Kreiss, director-general of Sheba Medical Center, was among those who attended.
The Sheba ceremony followed similar events held in recent months at Soroka and Beilinson to recognize the donation.
Cohen Khazon dedicated the contribution to her parents, saying they had instilled in her the values of generosity, humility and civic responsibility.
Donation to support cardiac care, Soroka recovery
At Beilinson, the donation was designated for the development of the hospital’s Cardiology Center in the Hope Tower, headed by Prof. Ran Kornowski, and the expansion of the Cardiac Intensive Care Unit, led by Prof. Katia Orvin.
The funding is intended to increase treatment capacity, improve infrastructure and support the introduction of advanced technologies for cardiac patients.
Cohen Khazon and her husband also visited Soroka Medical Center in Beersheba, where they met hospital director Prof. Shlomi Kodesh.
Their visit came following extensive damage sustained by Soroka during Operation Rising Lion.
The portion of the donation allocated to Soroka is intended to help restore and upgrade damaged infrastructure, reinforce critical departments and purchase equipment for the hospital’s emergency and trauma units.
When the donation was announced, Cohen Khazon said she viewed the contribution as a way of translating business success into a broader contribution to Israeli society.
“I dedicate this donation to the memory of my beloved parents: Nediva (Gisèle), who raised and educated generations of children with special needs, and Moshe (Musa) Cohen, one of the founders of Israel’s electrical industry, who also made a significant contribution to the industry worldwide,” she said.
Generosity, humility and civic responsibility
“They instilled in me the values of generosity, humility and civic responsibility. As the CEO of a company that operates internationally yet remains deeply rooted in Israeli society, I felt that this was the right time to translate business success into a positive social impact.”
Turpaz Industries operates in the flavor, fragrance and specialty ingredients industries. The company markets products to more than 4,900 customers in over 100 countries and operates manufacturing facilities, research and development centers, laboratories and sales offices around the world.
The company employs more than 1,100 people and has completed 28 acquisitions since 2017 as part of its international expansion strategy.

UK recognition of unlawful Israeli occupation marks 'huge' shift, but response falls short, scholars say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:43:44 UTC
04:43:44 KST

Britain's formal conclusion that Israel's continued occupation of Palestinian territory is unlawful marks a significant legal and political shift, but international law scholars say London's response still falls short of what that recognition demands.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced Tuesday that the UK government had formally concluded that the occupation was unlawful, bringing its position into line with a central finding of the International Court of Justice's (ICJ) July 2024 advisory opinion.
The announcement marks a departure from London’s previous position, as the government had not formally expressed a view on the legality of the occupation as a whole.
But while the UK has announced measures targeting Israeli settlements and settlement expansion, the broader relationship with Israel remains largely untouched -- a distinction some legal scholars question.
“The legal and political shift is honestly huge, although insufficient,” Luigi Daniele, an associate professor of international law at the University of Molise in Italy, told Anadolu.
The ICJ ruled in July 2024 that Israel's continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, was unlawful and that Israel was under an obligation to bring that presence to an end as rapidly as possible.
The court also said Israel must immediately cease all new settlement activity and evacuate all occupiers from the occupied territory.
Gerhard Kemp, a professor of criminal law at the University of the West of England, Bristol, said Britain's conclusion was significant because it brought the government's position in line with the ICJ's findings on the occupation.
"It is a good thing that the UK clearly concluded that Israel's occupation of the Palestinian Territory, including the West Bank and East Jerusalem, is unlawful," he told Anadolu.
But Kemp noted that the ICJ's advisory opinion went further, also addressing Israeli policies and practices in the occupied territory, including segregation and apartheid -- issues not specifically addressed in the British statement.
He said the British position appeared to be based not only on the ICJ's work, but also on its own assessment of the factual and legal situation on the ground.
Miliband announced a ban on imports of goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, alongside measures targeting companies and individuals that provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate for settlement expansion.
“The sanctions itself are very targeted and limited to goods and some services from the settlements and the sanctions are not broadly aimed at Israel,” Kemp said.
The UK also announced sanctions on a further group of extremist occupiers who have supported or incited violence against Palestinian communities.
For Kemp, however, the measures leave the central issue unresolved.
“The sanctions are aimed to stop the expansion of the illegal settlements. So, one can say this is an important first step, but more would be required to address the central issue -- namely the unlawful occupation itself.”
For Daniele, another key limitation is that Britain has stopped short of characterizing Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide.
"Miliband has spoken clear words about the illegality of the situation in the occupied territory, although he hasn't mentioned in any way genocide at all," Daniele said. "I would say this is the main issue."
British foreign secretary said Tuesday that the UK supports full and fair judicial processes to consider allegations of genocide, with final determinations made by competent courts before the British government reaches its own conclusion.
Daniele, however, argued that Britain's approach risks creating an artificial distinction between Israel and its actions in occupied Palestinian territory.
"Miliband seems to cultivate, with (UK Prime Minister) Andy Burnham and the other countries announcing these measures, the illusion that there is a good and lawful Israel within the green line, with which it's ok to continue trade, military assistance, surveillance assistance ... and then there is somehow it's a bad and unlawful Israel in the occupied Palestinian territory,” he said.
"But we know that this construct is false."
Daniele argued that such an approach allows governments to condemn settlements and sanction individual occupiers while continuing other forms of economic, military and security cooperation with Israel.
Daniele also questioned whether measures targeting individual occupiers can be effective without addressing what he described as the broader political and institutional system supporting settlement activity.
“It is simply impossible to just target the most blatant cases and actors of this rogue and criminal dynamic without targeting the state of Israel as exactly as it was done during apartheid in South Africa,” he said.
He argued that one of the most significant changes in Israeli politics over the past decade has been the growing influence of the occupier movement.
“Settlers have become a governing force of the state of Israel, with their movement and with their political expression,” he said.
The issue of occupier violence further complicates attempts to isolate settlement activity from the Israeli state, Daniele said.
In the occupied West Bank, he added, a network of actors openly seeking to "de-Palestinize entirely the land" has the support of Israeli institutions and political networks.
He pointed to Israeli banks, bonds and the World Zionist Organization as part of what he described as a broader system supporting settlement activity.
Daniele said the measures need to target Israel as a whole until future governments demonstrate that they intend to respect the fundamental rights of the Palestinian people, starting with their right to self-determination.
Britain's shift also shows that sustained public pressure can influence government policy, Daniele said.
“I think we should salute this development positively because it shows that the pressure of civil society mobilization has meaning and can radically affect how governments deal with the situation when they don't want to lose the consent of the majority of the working people in Western society,” he said.
But rather than viewing Britain's decision as an endpoint, Daniele argued that pro-Palestinian movements should build on it to push for more significant results in the coming years.
"We should also use this opening as an indication that we need to relaunch the global movement in a better organized manner," he said.

- Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it has blocked for months.
-The fresh attacks and fighting with the United States have sent oil prices above $100 per barrel again as Tehran chokes off the strait and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
-Donald Trump predicted that the war with Iran will end "immediately after" the US midterm elections in November but said that he didn't expect the price of oil to come down before then.
-Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has visited Jabal al-Shaikh (Mount Hermon) in Syria and said that the Iranian government was very close to being overthrown.
-Yemen's Houthi rebels have reported dozens of Saudi airstrikes days after renewed conflict broke out in the country.
Iran condemned on Wednesday a resolution adopted by the United Nations atomic watchdog's board of governors which referred the Islamic republic to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance".
"This resolution was passed under political pressure from the US and its allies and in our view has no basis and will not bring any results," Iran's representative to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Reza Najafi, told state television.
Saudi Arabia reports fresh Houthi attacks on kingdom's south
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen on Wednesday said the Iran-backed Houthis had launched fresh attacks on the kingdom's south, after the rebels launched an offensive seeking to control the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The coalition's spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in a statement the Houthis had "launched several ballistic missiles and drones toward the cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha, and Jizan", without mentioning any casualties as a result of the attacks.
Iran attacks more than a dozen vessels in Strait of Hormuz
Iran said it attacked more than a dozen vessels trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, as it announced an expansion of a no-go zone outside the strategic waterway it has blockaded for months.
The fresh attacks and fighting with the United States have sent oil prices above $100 per barrel again as Tehran chokes off the strait and Washington presses a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 "non-compliant vessels" that were trying to pass through the route crucial for oil and gas trade, Iranian state media reported.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said "several" vessels in the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf were "subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region".
The Gulf of Oman lies on the Indian Ocean side of the narrow Hormuz strait, a vital energy conduit that normally carries around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas.
Iran's Guards also for the first time added parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea to a new "prohibited zone" on Wednesday, saying that exact coordinates will be announced later.
"If a vessel enters that area without coordination, it will be subject to our sanctions," Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi told state television.
The IAEA board of governors on Wednesday voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council over its nuclear "non-compliance" in a diplomatic move to pile pressure on the Islamic republic.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel, joined by the United States, launched a 12-day conflict in June 2025 that included strikes on nuclear sites.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, which erupted on February 28, and the IAEA has repeatedly urged to be given access.
The resolution was adopted by 23 votes in favour, three votes against and eight abstentions, two diplomats told AFP. Russia, China and Niger voted against it.
It "requests the (IAEA) director general to report" Iran to the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations.
The resolution, submitted by Britain, France, Germany and the United States, marks the first time Iran has been referred to the Security Council in 20 years for failing to comply with its nuclear reporting obligations.
The move is seen as largely symbolic as Iran allies China and Russia hold power to veto any sanctions against Tehran.
Syria condemns Netanyahu 'illegal' entry into its territory
Syria condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's entry into its territory after he visited Israeli troops stationed in southern Syria on Wednesday, calling the move "provocative and a blatant violation" of its sovereignty.
"The Syrian Arab Republic strongly condemns the illegal entry of Israeli occupation Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu into Syrian territory and his tour of Mount Hermon, in a provocative move and a blatant violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic and of international law," the foreign ministry said in a statement.
Trump says Iran war will end "immediately after" US midterms
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday predicted that the war with Iran will end "immediately after" the U.S. midterm elections in November because Tehran was trying to influence the vote but would not be able to hold out more in the face of U.S. economic pressure.
"I think war is going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election," he told reporters before departing for the Republican National Convention in Dallas.
Trump's war with Iran has recently entered its seventh month with no immediate end in sight. On Wednesday, Iran said it attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers. The renewed fighting sent the price of oil surging with benchmark Brent crude future breaching $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
Trump's approval ratings recently sank to a record low due to frustration from voters over the Iran war and deepening cost-of-living crisis. Midterm elections, due to be held on November 3 this year, are typically a referendum on the occupant of the White House.
Oil prices would also come down right after the election, Trump said on Wednesday, once the war is over, while acknowledging diplomatic talks are still a possibility but not preferred.
"Yes, a negotiation could possible happen, but it's not something we're looking at," Trump said.

Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces Hit Russian Purovsky Gas Plant — It Is Located More Than 3,000 km From Border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:41:58 UTC
04:41:58 KST

Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces (SOF) have set a record during the full-scale war by hitting enemy targets more than 3,000 kilometers away.
The SOF press service reported this.
On September 9, SOF Deep Strike drone units hit two major Russian gas condensate processing enterprises — the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky plants.
Both enterprises are located in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, one of the key oil and gas-producing regions of the aggressor state.
The SOF reported the strike on the Purovsky plant. It is part of PJSC Novatek and is one of the company’s key enterprises.
The Purovsky Gas Condensate Processing Plant produces stable gas condensate, a broad fraction of light hydrocarbons and liquefied hydrocarbon gas.
The facility is designed to process deethanized hydrocarbon condensate from Novatek’s gas condensate fields: East-Tarkosolinskoye, Khancheyskoye and Yurkharovskoye, and in the future, fields within the Olympic license area as well.
The processing capacity of the Purovsky Gas Processing Plant corresponds to the combined production capacity of fields operated by Novatek and its joint ventures.
In 2019, the Purovsky Plant processed 10.8 million tons of deethanized gas condensate.
It produced 8.2 million tons of stable gas condensate, 2.5 million tons of broad fraction of light hydrocarbons and liquefied hydrocarbon gas, as well as 14,800 tons of regenerated methanol.
Militarnyi recently reported that Ukraine’s Defense Forces had hit the Novy Urengoy Condensate Pre-Transportation Preparation Plant. Before the strike, its combined capacity was approximately 19.5 million tons per year.
It is currently unknown which specific units were damaged or how much the plant’s capacity has been reduced as a result.

US judge denies bail for Tate brothers facing UK extradition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:37:40 UTC
04:37:40 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
A US magistrate judge denied bail on Wednesday to Andrew Tate and Tristan Tate, ruling that the brothers must remain in custody at the Federal Detention Center in Miami while they await the start of extradition proceedings to the UK. 
The brothers face serious charges in the UK, including multiple counts of rape, sexual assault and physical abuse. 
Judge Lauren Louis emphasized that unlike domestic criminal cases, the burden in foreign extradition proceedings lies entirely with the defendant to prove they do not pose a flight risk. 
“There is a well-established presumption against bond in extradition proceedings,” she noted, finding that the Tates failed to meet the legal burden required to prove they are neither a flight risk nor a danger to the community.  
Flight risk, social media persona 
The court rejected claims that the brothers lack the resources to flee, noting that the record “reflects that they possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction.” The judge also observed that the brothers' own online activities actively undermined their legal defense. 
“Respondents’ public-facing personae, from which they derive income, are self-proclaimed law-evaders,” said the judge, noting that the Tates previously boasted on social media about holding multiple passports and their ability to live “off the grid.” Louis also cited evidence that the brothers had engaged in witness tampering, involving between seven and 12 counts of “influencing witness testimony on a continuing basis,” while under supervision in Romania. 
The Tates had argued that their incarceration in administrative segregation was punitive and damaging to their health. The judge dismissed those claims, saying their testimony on isolation and weight loss was “thoroughly impeached” by evidence showing they had access to radios, commissary and work assignments as orderlies. 
Defense labels process 'punishment' 
Joseph McBride, legal counsel for Tates, strongly criticized the ruling, asserting that his clients have spent 53 days in federal custody without a conviction or an extradition order. “The process is the punishment,” McBride said on US social media company X, arguing that the UK is using its 60-day treaty window to build a case while the brothers endure the “severe restrictions of administrative segregation.” 
The British government has until Sept. 16 to submit its formal extradition materials. McBride said “every additional day belongs to the United Kingdom on paper and is taken from Andrew and Tristan in life,” warning that “no later victory can give that time back.” 
The defense attorney highlighted that Romania has recently indicted the brothers, leaving them separated from their local counsel and “approximately 30 terabytes of information” essential for their defense. He noted that attempts to conduct legal videoconferencing from the Miami facility failed, noting: “You cannot defend a 30-terabyte criminal case across an ocean through a jailhouse connection that does not work.”

I became a grandparent at 37 when our other kids were in primary school. We felt guilty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:36:46 UTC
04:36:46 KST

What does grandparenting look like today? Insight explores whether the demands on modern-day grandparents are keeping them physically fit and mentally well, or if the younger generations' wants and needs are being prioritised to the detriment of grandparents. Watch Insight episode Grandparenting on SBS On Demand.
Matt:
I love telling people I'm a grandfather at 39, then immediately stopping to leave dead silence between us.
Their eyes widen, and you see them do calculations in their head — wondering if they should ask the follow-up question: "How old were you when you had your first child?"
After a few seconds, I explain how my wife and I met when I was 18, and she was 22 and already had a three-year-old, Ethan. And Ethan and his wife, Maddy, had a child named Illyria when he was 22 years old — almost two years ago now.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
At times, I feel like I'm leading a double life.
One minute, I'm doing school pickup or coaching our second son Zander's U12 rugby team.
The next, my wife Esther asks if I remembered to put our two-year-old granddaughter Illyria's car seat in the car to pick her up for a sleepover.
We threw all our baby stuff out the moment our youngest Eden was too big for it five years ago. We weren't expecting to need it so soon — only three years later.
Unexpected guilt
But being a young grandparent brought a feeling I never expected: guilt.
Arguably, most older grandparents have children who are all grown up and they are retired — or close to it — and have the free time to put more energy into their grandchildren.
And sometimes, I feel a pang of jealousy for these older grandparents. I'm not jealous because it's a competition, but because they're at a stage of life with extra time to help their children.
It's a big juggling act trying to be there for everyone.
There are benefits to being a younger grandparent, though.
We have more energy (we like to think) and remember what it was like to have a baby in the house. I mean, it was only six years ago that Eden, 9, was a toddler.
She and our granddaughter absolutely adore each other, and their relationship is somewhat unconventional, with just a seven-year age gap.
Eden is known as 'Yaunty' (young aunty), and her duties look more like a sister's duties. I love watching her play with her niece and getting the experience of having a little sister.
And watching our 23-year-old Ethan become a dad has been the next best thing to becoming one myself.
He's not just attentive as a father, but he gives his heart fully to his wife and daughters. (I should mention they've just had another baby, Ananyah, who is one week old as I write this.)
He and I were extremely close when he was little, and we had a bit more distance when he was a teenager, becoming his own man, which is a normal and healthy rite of passage for parents and teens.
But Ethan moving into fatherhood has brought us closer once more. Now we bond over all the classic 'dad topics' such as lawns, what's the best decking oil and smoking meat.
My and Esther's life looks very different to our friends around us, although it always has.
Retirement will be very different too. There's a very good chance we won't just have grandchildren the day we retire; we might also have great-grandchildren.
Esther:
My son Ethan and his wife Maddy became serious quickly and married within two years. When they were pregnant a year into their marriage at 22, I had the brief, selfish thought, "I'm too young to be a grandmother."
But it passed quickly.
Matt, as always, helped me see the bigger picture. He was over the moon, crying tears of happiness from the moment they told us.
And I reminded myself how lucky I was.
The stigma I experienced as a young mum was never a reflection of what my life could become.
My life was the antidote to that judgement, and now I was going to be the best Granny I could be.
Being a teenage mum
Being a mum at 17 was not how I expected my story to go. I felt very alone when I was pregnant and realised how much my life was changing.
All my friends had a freedom I knew I wouldn't have anymore, and I felt the weight of responsibility like a backpack I carried everywhere.
But alongside those feelings was an immense love for my son Ethan and a real hope that I could give him a beautiful life.
I have always believed that everything happens for a reason. If my purpose was simply to be his mum, then that was enough — and I was going to give it everything I had.
Ethan and I were a tight-knit duo, and after recently being dumped, I was even more determined to prove I could navigate motherhood and life as a single woman.
But right when my career and independence were about to take off, I met Matt at a party in our hometown of Toowoomba. He made me laugh. A lot.
A natural parent
Neither of us thought it would go anywhere; he was 18, and I was a 22-year-old single mum to a three-year-old.
We also had eight weeks before we were both moving to different cities for work, so we spent as much of that time together as we could.
After six weeks, we both knew we were in trouble and decided to be together and try having a long-distance relationship.
Matt met Ethan after three months, and they hit it off immediately.
I had told him Ethan already had wonderful male role models in his life and that any relationship between them could develop naturally, without labels.
But it quickly became obvious that Matt naturally parented Ethan and that he was falling in love with my son.
I knew he loved kids and wanted a bigger family. Eventually, he simply came home from work one day and said, "I want another baby. It's never going to be a good time."
He was right; and we gave Ethan two younger siblings, who are now also a wonderful uncle and aunty to our granddaughters.
The greatest gift
Along with being a parent, being a grandmother in my early 40s has been one of the greatest gifts of my life.
At times, though, I wish I could spend more one-on-one time with Illyria because she is just coming along to our kids' sports and activities when we babysit her.
Watching my daughter and middle son adore their nieces and play with them like they are little again makes my heart so full.
And I get to love and spoil these beautiful little reflections of my son and daughter-in-law — without the hourly feeds and the 1,000 nappy changes a day.

Russia, Vietnam to strengthen cooperation in countering extremism

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Russia and Vietnam are committed to strengthening cooperation in countering extremism and radicalization, particularly among young people, according to a joint statement issued following talks between Presidents Vladimir Putin and To Lam.
In this context, Russia and Vietnam stressed the need for their competent authorities to exchange best practices and enhance cooperation.
"The parties <…> will continue to coordinate efforts to counter the use of information and communication technologies (ICT) for terrorist, extremist and other criminal purposes, as well as to interfere in states’ internal affairs and undermine their sovereignty," the statement reads.
Russia and Vietnam will also increase exchanges of information and experience in countering the plans and activities of unfriendly countries and their intelligence services aimed at interfering in internal affairs and influencing state, political and legislative institutions.
The parties intend to establish practical cooperation in information technology, including advancing an initiative to create a regional center to combat cybercrime in the Asia-Pacific region under the auspices of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. Russia and Vietnam also emphasized the importance of developing universal, legally binding norms under UN rule to build a fair and equitable system of international information security.
"The parties are ready to expand cooperation in preventing and combating crime in all its forms and manifestations, including crimes involving ICT, and to continue cooperation between the two countries’ law enforcement agencies," the statement notes.
