What Russia’s military elite is preparing for behind closed doors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:35:58 UTC
04:35:58 KST

What Russia’s military elite is preparing for behind closed doors
Every year, Russia publishes a private analytical report intended for a select group of military and defense industry leaders. The Russian Military Yearbook is designed strictly for senior officers, security agency staff, and executives of companies in the defense sector.
Unlike public reports on the state of the armed forces, the Russian Military Yearbook is meant for internal use. It addresses military planning, advancements in weaponry, and developments in the defense industry, along with the key priorities of the Russian military leadership amid ongoing conflicts. Consequently, the yearbook sheds light on the priorities of Russia’s defense apparatus.
Russia’s global plans remain unchanged and are based on two main principles
First principle: Russia should be responsible for the stability and development of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). While Moscow does not harbor imperial ambitions to annex former Soviet republics, Russian politicians and military officials view these nations as vital partners in trade, infrastructure projects, and security.
Therefore, countries of the “post-Soviet space” should not join other political and military blocs, especially the EU and NATO. Such blocs often pressure members to sever ties with Russia and are sometimes directed against Russia.
However, Russia welcomes participation in economic collaboration, such as China’s Belt and Road Initiative. What benefits neighboring countries also benefits Russia due to the close economic ties between them.
“The West is entertaining the idea of creating a geopolitical confrontation arena in the South Caucasus, attempting to push Russia aside from the normalization of relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Rejecting such attempts, the Russian Federation intends to do all it can to protect the region.” 
– Analytical report of the Institute of Contemporary International Studies of the Diplomatic Academy of the Russian Foreign Ministry
Second principle: Moscow views stability through the lens of a “multipolar world.” This refers to a situation in international relations where there is no single hegemon or “world police.” Decisions regarding security and regional organization are made either at the regional level or during global negotiations, rather than by one or two central powers.
It may seem that America’s recent setbacks – including conflicts with European allies and protracted crises in Iran and the Middle East – create an ideal situation for Russian strategists. As Washington’s influence wanes, America’s capacity to control global affairs may diminish as well. However, that perception is wrong.
Russian military and political leaders desire not only a world without hegemony but also one characterized by stability and adherence to international laws. Even setting idealism aside, this approach undeniably serves Russia’s interests. UN principles help maintain the status quo and ensure regional leadership.
Conflicts involving Russia are often caused by breaches of agreements (primarily regarding NATO expansion), leading to the use of force and the disruption of regional balance. This was true of the conflict with Georgia in 2008, the civil war in Syria, and the Ukraine crisis.
Moreover, America’s inability to manage conflicts (which are often instigated by its own government) only serves to destabilize the world. This compels Moscow to allocate more resources for potential interventions. The Kremlin is well aware of what happens when a crisis outside its borders spirals out of control.
“According to S.V. Lavrov, the Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs, ‘The USA could become one of the responsible centers of power together with Russia, China, and other powers of the Global South, East, North, and West in the foreseeable future’, but this is subject to them abandoning the counteraction to the objective process of multipolarity strengthening” 
– Analytical report of the Institute of Contemporary International Studies of the Diplomatic Academy of the Russian Foreign Ministry
Russian analysts do not believe that it is possible to return to the former Western-centric world order. They believe the Trump administration is too preoccupied with internal issues and is consistently souring relations with European allies, whom it views as ‘parasites’. Meanwhile, the EU is becoming increasingly reliant on rigid neoliberal institutions, making it less open to negotiations due to entrenched anti-Russia sentiments among its leaders.
Consequently, the only remaining option is to build a multipolar world.
Moscow sees China and India, as well as the nations of the Global South, as its partners in this new world order. These governments also seek independence from the US and Europe and are pursuing their regional agendas. However, experts point out that Russia’s goals may diverge from those of its partners and could even come into conflict with their goals; no one is willing to sacrifice foreign policy autonomy for the sake of “unconditional friendship.”
Despite the prevailing pessimism surrounding global politics, Russian experts believe that new conflicts can be avoided, even during such troubled times.
However, analysts are concerned about one particular region.
Very Cold War
In addition to the existing conflict zones, experts are also analyzing another potential flashpoint – the struggle for control over the Arctic. And this isn’t just about the vast reserves of valuable resources in the Arctic – estimates suggest that around 13% of the world’s oil and 30% of its natural gas lie beneath the ice.
Disputes over this “no man’s land” and its surrounding waters have been going on for nearly two centuries, and date back to the first attempts to carve out spheres of influence in the Arctic. Canada even attempted to occupy one of Russia’s Arctic islands during the Civil War, though this “occupation” was limited to a few settlers who were soon sent home by the Russian Navy.
Experts note that NATO countries have already begun a major arms buildup specifically aimed at potential Arctic operations. Military exercises are frequently held in the region, such as the recent Exercise Cold Response 26. In March, tens of thousands of service members participated in drills led by the Norwegian armed forces.
“During regular exercises in the Arctic, NATO countries carry out activities to conduct reconnaissance of all types, prepare and deliver missile, air, bomb, and torpedo strikes. Skills related to combat control and logistics, the interaction of dissimilar forces and means are honed.” 
– Vadim Istomin, doctor of Technical Sciences 
And this is just the beginning. NATO countries have initiated Arctic-aimed retraining and rearmament programs set to be completed by the early 2030s. NATO members call it preparation for possible threats. Yet analysts speculate that it could also be preparation for a coordinated attack.
Here are several examples:
Finland – HX / F-35 Program: As a new NATO member, Finland has acquired 64 F-35A fighters, as well as weapons and equipment for Arctic operations. It is also retraining pilots and technical staff. By 2028-2030, the F-35s are expected to fully replace F/A-18 Hornet aircraft.
Canada – North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) modernization: A new threat detection system for the Arctic is being developed. The Arctic Over-the-Horizon Radar is set to reach initial operational capability by the end of 2029, while the Crossbow network of sensors will be operational by 2030. The Polar Over-the-Horizon Radar is anticipated to become operational between 2032 and 2033. Infrastructure for aviation and the command system are also being upgraded.
Canada – Rearmament of the Air Force: Canada is purchasing 88 F-35As to replace its CF-18 fleet. Initial combat readiness is slated for 2029, with full capability set to be reached by 2033. This program aims to enhance the defense of Canada’s Arctic region.
Denmark and Greenland – Defense Program 2024-2033: Military infrastructure in the Arctic and North Atlantic is being strengthened through the acquisition of new Arctic ships and drones, alongside the deployment of additional surveillance assets in Greenland. The Joint Arctic Command is also being bolstered to support extended operations in the area.
This isn’t just speculation. In 2021, the Pentagon adopted a new strategic plan titled ‘Regaining Arctic Dominance’. It explicitly states that the US intends to push Russia and China out of the Arctic, including through threats and the use of force.
“It appears that, distracted by the conflict in Ukraine, the Americans have seemingly pushed the Russian Arctic to the periphery of their attention for the time being. But this is a dangerous delusion. Washington never abandoned the thought of redrawing borders in that area.” 
– Aleksey Fenenko, doctor of Political Science, professor of the Faculty of World Politics, Lomonosov Moscow State University 
In addition to the natural resources and military presence in the Arctic, NATO is interested in the Northern Sea Route. This corridor connects Asia and Europe via the Arctic Ocean, providing a faster alternative to the traditional southern route through India and the Suez Canal. Considering rising piracy and the Iran crisis, navigating the icy waters has become a safer alternative.
However, due to geographical factors, the Northern Sea Route heavily relies on Russian maritime infrastructure, effectively giving Moscow control over ship and cargo movements. Consequently, Russia could dictate terms to carriers or even halt traffic entirely. Of course, NATO doesn’t want this.
Canada is expanding its fleet of icebreakers, and Norwegian spy vessel the FS Marjata is increasingly being spotted in the Barents Sea. Meanwhile, Finland is deploying American F-35A fighters just 150 km from the Russian border. The US is ramping up its military presence in Alaska, launching new NAVSTAR military satellites over the region, and ordering amphibious vehicles, which are ideally suited for operations in the north. Swedish BvS10 Beowulf amphibious tracked all-terrain vehicles are a particularly popular choice.
The Russian military is already preparing for potential conflicts in the Arctic. The Russian Army and Navy traditionally have a strong presence in the North and benefit from developed infrastructure. New missile defense systems ensure aerial security. Tor-M2 missile systems, available in various configurations, also play a significant role. The specialized variant for naval vessels, the Tor-M2KM, is particularly easy to produce in mass quantities.
Russia is ready to respond to any challenge in the Arctic; yet this crisis can still be avoided.
Meanwhile, Russia is forced to address another issue on a daily basis – though one may call it more profitable.
Arms market shakeup
The armaments and military equipment (A&ME) sector, unlike many others, boasts consistent growth in both demand and supply, expanding by 28% over four years to reach $679 billion.
In 2022, the weapons market began to shift dramatically. Sanctions caused Russian exports to plummet from 18% to 12%, with lost contracts primarily shifting to American manufacturers.
The composition of imports has also changed, becoming more unstable and concentrated in regions of existing or potential conflicts. Warsaw has emerged as the world’s leading arms purchaser, spending $33 billion on weaponry in 2023 alone. Given Poland’s status as “NATO’s vanguard,” there’s little doubt about the purpose behind this arms buildup.
Clearly, supplies to Ukraine have significantly increased, but experts point out an important detail: Western allies mainly send legacy military equipment to Kiev, which allows them to quickly modernize their own arsenals. And it’s clear who benefits most from this situation.
“After getting rid of the obsolete weapon systems supplied to Kiev as military aid, the ‘collective West’ countries began large-scale purchases of modern and more expensive arms. At the same time, the USA became the main beneficiary and recipient in this situation, having practically monopolized the arms market of NATO member states.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
Since 2021, the Russian defense industry has grown approximately fivefold (with the output of some sectors increasing by six or even seven times). However, the bulk of this production is consumed by the Russian military, and exports are severely restricted due to sanctions. Nevertheless, analysts believe that after the end of the Special Military Operation, the Russian defense sector may dominate the market.
Experts note that the unique advantage of Russian weaponry developed during the Ukraine crisis is its proven adaptability to real-world battle conditions. Most Western and Asian arsenals have been tested only during military exercises, whereas new Russian models have been designed and adapted based on data gathered from the battlefield.
The primary goal of Russian defense companies was not to create a budget-friendly training model; they needed to design weapons that would prove reliable in real battle conditions. Developers also received ample feedback from soldiers who tested the weapons in battle.
Looking ahead, Saudi Arabia and India are expected to be major buyers of weapons; analysts predict these countries will focus on importing weapons in the coming years. China could also become a major buyer of Russian defense products, though Beijing consistently reduces foreign procurement in favor of satisfying demand through domestic production.
These imports extend beyond just rifles, ammunition, missiles, and aircraft. Analysts forecast that by 2030, 40% of the entire defense market will revolve around technological exchange – selling access to new developments, as well as training engineers and military personnel.
This sector is already evident in Russia’s partnership with India. For instance, Rosoboronexport is working on localizing AK-203 rifles and 125mm Mango APFSDS rounds in India, as well as upgrading T-72 tank engines at Indian facilities.
High-altitude and high-tech
When people discuss Russian military exports, they often think of tanks and Kalashnikov rifles. This makes sense, as the Russian Army is primarily viewed as a land power, and advancements in the development of rifles and tanks indeed play a significant role in its capabilities.
However, the Ukraine conflict has highlighted the crucial importance of air superiority, especially in the age of drone warfare. The Russian military employs a wide array of tools tailored for various tasks.
On the one hand, there are powerful systems like the S-400 Triumph surface-to-air missile system. Adopted by the Russian military in 2007, this system can detect aerial objects up to 600 km away and engage aerodynamic targets at a distance of up to 380 km. This system has repeatedly demonstrated its effectiveness, even though it was designed at a time when warfare was quite different.
“The S-400 Triumph is capable of fighting the entire range of modern air targets within its zone of responsibility. This isn’t only the merit of the developers but also of the General Staff which managed to predict long-term threats.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
But there are also small, mobile systems that are indispensable in urban combat and dynamic modern warfare.
A prime example is the Dzhigit support launcher. Without its Igla-S and Verba missile launchers, it looks like a sophisticated garden chair. However, fully equipped, it can fire powerful missiles in rapid succession or salvos, functioning on the ground, in buildings, or mounted on a combat vehicle. Military personnel particularly appreciate its stealth capabilities and battlefield survivability.
As for new Western radar and missile defense developments, analysts are skeptical about them. They note that while these new models often set records, they don’t necessarily enhance practical use.
“The TRLM-4D is also a leader in the number of simultaneously detected targets – 1500. However, the only thing that such a number of blips on the radar screen can give to the crew having just 24 ADMS is a sense of despair.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
Uncertainty is the new certainty
Overall, Russia’s strategy can be summed up as “active preparation for the worst, moderate hope for the best.” Politicians, military leaders, and defense industry representatives understand that the Special Military Operation may continue for an extended period, while adversaries seek to exploit any weaknesses that Russia may have; therefore, new crises are almost inevitable. Recent years have demonstrated the resilience of the Russian military and economy, but that alone may not ensure success.
At the same time, analysts believe that a peaceful resolution to all issues is possible. However, it probably won’t be brought about by the goodwill of politicians, but rather by the demonstration of strength and the readiness to respond to any threats.

New EU taxes will cut countries’ payouts to Brussels, Costa says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:35:37 UTC
04:35:37 KST

European Council President António Costa speaks during the final press conference as part of the EU Summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels, on June 19, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
European Council president António Costa said that new, EU-wide taxes could shield German taxpayers from sending more money to Brussels.
With less than four months to go until an informal deadline to reach a deal on the EU’s 2028-2034 budget, Costa signaled that new levies would reduce national contributions to the EU’s coffers. This is a key aim for Germany, which finances a quarter of the cash pot.
“We cannot ask more from the member states. We need to create new own resources in order to protect the national budgets,” Costa said in a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin.
Advertisement
“All national budgets need to be respected,” he added.
Costa’s visit came only three days after the far-right Alternative for Germany secured a historic landslide victory in the regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt. The Euroskeptics’ success risks hardening Merz’s stance in the budget negotiations, according to several EU diplomats.
Speaking alongside Costa, the German Chancellor reiterated calls to cut “several hundreds of billions” from the Commission’s near-€2 trillion proposal.
He described the budget increase as “simply prohibitive because at the end it is the European taxpayer who has to foot the bill.”
Costa countered that EU-wide taxes, known as own resources, are needed to finance common European policy areas such as defense and competitiveness that cannot be addressed by individual governments.
The Portuguese leader has previously signaled that he intends to narrow down several potential taxes that are acceptable to EU governments during a leaders’ summit on Oct. 15.
New own resources were expected to be €66 billion per year according to the Commission’s proposal from last July.
But after over one year of negotiations, EU governments have only agreed to proposed levies on foreign polluters, known as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, and on uncollected electronic waste, which are expected to jointly raise around €20 billion per year.

China: English to be removed as a graded core subject?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:34:00 UTC
04:34:00 KST

China: English to be removed as a graded core subject?
September 9, 2026
From business and academia to social media and entertainment — English is considered the dominant global language. One in five people on Earth actively uses this lingua franca. In China, a mathematics professor specializing in vector algebra is now challenging this dominance in no uncertain terms. Tang Jiafeng believes that English should be abolished as a core subject in elementary schools, secondary schools and universities.
Tang is convinced that no other country in the world has placed as much importance on English as China has.
"Our children desperately begin learning English even before they have properly mastered their native language. Yet we are a civilization that dates back thousands of years. English is just a tool. It's enough to be able to use it. The tradition of revering and emulating Western cultures must come to an end," Tang says in social media.
English as a required subject starting in third grade
English is considered difficult in China, since the Chinese language does not use an alphabetic script. It is a required subject starting in third grade. It is graded on par with Chinese and mathematics on the entrance exam for secondary schools, the central exam after 9th grade, and the high school graduation exam. A maximum of 150 points can be earned on the latter.
"How many resources and how much time do our children, parents and schools invest in a subject that is completely irrelevant to the majority of people in their future professional lives?" the mathematician asks, explaining his position.
He became well-known because many of his students achieved full scores on state math exams; in the class of 2011, six students from a single class did so.
Why English? 'AI translates'
Tang's opinion spread quickly online.
"Why cram for English when artificial intelligence can translate everything in seconds?" comments a user from Beijing.
Another suggestion from the southern province of Guangdong is to at least adjust the scoring — for example, to 120 points instead of 150 on the high school graduation exam.
Many parents invest in private tutoring that focuses specifically on exam questions. In addition, all bachelor's students must pass the English exam before being admitted to master's programs. Tang suspects that this could cause many young talents in the natural sciences to fail, even though they have great potential to become top researchers.
No English proficiency, no competitiveness
There is no question that English is also important for STEM subjects. Research on future-oriented topics is typically published in English. There are fears circulating online that cutting back on English instruction could lead to a decline in China's competitiveness. A prominent advocate for English as a required subject is Hu Xijin, former editor-in-chief of the state-run "Global Times," who has previously drawn attention primarily for his nationalistic statements.
Hu emphasizes that foreign language skills are of great importance for every global citizen, "because we live primarily in the present," alluding to a debate over the ungraded history exam. "This present is shaped by globalization. China's opening up is not only state policy but also expands people's scope of action as well as the range of their diverse material and immaterial interests in life."
Hu went on to say that connections to the outside world should not, therefore, be compared to intellectual ties to ancient history.
"Forcibly pitting them against each other — by asking whether foreign languages or traditional Chinese culture are more important — runs the risk of setting the wrong priorities and unnecessarily politicizing public discussions."
For him, an open engagement with the outside world is the top priority. English as a core subject also promotes equal opportunity, he noted, as it gives children in rural areas access to this important foreign language and thus to the world.
Little interest in language studies
Even Chinese universities specializing in foreign languages are feeling the pressure to adjust their educational goals and prepare incoming freshmen for future job markets. For example, fewer and fewer high school graduates are interested in German language studies, explains a university professor from Beijing who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity.
The new curriculum at Beijing Foreign Studies University has adopted a "foreign language plus major" model: English combined with law, information technology, or economics.
Similar cultural struggles already took place during the Self-Strengthening Movement in the late 19th century under the Qing Dynasty.
"Learn the superior skills from abroad so that you can later conquer the outside world," said Wei Yuan, a court scholar at the time.
Learning from abroad simply works better in the language used there. Even though it may be becoming apparent that, in some areas, other countries are more interested in learning from China— as is already the case today, for example in battery technology for the automotive industry, and humanoid robotics.
This article was originally published in German.

Moscow Rushes Bomb Shelter Repairs as Ukrainian FP-9 Puts Capital Within Reach

Moscow Rushes Bomb Shelter Repairs as Ukrainian FP-9 Puts Capital Within Reach
Moscow has ordered capital repairs on nine bomb shelters across three of its districts, with all the work due by November 30.
The tenders were reported on September 9, by the Telegram channel Ostorozhno, Moskva, which cited records from Russia's state procurement portal.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Authorities set aside 39 million rubles (about $455,077) for the overhaul, covering shelters on Azovskaya, Bolotnikovskaya, and Nagornaya streets, as well as one on Leninsky Prospekt. Contractors will rebuild entrances, partitions, and doors, refresh interior finishes, and repair the water, power, sewage, ventilation, and communication systems.
The repair tenders appeared only after Ukraine announced plans to launch its own ballistic missiles at Moscow, tying the repair drive to Kyiv's stated intent.
Those strikes could begin before the end of 2026, according to mid-August statements by the developer Fire Point and Ukraine's former defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov. The rocket earmarked for Moscow, the FP-9, can carry a payload of up to 800 kilograms and reach targets as far as 850 kilometers away.
"Such systems can pose a serious threat to facilities of Russia's military-industrial complex, its energy infrastructure, and other strategic targets," noted Anton Zemlianyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center.
Moscow sits behind three defensive rings that include more than 100 launchers and 50 mobile Pantsir systems, according to Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces.
The systems best suited to intercepting ballistic targets are the S-400 and S-500, though the S-500 remains scarce. Russia placed its first S-500-equipped regiment on combat duty in December 2025, its defense minister, Andrey Belousov, reported, without giving a figure. Newsweek put the country's S-400 stock at 56 in the early 2020s.
The Moscow contracts form part of a wider wave of shelter inspections and repairs unfolding across Russian regions through 2025 and 2026, as authorities work to bring civil-defense sites into readiness.
The repair drive fits a broader scramble to harden the capital against Ukrainian strikes. In late August, Moscow began erecting anti-drone netting around the Abramovo electrical substation, an $86.9 million facility standing just 350 meters from the Izmailovo Kremlin.
Weeks earlier, work had started on a third air-defense ring around the city, with a radius of roughly 40 kilometers. That build-out added about 24 Pantsir towers and two new sites for S-400 batteries.

The region, located 2,800 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, accounts for 80% of Russia’s total gas extraction, according to Agentstvo News.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Following the attack, a fire broke out on the grounds of an industrial facility in the city, according to Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug Governor Dmitry Artyukhov. The governor stated that there were no fatalities or injuries.

The UN resident coordinator for Nepal emphasized Wednesday that the country is suffering disproportionate consequences from global climate change following recent devastating floods.
“The devastation Nepal has experienced is an extraordinary stark illustration of the losses and damages that climate-vulnerable countries are increasingly facing,” Lila Pieters Yahia told reporters. She noted that the nation has contributed "very little" to global greenhouse gas emissions, but it is enduring profound human and economic impacts.
Yahia asserted that Nepal's situation highlights the core need for "climate justice" within the international framework. She argued that nations particularly vulnerable to climate change require adequate and accessible support to respond to damages "they did little to cause."
The briefing follows a massive disaster along the Nepal-China border on Aug 27. Authorities have recovered 1,369 bodies in Nepal, bringing the regional death toll to 1,412. More than 5,650 individuals are missing, including 848 foreigners.

Trump says Iran war will end ‘immediately’ after US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:27:06 UTC
04:27:06 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he expects the war with Iran to end “immediately after the election,” arguing that Tehran is trying to hold out until the November 3 midterms in hopes that Democrats will regain control of Congress.
Trump made the remarks while speaking to reporters before departing for a Republican conference in Dallas, as crude oil prices climbed above $100 a barrel amid renewed escalation with Iran. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the election,” he said. Asked why, Trump replied: “Because they can't hold out any longer. They're desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon. All they want is a nuclear weapon. And if they had a nuclear weapon, the whole world is in deep trouble.”
Trump also took responsibility for recent U.S. attacks on Iranian vessels and suggested more strikes were coming. “Well, the attacks are made by us. We've knocked out nine of their ships,” he said. “And you're going to see a lot more.” At the same time, he signaled that Washington’s objectives go beyond another nuclear agreement, saying the U.S. was “not looking for a deal” and was seeking “much more than a nuclear deal,” while adding that negotiations could still take place.
The president also said he would speak with Israel about sanctions imposed on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Britain announced new economic measures this week targeting companies and individuals involved in settlement activity, while Canada and France have also moved against settlement goods as part of coordinated pressure on Israel. The British move has sparked a diplomatic row with Jerusalem and criticism from leading Jewish communal figures in the UK.
Trump’s remarks came as Tehran faced a separate escalation on the diplomatic front. For the first time in 20 years, the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Board of Governors voted Wednesday to refer Iran to the UN Security Council after determining that Tehran had violated its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The resolution was backed by 23 of the board’s 35 member states, with Russia, China and Niger voting against, eight abstaining and one not participating.
The referral is not expected to produce immediate sanctions because Russia and China, both Iranian allies and permanent members of the Security Council, could block such measures. Still, sending the issue to the UN’s most powerful body marks a significant diplomatic escalation and follows an IAEA resolution adopted on June 12, 2025, one day before Israel launched its war against Iran, which found Tehran in violation of its nonproliferation commitments.
The dispute centers in part on long-running IAEA investigations into uranium traces found at undeclared Iranian sites and Tehran’s refusal to allow inspectors full access to facilities damaged in the war. Iran has consistently denied pursuing nuclear weapons, but since its nuclear sites were bombed in June 2025 it has sharply restricted cooperation with the agency.
A central unresolved question is the fate of Iran’s stockpile of uranium enriched to 60%, close to the 90% level associated with weapons-grade material. Before the 2025 war, Iran possessed 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60%, an amount estimated to be sufficient for at least 10 nuclear weapons if enriched further. Much of the material was reportedly buried underground near the damaged Isfahan facility, while Iran has denied inspectors access to Isfahan, Natanz and Fordow.
The survival of that stockpile remains a major concern in Israel, where officials fear Tehran could eventually move the material to a secret facility and enrich it rapidly to weapons grade. One site that has drawn particular attention is a deeply buried complex known in Israel as “Pickaxe Mountain,” which Israeli officials fear could be difficult to destroy even with bunker-busting bombs.
Iran had threatened to respond if the IAEA referred the issue to the Security Council, though no concrete retaliatory step had been announced by Wednesday evening. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi accused Western countries of exploiting conditions created by attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities, while Iran’s mission to the IAEA denounced the decision as political and blamed the United States and Israel for the current crisis.

Ukraine fighting for our freedom too warns UK
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:24:55 BST
04:24:55 KST

Britain will not flinch in its support for Ukraine, the Defence Secretary told allies as he announced a £100 million contribution towards the rapid delivery of air defence interceptors before winter, at a virtual meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group on Tuesday.
Wes Streeting, co-chairing the meeting alongside German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, put the money into the PURL mechanism, under which allies fund American weaponry for Ukraine. The announcement came against a requirement Kyiv had set out minutes earlier for 300 Patriot missiles from partner stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors with counter-cruise missile capability and $2 billion for drones.
Attending as, in his own description, the still relatively new Secretary of State, he said the commitment felt across the country was unshakable. “Our Prime Minister Andy Burnham and I, and in fact our entire country, feel to Ukraine, to its people and to its government as they fight on the front line, not just for Ukrainian freedom and democracy, but for all of our freedom and democracy.”
Having hosted President Zelensky in Britain over the summer and visited Kyiv alongside the Prime Minister, he said he had seen the consequences of Russian aggression at first hand along with “the resilience and strength and the courage that the people of Ukraine are showing”.
The message he wanted heard in Moscow was that the winter would change nothing. “We know that this will only end through a negotiated peace. It’s really important that Russia understands that we won’t flinch in terms of our support for Ukraine as they continue to fight for their freedom and, for that matter, for ours.”
On drones, where Britain committed to supplying 120,000 this year, progress is running at more than 25,000 delivered so far with thousands more due before winter. Those cover a range of capabilities, in his account, helping Ukraine “to take the fight directly to Russia, defend itself by taking out Russian drones, and also to see what’s happening both on the battlefield and behind enemy lines”.
Britain delivered its millionth round of large calibre artillery ammunition in July, with tens of thousands more to follow, funded by Germany, Denmark, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.
The Ukrainian ask
Evgeniy Khmara, attending his first meeting as Ukraine’s Defence Minister, opened by thanking partners for the munitions, the funding and the technology, but above all for the time it had bought. “We are still standing because we have strong people and we have strong friends,” he told the group. His assessment of the front was that Russia has failed to achieve strategic success and is compensating through terror against civilians. “We have built a drone kill zone. It halts the enemy’s advance and destroys over 30,000 Russian military personnel every month,” he said.
Describing the previous night’s attack, in which cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones were launched, he said Ukrainian air defences intercepted 31 of 32 cruise missiles. “The situation with ballistics is much more difficult, and that difficulty is precisely down to the lack of Patriot missiles. Russia is aware of this, which is why it’s trying to exhaust our air defence, our economy, and our society.”
Russia is planning to mobilise something in the order of 300,000 personnel on top of those already recruited, according to Ukrainian assessments, with the same expected for 2027, alongside increased production intended to turn the war into a competition of resources. Kyiv’s answer, Khmara said, is “smart technology and speed”. On money, of the 70 billion euros promised at Ankara, partners are so far providing 62 billion including bilateral assistance and the EU loan, leaving 8 billion outstanding against the declaration while the overall defence deficit stands at 23 billion euros. He asked that the necessary decisions be taken by November so results can be seen on the battlefield this winter, noting that up to 90 per cent of Ukrainian battlefield success now rests on drones.
Ukraine is contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles with partner help and through the EU loan, but the majority will not ship for some years, which is why he asked allies to supply from existing stockpiles now in exchange for improved missiles from those future contracts. “The support for Ukraine is not a subsidy; it is an investment,” he said.
“We are offering a win-win partnership. Together, we’re creating new capacities for the security of the free world.”

China slams US claims of ‘industrial-scale’ AI theft

China slams US claims of ‘industrial-scale’ AI theft
The response comes after three US agencies accused Chinese AI companies of exploiting American AI models.
China has issued a forceful reply against claims by the United States that top Chinese artificial intelligence companies have engaged in “industrial scale” theft of their US counterparts’ AI models.
The response on Wednesday comes after three US federal agencies – the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), National Security Agency (NSA) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) – accused Chinese AI companies of exploiting American AI models to benefit their own systems.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3OpenAI unveils latest AI model amid rising scrutiny and safety concerns
- list 2 of 3As the China-US AI race reaches Cairo, Egypt faces a strategic decision
- list 3 of 3AI researcher quits Anthropic saying AI race ‘could kill us all’
The joint advisory on Tuesday said Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot AI had distilled “billions of tokens” from US models since “at least late 2024”, likely with the Chinese government’s “awareness”.
Tokens are the smallest units of text that AI models read, or generate.
On Wednesday, China’s Commerce Ministry dismissed the allegations and accused the US of seeking a “monopoly of the AI industry”.
“If the U.S. suppresses Chinese AI companies under the pretext of targeting distillation, China will take resolute countermeasures,” the ministry said in a statement to the Associated Press.
Distillation is a method in which lesser AI models are trained on more advanced ones. The ministry said the practice is commonplace in the AI industry, including by US AI companies. But American firms say the volume in which it’s being done by Chinese AI models amounts to stealing.
“The sheer scale of these campaigns and their sophistication indicate that distillation is not a supplement to these companies’ AI model development, but the critical core of it,” the US advisory claimed.
The AP reported that China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called on the US to “refrain from making unfounded accusations or smears” against China.
“China’s AI development is the result of high-level technological self-reliance and strength,” ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters at a news conference. “We maintain that all parties should strengthen cooperation to promote AI development that is open, inclusive, universally beneficial and oriented toward the common good.”
Xi visit
The US advisory comes just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to visit the US, where President Donald Trump will host a summit on a range of topics, including AI.
In a rare move, Xi could be accompanied on his US visit by a large number Chinese executives, according to the Reuters news agency. It is not clear which executives would join the delegation, but past meetings between the two countries may indicate AI leaders could be in the mix.
Xi brought Alibaba founder Jack Ma during his 2015 visit to the US. When Trump visited Xi during a trip to Beijing in May, the US president was joined by more than a dozen American executives, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
Under Trump, the US government has taken a hardline against efforts to advance Chinese AI models. China is aggressively investing heavily in artificial intelligence and robotics, pouring nearly $300bn into what the government sees as the country’s next economic engine.
While speaking in Dallas on Tuesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told an audience that China can “never get ahead” of the US in AI.
“The Chinese distill our models and they can never get ahead of us,” Bessent said.
The Chinese companies named in the US advisory did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Everything Apple Announced: iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch, AirPods 5
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:21:18 UTC
04:21:18 KST

It’s a brand-new era for Apple. The company is turning over leadership for the first time in 15 years, with former CEO Tim Cook handing off the reins last week to the new CEO, former Apple VP of hardware John Ternus.
At the first Apple product soiree hosted by Ternus, the company made an even bigger change: It announced its first-ever folding device, the iPhone Duo.
The company also announced its new line of iPhone 18 Pro phones, some updates to its Apple Watch line, new AirPods, and new software capabilities powered by Siri AI.
As expected, there were no base-model iPhone 18 announcements; those are likely coming early next year. There was also no mention of Vision Pro, iPads, or Macs. Apple touted new desktop Macs in August.
Here’s everything Apple showed off today.
Apple iPhone Duo
Apple’s first ever folding device is the Duo, a “passport-sized” foldable iPhone. It starts at $1,999 for a model with 256 GB of storage.
It’s a product category that Apple has been working toward for a decade. Now, it hopes to do that very Apple thing where it may not be the first company to the new-tech party, but it definitely aims to be the snazziest.
The Duo is a landscape style foldable, meaning it has a vertical magnetic hinge that lets you open the device like a book. Closed, it has a 5.3-inch screen on the outside. Open it up and the landscape display is 7.7 inches. The Duo is also heavy, weighing in at 254 grams, which might be a little too hefty for some users.
The Duo is made with a titanium frame and what Apple calls a “custom polymer” screen for increased durability. It runs on Apple’s proprietary A20 Pro chip (the same chip in the new Pro-model iPhone 18s) and the company’s custom C2 modem. The horizontal format also means it's capable of running iPad-like apps, albeit ones that can adjust on the fly when folding the screen or setting the phone up at an angle. The Duo will also be able to work with the Apple Pencil Pro stylus.
On the back of the Duo are two 48-megapixel cameras, one standard, one for ultrawide shots. There are two 12-megapixel selfie cameras, one on the main screen and one on the inside when the screen is opened. The cameras can also capture 4K video.
Untypical of Apple, the Duo does not have Face ID. Instead, it uses a TouchID sensor in the power button. This is likely due to Apple’s desire to minimize the device’s bulk and allow for more components inside the device.
Like, for example, the massive battery. Apple says the iPhone Duo gets 31 hours of battery life, and up to 44 hours just using the smaller front screen. Storage options start at 256 GB for the base model, with options up to 2 terabytes of space. That top configuration puts the Duo at $3,199.
Expensive, yes, and very in line with Apple's upward adjustment to its prices due to the memory shortage. But Apple is also keen on enticing users to rent the most premium devices with Apple Upgrade, the leasing program the company introduced in July.
For more details about the Duo, check out WIRED’s deeper look at the company's very first foldable.
iPhone 18 Pro
As expected, Apple is not releasing a base model iPhone this year. Instead, the company focused on highlighting its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
These look almost identical to the iPhone 17 Pro models, albeit slightly smaller. The iPhone 18 Pro is 6.3 inches, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. They come in black, silver, glacier, and burgundy color options.
They feature Apple’s new A20 Pro chips, which have been repackaged into a silicone casing that can connect directly to the new, redesigned vapor chamber, a design flourish that aids in keeping the components from overheating and helps the phone last longer. Wireless charging is even faster, able to juice the phone up to 50 percent battery life in 15 minutes.
The iPhone 18 Pro battery is capable of up to 36 hours of video playback per charge. The 18 Pro Max gets around 45 hours of video playback.
The 18 Pro phones are also getting juiced up with a new and improved Siri AI. There is an all-new Siri AI app on the iPhone. Siri AI is rolling out as a beta in English now, and will be available in French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.
Adjustable Aperture
The iPhone 18 models also get a number of big improvements to their cameras. The biggest: a variable aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro's 48-megapixel main camera. Users can dial in their preferred aperture, which adjusts mechanically in the lens. This opens up new possibilities for shooting in different light environments, as well as adjusting the depth of field for adding real—not digital—bokeh effects to photos.
Apple is also touting improved photography and video-capture controls, called Pro Controls, that let you change settings like white balance, aperture, and shutter speed. So if you’re a camera nerd, you have new software and hardware tools to play with.
Apple is also introducing Apple Reference Image, a watermarking tech that maintains an image the way it was originally shot. Apple refers to it as something close to “a digital photo negative” that you can reference if you need to prove a photo’s provenance.
The iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is $1,299. You can preorder the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max this Saturday, September 12. Apple says they’ll officially start selling September 18.
Apple Watch
Apple announced some revamps to its Apple Watch. There is a reengineered Apple Watch 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.
Both watches get new sensor arrays. Apple’s new Health Sensing System includes LEDs that measure high-frequency heart rate data as often as every five seconds. This gives wearers a constant stream of health data all day long.
The Apple Health app gets some revisions that better track sleep and show personalized guidance about your daily readiness. This is something Google’s Pixel watches have had for a while, though Apple’s reports will benefit from its new sensor array.
Also on the watch are some features that make use of Apple’s ambient listening tech to record and log the things around you. That means the watch can transcribe the things people say and show the text right on your smartwatch’s screen. In a demonstration video today, Apple showed a server at a restaurant reciting menu specials, and the person sitting at the table was able to scroll back through a transcript of the last 15 seconds on their Apple Watch’s screen to read what the server said.
These features are opt-in—at least for the person wearing the watch—and the features that record audio will emit a chime when somebody uses them. You can learn more about how the Apple Watch listens in Lily Hay Newman’s report for WIRED.
The listening feature can also send alerts to your wrist when it detects important sounds like sirens, doorbells, and babies crying. Apple says the audio is not stored, the raw audio is inaccessible even by Apple, and that the transcriptions do not identify the people talking.
There are new ceramic cases and color options for the Series 12 Watch, including gray, black, light gold, and bronze. The Apple Watch Series 12 is $399. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is $799.
For more about the Apple Watch updates, read Boutayna Chokrane’s WIRED story about all the details.
AirPods 5
Apple’s new, cheaper AirPods 5 come with some of the features that the AirPods 4 had. The AirPods 5 come with noise canceling and adaptive sound controls. You can also use Siri AI directly on the AirPods and communicate via chat. They also have live language translation, though it’s not clear how well that will function out in the real world—of course, it works great in Apple’s demo videos.
The base model costs $129. There’s also a version with touch volume controls on the stems, a little more battery, and a wireless case-charging puck that also can charge your Apple Watch. Those nicer options cost $149.
Some rumors had predicted that Apple would show off a new pair of AirPods with cameras in the earbuds. Those are possibly still coming eventually, but Apple didn't say anything about them this time. We’re expecting at least one more Apple event before the end of the year, and they may show up then.

Canadian Muslim groups welcome Ottawa's decision to ban illegal Israeli settlement trade

Merve Gül Aydoğan Ağlarcı
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Canadian Muslim organizations and a leading human rights advocate on Wednesday welcomed Ottawa's decision to join 11 countries in the long "overdue" but "monumental" move to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Ahmad Al Qadi, Government Affairs and Public Policy Officer at the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM), said at a news conference in Ottawa that the organization was "here to welcome the government's announcement on a categorical ban on products emerging from illegal Israeli settlements."
"Although this step should have been taken long ago, September 8th, 2026, will mark a monumental day in Canada's history," he said.
Al Qadi said future generations of Canadians "will use this date as a precedent for Canada's commitment to upholding values of human rights, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, values that the Prime Minister (Mark Carney) spelled out clearly during his Davos address."
He added that the ban "demonstrates that, indeed, as the Prime Minister stated, Canada is not powerless," and it has "the capacity to build a new world order that respects these values."
Al Qadi thanked Carney and Foreign Minister Anita Anand on behalf of the NCCM for advancing the ban, stressing that "Canadian businesses operating internationally have a duty to respect human rights and ensure that activities do not contribute to adverse impacts."
Imam Sikander Hashmi, executive director of the Canadian Council of Imams, said Canada's trade policy "should not help sustain the dispossession and abuse of another people," calling the ban "overdue."
He said Islamic teachings do not bar business dealings based on ethnicity or religion, noting that Prophet Muhammad “conducted business with Jewish people and others."
"Honest and respectful trade can benefit everyone. It can build relationships and bring communities together," said Hashmi, adding that "trade that sustains injustice demands a different response," and "refusing to support dispossession is a matter of basic fairness and human dignity."
Amira Elghawaby, a human rights advocate and Canada's former special representative on combatting Islamophobia, said the decision was "grounded in clear principles of international law, including the Fourth Geneva Convention and numerous other United Nations resolutions and international court findings."
She said the move by Canada and its allies sends "an unmistakable signal" that they "refuse to be complicit in the violation of international law," describing it as "the mainstream of international law finally being enforced through policy."
Citing public opinion, Elghawaby said that "far more Canadians oppose illegal settlements than support them, and far more Canadians support banning settlement products than oppose that step."
"Canada's responsibilities do not end at our borders," she said, adding that upholding international law "consistently and without exception is how a country like ours earns the right to speak about human rights at all." 
12 countries announce measures on illegal Israeli settlements
The foreign ministers of the 12 countries announced in a statement Tuesday that they would impose or consider trade restrictions on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The countries said Israel's actions in the West Bank were undermining prospects for a two-state solution and stressed the need to preserve the possibility of establishing a Palestinian state.
Israel subsequently announced that it would close the UK's consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, which serves Palestinians, in response to the measures.

Poland has presented the domestically produced CBWP heavy infantry fighting vehicle (IFV).
A Militarnyi correspondent reported this from the MSPO exhibition in Poland.
The CBWP is being developed by companies from the Polish Armaments Group, including Huta Stalowa Wola, in response to the Polish Armed Forces’ need for a vehicle that is heavier and better protected than the Borsuk IFV.
In the configuration shown at the exhibition, the CBWP is equipped with the remotely controlled ZSSW-30 turret used on the Borsuk IFV and Rosomak armored personnel carrier, a 30 mm Mk 44/S Bushmaster II cannon, a machine gun and a Spike-LR anti-tank guided missile launcher.
Other CBWP weapon configurations are also possible, including a 40 mm or 105 mm cannon.
The IFV weighs approximately 40 tons, compared with 28 tons for the Borsuk. The demonstrator is equipped with an 800 kW MTU engine, producing more than 1,000 hp, as well as a U.S.-made transmission.
The CBWP will have two troop compartment configurations, with seating for 6-8 troops.
In this configuration, the vehicle meets the requirements of the SAFE program and uses at least 65% EU technologies.
According to Defence24, the Polish Armaments Group announced plans to produce two prototypes in 2027 and be ready to begin serial production of the IFV in 2029.
Huta Stalowa Wola first revealed the specifications of the new IFV, then known as the Ratel, at last year’s MSPO exhibition in September.

Rutte warns delays in Ukraine aid cost lives
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:18:52 BST
04:18:52 KST

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has urged allies to accelerate military support for Ukraine, warning that delays in delivering weapons and funding are costing lives.
Speaking at the latest Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting, Rutte said Ukraine’s war against Russia was directly affecting the wider security environment across NATO and called on countries to increase their contributions.
Rutte said: “Ukraine’s fight shapes the entire Euro-Atlantic security environment. It directly impacts, as we all know, our own security, and as we work on modernising the alliance and building a stronger Europe and a stronger NATO, we must continue to support Ukraine’s security and help them defend from Russia’s brutal attacks.”
He added: “That means supporting Ukraine with the utmost urgency. And here, let me say that delays simply cost human lives.”

The NATO Secretary General identified air defence, drones and extended-range ammunition as priority requirements for Ukrainian forces. Rutte also said allies were seeing changes in the weapons employed by Russia, including greater use of North Korean missiles and jet-powered attack drones.
He stressed the continuing role of the PURL mechanism, under which NATO allies and partners finance the purchase of American weapons for Ukraine. According to Rutte, around $10 billion had been allocated over the previous year through PURL and US foreign military sales for Ukraine, including $3.5 billion originating from the Ukraine support loan.
He described those figures as evidence of European countries taking on a greater share of the effort to sustain Ukraine. Rutte said continued deliveries were particularly important for maintaining Ukrainian air defences and enabling forces to hold positions on the front line.

Ukraine seeks 300 Patriot missiles from allies
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:18:38 BST
04:18:38 KST

Ukraine has asked allied countries to provide 300 Patriot interceptor missiles from their existing stocks as Kyiv attempts to strengthen its air defences before another winter of Russian missile and drone attacks.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara set out the requirement during his first appearance at the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, alongside requests for 500 air-to-air interceptors capable of engaging cruise missiles and $2 billion in funding for drones.
Khmara said a recent Russian attack had involved cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed-type drones. Ukrainian air defences had intercepted 31 of 32 cruise missiles, he said, but ballistic missiles were proving more difficult to counter because of shortages of Patriot ammunition.
He said: “Our air defence managed, among other things, to intercept 31 of the 32 cruise missiles, but the situation with ballistics is much more difficult, and that difficulty is precisely down to the lack of Patriot missiles.”
Ukraine is already contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles with support from partner countries and through European Union financing, according to Khmara, but most of those weapons are not expected to arrive immediately.
He therefore appealed to countries to transfer missiles currently held in their own inventories, saying: “we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today, in exchange for future improved missiles from our contracts.”
Khmara also warned that Ukraine faces a substantial defence funding gap. He said €70 billion in security assistance had been promised this year, with around €62 billion currently expected from bilateral assistance and European funding.
That leaves €8 billion of the earlier commitment outstanding, while Khmara put the wider Ukrainian defence funding shortfall at €23 billion, equivalent to around $27 billion. He asked partners to take the necessary funding decisions by November so that equipment could reach the battlefield during the winter.
Drones also featured prominently in the Ukrainian presentation. Khmara said: “Up to 90 percent of our success in the battlefield is down to drones.”
He said Ukrainian companies were developing lower-cost methods of intercepting jet-powered Shahed-type drones, with some interceptor systems already being tested in combat. Khmara also said Ukrainian assessments indicated that Russia was planning to mobilise around 300,000 additional personnel on top of existing recruitment and could seek a similar mobilisation effort in 2027.
He argued that Moscow was attempting to turn the conflict into a competition over manpower and resources, while Ukraine intended to rely increasingly on technology, drones and rapid battlefield adaptation.

====================================================================================================

Staggering price tag for states worst hit by rising seas revealed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:18:14 UTC
04:18:14 KST

Sea level rise threatens more than a quarter of a million properties as bill surges to $855b
Climate change means Australia's love of the coast is facing a multi-billion-dollar reckoning, research suggests, as rising seas threaten to turn its prized coastal lifestyle into a question of who will foot the bill: property owners or governments.
In the first nationwide assessment of economic losses from sea level rise, researchers from the University of Melbourne, the Australian National University and Global Environmental and Economic Modelling have found that all coastal states and the Northern Territory face hefty damage bills this century.
Australia could face damage costs of more than $850 billion, with more than $274 billion going to property losses and $580 billion spent on land-use damage.
Co-author Tom Kompas said the findings were "alarming", and the economic toll would mount as fossil fuel emissions continued to drive global temperatures higher.
"We keep warming the planet … so you get more sea level rise, you get higher tides, higher king tides, higher maximum tides," the professor of environmental economics and biosecurity at the University of Melbourne said.
"You get more intense, and maybe even more frequent storms and storm surges, and that causes localised flooding."
Sea level rise hits hard across the board
As temperatures rise, melting ice and the thermal expansion of warmer seawater raise sea levels, threatening coastal communities worldwide.
The Australian research found more than 267,000 coastal properties and 2 million hectares of land across the country will face flood damage by 2100 based on global carbon emissions peaking around 2040 and global warming being limited to about 2.7C.
The United Nations has warned that warming will reach at least 1.8C above pre-industrial levels and projects it could reach up to 2.6C by the end of the century under current policies.
The findings also put a price tag of more than a trillion dollars on impacts associated with global warming exceeding 4C. However, that level of warming was predicated on growing fossil fuel use, and scientists have deemed it unlikely to eventuate due to the uptake of clean energy.
Queensland has been identified as having 93,000 properties at risk of damage due to sea level rise, resulting in an expected damage bill of $214 billion for the state.
The Gold Coast is Australia's most exposed urban area, with projected economic losses of $84.4 billion.
Western Australia faces the largest total losses, while in New South Wales, communities in the state's north and Central Coast region face higher property losses than in Greater Sydney.
With Victoria the only jurisdiction where property damage costs exceed those associated with land use, Professor Kompas said the research underscored the significant costs of inundating farmland and recreational areas.
"Much of it is badly, badly damaged with sea level rise and storm surge … damaged reserves, parks, beaches," he said.
"So it's not just individual properties, commercial and residential properties; it's a wide range of assets that are being impacted."
Consequences with every centimetre
The economic assessment forms the basis of a Climate Council report, which highlights how coastal floods previously considered severe will become a regular occurrence in the future.
It found that every 10cm of sea level rise will triple the frequency of "once-in-a-century" flood events.
Global sea levels have already risen by over 22cm since 1900, with projections there could be an additional 14cm by 2050.
Narrowneck Beach and other northern Gold Coast shores suffered severe sand loss, exposed rock walls, and high tides crashing against infrastructure three months after Tropical Cyclone Alfred. (ABC News: Nicholas McElroy)
Report author and Climate Councillor Andrew Watkins said the impacts were already being felt.
"We have seen quite a rapid increase in what we call extreme water levels along the coast, and that gives coastal inundation, coastal flooding and coastal erosion as well," the Adjunct Professor at Monash University's School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment said.
Sea level rise can damage coastal land and infrastructure in multiple ways, including permanent inundation. Scientists often use the "1 to 100 rule" to describe this — meaning seawater will go about a metre inland for each centimetre of sea level rise.
So 10cm of sea level rise can actually move water 10 metres further inland, inundating any land or building in its path.
The Land and Environment Court has granted consent for a 90-metre seawall at The Entrance North, a coastal village in NSW's Central Coast. (Supplied: Horton Coastal Engineering)
Rising seas can also contribute to isolated coastal flooding events when combined with storms.
"When you have that sea level rise, and then you get a storm surge where the storm is pushing the water up against the coast, it makes the water go even higher," Dr Watkins said.
"Then you get waves on top of that, and if it happens at high tide, that's when you get the full combination of impacts."
Storm surges and wind-driven waves linked to Ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred led to severe erosion along the coastline between south-east Queensland and north-east NSW last year, with the Insurance Council of Australia announcing more than 125,000 claims totalling $1.36 billion.
Higher sea levels will push storm surges further inland. (X: Lisa Garnham)
Associate Professor of Climate Adaptation at Griffith University Johanna Nalau said recovery from that event was still ongoing.
"There has been a lot of work on beach nourishment and then more acute damage, so we talk about power, power networks, transport, water and sewage; those were resolved within weeks to months," she said.
"But the coastal erosion part is still an ongoing effort, and there has been some reporting in the news as well that some of the housing damage that people experience hasn't been resolved yet."
Bracing for the future
Experts are calling for improved efforts to help coastal regions adapt as climate change not only contributes to rising sea levels but is also expected to increase the frequency and intensity of storms.
Storms last year caused significant erosion damage at Fox Beach, Robe, SA. (Supplied: District Council of Robe)
Warnings of a mounting economic toll have also raised questions around who will foot the damage bills going forward, particularly given insurance generally does not cover "actions of the sea".
"Most coastal properties would have some level of insurance, although the insurance sector is also very, very aware of risks that come with climate change," Dr Nalau said.
"So insurance premiums are increasing quite heavily in some coastal areas."
Dr Watkins said it was becoming "prohibitively expensive" for some councils to pay for adaptation and recovery.
In the 1970s, old car bodies were used to prevent sand dune erosion in front of a sand mining site at Belongil in Byron Bay. (Supplied: NSW Public Works)
"A lot of councils are effectively having to dip into their own coffers to support resilience building, but also to recover from damage that's done when we have these storm events and sea level events along our coastlines," he said.
"We do need to look at this as a national problem and develop plans with the communities and with the local, state, and federal level about the best ways to go forward."

UK deepens NATO-first defence industry cooperation
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:18:03 BST
04:18:03 KST

The UK is expanding defence industrial cooperation with NATO allies and international partners, including the United States, as part of a wider effort to strengthen production capacity, supply chains and military readiness, the Ministry of Defence has said.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard set out the position in response to a written parliamentary question from Labour MP Callum Anderson, who asked what discussions the Government had held with allies on increasing defence industrial cooperation.
Pollard said work had accelerated since publication of the Defence Industrial Strategy in September 2025, with greater emphasis on exports, strategic partnerships, information sharing and what the department describes as a NATO-first approach to industrial cooperation.
He said: “Since publication of the Defence Industrial Strategy on 8 September 2025, the Department has strengthened collaboration with industry, NATO Allies and international partners, including the United States, to support UK defence exports, deepen strategic partnerships, improve information sharing and promote a NATO-first approach to industrial co-operation.”
The MOD also pointed to the role of National Armaments International in helping British defence companies compete for overseas contracts.
Pollard said: “National Armaments International is supporting UK companies to compete overseas, with record successes in 2025 including the UK’s biggest ever warship deal to Norway and the largest fighter jet exports agreement in a generation, promoting global security while boosting growth at home.”
The department is linking that international activity with efforts to expand industrial capacity inside the UK. This includes giving companies clearer indications of future demand, investing in priority capabilities and strengthening supply chains in sectors considered important to military readiness.
A further element is expected to come through the planned Defence Readiness Bill, which Pollard said is due later in the current Parliament. At alliance level, the UK is continuing work on NATO initiatives intended to increase defence production and make supply chains more resilient across member states.
The UK also backed a new NATO strategy for cooperation with industry at the recent Ankara summit.
Pollard said: “The UK also joined Allies in endorsing the new Strategy for Industry NATO Cooperation at the recent Ankara summit and maintains a strong partnership with the UK delegation to the NATO Industrial Advisory Group (NIAG), enabling senior industrialists to offer expertise and strategic insight on a wide range of security policy, defence planning, and capability issues.”
The NATO Industrial Advisory Group provides a route for defence companies and industrial specialists to feed expertise into alliance planning and capability discussions. Britain hosted the NIAG plenary in June 2026, an event the MOD said demonstrated a shared government and industry commitment to NATO capability development and further cooperation between allied defence sectors.

====================================================================================================

Pollard says he does not want kit that fails in Ukraine
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
20:17:19 BST
04:17:19 KST

Equipment that would not survive the war in Ukraine has no place in the British armed forces, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry has told an audience of financiers and defence firms at Mansion House, in a speech setting out how the government intends to bring private capital into defence.
Luke Pollard was speaking on Tuesday at an event hosted by the Lady Mayor, ahead of remarks by the Ukrainian Ambassador, and used the address to announce a Defence Finance Investment Strategy to follow the autumn budget along with a defence investment summit in December.
Warning that Britain must “discard the warm comfort blanket that we are used to, of polishing old things and pretending that that will protect us”, he put the test in a single sentence: “If our technology and kit will not work in Ukraine, I do not want it in our armed forces.”
That, he argued, opens the door to “new technology, new thinking, new weapons”, and to designing for “the conflicts of today and the battles of tomorrow”.
“The way that the United Kingdom would now fight is fundamentally different today than it was at the point when Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine only those four and a half years ago,” he told the room, adding that learning from Ukraine means changing how Britain itself operates.
Finding, funding and firing up
Much of the speech turned on speed, and on where the useful ideas are now coming from. Many of the most critical advances in defence, in the minister’s account, are emerging from technology startups and scale-ups, agile businesses “seizing the opportunities on offer and driving change at speed”. The challenge he set the room was framed as a question. “How can we get better at finding, funding and firing up the most creative minds and enterprise to get the best technology into the hands of our armed forces and those of our allies as fast as possible?”
He was unsparing about the position two years ago, describing a defence programme that was “to be honest and to be frank, unfit to counter the dangers that we now face”. Industry, he suggested, needs no reminding. “Those who work in our supply chains know how painfully slow, wasteful and costly the procurement the MOD previously undertook was,” he said, singling out small businesses and scale-ups with good products who “struggled sometimes to find the right buyer within the MOD”.
Small firms
Against that, Pollard set out the machinery now in place: a new National Armaments Director in Rupert Pearce, recruited from a FTSE 100 company and bringing what the minister called a new corporate approach and energy to procurement; the Defence Office for Small Business Growth, established to cut red tape and remove obstacles to entry; and an SME Action Plan published so the department can be held to account for the change.
The headline commitment is a 50 per cent increase in departmental spending with medium and small firms by summer 2028, which the minister described as “moving an extra two and a half billion pounds into the pockets of SMEs by changing the way we procure”.
Regional defence and security clusters have proved successful enough that more regions are developing them, he said, creating local routes that bring together major suppliers, devolved and local government, and giving investors a forum in which to meet them.
Bringing in the City
Running through the address was an argument that public money alone will not build the capacity required in the time available, however welcome rising budgets are. “As a defence minister, of course, I would like more defence spending,” he said.
“But it’s not just from the taxpayer that there’s opportunities for investing in defence. It’s how you crowd in private capital, how you use the institutions, the networks, the structures of the City of London and the UK’s place at the heart of global financial trade, to bring more private capital into defence, creating more good jobs and more deterrence.”
Waiting was not, in his view, an option: “In a more dangerous world, we need to build more capacity now, rather than just wait for the increase in defence money that we know is coming over the next 10 years.”
Whether the two sides can understand one another is a separate problem, and one he acknowledged. “There’s a risk that we sometimes speak past each other,” he said, arguing that a shared language and shared data would improve the department’s ability to deliver. The Defence Investment Unit announced in the Defence Investment Plan is meant to close that gap, giving investors a clearer interface with the department while bringing financial expertise in to turn priorities into market-facing propositions.
Companies already through the door
To show the approach producing results rather than remaining theoretical, the minister turned to firms that have already taken the route.
Thirteen British startups won contracts of up to £4 million in May under the Defence Unicorn Fund programme. Among them was Kraken Technologies, which builds maritime uncrewed surface vessels and has since raised $175 million in a Series B round on the back of a $1 billion valuation. Green Jets, one of three firms selected to develop a low-cost drone interceptor, has also secured significant funding. Both drew money from the National Security Strategic Investment Fund and the NATO Innovation Fund, with the British Business Bank financing Kraken as well.
JET Connectivity, a small business building 5G and 6G communications tools, was the only British firm admitted to the NATO DIANA mission track programme this year from more than three and a half thousand participants, which Mr Pollard called “fantastic recognition of British innovation at its best” while adding that it is “just the tip of the iceberg”.
There was a moment of self-deprecation over how the language has shifted under the current Prime Minister, with the Minister saying, “I used to be incentivised by the MOD press office to say defence is an engine for growth in all my interviews,” he told the audience. “With Andy Burnham in Downing Street I now say re-industrialisation, but the fundamental truth is there. Investment in defence creates good jobs. It provides opportunities in particular for our young people and we should be unafraid and unapologetic of saying that truth loudly.”
His closing argument was that none of this rests with his department alone, describing defence as “a whole of society endeavour, a whole of government endeavour” which the Ministry of Defence must lead but cannot deliver by itself.
He finished on deterrence, and on what follows if it does not hold, saying “That’s why increasing our deterrence matters with new technologies. But if deterrence fails, we must be ready to fight, and we must be ready to win.”
