Yemen's Houthis report dozens of new Saudi airstrikes as conflict exacerbates
Yemen's Houthi rebels reported dozens of Saudi airstrikes on Wednesday as daily attacks continued in a conflict that has reignited during the Middle East war, with hundreds of people killed in fighting near the Red Sea.
More than 50 attacks targeted several regions including Taiz and Hodeida, the scene of fierce clashes between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government, the Houthis said.
"It's a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing," said Mohammed Khudairi, one of nearly 20,000 people who fled the fighting, according to the International Organization for Migration.
"We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there," he said at a displacement camp of wood-and-straw huts near Khokha, on the Red Sea coast.
The latest salvos in Yemen's previously dormant conflict come a day after the Iran-backed Houthis set oil sites ablaze and wounded 73 in their heaviest missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia in years.
The Houthis' Al-Masirah TV Channel reported on Wednesday the toll from Saudi strikes on a prison days earlier had climbed to 32 dead and seven injured as rescue and recovery efforts continued.
The fighting comes against the backdrop of the Middle East war, which erupted in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
Over 500 killed; Hodeida in Saudi crosshairs
The fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people since the Houthis launched a major offensive last week to seize territory around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, gateway to the Red Sea shipping route.
The Houthis have also been attacking Saudi oil tankers, and are trying to tighten their squeeze on the shipments, analysts say -- a lifeline for exports after Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
"During the past 12 hours, the Saudi enemy's air force conducted 54 airstrikes targeting the provinces of Al-Jawf, Marib, Taiz, Hodeida and Saada," said Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree.
Footage released by the Iran-backed group showed what it said were attacks on Saudi-backed forces on Al-Jawf province's frontlines, with missiles heard flying overhead before impact, followed by flaming wreckage.
There was no official comment from Saudi Arabia.
Analysis by the Institute for the Study of War said the city of Hodeida, held by the Houthis, could be the "ultimate objective" of the Saudi backed forces.
The Red Sea port is "critical to both Houthi civilian and military goods, and its loss would be a significant setback for the Houthis", a report published by the institute said.
Saudi warnings
Saudi civil defence issued warnings twice for the southern governorate of Khamis Mushait, near Yemen, and once for Abha city, but quickly lifted the alerts without elaborating on the cause.
On Tuesday, Saudi authorities vowed to respond to the Houthi attacks, saying they caused fires and temporary shutdowns at oil sites.
The Houthis triggered the return to hostilities in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.
Yemen's internationally recognised government, which controls Aden and the south of the country, retaliated by striking the airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on its sponsor, Saudi Arabia.
The ongoing exchanges risk returning Yemen to a conflict that left hundreds of thousands of people dead and sparked one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Yemen's capital Sanaaand forcing out the internationally recognised government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.

The AfD has been classified as right-wing extremist by the local office of Germany's domestic intelligence service. In its election program in Saxony-Anhalt, it advocated for "remigration" policies to speed up deportations of rejected asylum seekers and foreign criminals and incentivize people to leave voluntarily.

"If what is being advocated here, namely 'remigration', were to become reality, it would be nothing other than a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin color," Merz said, in answer to an earlier speech by AfD co-leader Alice Weidel.

Merz spokesperson declines to comment on Trump post

At the same regular press conference, Kornelius said the government had postponed a planned phone call between Merz and Trump on the upcoming 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks in the US.
"The German side postponed this call today. A new date has not yet been set," he said, declining to give a reason for the postponement.
The US and Germany have traditionally been close allies, but their relationship has been put to the test since Trump's return to office.
Kornelius said Germany remains ready to stand up for the values that define and unite the two countries. "These are freedom, democracy and respect," he said.

 Quantum Field Theory (QFT) is the mathematical and conceptual framework for contemporary high-energy physics, or “particle physics” (but see the discussion of the problematic particle interpretation below). It is also a framework used in other areas of theoretical physics, such as condensed matter physics and statistical mechanics. Bessent bond plan details to be revealed as Treasury secretary warns FX traders he's 'the house now'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:43:32 UTC
03:43:32 KST

Markets are set to find out Wednesday just how aggressive the Treasury Department's bond-buying program will get, as Secretary Scott Bessent dared currency traders to challenge him.
The department is expected to announce around 11 a.m. ET the size of a buyback operation it unveiled Aug. 19, an aggressive move and part of a broader strategy to keep a lid on Treasury yields and ensure markets function as intended.
"I am the house now," Bessent said Tuesday at Southern Methodist University, referring more specifically to his department's parallel maneuver to support the Japanese yen. "And you can bet against me if you want."
In the case of the yen, Treasury stepped in to buy the currency so that the Bank of Japan wouldn't sell its Treasurys. At $1.1 trillion, Japan is the largest foreign holder of U.S. debt, so a move to sell Treasurys likely would boost yields at a time when the domestic debt has soared past the $40 trillion mark and the deficit is headed past $2 trillion.
On the home front, Bessent announced last month that Treasury would buy back at least $4 billion of already-issued long debt, focusing specifically around 10- and 20-year notes. That is double the normal size of the buyback operations, and speculation is growing that the $4 billion level is a floor, not a ceiling.
"The size of the increase in bond-sector repurchases remains highly uncertain – and the odds of a larger increase are rising," analysts at Wrightson ICAP said in a note earlier this week. "Something in the $5 billion to $6 billion range now seems likely to be the starting point for the discussion, and we cannot rule out something larger."
Bessent's comments represent an even starker warning to markets than previous remarks, though the actual impact has been unclear.
The benchmark 10-year yield has risen about 10 basis points, or 0.1 percentage point, since the buyback announcement. Moreover, the 30-year bond yield has edged higher as well, though it has remained below the 5.3% level that BMO Capital Markets analyst Ian Lyngen said is a "proverbial line in the sand that was effectively established by Bessent."
The secretary's staunch position, though, has rattled some investors as heavy-handed and potentially damaging to a market considered the deepest and most liquid in the world.
"Such a backdrop represents a departure from the Treasury's history of being predictable and gradual to change course, although it appears to be the undeniable direction of Bessent's leadership," wrote Lyngen, BMO's head of rates strategy. "Our concern is that it will have negative consequences for the credibility of Treasuries as an asset class."
An announced buyback of $6 billion would be "fairly aggressive," according to the Wrightson analysts. Going beyond that to tripling or quadrupling the normal level would be an "extreme case" that would "result in a much more visible deceleration in the net supply trajectory."
While the buyback level will be announced Wednesday, the actual operation won't happen until Thursday. Markets will be watching both the offered amount as well as the demand from debt holders.

Yemeni army says it captured 'vast areas' from Houthis in northern Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:41:48 UTC
03:41:48 KST

Mohammed Sameai
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The Yemeni army announced Wednesday that its forces captured "vast areas" from the Houthis in northern Al-Jawf province.
In a statement on US social media platform X, the army's media center said forces also cut off Houthis' supply lines on the eastern fronts of Al-Hazm, the provincial capital of Al-Jawf.
“Our armed forces today took control of the Al-Mutahaffat area, Al-Masariya Hill and the hills adjacent to Al-Faraid Hill, north of Al-Labanat Al-Olya in Al-Jawf province," it said.
It added that government forces took control of “earthworks and trenches extending for about 20 km (12.5 miles), from the Al-Duhaydah positions through Al-Saara to Bir Al-Maraziq, east of Al-Hazm.”
Several Houthi fighters were also captured or killed and others wounded during fighting, the army claimed.
Amid the field advances, the statement said army aircraft carried out “focused and precise airstrikes” on Houthi gatherings and positions, destroying military vehicles and equipment.
In a parallel development, the government-aligned National Resistance Forces announced in a statement carried by its 2 December news agency that their naval forces "engaged" Houthi boats in the Red Sea.
Maval forces forced Houthi boats "to retreat north toward the city of Hodeidah," it added.
The Houthis did not comment on the statements.
Yemeni government forces have previously announced on several occasions that they destroyed Houthi boats off the coast of the strategic port of Mokha, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.   
Fighting intensifies
Fighting has intensified in recent days on several fronts, particularly in Taiz, Al-Jawf and Al-Bayda, alongside airstrikes targeting Houthi positions.
The escalation has also spilled into neighboring Saudi Arabia. Riyadh said Tuesday that Houthi attacks targeting civilian and economic sites in the southwestern cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran injured 73 civilians, including women and children.
The Houthis, accused of receiving Iranian support, claimed that they targeted facilities belonging to Saudi energy company Aramco and an air base with dozens of ballistic missiles and drones.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the national capital of Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014. A Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

Breathing depends on a cylinder: Gaza faces medical oxygen crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:40:38 UTC
03:40:38 KST

Breathing depends on a cylinder: Gaza faces medical oxygen crisis
Only 12 of Gaza’s 34 oxygen-generation stations remain operational, worsening the health crisis in the besieged enclave.
Az-Zuwayda, Gaza Strip – Ali Humaida’s heart rate quickens as he watches the gauge on the oxygen cylinder sitting in the corner of his tent.
As the needle falls, he looks at his 14-year-old son, Abdulaziz, lying on a mattress in the family’s tent in central Gaza’s az-Zuwayda, worried about how long the remaining oxygen will last – and where he will find more when it runs out.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Inside Israel’s prisons, where Ben-Gvir’s cruelty is policy
- list 2 of 3As the UK sanctions Israeli settlements, is the two-state solution dead?
- list 3 of 3Gaza students with overseas university offers, scholarships remain trapped
Abdulaziz depends on a continuous supply of supplemental oxygen, his father says. One night, when the family’s cylinder emptied before they were able to replace it, his breathing rapidly deteriorated.
“The cylinder suddenly ran out in the middle of the night,” Ali recalled. “The minutes turned into a nightmare. We began fanning him with our hands and pieces of cardboard while watching his face turn blue, terrified he would lose consciousness or slip into a coma right before our eyes, while we stood completely helpless.”
For families caring for oxygen-dependent patients in Gaza, such emergencies have become increasingly difficult to avoid.
Gaza’s Ministry of Health warned on August 15 that only 12 of the strip’s 34 oxygen-generation stations remained operational, while only four of 30 devices used to fill oxygen cylinders were still working. The remaining equipment was overworked with repeated mechanical failures, the ministry said.
These conditions have made obtaining cylinders particularly difficult for patients such as Abdulaziz, who receive much of their care outside hospitals.
“Every minute that passes means the oxygen is running out,” Ali said. “I am constantly asking myself: How much is left in the cylinder? Will it last until morning? And if it empties, where will I get another one?”
Complicated medical history
Abdulaziz has lived with serious health problems since birth. He was born with a congenital heart defect and has underdeveloped lungs.
Since childhood, he has also suffered from hydrocephalus, or cerebrospinal fluid buildup in the brain. Abdulaziz underwent surgery to relieve pressure on his brain by inserting a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt that drains excess fluid.
In addition, he has autism spectrum disorder and requires extensive daily care – something that is extremely difficult in a displaecment camp in Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war.
Before the war, Abdulaziz received regular specialised treatment at a hospital in Israel. That has now stopped, leaving the family dependent on Gaza’s health system, which has been devastated by Israeli attacks.
The cost of caring for Abdulaziz has also increased. His father, Ali, estimates that medicine, diapers and transportation now cost the family between 950 and 1,100 shekels ($315 and $365) a month – double pre-war prices.
“Abdulaziz cannot express pain like other children because of his autism, but I can see the distress in his eyes,” Ali said. “I am not asking for the impossible, all I want is for my son to breathe freely.”
When oxygen runs out
Interrupting supplemental oxygen can be dangerous for patients who depend on the therapy to maintain adequate blood-oxygen levels.
Dr Ghada Hassouna, a physician at al-Aqsa Martyr’s Hospital in Deir el-Balah, said a patient whose oxygen saturation level plummet can develop rapid breathing, a faster heart rate and cyanosis – a bluish discolouration of the skin caused by poor oxygen and blood flows.
Inadequate oxygen can also damage vital organs, particularly the brain and the heart.
Hassouna explained that the brain cells are exceptionally sensitive to oxygen deprivation, and are the most vulnerable to rapid breakdown and damage. In Abdulaziz’s case, any drop in oxygen levels can cause severe or permanent nerve damage.
This is an issue that impacts more than just one family.
According to the Gaza Ministry of Health, the majority of oxygen-generation stations being out of service is the result of a systematic Israeli policy across border crossings.
Israeli authorities continue to restrict and ban the entry of spare parts and specialised lubricants for hospital generators and oxygen plants, as well as blocking new plants meant to compensate for the shortage.
Israel classifies oxygen cylinders, accompanying devices and electrical generators as “dual-use” items, prohibiting their entry or spare parts through closed crossings.
At the same time, the environment of forced displacement imposes an extra layer of suffering.
Hundreds of thousands live in open areas lacking basic proper ventilation, filled with dust and toxic emissions from burning plastic waste and alternative power generators, which doubles the number of patients suffering from acute pneumonia and respiratory ailments such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
This comes at a time when the Ministry of Health and several hospitals in the strip have completely halted external oxygen cylinder refilling services for patients receiving care at home or in displacement tents.
The decision was a forced measure taken by the health system after nearing collapse, in an effort to preserve remaining oxygen supplies for bed networks in critical hospital departments such as intensive care units, neonatal incubators, and operating rooms.
Facing this complex field reality, medical staff explain that the decision was not an administrative choice, but a response to a catastrophic reality imposed by war conditions and the systematic destruction of health infrastructure.
The United Nations estimates that about 350,000 people in Gaza are living with chronic diseases, with treatments severely disrupted by the war.
Mohammad Abu Salmiya, director of al-Shifa Medical Complex, said Gaza is coping with shortages of half of essential medicines and more than 80 percent of laboratory materials. He estimated that about 21,000 patients and wounded people needed treatment outside Gaza, including more than 4,000 cancer patients and more than 10,000 injured people requiring advanced surgical care.
For now, patients in Gaza have to make do with what is available inside the Palestinian enclave.
Abdulaziz’s family measures time by what remains in his oxygen cylinder.
“We want him to be able to travel and resume his treatment,” Ali said. “Until then, we need a stable supply of oxygen.”
“All we want is for our son to breathe with dignity, without the constant fear that his breathing could stop at any moment.”

Ukrainian Drones Knock Out About 60% of KINEF Oil Refinery Capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:39:50 UTC
03:39:50 KST

Satellite imagery has confirmed that Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit the Kirishi Oil Refinery (Kirishinefteorgsintez, KINEF) in the Leningrad region.
The Absolutely Reliable Source project reported this.
On August 30, 2026, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the facility. Later, on September 2, it became known that the refinery had halted operations.
Reuters reported damage to key units at the facility at the time, but details were not disclosed.
Now, favorable weather conditions have made it possible to obtain high-quality satellite imagery confirming that two primary oil-processing units and three secondary processing units were hit.
The following facilities were identified at the refinery: ELOU-AT-1 — hit and shut down, with a capacity of 1.7 million tons per year; ELOU-AT-6 — hit and shut down, with a capacity of 7.6 million tons per year; ELOU-AVT-2 — undergoing repairs following a previous strike, with a capacity of 2.8 million tons per year; and ELOU-AVT-6 — fully operational, with a capacity of 8 million tons per year.
The secondary processing units LCh/24/9 and LCh/24/10, which are diesel fuel hydrotreating units, as well as the LG-35/8-300B catalytic reforming unit, were also identified.
Of the refinery’s total design primary processing capacity of 20.1 million tons per year, more than 12 million tons are currently out of service, accounting for about 60% of its capacity.
The refinery is one of Russia’s largest oil-processing facilities, with an estimated capacity of approximately 330,000-350,000 barrels per day.
Ukrainian drones first hit the refinery on March 8, 2025. KINEF, which accounts for 7% of Russia’s total oil refining and produces 2 million tons of gasoline and 7 million tons of diesel fuel annually, had already been forced to halt operations for extended repairs twice this year due to UAV attacks — on March 26 and May 5.
The refinery had never been fully restored. In August, it was operating at approximately 50% capacity.

New maps reveal hidden landscapes inside a prehistoric supercontinent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:38:14 UTC
03:38:14 KST

More than 180 million years after the supercontinent Gondwana’s breakup, scientists are still learning the true reach of this prehistoric landmass that once stretched across the globe.
By analyzing more than 25,000 volcanic rocks, a new study finds that Gondwana likely accounted for around 80 percent of total global land area around 500 million years ago. The analysis identifies pieces of Earth’s crust deep beneath Asia, Europe and North America that were once part of the supercontinent. That’s far larger than scientists had thought: older studies estimated Gondwana’s size as equivalent to around 64 percent of global land area.
This massive size means Gondwana’s formation and development over time could have been instrumental in the Cambrian explosion of life, the authors write—a period from about 540 to 530 million years ago when nearly all modern-day animals’ ancestors appeared on Earth for the first time.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
To uncover the hidden landscapes, researchers analyzed the chemical composition of deeply buried rocks from different geochemistry databases and mapped Gondwana using the distribution of elements within the rocks.
The newly revealed geographical areas, combined with existing knowledge of the supercontinent, reveal that Gondwana could have had outsized effects on sea level, atmospheric gas and volcanic eruptions—together these factors would have influenced early life on Earth, the researchers write. The findings were published today in Science Advances.
It’s possible that still-undiscovered parts of the continent could have been submerged or recycled back into Earth’s crust, the authors write. That means that even this massive new scale could be an underestimate as scientists continue to piece together our planet’s early history.

Israel opened its first permanent embassy in Slovenia on Wednesday, marking a sharp turnaround after years of strained relations under the country’s previous government.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar inaugurated the embassy in Ljubljana alongside Slovenian Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer, months after Prime Minister Janez Jansa returned to power at the head of a center-right government that has moved quickly to rebuild ties with Israel.
“This is the first resident embassy in Slovenia, it is indeed a historic day,” Sa'ar said at a joint news conference. “This is a clear expression of Israel’s commitment to our friendship and to its future.”
Relations had deteriorated significantly under the previous Slovenian government, which recognized a Palestinian state, barred Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from entering the country, halted arms agreements with Israel and canceled Israir flights to Ljubljana.
Since taking office in June, Jansa’s government has reversed those measures and voiced support for Israel within the European Union. Sa'ar announced the decision to open the embassy on the day the new government was sworn in.
The opening also comes as Israel faces growing diplomatic pressure elsewhere in Europe over its policies in the West Bank, highlighting the contrast between worsening ties with some governments and the renewed relationship with Ljubljana.
Sa'ar said the timing of the embassy opening, just before Rosh Hashanah, carried particular significance.
“We are inaugurating the embassy two days before Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year,” he said. “It is a sign of new beginnings and new hopes.”
During Sa'ar’s visit, the two countries also signed agreements to expand cooperation in education, science, culture, youth and sports.
“We signed cooperation agreements today between the two countries in various areas, including youth, sports, education and scholarships for students,” Kajzer said. “We will strive for relations with Israel that are open, strong and based on trust.”
An Israeli business delegation representing major companies and economic organizations accompanied Sa'ar to Slovenia, where an Israeli-Slovenian business forum was also held with the participation of the two foreign ministers.
“After a long period of less intensive political contacts, it is time to shift cooperation between Slovenia and Israel into a higher gear,” Kajzer said.
The policy shift has faced opposition at home. The liberal Freedom Movement of former prime minister Robert Golob and the Left party submitted a proposal to parliament Wednesday seeking Jansa’s impeachment, accusing his government of pursuing a foreign policy overly aligned with Israel.
Student groups, left-wing activists and pro-Palestinian organizations were also expected to demonstrate against the embassy opening.
The new mission is the fifth Israeli embassy Sa'ar has inaugurated over the past year and a half, and the first permanent Israeli diplomatic mission ever established in Slovenia.

Zelenskyy’s plane ‘almost hit’ by drone on way to Oslo, Norwegian PM says
Jonas Gahr Store says incident happened when jet carrying Ukrainian president took off from Moldova.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store has said a plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Oslo was almost hit by a drone.
Zelenskyy, whose country has been fighting a Russian invasion that began in February 2022, arrived in Norway’s capital on Tuesday evening to attend the funeral of Norway’s King Harald V.
“His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova,” Store told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK on Wednesday. “That is the reality he lives in.”
Store did not say what his source was for this information or how close the drone was.
Later on Wednesday, a Moldovan government spokesperson confirmed the incident, saying in a statement that it happened on Tuesday before the take-off, and involved a Russian drone.
The spokesperson said the departure was delayed when authorities closed Moldova’s airspace over a drone alert and Zelenskyy’s aircraft was cleared for take-off once it had been established that the drone had come down on Moldovan territory.
While in Oslo, Zelenskyy held talks with Store, with the two leaders also meeting defence industry executives to discuss advancing a European anti-ballistic system codenamed FREYJA.
In a social media post, Zelenskyy said the meeting focused on dividing responsibilities between governments and defence companies and agreeing on steps needed to produce the first practical results from the programme.
“We expect to see the first practical results. I am grateful to Norway for hosting this meeting. I thank our partners for their readiness to work together. Protecting Europe’s skies is our shared responsibility,” said the Ukrainian president.
His comments came as Ukrainian regional officials said at least eight people were killed in Russian attacks on Wednesday, including along the Ukraine-Moldova border and in the southeast.

Russia Takes Ukrainian Children From Temporarily Occupied Territories Under “Recreation” Program
Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) has received information indicating that Ukrainian children have again been removed from temporarily occupied territories and taken to Russia, with at least two placed under guardianship in the Moscow region.
According to the intelligence service on September 9, children from an orphanage in the Russian-occupied part of Ukraine’s Donetsk region were taken to Russia this summer under the pretext of a “recreation” program.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The SZRU said it is currently working to establish their whereabouts and circumstances.
The intelligence service described the case as part of an established practice in which Ukrainian children are taken to Russia under the guise of vacations, rehabilitation programs, or participation in cultural and educational activities. Some of those taken away are then not returned.
According to the SZRU, Russian occupation administrations, guardianship authorities, and organizers of such trips are involved in the process. Once in Russia, the children come under the control of local authorities, which can determine where they will subsequently live and their legal status.
The SZRU warned that the reported removals form part of a broader system in Russia that exposes children to various forms of exploitation.
According to the agency, this includes state-linked practices such as involving children in work at defense industry enterprises or their potential recruitment by Russian intelligence services. The SZRU also alleged risks of criminal exploitation, including sex trafficking, human trafficking, illicit organ transplantation, and other abuses.
The latest case comes amid ongoing Ukrainian efforts to locate and return children forcibly taken by Russia. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier this year that more than 2,100 Ukrainian children had been brought back through the Bring Kids Back UA initiative.
In a Telegram post on April 22, Zelenskyy said that 150 of those children had been returned since the beginning of 2026.

Bones and tools found in bat cave in China reveal Denisovan culture for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:35:46 UTC
03:35:46 KST

Since the discovery of the Denisovan human species in Siberia in 2010, the world has been agog to know more about them. But discoveries have been confined to isolated bones in Asia, and we had no unqualified information about their material culture. Now for the first time, a cave only Denisovans could have used for more than 100,000 years has been found in a cave on the Chinese Tibetan Plateau.
The fossil bones of the Denisovans in Bianfu Cave date to around 167,000 to 134,000 years ago. The artifacts range from about 190,000 to 70,000 years and include mostly stone but also a handful of bone tools, Qijun Ruan, Bo Li, Fahu Chen and colleagues reported Wednesday in Nature. The dates aren't inconsistent – Denisovans plausibly made and dropped tools in the cave throughout the 120,000+ year span, but the vast majority of their remains were not preserved. Some paleo-hyena remains may help explain that.
There may have been gaps in the cave's occupation, but the sequence stands and not only were Denisovan bones actually found, they're also the likeliest candidate for occupant. Homo erectus only went extinct in Asia about 100,000 years ago, but he isn't considered a candidate for this cave. Thus, the Bianfu bat cave finds represent "one of the longest cultural records most parsimoniously attributed to Denisovans," according to a second paper on the cave also published Wednesday in Nature by Huiyun Rao, Feng Liu, Qiaomei Fu and colleagues, discussing the analyses that identified some of the 60,000 bones in the cave as Denisovan.
So the finds, including fossil pollen, animal bones from their meals and hyenas, bring us the first direct insight into the way Denisovans were. At least those in a pine forest on the slopes of the Hengduan Mountains in the Middle Pleistocene.
Hitherto and still, we don't know much about the Denisovans. They were only discovered in 2010 after a fossil pinkie bone discovered in Denisova Cave, Siberia was identified to the general shock of all: neither Neanderthal nor Homo sapiens as assumed, but really an unknown human species. They were called the Denisovans.
Most of the roughly 20 fragmented Denisovan bone fragments and teeth found so far were in Denisova Cave. In 2019 a jawbone was found in Xiahe on the Tibetan plateau; a tooth unearthed in a cave in Laos in 2022 turned out to be Denisovan and last year, 2025, another jawbone dredged up from the Taiwanese seabed years earlier was identified as a huge Denisovan, probably male. A rib found in Baishiya Cave, Tibet was outed as Denisovan too.
Evidently Tibet was blessed with Denisovans. But that collection doesn't tell us much about them. The happiest day for paleoanthropologists arrived when a fossil skull found in Harbin, China a century earlier was belatedly reclassified in 2025 as Denisovan. At least some researchers suspect that several more ancient skulls in Asia are too.
The few bones found so far were starting to suggest that the Denisovans were a beefy lot, similar to the biggest erectuses and taller on average than sapiens. Yet about their material culture, we knew zip.
Denisova Cave has tons of tools and some were presumably Denisovan but the cavern also has remains from all three species, Denisovan, Neanderthal and Homo sapiens, and proving which species used what implement is a challenge. Now at Bianfu, we have a protracted Denisovan sequence with about 1,300 artifacts they made. That, Dorothy, is material culture.
By and large the finds support the assumption that Denisovans lived much like their sister species, the Neanderthals (sister species means they had a common ancestor), even if they were bigger.
What bones were found at Bianfu? Four teeth, expanding the recognized dental variation of Denisovans, the team says. The molars resemble Denisovan teeth found in Xiahe and Laos, and also teeth of an archaic hominin from Hualongdon from 300,000 years ago, which some now suspect was an early Denisovan. Bianfu also produced two cranial fragments and a forearm bone, which shows similarities with Neanderthal characteristics but is shaped more like ours, they say.
It all fits with the little we know.
The human family
This is the thinking: Homo sapiens, Denisovans and Neanderthals all sprouted from the same root, in Africa, possibly 800,000 years ago – we really don't know. At some point, perhaps around 550,000 years ago, the lineage that would produce Homo sapiens split from the lineage that would produce the Denisovans-Neanderthals. Homo sapiens continued to evolve in Africa, but the common ancestor of the Denisovans-Neanderthals continued its story in Eurasia. Neanderthals would emerge in Europe while Denisovans surfaced in Asia, mastering territory that ranged from freezing lands at extreme altitudes to humid subtropics.
So we already know that Denisovans and Neanderthals are sister species and we might expect similarities. Note that shortly after Homo sapiens' emergence in Africa, we began to roam beyond the continent; there is evidence suggesting a confab of Neanderthals and early sapiens 250,000 years ago.
Note that our very beings hint at the Neanderthal and Denisovan ranges. All modern non-Africans have traces of Neanderthal genes, so the common ancestor to all living Europeans and Asians mixed with Neanderthals. Westerners typically have no Denisovan DNA but Asian peoples do have Denisovan genes as well as Neanderthal. The strongest signals are in Southeast Asia and Oceania, where the Denisovan component can be as high as 6% (inferring relatively recent admixture).
The stone tools were stone tools and the bone tools at Bianfu were "unmodified" – which means they used bones to achieve things without knapping or otherwise changing them. The artifacts smack of Neanderthal techniques, Chen and his team reported – "Despite the considerable geographic separation, these bone tools show clear technological parallels with Middle Palaeolithic bone implements associated with Neanderthals," they wrote, suggesting shared cultural capacities. They add that the find suggests "bone tool use may have been more widespread among Pleistocene populations than previously recognized."
Once, in our condescension, we thought that only Homo sapiens cleverly made tools out of bone, but this has been disproved. In fact, the thinking now is that hominins utilized bones a lot more than had been realized, because stone tools don't decay but bones do. Separate research suggests bones were being used as tools in Ethiopia 2.5 million years ago and another study identified bone tool manufacture in Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania 1.5 million years ago.
So finding bone tools in the Denisovan context is no surprise, merely a delight. Of bone tools, seven were identified of which five are believed to have been "retouchers," the archaeologists say, which refers to a piece of bone, antler or tusk that hominins used to shape and/or sharpen other, stone tools. Why would they use feeble bone to achieve that? Apparently precisely because bone is softer than stone so enabled finer adjustments of the implement, compared with the brute force of a blow from stone.
Of stone tools, the team reports 1,366: cores, flakes and manufacturing waste. They used the locally available sandy mudstone, the teams say.
Other bones found in the cave that weren't too fragmented to be identified by paleozoologists, reveal the secrets of the Denisovan diet: They had no secrets; they ate the same animals Neanderthals and we would have. Previous work in Tibet, at Baishiya Cave, found predominantly blue sheep. At Bianfu, the Denisovans doted on Cervidae (deer) and Bovidae (cattle), and also ate buffalo and bison, which were likely the biggest herbivores left around. Some goat was found and the analyses also identified a smidgen of rhinoceros, which they may have eaten.
We know that Neanderthals ate of the rhino as well as the mammoth. The Denisovans probably didn't eat the hyenas of whose bones were found – in fact the reverse might be true.
Note that rhinos only went extinct in China in the 20th century, due to hunting pressure and habitat loss. In Tibet, there had been a woolly rhinoceros on the plateau but it vanished around 2.6 million years ago, so we and the Denisovans are off the hook for its extinction there.
What do we learn? That like the Neanderthals and us, the Denisovans were hunters of large to medium prey. The archaeologists identified a prime-dominated hunting strategy, meaning, Denisovans deliberately hunted mature adult animals. Like us and the Neanderthals, they smashed long animal bones to obtain marrow and grease, which separate research has demonstrated to be key to the paleodiet, the archaeologists deduced.
The identity of the animals and analysis of fossil pollen show the Denisovans were living either in a pine forest or forest-steppe, which means grassland interspersed with tree clusters. Sounds nice. Ultimately, the Denisovans seem to have successfully occupied a vast range of habitats in Asia, with at least some adapting to life at high elevation and thin air. Some of us were lucky enough to have inherited that trait, for instance Tibetan sherpas.
The bottom line is that the seven Denisovan bones found in Bianfu Cave join isolated Denisovan remains around Asia below the glaciers; and being associated with tools, we gain a glimpse at their culture, which was like that of their sister species the Neanderthals, which is as anticipated. We wanted to know and now we do.

With the digital age comes the scramble for minerals below us and the scramble to master the heavens above us. Donald Trump wants a thousand rocket launches a year and with SpaceX’s reusable modules leading the way, the United States towers over the competition. It’s why for instance Ukraine’s president has to beg Elon Musk to use his Starlink low orbit satellite system to take out the Russian cruise missile launchers.
Europe’s late to the game. Its Ariane rocket only plans between nine and 11 launches next year. We’ll ask about Norway’s first private launch of a German satellite this past weekend and more broadly, whether there’s room for everyone in an orbit already littered with debris. The Germans dropped out of co-hosting the Paris International Space Summit and the White House reportedly leaned on US aerospace leaders to stay away. Does space need regulating? How urgently? How Emmanuel Macron brought France’s AI darling to the world stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:32:49 UTC
03:32:49 KST

It’s not every AI company that can count the French president as its top salesman.
On June 11, 2025, the founder of French AI company Mistral took to the stage alongside Jensen Huang, the powerful CEO of chip giant Nvidia, to announce a partnership between the two companies. As President Emmanuel Macron joined them, the Taiwanese-American executive turned to Mistral’s young CEO Arthur Mensch and said something just audible to the Parisian audience of techies and public officials: “Your president worked really hard for you.”
The Nvidia boss was referring to the deal his company had just sealed with Mistral to roll out AI infrastructure across Europe. “I told the president that Arthur and Mistral needed support from France’s biggest companies. Mr. President said to me: ‘Which ones? Let me call them!’” Huang said.
Advertisement
By the time the deal was official, the companies could announce that BNP Paribas, Orange, SNCF and Thales had all expressed interest in the partnership — boosting Mistral’s official entry into the global race for computing power.
Even for the head of Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, such presidential proactivity was remarkable, illustrating the French government’s dedication to championing its homegrown startup and showing how Mistral has leveraged ties to the executive branch in Paris to try and reach the level of some of the biggest generative AI companies.
Mistral’s rise over the past three years, according to a dozen public officials and representatives of France’s tech ecosystem interviewed by POLITICO, owes much to the privileged relationship it built with Macron — enabling the company to secure both strong ties with the French state and a seat at the table with the world’s leading AI companies.
Now, with a French presidential election bringing to a close Macron’s two-term reign, details on the depth of that relationship — many of which are reported here for the first time — also raise questions about Mistral’s future under a different president.
The company on Tuesday announced a new €3 billion funding round including investments from the European Union and South Korea’s electronics giant Samsung, valuing Mistral at more than €21 billion. While that falls well short of the valuations of Anthropic and OpenAI, the news confirms the French startup as the only serious European player in the AI race.
As Europe questions its ability to challenge Chinese and American tech giants, Mensch and his team must now plan for life after Macron.
‘Fairy godmothers around the cradle’
Launched in 2023 by three co-founders — Mensch, Guillaume Lample and Timothée Lacroix — Mistral AI set out to build a full-fledged large-language model to compete with the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. To do so, the Paris-based startup put forward a clear strategy from day one: cultivate a relationship with the French executive, and Macron in particular.
From its first funding round, the startup — which declined to respond to questions for this article — made a point of forging ties with the public sector. First among them was Bpifrance, France’s public investment bank and one of its earliest investors.
“We were aware of the sovereignty issues linked to AI,” recalls Arnaud Caudoux, deputy CEO of Bpifrance. “We had a good idea of the few — a few hundred in the world at the time — credible experts in the sector, among whom were Mistral’s founders.”
Advertisement
The BPI investment was part of a record €105 million total for a French seed round. But Caudoux noted: “There were a lot of fairy godmothers around the cradle.”
Those looking out for the startup came from the cream of French business and tech, playing crucial roles as matchmakers, patrons and fundraisers. They included telecom billionaire Xavier Niel, as well as Jean-Charles Samuelian-Werve and Charles Gorintin, co-founders of insurance startup Alan.
They were driven by the same goal: helping a European AI giant emerge. They tapped their networks to identify the most promising French AI researchers. These three businessmen were the ones who played matchmaker, bringing together Mensch, Lacroix and Lample.
When the Alan team struck a deal with the three young co-founders, it secured a strategic recruit to forge ties with the public sector: Cédric O, a former digital affairs secretary of state and early Macron supporter, would play a crucial role in the startup’s launch.
It was O who went into battle in Brussels to try to secure looser rules under the European Union’s AI Act, first proposed in April 2021. For Mistral, the burgeoning legislation posed a threat: How could Europe build a giant of its own if it stifled innovation?
In 2023, O intervened on Mistral’s behalf in EU talks in an effort to influence the negotiations — to the point that some lawmakers accused him of a conflict of interest. He also drew a rebuke from Thierry Breton, then European commissioner for the internal market.
Advertisement
Mistral “is lobbying, that’s normal,” French-born Breton said during the final weeks of negotiations over the AI Act. “But we are not fooled by anything. It is defending its business today, and not the general interest.”
“Cédric O’s role was, in a way, that of a lightning rod,” said a private-sector official who followed Mistral in its early days. By taking the hits, O allowed Mensch “to grow and develop as a CEO.”
Behind the scenes
From the outset, Mistral played the French and European card. The three co-founders may have built their careers in U.S.-based AI labs — Google DeepMind for Mensch and Facebook AI for Lample and Lacroix — but the first concept notes drafted for the startup’s launch put technological sovereignty at the heart of the project.
At the time, Mensch was a discreet 30-year-old engineer who needed to transform himself into the public face of Mistral on the international stage. Just a few months after launching the startup, the alum of the prestigious École Polytechnique made his first public appearance at VivaTech 2023 — Europe’s largest annual technology event — alongside Macron, who had already begun making the appeal for European technological autonomy.
The two were clearly in sync. “How do France and Europe intend to enable European champions to emerge, and how do we make sure that AI regulation does not hinder innovation?” the young sneaker-wearing entrepreneur asked the French president on the main stage.
Mensch would himself be tasked with helping come up with the answers. A few months later, the prime minister’s office formed a committee of experts to devise a French AI strategy. Alongside Mensch and O, its members included Gaël Varoquaux, a top researcher at France’s national digital research institute and Mensch’s former Ph.D. supervisor, as well as future Nobel economics laureate Philippe Aghion and Meta researcher and Turing Award recipient Yann LeCun.
By 2024, the committee delivered its report and Mistral unveiled Le Chat, its rival to OpenAI’s ChatGPT. But the AI landscape was already changing rapidly — and Europe was having second thoughts.
German rival Aleph Alpha, the continent’s other great hope in generative AI, announced it was moving away from developing its own models. Its CEO, Jonas Andrulis, offered a gloomy assessment: “Simply having a European LLM is not enough as a business model. It does not justify the investment.”
Advertisement
Mistral was not spared those doubts. Many observers feared its technology could fall behind American or Chinese rivals — even raising concerns that the startup might be acquired from abroad.
In 2025, reports of talks with Apple sparked panic at the highest levels of the French state. France’s embassy in the United States and the Elysée presidential palace asked Mistral whether the reports were true, according to two advisers who spoke to POLITICO. The company eventually reassured them: There had been no discussions “at the highest level.”
The French champion instead turned to a partner closer to home, and at the heart of Europe’s drive for technological sovereignty: the Netherlands’ microchip-printing giant ASML. The Dutch pioneer in the chips supply chain poured €1.3 billion of fresh investment into Mistral in September 2025 in a bid to speed up industrial AI development and keep Mistral’s know-how in European hands.
The deal was a boon for politicians — including Macron — seeking to keep the United States out of Europe’s most prized critical technology players.
Strategic partner
Three years into the company’s existence, the French government is no longer simply promoting a promising young startup. The state is now prepared to bend over backward to preserve a company whose technologies are being integrated across government.
After signing a strategic partnership with France’s national employment agency in early 2025, Mistral secured a deal with the French Armed Forces Ministry to develop AI for defense. Since 2025, Le Chat has also been in the process of being rolled out to 10,000 civil servants.
Advertisement
In public, Mensch has played down the importance of public subsidies and government support for his company. But Mistral’s teams in private conversations readily acknowledge that this privileged relationship is a major asset.
With Macron’s help, the French company has also opened the doors to the world’s biggest international summits — all the way up to the G7.
Mensch has been brought along on almost every presidential trip abroad in the past two years, giving him repeated opportunities to sharpen and spread his AI counter-narrative to contrast with the all-powerful Silicon Valley vision.
For several months, the Mistral boss — who readily appropriates the École Polytechnique motto, “For the Nation, Science and Glory” — has hammered home a position aligned with Macron’s: Europe must promote technological sovereignty and offer the rest of the world a model that is more sensitive to cultural and linguistic nuances than American and Chinese rivals.
In February, on stage at the New Delhi AI summit attended by Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind and Sam Altman of OpenAI, Mensch defended AI as “a tool for empowerment, not domination.” He spoke about the importance of deciding who controls the deployment of AI, who benefits from it and how to ensure that it serves the general interest, not just a few powerful players.
That landed as countries across the world were scrambling to get insights from U.S. firms and the Trump administration into how new AI models were creating major new hacking risks.
Advertisement
And in June, in Evian-les-Bains at Lake Geneva, Mensch had lunch with G7 leaders and AI executives, including Altman. He once again took on the role of maverick to confront his American rivals, who were calling for technological standards to be drawn up under U.S. leadership.
“We still need to be very wary,” Mensch told POLITICO in an interview after the meeting. “It’s true that American actors tend to make that argument, which is, ‘Trust us—we’ll set standards here, and then we’ll export them to you.’”
Succession planning
As Mistral moves into infrastructure by building data centers and continues rolling out its solutions at major companies, some are beginning to doubt whether it can remain in the race to produce “frontier” models — the most powerful models available.
For Macron, the June G7 meeting was one of the last opportunities to leave his mark on the global AI debate before his presidency ends next spring. For Mistral, its relationship with Macron’s successor has yet to be built.
Gabriel Attal, former prime minister and presidential candidate for Macron’s pro-business bloc, readily showcases his ties to Mistral and has put AI at the heart of his campaign platform — even incorporating Le Chat into his communications toolkit. Attal’s centrist rival Edouard Philippe would also almost certainly continue backing Mensch.
Advertisement
While Mistral does not publicly associate itself with the far-right National Rally of Marine Le Pen, the nationalist party sees the company as a sovereign asset. On the left, the parties have unanimously backed the company — and called for sovereign AI — in response to the risk of American models being weaponized against European countries.
Yet Mistral relies on international funding and major partnerships with American giants including Amazon, Nvidia and Microsoft. While bringing in ASML as a key investor meant Mistral would remain firmly rooted in Europe, it also shifted some of the power to ASML’s headquarters in Veldhoven, the Netherlands.
This detail could undermine the French consensus in favor of Mistral, just as AI is emerging as a key campaign issue for the presidential election.
“We need to kill this very bar room idea that it would be feasible to own the capital, and therefore finance on our own, at French or European level, the hundreds of billions that AI infrastructure requires. It’s simply impossible,” said Bruno Bonnell, a French businessman who runs a major public investment program, France 2030, under the prime minister’s office.

‘Baggage reclaim was pandemonium’: passengers hit by airport IT chaos in UK recount their ordeals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:31:30 UTC
03:31:30 KST

More than 2,000 flights have been cancelled after an air traffic control system failure that has thrown airports across the UK into chaos. Nats, the air traffic control provider, fixed the problem within hours on Tuesday, but hundreds of thousands of passengers were hit by further delays and cancellations on Wednesday.
Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of Nats, has been given a week to report back on the reasons for the technical failure.
People affected by the disruption talked about their frustration during the two days of chaos – from hours spent stuck on planes waiting to take off, to spending the night sleeping on the floor of Heathrow airport. Here are some of their experiences:
‘People were sleeping on every spare inch of flooring’
Daniel Garrick, 32, a software engineer, was scheduled to leave Heathrow on a flight to Austin, Texas, on Tuesday. After waiting for seven hours on the asphalt, “we were released from the plane only to find Heathrow in absolute chaos”, he says.
“My baggage was lost, and British Airways employees were nowhere to be found. People were sleeping on every spare inch of flooring, in arrivals and at security.”
Baggage reclaim was “pandemonium”, he says. “All the screens just said it was closed. You couldn’t tell where your baggage was supposed to be.
“I found some other Texans going back to Austin on our flight. Someone had an air tag in their luggage and we figured out that the bags were still on the plane. Eventually, there was some announcement where we were told they were not going to finish getting all the bags off the planes tonight, so we’re just going to have to leave.” At the time of writing, Garrick still had not retrieved his case with a week’s worth of clothes.
Garrick’s airline, British Airways, sent a mass email apology at about 9pm on Tuesday. “Then in the app, it automatically rebooked me for a flight tomorrow [Thursday] morning, 48 hours after my first flight. Luckily I’m staying with a friend of a friend in Surrey. It was over £100 just for the Uber here.”
‘We were left to our own devices’
Melanie Thompson, 71, an interdisciplinary artist, was on a 14-hour flight returning from her performance at a mixed media festival with her son in Tokyo on Tuesday when she was told the flight would not land in London. “We were exhausted. About 40 minutes before we arrived, the pilot very politely said, ‘because of IT problems and disruptions at Heathrow, we are going to have to divert to Edinburgh’.
“There was a big silence. About 20 minutes later, he said: ‘We were hoping we could refuel and then take you on to Heathrow. But we can’t do that, so we would like you to stay in Edinburgh tonight.’ Then we were left to our own devices to find travel and accommodation for the night.
“We suddenly found ourselves in Edinburgh with nowhere to stay because all the hotels and Airbnbs had been filled up,.
“We finally found a flat for £500, paid for the taxi to get there and stayed the night there last night.”
Thompson spoke to the Guardian on her train journey from Edinburgh to London as there were no flights available on Wednesday.
‘It’s Kafkaesque’
Thomas Reilly, 55, was due to fly with BA from Marrakech to Gatwick on Tuesdayand then on to Marseille, where he lives and works as a freelance geopolitical adviser. It was only when he got to the airport that he was told his flight was cancelled.
“I am currently stuck in Morocco,” says Reilly. “I did not receive any information from BA about the disruption before getting to the airport.”
He says that, once at the airport, BA staff were helpful and courteous but he has been left with no option but to book a hotel to stay an extra two nights in Marrakech – at his own expense. (BA staff at the airport did tell him he could “pay and reclaim” for his hotel expenses.)
He has been trying to rearrange his journey, attempting to cancel with BA and fly directly to Marrakech through a different airline.
He says: “BA’s customer services operator is not taking calls as ‘the lines are too busy’. There is no email address. And their chatbot cannot help. It is Kafkaesque.”
Reilly says he has worked out “alternative travel arrangements, namely to fly direct from Marrakech to Marseille on Thursday 10 September” but he wanted to get his “refund agreed first before outlaying more money on the replacement flight.”
When Reilly got through to someone at BA, he says the airline told him they “would not refund the Heathrow-Marseille ticket”. “It’s absurd,” Reilly adds.
A spokesperson for British Airways said: “Since yesterday, we’ve rebooked more than 60,000 customers to travel on alternative flights, getting them to their destinations as quickly as we can. Today, we’ve been able to operate almost 80% of our schedule across our whole network.
“We know this has been a very challenging and frustrating time for our customers, and we’re incredibly sorry for the experience they’ve endured because of an issue that has been entirely out of our control.”
‘We have also lost two days of our trip’
Keith Sessions, 74, a computer engineer from Cobham, Surrey, and his wife were due to fly from Heathrow to Tahiti via LA on Tuesday with a five-hour stopover at LAX airport.
For the first leg of their journey, they were to fly Virgin, but once on the plane it was clear there were problems.
He says the pilot informed them there were delays. Five and a half hours later, with the plane still on the asphalt, the pilot announced that the flight had been cancelled.
Sessions says they were not offered a meal in that time, “only water, soft drinks and courtesy snacks”.
The couple decided to return home via taxi and their flights were auto-rebooked. They will now fly out on Thursday with an 11-hour stopover at LAX airport. They will arrive in Tahiti at 5.30am on Friday.
“The 11-hour stopover is not ideal,” says Sessions. “We have also lost two days of our trip and had to spend an extra £340 when you factor in extra cabs to and from the airport and the cost to reserve seating on our flight. Communication from Virgin has been very poor, diabolical.”
A Virgin Atlantic spokesperson said: “We’d like to sincerely apologise to our customers for the widespread disruption … We know how frustrating delays and changes to travel plans can be and appreciate our customers’ patience.”

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia could activate defence pact, Pakistan says
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif says agreement between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia may be activated if Yemen’s Houthis continue targeting the kingdom.
Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said any attack on Saudi Arabia could activate the recently signed Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, days after Yemen’s Houthis launched a barrage of missiles at the kingdom.
“If there is unprovoked aggression, or a spillover of whatever is happening in Yemen into Saudi Arabia, definitely the Mecca agreement will become operational,” he told Pakistani media outlet Geo News on Tuesday night.

list of 3 items

- list 3 of 3Yemeni forces launch counteroffensive against Houthis, vow to retake Sanaa
“There should be no doubt about that. We are bound by the terms and conditions of this pact, and … we will honour them in case there is a need.”
Yemen’s Houthi group on Tuesday carried out attacks in southern Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh saying that at least 73 people were wounded, as fighting escalates in Yemen between the Iran-aligned group and forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
Leaders from Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan last month signed the Mecca agreement, committing to reinforce collective deterrence against any aggression.
The agreement mirrors a key NATO stipulation – a strike on any single member is to be considered a strike on the entire group, though the precise mechanisms for implementing this pledge have yet to be clarified.
The deal was agreed as the three nations grapple with heightened regional frictions, including worries over Israel’s expanding military capabilities and Iran’s growing influence across the Middle East.
Combined, the three states field close to 1.4 million active troops, some 3,400 military aircraft, 6,000 tanks and more than 340 naval assets, according to the 2026 Global Firepower Index, which assesses the military strength of 145 countries.
Yemen fighting
On Wednesday, the Houthi-run Al Masirah TV reported that Saudi Arabian warplanes carried out a series of air strikes across Yemen’s Marib, al-Jawf and Taiz governorates.
It said five air strikes targeted the Khab wa Sha’af district in al-Jawf, 10 other air attacks targeted areas in the Sirwah district of Marib, and five hit the al-Barh area in Taiz.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi forces.
The ongoing hostilities mark the most serious escalation since a United Nations-brokered truce halted large-scale fighting in 2022.
The war in Yemen started in 2014 after the Houthis took Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year. Diplomats had hoped the truce would evolve into a durable political settlement, but those efforts have faltered amid regional tensions triggered by the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
The fighting resumed in July, when government forces struck the Houthi-controlled airport in Sanaa, blocking the landing of an aircraft from Iran. Then last week, the Houthis launched a major offensive, trying to advance through western Taiz and southern Hodeidah, towards the port city of al-Makha (Mocha) and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea.
The Houthis had declared a blockade against Saudi vessels transiting the waterway, which is a vital corridor for shipping between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The strait has taken on new significance for Saudi oil exports since Iran began restricting passage through the Strait of Hormuz at the outset of the US and Israel’s war on the country.

Apple unveiled the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max: a new camera, the A20 Pro chip, and the first foldable iPhone
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:30:56 EEST
03:30:56 KST

Apple unveiled the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max: a new camera, the A20 Pro chip, and the first foldable iPhone
Kyiv • UNN
Apple unveiled the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max with the A20 Pro chip, an adjustable aperture, and the new Siri AI. The company also announced a foldable iPhone.
On September 9, Apple held its annual presentation of new products, with the main premieres being the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max smartphones, as well as the first foldable iPhone. The event was also significant for the corporation itself, as it was Apple's first major presentation under the leadership of its new CEO, John Ternus, UNN reports.
Apple's first presentation with its new CEO
Ternus took over as Apple's CEO on September 1, replacing Tim Cook, who had led the company for 15 years. Cook remained at Apple as executive chairman of the board of directors. Before being appointed CEO, Ternus was responsible for hardware development at the company.
He began the presentation with a humorous video in which Apple showed several possible cinematic versions of how the event could begin. At the end of the clip, the camera moved to Tim Cook. Cook joked that this time viewers should not be watching him, after which John Ternus appeared in the frame. In this way, Apple symbolically introduced the company's new leader to the audience.
The main focus of the event was the new iPhone lineup and the development of artificial intelligence within the Apple ecosystem.
Four colors and a new body design: what the new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max turned out to be
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will be available in four colors. The lineup includes silver, deep black, light blue, and a unique burgundy. The latter became one of the most notable new design options. The smartphone's rear glass panel is now made in the same tone as the body, making the device's design appear more cohesive and aesthetically pleasing to the user.
Battery life and even faster charging
Apple also announced during the September 9 presentation that the iPhone would have the longest battery life in its history. The iPhone 18 Pro can now operate for up to 24 hours on a single charge, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max can last up to 30 hours. The larger model is also said to offer up to 45 hours of video playback.
The company also changed the battery's construction. The larger battery is intended to provide greater battery life without the need to constantly look for an outlet, which, for some reason, still remains a separate achievement for a modern smartphone.
Charging speed has also improved. Apple says the iPhone 18 can be charged to 50% in approximately 15 minutes. At the same time, the company did not specify separately which adapter is required to achieve this speed.
The new 2-nanometer A20 Pro processor for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max received the new A20 Pro processor, manufactured using a 2-nanometer process. The chip has six CPU cores, seven GPU cores, and 32 Neural Engine cores. According to Apple, the central processor is approximately 20% faster, graphics performance has increased by 40%, and the Neural Engine has twice as many cores as the previous architecture.
The company placed particular emphasis on the smartphone's performance under prolonged workloads. For the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Apple developed an updated cooling system. The vapor chamber was enlarged approximately threefold, which should help dissipate heat more effectively when running demanding games, processing video, and using artificial intelligence features.
According to Apple, the new cooling system is 80% made from recycled steel.
How Siri gained new artificial intelligence capabilities
One of the central topics of the presentation was Siri AI. Apple substantially redesigned its voice assistant and expanded its capabilities based on Apple Intelligence. Siri can now take into account the context of previous requests, information displayed on the smartphone screen, and user data. For example, the assistant can find the necessary information in messages, email, or photos.
In addition, Siri can perform actions in different applications. The user only needs to formulate a request by voice so that the assistant can, for example, find the necessary information, send a message to the right contact, or start music in one of the compatible services.
Also during the presentation, the company announced the possibility of Siri interacting with more than 250 applications. The assistant will also be able to answer questions about information displayed directly on the screen.
Apple even created a separate app for Siri, where users can continue previous conversations. The interface is also integrated with Dynamic Island, allowing users to contact the assistant without having to open a separate full-screen interface.
Apple has also expanded Siri's personalization options. Users will be able to change the assistant's voice, intonation, and speaking speed. Initially, these settings will be available in English. Some operations will be performed directly on the device by artificial intelligence. For more complex tasks, Apple will use secure cloud infrastructure.
The new Siri AI capabilities are expected to initially be released in beta later this year. Their rollout will depend on the region and language, so the full set of features will not be available to all users immediately.
The iPhone 18 Pro camera now has a variable aperture
One of the most notable hardware innovations in the iPhone 18 Pro is the camera. The main 48-megapixel module has received a variable aperture. It allows users to adjust the amount of light reaching the sensor, as well as affect the depth of field and background blur. In dark environments, the system can automatically increase the aperture opening to let in approximately 50% more light. This should improve photo quality in low-light conditions.
Apple has also provided manual camera settings for professional users. They are available exclusively on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max.
The Camera app itself has also been updated. New features include a professional mode, improved audio controls after filming, subject tracking, updated Photographic Styles, and support for recording 4K Timelapse video with Dolby Vision HDR.
How much will the iPhone 18 Pro cost, and when will it be available for purchase?
Sales of the new models are expected to begin on September 18.
In the United States, the iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for the version with 256 GB of built-in storage.
The 256 GB iPhone 18 Pro Max will cost from $1,299. For users who find even 256 GB frustratingly little, versions with up to 2 TB of storage will be available.
Apple enters the foldable smartphone market
The company's first foldable iPhone was a separate technological premiere at the September 9 event. Apple had not been in a hurry to enter this market for years, while Samsung, Google, and other manufacturers had already managed to establish a separate segment of foldable smartphones.
The foldable iPhone is expected to be a "book-style" device: when folded, it will function as a regular smartphone, while unfolding it will give the user access to a larger internal display. One of Apple's key challenges was the hinge design and reducing the visibility of the crease on the screen. These characteristics have traditionally remained among the main drawbacks of foldable smartphones.
At the same time, some specifications of the first foldable iPhone had circulated before the presentation mainly in the form of "leaks." In particular, earlier reports mentioned the possible name iPhone Duo and a starting price of around $2,000.
According to preliminary data, deliveries of the foldable model may not begin before October. The device's final specifications, name, and price should be assessed separately from the confirmed specifications of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.
Apple-2026 presentation: what has changed in a year
This year's presentation demonstrated two directions in Apple's development at once. The first is the gradual improvement of the traditional iPhone Pro lineup through a more powerful processor, better cooling, a camera with a variable aperture, and greater battery life.
The second is the more active integration of artificial intelligence. Siri is gradually ceasing to be merely a voice assistant and is becoming a tool that can work with the user's context and perform more complex sequences of actions across different applications.
The third direction is Apple’s entry into the foldable smartphone market. The company has joined a category that competitors have been developing for several years, but intends to use its own approach to design, software, and integrating the device with the Apple ecosystem.

This week on The Ring, EU lawmakers clash over the Ceuta migration crisis. From Morocco’s role and Spain’s response to whether EU member states are doing enough to help out when one member state comes under pressure, the debate raises more questions than answers.
The same week that Ceuta’s president, Juan Jesús Vivas, travelled to Brussels in a cry for help, we are joined by Czech centre-right MEP Tomáš Svetechovský and German Socialist MEP Birgit Sippel for their points of view. One month on from the arrival of thousands of irregular migrants in the Spanish city, we hear how EU countries could have shown more solidarity and what more can be done to help Ceuta.
Tomáš Svetechovský criticised the Spanish government’s handling of the situation, arguing that it should have acted sooner and requested more European support.
“I think that the Spanish government did not react to the situation very well,” he said, calling for additional police and security support.
German Socialist MEP Birgit Sippel defended Spain’s response and said the priority should be European solidarity.
“Whenever things like that are happening to whatever country, the first thing that we have to do is show solidarity,” she said.
The two MEPs also disagreed over the treatment of unaccompanied minors remaining in Ceuta. Sippel stressed the need to relocate children to other EU member states under the EU migration pact, while Svetechovský rejected mandatory relocation quotas and said the Czech Republic would not be welcoming anyone from Ceuta.
“We are absolutely strict against these quotas,” he insisted.
The role of Morocco remains another point of debate. Some have accused Rabat of allowing the crossings to happen and during his trip to the EU capital, Juan Jesus Vivas said he believes the Ceuta incident should prompt Brussels to reconsider its collaboration with Rabat.
