I Let an AI Agent Hack All My Gadgets—and I’d Do It Again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

As the author of a newsletter about artificial intelligence, I consider it my duty to experience the bleeding edge of this technology firsthand. This week, that meant embracing some agentic mayhem.
You’re probably aware that frontier AI models have attained advanced cybersecurity capabilities in recent months. They can find zero-day bugs in large codebases and scan computers for vulnerabilities at lightning speed. To make things even more exciting, cybersecurity agents sometimes go rogue, colluding with one another and hacking into outside systems to gain an edge.
To get a closer look, I decided to unleash one in my own home network. Over the course of a few days, I watched as my own rogue agent found vulnerabilities in various household devices, hacked into a PC, and showed me that several vibe-coded projects were—unsurprisingly—riddled with bugs. (My wife knew what I was up to, and rolled her eyes each time I proudly announced the discovery of a new vulnerability.)
But Will, you might be thinking, giving an impish, all-powerful cybersecurity agent access to your home network is batshit. And you would be correct! Nevertheless, I believe that a good way to understand the cybersecurity hellscape in front of us is to pay it a visit.
In the end, my experiment was revealing, but oddly reassuring, too. My little network gremlin showed me how vulnerable my home life would be to AI hacking, but it also told me how to make everything a lot more secure. In the end, I discovered that the best way to deal with AI hacking may well be having your own AI hacker.
Maverick Model
I got the idea for the experiment after discovering Abliteration AI, a startup that offers access to powerful AI models with the usual guardrails removed.
Most mainstream AI models will refuse to respond to certain queries, and they will certainly refuse to find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. But it’s possible to remove these restrictions by finding and modifying certain patterns within an open-weight model’s internal parameters. You can tweak the patterns that lead to refusals through a process known as abliteration.
Removing AI’s guardrails might seem risky, but it’s not uncommon. Academic researchers use these de-aligned models to better understand how AI actually works, while cybersecurity firms use them to probe software and systems for vulnerabilities. Technically speaking, Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s Astra work similarly: They’re basically conventional models that lack the usual cyber controls, with access limited to trusted customers for the time being. (The companies also offer wider access to models with a medium number of guardrails so that companies can vet their code and systems for problems.)
Abliteration AI offers several fully de-aligned models, the most powerful of which is a version of Z.ai’s latest agentic coding model, GLM 5.3. This puts similar cyber capabilities to Mythos and Astra right in your hands for as little as the cost of a pizza.
Devon, Abliteration AI’s CEO, believes that making de-aligned models widely available is smart defense: It will help good guys counter bad guys by probing systems for vulnerabilities and by mimicking the behavior of hackers, scammers, and, yes, rogue AI agents. (Devon asked that I use his first name only because his day job doesn’t know about his side project.)
“You have all these critical infrastructure companies, from airlines to banks, that are rolling out agents like crazy,” Devon says. “How do you make sure that a nefarious actor can't use some of these agents in a bad way?”
To start, I created an Abliteration AI account and installed a software harness called CyberStrike, which helps guide a large language model through different cybersecurity tasks.
Using CyberStrike, I asked the abliterated version of GLM-5.3 to take a look at my local network. A few moments later, it found around a dozen hardware systems on the same network—and catalogued several vulnerabilities.
My unruly helper told me, for instance, that my printer was misconfigured, which meant that anyone on the network could log into it. That could be a problem if there were sensitive documents—tax returns, bank statements, medical records—in the print queue.
The agent also noted that my Wiim stereo was leaking a lot of information. (It knew that the last song played was Rein Me In by Sam Fender and Olivia Dean, if you must know.) Anyone on the network could play what they wanted or adjust the volume. The model also found a bunch of internet-of-things (IoT) devices on the network with firmware that needed updating.
An ungovernable agent could be very useful to a hacker. But mine offered a number of helpful tips for keeping my network secure. Besides updating outdated firmware and securing the printer, it recommended putting IoT devices like smart speakers on a guest network; if one were compromised, it wouldn’t be able to see any of my PCs. Not bad for a model with no morals.
I also asked the agent to take a look at a directory containing a bunch of vibe-coded projects, including some that I turned into simple websites. It found dozens of problems, including unprotected API credentials and a misconfiguration that might let an attacker send out emails. Hardly surprising for a bunch of casually vibe-coded stuff, but still chastening. The sheer number of bugs makes me think I won’t be deploying a line of code without doing some AI vetting first.
Fear Factor
Running an abliterated model is, to put it plainly, a bit scary.
I asked my agent to probe a Linux machine on my network for vulnerabilities. After running a bunch of scans, it reported that the machine seemed relatively secure. I then asked if it could figure out how to log in. It cleverly figured out a working username based on the name of other systems on the network. It tried a bunch of obvious passwords, which didn’t work. It also offered to write a script to try “brute forcing” the password, but I told it to stand down.
To my amazement, the agent then found a cryptographic key on my machine, used it to log in without a password, and started hunting for the password in order to gain root access. I felt a moment of pure panic as I saw it rummaging around the directories. It made me wonder how far the agent might go in order to achieve its goal. Might it have hacked into something else, like a machine outside of my network, in search of the key? Probably not, but who knows with these agents.
Some behavior could prove even more precarious. When I connected to my Wi-Fi network a few hours later and asked the model to see if it could find any new machines, it not only found the router, but decided to try logging in by trying several common “admin/passwords” combinations. If it had decided to do this on an outside network, I could have been in big trouble.
Shaanan Cohney, a computer scientist at Tufts University who specializes in cybersecurity and the law, says that a cyber-reckoning does seem to be coming.
“Attackers are often early adopters,” Cohney says. “There’s also an asymmetry, in that to secure a castle, you need to make sure that there are no holes anywhere or no loose bricks in your wall. To invade a castle, all you need to do is to find that one loose brick.”
Over the long term, Cohney says, the proliferation of cyber-capable models may make software more secure in general. The challenge is that many companies aren’t thinking about shoring up their defenses. “Most organizations have other things to worry about,” he says.
After all that, I shut down the model and went back to using a regular, fully aligned version. Claude Code or Codex will only do certain things related to cybersecurity, like help you configure your laptop’s firewall. But at least they won’t hack your system before you know it. Hopefully.
AI Hacking for All
Unless open-weight models are banned outright, advanced AI hacking capabilities will soon be very widely available. My experiment made me think that this might be just what we need. Assuming that bad guys will have access to AI, shouldn’t we all use it to defend ourselves?
“We need to help people use these capabilities,” says Aleksander Mądry, an MIT professor who studies AI safety and who is currently on leave while he works for OpenAI. “I do think there will be room for open source and independent tools. If only because, ultimately, these kinds of approaches have the real staying power in the world of security.”
Mądry notes, however, that a key issue may be ensuring that those who manage critical infrastructure like power plants or financial markets have access to more powerful AI than the average script kiddie (or AI writer).
Using AI that lacks regular guardrails is both thrilling and alarming. But if a cyber-reckoning is coming, then it’s probably time to tool up.
This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Practical Magic 2 is practically magic, with a few missing ingredients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Practical Magic 2 brews up the goods, but has a limited shelf life
As a 30-something millennial with not-so distant memories of backyard potion brews, whimsigoth magazine spreads, and (unsuccessful) sleepover seances with my little sister, 1998's Practical Magic holds a special place in my heart.
Returning to a story that meant a lot to you as a kid is a load-bearing experience, and often comes with a complimentary pair of rose-tinted glasses (a margarita glass, in this case). I understand deeply the caveats of nostalgia-bait, what with me being in the prime age for all my beloved childhood IP to be blatantly mined for another crack at relevance. Still, I had a lot of fun with Practical Magic 2.
It's 28 years (ouch) since the Owens sisters first buried a body beneath the rose garden and drank midnight margaritas in their envy-inducing New England kitchen.
The sequel to Practical Magic (based on the series of books by Alice Hoffman) has brought the witchy family back to the big screen for a spell.
Sally (Sandra Bullock) has lost another husband to the Owens family curse that causes everyone they love to die, and she's given up on magic for good.
Her girls, Kylie (Joey King) and Antonia (Maisie Williams), have grown into adulthood with all memories of magic erased. Now, Kylie has taken a romantic interest in fellow college student Gideon (Xolo Maridueña), and Gillian (Nicole Kidman) is imploring her sister Sally to restore those memories and confront reality as the curse manifests again.
Given the film is more than two hours long, the plot moves along at an impressive pace: when Gideon's life is threatened and Kylie absconds to England in search of her witchy roots, Sally and Gillian quickly enlist the help of across-the-pond witchcraft expert, Professor Ian Wright (a tattooed and often shirtless Lee Pace), and go after her.
Thankfully, very little time is spent re-explaining concepts from the first film, and director Susanne Bier does an impressive job of visually recreating the tone and feel of the original so it feels cohesive without having to be constantly justified via dialogue.
It's nicely shot and colour graded, though the fish-eye lens becomes a little grating after a while.
Yes, the house that every girl dreamed of owning in 1998 is back, and you better believe it's packed to the rafters with candles, flowers and gilded frames of ancestral portraits.
It's a living Pinterest board that somehow still manages to feel lived in, despite its impractical decor.
It may be frustrating to some that things have not really changed in the time between films, but given the plot draws heavily on the idea of returning to ancestral roots/not denying your family traditions, it makes sense that it's largely remained the same. We're instead meant to focus on the trajectory of the Owens juniors, both of whom have taken up more 'normie' roles — Kylie is a grad student and Antonia is a nurse.
King and Williams look enough like Evan Rachel Wood and Alexandra Artrip that most people won't notice they've been recast — but their characters being aged down from the original does cause timeline confusion which director Bier has attempted to explain. They do a decent job at carrying the legacy, but Bier has wisely chosen to keep the focus on Sally and Gillian so Bullock and Kidman can remind us what made the first foray so spellbinding.
Bigger in scale, star power, and special effects, Practical Magic 2 obviously has the self-assured confidence of a returning IP that brings with it a giant fan base.
However, something is lost. What remains is a decently packaged, feminist-forward flick that is undeniably pretty to look at, and one that still carries an important central theme from its predecessor: witchcraft has always been a metaphor for women's power — the kind certain men can't stand to see, and insist is their oppression.
While the sequel still absolutely nails this thesis, it loses the power its original had in centring that around a domestic abuse case. Practical Magic lingers in cultural memory because, among all the elixirs, love spells and corpse-reanimating, there was a very real threat that millions of women have actually experienced.
In being more magic-focused, Practical Magic 2 misses the mark.
One thing is evident above all else: the original cast members are having a blast revisiting this world. Kidman and Bullock sink back into their roles quite naturally (Bullock especially — her comedic timing and Type-A neuroticisms are razor sharp), and the elder aunts Jet and Frances, played by Diane Wiest and Stockard Channing, bring wizened charm and eccentricity in spades. All four have an undeniable chemistry that makes you believe they really could be blood relatives.
The younger Owens don't get a great deal of screen time together, which is a shame (even if it makes sense narrative-wise), and it left me feeling like we missed out on another generation of the kind of sisterly antics that made the first film gain its cult following. But overall it's the sparks between the Owens women that elevates this film from 'meh' to memorable.
Fans of the original will be satisfied, and newcomers definitely won't be lost in the details. And if all else fails, you can always have another midnight margarita.
Practical Magic 2 is in cinemas now.

David Byrne never planned to be a musician
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

From Talking Heads to American Utopia, David Byrne has stayed curious
For someone who never intended on becoming a musician, David Byrne started strong.
"I remember the first [song] I wrote, and I got help from some of the others, was Psycho Killer," he says on Take 5 With Zan Rowe.
Released more than 50 years ago, that song features in just about any "best songs of all time" lists you happen across. But Byrne didn't set out to write a timeless classic.
"That was, for me, a test to see if I could write a song. And people really liked it. I thought, 'Oh, OK, check that box. I can write a song.'"
When it comes to music, curiosity has gotten David Byrne everywhere, stretching right back to his earliest years.
"My parents played music," he considers. "It felt like it was nice enough, but it's not really for me."
One night, The Byrds' version of Bob Dylan's Mr Tambourine Man came on his transistor radio. That curiosity kicked in, and it never went away.
"These mysterious words seemed to be in some kind of code," he says of the song.
"The music sounded really different than any of the kind of folk music or classical or anything that my parents were listening to.
"I thought, 'Oh, There's a whole world out there of other things.' That got me going, and then I started hearing other things."
New York state of mind
Exploring different forms of creativity led the art school student to form his first band.
"I didn't think that music would ever be my career," he says. "I thought that I would focus on being some fine artist of some sort.
"Music was a hobby. Music was something I did with friends or myself, just for fun. It was immensely satisfying, but I thought, 'No, no, no, there's people who are much, much better at this than I am. Don't get your hopes up, but you can enjoy yourself at the same time.'"
After college, Byrne moved to New York City with his bandmates, where they realised there were places that would let them play and people who might listen.
"There was a club around the corner, CBGBs, and a couple of bands were playing there," he says.
"A band called Television, Patti Smith was playing there … we thought, 'Well, there is a place. We could audition there and maybe play?'
"Sometimes we create things based on knowing [that], 'Yes, there's an outlet for what I want to do.'"
The Artistics became Talking Heads, who would become one of the defining bands of new wave, helping reshape the sound of rock music.
Byrne became a sponge. New York City was a great place for a mind as inquisitive as Byrne's, its funk, Latin and jazz clubs opening Byrne up to sounds and experiences well beyond his comfort zone.
"There was so much on offer," he says. "It gave me the opportunity to sample and hear all these different things."
He became hooked on the culture of dancing in these clubs, thrilled by the almost-involuntary way people let the music take over their bodies.
"You kind of lose yourself," he says. "You become part of the larger group of all the dancers and the music, and you just kind of go somewhere, and it's a wonderful feeling.
"There's such an emphasis on individuality, but giving up that self — or part of it — actually feels really good.
"If there were other things going on, and there might have been, I didn't know about it," he says. "I was blissfully unaware, I just saw everyone dancing. I thought, 'This is pretty great.'"
Byrne says the first time he heard his own music in the club came following the release of My Life In The Bush Of Ghosts, his legendary 1981 album made in collaboration with Brian Eno.
"I thought, 'Whoa, now we're making it … We've been validated.'"
While his relationship with Talking Heads is famously fraught, collaboration remains key to much of Byrne's work.
He made an album with St. Vincent, has appeared on songs from indie favourites Dirty Projectors and Montaigne, and worked with everyone from Arcade Fire and De La Soul to Robyn and Selena Gomez.
It's another by-product of Byrne's exploratory approach to creating.
"Pretty early on, I realised that you can work with other people in all these different ways, and you learn something," he says. "It takes you somewhere where you might not go yourself. I never stopped doing that."
Breaking it all to pieces
Part of that long-held curiosity came out for Byrne's highly celebrated American Utopia tour, where he dismantled the arrangements to his most enduring songs to show audiences how his band crafted their performances.
"We'd heard from critics or fans or whatever saying, 'You're playing to tracks, aren't you? You're playing pre-recorded music.' And we thought, 'Absolutely not. We're playing this live.' So, I thought we had to show that," Byrne explains.
"We took one of the songs and broke it apart. We'd start with one instrument, add the next, add the next, add the next. The audience can hear how the sausage is made and see how it's all put together."
His curiosity convinces Byrne to turn the lens on his past work.
"The old ones get rearranged," he says of playing Talking Heads classics. "They're recognisable. We're not like, 'Oh, we've turned Psycho Killer into a waltz.'"
At 74, Byrne still tours, records, collaborates, and generally remains creatively active. That curiosity that drew him to music has gone nowhere.
While not everyone can have the same musical talent and creative as David Byrne, he reckons being open to new ideas and ways of working can help us all.
"Sometimes I have inklings of answers, little bits, and that sometimes just then leads to more questions. But it's fine. It certainly has worked for me.
"I would like to think that being inquisitive that way would work for other people too. I can't be sure, but I've been very lucky. I've been able to do that and do OK and survive doing that."

How Hezbollah uses Lebanon’s schools to indoctrinate the next generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:25:26 UTC
03:25:26 KST

- i24NEWS
- Middle East
- Levant & Turkey
- How Hezbollah uses Lebanon’s schools to indoctrinate the next generation
How Hezbollah uses Lebanon’s schools to indoctrinate the next generation
Recent IDF operations in Lebanon have uncovered an increasing number of weapons caches and armories hidden in Shia schools
For decades Hezbollah has been exploiting Lebanon's fractured political system to dominate the country's south, but it has also stepped into the place of the Lebanese state and usurped its position as the provider of education and social welfare.
In particular, Hezbollah has opened private educational institutes in the country that cater to its Shia constituency. However, rather than provide a quality education to improve the lives of its base, Hezbollah has instead developed its education sector as an "ideological and doctrinal incubator," which according to The Beiruter, can be described as "educational mobilization."
These educational institutions vary from basic elementary schools all the way to higher education institutions like the Al-Mustafa International University. Their goal is to create a "Resistance Society" capable of supporting the development of a theocratic Shia government similar to Iran's, which necessitates total control over education.
The two primary educational institutions used by Hezbollah are the Al-Mahdi and Al-Mustafa networks, which operate schools throughout the Shia community, particularly targeting working- and middle-class Lebanese Shia. Both networks operate outside of the Lebanese Ministry of Education, meaning they have different programs and educational goals from those of state schools, according to the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA).
The Al-Mustafa network predates Hezbollah, having been founded in 1974, but remains extremely close to the party and largely operates according to its standards. It is considered to have a more ‘rigorous’ educational reputation. The Al-Mahdi network was founded by Hezbollah's Educational Unit in 1993 and remains interwoven in the party's apparatus.
"While Al-Mahdi schools have mass reach, Al-Mustafa schools focus on quality and elite education," The Beiruter reported. Before his ascension to the leadership of Hezbollah, Naim Qassem was the spiritual supervisor of both networks, indicating the importance Hezbollah places on these institutions.
The JCFA identified four core pillars of both educational networks: Ideological Monopolism, the Cult of the Martyr, the Militarization of Childhood, and the Dehumanization of the Other. These four pillars allow Hezbollah to mould the future Lebanese Shia into a "disciplined, ideologically uniform base" that will support Hezbollah without question.
Although the schools are private, Hezbollah offers substantial subsidies to working-class Lebanese. However, due to Hezbollah’s recent financial difficulties, it has begun restricting these subsidies and requiring payment in US dollars to offset financial losses from Al-Qard Al-Hassan.
One element key to Hezbollah's dominance is the Imam al-Mahdi Scouts. The al-Mahdi scouts are one of Lebanon's largest youth movements, comprising nearly 100,000 members. According to the JCFA, "Unlike mainstream scouting that focuses on civic duty and nature, the al-Mahdi Scouts integrate paramilitary training." Children as young as eight are organized into tribes and wear military-style uniforms. The scouting organization acts as a vetting system to give Hezbollah a sense of who should be recruited into Hezbollah's militias. The JCFA notes that "By the time a young man enters Hezbollah's military ranks (16/17), he has already undergone years of ideological conditioning, physical discipline, and loyalty oaths."
"The educational system accomplishes what researchers call the 'militarization of the imagination.' Standard schools try to shield children from political violence; Hizbullah’s schools actively normalize it," the JFCA says. "By the time a teenager is old enough to be recruited into the armed wing, they don’t see themselves joining a militant group; they see it as the natural, honorable graduation from their childhood."
Since 2020, the educational system has been under what The Beiruter described as a "financial and legal siege," as the sources of funding for the system have come under direct attack by US sanctions. The five major sources of funding have come under increased scrutiny in the past few years. Funding from Iran has dwindled as it is needed to defend against US and Israeli strikes in the country, while Hezbollah's own financial portfolio has collapsed in the face of military attacks on Hezbollah’s bank, the Al-Qard Al-Hassan Association. The fall of Assad also severed Hezbollah's connection to the illicit drug trade which had allowed it to profit from the Assad regime’s Captagon trade, primarily by trading Captagon for South American cocaine through Italian and Albanian criminal organizations.
Recent IDF operations in Lebanon have uncovered an increasing number of weapons caches and armories hidden in Shia schools throughout Lebanon as well as ideological indoctrination material, including 130 weapons such as Kalashnikov rifles, handguns, and anti-tank missiles, at a school in the Bint Jbeil area.
"There is no expectation that the education system in southern Lebanon will educate children to love Israel. However, the basic requirement is that the education system not be used as a tool for incitement, training for terrorist activity, or harming Israeli civilians," the IDF said following the discoveries in southern Lebanon.

Sheinbaum says Mexico will not sign USMCA deal affecting sovereignty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:24:03 UTC
03:24:03 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Wednesday that her government will not sign any agreement with the US that affects Mexico’s sovereignty, as negotiations on the North American trade agreement continue.
“We are not going to sign anything that affects our sovereignty,” Sheinbaum said at a news conference, outlining Mexico’s position in talks on the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, known as T-MEC in Spanish and USMCA in the US.
The US decided to negotiate separately with Mexico and Canada rather than bringing the three partners together at a single negotiating table, she added.
Sheinbaum said Mexico is conducting its discussions with Washington and is not involved in issues between the US and Canada.
The negotiations are focused on several issues, including US tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and automobiles, with Mexico seeking better conditions for its exports and opposing additional tariffs on key sectors of its economy.
Sheinbaum stressed that Mexico is willing to address issues related to trade and economic cooperation as long as they do not compromise its sovereignty.
She cited areas such as intellectual property and the recognition of certain US drug patents through Mexico’s health regulator as examples of issues that can be negotiated.
She ruled out, however, accepting conditions that would undermine Mexico’s ability to make decisions independently.
Despite the talks, Sheinbaum reiterated Mexico’s interest in preserving the trade agreement between all three North American countries.
“We obviously want the three countries to continue in a trade agreement. It benefits all three,” she said.
The T-MEC took effect in 2020, replacing the North American Free Trade Agreement and establishing the framework governing trade among Mexico, the US, and Canada.
The negotiations come amid broader trade tensions between Washington and its North American partners, with tariffs and market access remaining central issues in relations between the three countries.

Treasury Department to buy back up to $6 billion in longer-term debt, triple the normal level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:23:59 UTC
03:23:59 KST

The Treasury Department on Wednesday said it will buy back up to $6 billion of government debt in an operation aimed at keeping bond markets functioning.
The much-anticipated announcement triples the normal buyback operation and follows a statement Aug. 19 from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that the department would at least double the normal amount for already-issued securities.
Treasury also said future operations will be at least $4 billion.
Though the operation ostensibly is aimed at keeping government debt markets liquid — in this case for 10- and 20-year notes — the extraordinary measure also has been seen as an effort to put a lid on Treasury yields, which had hit highs not seen since prior to the global financial crisis in 2008.
Market reaction, however, was negative. Treasury yields rose further but were volatile with long-dated securities increasing as much as 5 basis points each before easing.
The benchmark 10-year issue hit 4.841% around 11:30 a.m. ET. The 20-year climbed to 5.314% while the 30-year bond rose 5 basis points to also punch through what had been seen as the important 5.3% level, most recently yielding 5.307%. One basis point equals 0.01%.
"Hank Paulson's bazooka this is not," said bond fund manager Mark Spindel, chief investment officer at Potomac River Capital, referring to the former Treasury secretary's actions during the financial crisis. "And it took an act of Congress in that crisis."
There had been speculation heading into Wednesday's announcement that the buyback level could be many times the initial release, in which Treasury said the amount will "at least" double the normal $2 billion operation.
"At the end of the day, the Treasury is issuing a spectacular amount of securities, and they're trying to control the price level at the back end of the curve with really what, in the big scheme of things, is not necessarily a major operation," said Robert Tipp, chief investment strategist and head of global bonds at PGIM Credit.
"When they came out and said we would be buying at least 4 billion, I think market expectations were kind of thinking six to 10, and they've come in at the bottom end of the market's expectations," he added. "As a result, you're seeing a negative reaction here in the market with the sell-off at the back end of the curve."
The actual buybacks will happen Thursday in a 20-minute operation that will conclude at 2 p.m. ET.
Higher Treasury yields have come against a confluence of factors: surging government debt that recently passed $40 trillion, elevated inflation fears from tariffs and the Iran war, and a corresponding resurgence in energy prices that saw crude oil top $100 a barrel Wednesday.
At the same time, the long end of the Treasury curve is the less active part of a market that is considered the deepest and most liquid in the world.
Treasury issuance this year has jumped 11.8% from 2025, and the $31.8 trillion in publicly held debt is up 8.2%.
"Treasury announced buybacks less than hoped for (or feared depending on your point of view)," Mizuho economist Alex Pelle wrote. "The risk is that the Treasury ratchets this up in some manner given the market's reaction. However, I think the pressure to go against standard operating procedure will abate somewhat on the other side of the midterms."
The accelerated buybacks have faced critics, with some questioning what impact the amount would have on such a massive market, as well as the action being a break from Treasury moving in a predictable manner on the process.
One prominent critic was Stanley Druckenmiller, head of Duquesne Family Office and a former mentor to Bessent.
"Once markets believe Treasury is defending a price, every rise in yields becomes a test of official resolve, and the operations must grow to survive the tests," Druckenmiller wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed.
"Governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose. The only variable is how much they spend before conceding," he added.
Treasury's maneuvering, which also has included a parallel move to support the Japanese yen, come as Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has preached less involvement in financial markets. The Fed has a rate decision coming in a week, with traders pricing in a hike.
"Actions not words are what matter, and action in this case mean changes in the direction of fiscal policy or interest rates," said Anil Kashyap, a University of Chicago economist.
— CNBC's Steve Liesman contributed.
Correction: Anil Kashyap is a University of Chicago economist. An earlier version misspelled his name.

But a source in the Ukrainian presidency described the claim that Zelensky was at risk as “exaggerated”.
“It was an alert in Moldova when a Russian (drone) entered Moldovan and Romanian airspace,” the source told AFP.
In Chisinau, government spokesman Dumitru Ciorici said Moldova closed its airspace on the afternoon of Sept 8 just after 4.30pm local time due to a Russian drone that entered from the direction of Ukraine.
“The airspace was closed to protect aircraft flying over Moldova at the time: three departures and four arrivals were delayed as a result,” he added.
“After 1720, the authorities confirmed that the drone had come down and exploded... some 160 kilometres from Chisinau International Airport.
“Flight restrictions were then lifted. For the same reason, the plane of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky took off... later than scheduled.”
Zelensky arrived in Oslo on the evening of Sept 8 and held talks with Store, Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg and Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide on Norwegian military aid, including air-defence support, and civilian assistance.
On Sept 9, he joined a host of other foreign dignitaries at the funeral of Norway’s King Harald, who died on Aug 28 aged 89.
Zelensky left Norway afterwards, headed for Canada and talks with leaders there, Store told NRK. AFP

France says illegal Israeli settlement expansion risks becoming ‘irreversible,’ backs EU-wide trade ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:21:34 UTC
03:21:34 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
France has decided to ban trade in goods originating from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories and supports extending the measure across the EU, the Foreign Ministry said Wednesday.
“There is now a political decision that has been taken to ban in France products originating from the settlements. It is decided, and it is major,” said spokesperson Pascal Confavreux.
The decision comes in response to “the deterioration of the situation in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, the intensification of settlement activity, the possible irreversibility of this, and the non-respect of international law on the ground,” said Confavreux.
He pointed in particular to Israeli plans for the E1 settlement area, saying that demands for tenders published in August for construction of part of the settlement’s housing “directly threaten the territorial continuity of the West Bank and therefore, de facto, the two-state solution.”
“The decision we have taken is in accordance with international law, since Israeli settlements are illegal under international law,” said Confavreux.
He cited a July 2024 advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice, which he said established an obligation not to maintain economic or commercial relations with Israel concerning the occupied Palestinian territory when relations would strengthen its unlawful presence there.
Confavreux rejected describing the measure as a boycott of Israel.
“This measure prohibiting [such trade] absolutely does not constitute a boycott of the State of Israel. It specifically targets the occupied Palestinian territories,” he said, stressing that the territories “do not belong to the internationally recognized territory of Israel.”
“Israel remains an economic partner of France, and we will continue to work to strengthen economic and commercial exchanges between our two countries,” he added.
France has already carried out significant preparatory work for the ban, but additional work is needed to settle legal and technical details, including the traceability and verification of goods, the legal mechanism and the timetable for implementation, according to the Confavreux.
He said France wants the measure to be extended across the EU and is awaiting a proposal from the European Commission.
“There is no majority at the European level, so we are moving forward at the national level, collectively with other states,” said Confavreux.
He said the decision was driven by “an urgency on the ground, colonization and violence,” as well as the need to act despite the lack of an EU-wide majority.
“The Commission must put a proposal on the table to act, and at this stage, it is the Commission that refuses, and that is why we are acting at our level,” he said.
Confavreux denied any link between the decision and Israel’s upcoming elections. “Absolutely not, absolutely not,” he said.
He said the measure was part of France’s continued efforts to preserve the possibility of a two-state solution amid accelerating settlement activity and violence.
“The application of international law does not merit retaliatory measures,” he said on possible Israeli retaliation.   
12 countries announce measures on illegal Israeli settlements
The foreign ministers of the 12 countries announced in a statement Tuesday that they would impose or consider trade restrictions on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The countries said Israel's actions in the West Bank were undermining prospects for a two-state solution and stressed the need to preserve the possibility of establishing a Palestinian state.
Israel subsequently announced that it would close the UK's consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, which serves Palestinians, in response to the measures.

Opposition and NGOs urge Finland to restore UNRWA funding
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:21:17 EEST
03:21:17 KST

Finnish opposition politicians and development organisations are pressing the government to reverse its decision to end direct funding for the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, arguing that other humanitarian organisations cannot replace UNRWA's operations in Gaza and the occupied Palestinian territories.
Finland has provided UNRWA with €5 million a year under its 2023–2026 funding agreement.
Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Ville Tavio announced on 27 August that Finland would not renew the agreement when it expires. He said Finland's overall funding for the Palestinian territories would not decline and that money would instead pass through other organisations, including the World Food Programme.
The decision has prompted criticism from opposition MPs and Finnish civil society groups, which question the basis for ending support while humanitarian needs in Gaza remain high.
Green League MP Inka Hopsu called for the government to reverse the decision, saying no other organisation has UNRWA's personnel, logistics and operating network in the Palestinian territories.
Israel has accused UNRWA of Hamas links and restricted its operations. Finland suspended funding in January 2024 over allegations against agency staff, then resumed payments in March after reviewing UNRWA’s safeguards, with 10 per cent earmarked for oversight.
Finnish development organisation Fingo said the government has not explained what new assessment led to the latest change.
Fingo executive director Linda Konate said the decision was taken during a continuing humanitarian emergency and called on the government to disclose the evidence used to support it.
Fingo also referred to proceedings at the International Court of Justice concerning Israel's obligations towards the United Nations and humanitarian organisations in the occupied Palestinian territory.
The UN General Assembly asked the court to consider Israel's obligations in relation to the presence and activities of UN bodies, including UNRWA. UN documents submitted in the proceedings describe UNRWA as a central part of humanitarian operations for Palestinian refugees.
Fingo said the court's October 2025 findings did not support allegations used to question the separation between UNRWA and Hamas. The organisation asked why concerns addressed by Finland when funding resumed in 2024 were now being cited as grounds for withdrawing support.
Fingo international policy specialist Johannes Hautaviita said Tavio had previously concluded that UNRWA's safeguards provided sufficient assurances for Finland to continue funding.
The Social Democratic Party has also criticised the decision. MP Kimmo Kiljunen said Finland risked weakening the UN humanitarian system at a time when the United States has withdrawn funding and Israel has restricted UNRWA's activities.
Kiljunen said Finland should maintain long-term support for humanitarian organisations operating in Gaza rather than reduce their ability to work.
The Finnish-Palestinian organisation Sumud is accusing Finland of contributing to efforts to dismantle UNRWA and calling the decision part of Finland's alleged complicity in Israel's genocide in Gaza.
Sumud also called for Finland to end military cooperation with Israel and support the suspension of preferential trade arrangements between Israel and the European Union.
Pressure on UNRWA has increased alongside Israeli measures against the agency. Israeli forces raided and seized UNRWA's Qalandiya vocational training centre in occupied East Jerusalem shortly before Finland announced its funding decision and removed staff from the premises. UNRWA said the entry violated the protections afforded to UN facilities.
Finland's government has maintained that its humanitarian support for Palestinians will continue despite the end of direct UNRWA funding, with assistance redirected through other organisations.
Its critics argue that the issue concerns not only the amount of aid but also whether other agencies possess the staff, facilities and logistical network required to replace services that UNRWA has provided for decades.
UNRWA provides healthcare, education, water, shelter and other services to Palestinian refugees. Its clinics in Gaza recorded 19.3 million visits between October 2023 and July 2026. About 800,000 people relied on its water assistance in July, while 65,000 displaced people were staying in UNRWA emergency shelters.

Aemet says summer 2026 is hottest on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:16:13 UTC
03:16:13 KST

The state agency also confirms that Spaniards have already endured 61 days of heatwave conditions so far this year, more than in any other year.
Spain has surpassed the dreaded and much-remembered summer of 2022 in terms of the number of days endured under a heatwave: 61, according to the State Meteorological Agency, 20 more than in that year. The summer of 2026 has also recorded an average temperature of 24.5°C, making it the hottest in the historical series since records began in 1961 and surpassing last year, 2025, by 0.3°C, and 2.4°C above the long-term average.
Aemet recalls that the ten hottest summers in the historical record have all occurred in the 21st century, and seven of the eight warmest have taken place since 2015. The agency also warns that the meteorological summer keeps getting longer.
"At the end of May, temperatures typical of July were recorded across large areas of the country. And then, in September, already in the meteorological autumn, there was another heatwave which, provisionally, ran from the 2nd to the 7th, lasting six days and affecting 16 provinces." Only in four other years has a month of September (1987, 1988, 2006 and 2016) seen such extreme heatwaves, more typical of the height of summer.
The heavy winter rains have meant that Spanish reservoirs have remained in very good condition after the summer season, with an average level of 62.58% despite tourist pressure, and above half of their capacity in basins that are usually under stress, such as the Júcar, Segura, Andalusian Mediterranean and Catalan catchments.
Even so, this has not spared the country from suffering, as in the rest of Europe, large-scale fires that have exposed the lack of forest fire prevention and of sufficient personnel with good working conditions, in regions such as Madrid, Aragón or Castilla y León.

Nuclear agency board refers Iran to UN Security Council for first time in 20 years
IAEA remains blocked from key sites damaged during June 2025 military strikes by the US and Israel
The UN atomic watchdog’s board on Wednesday reported Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, citing it for failure to cooperate in a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites.
Western officials suspect that the traces could provide evidence that Iran had a secret nuclear weapons programme until 2003. Iran says that it is not pursuing nuclear weapons, and that its programme is entirely peaceful.
Reporting Iran to the Security Council opens the country to possible sanctions and asset freezes, though such punitive measures are unlikely because Iran’s allies Russia and China hold veto power on the panel.
Twenty-three countries on the International Atomic Energy Agency’s 35-member board of governors voted for Wednesday’s resolution at IAEA headquarters in Vienna.
China, Russia and Niger opposed it, while eight countries abstained and one did not vote as it was in arrears, according to diplomats who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the outcome of the closed-door vote.
The resolution was put forward by the United States, Britain, France and Germany.

He expressed hope that renewed engagement between the two countries would contribute to stability and security in the Indian Ocean, "particularly at a time of increasing global uncertainty." 
The Chagos Archipelago, a group of seven atolls comprising more than 60 islands in the central Indian Ocean, lies about 500 kilometers (310 miles) south of the Maldives.

====================================================================================================

Everyday Recycling Mistakes You're Making—And What You Should Do Instead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:06:28 UTC
03:06:28 KST

Public confidence and trust in recycling systems is on the decline. While 87% of Americans say recycling is important, only about 32% of household waste is recycled or composted, according to 2025 data. More Americans believe that recycling feels harder today than it did four years ago.
But from plastic bottles to cardboard boxes, recycling is important—and has an impact. Recycled materials are key to reducing the extraction of natural materials like timber and aluminum. “It’s a really low-hanging fruit of something that you can do that does have a difference,” says Shelie Miller, professor in the School for Environment and Sustainability at the University of Michigan.
Sustainability experts say recycling doesn’t have to be that hard. Here are some of the biggest recycling mistakes people make—and what you should be doing instead.
Why is recycling so complicated?
What is recyclable varies greatly depending on where you live. “Recycling is unfortunately more complicated than we'd like it to be,” says Miller. “Everybody's recycling rules are going to be slightly different, which is what makes it so hard.”
That’s because different recycling plants use different equipment, and so they have different recycling rules.
Seven states, including California, Maryland, and Maine, have taken steps to fix that by introducing Extended Producer Responsibility laws aimed at standardizing recycling practices statewide.
Until that becomes more widespread across the country, there’s a simple rule you can follow, experts say. “Think about your bottles, cans, and containers that are in your laundry, kitchen, and bathrooms… and paper and cardboard,” says Cody Marshall, chief programs officer at The Recycling Partnership, a nonprofit dedicated to creating a better recycling system. “Those are things that are recyclable.”
What should you avoid recycling?
Avoid recycling things like plastic bags, which can jam machinery, and batteries, and refrain from bagging your recycling in trash bags. While many plastic products have a recycling symbol with a number in the middle, it doesn’t always mean it can be tossed in the recycling bin. The label simply denotes what kind of plastic it is.
In fact, plastic is one the biggest sources of confusion when it comes to recycling. Most places only accept plastics 1 and 2—commonly used to make soda bottles or laundry detergent containers. Some places might accept plastics 4 and 5 (think a yogurt container or plastic straw.) “The rest are not really recyclable at all, and some are really bad to put into the recycling system in practice,” says Jennifer Russell, associate professor of Sustainable Biomaterials at Virginia Tech. Incorrect recycling can cause the machinery to break down, or contaminate the batch, degrading its value.
Perhaps surprising to some, however, it turns out it is okay to recycle a greasy pizza box—as long as you eat the last slice. “A little bit of food residue is not a problem,” says Marshall. That’s because processing technologies have gotten better with time, and are now able to handle a small amount of residue. “Just don't throw anything in your container that a raccoon would still want to eat off of.”
Meanwhile, if something is compostable, it does not mean it can be recycled. “Compostable and recyclable are two different things,” says Miller. “If you have something that says it's a compostable cup, often that means it's compostable plastic. Compostable plastics can't be recycled, and they have to go into a facility marked as [able to break-down] compostable plastics, if they're actually accepted in your community.”
Why you shouldn’t ‘wish-cycle’
Refrain from what Russell calls “wish-cycling,” the practice of putting something in the recycling bin and hoping it's recyclable. “People really want to do the right thing and err on the side of caution, and that's just a big problem because recycling systems are designed on the basis of material, not on the basis of product,” says Russell, who notes that incorrect recycling can lead to more harm than good.
“Wish-cycling is actually one of the biggest drivers of the high costs of the system. If we were putting just the right materials that are being asked for—aluminum cans, number 1 and number 2 plastics, the systems would have less contamination, less shutdown issues, and the materials coming out the other side would be of much higher value.”
Another important change? Cut down on the number of things you buy—and reuse what you can. “Reduce and reuse are two important R's before recycle,” says Marshall. Bring reusable grocery bags when shopping, and consider seeing if there’s a refill or zero-waste store in your neighborhood where you can shop for household items in your own reusable containers rather than single use plastic packaging.
These small changes really can make a difference. “That one choice that each of us makes every day to buy or use a single-use option instead of a reusable one, or to put it in the garbage can instead of the recycling one, they aggregate across the millions of people in the country who are making the same decisions every single day,” says Russell. “It’s important to remember that every one of those decisions actually does matter. Making the right decision can be very important if you're trying to make the system better.”

The star-spangled map was part of a wider burst of Truth Social posts over recent weeks in which Trump claimed Apple Maps had joined Google Maps in renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America,” declaring the change “complete, ratified, and binding.”

Thirty years of Italian creativity through the vision of architect and designer Marco Poletti. A traveling exhibition that explores Italian design as culture, research, and a vision of the future. Italian design takes center stage once again in Central Asia. “The Languages of Time in Design (1995–2026),” the exhibition curated by architect Marco Poletti in collaboration with Gaia Zanotti, opens on September 11 at the “Kulyash Baiseitova” National University of Arts of Kazakhstan, in the heart of Astana. The third stop on an evolving journey—following the successes in Almaty and Bishkek —the project is sponsored by the Italian Embassy in Kazakhstan, the ICE Agency, and the Italian Cultural Institute in Almaty to place Italian creativity at the center of cultural dialogue with Central Asia. The exhibition presents “Made in Italy” in its broadest sense: not merely as an object, but as a synthesis of creativity, research, entrepreneurship, innovation, and memory. Thirty years of design interpreted as a living expression of contemporary Italian culture. By supporting the exhibition’s international tour, the embassy thus strengthens its efforts to foster dialogue between Italy and Central Asia, building bridges between institutions, universities, businesses, designers, and new generations. A universal language that transcends borders and connects Italy’s creative heritage with the emerging sensibilities of the region. As Italian Ambassador Antonello De Riu emphasizes: “The exhibition should not be understood as a mere collection of works, but rather as a cultural device that reflects on the very act of exhibiting, going beyond its original form. A journey that illustrates design’s ability to interpret society, anticipate its needs, and transform innovation into new ways of living. Step by step, the exhibition has captured and conveyed the various “languages” that design has adopted in its dialogue with technology and contemporary sensibilities.

Earliest known drug use and its consequences discovered in Indonesia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:02:35 UTC
03:02:35 KST

Who doesn't love to get stoned out of their gourd? Use of intoxicants isn't even confined to our species – Egyptian fruit bats are known to get drunk on fermenting fruit.
They seem aware of the potential consequences, which include the mucking up of their flying and navigational skills. This explains why some apparently avoid eating overripe fruit and why fruit bat alcoholics aren't a thing.
If only we had bat brains. Some researchers even suspect that agriculture arose around 10,000 years ago as a reliable way to make beer, as opposed to a reliable way to eat.
We already knew that prehistoric peoples used mind-altering substances, but now a report provides the earliest evidence of drug use yet. The skeletal remains of two hunter-gatherers in Sulawesi, Indonesia, indicate that they sucked on mind-altering betel nuts, one as long as 16,000 to 25,000 years ago.
The other one was doing that 6,300 to 7,600 years ago, Adam Brumm of Australia's Griffith University and Marlon Ririmasse of the Pusat Riset Arkeologi Lingkungan research institute in Jakarta reported with an international team in Science Advances on Wednesday.
Why is there such a wide margin of error on the dating for these addled hunter-gatherers? "The site has been challenging, as no charcoal for radiocarbon dating is preserved, so we had to use a combination of methods, including luminescence dating of sediments and uranium-series dating of bones, teeth and stalagmites," Brumm says.
The smoking spliff isn't cave art portraying this horrible habit but the parlous state of the two hunter-gatherers' teeth. Both exhibited hollowed-out rounded grooves in specific molars. The archaeologists believe that this erosion was caused by the compulsive sucking on hard spherical objects – not stones but betel nuts, a thesis supported by the presence of the betel intoxicant arecoline in the hunter-gatherers' dental plaque.
Also, the object clenched between the rear molars of these people was 10 to 20 millimeters (0.8 inches) in diameter, which fits betel nuts on Sulawesi, one of Indonesia's biggest islands.
In any case, the wear pattern on the teeth wasn't typical of routine consumption of anything. The researchers note that betel nuts, also known as areca seeds, have no nutritional value, so they weren't being held in the mouth for that.
Modern folk don't suck betel nuts, we chew them in the form of "betel quids." The quid is made by shelling the nuts and crushing or slicing their seeds, and mixing the mash or slices with calcium hydroxide (slaked lime).
Sometimes the mixture is flavored with spices such as cardamom. The plain or flavored mash is wrapped in a leaf to create a quid, which is inserted into the mouth and chewed. The drug reportedly causes mild stimulation, helping you stay awake, and even mild euphoria.
Regular indulgence leads to tolerance, leading the user to increase the dose, which can cultivate chemical dependence, aka addiction. Side effects of habitual quid chewing include staining your teeth and mouth red, eroding your teeth, and triggering oral or esophageal cancer. Even so, the scientists say that one in 10 people today, from Africa to Asia to Micronesia, chews betel quids.
Well, almost two in 10 people today still smoke cigarettes, knowing full well how bad that is. Withdrawal from betel dependency can involve mood swings and anxiety, not to mention the wicked combo of fatigue and insomnia.
The question is when humankind began to ride the betel beast, and now we learn that in Indonesia it started possibly as long as 25,000 years ago.
Inconveniently for the archaeologists, sucking the nut whole does not stain the teeth red like the modern custom of chewing betel mash in a quid with slaked lime, Brumm explains. The lime triggers a chemical reaction that turns the saliva bright red. But the hunter-gatherers didn't have crimson teeth, just damaged ones.
Did holding a nut in the mouth without accessing the inner seed make these people high? Yes. Remember, today the main neuroactive alkaloid in betel nut, arecoline, is released by chewing the nut processed with slaked lime, but stick that nut in the mouth for a decent while and it releases the desired arecoline, albeit less than one would get by crushing and processing the nut, the team reported based on experimentation.
So plausibly the betel habit began as simply sucking the nuts, and the common assumption that betel addiction began with the onset of agriculture was simply wrong.
In any case, this is the earliest known instance of deliberate inebriation, the team says, helpfully listing known intoxicants of prehistory, as detected by archaeologists. Hitherto the earliest was beer made using barley 11,000 to 13,000 years ago in Israel. Then we have the psychedelics San Pedro cactus and Mescalbean that were used 10,400 years ago in Peru and Texas, while paleo-Indians painted pictures of psychedelic datura 10,000 years ago, and our friend the coca leaf was used 8,000 years ago in Peru. Finally, Psilocybian mushrooms were used 8,000 years ago in the Sahara.
The researchers note that we have no idea when use of any of those began, let alone how the ancients discovered their delights. In short, the list and now the new discovery debunk the vague notion that intoxication began with farming.
The scientists note that early betel use in some form had been suspected in certain ancient teeth, such as 13,000 years ago in Thailand, but the dates were unsure. The earliest proven betel user was also in Thailand but just 3,500 years ago. Now the timeline is much further back.
So we don't know origins or prehistoric rationale, but we know what we like, and one in 10 likes betel quids. What's betel to the other 90 percent?
It is the drupe fruit (which means it has flesh and a pit like a peach) of areca palm trees in tropical regions of South Asia, Southeast Asia and the wider Pacific. We do not chew on its shell; we crush its seed. In time, once we chew the quid and turn our saliva bright red, our teeth will be stained as well.
Sadly, as Brumm and the team suggest, like many an addict today whose habit alleviates the pain of anticipating bad effects in the future, these ancient hunter-gatherers could have found themselves trapped in a loop of sucking on betel nuts to relieve toothache – as this habit worsened their oral health.
Today's betel buffs aren't in a good place either. "Betel quids are chewed in the buccal cheek cavity, with the blood-rich tissue in this part of the mouth allowing the plant compounds to enter the bloodstream more rapidly," the team writes. This practice elevates the risk of oral cancer. The compound's absorption is facilitated by the slaked lime.
When people stopped mouthing the mind-altering nut and began to convert it into chewable quids is a mystery. Maybe in the Neolithic, the scientists suggest.
The researchers note that people sometimes stick stuff in their mouth and just keep it there, not for eating or anything else really – a blade of grass, for instance. But holding a betel in the oral cavity and gnawing or chewing or just sucking on it had deleterious effects, hence the sense that the behavior was compulsive, which suggests that these people were getting high.
And the scientists add that skeletal remains of preagricultural foragers are extremely uncommon in southern Sulawesi. So probably the compulsion and physical dependence goes back far, far before our hunter-gatherers from 16,000 to 25,000 years ago.
Who knows, maybe the inspiration behind the earliest figurative art ever found, the portrait of a warty pig on the very same island of Sulawesi from over 54,000 years ago, wasn't only the swine's charms.

Betel nut traces in 25,000-year-old teeth point to early human drug use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:01:00 UTC
03:01:00 KST

Traces of betel nut in 25,000-year-old teeth earliest-known evidence of human drug use
In short:
Archaeologists have found evidence of a person who used a psychoactive drug up to 25,000 years ago.
Tooth fossils in Indonesia suggest that ancient foragers in the region were sucking on betel nut, possibly as a painkiller.
What's next?
Human drug use is probably older than this sample, but evidence is harder to come by.
Betel nut, one of the most commonly used drugs in the world, appears to have an ancient history.
Fossilised remains of two people, found by archaeologists on the island of Sulawesi in Indonesia, carry traces of the psychoactive substance in their jaws.
One of the fossils is dated between 16,000 and 25,000 years old, making it the oldest known example of human drug use by at least 3,000 years.
The discovery was published today in the journal Science Advances.
Adam Brumm, the study's lead author and an archaeologist at Griffith University, said the two people probably sucked on betel nuts like "gobstoppers".
Professor Brumm, who tried the method himself, said it numbed the mouth.
"I suspect that was the effect that they were after," he said.
Mysterious damaged teeth in Sulawesi caves
A team of Indonesian and Australian archaeologists uncovered the fossils at two separate sites in South Sulawesi.
Both individuals, the younger of which was 6,300 to 7,600 years old, predate the arrival of agriculture on Sulawesi.
Both hunter-gatherers had puzzling, deep marks on their teeth.
"Although they were separated by about 10,000 years of time, they had these really distinctive and very unusual tooth grooves," Professor Brumm said.
"We couldn't explain them."
An analysis of the marks suggested they had been created by repeatedly sucking on a round object, one or two centimetres in size.
"I thought, immediately, betel nut is the most likely possibility," Professor Brumm said.
Betel nut by another method
Betel or areca nut is the seed of a palm native to South-East Asia.
It is one of the most commonly used psychoactive substances in the world, alongside alcohol, caffeine and nicotine.
Today, people typically grind betel nut and mix it with substances such as slaked lime to enhance its psychoactive properties before chewing it.
"We hypothesised that before the development of the betel nut chewing custom, there may have been an earlier stage in the human use of betel nut where they just sucked on the nut itself," Professor Brumm said.
To test this, the team designed an experiment to simulate betel nut sucking.
They soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva, then tested the saliva on frog egg cells genetically engineered to grow human brain receptors.
The results suggested betel nut sucking would affect human brain cells.
"It will alter human brain function, but not to the extent of modern betel nut chewing with slaked lime," Professor Brumm said.
The team then investigated residues on the fossil teeth and found arecoline, the main psychoactive substance in betel nut.
Sofia Samper Carro, an archaeologist at the Australian National University who was not involved in the research, agreed with the conclusion that betel nut sucking caused the tooth marks.
"The early evidence of drug consumption presented here predates any published evidence by thousands of years,"
Previously, the oldest known evidence of drug use was 13,000-year-old beer brewing in Israel.
A painful, addictive treatment
The researchers believe betel nut sucking would have produced a numbing effect on the mouth, and may have been used as a painkiller.
But betel nuts would have damaged teeth in the process, producing deep grooves that would have prompted painful toothaches.
Professor Brumm suggested the damaged teeth were evidence of a "vicious cycle".
"The more they sucked the nut for pain relief, the worse it damaged their teeth and the more they became addicted to sucking the nut to treat that."
Modern-day betel nut use also affects the mouth and teeth, and has been linked to an increased risk of oral cancer.
"You can see the pretty serious negative health consequences and how humans have grappled with those for at least 25,000 years on this island," Professor Brumm said.
Dr Samper Carro said the research could help identify even older uses of betel nut or other drugs.
"I'm convinced that even earlier hominids, such as Neanderthals, would have used natural remedies [like plants, natural compounds and maybe even insects or fungi] to fight pain and infection," she said.
Professor Brumm agreed the practice probably stretched further back into history than their 25,000-year-old sample.
"There's no human society today that doesn't use drugs of some kind,"
"But we just know so little about the deep antiquity of these practices."

A six-decade study links teenage school anxiety to late-life memory complaints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:00:49 UTC
03:00:49 KST

Feeling anxious or struggling to keep pace in school during early adolescence is linked to how people view their own memory abilities more than fifty years later. The findings suggest that early-life psychological health can have a lasting association with how individuals perceive their cognitive decline in older age. The research was published in Journal of Gerontology: Psychological Sciences.
Subjective memory refers to a person’s own perception of their everyday memory functioning. This includes noticing how often they forget where they placed an item, lose track of a conversation, or fail to recall something they were just told. As people age, it is incredibly common to experience and report these types of memory difficulties. Some older adults report no changes, whereas others feel their memory is steadily declining.
Scientists are interested in these self-reported memory complaints because they can sometimes serve as an early warning sign for dementia. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that greater declines in self-reported memory over time were associated with higher levels of Alzheimer’s-related proteins in the brain. At the same time, a 2014 meta-analysis found that people’s self-rated memory issues only weakly match their actual memory test scores. Because subjective memory and objective memory often differ, researchers have begun exploring how emotional and psychological traits influence self-reported cognitive decline.
Historically, much of the research on cognitive aging has focused on risk factors present in middle or late adulthood. However, scientists are increasingly looking to the very beginning of life to understand how early experiences shape the aging process. For example, a 2004 study demonstrated that cognitive abilities measured in childhood continue to predict mental performance and health many decades later in old age. Conditions such as a family’s socioeconomic status can dictate a child’s early opportunities, setting them on a path that affects their long-term brain health.
The research, led by Gideon Neidenmark, a doctoral student at Örebro University in Sweden, aimed to understand how an array of childhood factors might forecast memory complaints in old age. The authors noted that existing research rarely tracks individuals from early childhood all the way into their late sixties. By bridging this gap, they hoped to see whether childhood intelligence, social well-being, or school anxiety could predict how people evaluate their own memories nearly six decades later.
“I am fortunate enough to be involved in a longitudinal study called the IDA-project with data spanning six decades,” Neidenmark told PsyPost. “This has enabled questions regarding how our childhood and adolescence are related to our abilities when we get older.”
“I became especially interested in subjective memory because previous research has demonstrated that our own experience of our memory abilities usually does not overlap substantially with our actual memory performance and wanted to understand why that is,” he added.
To investigate this, the researchers used data from the IDA-project, a massive Swedish longitudinal study that began in 1965. They tracked a cohort of participants who were around 10 years old at the start of the study, assessing them again in 1968 at age 13. During these childhood visits, participants completed standardized tests measuring their verbal, spatial, and reasoning abilities. The researchers also gathered official school grades, collected information on the families’ socioeconomic status, and asked the children to fill out questionnaires about their social well-being and any anxiety they experienced in the school context.
In 2022, the researchers sent follow-up questionnaires to the surviving participants, who were now about 67 years old. A total of 625 people completed this phase of the study. The participants filled out a standardized survey detailing their current subjective memory, answering questions about how often they forget things in their daily lives. They also completed a widely used assessment to measure their current levels of anxiety and depressive symptoms.
When analyzing the data, the researchers found that participants who reported higher levels of school anxiety at age 13 tended to report worse subjective memory at age 67. This association was specific to psychological health during early adolescence. Interestingly, the researchers did not find evidence that school anxiety at age 10 predicted memory complaints later in life.
This link between early adolescent anxiety and late-life memory complaints remained steady even after the researchers accounted for the participants’ current anxiety and depressive symptoms.
“I think the most important take-home message is that our childhood and adolescence are related to our abilities in later life, particularly that our psychological health in our youth is related to how we perceive and rate our own memory abilities,” Neidenmark said. “This also persists even when we account for current psychological health.”
In contrast, several other childhood factors did not predict subjective memory in older age. The researchers found no evidence that cognitive ability, school grades, social well-being, or family socioeconomic status at ages 10 or 13 had any bearing on how participants viewed their memory at age 67.
“I think what surprised me the most was that social well-being, socioeconomic status, cognitive ability and school performance during childhood and adolescence were not related to subjective memory in later life,” Neidenmark explained. “It really emphasized what previous literature has found, i.e., that subjective memory may better reflect psychological factors than actual memory performance.”
The findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that depression during adolescence was associated with lower cognitive performance over the next six years. The new study extends this timeline considerably, tracking participants over nearly six decades. It is worth noting, however, that the new study focused exclusively on self-reported memory complaints in older age rather than objective cognitive test performance.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The childhood questionnaires used to measure school anxiety and social well-being relied on only a few items, which resulted in relatively low statistical reliability for those specific measures. This lack of precision might explain why factors like early social well-being did not show a relationship with late-life memory complaints. Better measurement tools might yield different results in future studies.
“Like with any articles, we should be cautious about considering these findings as fact or infer causality,” Neidenmark pointed out. “As mentioned, we should be cautious about considering lower psychological health as causing lower subjective memory. Rather, they are related to each other even over such a large time span.”
Additionally, the recent follow-up phase of the study did not include objective memory tests or medical screenings for dementia. Because of this, the researchers could not determine if the participants’ memory complaints reflected actual cognitive decline or merely a pessimistic view of their abilities. The study also experienced attrition over its 57-year span, and the individuals who remained in the project at age 67 generally had better childhood grades and better psychological health than those who dropped out.
Future research could explore whether there is a direct chain of events linking early-life psychological health to late-life memory. Scientists might also look at mid-life factors that could bridge the gap between teenage anxiety and aging. Understanding these pathways could help health professionals design interventions that support both emotional well-being and lifelong cognitive health.
“However, this study and findings could indicate the importance of considering early-life for prevention,” Neidenmark noted. “This study in particular may point to psychological health (in particular school anxiety) as an important factor to consider in this work.”
“My next step is to investigate how these factors in childhood and adolescence are related to actual memory performance and brain structure in later life,” he said. “I hope to understand how this differs to my results from this study, and how they are related.”
The study, “Early life predictors of subjective cognitive function in older age: Emerging longitudinal associations over six decades,” was authored by Gideon Neidenmark, Catherine Tuvblad, and Jonas Persson.

Indonesian foragers may have sucked on mind-altering nuts 25,000 years ago, research finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:00:02 UTC
03:00:02 KST

What may be the earliest known evidence for human drug taking has been traced to ancient Indonesian foragers who sucked on mind-altering nuts as long as 25,000 years ago.
Analysis of two exceptionally rare skeletons from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi revealed dramatic tooth wear and traces of a psychoactive substance in the individuals’ remaining teeth, suggesting they routinely sucked on hard, abrasive betel nuts.
Although little known in western societies, betel nuts are the world’s fourth most widely used psychoactive substance after alcohol, caffeine and nicotine, with an estimated tenth of the global population chewing the seeds.
“We’ve found evidence for how this very common drug use habit, which is found throughout a lot of the Asia-Pacific region today, might have evolved,” said Prof Adam Brumm at Griffith University’s Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution in Brisbane.
The work began when the team examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers unearthed at two different sites on the island. One was dated to about 7,000 years old, the other more ancient at 16,000 to 25,000 to years old.
Writing in Science Advances, the researchers describe how both adults had deep, rounded grooves in their teeth. Some went so deep they would have exposed the dental pulp. “I was thinking, what the hell were these people doing? It’s like someone had a drill head shaped like a gobstopper and wore away the inner part of the tooth,” said Brumm.
Betel nuts are actually the seeds of the Areca catechu palm, but are misnamed because they are often wrapped in betel vine leaves for chewing. Today, the nuts are typically chewed after being mixed with slaked lime made by grinding burnt shells to form a “quid”.
Brumm suspected the bizarre tooth wear was caused by the foragers holding hard, round and abrasive objects in their mouth, but what sort of object? “Imagine you kept a stone in your mouth and you moved it from one part of your mouth to another, and if you did that day after day, hour after hour. Eventually it would wear down your extremely hard dental tissue to form these grooves,” he said.
The team wondered whether the grooves were the result of foragers sucking on betel nuts before people realised that mixing the nuts with slaked lime helped release more of the psychoactive drug and intensify the “high”.
To test the hunch, the scientists soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva and found that it soon contained enough of the psychoactive compound arecoline to induce a high, albeit a milder one than when the nut is chewed. Analysis of the foragers’ teeth found traces of arecoline in the tissues.
“I’ve sucked on a nut as an experiment and it’s a really bitter, astringent taste. It makes your mouth go numb and I think that’s what they were interested in,” Brumm said.
“This might have been a traditional remedy for toothache, but if they did it for too long, sucking on the nut wore down their teeth so badly that it actually created much worse dental pain in the long term. These individuals were seemingly caught in a self-perpetuating cycle where they were continually sucking on the nuts to treat the tooth pain caused by this nut-sucking habit.”
While humans probably began using mind-altering plants as soon as they encountered them, the oldest traditions of psychoactive drug use are thought to have arisen about 13,000 years ago with fermented drinks such as barley beer.
Dr Elisa Guerra-Doce, an associate professor in European prehistory at the University of Valladolid in Spain, said the study provided “direct evidence of the antiquity of human drug use”.
“These findings not only represent the earliest known evidence to date of the use of psychoactive plants anywhere in the world, but also demonstrate that the consumption of Areca nuts is a millennia-old tradition dating back to prehistoric times,” she added.
