Taiwan’s defense efforts sending signal to US, not China, security expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:38:10 UTC
01:38:10 KST

Taiwan’s growing defense preparations might be sending a stronger signal to the US than to Beijing, highlighting the need for Taipei to tailor its deterrence efforts to different audiences, a US security academic said yesterday.
Stanford University Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies fellow Oriana Skylar Mastro made the comment during a Taipei Security Dialogue panel examining lessons Taiwan could draw from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Mastro said she was impressed by Taiwan’s increased defense spending, emphasis on asymmetric capabilities and efforts to prepare society for conflict, but questioned whom those initiatives were influencing.
Photo: CNA
She said when she asked senior Chinese figures and analysts whether Taiwan’s improving capabilities were making Beijing more cautious, their responses generally amounted to: “We don’t really know. We’re not paying attention to that. That’s not the point.”
Although Taiwan’s efforts contributed to improved deterrence, “the audience is the US,” she said.
Taiwan’s message that it is doing more for its defense, particularly its ability to defend itself without outside intervention, is largely directed at Washington, Mastro said.
That is an appropriate strategy, because it reassured Washington of Taiwan’s determination to defend itself, she said, but added that Taipei needed a separate approach to ensure that its capabilities also affected Beijing’s calculations.
“There’s no situation under which Taiwan can defend itself without direct US military intervention,” Mastro said.
Taiwan should communicate its newly acquired capabilities more effectively to Beijing so that its defense investments can deepen relations with the US and deter China, she added.
National Chengchi University Department of Diplomacy professor Chen Ping-Kuei (陳秉逵) agreed with Mastro, saying: “I think the public believes that we have sent an effective signal to the US, but we haven’t sent a very effective deterrent signal to Beijing.”
US arms sales to Taiwan is an important signal of Washington’s commitment, he said, adding that their political significance could be more important than the size of individual packages.
If Washington were to begin discussing proposed arms sales packages for Taiwan with Beijing, it would send “a very, very bad signal” to Taipei, Chen said.
He was referring to concerns raised after US President Donald Trump confirmed he had spoken to Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) about arms sales to Taiwan when they met in Beijing in mid-May.
That violated a key tenet of the “six assurances” — that the US would not consult China on arms sales to Taiwan.
Trump seemed to brush aside such a pledge.
“What am I going to say? I don’t want to talk to you about it because I have an agreement that was signed in 1982?” he said after the meeting.
Beyond military capabilities and signaling, Taiwan must prepare to remain functional if China seeks to isolate it, German Institute for Defence and Strategic Studies senior research fellow Wolfgang Muller said.
Isolation would not necessarily require a formal blockade, because heightened risk alone could alter the behavior of shipping companies, insurers, suppliers and maintenance providers, Muller said.
“Do not ask only how China would invade Taiwan. Ask also how China could make an invasion unnecessary,” he said.
Rather than pursuing complete self-sufficiency, Taiwan should measure how long essential services could continue if external supplies were interrupted, Muller said.
He also urged Taiwan to identify bottlenecks linking infrastructure systems and pre-position critical items that could be difficult to obtain during a crisis, including transformers, medicine, chemicals, communications equipment and machine parts.
“Taiwan cannot make its critical infrastructure invulnerable, but it can make failure more temporary,” Muller said. “Recovery capacity is combat power.”

Reform UK’s conference was to showcase a party ready for government. It did so with two top aides removed after an investigation aired on Channel 4, its finances under police scrutiny and seven in 10 voters, polls indicate, regarding its leader, Nigel Farage, as sleazy — double the number who thought the same of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Reform, a rightwing populist party, says it would take power back from a corrupt establishment. The scandal raises a question: Does Reform oppose the influence of big money — or just who benefits from it?
Reporters from Verbatim Investigations, founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a wealthy American father and his UK-based son who wanted to donate to Reform. In the UK, foreign donations are banned from politics. That “allegedly” was ignored. Verbatim’s team filmed their meetings with James Orr, a Cambridge academic specializing in ethics and Reform’s head of policy, as well as with Dan Jukes, Farage’s close aide. Both have been “removed” from their posts.
Reform officials allegedly commissioned ￡32,500 (US$44,060) of polling, arranged for what they believed was a US company to pay the bill, hid the party’s role and used the results to generate favorable newspaper headlines. Verbatim wired the money from a US firm to polling firm JL Partners, whose boss was filmed saying that he should have disclosed that his client was Reform. JL Partners admits procedural “weaknesses.” When the supposed American benefactor explained the arrangement to Farage over lunch, the Reform leader’s filmed response was not alarm, but celebration: “It worked. Boom.”
The second allegation is that the American father was willing to provide Reform with ￡500,000 through a “permissible” British intermediary — his son. This, if true, would be unlawful. At the lunch Farage does not say that the father cannot be the cash’s source or that the son can legally only donate his own money. He is filmed saying “thank you both” when it was explained.
Gavin Millar, a media lawyer, told reporters that “there is enough being said, in the presence of Farage and to Farage, for it to be a red flag — for it to be understood as the reality that this money is coming from an American in a disguised form. And he should be questioning that … On the contrary, he seems to be quite happy to receive the money.”
In response, Reform said that it has “broken no laws.” Farage told LBC that while his party had done “nothing wrong,” the footage looked bad and hence party aides were suspended. Reform has not offered much of an explanation, preferring to claim that it has “been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate change activists.”
Reform has been reported to law enforcement and the Electoral Commission.
Reform’s problem is not that two aides forgot about the rules. It is that senior figures appear to have understood them, discussed how to circumvent them and assumed that nobody would find out. A party accused of plotting how to get around the law is saying it would impose a “national emergency” so that judges and officials would not get in its way. That is a telling and ominous indicator about how Reform understands power.

US to ban Canadian dairy and alcohol
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:38:04 UTC
01:38:04 KST

The US on Tuesday banned a broad swath of Canadian alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and dairy products from import, sharply escalating an already acrimonious trade spat.
The import bans, which go into effect on Sept. 29 and were published on the White House’s Web site, came after Canada’s own retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect after midnight on Tuesday.
Those Canadian levies themselves followed 50 percent tariffs that the US imposed on US$20 billion of Canadian goods last month, after several rounds of negotiations collapsed.
Photo: AFP
The breakdown has widened a rift between the longtime allies, who have blamed each other for the failed talks, spurred Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to urge a further shift away from Canada’s biggest trading partner and cast doubt on the viability of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
“We have everything we need to pivot and prosper,” Carney said on Tuesday in a video posted on YouTube.
“That pivot will come at a cost. There’s always a cost to action, but it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still,” he said.
The US bans appeared to cover most alcohol products, including beer and various types of wine, whisky, bourbon, rum, vodka, vermouth, tequila, mezcal and brandy. The dairy ban covers whey protein, invert molasses, cane molasses and nonalcoholic beer, per notices on the White House’s Web site.
In addition to the import bans, cheese products were added to a list of products subject to a 50 percent tariff, but not banned outright. Some paper, aluminum, wood, furniture, lighting and other products were also added to the list.
A US official said US President Donald Trump’s pre-existing threat to increase tariffs on Canadian autos from 25 percent to 50 percent on Jan. 1 remained in effect.
The official added that US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer had spoken with Canadian Minister for International Trade Dominic LeBlanc over the past couple of days, and the pair were expected to speak again in the coming days to see if there was an alternative path for the two countries.
In a social media post on Tuesday night, LeBlanc criticized the latest US measures and said he was in contact with Greer regarding a path forward.
“As has been the case for the last 18 months, our first priority remains on protecting and supporting Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses from these unjustified actions,” he wrote.
Ottawa’s retaliatory measures, which in turn provoked Washington’s move on Tuesday night, were designed to put economic and political pressure on Washington, Canadian government officials said.
Those counter-tariffs cover US$20 billion of US goods, with duties ranging from 15 percent to 50 percent across products from steel and furniture to clothing and electronics, and are expected to hit sectors in some competitive states such as Michigan and Ohio, ahead of US midterm elections in November.
While the tariffs affect a small amount of exports compared with total trade between the US and Canada, some analysts worry the standoff could destabilize the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, the free-trade pact that succeeded North American Free Trade Agreement. Together they have underpinned commerce across North America for decades.
“What we are worried about is an escalatory spiral,” said Michael Harvey, executive director of the Canadian Agri-Food Trade Alliance and a member of Carney’s advisory committee on bilateral US economic relations. “But at the same time, we totally understand that the prime minister needs to find areas of leverage.”

16:38:03 UTC

A car racing team whose injured driver was rescued by another competitor after a horrific crash in Shanghai on Saturday has called the organizers “grossly negligent in the safety response” and said it is withdrawing from future events in China.
The car of British driver Ollie Millroy exploded into flames in a GT race at the Shanghai International Circuit. And it was another driver, Loek Hartog, who stopped his car and, armed with a fire extinguisher, pulled Millroy out of the burning wreckage.
“I am still alive tonight, entirely thanks to one man. Loek Hartog stopped instantly with no flag marshals or fire crews in sight and risked his own life to get me out of the car,” Millroy wrote on his Instagram account. “I don’t remember anything between 30 seconds before the crash and 1 hour after it, but I will remember his incredible act of bravery for the rest of my life.”
Photo: AP
Hartog responded with humility to the praise.
“You have nothing to thank me for,” he said. “I wish to live in a world where this would not be considered as bravery — but as the instinct of others, too. I am so grateful to have been at the place I needed to be.”
According to his Instagram account, Millroy sustained six broken ribs, a broken collarbone, a broken hand and a punctured lung. He underwent a four-hour operation in a Shanghai hospital to insert plates and screws into the broken bones. Doctors also inserted a drain line into his abdomen to release gas and fluid leaking from his lung.
Millroy’s team, AAI Motorsports, in a long statement was scathing about the conduct of Chinese organizers.
“The event organizer was grossly negligent in its emergency response and safety rescue arrangements, with serious deficiencies in the rescue response that nearly resulted in a tragedy,” the team said.
“Even more outrageously, during the live broadcast of the accident, event staff failed to verify the on-site situation and hastily reported that the driver had left the wrecked vehicle on his own. In fact, the driver of our No. 91 car was pulled out of the burning car by Loek Hartog, driver of the No. 79 car of Phantom Team who risked his own life to carry out the rescue.”
AAI Motorsports called for a “comprehensive investigation” and public disclosure around the accident, track safety and the emergency response. It said it would withdraw from all GT events in China until its demands were met.
“We will not return until the event organizing committee conducts a comprehensive, independent and transparent investigation into every aspect of the incident, including the failures in the rescue response, and provides our team with an official response.”
In a statement, event organizers apologized for the “incident and the distress” it caused and offered “sincere sympathy” to the injured driver.
The organizers also defended some of the conduct.
“According to our preliminary review, the event’s overall staffing and resources met the standards required for a national-level motorsport event, although there remains room for improvement in detailed operational management,” the organizers wrote.
“We will conduct a further review and investigation into the accident and develop more comprehensive plans to address shortcomings in race organization, support arrangements, emergency response, rescue operations and medical services, they said.”

EDITORIAL: Rental scams, housing woes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:38:01 UTC
01:38:01 KST

The Criminal Investigation Bureau (CIB) is warning people about fake rental listings targeting students and other inexperienced renters as demand rises. Scammers often advertise properties below market rates, claim to be out of town and offer to mail keys via convenience stores for self-guided viewings before directing people to fake delivery Web sites.
A woman who lost NT$55,000 (US$1,746) after responding to a Taipei rental advertised at NT$10,000 a month, the CIB said. She was tricked into transferring NT$30,000 and buying NT$25,000 in game credits.
People should view properties in person, verify landlords’ identities and sign a lease before paying, it said, adding that legitimate delivery services never require bank transfers or online banking for real-name verification.
Scams are not the only challenge renters face. Despite the government doing more to help renters, rents continue to rise and markets remain tight — particularly in urban areas. Taiwan’s median monthly rent was NT$8,600 in the latest Ministry of the Interior data, up 1.2 percent from a year earlier, while median rents were NT$12,500 in Taipei, NT$13,000 in New Taipei City and NT$10,000 in Taoyuan.
The government has expanded its rent-subsidy program to NT$30 billion annually and promoted social-housing and subleasing programs to bring more homes onto the market.
However, the vacancy rate fell to 9.4 percent in the second half of last year from 10.4 percent in the first half, with rates below 8 percent in Taipei, New Taipei City and Hsinchu. Although a lower vacancy rate can reflect homes being brought into use, in high-demand areas it also points to tight markets in which government assistance has yet to make housing substantially cheaper or easier to find.
Greater government involvement could help address the problems. A government-run or certified rental platform could verify landlords’ identities and property ownership while requiring renters to verify their identities as well. With appropriate privacy and appeal safeguards, renters could potentially be flagged for documented histories of serious problems such as repeated non-payment of rent or significant property damage. Such a system could protect both sides while making it much harder for scammers to pose as landlords.
The platform could also allow verified landlords to list vacant units, giving renters a searchable source of legitimate housing and the government a clearer picture of available supply. It could be linked to rent-subsidy programs, allowing eligible students and low-income families to apply through the same system. The government could pay approved subsidies directly to verified landlords, reducing paperwork for tenants while ensuring public funds go toward legitimate rental arrangements.
There are precedents for greater government involvement. Singapore’s Housing and Development Board operates government-backed rental housing and requires some landlords to obtain approval and register tenants. The Netherlands has also moved toward regulation of private rentals, and proposed a national register for landlords and rental properties.
Taiwan could draw on those models while developing a system suited to its own housing market.
Another challenge is Taiwan’s aging housing stock, including buildings that might be vulnerable to earthquakes. Building renewal can be difficult when residents disagree over reconstruction or when elderly or financially vulnerable residents cannot afford renovation costs, higher housing payments or a new mortgage.
The government could consider lowering the resident-approval threshold for major renewal projects when buildings pose significant safety risks, combined with independent safety assessments and appropriate protections for dissenting residents.
Building renewal is not simply a property issue. For many long-term residents, an apartment is their home and largest financial asset. A policy that leaves people choosing between remaining in an unsafe building and taking on housing costs they cannot afford is unlikely to be sustainable.
The government could instead help balance residents’ property rights and financial circumstances with the broader need to ensure that Taiwan’s aging housing stock is safe.
Housing remains a challenge for many people in Taiwan, and greater government involvement could improve access to safe, affordable homes for those who need them most. Making greater progress on building renewal is particularly important. Replacing aging low-rise buildings with taller, modern buildings with elevators would make better use of Taiwan’s limited land, create more housing units and improve accessibility for an aging population.
Overcoming the financial and legal barriers to renewal while protecting vulnerable residents could help address Taiwan’s housing shortage, building-safety concerns and accessibility challenges at the same time.

Iran yesterday said it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the US sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war.
The attacks in and around the vital waterway sent the price of oil surging, with the international Brent crude benchmark breaching US$100 a barrel for the first time since July. The politically sensitive average retail price of diesel fuel in the US hit an all-time high of US$5.94 a gallon.
Iran also said it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by US forces in Jordan.
Photo: US Naval Forces Central Command Public Affairs via AFP
Attacks by both sides since the end of last month have shattered a month of relative calm, with the US and Iran hitting military, shipping and energy assets.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it would sharply escalate their response to any further attacks, and if the enemy struck two or three Iranian targets, Iran would respond by hitting 20.
Iran would soon release maps of a new, much larger off-limits zone at sea that would extend as far as the Arabian Gulf off Chabahar on the far reaches of Iran’s coast near Pakistan, the IRGC said.
The US said they destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, releasing video of ships ablaze before they sank.
The US Central Command called its attacks a response to the IRGC targeting a US Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days.
No Americans were harmed, the US said.
Washington has announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers in retaliation for fire that threatens its warships, and first said it hit three tankers on Saturday.
Iran said it is using new, more capable missiles to attack US ships.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.

Taiwan not on right drone track: ex-official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:38:00 UTC
01:38:00 KST

Taiwan is “not on the right track” to acquire drone capabilities sufficient to deter a Chinese attack, a former top US defense official told the Taipei Security Dialogue yesterday.
The Legislative Yuan-approved NT$240 billion (US$7.62 billion) drone budget act, although a welcome development, was too modest and took too much time to pass, former principal deputy assistant secretary of defense for Indo-Pacific security affairs Jedidiah Royal said.
The budget was significantly lower than what he and many others in Washington had expected, Royal said, adding that it was a “base hit, not a home run.”
Photo: Fang Wei-li, Taipei Times
The security situation in the Taiwan Strait is governed by two clocks: the “threat clock” posed by China’s growing capabilities and increasingly aggressive actions, and the “delivery clock” of Taiwan’s force-building efforts, Royal said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) policy directives that the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) achieve performance benchmarks for invading Taiwan and fighting the US, China’s military drills surrounding Taiwan proper and threatening statements should be taken with utmost seriousness, he said.
These actions do not mean war is inevitable or impose limits on Beijing’s policies, but speak to the urgency and diligence with which China pursues its strategy of achieving military superiority over its neighbors, peers and the international system, Royal said.
To push back the schedule of Xi’s designs on Taiwan, the nation must buy time by matching its delivery clock with China’s threat clock, he said.
From this perspective, Taiwan’s investment in drone capabilities is inadequate, Royal said, adding that the nation made significantly less progress than he expected a year ago.
Drones are a necessary supplement to Taiwan’s military capabilities, he said.
A reliable, networked and responsive system of military drones is a crucial ingredient for Taiwan’s deterrence strategy, he added.
Political strife surrounding the drone and defense funding was regrettable, as it wasted valuable time and opportunity for Taiwan to claim a dominant position in non-Chinese defense supply chains, he said.
Taiwan’s inability to achieve a consensus on a healthy and viable defense budget is a gift to the nation’s competitors in the military drone sector, he added.
Only through increasing military spending and focusing on key systems could Taiwan buy back time it has lost, he said.
Should Taiwan fail to display its resolve to defend itself, it would become more isolated than ever on the international arena, face greater pressure from China and have fewer options for determining its future, Royal said.
Taiwan has made progress in other areas, including increasing the realism of military exercises, simulating realistic scenarios in war games, incorporating new doctrine, delegating command authority and applying innovative technologies, he said.
There is still time for Taiwan’s delivery clock to catch up with China’s threat clock, but that time is rapidly diminishing, he added.

Intensive sports training may affect schoolwork: survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:58 UTC
01:37:58 KST

While a majority of elementary-school students in sports-focused classes feel a strong sense of achievement from their training, about half fall behind in their schoolwork due to frequently missing class for competitions, a survey by the Child Welfare League Foundation found.
The non-profit organization disclosed the survey results after the Executive Yuan on Thursday last week approved amendments to the National Sports Act (國民運動法), which are designed to protect student athletes in elementary schools from high-intensity sports training.
The Executive Yuan also ruled that no new sports-focused classes would be established at the elementary-school level. The existing sports-centered classes would be transformed into sports clubs and community sports to balance learning and sports training, and to prevent students from undertaking high-intensity sports training.
Photo courtesy of the Keelung Department of Education
The survey found that 66.6 percent of respondents had experienced training for more than three hours in a single day during the week, while 18.6 percent underwent extreme training sessions lasting three consecutive hours without a single break.
Some schools did not follow the Regulations Governing the Establishment of Physical Education Classes in Senior High Schools and Below (高級中等以下學校體育班設立辦法), which limits the training to no more than three hours per day during the week, the foundation said.
Of the respondents, 60.6 percent said that they had experienced training for more than three hours in a single day, while 15.6 percent said they had endured training sessions of more than eight hours in a single day.
In addition, 38.7 percent of the student athletes said training had taken up so much of their time that they had little time left to study their academic classes. About 26 percent of respondents said they had undergone sports training during times when they were supposed to be attending academic classes.
Close to 32 percent said that they had taken a leave of absence for more than 16 days in one semester due to sports competitions and training.
Close to 50 percent reported they were at one point having trouble keeping up with schoolwork because of training and sports competitions, the foundation said.
More than half of the respondents said that it was difficult for them to regain energy after training even with sufficient time to rest, while 20.4 percent said that they had undergone operations, undertaken long-term therapies or been hospitalized due to sports-related injuries.
About 27 percent said they were asked to undergo high-intensity training when they were injured.
Regarding the mental health of student athletes, 56.4 percent said they had questioned the meaning of athletic training, while 46.5 percent said that their passion for the sports had gradually faded.
Meanwhile, 47 percent said they were concerned that poor academic performance would hurt their job prospects, while 17.8 percent said they were concerned that they lack other skills and have very limited career options.

Reclaiming the streets: the architects clawing back Europe’s car-centric spaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:57 UTC
01:37:57 KST

In the words of Joni Mitchell, the planners of many urban centers around the world “paved paradise and put up a parking lot.” The European Prize for Urban Public Space tries to show that cities don’t have to be locked in the automotive age for ever.
The prize’s latest shortlist, announced yesterday, highlights architectural projects that convert infrastructure for cars into spaces that help urban dwellers cope with the soaring temperatures of the climate crisis: roundabouts that have become splash pools, thoroughfares turned into green havens, and car parks into gardens.
Among the most eye-catching of the five finalists is Leopold Banchini’s Round About Baths in Logrono, northern Spain. The Swiss architect’s project sought to revive what he called a “lost space” on one of the main thoroughfares in the city, a concrete island with a broken fountain.
Photo: AFP
Inspired by 19th-century public baths, Banchini’s studio used uncut timber panels to build and place a simple structure directly on to the fountain. The existing water basin became a shallow pool, while cast-iron flower pots were repurposed as fire bowls that heat a steam room.
“We have given up so much public space to cars, and if you live in a city with kids you live in constant fear that they will be hit by a passing vehicle,” Banchini said. “It restricts our movement so much that we almost can’t see it anymore.”
Those trying to catch a glimpse of the roundabout baths in situ will be disappointed, however: Banchini’s structure was only erected for a week as part of the city’s Concentrico architecture festival in June last year — inadvertently showing how difficult it is to permanently alter car-centric infrastructure.
“If we had built something more permanent, we would have had to engage with safety concerns”, said Banchini, noting that bathers were only able to access the roundabout via a zebra crossing on one side.
“The rules around car traffic are hard to modify, and any requests usually go all the way up to municipal authorities”, he added. “And politicians are really scared to touch anything with cars, because they fear it will cost them in votes.”
The creators of another Spanish finalist, Barcelona’s Placa de les Glories Catalanes, were more successful: the three thoroughfares that used to bring traffic into the Glories cloverleaf interchange were partly laid underground to make room for open green space.
Antwerp’s Zuidpark is the result of a similar attempt to banish cars from cityscapes. Located in the southern Zuid district of the Belgian city, the 800-meter green space covers an area that used to be taken up by a large free car park.
In 2015, municipal authorities launched a competition for a public space to fill the site.
“I have done projects like this for 25 years, but this park had to be completely different to anything we’ve done before, and that’s because of the climate issue,” said Bart Van Gassen of Tractebel, the urban architecture company that won the commission.
The firm decided to excavate 70 percent of the new park’s area and put in place a 1.5-meter top layer of soil that would allow trees and bushes to grow more rapidly. Two years after its opening in 2024, Zuidpark is lined by double rows of 500 new trees that provide shade during heatwaves.
“The planting is really booming,” said Van Gassen. “We have projects we constructed 10 years ago and the trees are still smaller than here.” He said recent research by the University of Antwerp showed there were significantly lower temperatures inside the park than elsewhere in the city.
Climate breakdown is bringing not just waves of intense heat but also extreme precipitation, which Zuidpark seeks to anticipate with lowered spaces, called “rain gardens”, designed to collect rainwater. Filled with old bluestone blocks unearthed during construction and vegetation that can grow in a wet environment, these wilder spaces have become popular play areas for children.
Still, the cars haven’t vanished altogether: a new car park, no longer free, is now positioned across four storys underneath Zuidpark’s northern and southern wings, and can be accessed from entry points outside the park.
“You could be critical because it’s still a car park with 2,000 spaces that is very close to the city,” said Van Gassen. “If you’re thinking sustainably, maybe it should have been built more outside of the city. But then, maybe if there was no parking we wouldn’t have been able to build a park at all.”
Also on the shortlist for the prize, which is held every two years, are the Leca Green Corridor in northwest Portugal and Peace Park in Vicenza, Italy.
The winner of the award, organized by Spain’s Center de Cultura Contemporania de Barcelona with six other European architecture institutions, will be announced on 15 October.

Attempts to circumvent political opposition and institutional checks can begin a slide toward authoritarianism, even when presented as short-term solutions to gridlock. While that might solve problems in the short term, it inevitably evolves into a system that serves the rulers and the powerfully connected at the expense of the rights of regular folks. President William Lai (賴清德) on Tuesday met with a Japanese cross-party parliamentary group, with both sides calling for closer Taiwan-Japan cooperation, the Presidential Office said yesterday.
During the meeting with the Diet Members’ Association for Peace and Stability in the Taiwan Strait, Lai said that he believed the group would would draw greater attention in the Diet to issues concerning the Taiwan Strait and help advance former Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe’s vision of a free and open Indo-Pacific.
China’s continued military exercises, “gray zone” tactics and transnational repression pose a compound threat to Taiwan and undermine regional security, Lai said, urging Japan and other democracies to join Taiwan in enhancing their defense and deterrence capabilities to safeguard democracy, peace and prosperity.
Photo courtesy of the Presidential Office
Taiwan’s defense spending has reached 3 percent of GDP this year and would remain above that level next year, with spending expected to reach 5 percent by 2030, he said.
Taiwan is also working to bolster its defense industry and boost its artificial intelligence and drone capabilities, he said, adding that the nation is developing a resilient, all-out national defense system.
Lai said he looked forward to deepening Taiwan-Japan cooperation on national strategy, economic and trade security, and high-tech industries.
The delegation was led by Haruo Kitamura, a member of the Japanese House of Councilors from the Conservative Party of Japan.
The delegation’s visit aimed to turn the Taiwan-Japan friendship into concrete action and continue moving bilateral relations forward, Kitamura said.
Taiwan had demonstrated its friendship with Japan by sending disaster-relief teams and raising ¥25 billion (US$162.73 million) in donations after the 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, Kitamura said.
If Taiwan faces a crisis, Japan would do everything in its power to stand with the nation, he said, adding that Taiwan and Japan must show their determination to support and defend friends in times of need.
Kitamura said he would promote Japanese versions of the US’ Taiwan Travel Act and Taiwan Relations Act, facilitate senior government exchanges and advance defense cooperation.
He also said he would rally like-minded lawmakers to lobby the Japanese government for improved Taiwan-Japan ties and peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait.
Separately, Japanese lawmaker Seki Hei, also known by his Chinese name Shi Ping (石平), yesterday said that he supports restoring diplomatic relations between Taiwan and Japan and establishing an alliance, including a trilateral alliance with the US.
Speaking at the Taiwan-Japan Foreign Affairs and Defense Forum in Taipei, Shih said that the US-Japan alliance is important to Japan and regional peace, but insufficient to safeguard peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait and across East and Southeast Asia.
“The US-Japan alliance is missing a crucial leg, and that leg is Taiwan,” Shih said, adding that an ideal alliance would bring the US, Japan and Taiwan together to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).
Shih said he would promote a Japanese version of the Taiwan Relations Act to bolster bilateral cooperation.
He also urged Taiwan and Japan to abandon any illusions about the CCP and jointly defend freedom and shared values, adding that “any compromise with the Chinese Communist Party will lead to our own destruction.”

01:37:56 KST

Drones are widely recognized as a critical weapons technology of the future. Because of this, the pro-China Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) appear to be obstructing their development. One approach to handling this obstruction is to circumvent it by building robust drone capabilities across a wide swathe of the population. Taiwan is doing just that, but more is needed.
The Penghu County Government on Monday said it was testing flying drones on routes from Magong City (馬公), the county seat, to Jibei Island (吉貝嶼). Because all of the inhabited islands lie within 40km of Magong, drones can easily reach them. The drone program, which may include uncrewed sea vessels, is aimed at offering Penghu residents daily necessities. Whether intentional or not, the program mimics the use of drones to provision front line troops and residents in occupied areas, a key function of drones.
Similarly, the Taipei Times reported this week that healthcare providers on the east coast are building a delivery network for medical goods using drones. Authorities held a live demonstration of a medical drone flight designed to service remote mountain communities. Drones for both routine delivery of medicines and emergency treatments are being studied. The program was inspired in part by the situation after the April 2024 earthquake in Hualien, which saw many mountain communities cut off from medical services.
Photo: AFP
Torrential rains, typhoons and earthquakes can easily cut off services to remote communities and offshore islands. In wartime islands are likely to be without transportation as ferries and aircraft are mobilized for wartime service, and roads to remote communities blocked. It is easy to see how an existing integrated drone-based medical delivery system could be repurposed for wartime use.
Tainan city and the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCIST) in December last year participated in a demonstration of drones in disaster response. The wartime applications of such a system are obvious.
Taiwan Water Corp is already using drones to monitor water quality. It presently operates 11 drones and plans to acquire 10 more by the year’s end. It also uses an unmanned boat to monitor water quality in an artificial lake in Nantou County. Since water facilities will surely be targeted in a Chinese invasion scenario, these are key technology capabilities.
The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI), long at the forefront of technology development, has supported a range of civilian drone applications with obvious wartime uses. For example, it developed a drone-based inspection system for assessing damage to bridges and other structures for the high speed rail. It has also developed an automated drone-surveillance system for police use. Both of these have clear wartime applications.
Though at present these systems are technology demonstrations, the existence of local and government agency drone initiatives suggests how the antics of the pro-China parties in the legislature can be circumvented: encourage local governments to develop local drone initiatives that move beyond technology demonstration to actual implementation across a wide range of activities that will be useful in an invasion scenario. The purpose of such programs is to build drone-based capabilities for use in wartime and create robust expertise in drone use at the local level. For areas controlled by pro-Taiwan politicians from the pan-Green parties, this should be considered mandatory.
Such programs could include search and rescue operations, emergency response and border surveillance. Recall that “borders” in Taiwan are watery and have already been penetrated by operatives of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) using small craft. Drone patrols by local governments would be an ideal response, especially if they are rhetorically positioned as safety patrols. Drone-based monitoring of cables, bridges, roads, dikes, wells and other vital infrastructure should be widely implemented across the country.
Photo courtesy of the Hengshan Police Station
Medical deliveries and provisioning of daily necessities should be extended across all the nation’s remote areas and all of its associated islands. In wartime, the skills used to deliver to remote areas and islands will come in handy delivering to friendly areas surrounded by enemy-occupied areas, which will functionally be “islands” and “remote areas.” Even programs that track and map vegetation, wildlife and agriculture would be useful in wartime. Taiwan is already thinking about or implementing some of these programs, but local governments need to start aggressively funding and expanding them.
Note that many of these programs could be implemented on a volunteer basis using Taiwan’s plentiful pool of senior volunteers. Numerous private organizations already offer drone training, as do higher education institutions, since operating drones weighing 2kg or more requires a license. Even schools are now offering summer programs. Local governments should be pushing harder to fund and expand these organizations.
Taiwan wants to turn out 100,000 drones a month by the end of the decade. Wartime assaults will involve tens of thousands of drones on both sides. Ukraine has 80,000 personnel involved in its drone programs, with an estimated 25-40,000 pilots. By contrast, even the well-known Kuma Academy’s introductory course only has capacity for 75 civilian trainees per month, roughly 900 people a year, according to a recent Guardian article.
Taiwan’s civilian drone programs are thus woefully undersupported and underproductive, the more so when the inevitable losses due to combat and psychological trauma in an invasion are considered. They are also out of sync with Taiwan’s potential drone output, even if a large chunk of that is exported as the government plans. Demand for drone operators is going to massively outstrip supply. Taiwan does not have the luxury of trading space for time to implement drone operator training as Ukraine does. It has to enter the war with a large pool of drone operators already well-trained and experienced.
Another reason to get local governments to operate robust drone programs is decentralization. In a Taiwan invasion scenario central government control is going to be spotty and focused on making sure the military responds, especially early in the invasion. The more local governments can cultivate civil defense capabilities, the better off Taiwan will be, and the more Taipei can focus on the national situation. Moreover, independent drone capabilities integrated with local government agencies and officials will also be useful if local governments are cut off from Taipei.
Finally, massively expanding local government and government agency drone operations will force the pro-China parties in the legislature to face the politically unpalatable choices of either attempting to suppress local drone training programs — affecting local voters and displaying their pro-China positions for all to see — or letting drone programs flourish and angering their friends across the Strait. It will also be good for Taiwan and the pro-Taiwan parties to get more locals engaged with drones and civil defense.
If local drone production ramps up, drone pilot production must follow. Local governments need to vastly expand their investment in local drone training and applications. Time may be running out.

The US now learns what Taiwan knew before
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:55 UTC
01:37:55 KST

Taiwan does not need a CIA deputy director to explain that Beijing treats commerce as a battlefield. It has been living that lesson for decades, watching its chip designers get poached, its retired officers get recruited for cash, and its companies get pressured to choose between the Chinese market and their own government’s security priorities. What changed this month is that Washington finally said the quiet part out loud.
CIA Deputy Director Michael Ellis told a Washington audience that China’s threat to the US is now “fundamentally different,” because the competition is economic, not military, and that a Chinese company cannot be treated as genuinely private when the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) can absorb or direct it at will.
This is not a new insight in Taipei. It is the working assumption behind every export control on advanced lithography equipment, every debate in the Legislative Yuan about Chinese investment in the semiconductor supply chain, and every prosecution of a retired general caught building a spy network for a bowl of noodles and a modest stipend. Taiwan has spent 30 years treating Chinese capital as a potential delivery mechanism for state power. Washington is only now updating its assumptions to match the country Taiwan has always had to live next to.
The same week Ellis spoke, federal agents in Detroit charged a Chinese national, Zeng Weiheng, with lying about why he had spent 20 minutes photographing cargo planes at O’Hare International Airport. Zeng was not a trained intelligence officer. He was a college student in Canada, allegedly paid by a contact he believed was tied to the CCP to photograph specific aircraft and tail numbers, a task cheap enough and deniable enough that losing him cost Beijing nothing.
Taiwan’s own counterintelligence record is full of Zengs: low-ranking, financially motivated, recruited through family ties or business contacts and disposable by design. The scale is different, the method is not. What the O’Hare case demonstrates on US soil, Taiwanese security services have been documenting for a generation, usually with far less international attention.
The useful thing about Washington’s shift is not that it discovered anything new. It is that it removed a piece of cover that Beijing-friendly voices in Taiwan have relied on for years: the argument that treating cross-strait economic integration as a security risk is paranoid, protectionist or an overreaction driven by Taipei’s politics.
If the CIA argues publicly that a Chinese semiconductor firm cannot be assumed independent of the CCP, then the same logic applies with more force, not less, to a Chinese-linked investment vehicle courting a Taiwanese supplier or to political factions here who insist that deeper economic ties with China are merely business. That argument was always thin; it just got a lot thinner.
None of this should be read as vindication for its own sake. The point of Washington catching up is not that Taipei gets to say it told you so, although it would be entitled to. The point is that shared threat assessment is the precondition for shared policy, on export controls, on investment screening, on the defense package still stalled in the legislature by parties more interested in denying the threat than countering it.
Taiwan has spent years explaining what it is like to share a border with an authoritarian state that does not recognize the line between its companies and its intelligence services. It is a strange kind of relief to watch Washington arrive, slightly out of breath, at the same conclusion.

MOL warns foodpanda over docking couriers’ pay for late deliveries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:55 UTC
01:37:55 KST

Delivery platform Foodpanda could face fines up to NT$100,000 per affected worker for illegally docking couriers’ pay for late deliveries based on unilaterally imposed time limits, the Ministry of Labor (MOL) said yesterday.
At multiple recent meetings with local labor officials, the ministry said that such practices by Foodpanda contravene the Delivery Workers’ Rights Protection and Delivery Platform Management Act (外送員權益保障及外送平臺管理法), the ministry said in a statement.
Local labor bureaus can impose fines ranging from NT$20,000 to NT$100,000 per affected courier once they determine the validity of the complaints filed by workers, said Wang Hou-wei (王厚偉), director-general of the ministry’s Department of Labor Relations.
Photo: Chiu Chiao-jen, Taipei Times
Wang did not disclose how many complaints had been filed with local authorities, citing a lack of complete data, but said that all reported cases involved Foodpanda.
Delivery couriers reported facing pay deductions for exceeding estimated delivery times by as little as one to five minutes, calling the policy “unfair” due to “numerous unforeseen and uncontrollable factors on the road,” Wang said.
When delivery delays occur, platforms should look into the causes and handle them via proper mechanisms instead of making unilateral pay deductions, the ministry said.
“Unlawful practices would absolutely not be tolerated,” it added.
Under the law, which came into force on July 21, platforms must pay riders based on the exact time a delivery takes, using a rate of 1.25 times the minimum wage, and no order can pay less than NT$45.
Earlier yesterday, the National Delivery Industrial Union and two other unions issued a joint statement accusing Foodpanda of “maliciously scapegoating delivery workers for order delays” as a pretext for unlawfully docking their pay.
Separately, the Preparatory Committee for the Taiwan Federation of Delivery Industrial Unions said that couriers frequently encounter delays caused by factors beyond their control.
Such situations include understaffed retail stores, long peak-hour restaurant waits, GPS and system glitches, unreachable customers or incorrect delivery addresses, as well as traffic congestion, road closures and severe weather, it said.
It called on couriers to submit formal complaints to local labor departments if they experience illegal pay deductions.
In response, Emma Kuo (郭昕宜), Foodpanda’s director of public affairs and public relations, told reporters that the platform has never refused to disburse riders’ pay due to delivery delays.
The company only asked delivery couriers to clarify unusually long trips, Kuo said, adding that full pay is disbursed as long as a valid explanation is provided.
Kuo made the remarks yesterday afternoon at a news conference announcing a new commercial partner, reports by local Chinese-language media said.

Seyit Şamil Kurt
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The foreign ministers of Türkiye, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates on Wednesday welcomed the UK government's decision to ban imports of goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory and restrict services linked to such settlements.
In a joint statement, the ministers expressed hope that the decision would help mobilize the international community to take similar action in line with international law and hold accountable settlement organizations and individuals engaged in illegal settlement activities.
They also welcomed a joint statement on the two-state solution issued by the foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden and the UK.
The 12 countries confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions and/or support European restrictions on trade in goods with settlements that are illegal under international law, or to actively consider these and other measures in accordance with their respective national procedures.
The ministers of the eight countries urged the international community to build on these steps and adopt concrete measures to end activities that support or sustain illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory.
They said the announced measures were in line with international law and relevant UN resolutions, including UN Security Council Resolution 2334 and the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion of July 19, 2024.
The statement cited the obligation of all states not to recognize as legal the situation arising from Israel's unlawful occupation of the Palestinian territory and not to provide aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by the occupation.
The ministers reiterated their call for Israel to rescind all measures taken in connection with settlement activities, as well as other measures aimed at altering the geographic and demographic character of the occupied Palestinian territory.
They also stressed that Gaza is an integral part of the occupied Palestinian territory and called for the "full and immediate implementation" of US President Donald Trump's Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict.
The ministers said the plan should be implemented to ensure security and stability, address the humanitarian situation, facilitate reconstruction and recovery, and lay the foundations for lasting peace.
They reaffirmed that "the only viable path" to achieving a just, lasting and comprehensive peace is the implementation of the two-state solution through the establishment of an independent, sovereign, contiguous and viable Palestinian state based on the June 4, 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

The countries said Israel's actions in the West Bank were undermining prospects for a two-state solution and stressed the need to preserve the possibility of establishing a Palestinian state.
Israel subsequently announced that it would close the UK's consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, which serves Palestinians, in response to the measures.

Who controls the data controls the future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:52 UTC
01:37:52 KST

In March, Iranian drones targeted three Amazon Web Services (AWS) facilities in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), striking two directly and almost hitting the third. It was the first time a commercial data center had been a military target, yet almost nobody outside specialist circles noticed. They should have. The servers holding a country’s data, and the chips running the artificial intelligence (AI) models on which its economy increasingly leans, are no longer background infrastructure. They are as strategic as ports or power grids — and just as exposed.
For most of the past decade, data was something companies mined, and AI was something companies sold — regulated at the margins through privacy law, if they were regulated at all. This framing no longer works. AI now sits inside finance, defense, healthcare and public administration, and it runs on two things most governments do not actually control: the data that train it and the compute that processes it. Countries that ignore this would find their futures being decided in boardrooms where they have no seat.
Many governments have taken note. Global spending on “sovereign AI” would reportedly surpass US$100 billion this year. Over the past few months, Canada, France, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have rolled out national compute funds and GPU allocations. The EU has gone further, treating sovereign AI infrastructure almost as doctrine, which has meant backing Gaia-X to build out European data infrastructure and financing projects such as Mistral AI’s new data center outside Paris.
Illustration: Mountain People
On paper, this looks like sensible diversification away from a handful of US and Chinese firms. In practice, it risks creating something more brittle: a patchwork of national fortresses, each self-sufficient and none capable of talking to the others. Part of the problem is that “AI sovereignty” encompasses at least three things, and most governments are only working on one.
Data residency — keeping citizens’ data within national borders — is the oldest of the three, the easiest to legislate, and the one most policy actually addresses. Compute sovereignty — who owns the chips and data centers doing the processing — is more difficult: a country can wall off its data, but it loses control if those data are processed on infrastructure someone else owns. Governance sovereignty — the ability to set the rules AI systems have to follow, rather than importing whatever standard the country hosting the dominant developers happens to set — is the one almost nobody talks about.
A fragmented regulatory landscape does not help any of this. Roughly 90 countries have some kind of national AI strategy; at least 33 have passed binding legislation. The approaches often clash. The EU’s AI Act, whose main provisions became applicable last month, carries penalties of up to 35 million euros (US$40.6 million) or 7 percent of the offender’s global annual turnover. The US’ AI Action Plan takes the opposite approach, treating deregulation itself as a competitive edge. China’s Global AI Governance Action Plan offers cooperation on AI governance with developing economies, but on Chinese terms.
The Council of Europe’s Framework Convention on AI — the first binding international AI treaty — represents real progress, but its enforcement is modest next to the scale of what it is meant to govern. Coordination beyond that has barely started. The UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI has warned of a “race to the bottom,” with jurisdictions competing to offer the most permissive rules rather than the safest ones. Companies running high-risk AI deployments are already shopping for the softest jurisdiction.
Genuine AI sovereignty requires four things, none of which is complicated in concept. Start by putting AI data infrastructure in the same legal category as power grids, with someone clearly on the hook for physical and digital security.
Next, countries building sovereign compute need shared interoperability standards, not just national champions — Gaia-X’s work on data portability is a useful template. A hospital in Lagos or a ministry in Warsaw ought to be able to verify that a system meets baseline safety requirements, regardless of whose infrastructure it is running on.
Oversight needs teeth: audit rights, mandatory incident reporting, and licensing for the handful of frontier models capable of touching critical infrastructure or financial stability. These models should be treated more like nuclear material than ordinary software.
The world needs a real mechanism to stop AI sovereignty from turning into just another axis of inequality. That US$100 billion investment in sovereign compute is happening almost entirely in rich countries. Pooled regional compute, financed and governed jointly by smaller countries, would deliver better results than each of them trying to go it alone.
None of this requires a grand global treaty. The components of a governance framework — including the EU AI Act, the Council of Europe convention, Gaia-X, and the UN’s scientific panel — already exist. The scaffolding connecting them is missing, and building that takes deliberate work. Every year it is delayed, the infrastructure gets bigger and harder to reconfigure. Nobody pouring billions of dollars into data centers and GPUs is waiting around for governance to catch up.
The strikes on those AWS facilities in the Gulf sent a message (whether or not anyone intended it): The infrastructure underpinning a growing share of consequential decisions — who gets a loan, which patients get flagged for treatment, which factories keep running — sits in buildings most governments do not control and cannot fully protect. Data sovereignty, compute sovereignty and governance sovereignty are not conference-room abstractions. They are the precondition for a future shaped by countries’ own citizens — not whoever happens to own the servers.

Kenyan start-up makes limbs to sign for deaf kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:50 UTC
01:37:50 KST

In a school for the deaf in Kenya, children signed their excitement as a team demonstrated how a robotic arm could revolutionize their studies.
About 300,000 children in the east African nation have a hearing impairment, according to the Kenya Society for Deaf Children, but just 20,000 were enrolled in schools as of 2024.
Kenyan start-up ZeroBionic, cofounded by 22-year-old Norah Kimathi, hopes to tackle some of the educational difficulties they face.
Photo: AFP
It has built a mechanical hand that can translate a teachers’ voice into sign language in real time, allowing deaf children to learn alongside their hearing counterparts.
For the pupils at the Kasarani Treeside Secondary School for the Deaf in Nairobi, there is another element of the technology that is even more promising.
The robotic arms are trialed by deaf teachers to record and store signs using a bodysuit, which ZeroBionic imported for the task.
In the process, they are building a database of technical terms — drawing on English, American and Kenyan signs — that is helping to expand the language and make it easier for deaf children to learn and communicate.
“The biggest challenge we faced actually was in Africa we don’t have a standardized African sign language dataset,” Kimathi said at the company’s tiny lab in Nairobi.
“No one else had built this on the continent... We had to start from scratch,” she said.
Many deaf children in Kenya learn a patchwork of makeshift signs, and the local dialect lacks many technical terms used to teach subjects like math and biology.
Sharon Mumbe, 19, one of the pupils at the deaf school, said it gives her “hope for the future.”
“I’ll be able to understand different concepts better,” she said.
Numerous prototype limbs litter the surfaces in Kimathi’s lab.
The team works with Africa One, a humanoid robot they built, to refine and expand the signs their mechanical arms are able to produce.
Everything has been designed and built in-house, using recycled materials to reduce costs and environmental impact, produced using 3D printers that thump away constantly in the background. Each hand costs about US$350 and can last for up to two years. They are already in 78 schools across Kenya.
They boast a 92 percent speech-to-sign accuracy rate and Kimathi said the results have made all the long hours in the lab worthwhile.
“We know we’re going to put a smile on someone else’s face,” she said.

Thailand investigates after Briton dies from penis enlargement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:50 UTC

Thai authorities yesterday said they are investigating a Bangkok clinic where a Nigerian-born British businessman and influencer underwent a penis enlargement procedure that led to his death.
A coroner in London last month ruled that the March 6 death of Igho Ubiribo, 43, in the Thai capital was caused by the hyaluronic acid injection he received hours earlier.
The case has reignited debate about medical tourism, with Thailand a leading destination for visitors from abroad seeking healthcare, including aesthetic procedures.
Photo: AFP
Ubiribo, reportedly known as “Tiny” and “Ego,” had 185,000 followers on Instagram, regularly posting pictures with his wife, Daniella Simba Allen, enjoying a luxury lifestyle.
The Thai Ministry of Public Health ordered an investigation into his death and officials on Monday visited the central Bangkok clinic where Ubiribo was treated.
Authorities are looking into whether it holds a valid license and followed health and safety protocols, a health ministry official said.
He was having a massage after receiving the filler when he complained of chest pains and collapsed, according to a report last month from the British coroner, which formally determines cause of death.
He was taken by ambulance to hospital, suspected of having a pulmonary embolism, but lost consciousness before he could have a computed tomography scan.
Medics tried to resuscitate him for more than 100 minutes, but he was declared dead around 1am.
“Post-mortem examination and toxicology determined the cause of death to be due to the hyaluronic acid injection,” the report said.
Senior Bangkok police official Utit Soodjai told AFP his officers were also investigating.
“When it comes to medical procedures, we advocate for the highest level of caution,” Thai Minister of Public Health Pattana Promphat told reporters.
The probe was intended “to ensure fairness for everyone and to reassure both local and international patients that they are receiving safe, high-standard and valuable care in Thailand,” he added in a statement.
The clinic’s managers said Ubiribo had been a regular patient since 2024 and had undergone five penile enlargement injections, according to the health ministry.
The first four procedures took place in 2024 and last year, while on his fifth visit on March 5 he received 40 milliliters of filler.
The doctor had recommended splitting the procedure into two sessions, but Ubiribo requested that the entire amount be injected in one session, clinic management told investigators.
Hyaluronic acid fillers are widely used in aesthetic medicine, considered minimally invasive and relatively low risk.

Global notebook shipments tipped to drop 8%, MIC says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:48 UTC
01:37:48 KST

Global notebook computer shipments are expected to fall 8 percent year-on-year to 167.9 million units this year, dragged by weak demand, high component prices and supply constraints, the Market Intelligence and Consulting Institute (MIC) said on Tuesday.
Next year, shipments are expected to decline by a further 4.7 percent to 160 million units as higher retail prices weigh on consumption, MIC deputy director-general Edward Lin (林柏齊) told a news conference in Taipei.
The downtrend is expected to extend into 2028, with replacement demand unlikely to recover before supplies of key components rebound and costs decline, Lin said.
Photo: AFP
Surging demand for artificial intelligence (AI) servers has led to a broader tight supply of standard DRAM and high-bandwidth memory chips, high-end multilayer ceramic capacitors, advanced microscopic bridge substrates and build-up films, high-end copper-clad laminates and T-glass, which is likely to persist until 2028, he said.
However, NAND flash memory shortages could ease by the end of next year, he added.
MIC expects wider adoption of AI PCs in 2028, with penetration rate projected to reach 76.1 percent, from 54.1 percent projected for this year and 66.3 percent next year, Lin said.
The next AI PC opening is in devices that run meaningful agentic workloads locally, he said.
Unlike basic AI assistants, the systems can handle workflows and execute tasks, requiring greater computing power and memory, he added.
A trend among PC makers to cut memory specifications to offset rising costs in the past year is likely a short-term response rather than a lasting strategy, Lin said.
The measure can help maintain prices, but could weaken the user experience for AI, he said.
As AI shifts from an optional feature to an expected capability, products with overly compromised specifications could lose competitiveness, he added.

Book review: The Cold War’s hidden hands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:45 UTC
01:37:45 KST

Alfred McCoy has been a thorn in the side of the CIA at the very least since 1972, when he published The Politics of Heroin in Southeast Asia, a book the agency tried — and failed — to kill.
Now, with his latest, The Cold War on Five Continents, McCoy continues to hammer the CIA for its crimes of the Cold War, including anti-democratic political assassinations, coups and other covert foreign interventions. At the same time, he also presents a startlingly novel analysis of the Cold War itself — this is most of the book, and it’s great — and a less good prediction for the advent of a new Cold War.
Taiwan is mentioned only a few times in the book, but McCoy’s grand narrative of the late 20th century has big implications for the country. It allows us to consider the nation’s post-World War II history against broader trends, and shows this history to be less unique than is often assumed.
McCoy’s theory of the Cold War goes something like this. The 40 or so years following World War II combined two defining historical moments, the Cold War and the era of decolonization. These overlapped almost perfectly.
As scores of new nations stepped out from under the yolk of colonialism to be born in Asia, the Americas, Africa and Eastern Europe, two major powers — the Western liberal bloc led by the USA and the Communist bloc led by the USSR — vyed to bring them into their respective folds. It was a geopolitical competition for influence, and the superpowers played it by carving up the globe.
But with the horrors of World War II fresh in the world memory, there was little appetite for “hot war.” There were a few exceptions of course — Korea and Vietnam for the US, Afghanistan for the USSR.
But on the whole, the superpowers preferred covert operations — espionage, insurgencies and secret wars. (Think: Laos, Angola, Congo, Nicaragua). These types of interventions were much cheaper, didn’t kill off hometown boys and there was no moral backlash as long as the news stayed in the back pages.
The chaotic milieu of new nations — which especially from the late 1940s to the 1960s mixed nationalists, democrats, communists and warlords — was perfect for the deployment of covert operatives, or spies.
McCoy calls these “men on the spot,” an archetype he models on 19th century solo agents like T.E. Lawrence, or “Lawrence of Arabia,” and James Brooke, the “White Raja of Sarawak.” One could also imagine Joseph Conrad’s Colonel Kurtz or Lord Jim.
Such men were parachuted into local, factional conflicts and, based on their personal wiles, often managed to win the day for one empire or another.
Characterizing these men on the spot as “ambitious, cunning and often amoral,” McCoy identifies around three dozen such Cold War operatives, from French military officer Roger Trinquier, who pioneered methods of counter-insurgency in Indochina in the late 1940s, to US marine Oliver North, who ended his career at the center of the Iran-Contra scandal in the 1980s.
Such covert actors often fueled what were essentially civil wars — though in the new Cold War terminology, they were labeled anti-communist or anti-imperialist insurgencies--with arms, cash and secret directives from Washington or Moscow.
The pity here is that each of McCoy’s spy stories offers a potential thriller, but he is so ploddingly deadpan in the telling. Mainly, we are left with a history lesson.
As the superpowers squared off throughout the third world, McCoy argues that the US found it much easier to achieve its political goals by backing “absolute monarchies, dictatorships and juntas,” as long as they were reliably pro-Western.
The pattern was perhaps predicted by US president Franklin D Roosevelte, who, after having backed Nicaraguan dictator Anastasio Somoza Garcia in 1939, is supposed to have said, “He may be a son of a bitch, but at least he’s our son of a bitch.”
For Washington, autocrats were often easier to deal with. Democracies, by comparison, were messier and far less predictable.
So the US, in large part through the CIA, funded dictators who ruled with iron fists, jailed and killed their political opponents and in many cases operated death squads. Cumulative death tolls ran up into the millions.
Many of these Cold War autocracies however came to an end in the late 1980s and early 1990s. As the Berlin Wall came down and the Soviet Union split apart, a series of “people power” revolutions sprung up across the globe, spurring their downfall. The US Congress also became far less tolerant of anti-democratic rulers and the CIA’s dirty tricks.
In this new climate, repressive regimes from the Philippines to Eastern Europe suddenly fell apart. With varying degrees of success, they were replaced by democracies.
These overarching trends were geographically dispersed and remarkable in their variety. The way McCoy weaves them together is extraordinary.
Taiwan’s Cold War history is not specifically described, but it fits McCoy’s pattern almost perfectly. (McCoy probably found Taiwan less interesting, as the country didn’t contain rival superpower proxies fighting it out.)
Following Taiwan’s decolonization from Japan at the end of World War II, the US backed an authoritarian ruler Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石). Then Washington stuck with his regime through 38 years of martial law, largely turning a blind eye to the human rights abuses of the White Terror.
Taiwan’s martial law came to an end in 1987 — right at the tail end of the Cold War and marking the twilight of what some would call the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) colonization of the country. Domestic democracy movements were key in pushing this change.
Viewed in McCoy’s framework, it becomes easy to place Chiang alongside other US-supported dictators like Mobotu in the Congo (then called Zaire), Chilean president Augusto Pinochet, Philippines president Ferdinand Marcos and Indonesia’s General Suharto.
It also reminds us that Taiwan’s democratic era arrived in the same wave with the Philippines’ People Power Revolution (1988), the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989), and the end of apartheid in South Africa (1994).
Where McCoy directly addresses Taiwan is in looking towards a “New Cold War.” Here, he sets it alongside Ukraine and Gaza, but it is hard to see how these conflict zones fit his classic pattern. Though Taiwan and Ukraine can be considered as part of great power competitions, Gaza is a harder fit. If anything, what these places have in common is that they are resisting the annexation of aggressors who are not only intent on taking their territory, but on obliterating their cultural identity as well.
No matter where one sits on the political spectrum and who one blames for the ongoing struggles between the executive and legislative branches or the latest food scandal, there has been noticeable frustration with the way democratic institutions are functioning. Attempts to circumvent political opposition and institutional checks can begin a slide toward authoritarianism, even when presented as short-term solutions to gridlock. While that might solve problems in the short term, it inevitably evolves into a system that serves the rulers and the powerfully connected at the expense of the rights of regular folks. One interesting lens to examine the

They were not simply trying to sell programs. They were trying to change an idea of Taiwan. Caring for migrant care workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:37:44 UTC
01:37:44 KST

Taiwan has nearly 1 million people in need of long-term care, yet the proportion of people with severe disabilities receiving long-term care benefits has been declining year by year. The gap is not being filled by the government, but by more than 200,000 live-in migrant care workers who are not covered by the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法).
Wages are rising in the home countries of most of Taiwan’s care workers, such as Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam. Meanwhile, Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong are competing to attract those workers. The question is not whether families can afford carers, but whether any will still be willing to move to Taiwan three years from now.
The Ministry of Labor’s Diversified Companion Care Service Pilot Program is a step in the right direction. Under the program — which was launched last year — nonprofit organizations hire care workers who are covered by the Labor Standards Act. After 90 hours of training, they provide in-home services in shifts of at least two hours, demonstrating that migrant workers do not have to be tied to a single household to work with dignity.
However, with just 13 participating organizations and 41 foreign care workers, the program is nowhere near large enough to meet the demands of even a single district of Taipei.
There are three keys to solving the problem:
First, care services should be a part of long-term care benefits. Under the diversified companion-care system, services running at NT$300 to NT$400 per hour are difficult for struggling families to afford.
If the services provided by migrant domestic care workers for people with severe disabilities were incorporated into the long-term care benefits system — with partial subsidies based on the individual’s level of disability and the household’s financial circumstances — that could ease the burden on families, and improve migrant workers’ pay and access to days off.
The long-term care budget for this year has already exceeded NT$100 billion, yet people with severe disabilities have among the lowest takeup rates. Redirecting funding toward those who need it most should be at the heart of long-term care policy.
Second, talent pools and career pathways must be built up. The system treats migrant workers as disposable labor: When their work permits end, one group is replaced by another and the process starts over. Japan, by contrast, allows skilled care workers pathways to extend their work visas and transition to other forms of residency. Taiwan should allow trained foreign care workers who have accumulated experience to move into institutional care, advance to supervisory positions and ultimately qualify for long-term residency.
Third, cultivate differentiated pathways rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.
People with mild or moderate care needs could receive services through institutional staffing agencies, using multiple caregivers working in shifts and flexible hours. For people with severe or profound disabilities, one-on-one care could be retained, but wages should be supported through long-term care benefits, with mandatory respite care shift rotations implemented.
Neither employers nor the government wants to shoulder the additional costs, but the cost of care does not disappear simply because no one is willing to bear it; it is merely shifted onto people with disabilities, the careers of family members and the years of migrant workers’ lives.
Taiwan is using the silence of more than 200,000 foreign care workers to subsidize a society that refuses to confront the true cost of care.
As Long-Term Care 2.0 enters its 10th year, migrant domestic care workers have been waiting outside the system for two decades. The overdue bill for care is one the government must start facing up to.
Huang Jin-shun is a former Presidential Office national policy adviser and an honorary president of the Federation of Taiwan Pharmacists’ Associations.
