Die EU will öffentliche Aufträge zu Herzstück ihrer neuen Industriepolitik machen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:25:40 UTC
01:25:40 KST

The proposal also spells out how public authorities can favor EU goods and services — a power that they enjoy under existing rules but rarely use. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
BRÜSSEL - Die EU will die Vergabe öffentlicher Aufträge zu einem wichtigen Instrument ihrer neuen Industriepolitik machen. Hunderte Milliarden Euro für Infrastruktur, Schulen, Energie oder das Gesundheitswesen sollen bevorzugt an Unternehmen aus dem Binnenmarkt gehen.
Dazu stellte die EU am Mittwoch ihren Public Procurement Act (PPA) vor, das Gesetz über das öffentliche Beschaffungswesen. Die Kommission folgt damit einer der Empfehlungen des Draghi-Reports für eine bessere Wettbewerbsfähigkeit.
Es geht um riesige Summen. Mit einem Volumen von rund 2,5 Billionen Euro pro Jahr machen öffentliche Aufträge knapp 15 Prozent des BIP der EU aus. Davon fallen etwa 600 Milliarden Euro unter die neuen Vorschriften, sagte Industriekommissar Stéphane Séjourné.
Advertisement
„Es handelt sich um öffentliches Geld, das auch unseren gemeinsamen Zielen dienen muss“, sagte der französische Kommissar. „Das entspricht einem jährlichen Konjunkturprogramm und ist, gemessen an den Ausgaben, etwa vier- bis fünfmal so hoch wie der EU-Haushalt.“
Die Kommission verspricht zudem jährliche Kosteneinsparungen von 650 Millionen Euro für die Behörden, da drei Richtlinien und zwei Dutzend kleinere Gesetze zusammengefasst werden. Dies soll Bürokratie abbauen.
Um die Beschaffung zur Stärkung der europäischen Industrie zu nutzen, setzt die EU-Exekutive nicht mehr auf den Preis allein. Auch die „Qualität“ soll Hauptkriterium bei der Vergabe öffentlicher Aufträge werden. Qualitätskriterien erhalten ein Gewicht von mindestens 30 Prozent, bei arbeitsintensiven Aufträgen auch bis zu 50 Prozent. Zur Qualität zählen auch die Themen Umwelt, Soziales, Innovation, Sicherheit und Resilienz.
Wenn die Qualität durch technische Spezifikationen definiert ist, können Behörden Aufträge weiter allein nach dem Preis vergeben. Öffentliche Auftraggeber können bereits heute ökologische oder soziale Kriterien in den Mittelpunkt stellen. Laut einer Untersuchung der Kommission wird dies aber weder optimal noch EU-weit einheitlich gemacht. Einige Vergabestellen fürchten Rechtsstreitigkeiten, wenn sie das Angebot mit dem niedrigsten Preis ablehnen.
Europäische Präferenz wird eingeführt
Der Vorschlag des PPA gibt öffentlichen Auftraggebern weitere Instrumente, um Waren und Dienste aus der EU zu bevorzugen. Sie können die Teilnahme an Ausschreibungen beschränken, Ursprungsanforderungen festlegen und Angebote ablehnen, bei denen der Anteil an EU-Leistungen weniger als 50 Prozent des Auftragswerts ausmacht.
„Künftig kann man dem EU-Kommissar keinen Vorwurf machen, wenn öffentliche Auftraggeber chinesische Busse europäischen vorziehen, da im Text alles genau festgelegt ist und die Bevorzugung europäischer Busse zulässig ist“, sagte Séjourné. Die Behörden der Mitgliedstaaten können chinesische Anbieter auch ganz von Ausschreibungen ausschließen.
Kritiker geben zu bedenken, dass die EU gleichzeitig versucht, bei Handelsabkommen mit anderen Ländern wie Indien europäischen Firmen Zugang zu öffentlichen Ausschreibungen dort zu erleichtern - während sie diesen Zugang in der EU nun einschränkt.
PPA soll die Regeln vereinfachen
Séjourné bezeichnete den Entwurf als „Akt radikaler Vereinfachung“. Die Kommission entschied sich gegen die Einwände einer Mehrheit der Mitgliedstaaten für eine Verordnung anstelle einer Richtlinie. Eine Verordnung schränkt den Spielraum der Länder bei der nationalen Umsetzung ein.
Der PPA soll es Unternehmen erleichtern, Ausschreibungen in der gesamten EU zu finden und daran teilzunehmen. Dazu wird ein Netzwerk digitaler Plattformen eingeführt. Derzeit gibt es EU-weit 123 Plattformen – entweder auf nationaler oder auf lokaler Ebene. Die Kommission will sicherstellen, dass alle miteinander kommunizieren. Auch die Verfahren werden vereinfacht.
Innovation fördern
Die Kommission will zudem das Problem angehen, dass Forschungsergebnisse aus der EU nicht zu innovativen Produkten oder Diensten im Markt führen - auch weil Start-ups keinen Zugang zu dem nötigen Kapital finden.
Die Antwort der Kommission ist der „European Innovation Act“, der ebenfalls am Mittwoch angekündigt wurde. Er zielt darauf, staatlichen Auftraggeber zu Ankerkunden für neue Produkte zu machen.
Advertisement
„Innovative Ideen, die in Europa entwickelt werden, schaffen es zu oft nicht, den Markt zu erreichen, grenzüberschreitend Fuß zu fassen oder neue Wachstumsbranchen zu erschließen“, heißt es darin.
Der „Innovation Act“ wurde von Forschungskommissarin Ekaterina Zaharieva vorangetrieben und war ursprünglich ehrgeiziger angelegt. Laut Dokumenten, die POLITICO vorliegen, wurde der Geltungsbereich nach zwei negativen Stellungnahmen der Kommission eingeschränkt.

The SEPTEMBER FEST 2026 urbanism festival, previously scheduled for September 18 at A-STATION in Kyiv, has been rescheduled for November 5, 2026. The event will take place at the “Parkovy” Exhibition and Convention Center in conjunction with the UBC Congress under the format “SEPTEMBER FEST + UBC,” according to the DMNTR media group, the festival’s organizer.
The decision to reschedule was made following the introduction of new restrictions in Kyiv on mass gatherings due to the deteriorating security situation.
On September 7, the Kyiv Defense Council decided to temporarily ban entertainment and physical education/sports mass events in open areas, as well as in buildings and structures that lack shelters capable of accommodating the expected number of participants.
The new rules take effect at 12:00 a.m. on September 10, the Kyiv City State Administration reported on September 9.
“In connection with the decision of the Kyiv Defense Council and the announcement by Mayor Vitali Klitschko, starting September 10, entertainment and mass events in open areas and in premises without appropriate shelters are temporarily prohibited in the capital.
Therefore, we are rescheduling the September Fest urban festival for November 5 and will hold it jointly with the UBC Congress at the “Parkovy” Exhibition and Convention Center in the format of SEPTEMBER FEST + UBC,” the organizers stated.
According to DMNTR, the festival’s announced program, speakers, and concert lineup remain unchanged.
SEPTEMBER FEST 2026 was previously planned as an open-air event. The festival is positioned as a professional platform for representatives of the real estate development, architecture, and municipal government sectors, as well as investment companies and related industries. Over 150 speakers were scheduled to participate in the professional program.
Key topics of the event include the development of Ukrainian cities, architecture and real estate development during the war, post-war reconstruction and revitalization of territories, investments in real estate and infrastructure, labor shortages in construction, the industry’s digital transformation and BIM technologies, energy independence, the design of public spaces, and the shaping of a modern urban environment.
Previously announced international participants in the professional program include Christos Passas, Design Director at Zaha Hadid Architects; British industrial designer Ross Lovegrove; and German designer Konstantin Grcic. The Ukrainian portion of the program will feature developers, architects, investors, mayors, and chief city architects, as well as representatives of government agencies and industry organizations.
The organizers expect that combining SEPTEMBER FEST with the UBC Congress will allow them to preserve the professional and cultural components of the festival in a new, safer format and bring together representatives of the development, architectural, investment, and urban communities in a single venue.
The general sponsors of SEPTEMBER FEST + UBC are A Development and “Creator-Bud.” The organizer is the DMNTR media group.
The new date is November 5, 2026.

A criminal investigation is underway in Britain into allegations that the Reform UK party broke the law in relation to foreign funding, according to media reports Wednesday.
The investigation by the Metropolitan Police Special Enquiry Team is being folded into an inquiry that has been underway into other donations to the party, the BBC reported.
It came after a broadcast by Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations last week showing an undercover reporter recording two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations.
A Reform UK spokesman said the party "denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation," in response to the investigation. "We won't be commenting further while a live investigation is under way."
The Metropolitan Police said the investigation was launched after it received "a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party."
Police said that "All allegations under investigation relate to potential offences under the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000."
The spokesperson added that detectives were seeking to obtain footage relating to the broadcast.
The two key figures in Reform UK, Dan Jukes, chief of staff to leader Nigel Farage, and James Orr, head of policy, have resigned amid the row.
Jukes has denied "any wrongdoing" and said he "stepped back from politics in order to clear” his name.

Ukraine and its partners have agreed on concrete steps to implement the Freyja anti-ballistic program, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:22:06 EEST
01:22:06 KST

Ukraine and its partners have agreed on concrete steps to implement the Freyja anti-ballistic program, Zelenskyy says
Kyiv • UNN
A meeting was held in Norway with the heads of defense companies from partner countries, dedicated to the implementation of the Freyja anti-ballistic program.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Prime Minister of Norway Jonas Gahr Støre held a meeting with the heads of defense companies from partner countries dedicated to the implementation of the Freyja antiballistic program. The President of Ukraine reported this, UNN writes.
"The main topic is the Freyja antiballistic program, which can provide Europe with integrated protection against air threats through the joint efforts of Ukraine, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom," Zelenskyy noted.
The meeting was attended by the heads of the defense companies FirePoint, Kongsberg, Weibel, Saab, Diehl Defence, Hensoldt, Thales, Safran, Sener, and Leonardo.
"We agreed on what exactly the leaders and government officials should do at their level, and what the manufacturers and developers should do at theirs. We expect the first practical results," the President reported.
He also thanked Norway for hosting the meeting and the partners for their readiness to work together.
"Protecting Europe's skies is our common cause," Volodymyr Zelenskyy emphasized.
Earlier, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced meetings with representatives of the states and defense companies involved in developing the joint Freyja antiballistic program.
What is Freyja
Freyja is a project initiated by Ukraine for a joint European antiballistic system, the first track of the Antiballistic Coalition, which includes 10 states and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
The project is being built around the Ukrainian FP-7.x interceptor missile developed by Fire Point, while other components are supplied by European manufacturers. As UNN reported, Fire Point's General and Technical Director Iryna Terekh said that development has reached the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem — radars, a launcher, a data transmission channel, and a command center — while tests are conducted up to twice a week. The first interception of a ballistic target by the system is scheduled for 2027.

Joint List submits Israel election slate, vows to fight racism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09

Breadcrumb
Joint List submits slate for Israel election, vowing to fight racism, supremacy
The Joint List, predominantly made up of Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, has submitted its final slate for Israel's October election, vowing to fight "racism and supremacy" and setting out conditions for potentially backing a government to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The alliance of Hadash, Ta'al and Balad formally submitted its candidates to Israel's Central Elections Committee on Tuesday ahead of the 27 October election, declaring itself "the only alternative to racism and supremacy".
Hadash chairman Yousef Jabareen heads the ticket, followed by longtime Ta'al leader Ahmad Tibi and Balad chairman Sami Abou Shahadeh.
Hadash's Faten Ghattas is fourth, followed by Balad's Bakr Awawdeh and Hadash lawmaker Ofer Cassif. Former Hadash lawmaker Youssef Atauna is seventh, followed by Balad's Maha Karkabi Sabbah.
The slate underwent a late change after Hadash replaced Jafar Farah in fourth place with Ghattas, a longtime party activist, following an internal examination of sexual harassment allegations against Farah.
The Joint List said it wanted to turn the electoral and political weight of Palestinian citizens of Israel into an effective force capable of influencing the balance of power, with removing Netanyahu and his far-right allies from government among its main priorities.
The alliance said the past four years had seen democratic space restricted and legislation targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel and democratic forces, while pledging to oppose "the destruction of Gaza, ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and the political persecution of the country's Arab citizens".
It also pointed to increasing home demolitions, rising crime and violence within Palestinian communities and Israeli incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque, as well as expanding settlements and displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
But the Joint List made clear that any support for an alternative government seeking to replace Netanyahu would "not be a blank cheque".
It said its position would depend on the political commitments made by any prospective government and its ability to deliver meaningful change on issues affecting Palestinian citizens of Israel and Palestinians more broadly.
Its demands include an end to home demolitions and fairer planning policies for Palestinian towns, serious measures to tackle crime and violence, as well as an end to the war on Gaza and displacement in the West Bank, with a political process recognising the Palestinian people's right to self-determination and an independent state.
The Joint List also said it would only to provide a confidence and supply arrangement to an alternative Israeli government in exchange for what it described as a "real safety net" for its constituents, including its demands for an end to home demolition and action against crime.
Joint List projected to win seven seats
Recent polling projects that the Joint List will win seven seats in the next Knesset.
The three-party alliance was revived in August, four years after Balad split from Hadash-Ta'al ahead of the 2022 election.
Another Palestinian party, Ra'am led by Mansour Abbas, is not part of the alliance and submitted a separate electoral slate. The fledgling Jewish-Arab Makom LeKulanu party, meanwhile, withdrew shortly before the deadline amid low polling numbers.
The Joint List also includes Jewish candidates. Cassif is among its leading candidates, while Orly Noy, the first Jewish member of Balad, is in 15th place.
Jabareen said the alliance's return offered Palestinian citizens of Israel an opportunity to strengthen their political and parliamentary influence.
"We agreed on the Joint List because the interests of our people are greater than any disagreement," he said.
"Our goal now is to restore hope to our people, raise voter turnout and transform the weight of our community into a political force that cannot be ignored."
A total of 38 lists have registered to compete for the Knesset's 120 seats, with a governing coalition requiring the support of at least 61 lawmakers.

President Volodymyr Zelensky and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre met with heads of defense companies from partner nations in Oslo to push forward the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program – a defense initiative aimed at building alternatives to the US-made Patriot interceptors.
Zelensky detailed the meeting in a statement on Wednesday, Sept. 9, saying the talks brought together leadership from companies including FirePoint (a Ukrainian company that initiated and leads the FREYJA program), Kongsberg, Weibel, Saab, Diehl Defence, Hensoldt, Thales, Safran, Sener, and Leonardo.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The discussions covered what governments and manufacturers each needed to deliver going forward.
“The main topic was the FREYJA anti-ballistic program, which can provide Europe with integrated protection against aerial threats through the joint efforts of Ukraine, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom,” Zelensky said.
“Protecting European skies is our shared cause,” he continued.
Norway’s role in protecting Ukraine’s skies
Norway allocated NOK 85 billion ($9.2 billion) to Ukraine under the Nansen Support Program for 2026, including NOK 70 billion ($7.6 billion) in military assistance and NOK 15 billion ($1.6 billion) in civilian and humanitarian aid.
Oslo has also proposed maintaining the same NOK 85 billion ($9.2 billion) level of assistance next year, with most expected to go toward military support.
Ex-CIA Chief: NATO Is Weak and the Baltics Are Next
Building on prior agreements
The most recent meeting on Wednesday followed a broader visit that began on Tuesday, Sept. 8, when Zelensky and Støre held talks focused on Ukraine’s air-defense needs, interceptor missile supplies, and preparations for the upcoming winter.
The discussions centered on expanding Ukrainian-Norwegian defense cooperation agreed to less than three weeks earlier, during Støre’s visit to Kyiv on Aug. 23, when the two leaders signed an Agreement on Defense and Security Cooperation under the Drone Deal format.
Zelensky and Støre also signed a declaration establishing the Ellisiv Accord strategic partnership.
“I am grateful to Norway for hosting this meeting. Thank you to our partners for their willingness to work together,” Zelensky said in his latest statement.
Separately on Monday, Russia threatened to take unspecified “additional measures” in response to Norway’s expanding military presence along its northern border following Norway’s establishment of an artillery battalion. Norway has defended the buildup as necessary for modern defense, citing the war in Ukraine.
Although European officials stated there is no intelligence indicating Russia is preparing for a conventional military attack on NATO or the Baltic states, many member states have deliberately increased their defenses in case Russia’s aggression spreads beyond Ukraine’s borders – particularly as hybrid attacks from Russia escalate.
A fifth winter of war
The upcoming winter will mark Ukraine’s fifth winter since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, prompting Ukrainian authorities to reassess and intensify their winter preparations across all sectors.
This year, Russia is expected to shift its winter campaign away from targeting only Ukraine’s power grid, including heating and electricity, toward targeting water infrastructure as well.
At the same time, Ukraine continues to rely on foreign partners for the delivery of Patriot interceptors, which are the only weapons system that can intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
Zelensky’s trip to Oslo came just hours after Russia launched a large-scale missile and drone barrage on Kyiv, killing five people and injuring 35 in strikes on civilian infrastructure. The barrage began just as senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner left the country, following meetings that centered on brokering an end to Russia’s war.
“Our priority right now is the winter package,” Zelensky said in a statement on X. “The main issue is strengthening air defense and assistance in other areas important for getting through the winter.”
On Tuesday, Ukraine announced it was signing contracts with partners for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles for its air defense systems ahead of the winter.
Germany said it would urgently transfer PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from its own Bundeswehr stocks.

Trump claims he will send $5,000 to every citizen if Republicans hold on to control of Congress

“So if the Republicans win, you win with us … it will be called the Trump dividend,” the president said.
Here's a recap of the first night of the GOP midterm convention
In a nearly two-hour speech, Donald Trump capped off his first night remarks at the GOP midterm convention by pleading with Republicans to “pretend that I’m running”. The president centered himself in the battle to control Congress, and acknowledged that candidates are more successful when he is on the ballot. He offered an ominous outlook if Republicans fail to retain power. “If we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security. You’re going to lose your wealth. Our country is going through hell. You will be going through hell just like you did just two years ago,” Trump said.
The president made the stunning claim that he wouldsend every citizen $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the US House and Senate. However, he provided no details about where he would source this money from or the legality of the incentive. “It will be called the Trump dividend,” the president said. A reminder that it’s against federal law to “make or offer to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote”. It would cost over $1tn, accounting for more than 235 million adult citizens across the country.
Throughout his remarks, Trump also tried to campaign on behalf on Republicans in competitive midterm races. While he made fun of Ken Paxton’s clothing choices and the way he speaks, he praised the Republican nominee for US Senate in Texas as “the single greatest attorney general” in the state’s history, while also branding his opponent James Talarico as a “disaster”. He also praised Michael Whatley, who is running to keep the open Senate seat in North Carolina red, and blasted his challenger – the state’s former Democratic governor Roy Cooper – over his handling of the devastating hurricane that swept through the state in 2024.
Earlier, Democratic senator John Fetterman made a surprise virtual appearance at the Republican midterm convention, delivering a video address supporting Dave McCormick, a Republican senator in Pennsylvania. Fetterman, who has increasingly broken with his party since his election in 2022, said in the video that he would always reject “extremes and socialism”, repeating an oft-used Republican critique of the Democratic party’s increasingly popular left wing. “Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today? Because well, I’m a commonsense Democrat. I’m always going to stand with America,” the Pennsylvania lawmaker said in the pre-recorded message. Fetterman, for his part, insisted that he would not be switching parties in the next Congress. ““I’m a lifelong Democrat who votes overwhelmingly with my party-and should the Senate flip in November, I will still be the 51st vote that I ran on,” he said in a statement.
Meanwhile, several Republicans who are facing tough races have chosen not to attend the convention in Dallas. This include Susan Collins, the five-term incumbent senator from Maine, and Dan Sullivan – the Republican senator from Alaska who is facing a tough contest against former Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola. By showing up at the convention, these nominees run the risk of isolating swing voters they need to court in competitive districts and states where the administration’s policies have proven unpopular.
Trump caps nearly two-hour speech by repeating his plea to 'please pretend that I'm running'
In a nearly two-hour speech, Donald Trump capped off his first night remarks at the GOP midterm convention by repeating his plea to Republicans.
“Please pretend that I’m running,” he said. “Get out and vote on November 3rd or sooner, because in actuality, I really am running … we have to take Congress.”
The president noted that he’ll also speak on the second and final night of the convention, but it won’t be as long.
“I’m not doing a big deal like this because I don’t have to say the same stuff twice. I gave you a lot of material,” he said. “I’m going to be just sort of getting up here and saying, good luck. We love you all.”
Also in his speech, Trump referenced the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk – which happened a year ago on Thursday. Erika, Kirk’s widow who is now leading his organization, Turning Point USA, was in the audience.
Those at the American Airlines Center gave Erika a standing ovation, while Trump chided people who “cheered” Kirk’s death. “The mask came off the radical left,” the president said.
As we’ve previously reported, by November of 2025, a Reuters investigation estimated that 600 people had been terminated, disciplined, investigated, suspended or otherwise admonished for their Kirk posts, likening the reaction to an ideological purge.
The president has given shout outs to several Republicans running for Senate in a number of competitive races throughout his speech.

“[Cooper] did nothing to help. He was a disaster during that very traumatic time,” the president said.
However, as my colleague Chris Stein has reported, when Trump visited the state shortly after returning to office, he said Whatley would be “in charge of making sure everything goes well” with the recovery. That’s led to Whatley being known in the state’s press as the “recovery czar”, a title the Republican’s campaign said he was never given, but which Cooper has wielded to argue that his opponent is the one letting North Carolinians down.
Trump defended the war in Iran during his speech today, and appeared to downplay concerns about the price of gas – now more than a dollar higher per gallon than this time last year.
“Let me ask you one question: Can Iran have a nuclear weapon? Absolutely not,” he said.
The economic ramifications of the conflict, including record-high inflation, have had an impact on voters. Poll after poll shows a majority of Americans disapprove of Trump’s decision to go to war.
Earlier, the president spoke about his prized White House ballroom. The supreme court recently allowed construction to continue after several legal challenges.
Again, Trump claimed that this is a “tax free” project. “I’m giving you a ballroom free of charge,” the president insisted. But the Guardian previously reported that the administration quietly redirected $352m in federal funds designated for the Secret Service toward the ballroom project, despite repeated promises by Trump that the construction would be financed by private donations.
The funds were drawn from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Trump’s signature tax legislation passed last summer on Republican-only votes. The law stipulates the money may only be spent on Secret Service personnel, training facilities, technology and related costs, not construction.
A reminder that Congress explicitly refused to provide $1bn in funds for the “East Wing Modernization Project” in June.
It’s unclear on what legal grounds the president can offer a cash incentive to vote for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections. It is against federal law to “make or offer to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote”.

Donald Trump falsely claimed that there have been “zero” border crossings over the last 16 months. He also falsely claimed there were “25 million” under his predecessor Joe Biden.

Russia markets drone-like missiles in Egypt during Su-57 jet's Africa air show debut
EL ALAMEIN, Egypt, Sept 9 - Russian state-owned arms exporter Rosoboronexport showed off drone-like missiles for its Sukhoi Su-57 fifth-generation stealth jet fighter in Egypt on Wednesday as the warplane made its African air show debut.
The jet roared over the arid landscape outside the El Alamein International Airport near the Mediterranean coast during the second installment of an exhibition meant to position Egypt as a gateway to African and Middle Eastern markets.
On display in Russia's section of the airfield were S-71M and S-71K missiles, which combine features of cruise missiles and low-cost attack drones, according to defence industry outlets.
The airshow in El Alamein marked the first time the missiles were displayed publicly, though they have previously been used in combat, said a Rosoboronexport representative, who spoke on condition he not be named.
"It's not a drone, it's not a missile, it's something [like] both," he told Reuters.
The export model of the Su-57, a rival to Lockheed Martin’s F-35 Lightning II, has previously been shown in China, India and the United Arab Emirates. Ukraine said it hit an Su-57 at an air base inside Russia in 2024.
Elsewhere at the airshow, China displayed its J-16 fighter jet, just weeks after the warplane took part in joint military exercises with Egypt in the aircraft's first deployment to Africa.
Companies from Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt also featured heavily at the exhibition, hawking products for an era of war increasingly dominated by drones as military delegations from countries such as Sierra Leone, Tanzania and Kuwait browsed their booths.
Mohammed Al-Sayed, a consultant at the Egyptian private defence company Amstone International Group, said turnout reflected interest in Egypt as a gateway to African and Arab defence markets. REUTERS

"Its efforts in Gaza and the West Bank are known to everyone," he said.
"The Israeli government and its various agencies are aware of the scale of the efforts made by the State of Qatar, in cooperation with its partners, to contain the escalation and reach truces and agreements that contributed to saving lives."
"If Israel chooses to target this role or undermine the model of mediation, despite the international appreciation and support it enjoys, this is a crisis that reflects its own choices, not a crisis in the role or positions of the State of Qatar," he added.
Al-Ansari also stressed that Qatar's sovereignty and territorial integrity remained a "red line".
"We affirm that while the State of Qatar seeks peace and works to facilitate dialogue and de-escalation, its sovereignty and territorial integrity are a red line," he said.
"We will not hesitate to defend them and take all necessary measures to safeguard them, in accordance with the guarantees provided by international law and the UN Charter."
Asked about competition between Israel's government and opposition over moves to classify Qatar as an "enemy state", Al-Ansari said Doha did not pursue a policy of hostility towards any country.
"The State of Qatar does not adopt a policy of hostility towards any state," he said.
"Its foreign policy is based on the principles of dialogue and cooperation and respect for international law. Its positions are clear and consistent in supporting the legitimate rights of the brotherly Palestinian people and working to achieve security and stability in the region."
He said attempts to portray Qatar as an enemy amid Israel's domestic political rivalries were aimed at undermining the approach Doha represents.
"Attempts to manufacture a state of hostility with the State of Qatar and exploit it in Israel's internal political disputes and competitions do not target Qatar as much as they target what it represents: an approach based on mediation, dialogue and support for rights," Al-Ansari said.
He added that such campaigns would not change Doha's position on Palestine or its mediation efforts.
"Such claims and campaigns will not deter the State of Qatar from its steadfast positions towards the brotherly Palestinian people, nor will they affect its efforts to de-escalate and enhance security, peace and stability at the regional and international levels," Al-Ansari said.

How a French Foreign Legion soldier dramatically escaped Colombian captors

How a French Foreign Legion soldier dramatically escaped Colombian captors
A French Foreign Legion soldier kidnapped by Colombian guerrillas escaped after nearly a month in captivity by overpowering a guard, jumping into a river with his hands tied and trekking for four days through the Andes to reach safety, according to a Colombian military source.
A French Foreign Legion soldier overpowered one of his Colombian captors and then jumped into a river with his hands tied in a dramatic escape from a guerrilla group that reads like the plot of a thriller.
A senior Colombian military source told AFP on Tuesday how Jose Melo Charry made it to safety after nearly a month captive at the hands of drug-trafficking rebels.
Read moreFrench Foreign Legion soldier kidnapped in Colombia
Melo Charry, a Colombian citizen, was on leave in his homeland when he was abducted in southwestern Narino department on August 6 by a dissident faction of the defunct FARC guerrilla group.
He escaped by asking to be taken to the bush to relieve himself.
Once he was away from the rebel camp, he wrestled with his guard, immobilised him and took his rifle.
He still hand his hands bound but jumped into a river and managed to free himself, the military source related.
The soldier, who is in his mid-thirties, then walked for four days through a region of the Colombian Andes that is bristling with armed groups before locating a police station where he sought help.
Along the way, he stopped to eat at a farmer's house but was fearful that the family would betray him to the guerrillas.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
During his escape, he found a way to contact his family, through whom he sent a message to the security forces notifying them that he was roaming the mountains.
"He managed to escape by hiding at night. Every time a motorcycle passed, he hid," behind rocks and in trees, the source, who requested anonymity, told AFP.
The source added that Melo Charry was considered a "big fish" by the guerrillas and had his hands, feet and neck bound for most of his captivity.
A photograph shared by the French Armed Forces with AFP showed him dressed in an olive T-shirt and pants at a hospital, where he was airlifted for medical tests, with no visible injuries.
Read moreColombian rebel group say kidnapped French Foreign Legion soldier is still alive
On Monday, authorities reported he was in good health and remained under military protection at the hospital.
The Central General Staff (EMC), the biggest of the dissident FARC factions that rejected a historic 2016 peace deal between the rebel army and the state, claimed responsibility for his abduction.
The EMC did not demand a ransom for his release but had warned Colombia's new right-wing president, Abelardo De la Espriella, against "any attempt at a rescue operation".
France's defense ministry said that Melo Charry had not received authorisation to travel to Colombia.
He was traveling with a woman who was also taken hostage and released hours later.
Kidnapping is commonly used by Colombian armed groups for extortion purposes or to exert political pressure.
Colombian-French politician Ingrid Betancourt became a symbol of the scourge of kidnappings in Colombia when she was captured by FARC in a jungle area in 2002, while campaigning for the presidency.
Read moreIngrid Betancourt faces ex-FARC captors nearly 20 years after kidnapping
She was rescued six years later in a military operation.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Estonian Ambassador Aino Lepik von Wirén elected to chair working group on Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:16:16 UTC
01:16:16 KST

The working group is tasked with preparing for the launch of the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression, which is being established under the auspices of the Council of Europe. Estonia has been one of the most consistent members of the working group and one of the most vocal advocates for establishing the Special Tribunal within the Council of Europe.
“At a time when Russia’s full-scale aggression against Ukraine is already in its fifth year, we must use every international mechanism available to hold the aggressor accountable for its crimes,” Ambassador Lepik von Wirén stressed. “The purpose of the Special Tribunal is to bring the perpetrators of the crime of aggression before the Tribunal.”
According to the Ambassador, active efforts to make the Special Tribunal operational must continue. She also thanked the working group’s previous chair, Tanja Gonggrijp, who was recently elected Vice-President of the Council of Europe, for her commitment.
An agreement on the establishment of the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression has been concluded between the Council of Europe and Ukraine. The Tribunal’s task is to investigate and prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for the crime of aggression. The founding documents of the Special Tribunal were drawn up by the Core Group established in 2022, which comprised legal experts from 40 countries – including Estonia – as well as representatives of the European Union and the Council of Europe. In June 2025, Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed an agreement on the establishment of the Special Tribunal.
On 15 May 2026, 36 countries, including Estonia, together with the European Union, confirmed in the Moldovan capital Chișinău their readiness to contribute to the establishment of the Special Tribunal. Estonia has completed the necessary domestic procedures: in February this year, the Riigikogu approved the agreement establishing the Management Committee of the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression.
Aino Lepik von Wirén was born in Stockholm on 28 October 1961. She graduated in law from Stockholm University in 1987 and also studied at the University of Surrey in England. She began her diplomatic career in 1994 as Director of the Human Rights Division in the Legal Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and served as Director General of the Legal Department from 1997 to 1999.
From 1999 to 2003, she served as State Secretary, after which she was Estonia’s Ambassador to Portugal (2003–2006), Israel (2007–2010), the United Kingdom (2010–2014) and Ireland (2018–2022). She has also served as Undersecretary for Legal and Consular Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and as Director General of the Department for European Affairs. Before taking up her current post, she served as Director General of the Department for International Organisations and Human Rights.

Israel sanctions will not hurt intelligence sharing between spy agencies, says Miliband

2026-09-09

01:14:41 KST

British intelligence has been given assurances by its Israeli counterpart that information sharing with the UK will continue as before, Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has said.
The disclosure counters predictions that his decision to impose a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements would lead to a collapse in cooperation between the agencies.
The exchanges of information are seen as mutually beneficial and it is understood that Israeli intelligence was never willing to become mired in any political dispute between the two governments.
Miliband insists the intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
Miliband also expressed confidence that the US shared some of his exasperation with Israel’s reluctance to constrain the settlers in the West Bank, or to engage fully with the 20-point plan for Gaza set out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace.
As yet there has been no explicit criticism of the UK’s actions by the White House.
Trump avoided taking a hard stance when pressed about the coalition of countries, including the UK, France, and Canada, that have imposed new sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
“I’ll be speaking to Israel, I’ll be speaking to them, and I’ll find out what’s their thinking,” he said on Wednesday.
Trump, now locked in fighting midterm elections, appears reluctant to leap to the aid of Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, who persuaded him to go to war against Iran. That decision has pushed oil prices beyond $100 a barrel, helping to swell a threatened “blue wave” that could leave the Democrats in charge of both the House and the Senate.
There is also cross-party concern in the US at the violent tactics adopted by some Israeli settlers.
Miliband said on Sky News on Wednesday: “We obviously talked to the Americans in advance of our announcement. I think the whole international community, let me say this, has been quite frustrated, to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government.
“I think there is real concern about what is happening … underlying so much of the conflicts in the Middle East is this failure to really grasp the situation between Israel and Palestine.
“It’s in our interest to act not just because it’s standing up for our values, but because it’s in our interests to have this two-state solution as a rock of stability in the Middle East.”
The US decision not to oppose the UK over its sanctions and ban on trade with the Israeli settlements follows conversations between Trump and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, on Monday, as well as previous diplomatic exchanges at lower levels.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, was careful not to endorse the UK sanctions, but affirmed he shared the objective of securing greater stability.
Miliband can also claim credit for persuading Canada and France to join the trade ban, the surprise element in the package announced on Tuesday.
The agreement came together late in the process. Eight other European countries have announced their intention to introduce such measures or to support the measures within the EU, a statement of solidarity that represents probably less of a shift than headlines might suggest.
Some of the signatory countries had already taken steps independent of the EU, or had long been advocating for measures such as suspension of the Israel-EU trade agreement.
For France, the decision to join the British initiative was formalised relatively late during Emmanuel Macron’s trip to London, when he met Burnham on 3 September and celebrated the display of the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum.
France acted after a Franco-Swedish proposal made to the EU27 in April appeared to be making little progress.
The French plan aimed to establish an embargo or tariff on products from the occupied territories, but resistance from a constellation of countries including Germany, Italy and Bulgaria blocked progress. The commission also appeared to raise objections.
Paris last year had led the push to recognise the state of Palestine as critical to the two-state solution, but much of the French diplomatic energy had subsequently drifted. The UK, along with Jordan, will hold a meeting concerning improving humanitarian supplies into Gaza at the UN general assembly later this month.
In advance of Miliband’s statement, Trump had been hinting that he might support the Argentinian claim to sovereignty over the Falklands, a proposal mooted by Netanyahu’s son.
But in a little-noticed move likely to please Washington, Miliband this week supplemented the action against Israel by announcing fresh nuclear-related sanctions against Iran, including targeting Iranian ships involved in “malign behaviour”.
The UK also said it was backing a motion to be put to the UN stating Iran was in breach of its obligations on nuclear proliferation.
The new sanctions are extended to cover energy, software, metals, gold and related activities such as shipping, insurance and banking. Most Iranian aircraft will be prohibited from landing in the UK.
In response to the UK ban on goods, not due to come into force for at least six months, Israel has said it will: close the British consulate in in occupied East Jerusalem; remove British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel; terminate the UK’s role in training Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank; and deny 12 mainly leftwing MPs entry to Israel.

Tributes flow in as Hong Kong mourns Tung Chee-hwa, pioneering first leader
Former business magnate faced difficult crisis during tenure, but officials and former colleagues praise his compassion and ‘brave leadership’
Hong Kong is mourning the death of Tung Chee-hwa, the city’s first leader after its return to Chinese sovereignty and a respected elder statesman, who died on Tuesday at the age of 89.
Tung was surrounded by his family when he “passed away peacefully” at 9.57pm, according to state news agency Xinhua.
Tributes and messages of grief poured in on Wednesday from across Hong Kong and mainland China, as well as from overseas, with top officials, politicians, business leaders and others praising his pioneering role as the first steward of the “one country, two systems” policy under which the city would be administered after the end of British colonial rule in 1997.
They remembered him for steering the city through its uncertain transitional years and laying the groundwork for its post-handover prosperity, and hailed his later role as an elder statesman who worked tirelessly to help improve US-China relations.
Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong issued a statement, describing Tung as a “close friend of the Communist Party of China”, an “outstanding contributor to ‘one country, two systems’” and a “renowned patriot”, while the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office sent a condolence message to his wife, Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping.
The offices said Tung had made “major historic contributions” to Hong Kong’s smooth return to China, while crediting him with tackling complex political, economic and social challenges during the formative years of the special administrative region.
They also highlighted his work after leaving office, saying he continued to support successive chief executives and governments, promote closer ties between Hong Kong and the mainland and use his extensive international connections to foster exchanges between China and the rest of the world.

Auditors stated that the EU’s process of phasing out Russian energy resources is &quot;stalled&quot;
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:13:38 EEST
01:13:38 KST

Auditors stated that the EU’s process of phasing out Russian energy resources is "stalled"
Kyiv • UNN
EU gas storage facilities are 67% full, while investments in phasing out Russian energy resources amount to €54.3 billion instead of €300 billion.
The EU's efforts to achieve independence from Russian oil and gas are stalling just as the 27-country bloc enters winter with exceptionally low gas reserves. Reuters reports this, citing a statement by auditors, according to UNN.
Details
A report by the European Court of Auditors says that the EU is not investing enough to achieve its goals of completely replacing Russian energy supplies by diversifying fossil fuel supplies, as well as expanding the use of renewable energy sources and developing grid infrastructure to increase energy flows between member states in the coming years.
The European Union has been gradually reducing its imports of Russian fuel since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Thanks to sanctions on seaborne Russian oil, the EU has almost completely abandoned imports of Russian crude oil, while Russia's share of the bloc's gas imports has fallen to 12% (compared with 45% before 2022).
However, the EU's plan to abandon Russian energy supplies is "stalling just as Europe's energy security is facing new threats due to instability in the Middle East," auditors said.
Europe is struggling to fill its gas storage facilities ahead of winter, as the conflict involving Iran is restricting global supplies. According to the Gas Infrastructure Europe association, underground gas storage facilities in the EU are only 67% full, significantly below the 80% level reached by this point last year.
Analysts warn that this could lead to a sharp rise in prices in winter, particularly given that the EU's plan to abandon Russian gas provides for a complete ban on imports of Russian LNG from January 1, 2027.
Auditors noted that the EU had managed to replace Russian gas partly thanks to mild weather and high energy prices, which reduced demand, rather than through policy measures. They recommended that Brussels intervene more actively in the situation to ensure that countries continue on the path toward abandoning Russian energy supplies.
A European Commission spokesperson said that EU action and funding had accelerated the implementation of renewable energy projects and contributed to a significant reduction in Russian gas consumption.
"The Commission will take note of the Court of Auditors' recommendations," the spokesperson added.
Initially, the Commission estimated the investments needed to implement the plan to abandon Russian energy supplies at 300 billion euros and provided for these funds to be allocated from the EU budget. However, countries have so far allocated only €54.3 billion for these purposes; in the auditors' view, this indicates either that the Commission incorrectly assessed the investment needs or that countries are having difficulties implementing the plan.

Passenger killed after train hits truck at Poland level crossing

A passenger has been killed in Poland as a train derailed after colliding with a concrete mixer truck at a level crossing.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the accident was "very serious and also means that we must immediately begin urgent work on tougher regulations".

It is still too early to determine the sequence of events.

Last week, a lorry driver crossed the first set of barriers at a level crossing as they were closing and dramatic footage showed him reversing, then moving forward in an unsuccessful attempt to evade another PKP train which was coming at speed.

Merz accuses AfD of ‘ethnic cleansing’ as Trump hails far-right win with ‘MGGA’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:10:52 UTC
01:10:52 KST

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz accused the far-right Alternative for Germany party on Wednesday of advocating what he called “ethnic cleansing” through its mass “remigration” policy, three days after the AfD scored a historic election victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The bitter parliamentary clash came as President Donald Trump openly celebrated the AfD’s breakthrough, posting “MGGA,” apparently meaning “Make Germany Great Again,” in a German variation of his MAGA slogan.
A telephone call between Trump and Merz planned ahead of the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks was subsequently postponed. The German government did not say why, but its spokesman pointed to Merz’s longstanding opposition to foreign leaders intervening in or commenting on Germany’s domestic politics, particularly elections.
Merz confronted AfD co-leader Alice Weidel in the Bundestag after her party won nearly 44% of the vote in Sunday’s Saxony-Anhalt election, putting it within three seats of an absolute majority and raising the possibility that it could lead a German state government for the first time.
Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union suffered a crushing defeat, winning just over 17% and losing roughly half the support it had received in the previous state election.
The AfD’s victory has reverberated across Germany and Europe. Germany’s domestic intelligence service has classified the party as right-wing extremist.
During Wednesday’s parliamentary debate, Merz called the AfD a “destructive force” and accused it of acting against German interests through its support for Russia.
He reserved his sharpest attack for the AfD’s policy of “remigration,” a term the party uses for policies aimed at sending migrants back to their countries of origin.
Merz said one in six skilled workers in Germany has a migration background and argued that implementing the AfD’s plans would amount to “nothing less than ethnic cleansing of skilled workers based on skin color and origin.”
Millions of immigrant workers are essential to the German economy, he said, warning that nursing homes, hospitals and restaurants would be unable to function if the AfD’s plans were implemented.
Merz said his government accepts that some migrants must be deported, but insisted on a distinction between those who work in Germany and contribute to its prosperity and people without a legal right to remain who, he said, “must leave our country.”
AfD lawmakers repeatedly interrupted the chancellor during his speech, prompting the Bundestag president at one point to threaten disciplinary action and remind lawmakers that “we are not at a football stadium.”
Weidel, who as leader of the largest opposition party spoke before Merz, used the AfD’s election triumph to attack the chancellor.
She told Merz that his CDU had been “ground into dust” in Saxony-Anhalt and accused his government, as well as the Social Democrats who led its predecessor, of pushing Germany toward bankruptcy.
Weidel also argued that mass immigration had left Germans facing knife attacks and violence at train stations.
“Your time is up,” she told Merz. “The public wants a change in policy, and it will get one.”
The AfD now hopes to translate its state-level breakthrough into national power. Weidel said the party’s goal remains victory in Germany’s next federal election and the formation of a national government.
For now, however, its path to power in Saxony-Anhalt remains uncertain. The party fell three seats short of the majority needed to govern alone, while most other parties have long rejected entering a coalition with it.
AfD state leader Ulrich Siegmund is seeking potential partners, with attention focused in part on the populist left-wing BSW.
Merz also attacked the AfD over its Russia policy, pointing to the party’s response to an explosive-laden drone found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig airport last month. Germany has blamed Russia for the incident, an accusation Moscow rejects.
The political fallout from the Saxony-Anhalt election has now crossed the Atlantic.
Trump praised the result on Truth Social, writing that “the populist party in Germany just had a really big night” and saying voters had “finally gotten tired” of what he described as Germany’s “absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations.”
“They are on the rise, and are not going to take it anymore!” Trump wrote, before signing off: “MGGA!!!”
Trump did not name the AfD directly, but the reference was clear.
His comments followed repeated expressions of support over the past two years by Trump, members of his administration and allies including Elon Musk for the AfD and other far-right European parties.
Later Wednesday, a German government spokesman said a planned conversation between Merz and Trump had been postponed and that no new date had been set.
The spokesman declined to say whether Trump’s comments about the AfD were behind the decision. He noted, however, that Merz has repeatedly opposed foreign “interference or commentary on the domestic political situation, particularly when it comes to elections.”
German public broadcaster ARD separately reported that the government described the call as postponed, rather than canceled, and said officials did not confirm that Trump’s AfD post was the reason.

We expect to see the first practical results,” Zelensky said.
He expressed his gratitude to Norway for hosting the meeting.
“I thank our partners for their readiness to work together. Protecting Europe’s skies is our shared responsibility,” Zelensky emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, during his visit to Norway, Zelensky discussed with Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre a number of important issues related to strengthening Ukraine’s defense.

Ukraine Unveils New 110-Km Vilkha Guided Missile With 220-Kg Warhead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:09:19 UTC
01:09:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Unveils New 110-Km Vilkha Guided Missile With 220-Kg Warhead
Ukraine’s Luch Design Bureau has developed a new guided missile for the Vilkha rocket system, with a stated range of up to 110 kilometers and a 220-kilogram warhead. The weapon is currently in the final stage of testing.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 9, the upgraded missile was presented at the MSPO 2026 defense exhibition in Poland. The new 300-mm missile is 7.6 meters long and has a total weight of 907 kilograms.
The missile is designed to strike ground targets and adjusts its trajectory toward predetermined coordinates throughout its flight. Its guidance system combines satellite navigation with an onboard inertial navigation system.
According to Oboronka on September 8, representatives of Luch described the missile, designated R-624MS, as a further development of the Vilkha-M project. The new version has a maximum stated range of 110 kilometers.
The missile can be used with Vilkha launchers carrying either 12 or eight rounds. Oboronka reported that these could include existing 300-mm Smerch multiple-launch rocket systems as well as a newer eight-round launcher.
The new missile also differs significantly from earlier Vilkha-family designs. The previously used belt of 90 small gas-dynamic thrusters, which helped alter the missile’s flight vector, is no longer visible on the new version.
Instead, the R-624MS features a redesigned tail section with a rotating aerodynamic control assembly. According to Militarnyi, the new configuration allows the missile body itself to remain stabilized during flight, unlike earlier versions in which the entire missile rotated around its longitudinal axis.
Oboronka suggested that keeping the main body stable while only the tail assembly rotates could improve the continuity of satellite navigation and potentially increase accuracy. Luch has not disclosed further technical details about the missile.
The R-624MS is one of several missile projects recently presented by the Ukrainian defense industry. LUCH has also developed a new air defense missile based on technology from its Stugna missile family.
The new Vilkha missile is part of a broader push by Ukraine to expand domestically produced missile systems. Luch has also developed the RK-19 surface-to-air missile, designed to replace Soviet-made 9M33-series interceptors used by the Osa-AKM short-range air defense system.

Air traffic control boss given a week to report after UK flight chaos causes 2,000 cancellations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:09:18 UTC
01:09:18 KST

The head of the air traffic control provider Nats has been given a week to report back on the reasons for a technical failure that grounded thousands of flights, as the transport secretary said she did “not believe the issue was unavoidable”.
Heidi Alexander said on Tuesday she had also commissioned an independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) into the latest Nats meltdown, which severely disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers.
The comments will pile pressure on the Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, despite Downing Street saying the government still had confidence in him after a morning meeting with Alexander, and as the number of flight cancellations passed 2,000.
The minister told the Commons: “Safety must remain air traffic controllers’ overriding priority, and this morning I have spoken to Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, who informed me this outage was due to a technical issue at their Swanwick site.
“So, while my understanding from Nats is that we can rule out a cyber-attack on this occasion, I do not believe this issue was unavoidable.”
The CAA said passengers were “unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays and cancellations” as the problem was likely to be considered the result of “extraordinary circumstances”.
Airlines have urged action, with Rolfe facing increasing pressure to quit, after the third large-scale stoppage to flights in just over three years.
Latest industry estimates say about 330,000 passengers had their travel disrupted and delayed, with many stuck on grounded planes for hours during the incident . Other passengers were stranded overnight at airports in the UK and abroad. More than 155,000 passengers had flights cancelled, while flights were delayed for more than 180,000 passengers.
A Downing Street spokesperson earlier said Alexander had asked Rolfe to “carry out a full investigation into what happened to make sure that lessons are learned, so that this doesn’t happen again”.
Alexander said she would “leave absolutely no stone unturned in understanding what has happened here, and what can be done to drastically reduce the likelihood of something like this ever happening again.
“I do think we need to ask tough questions about the resilience of Nat systems … We also need to think about consumer redress issues as well.”
The prime minister’s spokesperson added: “We have confidence in him and he’s been tasked with the investigation, which will report in a week’s time.”
Airlines including Ryanair and Wizz called for Rolfe to resign or be sacked by Alexander. He had earlier defended the resilience of the systems run by Nats, which provides services to 15 UK airports.
“We will be doing a very thorough and full investigation,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We have at this point ruled out a cyber-attack … This will be something we haven’t seen in more than 50 years of operation.”
Nats said the problem occurred in its flight processing system but was not the same fault as the issues that caused outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025.
Ryanair queried the explanation and said lessons had not been learned. The carrier, which on Tuesday said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted when 50 flights were cancelled, said it had now cancelled more than 250 flights and that its costs would run into millions.
The airline’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, said: “Martin Rolfe’s position as Nats CEO is untenable. We don’t need more investigations, we don’t need more reports, and we don’t need another parliamentary committee hearing where Martin Rolfe will promise change, will promise resilience, and will promise an effective backup system.”
He said the UK’s air traffic control services were one of the most expensive in Europe “and yet it keeps repeatedly failing”. O’Leary said Alexander should “today demand that failing Martin Rolfe must quit, or be dismissed”.
Yvonne Moynihan, the managing director of Wizz Air UK, called on Rolfe to consider resigning. “In any industry when you’ve had three failures, you need to consider three strikes and you’re out,” she told Today. “A third time and a third excuse is not enough any more. What we need to see from leadership is accountability.”
Luke Petherbridge, the director of public affairs at the travel association Abta, said: “While the immediate priority is supporting customers … the industry and the public will want answers as to what has gone wrong.”
Nats said the fix it eventually implemented on Tuesday, almost four hours after the incident first occurred, had been a “very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover”.
More than 300 flights were cancelled on Wednesday in the continuing fallout from the outage. According to data from the analysts Cirium, nearly 2,100 flights in and out of UK airports have been cancelled because of the failure, including 1,750 on Tuesday out of 5,800 scheduled flights. Of these, 541 were at Heathrow.
A spokesperson for British Airways said: “Tuesday’s air traffic control issue has forced us into cancelling almost 550 of our flights, affecting more than 85,000 of our customers. We’re incredibly sorry for the experience they’ve endured because of an issue that has been entirely out of our control.” The airline operated nearly 80% of its typical flight schedule.
Rail passengers affected by flight disruption could use booked tickets on a different date or to a different airport if needed, or apply for a refund, the Rail Delivery Group said.
The airport breakdown started at about 1pm on Tuesday and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted.
London airports as well as Manchester were among the most directly affected, with operations in effect suspended for hours in the afternoon. While Heathrow said the fault initially only stopped takeoffs, the airport was soon too full to accommodate more planes, with arriving flights diverted to other European airports.
Flights to and from other airports around the UK, including Birmingham, Edinburgh and Belfast, were also disrupted.
The air traffic control problems follow an “isolated event” a year ago that caused widespread disruption, and appeared less severe than the full grounding of flights in August 2023, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry.

Ukraine Knocks Out Two of Russia’s Irreplaceable Tu-95 Strategic Bombers in Just Six Weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:08:35 UTC
01:08:35 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Knocks Out Two of Russia’s Irreplaceable Tu-95 Strategic Bombers in Just Six Weeks
Ukraine has disabled two Russian Tu-95 strategic bombers in separate long-range drone strikes on the Engels-2 airbase in Russia’s Saratov region over a six-week period, targeting aircraft that Moscow can no longer replace.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Telegraph on September 9, both strikes were carried out by a specialized long-range unit of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU). Satellite imagery indicates that one Tu-95 lost its tail in a July 19 attack, while another sustained major damage to its right wing during a second strike on August 28.
Analysts cited by The Telegraph assessed that neither aircraft is likely to return to service. Russia has not produced new Tu-95 bombers since 1992, making losses from its existing fleet effectively irreversible.
“They’re part of Russia’s nuclear triad,” Justin Bronk, a senior research fellow for Airpower and Technology at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The Telegraph.
“They’ve been used to conduct intensive missile raids against Ukraine for four and a half years. Destroying one, especially at its home base, is a politically poignant thing to do,” he added.
The Telegraph reported that the SBU used MICH-2000 long-range drones in the operations. The system has an estimated range of about 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles), substantially exceeding the roughly 800-kilometer direct distance between Ukrainian-controlled territory and Engels-2.
The additional range allowed Ukrainian operators to plan indirect routes around areas with concentrated Russian air defenses. According to the report, the drones also used terrain to reduce their exposure to radar.
“There’s just less dense air defence cover that the Russians can put at any one site than they used to,” Bronk said. “Even something as important as Engels.”
Engels-2 is a major base for Russia’s strategic aviation and one of a limited number of facilities equipped to operate and maintain its nuclear-capable bomber fleet.
The Tu-95, together with the Tu-160, is one of two Russian aircraft capable of launching Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles. The missiles have a range exceeding 3,000 kilometers and have been repeatedly used in Russian long-range strikes against Ukraine.
Robert Tollast, a researcher with RUSI’s Land Warfare team, told The Telegraph that Russia may have only around 20 to 30 operational Tu-95 bombers remaining, potentially fewer, as the aging aircraft require extensive maintenance.
“The Tu-95s are obviously really important for Russia’s deep-strike campaign, which tends to prioritise, particularly over the winter, Ukrainian power infrastructure,” Tollast said. “So the fewer Tu-95s Russia has, the fewer of these missiles can be fired with the devastating warheads and the long range,” he added.
The two Engels strikes follow earlier Ukrainian operations against Russia’s strategic aviation. The open-source monitoring project Oryx has documented at least 10 Tu-95 losses since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, excluding the two aircraft recently struck at Engels-2, according to The Telegraph.
The Telegraph reported that further reductions in Russia’s Tu-95 fleet could affect not only Moscow’s ability to conduct large-scale missile attacks against Ukraine but also the number of strategic bombers available for Russia’s nuclear deterrence and potential operations involving NATO.
In June 2025, Ukraine also targeted Russian strategic aircraft during Operation Spiderweb, when drones launched from inside Russia struck bombers at several airbases.

Is Britain leading a European shift on Israel?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:08:34 UTC
01:08:34 KST

Breadcrumb
Is Britain leading a European shift on Israel?
Britain has imposed its most extensive measures yet against Israel's illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, prompting a furious response from Israel and raising questions over whether London is leading a broader European shift in relations with the country.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced on Tuesday that the UK would ban imports from Israeli settlements and introduce new sanctions targeting companies and individuals involved in financing, constructing or otherwise facilitating their expansion.
France and Canada announced similar import bans alongside Britain, while nine other countries backed further restrictions on settlement trade.
Israel responded by ordering the closure of Britain's consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, expelling UK personnel involved in coordinating aid to Gaza and supporting the Palestinian Authority, and banning 12 British politicians and other nationals from entering the country.
The measures mark a significant escalation in British pressure on Israel, but stop well short of broader sanctions or a boycott of the country itself.
So how far has British policy actually shifted, and is London leading a wider European move from diplomatic condemnation of Israel towards imposing tangible economic costs?
What has the UK actually done?
At the centre of the new British policy is a ban on imports of all goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, which the government says will be implemented within six to nine months.
London is also establishing a broader sanctions regime allowing it to target companies and individuals providing construction, infrastructure, financing and real estate services that facilitate settlement expansion.
Advertising Israeli settlement properties in Britain will be prohibited, while additional extremist settlers accused of supporting or inciting violence against Palestinians have been sanctioned.
The government has also widened restrictions on arms exports. Britain had previously suspended more than 30 licences for weapons that could be used by the Israeli military in Gaza, but will now refuse applications for arms and other exports that "materially contribute to the occupation".
Miliband also formally accepted the International Court of Justice's conclusion that Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territories is unlawful.
Chris Doyle, director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu), told The New Arab that the measures had represented a "major departure for Britain".
"It transforms the British official position from being a declaratory one that says that Israel's settlements are illegal and an obstacle to peace to one where it is prepared to take action to uphold international law," he said.
Previous British measures had largely focused on individual extremist settlers and a small number of organisations, Doyle said, whereas the latest package targets the wider economic structures supporting settlement expansion.
"The broad nature of the measures demonstrates that this is a significant step change," he added.
But there are clear limits to that change.
The government has explicitly confined its new trade measures to settlements rather than Israel itself and has pledged to maintain what Miliband called "important and valued trade" with Israel within the Green Line.
Miliband also reiterated his opposition to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, which advocates broader economic pressure on Israel. The measures therefore remain considerably short of the comprehensive economic sanctions and boycott demanded by Palestinian civil society groups and other advocates of isolating Israel economically.
Is Britain leading Europe?
The announcement nevertheless comes amid a broader change in European policy towards Israel.
France and Canada joined Britain in announcing settlement import bans on Tuesday, while Ireland, Spain, the Netherlands, Norway and Belgium have already introduced or begun developing restrictions on settlement goods.
Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal and Sweden have meanwhile pledged to support further action.
Doyle believes Britain has played a leading role in accelerating that process.
"It was Britain that signalled it was going to do it. It was Britain that took all the flak from Israel and the United States and their supporters," he said.
"The other countries, some of whom had already made such bans, sailed in behind the British position."
The distinction is important. Britain is not the first European country to take action against settlement trade, and several European governments had already moved ahead of London.
But its position as one of Europe's largest economies and Israel's longstanding allies makes the shift politically significant, particularly if it encourages coordinated action outside the European Union's often divided foreign policy structures.
The measures also go beyond simply banning settlement produce.
Targeting financing, construction and other services potentially exposes companies with links to the settlement enterprise to sanctions, increasing the possible economic consequences beyond the relatively small value of goods directly exported from settlements.
Whether that develops into broader pressure on Israel remains an open question.
Europe collectively possesses considerably greater economic leverage through its trade and investment relationship with Israel, but governments remain divided over how far they are prepared to use it.
Britain's own policy illustrates that boundary: it is increasingly prepared to impose economic consequences over the occupation while simultaneously maintaining normal commercial relations with Israel itself.
Will the pressure change Israeli policy?
Israel's response suggests Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government views the measures as more than symbolic.
Israel has given Britain 30 days to close its historic consulate in occupied East Jerusalem and is removing British personnel involved in Gaza aid coordination and programmes supporting the Palestinian Authority.
Doyle argued that the retaliation would primarily harm Palestinians rather than Britain.
"All of these measures impinge far more on Palestinians than they do on Britain," he said, arguing that they would hinder British assistance to Palestinians in the occupied territories and Gaza.
Closing the East Jerusalem consulate, he added, also "significantly tries to sever the link between Palestinians and East Jerusalem by closing down that British diplomatic presence in the city".
London has so far shown no indication that the Israeli response will force it to reverse course.
"I do not think that the British government is in the mood to be bullied on this and is not going to back down as a result of these measures," Doyle said.
But he was equally sceptical that the new international pressure would force Israel to change course.
"Nor, on the other hand, do I believe that this current Israeli government is going to back off as a result of all the measures announced by the 12 states."
That leaves Britain's policy at an important juncture.
The latest measures represent a substantial change from years in which London condemned illegal settlements while imposing relatively limited material consequences for their expansion.
But whether Britain is leading a lasting transformation in Europe's relationship with Israel will depend on what comes next - whether other governments follow with stronger measures, whether pressure expands beyond the settlements, and ultimately whether European states are prepared to use their much greater economic leverage over Israel itself.
