Scientists unlock new clues to what a mysterious ancient human ancestor looked like
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:01:38 UTC
01:01:38 KST

The Denisovans are considered one of modern humans’ closest ancient ancestors, yet we know very little about how they looked or lived. But new analyses of remains from Bianfu Cave in Yunnan province, southwestern China, reveal not only clues to how these ancient hominins looked, but also how they survived and thrived at the site more than 130,000 years ago.
The findings could help place other ancient hominin remains as Denisovans—helping to color in more of their shadowy history.
“People recognized that maybe other archaic hominins were also Denisovan, but we needed more evidence,” says archaeologist Hao Li of China's Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research; Bianfu Cave is on the Tibetan Plateau. Until now, the only solid evidence of Denisovan life was confined to just two places: Siberia’s Denisova Cave, where the ancient hominin species was discovered in 2008, and China’s Baishiya Karst Cave in the northeastern Tibetan Plateau. The analyses by Li and his colleagues show Bianfu Cave is among the richest Denisovan sites known to exist: it includes many Denisovan bones, as well as simple stone and bone tools that Denisovans made and traces of the animals they hunted.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Li is a co-author of one of two studies published 9 September in Nature describing the remains and artifacts. The bones were unearthed in 2019, but have only recently been identified as Denisovan, thanks to a distinctive amino acid found in tooth enamel. Identifying the samples using ancient DNA analysis was not an option, says geneticist Qiaomei Fu of China’s Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, who led the research team. The cave is very old and relatively warm: “These conditions were unsuitable for DNA preservation,” she says.
“These are great studies," says University of Toronto paleoanthropologist Bence Viola, who wasn't directly involved. The new discoveries add much about the species that was not known before—and especially about their teeth, which can now be compared to the teeth of unknown hominins from other sites, he says.
The newly described Denisovan remains include four teeth, part of an arm bone, and two skull fragments. Roughly 60,000 animal bone fragments were also recovered from the cave, which indicate these Denisovans mainly hunted deer and wild bovids, including water buffalo and gaur.
One skull fragment is between 167,000 and 161,000 years old, while the other skull fragment, arm bone and teeth are between 142,000 and 134,000 years old. The arm bone analysis is especially interesting: It suggests Denisovan bones were shaped more like those of modern humans than robust Neanderthals, which implies Denisovans may have looked more like modern humans than Neanderthals, too.
Genetic studies show Denisovans and Neanderthals were closely related. But while evidence of modern human interbreeding with Neanderthals is found in the genomes of all modern humans outside Africa, evidence of Denisovan interbreeding is found mainly in some modern populations in Southeast Asia and Oceania and in traces in human genomes from the rest of Asia, but not in genomes from Africa or Europe. More work will be needed to tease out exactly how the three species’ histories intertwine.

Israel to open embassy in Slovenia after shift to the right
Israel will open its first embassy in Slovenia on Wednesday in a turnaround in relations after a government led by right-wing Prime Minister Janez Jansa came to power this year.
The rapprochement comes as Israel faces growing diplomatic isolation elsewhere over its settlement expansion in the West Bank, including import bans by Britain, France and Canada on products from Israeli settlements.
"This is the first resident embassy in Slovenia, it is indeed a historic day," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said at a news conference with his Slovenian counterpart Tone Kajzer.
"This is a clear expression of Israel's commitment to our friendship and to its future," Saar added, thanking the Slovenian government and Prime Minister Janez Jansa for their friendship towards Israel.
At the start of a two-day visit, Saar and Kajzer signed a memorandum on cooperation in the fields of education, science, culture, youth and sports between the two countries.
A delegation of Israeli businessmen will also attend an economic forum later in the day which is expected to result in new investment, Kajzer said.
"After a long period of less intensive political contacts, it is time to shift cooperation between Slovenia and Israel into a higher gear," he told reporters.
However, there was some opposition to the move in Slovenia.
The liberal Freedom Movement of former Prime Minister Robert Golob, joined by the Left party, on Wednesday submitted to parliament a proposal for impeachment of Jansa, primarily over his government's foreign policy which they said was exclusively in the interest of Israel.
Protests against the opening of the embassy are scheduled on Wednesday evening by student movements, a leftist opposition party and pro-Palestinian groups.
It marks a change in approach Slovenia, a small Alpine country which is a European Union and NATO military alliance member. Under the previous liberal government, it recognised a Palestinian state.
Slovenia was also among the first EU countries to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank and entry for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes, as well as extremist ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir.
These decisions were quickly revoked by the new government.

Will the US ever recover from its Covid wounds?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:00:43 UTC
01:00:43 KST

Annapolis, the waterfront capital of the US state of Maryland, is a vibrant coastal city with an active civic life. In 2020, it was also among numerous American cities swept up in Covid-era protests.
At the height of the pandemic, politically charged demonstrations gridlocked its streets. Crowds denounced government lockdowns and challenged the science behind vaccines. Six years later, some of that scepticism still lingers.
"When Covid came around, people were gonna get vaccinated because that's what we were trained to do. So then, then you get vaccinated again, and then you get vaccinated again. And now people start to wonder, 'What is this about?'," Penelope, an Annapolis resident tells TRT World.
Penelope is not alone. The latest research indicates that more Americans than ever before do not trust vaccines, the science supporting them, or their government.
"I won't get another vaccination, you know. I just have to deal with the consequences, you know, because it didn't, it didn't help because I still caught Covid. I really don't think they work, you know. And then again, I don't know what they really injected in me," says another Annapolis local.
The vaccine hesitancy has grown in US in recent years. Under US President Donald Trump, Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr. has pursued changes to childhood vaccination policy that have drawn criticism from parts of the medical community.
According to pediatrician Dr. Paul Offit, who was dismissed from a government vaccine advisory board last year over his criticism of Kennedy, the Covid pandemic supercharged the lack of trust in public health institutions.
"This was a virus that was spread person to person, and it could be spread from somebody who had no symptoms. So all we could do was prevent human to human contact. So we closed schools and shuttered businesses, restricted travel, social distanced and quarantined," Dr. Offit tells TRT World.
He notes that a section of the American public perceived the measures as significant government overreach.
"You couldn't go to your favourite restaurant or sporting event without your vaccination card. You may be fired from your job. That too was seen as government overreach. People didn't like being told what to do."
Dr. Offit argues that official messaging could have been clearer, noting public scepticism stemmed from broader distrust of government rather than healthcare policies alone.
Public health is not the only sector experiencing an erosion of confidence; trust has also declined in public education, the US Congress, the Supreme Court, and the media. Twelve of the 14 core US institutions monitored annually since 1993 are currently at or near their lowest-ever approval ratings.
Americans remain protective of their constitutional rights, particularly protections such as freedom of religion, speech, and the press, and the right to bear arms. But how concerning is it when it relates to public health policy, and where does that leave the country if there is no perceived standard bearer of trusted information?
Dr. Offit notes that distrust of government often translates into opposition to public health under the guise of "medical freedom", disregarding collective well-being.
"It's very concerning. I mean, basically, what you're saying is that it's my right to catch and transmit a potentially fatal infection, knowing that there are a certain number of people, millions of people in this country, for example, who can't be vaccinated, who depend on me and the, the people around them to protect them. And what you're saying is, 'I'm gonna do whatever I wanna do. I don't care how it affects others'."
Asked what will restore the public trust in America's institutions, the vaccine expert says, "I think the viruses and bacteria are gonna be doing the educating.
Eroding trust in US institutions
Ameshia Cross, a Democratic political analyst, and Matthew Hurtt, an Arlington Republican Party official, offer TRT World contrasting diagnoses of why Americans have lost faith in government, public health agencies and the media, tracing the problem from the Covid-19 pandemic to today's polarised information environment.
Hurtt says the pandemic "exposed something that had been happening" for years: falling confidence in government and even neighbourhoods.
He points to shifting guidance from former Chief Medical Advisor to the President, Dr. Anthony Fauci, vaccine mandates he described as involving "untested" shots, and parents’ subsequent questions about what they were putting in their children’s bodies.
He notes that his own childhood vaccine schedule in the late 1980s was shorter and more spaced out than the schedules followed by his young niece and nephew.
"And the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention), in June of last year, said that some of these vaccines, particularly related to Covid-19, have led to and can be related to the myocarditis that we're seeing among young people," he adds.
Cross, a Democrat, argues that the federal government "lost America’s trust a long time ago," though many people still had more faith in state and local officials.
She says the rapid changes — from social distancing to restaurant curfews — left people frustrated that "the science seemed to be changing month after month, and in some cases week after week."
Extended isolation, she adds, damaged the "social, emotional, and mental psyche" of many Americans.
Cross defends officials who "did what we had to do with the information we had at the time".
Handling another crisis
Cross notes that then-President Donald Trump launched Operation Warp Speed and received a Covid-19 vaccine himself, while also publicly questioning aspects of the pandemic response.
Hurtt acknowledges Trump's role in Warp Speed but says vaccine scepticism and questions about the programme were expressed across the political spectrum during the 2020 election period.
Distrust, he adds, now cuts both ways: many Democrats question the Justice Department's use under the current administration, just as conservatives have long accused prior administrations of weaponising government.
Cross also blames declining trust in part on media outlets whose claims have been "debunked," the rise of non-journalists on social media with large followings, and poor media literacy.
"It's the Wild Wild West across social media, and everybody is picking one that confirms what they already believe," she says.
She says Americans now fear lettuce and grocery-store produce and are seeing measles outbreaks "we eradicated generations ago."
Hurtt, however, insists that listeria outbreaks in vegetables occur every 18 to 24 months regardless of who is president, and that healthy skepticism of government at any level is valuable.
Asked whether the country has enough "institutional capital" left to handle another national crisis, Cross says the US already faces daily crises and that the structure has been "so badly disrupted" that a coordinated response would be extremely difficult.
Hurtt, a Republican, largely agrees on health and vaccine issues but insists communities still produce effective responses to natural disasters, which gives him hope.

How will AI change the future of work? Ravi Kumar S has a few ideas. As the CEO of Cognizant, which employs more than 350,000 people around the world, Kumar isn’t just helping other companies figure out how best to use this technology. He's also testing his theories across a large global workforce.
Since becoming CEO in January 2023, Kumar has been a prominent voice in the debate on AI, offering his views on which jobs will last, how work will evolve, and how society should best take advantage of the technology. Kumar joined The CEO Moment, TIME’s interview series, to discuss AI’s potential and where it is currently falling short.
How is AI going to change how companies are structured?
You’re going to see more modular, agile, small teams. Managers are going to be expected to be player-coaches…They're going to be more hands-on. The path to expertise is going to be much faster. The asymmetry between individuals and institutions is no longer going to be expertise. Expertise is going to be at your fingertips. The asymmetry is going to be interdisciplinary skills.
You recently celebrated 20,000 entry-level grads hired at Cognizant. At the same time you announced a plan for spending $270 million on severance. How many jobs has Cognizant eliminated because of AI adoption?
The net addition of people is still positive for the company. We're still growing.
Do you find that new employees who used AI in college lack curiosity or resilience?
Somebody asked me this question saying, how do you keep that curiosity if you're outsourcing everything you would like to do to a machine? I think we need massive transformation in K-12 schools. It's funny, if you use AI in schools, schools will fire you. If you don't use AI in workplaces, your employer will fire you. Schools should teach native skills in classrooms without AI. They should give homework, which you should do with AI.
Do you believe we’re in an AI bubble?
If you see this buildout, and if it is real, money will flow into the bridges. Money will flow into the end user industries and the end user industries will benefit out of it. If that flow is not happening, then this bubble is going to burst. I am convinced the capability is there. I'm equally convinced the production value is not there.
You’ve proposed taxing digital labor. This idea can’t be popular with your customers.
I'm not saying that universally. I'm actually saying if you are positioning this technology to eliminate human work, and you are not positioning this technology to amplify human work, labor is getting taxed. Why should human labor be getting taxed? Why shouldn't digital labor be carrying the same overhead?
How do you worry America has turned against immigrants and immigration?
Do we need the best talent in the world to be in the United States? Absolutely. That's been the strength of America.
The endeavor of enterprises is to attract the best talent across the world and to create domestic talent pools in a sustained manner. Now, if we lose that mojo of doing it, then we wouldn't be able to create these innovation ecosystems. Even today, the United States is the best place for upward social mobility… Whoever you are, it doesn't matter. Whatever background you come from, it doesn't matter. You could live the American dream.
TIME editors independently oversee the content of The CEO Moment, including this episode with sponsor Cognizant.

Self-perceived romantic desirability is strongly linked to overall self-esteem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:00:10 UTC
01:00:10 KST

People who consider themselves highly desirable romantic partners also tend to report higher overall self-worth. A recent meta-analysis of data from nearly 12,000 individuals confirmed a strong positive association between self-perceived mate value and global self-esteem. The research was published in the Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy.
Psychologists use the term “mate value” to describe how desirable a person is within the dating market. Historically, researchers tied this concept to evolutionary traits like physical health, financial resources, and social status. More recent approaches emphasize that mate value also depends on specific relationship contexts and personal preferences.
Self-perceived mate value refers to an individual’s own assessment of their romantic desirability compared to potential competitors. It acts as a form of internal bargaining power. This self-assessment guides people toward partners who match their own perceived level of desirability, helping them minimize the risk of romantic rejection.
Self-esteem represents a person’s broad emotional evaluation of their own worth. One prominent psychological framework, known as sociometer theory, suggests that self-esteem functions as an internal gauge of social acceptance. According to this model, people experience high self-esteem when they feel included and valued by others. They experience low self-esteem when they feel rejected.
Evaluating oneself as a good romantic prospect is a highly specific form of social inclusion. Theoretical models suggest that self-perceived mate value and self-esteem operate in a continuous feedback loop. Feeling like a desirable partner might elevate self-esteem, which then breeds the social confidence needed to attract potential mates.
Evolutionary psychology provides additional context for this relationship. From an evolutionary standpoint, human beings possess deep-seated motivations to survive and reproduce. Individuals who believe they possess highly prized mating traits often feel a sense of biological and social fitness, which bolsters their overall self-worth.
Relationships can also be viewed through the lens of social exchange theory. This framework assumes people seek to maximize rewards, like companionship and support, while minimizing emotional costs. People with high self-perceived mate value often feel they bring substantial resources to a relationship, so they expect an equitable exchange and are less likely to settle for imbalanced partnerships.
Early childhood experiences shape how adults navigate these romantic domains. Securely attached individuals generally develop stable self-esteem and hold positive, accurate views of their mate value. Those with anxious or avoidant attachment histories often struggle with fluctuating self-worth and may undervalue what they offer to a romantic partner.
Finally, self-verification theory suggests that people have a strong psychological drive to maintain consistency between their self-concept and the way others treat them. Individuals who view themselves as highly desirable will seek out partners who validate that belief. Conversely, those with low self-perceived mate value might gravitate toward relationships that confirm their negative self-evaluations.
To better understand the strength and consistency of the relationship between self-esteem and romantic desirability, a team of researchers conducted a comprehensive review of existing literature. The team included Sreedevi J. and Saurabh Maheshwari of the Indian Institute of Technology Jodhpur, along with Jeshmeen Deb Barman of the Sikkim Manipal Institute of Technology. They wanted to see if the link between these two psychological concepts held true across different demographics and survey methods.
The investigators performed a meta-analysis, a statistical technique that combines the results of multiple independent studies to identify overarching trends. They searched academic databases for papers containing keywords related to self-esteem and mate selection. They also contacted the authors of previous studies to obtain unpublished correlation data.
The team ultimately gathered 23 research records containing 26 distinct datasets published through the end of 2025. This yielded a large sample of 11,837 participants. The vast majority of these participants were young adults living in Western countries.
The pooled data revealed a strong, positive mathematical correlation between self-perceived mate value and self-esteem. Individuals who rated themselves highly on traits related to romantic desirability consistently reported higher overall self-worth.
Next, the researchers tested whether other variables influenced the strength of this connection. They categorized the data by participant age and gender to see if demographic differences changed the statistical relationship. They also looked at whether the original studies used specific types of survey tools.
Some of the original studies measured mate value by asking participants to rate their own specific traits, such as physical attractiveness or wealth. Other studies used non-trait methods, simply asking participants how desirable they believed they were to the opposite sex. The researchers compared these different survey styles to see if the measurement method altered the results.
The results of these secondary analyses were not statistically significant. The type of survey used to measure self-esteem or mate value did not change the core relationship between the two variables. The researchers noted that both survey styles likely capture the same internalized beliefs about personal desirability.
Gender and age also failed to alter the connection. The link between romantic desirability and self-esteem remained consistent across the board. Men and women of various age groups all demonstrated a strong association between their perceived mate value and their global self-esteem.
This research relies entirely on correlational data. The mathematical association does not prove that feeling like a good catch directly boosts a person’s self-esteem. It is equally possible that possessing high baseline self-esteem makes people view their romantic prospects more optimistically.
The original study authors suggest that the relationship is likely bidirectional. Self-perceived mate value and self-esteem probably feed into one another over time. A positive self-evaluation in the dating market enhances overall confidence, which then makes a person feel even more desirable.
The underlying studies predominantly featured young adults from Western populations. This heavy reliance on specific demographics limits the ability to generalize the findings to older individuals or non-Western cultures. Cultural norms surrounding dating and self-worth can vary widely around the world.
The current data only addresses how people view their own desirability. Future investigations could incorporate external evaluations from peers or independent interviewers. Comparing a person’s internal self-assessment with how others actually perceive them might provide a more complete picture of how dating market dynamics relate to personal self-worth.
The study, “Association Between Self-Perceived Mate Value and Self-Esteem: A Meta-Analysis,” was authored by Sreedevi J., Jeshmeen Deb Barman, and Saurabh Maheshwari.

Kurdish expert: Israel knows how to recognize a nation. It should recognize ours - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

This weekend, on September 5 and 6, the second Jewish and Kurdish diaspora gathering met, and Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar sent a message. For his office, it was a small courtesy. For us it was not small at all, and it is worth explaining why a paragraph from Jerusalem lands so heavily on a people of 40 million.
Kurds are the largest unrecognized nation on earth. Not unrepresented, which is a lesser condition. Unrecognized. There is no seat, no flag at Turtle Bay, no ministry anywhere that receives our envoys as envoys.
Compare us to almost any other stateless national claim and the asymmetry is immediate: Palestinians hold observer status at the United Nations and full diplomatic representation across most of the Western world, and their cause commands parliamentary time in capitals that could not locate Kurdistan on a map.
I do not raise this to diminish anyone’s claim. I raise it because the same international system that found room for one has found none for a nation four times larger.
What that absence looks like on the ground is worth spelling out, because it is not abstract.
In Turkey, when Kurdish is spoken in parliament, whether by an elected member or by a citizen addressing a committee, the official record has entered it as speech “in an unknown language.” The state broadcaster runs a Kurdish channel, TRT Kurdî, funded by the same government whose parliamentary stenographers cannot name the language it broadcasts in.
That is not repression at its most violent. It is repression at its most absurd, and the absurdity is the point: a century of policy has been built on the proposition that we are a clerical error.
The reach extends past Turkey’s borders. In Germany, Kurdish parents holding Turkish passports have found their children’s names constrained by what Turkish law permits, because German registry practice deferred to the naming rules of the applicant’s state of nationality.
Turkish orthography excludes the letters Q, W, and X. Kurdish requires them. So a Kurdish family in Cologne discovers that Ankara has a say in what their daughter is called. Denial of identity does not stop at a frontier. It travels in the passport.
Against that background, consider what Jerusalem has just proved it is willing to do. In December 2025, Israel became the first state in the world to recognize Somaliland. Sa’ar flew there in January. Ambassadors were exchanged by the spring.
Israel looked at a functioning, self-governing people that the international system had spent three decades pretending not to see, and decided that the pretense was not binding. Mogadishu objected. Israel proceeded anyway.
Kurds noticed.
Asking for advocacy
I am not asking for a declaration tomorrow, and I am not going to pretend we have earned one on our present performance. Israel represents its people. We cannot yet say the same. Our political factions have not produced a national congress or any body with standing to speak for the nation, and until they do, no partner has an address to write to.
That failure is ours. I have said so in these pages before, and I will keep saying it, because a movement that will not name its own weakness has no business asking anyone to invest in its strength.
But the fracture is in Kurdish politics, not in Kurdish identity. Where our politicians have failed to build a representative body, our people have not failed to remain a people. And the place where that distinction can be turned into something usable is the diaspora.
This is familiar ground for Jewish readers. The State of Israel was conceived in exile, argued into existence in Basel and Vienna and London long before it was defended at home. Kurds are at the beginning of that road, second generation at most in the societies we now live in, where Jewish communities are measured in centuries.
We are not equals in this. But we are in the same rooms, which is new, and the gatherings of the past two years are where it is happening.
So the practical proposal is narrow. The Jewish Diaspora is the most effective advocacy network any group of people has ever built, and Sa’ar has spent his term strengthening precisely those ties, most recently at the J50 Forum in Jerusalem five days before our own gathering met.
That machinery, turned even partly toward the Kurdish question, would do more for our international standing in a decade than we have managed in a century of asking. Not charity. Advocacy for a cause that pays.
Because it does pay. The governments that guarantee Kurds never see daylight are, with striking consistency, the same governments organized around Israel’s disappearance. Relations with Ankara are at their lowest point in the history of the two states; Sa’ar himself described the Turkish foreign minister’s remarks this July as a call for genocide.
Whatever deference to Turkish sensitivities once constrained Israeli policy toward Kurds, it is difficult to see what remains of it now.
Kurds have been misled and abandoned by Western partners often enough to be careful about who we thank. This is not one of those cases. Israel is doing the one thing we cannot do for ourselves: treating us as a nation in public, at cost, without asking permission. More is possible, and Somaliland is the proof that it is possible.
Israel has been bold before, and recently. Kurds will answer boldness.
The writer, based in Vancouver, is a commentator on Kurdish affairs, Kurdistan, and international politics.

Diehl Develops Ziesel UGV That Can Follow Infantry Soldiers Autonomously
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:58:14 UTC
00:58:14 KST

German company Diehl Defence has presented the Ziesel tracked unmanned ground vehicle (UGV), designed to support infantry units.
The presentation took place at the MSPO exhibition in Poland, Militarnyi reports.
The 350 kg tracked platform can carry a payload of up to 500 kg. The unmanned vehicle measures 1,310 mm in length, 1,230 mm in width, and 600 mm in height, excluding the payload.
The all-electric powertrain provides a maximum torque of 1,000 Nm and allows the vehicle to reach speeds of up to 20 km/h. The platform has a range of up to 40 km and an operational endurance of up to 24 hours. Its design allows it to climb slopes with an inclination of up to 60%.
Diehl Defence’s PLATON-Kit system provides the system’s high level of autonomy. It integrates several control and autonomous-following modes to ease the operator’s workload in combat conditions.
The platform supports remote manual control with assistance functions, as well as a mode that allows it to follow a soldier or another vehicle while maintaining a safe distance.
In Push mode, the UGV moves ahead of the infantry soldier at a set distance, serving as mobile cover. Waypoint-based movement using map data provides autonomous navigation.

Despite recent public pronouncements by Russian President Vladimir Putin that rumors of a fresh troop mobilization were ‘complete nonsense’ and that ‘there is no scenario today that would require mobilization’ recent events suggest the process may have already begun.

According to an article in Deutsche Welle’s Russian service (DW), large numbers, which some estimates put as tens of thousands, are increasingly being summoned to military enlistment offices to verify, clarify and update their military registration records.
Having done this they find that their military ID cards have been modified to include a ‘mobilization order’ that requires them to report to a specific collection point in the event of mobilization,
Such orders were issued prior to the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the previous mass mobilization in the autumn of the same year, but the current level of summonses is unprecedented. DW quotes the Russian internet search engine Yandex Wordstat which has seen a 800% upsurge in the number of searches for ‘mobilization order’.
A Russian lawyer, Artem Klyga, is quoted in the article noting that a summons to an enlistment office to clarify data does not necessarily mean the individual will be mobilized but it will be used to rapidly bring them in once the order is given. He adds that officials have been instructed to prepare the system for any decision Putin makes.
Ukraine Presents Domestically Developed Pegas IFV
Putin’s assurances are not shared by many of those summoned particularly after reports in June told of men reporting to military enlistment offices being taken and pressured into signing military contracts in Russia’s Penza region. According to local reports many were transported to military units where they were held before being sent to the front. Some see this as a ‘dress rehearsal’ for what is to follow.
Western estimates, including those of the US Institute for the Study of War (ISW), suggests that Russia is losing more than 40,000 men killed and wounded at the front compared with around 35,000 volunteers being recruited every month. ISW argues that this gap cannot be supported indefinitely and can only be remedied by ‘mobilization in some form’.
Western intelligence agencies say they are also seeing the signs of preparations for mass conscription in a number of regions that could be a precursor to establish training grounds, feed and arm new recruits. In late July, advertisements began to appear offering vacancies in ‘mobilization preparedness’ and ‘military registration’.
As Politico reported in late August concern among young Russians was such that more than 110,000 had fled in the previous week across the Upper Lars checkpoint between Russia and Georgia, ostensibly for summer holidays, — a loophole that has since been closed off.
DW also pointed out that the 2022 decree on partial mobilization in Russia has never been formally revoked and technically remains in force – another cause for disquiet among those eligible for call up.
The combination of summonses, changes to the military registration systems and aggressive recruitment efforts help explain why Putin’s denials have failed to put the rumors to the rest.

The vessel took part in missile strikes on Syria in 2017 and has been involved in strikes on Ukraine since 2022. It is armed with 3M14 Kalibr cruise missiles, the Shtil-1 surface-to-air missile system and a 100mm A-190 gun.
The R-360 Neptune cruise missile is designed to destroy ships with a displacement of up to 5,000 tonnes and, like other missiles of its class, can be launched from land, surface and air platforms. In April 2022, a Neptune missile was used to sink the Russian cruiser Moskva.
In late 2025, Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine was also using the upgraded Long Neptune version. The Neptune-D system uses RK360L cruise missiles with a range of up to 1,000 km and a 260kg warhead. The missile is designed to strike both land and maritime targets.
Background: It was reported earlier that Ukraine's defence forces and the Unmanned Systems Forces struck a number of Russian military assets in Novorossiysk and Anapa on the night of 8-9 September. Confirmed hits included a Su-33 carrier-based fighter and an Mi-8 helicopter, two Russian radars – a Kasta-2E2 and a 92N6 radar from an S-300/S-400 air defence system – near Gelendzhik, as well as the Project 11356 frigate Admiral Essen.

Could US retaliate against UK over Israeli settlement sanctions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:55:12 UTC
00:55:12 KST

Breadcrumb
Could US retaliate against UK over Israeli settlement sanctions?
The UK's landmark decision to sanction Israeli settlers marks a significant shift in Middle East foreign policy, but could the move expose London to retaliation from the United States over its support for ally Israel?
The possibility emerged after US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee warned of "significant" repercussions if Britain imposed a "boycott and sanctions" on Israeli targets.
Israel has already responded furiously to the measures, including with plans to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem.
Israel also announced that Britain would no longer be permitted to train Palestinian security forces in the West Bank, while 12 British lawmakers and other nationals, including former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn, would be barred from entering the country.
But analysts who spoke to The New Arab said the prospect of Washington following Israel with punitive action against Britain is more complicated, particularly given conflicting signals from the Trump administration amid escalating Israeli settler violence in the West Bank.
What has Washington actually said?
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that Washington would not follow the UK in imposing new measures related to Israeli settlements in the West Bank, but stopped short of directly criticising London's decision.
Rubio's comments contrasted with those of US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, who told the BBC that if Britain imposed a "boycott and sanctions" on Israeli targets, "the repercussions are going to be significant".
Michael Hanna, US programme director at the International Crisis Group, told The New Arab that Rubio's comments carry greater official weight given his position as Secretary of State.
He said the remarks suggested that no major shift in US policy was imminent, indicating that the Trump administration may tolerate the UK's actions for now.
This comes as Axios reported, citing a White House official, that Huckabee's comments were not coordinated with either the White House or State Department and did not reflect the administration's policy.
The report also said US President Donald Trump did not push back against British plans to sanction Israeli settlements when he was briefed on the proposal by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham during private conversations ahead of Tuesday's announcement.
"If we don't see further action and Rubio's stated policy is in fact what prevails, I think it tells us that even this administration, which has been so acquiescent to Israel and Israeli maximalism, that even they have some friction over this issue," Hanna told The New Arab.
"It's reached such a point that even the Trump administration is not willing to stick its neck out to defend Israel on this one set of issues."
Could the US punish Britain?
Daniel Levy, president of the US/Middle East Project (USMEP), told The New Arab that punitive action against the UK was unlikely to be led by the current US administration, despite measures already introduced against entities sanctioning Israel.
"I expect there at most to be warnings rather than actual measures on that front," Levy said. "The fact that the UK showed leadership and brought other countries along and did not do this alone, I think further complicates the picture for the US."
The international nature of the move could therefore make retaliation against Britain more difficult, particularly as Washington is already grappling with several international crises.
"As unpredictable as Trump is, let's acknowledge the context – the US is putting out fires on multiple fronts, and while you can never rule out it starting another fire in its relations and going into another trade and economic sanctions battle, it wouldn't exactly be helpful to an American economy that is not going well, and that is really costing the Republican Party in the lead-up to the midterms," Levy said.
Levy also cited reports detailing US frustrations with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over his handling of the Gaza war, Israel's offensive in Lebanon and hostilities with Iran.
However, he stressed that this did not necessarily translate into direct US pressure on the Israeli government.
"It may mean that the US is rather okay with others taking measures right now," Levy added.
Why could these sanctions matter?
The nature of the British measures could also prove important in determining Washington's response.
"Importantly, the UK measures announced were not just a ban on trade and goods, but also moved into the financial services sector, which is far more consequential," Levy told The New Arab.
"In that respect, there could be a knock-on effect with Europe and others in beginning to move the dial on more serious consequences."
He continued: "The measures announced were serious, but perhaps any US response will be reconsidered when it comes to the details of the sanctions regime being implemented, which, as the Foreign Secretary Miliband noted, will take a little time."
The Times of Israel, citing a White House official, reported that Washington could take further action in the coming days, although any response may be less severe than the measures threatened by Huckabee.
That leaves open the possibility of some form of US response even if Washington stops short of the kind of economic retaliation initially raised by the ambassador.
How has Israel responded?
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called Britain's latest action "morally distorted" and accused the UK of "blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process" ahead of next month's Israeli election.
During Tuesday's announcement, UK Foreign Secretary Miliband told lawmakers that, alongside banning imports of goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, Britain would also introduce measures against companies and individuals providing services to settlements, including "construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate".
France and Canada also said they would ban imports of products from Israeli settlements, while nine other countries, including Denmark and Portugal, endorsed the British action.
Rights groups and politicians have widely described the sanctions as an important, albeit symbolic, step, particularly in relation to goods.
However, critics in the UK have called for more robust action against Israel's settlement project.
Britain, France and Canada were also among the countries that formally recognised the State of Palestine in 2025, as well as having previously imposed sanctions targeting settlements and Israeli ministers over accusations of inciting violence against Palestinians.

Drone threat beyond the Arctic Circle: Russia complains that Ukraine attacked a plant in Yamal
Kyiv • UNN
A drone threat was declared in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug; the likely target was Gazprom Pererabotka’s Novy Urengoy plant. The facility being hit has not been officially confirmed.
On September 9, a drone threat was declared in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug. According to preliminary data, the Novy Urengoy Plant for Preparing Condensate for Transportation may have come under attack, UNN reports, citing the press service of the region’s governor.
Residents have already been urged to remain indoors and stay away from windows.
It should be emphasized that, as of now, there has been no confirmation in the information space from the Russian authorities or Gazprom regarding damage to the facility. Russian official bodies have also not reported that a drone struck the Novy Urengoy Plant for Preparing Condensate for Transportation specifically, nor have they reported a fire or damage to technological equipment. There is also no confirmation regarding possible consequences for the facility’s operations.
What is known about the plant that may have been hit by attack UAVs
The facility is located in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, more than 3,000 km in a straight line from Ukraine. The Novy Urengoy Plant for Preparing Condensate for Transportation is one of the region’s key gas-condensate infrastructure facilities. The facility is part of the Gazprom Pererabotka structure and prepares gas condensate for further transportation and processing.
The plant’s design capacity after modernization is approximately 19.5 million tonnes of raw materials per year. The facility receives unstable gas condensate from fields in Western Siberia, including the Yamburg, Zapolyarnoye, and Urengoy fields. The plant produces, among other things, stable and de-ethanized condensate, a broad fraction of light hydrocarbons, and liquefied hydrocarbon gases. Some of the prepared raw material is sent by pipeline for further processing.
In 2021, a large-scale fire occurred at the Novy Urengoy Plant for Preparing Condensate for Transportation, at the condensate de-ethanization unit. After the accident, Gazprom implemented a project to build a new unit, which was commissioned in 2024.
In addition
Amid the alleged UAV threat, restrictions on the operation of aviation infrastructure were also recorded in Novy Urengoy. In particular, flights from and to the city were delayed.
We remind you
As reported by Denis Shtilerman, co-founder of the attack-drone manufacturing company Fire Point, the Ukrainian long-range FP-1 UAV traveled approximately 3,200 km and struck the Novy Urengoy Plant for Preparing Condensate for Transportation (ZPKT) in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug.

Nigeria names new commander to lead military operations against Boko Haram
ABUJA, Sept 9 - Nigeria has appointed a new commander to lead military operations against Boko Haram and its Islamic State-backed splinter faction in the northeast, replacing the head of the operation less than two years after his appointment, an army spokesperson said on Wednesday.
The appointment comes ahead of presidential elections due in January, with insecurity remaining a major concern after years of insurgent violence, banditry and kidnappings across parts of the country.
Major General Ibikunle Ademola Ajose, who previously served at Army Headquarters in Abuja, takes over from Major General Abdulsalam Abubakar, the 15th commander of Operation Hadin Kai, who assumed the role in April 2025.
The insurgency by Boko Haram and its splinter group, Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), has killed more than 40,000 people and displaced millions since 2009, according to data from the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED).
Security concerns disrupted voting in parts of northeastern Nigeria during the last presidential election and remain a challenge ahead of next year's polls.
The army did not link the reshuffle to any recent attacks in the northeast. The change was part of a wider military shake-up involving 14 other generals, which the army said was aimed at improving operational effectiveness, strengthening leadership and aligning command structures with Nigeria's evolving security challenges, spokesperson Appolonia Anele said in a statement. Netanyahu calls claim he was warned of Oct. 7 attack "malicious libel"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:50:34 UTC
00:50:34 KST

Netanyahu rejects claim he was warned ahead of Oct. 7, as 2023 attack fuels pre-election furor
As Israelis prepare to vote next month in a tightly contested legislative race that will determine the country's next government, they're still debating how their country was caught by surprise on Oct. 7, 2023, when the U.S.-designated terrorist group Hamas stormed across the border and killed more than 1,200 people and kidnapped hundreds more.
The discussion got new fuel when the Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported Monday that, just days before the attack that sparked the war in Gaza and arguably the much wider conflict across the Middle East, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned in a phone call by the leader of the United Arab Emirates that Gaza's Hamas leaders were planning a major assault.
The Haaretz report said Netanyahu did not pass on the warning to Israel's security leaders.
CBS News has not independently confirmed Haaretz's reporting, which the Israeli newspaper said it stood by in a Tuesday statement.
The day Hamas attacked, Israel was caught by surprise, despite having observed preparations by Hamas for the assault, some of which the group itself posted in videos online.
Netanyahu's office denied in a Tuesday statement that he had received any explicit warning from the Emirati leader leading up to the attack, and said he had "instructed his attorneys to file a defamation lawsuit" against Haaretz and the reporter who filed the story.
"No conversation took place between the Prime Minister and the President of the United Arab Emirates," Netanyahu's office said. "This is a malicious libel with clear political timing, as part of the left's election campaign, and more such false smears will follow."
Israel's national legislative elections take place on Oct. 27, and there is currently no clear front-runner.
Former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who is running against Netanyahu in the upcoming election and has met with the Emirati leader himself several times in recent years, wrote in a social media post Tuesday that he believed the Haaretz report was true, adding that Netanyahu's "ignoring of the warnings is criminal negligence."
The Haaretz report and subsequent denial by Netanyahu also gave a rare look into the high-stakes diplomacy of the Middle East.
Netanyahu's office confirmed in its statement that, as reported by Haaretz, whenever the Emirati leader does wish to speak with the Israeli leader, a representative from the UAE travels to Netanyahu's office and provides a specially encrypted phone for the conversation.
Netanyahu's office said Tuesday that there is no record of a call between the Israeli and Emirati leaders from the beginning of September until Oct. 7, 2023. There was no record of an Emirati visitor to the prime minister's office during that period either, Netanyahu's office said.
The check for any such visit or phone call was conducted by the Prime Minister's Office, the National Security Council (NSC) and the Military Secretariat, Netanyahu's office said.
The UAE government said in a statement Tuesday that, since the country established normal ties with Israel five years ago, it has maintained "open and direct lines of communication." The statement neither confirmed nor denied the Haaretz report about the phone call.
Netanyahu has argued that none of his advisers or security officials woke him up on Oct. 7 until Hamas' attack was underway, and that it wasn't he who failed to protect Israel that day, but the heads of the country's security agencies.
Questions over Netanyahu's actions on that day burst back into public debate last week after Israel's national broadcaster Kan News revealed that three hours passed between Netanyahu being woken up by his military secretary at 6:27 a.m., as the invasion began, and when he first requested to speak with the country's top general.
Netanyahu's office released a schedule roughly confirming that timeline, but it added that he spoke with Israel's defense minister around 8 a.m. that day, on his way to the ministry of defense.
In the weeks and days leading up to the attack, Netanyahu was warned by top security and political officials that Israel's enemies were considering an attack while the country was being rocked by protests against an effort by Netanyahu's government to overhaul the judicial system, according to statements issued by Netanyahu and security officials at the time.
Netanyahu has argued that those warnings did not specifically mention an attack originating from Gaza, or a clear timeline. He has also argued that the assessment of his security chiefs at the time was that Hamas was not interested in a major escalation.
So far, the Israeli leader has rejected demands for a formal state inquiry into the Oct. 7 attack, which is regular procedure in Israel after national catastrophes.
Netanyahu's political opponents have said they would establish one immediately, if they win power in October.

BEIJING, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese mainland remains the "best choice" for Taiwan businesses seeking to invest and expand, a mainland spokesperson said Wednesday, rejecting a recent claim by Taiwan authorities that businesses on the island should exercise caution over such investment.
Chen Binhua, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said the mainland also offers fertile ground for innovation and development, as well as strong support for businesses seeking to defuse risks.

Mainland exports to Taiwan rose 31.6 percent to 62.17 billion dollars, while mainland imports from Taiwan increased 24.7 percent to 159.63 billion dollars, he said.
"The figures showed the close economic links between the two sides and the strength of their shared interests, as well as stable and resilient industrial and supply chains across the Taiwan Strait," Chen said.
The mainland economy's vitality and resilience have provided a source of momentum and "hard-won certainty" for the global economy, while creating new opportunities and space for greater cross-Strait economic cooperation and integration, Chen said.
The Taiwan-based Straits Exchange Foundation (SEF) plans to increase its budget by 10 million New Taiwan dollars (about 320,000 U.S. dollars) in 2027 for raising awareness of travel safety on the mainland. "My response to the SEF's recent move is to remember its original mission and do more useful work," Chen said.

"They all came happily and returned safely," Chen said.

Chen called the measure another attempt by the DPP authorities to intimidate Taiwan residents and obstruct cross-Strait exchanges and travel.
Taiwan residents traveling on the mainland enjoy the same legal protection as their mainland counterparts, he noted.
If their lawful rights and interests are harmed, they could file complaints with the tourism department where the tourism operator is located, where the travel contract is signed, or where the dispute occurs, he said, adding that they can also call the government service hotline or contact local Taiwan affairs offices for assistance.
"None of these are problems. The ones creating problems are the DPP authorities," Chen said.
The Taiwan question is left by a full-blown civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. In 1949, the remnants of the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation, though the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. ■

PACE says Russian assets should be used to pay compensation to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:50:00 UTC
00:50:00 KST

PACE says Russian assets should be used to pay compensation to Ukraine
As reported by Ukrinform, this is stated on the institution’s website.
The committee approved a draft resolution and recommendation based on a report by Tony Vaughan (the United Kingdom).
In two interstate cases brought by Ukraine, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has already found Russia responsible for serious human rights violations caused by its war of aggression. At the same time, the amount of just satisfaction that Russia must pay Ukraine has not yet been determined.
“But given the scale of the damage inflicted on Ukraine, which is unprecedented in the history of the Council of Europe, any awards could potentially amount to billions, tens of billions, or hundreds of billions of euros”, PACE’s Legal Affairs Committee pointed out.
The parliamentarians concluded that directing Russian state assets toward compensation payments to Ukraine in war-related cases would be consistent with international law.
“The repurposing of Russian state assets to pay compensation to Ukraine in cases concerning the war would constitute a lawful countermeasure under international law,” the approved document states.
Following the launch of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, about €260 billion in assets belonging to the Central Bank of Russia were immobilized. Of this amount, approximately €210 billion is held in the EU.
The Committee proposed establishing a special funding mechanism under the auspices of the Council of Europe that would receive these assets and disburse the funds to Ukraine.
PACE recalled that Russia was expelled from the Council of Europe on March 16, 2022, and six months later ceased to be a party to the European Convention on Human Rights. However, Russia remains obliged to comply with ECHR judgments concerning violations committed before the Convention ceased to apply to it.
“This obligation under international law does not diminish with time and cannot be set aside by Russian domestic law,” the parliamentarians pointed out.
The Committee also called on states to ensure that ECHR judgments against the Russian Federation can be enforced at the national level. To this end, national legislation should allow applicants to seek recovery of the compensation awarded to them for as long as Russia refuses to pay voluntarily.
In addition, the Committee proposed creating a public list of individuals responsible for large-scale human rights violations established by ECHR judgments who have not yet been held accountable. The list should be regularly updated and shared with Council of Europe member states, the EU, and the ICC to facilitate targeted sanctions or criminal prosecution.
The draft resolutions and recommendation approved by the committee are scheduled to be submitted to the PACE plenary session on September 30.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukraine supports revisiting the idea of using frozen Russian assets.

The victim, a resident of Antalya's Aksu district, was affected by smoke from the wildfire before suffering the heart attack, Aksu Mayor Isa Yildirim said in a social media post.

Aerial operations began early Tuesday, with five aircraft and more than 10 helicopters joining the response. Around 110 firefighting vehicles and more than 600 personnel were also deployed to contain the blaze.
A highway connecting Antalya with the neighboring province of Isparta was also temporarily closed as a precaution, the reports said.
Firefighting continued on Wednesday with ground crews backed by aircraft and helicopters. Local residents also helped emergency teams keep the flames from reaching populated areas, private broadcaster NTV reported.
More than 2,000 homes in the region were affected by power outages, Anadolu Agency reported.
Antalya is scheduled to host the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in November, bringing together world leaders and climate negotiators to discuss global action on climate change. ■

Direct elections of county-, township-level lawmakers underway orderly in China: official

2026-09-09
23:49:07 CST
00:49:07 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- China is currently carrying out a new round of direct elections of county- and township-level lawmakers in an orderly manner, according to a senior legislator on Wednesday.
More than one billion voters will directly elect over 2.6 million deputies to the people's congresses at the county and township levels, representing a vivid practice of whole-process people's democracy, said Song Rui, deputy secretary general of the National People's Congress (NPC) Standing Committee, at a press conference.
Song noted that deputies to people's congresses at all levels serve as a bridge between the Party and the state and the people. He urged further support for the deputies in performing their duties, maintaining close contact with the people, conveying their views and concerns, and helping resolve practical problems in accordance with the law.
China's people's congress system has a multi-tiered structure, with the NPC at the top and congresses at the provincial, municipal, county and township levels. Deputies are elected at each level every five years to represent the people's interests.
Under the country's electoral law, deputies to county- and township-level people's congresses are directly elected by voters, while deputies to people's congresses above the county level are elected by deputies at the next lower level.
In the previous round of elections, which wrapped up in 2022, 2.62 million county- and township-level deputies were elected by more than one billion voters through "one person, one vote," making it one of the world's largest democratic practices. ■

India launches ORV Sagar Manthan, boosting ocean research fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:48:06 UTC
00:48:06 KST

ORV Sagar Manthan, built under the Deep Ocean Mission at a cost of around Rs 840 crore, will boost India’s ocean research capabilities.
NEW DELHI: The Government on Wednesday launched state-of-the-art ocean research vessel ORV Sagar Manthan at Rishi Bankim Shipyard in Kolkata, boosting India’s efforts towards self-reliance in oceanographic science and maritime technology.Constructed under Vertical-4 (Deep Ocean Survey and Exploration) of the government’s flagship Deep Ocean Mission (DOM) at a cost of around Rs 840 crore, the vessel is an all-weather, multidisciplinary platform. It is engineered to operate in extreme oceanic environments, including the Southern Ocean, with a projected service life of 30 years.The ORV Sagar Manthan, designed, engineered and constructed by defence public sector undertaking Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Limited (GRSE), will gradually replace the iconic 43-year-old ORV Sagar Kanya, procured from Germany in 1983.
“Today, the world knows very little about our oceans, yet they provide vital inputs about melting polar glaciers, maritime impact, and climate dynamics. Solid data collected by vessels like ORV Sagar Manthan will allow India to lead the global path in disaster prevention, take corrective environmental measures, and play a pivotal role in global ocean geopolitics,” said Union minister of earth sciences Jitendra Singh, who virtually joined the launch event.
ORV Sagar Manthan will support multidisciplinary exploration along Indian Ocean mid-oceanic ridges to identify multi-metal hydrothermal sulphide mineralisation, establish environmental baselines and collect upper-air data. It integrates dynamic positioning, multibeam bathymetry, multichannel seismic systems, sub-bottom profiling, weather radar, drop keels and deployment facilities for remotely operated and autonomous underwater vehicles.
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. stefano boeri plans gardened affordable housing in ibiza as four modular timber blocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:45:57 UTC
00:45:57 KST

Stefano Boeri Architetti has won the competition for Sa Casa, a new affordable housing complex in Ibiza built around a modular timber system. Developed for Spanish public housing agency Casa 47, the proposal divides roughly 190 apartments among four residential volumes, leaving the center of the site open as a planted communal space. The buildings step and shift across the sloping plot instead of forming one continuous perimeter, creating a series of passages and courtyards that lead toward a public square at the center.
The project is planned for Ca n’Escandell, a large public housing development on the edge of Ibiza Town. Here, Sa Casa occupies a 5,505-square-meter parcel and forms part of a wider neighborhood planned to contain more than 500 protected apartments. The winning scheme was selected from 13 competition entries, with the jury pointing to the way its separated volumes negotiate the terrain and open the housing toward the shared landscape between them.
Stefano Boeri Architetti divides Sa Casa into four residential volumes around a planted center
CLT MODULES GIVE THE APARTMENTS ROOM TO CHANGE
Stefano Boeri Architetti plans the main structural system with cross-laminated timber, with a high degree of prefabrication intended to shorten work on site and reduce construction waste. The logic of the CLT frame extends directly into the apartments. Instead of fixing each unit around one household type, the architects use a modular layout that can be reconfigured as occupants and their needs change over time, including homes adapted for residents with reduced mobility.
With this flexibility, shared work areas and communal rooms can be reorganized within the same architectural system, giving the building a degree of elasticity long after construction is complete. It is a useful idea for public housing, where the people moving through one apartment over decades may have very different ideas of what a home needs to contain.
CLT construction gives the apartments a modular structural system
FOUR BUILDINGS GATHER AROUND A GARDEN
From the outside, the fragmentation gives Sa Casa much of its character. Long timber-framed elevations face one another across planted paths and terraces, while deep balconies introduce another layer between each apartment and the landscape. Mediterranean vegetation runs through the courtyards and continues onto the roofs, where planting becomes part of the environmental strategy as well as the architecture.
The open center is especially important to the proposal. Instead of treating circulation as leftover space between apartment blocks, the architects use it to build a loose sequence from the surrounding neighborhood toward the central square. The buildings frame this route without sealing it off to give residents shared outdoor space while keeping the complex connected to the city around it.
Mediterranean planting moves through the paths and onto the roofs
SHADE, AIR AND WATER BECOME PART OF THE PLAN
To reduce reliance on mechanical cooling within each home, the climate of Ibiza enters the architecture through orientation and cross ventilation. Green roofs add shade and help temper exposed surfaces, while photovoltaic panels provide renewable energy. Rainwater collection and greywater reuse are also integrated into the scheme, with native planting selected to work within the island’s Mediterranean conditions.
Sa Casa is currently an ongoing project, with Stefano Boeri Architetti responsible for the architectural design and SOCOTEC Spain working as local architect and sustainability consultant. The scheme also arrives at a moment when Ibiza faces heavy pressure on its housing supply. Here, the studio’s familiar interest in vegetation moves into a different area: publicly funded rental housing built from repeatable timber pieces, with enough flexibility in the plan to keep changing after residents move in.
deep balconies create shaded outdoor extensions to the apartments

Jamaica’s plea to the king: use your authority to ensure colonial slavery is examined | Olivia Grange
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:44:11 UTC
00:44:11 KST

On 6 September 1781, the Zong slave ship set out on the final leg of its voyage to Black River, Jamaica. Four hundred and forty two enslaved Africans were on board – twice the number of people the ship could safely accommodate.
Twelve weeks later, 132 enslaved people were murdered by the ship’s crew by being pushed overboard to their deaths. The crew’s justification was the ship had insufficient water supplies to keep everyone alive for the rest of the voyage – a claim later proved false in the British courts.
This event, and the legal case that followed, added significant weight to the abolitionist movement in the UK, as did uprisings throughout the Caribbean led by the enslaved.
My ancestors achieved their emancipation in 1834, more than 50 years on from the horrors of the Zong. It took a further 128 years for Jamaicans to achieve our independence, on 6 August 1962.
At that time, Jamaica ceased to be a British colony. But the legacies of our colonial past linger, not least because we remain a member of the Commonwealth, with King Charles as our head of state.
The consequences of the slave trade reverberate deeply to this day. The UK drew immense wealth from Jamaica during the colonial era, but centuries of exploitation left us with an economic and social deficit we are still fighting to overcome.
Our natural resources were ravaged during the colonial period, leaving us one of the most vulnerable regions in the world in relation to the climate crisis and extreme weather events.
Our infrastructure is massively underdeveloped; our most talented young people often choose to immigrate to the US or come here to the UK. Poverty levels remain high; educational disadvantage persists; health outcomes are poor – all of this can be directly linked to our history of enslavement and colonialism.
While the government of Jamaica works tirelessly to address the economic and social deficits, legacy issues persist.
Here in the UK, meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of people have African-Caribbean heritage.
It is against this backdrop that we have, this week, filed a petition with King Charles, asking him to refer three specific questions on transatlantic chattel enslavement to the judicial committee of the privy council. The questions focus on whether enslavement in Jamaica was ever lawful and whether there is an obligation on the UK to provide some form of reparatory remedy.
It is important to stress we are not asking King Charles to answer these questions himself. Rather, the people of Jamaica are asking him, as our head of state, to allow our case to have a fair hearing in the British courts.
Drawing on the Judicial Committee Act of 1833 – which confers a special power on King Charles to refer questions of legal and constitutional importance to the judicial committee – this is the first time any Commonwealth state has pursued this legal route for the cause of reparatory justice. It is, in fact, such a rarely used legal route that it took us some time – with both the palace and the privy council – to confirm the exact process for filing the petition correctly.
In pursuing this route, we are placing our faith in the British legal system, one of the longest-established in the world.
We are seeking a chance to put forward the legal argument for reparations – and our legal case coincides with growing political and public momentum on this issue.
In March, the UN passed a motion, recognising enslavement as “the gravest crime against humanity”. In May, Pope Leo XIV made a historic apology for the Vatican’s role in legitimising enslavement.
In June, heads of state, policymakers and activists from more than 80 countries (including some former European colonial powers) gathered in Ghana for the Accra Reparatory Justice Conference. A Global Advisory Council on Reparatory Justice was established after the event, of which our own prime minister, Dr Andrew Holness, is a member.
Just last week, the UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) issued guidance stating countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and to take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination.
Now, through our petition, Jamaica is adding our own distinct effort to the global campaign for reparatory justice, aiming to test the legal principles of relevance to this issue.
Our petition has been endorsed by the heads of government of all Caricom countries, while Ghana’s president, John Dramani Mahama, has also expressed his strong support.
King Charles has previously expressed deep personal sorrow about the history of enslavement. He has the constitutional power and the personal moral authority to allow this question to now be legally examined. Two hundred and forty-five years on from the Zong massacre, we are asking him to grant this request.
Olivia Grange is the Jamaican government’s minister for culture, gender, entertainment and sport

====================================================================================================

As the UK sanctions Israeli settlements, is the two-state solution dead?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:43:29 UTC
00:43:29 KST

As the UK sanctions Israeli settlements, is the two-state solution dead?
Analysts say UK move far from enough to drive momentum for Palestinian statehood.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the United Kingdom will sanction illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, describing the move as “overdue” and necessary to “salvage” a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
He made the comments on Tuesday as 11 nations joined the UK in supporting or considering curbs on trade in goods with settlements that are a barrier to a future Palestinian state.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3UK bans goods from Israeli West Bank settlements: What that really means
- list 2 of 3Nicaragua urges ICJ to reject Germany’s bid to throw out Gaza genocide case
- list 3 of 3Israeli parties submit slates for October Knesset elections
But analysts say the step is far from enough to drive momentum for Palestinian statehood, threatened by ever-expanding settlements in the West Bank and an increasingly hostile Israeli political environment.
Tahani Mustafa, a lecturer in international relations at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera the latest anti-settlement measures are “modest” and unlikely to have a significant impact on ambitions for Palestinian statehood.
“After three decades of breakneck settlement expansion, Palestinian territory is only being held together by its sinews,” said Mustafa. “If what remains is still territorially viable as a state, it is only barely so. Much more decisive action is needed to salvage the two-state solution and a durable lasting solution to the conflict.”
Settlements dividing Palestinian territory
More than 30 years after the Oslo Accords set out a negotiating process aimed at resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, the creation of a Palestinian state alongside Israel has remained the foundation of international efforts to forge peace.
But since the Oslo process began in 1993, the number of Israeli settlers in the West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, has ballooned from about 260,000 to more than 700,000, according to the Palestinian Bureau of Statistics, posing a glaring roadblock to the plan.
The challenge is not just the raw number of settlers, but their geographic spread. Today, many Israeli settlements are embedded deep inside West Bank areas that would be needed for a contiguous Palestinian state, including near major Palestinian urban centres such as Nablus, Salfit and Hebron.
Israel’s recent E1 settlement plan, which would build thousands of illegal housing units between the Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim and East Jerusalem, is a case in point. The plan would effectively split the West Bank in two and fully sever it from East Jerusalem, which Palestinians seek as their future capital.
Experts have long said Israel will need to dismantle some of its West Bank settlements, as it did in the Gaza Strip in 2005, to make room for a cohesive Palestinian state. But many Israeli settlements, especially those closer to Israel’s pre-war 1967 borders, would likely need to be addressed through land swaps.
“A complete withdrawal from some of the deeply embedded settlements is highly unlikely,” so land swaps would be the only way to create some form of Palestinian “territorial integrity”, Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
However, such an arrangement – under which Israeli settlements close to the pre-1967 borders would become part of Israel and some “northern Arab-Israeli communities would be integrated into a Palestinian state” – would be “highly controversial” and face blowback from multiple communities, said Krieg.
He argued that Israelis would be certain to oppose any forced withdrawal from West Bank settlements, while some “Arab-Israelis may not want to live within a Palestinian state”.
Palestinian citizens of Israel make up approximately 21 percent of Israel’s overall population but are treated as second- or third-class citizens at the institutional level. According to rights groups, several dozen Israeli laws actively discriminate against Palestinian citizens across a number of issues, including education and housing.
Israeli ‘consensus’ against Palestinian state
Beyond the physical obstacle created by settlements is the Israeli political landscape, in which the idea of a Palestinian state has become toxic.
The government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appears to be among the most hardline in Israel’s history on the issue. Netanyahu has emphatically ruled out the prospect of a Palestinian state, while his far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also oversees Israeli settlements in the West Bank, has celebrated blocking Palestinian statehood as a badge of honour.
The views of Netanyahu’s most influential domestic critics do not deviate much. His top rival in elections slated for October, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has promised not to allow the establishment of a Palestinian state. And Naftali Bennett, a Netanyahu rival from the far right, fervently opposes Palestinian statehood.
As for the Israeli public, a June poll by the Council for a Secure America found that only 22 percent of Jewish Israelis favour a two-state solution, while 63 percent oppose it.
“The consensus within Israel, socially and politically, does not allow for any party to make any steps towards a Palestinian state,” said Krieg.
Meanwhile, Israel’s closest ally, the United States, is unlikely to apply significant pressure over Israel’s settlement policy so long as President Donald Trump remains in office for the next two and a half years, he added.
Krieg said a “best-case scenario” is for Israel’s next elected government to reverse some of the country’s recent settlement advances.
John Strawson, professor at the University of East London, said that any new Israeli government is “unlikely to support a Palestinian state”, but that a more moderate Israeli government may at least “stop the ethnic cleansing and other moves which are aimed at making that impossible”.
“Removing Netanyahu is the first step towards a two-state solution,” said Strawson.
Two states are the ‘only alternative to violence’
If the two-state model is still alive at all, it is largely due to pressure from the international community.
More than 150 countries, including the majority of European Union nations, have recognised Palestinian statehood. And several Arab states with whom Israel seeks better ties have indicated Palestinian statehood is a precondition for normalisation with Israel.
Krieg said Tuesday’s move by the UK and the 11 other mostly European nations is an “overdue step in the right direction”, but also “shows the laziness and lack of creativity on the part of the international community to actually think outside the box in terms of a two-state solution”.
Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, said that while the settlement sanctions are concerning to Israel, other previous anti-settlement measures, such as 2013 EU restrictions on funds for Israeli entities operating in occupied Palestinian territory, “changed little on the ground”.
He said the latest sanctions may be “too late” and “too limited … to save the two-state solution”.
Strawson said that while a two-state solution may “seem optimistic”, it is the only alternative to “permanent war and violence”.
