Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:43:00 UTC
00:43:00 KST

Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes
September 9, 2026
Iranian authorities have launched a clampdown on cafes in the capital, Tehran, in recent months, suspecting them of fostering anti-government sentiment and facilitating protests.
According to the human rights organization HRANA, at least seven cafes and restaurants were shut down on July 19 alone for allegedly failing to comply with mandatory hijab rules.
Previously, some media outlets, including Javan, a newspaper affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have described cafes as "gathering places for protesters" who, in their view, pose a threat to "national security."
Most recently, the "Vanak Park" cafes in Tehran were sealed, resulting in at least 200 people losing their jobs.
Crackdown on cafes
Authorities believe cafes, because of their widespread presence and popularity, could play a role in organizing mass protests.
The government's fears are rooted in the latest wave of protests in Iran, which began on December 28, 2025, and grew into the country's largest uprising since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
Saediniya, a well-known cafe chain with 10 branches in Iran, closed its branches on this day in support of calls for strikes. It was subsequently accused of engaging in "propaganda against the state."
Iran's Supreme Court has now upheld the sentence of Sadegh Saedinia, the owner of the cafe chain, to 12 years and six months in prison, along with the confiscation of his assets.
He was arrested over his support for the protests, and all branches of his cafe chain were confiscated and shut down by judicial order.
Other cafes, including "Lamiz" and "Voria," faced a broadly similar fate. Voria is owned by a prominent Iranian footballer. Both were sealed by judicial order because of their indirect support for calls to protest. Cafe closures have not been confined to periods of protest, however, and the practice continues.
The rise of the cafe culture
Tehran has seen a surge in the number of cafes over the past decade, rising from around 300 in the early 2010s to as many as 4,000 now, according to various estimates.
Some experts attribute the growing number to changes in urban lifestyles in recent years. They see this as more than the expansion of a particular type of business and describe it as a sign of wider social and cultural changes within Iranian society.
"The explosive growth of cafes in society can, to some extent, be seen as a social response to living in a state of chronic crisis," Saba Alaleh, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst whose work focuses on political and social issues, told DW's Persian service.
"In such circumstances, people are not simply looking to consume or be entertained. They are looking for a place to temporarily distance themselves from the pressures of everyday life," she said.
"In this sense, the cafe becomes a third space. It is neither home nor the workplace, but a space between the two where people can briefly step away from their everyday roles and pressures, connect with others, and feel that life is still somewhat manageable and normal."
The cafe trend has become particularly popular among Gen Z, who are bearing the brunt of runaway inflation and steep living costs in Iran.
"The young people who gather in these cafes do not necessarily come from affluent backgrounds," Nasser, a cafe owner in Tehran, told DW. "In many parts of Tehran, young people from the middle class also meet at cafes, and many of our customers belong to this group."
The political role of cafes
Even before the latest bout of nationwide protests that began at the end of last year, shutting down cafes was common practice for the Iranian government.
Most of these crackdowns and closures, however, were carried out under the pretext of enforcing compulsory hijab.
The protests that began in late December 2025 changed that, with cafes becoming the target more often and for varied reasons.
"They shut down our cafe on the pretext that we had served customers who were not wearing the hijab, but that is only an excuse," Nasser said.
"Outside, on the streets of Tehran, women and girls have effectively abandoned the compulsory hijab, yet the government expects us not to allow them into the cafe," he added.
Maintaining control over social spaces
Alaleh said the issue is no longer simply about cracking down on women for not wearing the hijab.
"Authoritarian governments generally seek to control the flow of information, social interactions and the organization of citizens," she pointed out. "Any space beyond the direct supervision of those in power that allows trust, dialogue and social ties to develop can weaken part of the government's monopoly over the social sphere."
The expert said the crackdown on cafes and cafegoers is part of the government's efforts to preserve its monopoly over social spaces.
She underlined that to a security apparatus, even a group of young people casually sitting together can represent the emergence of an independent social network outside the formal structures of power.
"The broader and more deeply rooted these independent networks become, the more difficult it is for the government to maintain exclusive control over the public sphere," added Alaleh.

Gold Medal of Catalonia Awarded to Italian Scientist Caterina Biscari
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
17:42:18 CEST
00:42:18 KST

The president of the Generalitat of Catalonia, Salvador Illa, awarded the “Medalla d’Or de la Generalitat” to Italian scientist Caterina Biscari during a ceremony in Barcelona attended by the Italian Consul General in Barcelona, Gabriele Luca Fava, and the Embassy’s scientific attaché, Sergio Scopetta.
                                    
                                       
				   Established in 1978, the Gold Medal of the Generalitat is the highest honor bestowed by the Autonomous Community of Catalonia and has been awarded to universally renowned figures such as Salvador Dalí, Joan Miró, Pau Casals, Josep Carreras, and Montserrat Caballé.
                                    
                                       
				A physicist and director of the Alba Synchrotron—one of Spain’s major research facilities—Caterina Biscari is the first non-Spanish citizen to receive this honor. 
    The official citation states that “Biscari has strengthened the international profile of research conducted in Catalonia. Her scientific career combines scientific excellence, service to society, and collaborative leadership. She serves as a role model for women in science and has helped raise the visibility of women in decision-making positions within European research.”
   Caterina Biscari, born in Sicily, attended the Italian State School in Madrid and earned her bachelor’s degree from the Complutense University. She subsequently earned her Ph.D. from the University of Naples Federico II. As a researcher at the National Institute of Nuclear Physics (INFN), she specializes in particle accelerator physics, a field in which Italy boasts a long tradition of excellence, dating back to the pioneering studies of Edoardo Amaldi and Bruno Touschek at the INFN’s Frascati National Laboratories (LNF), where Biscari began her career. 
  From there, her work expanded to other major institutions, such as CERN in Geneva and, more recently, the National Center for Oncological Hadrontherapy (CNAO) in Pavia, where she has conducted fundamental, applied, and health-related research. Since 2012, she has been the director of the Alba accelerator in the Barcelona area. Alba is a synchrotron light source that enables the study of the properties of matter with a wide range of applications in the life sciences and materials science, relevant to both academia and industrial research. Since its founding, more than 10,000 researchers and over 100 companies have used Alba for their studies.
                                    
                                       
				     Already an Officer of the Order of the Star of Italy and winner of the “Aldo Olcese 2026” award—established by the Italian Embassy in Madrid in memory of the distinguished compatriot who passed away prematurely last year— Caterina Biscari has consistently collaborated with the numerous scientific outreach initiatives organized by the Embassy and the Consulate General in Barcelona. The awarding of the “Medalla d’Or de la Generalitat” is further recognition of the excellence of the Italian education and research system and of our tradition in accelerator physics.

China responded to U.S. statements about the “harmful” development of artificial intelligence ahead of the planned talks between the American and Chinese leaders — Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, UNN reports, citing AP.
Details

Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:38:58 UTC
00:38:58 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities.
The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds.
The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools.
In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508).
Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463).
In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU.
A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497).
Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading.
In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading.
In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland
Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”.
However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”.
Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports.
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Daniel Tilles is editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland. He has written on Polish affairs for a wide range of publications, including Foreign Policy, POLITICO Europe, EUobserver and Dziennik Gazeta Prawna.

‘Wanted to teach him a lesson’: Accused on assault that killed Delhi musician

Accused wanted to ‘teach him a lesson’, police say
NEW DELHI: The men accused of killing Manipuri musician Chongtham Vikram Singh in southeast Delhi allegedly wanted to “teach him a lesson” for objecting to noise outside his home, but did not expect the assault to turn fatal, police said on Wednesday.During questioning, the accused allegedly told police that they assaulted the 54-year-old musician with fists and blows after he objected to the commotion outside his residence in Kilokari, according to the police, as cited by news agency PTI.Singh had on some occasions complained to the owner of a nearby dhaba about the noise caused by people gathering there, a senior police officer said. However, police had not received any formal complaint from Singh regarding the noise.The dhaba remained open until around midnight and attracted customers from neighbouring areas as well as students living nearby, police said.
Police examine racial angle, dhaba owner’s role
Police said they were examining all aspects of the case, including whether there was any racial angle. So far, the investigation has not revealed any instance of a racial slur being used against Singh during the altercation, a police source said.The FIR registered at Sunlight Colony police station on the complaint of Singh's son mentions Section 103(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, pertaining to group murder in circumstances covered by the provision.
Police are awaiting the post-mortem report to ascertain the exact nature of the injuries sustained by Singh. Prima facie, he appears to have suffered internal injuries that led to his death.The police are also examining the role of the dhaba owner and its operations. So far, no irregularity in the functioning of the establishment has come to light, sources said. Action would be taken against the owner if anything emerges during the investigation.CCTV footage is being scrutinised and witnesses are being questioned to establish the sequence of events and the circumstances that led to the assault.
Singh died hours after assault
The incident took place around 11.30 pm on Sunday when Singh went downstairs after hearing a commotion outside his home.According to the complaint, when his son heard his father shouting, he opened the door and saw a group of men kicking and punching him.Singh subsequently returned upstairs but complained of breathlessness. His 20-year-old son Yaiphaba took him to Holy Family Hospital, where he succumbed to his injuries around 6 am the following day, police said.Seven men have been arrested and a juvenile apprehended in connection with the case. The accused have been identified as Bharat Kumar, 19, Pramod, 26, Ramzan Khan, 22, Deepanshu, 21, Mohan Vishwakarma, 32, Vijay, 36, and Mannu, 26.
Northeast body seeks swift, impartial probe
The killing has sparked concern among members of Delhi's northeastern community, with several residents alleging that people from the region face racial slurs and discrimination in the national capital.The North Eastern Students' Organisation (NESO) on Wednesday condemned Singh's killing and demanded a swift and impartial probe.NESO chairman Samuel B Jyrwa said the incident was deeply disturbing and called for all those responsible to be brought to justice.“It is deeply disturbing that a person can lose his life merely for raising an objection to disturbance outside his own home. We demand a transparent and impartial investigation and exemplary punishment for every person found responsible,” Jyrwa said in a statement, as cited by PTI.Jyrwa said the killing could not be viewed in isolation from what he described as continuing harassment, racial discrimination, stereotyping, intimidation and violence faced by people from the Northeast in different parts of mainland India.“For years, Northeastern citizens living, studying and working outside the region have repeatedly reported being subjected to racial slurs, verbal abuse, physical attacks, social discrimination and other forms of humiliation because of their appearance, identity and place of origin,” he alleged.NESO urged authorities to treat the matter with seriousness and urgency and ensure that nobody responsible for the crime evades accountability.“The law must be applied firmly and equally, irrespective of the identity or background of the perpetrators,” Jyrwa said.
The organisation also called for stronger preventive measures, effective enforcement of the law, sensitisation of police and public institutions, and mechanisms to ensure the safety and dignity of people from the Northeast.“The loss of Chongtham Vikram Singh is not merely a personal tragedy for his family and loved ones, but a matter of deep concern for the entire Northeastern community,” Jyrwa said.
Who was Chongtham Vikram Singh?
Singh had lived in Kilokari for more than two decades. He was a well-known musician and guitarist, and had been the lead guitarist of the Manipur rock band Phoenix in the early 1980s.He later worked as a music teacher and performer in Delhi.NESO expressed solidarity with Singh's family and the people of Manipur and demanded justice for him and accountability for everyone found responsible for his death.

Explainer: How a corruption scandal and loyalty to Zelensky brought down Ukraine’s prosecutor general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:36:13 UTC
00:36:13 KST

Explainer: How a corruption scandal and loyalty to Zelensky brought down Ukraine’s prosecutor general
Then-Prosecutor General of Ukraine Ruslan Kravchenko holds a briefing in Kyiv, Ukraine, on July 23, 2025. (Danylo Antoniuk / Ukrinform / NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko once helped lead the crackdown on Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU). On Sept. 7, a corruption scandal ultimately led to his downfall after the same bureau broke through the gates of his office.
Kravchenko, long seen as a staunch loyalist of President Volodymyr Zelensky, resigned on Sept. 7 after NABU detectives exposed an alleged scam call center protection racket run from the Prosecutor General's Office — only the latest in a string of scandals that had forced out top Zelensky allies.
During his more than a year in office, Kravchenko has accumulated plenty of baggage: from helping the presidential administration's failed attempt to destroy the independence of anti-corruption bodies to earning the reputation of a "last line of defense" for lawmakers fearing charges.
But even some in Zelensky's party had come to see him as more trouble than he was worth.
While Kravchenko himself has not yet been charged in the scam call center case, he appears in incriminating recordings, and one of his top prosecutors has been detained.
The NABU operation that brought down the prosecutor general was codenamed Carthage — an apparent reference to a Roman refrain that "Carthage must be destroyed," here referring to the corruption that has taken root in the Prosecutor General's Office.
But anti-corruption activists and some lawmakers argue that replacing Kravchenko with another loyalist will not solve the problem.
The only remedy, they believe, is a transparent selection process for the next top prosecutor and a thorough reform of the prosecutorial system.
read also
Is Kravchenko implicated?
The NABU raid that cost Kravchenko his job started late on Sept. 4 with searches at the office of Serhii Kropyva, a deputy head of the Prosecutor General's Office's international cooperation department and an alleged "confidant" of the prosecutor general.
Kropyva was later charged with organized crime and laundering Hr 90 million ($2 million).
Anti-corruption detectives on Sept. 4 also searched the offices of Kravchenko, his senior deputy Maria Vdovychenko, and Oleh Kiper, governor of Odesa Oblast. None of them has been charged, though Vdovychenko resigned on Sept. 8 nonetheless.
It would be impossible for a prosecutor general not to know about such extensive corruption, a former top employee of the Prosecutor General's Office told the Kyiv Independent.
"There's no way something like this could be going on behind the prosecutor general's back," he said. "No prosecutor general would allow it. He would either put a stop to it — or take charge of (the scheme) himself."
While NABU has not named Kravchenko, evidence released as part of its investigation points squarely to him.
The bureau's recordings refer to a "boss" allegedly protecting the group, a figure whose patronymic, Andriiovych, and prior role as head of the State Tax Service correspond to Kravchenko.
An earlier Telegram post by the Prosecutor General's Office confirms that the investigators understand the term "boss" as referring to Kravchenko.
An anti-corruption prosecutor also described Kropyva as a confidant of Kravchenko during court hearings.
"The problem with the Prosecutor General's Office lies with the prosecutor general, who essentially trades his political loyalty to the president for control over the law enforcement system and the financial benefits he derives from it.
According to NABU recordings, Kropyva arranged repair work at Kravchenko's house in Kozyn, an elite residential area south of Kyiv. Kravchenko said he had chosen the house last winter and had been living there since May.
The house has not been included in Kravchenko's latest asset declaration, with the prosecutor general saying he would declare it in his 2026 disclosure. Kravchenko was supposed to declare the rental if the expenses exceeded Hr 166,400 ($3,748), but there is no information on whether they did.
Kravchenko's own handling of the NABU raid's fallout only deepened the suspicion.
The Prosecutor General's Office initially denied the searches at Kravchenko's personal office — before admitting them the next day. Kravchenko went incommunicado until Sept. 6, when he made a statement denying complicity in the scheme.
"From a communications standpoint, the whole thing was a complete failure — very amateurish and deeply unprofessional," political analyst Ihor Reiterovich told the Kyiv Independent. "His explanations only raised more questions."
read also
Kravchenko's resignation saga
Before Kravchenko’s resignation late on Sept. 7, some lawmakers within Zelensky's own party felt that the situation with the prosecutor general was getting out of control.
"And the situation has only gotten worse," one of them told the Kyiv Independent. "That's why we started discussing within the parliamentary faction that enough is enough — we're going to start collecting signatures calling for Kravchenko's resignation, because this simply cannot go on."
"Kravchenko has accumulated so much negative baggage that they needed to cut him loose before the backlash started spilling over onto Zelensky."
If Kravchenko had not resigned, quite a few lawmakers from the ruling party would be unhappy, the member of parliament said.
Eventually, Kravchenko resigned after Zelensky met with him, David Arakhamia, the parliamentary leader of the president's Servant of the People party, and the heads of NABU and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) — Semen Kryvonos and Oleksandr Klymenko, respectively — on Sept. 7.
"Kravchenko has accumulated so much negative baggage that they needed to cut him loose before the backlash started spilling over onto Zelensky," Yaroslav Yurchyshyn, a lawmaker from the liberal opposition Holos party, told the Kyiv Independent.
Another lawmaker from Zelensky's party told the Kyiv Independent that they were not sure parliament would support Kravchenko's resignation.
"They see him as something of a last line of defense — someone who can prevent, for example, lawmakers from being charged," the lawmaker said.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comments from the President's Office and the Prosecutor General's Office and will publish their responses once they are received.
read also
Long-running controversy
Kravchenko's reputational problems began long before he resigned.
When he was appointed in June 2025, Kravchenko was widely seen as a staunch Zelensky loyalist.
He played a crucial role in the authorities' attack on NABU and SAPO in July 2025.
At the time, Zelensky attempted to eliminate the independence of the anti-corruption agencies by subordinating them to the prosecutor general. However, the bureau's independence was later restored amid protests and Western pressure.
The same month, Kravchenko's Prosecutor General's Office, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and the State Investigation Bureau conducted at least 70 searches at NABU. Two detectives of the bureau were arrested and charged with high treason and aiding Russia.
Critics argue that the cases were a political vendetta for the NABU cases against Zelensky allies involving state nuclear power monopoly Energoatom, the biggest corruption investigation during Zelensky's presidency.
Kravchenko's public image took a further hit in December, when he publicly threatened to go after his opponents who demanded his resignation.
read also
Conflict subsides
Kravchenko's conflict with NABU and civil society appeared to have subsided after Zelensky's powerful chief of staff, Andriy Yermak, resigned following NABU's search of his premises in November.
The next month, the two detained NABU detectives were released. Some commentators saw it as a sign that the political will to continue the crackdown on the anti-corruption bodies had evaporated.
Despite his loyalty to Zelensky, Kravchenko reportedly began refusing certain orders from the President's Office in late 2025 and even clashed with Zelensky's controversial deputy chief of staff, Oleh Tatarov, who is responsible for law enforcement, Ukrainska Pravda reported in August, citing its sources.
"I don't think Zelensky has trusted Kravchenko since last year, when Kravchenko failed to prove himself a strong defender of the president's interests, both in the situation involving Yermak and later in his dealings with NABU," political analyst Volodymyr Fesenko told the Kyiv Independent.
What is Arakhamia's role?
Arakhamia, the parliamentary leader of Zelensky's party, reportedly played a major role in keeping Kravchenko afloat.
Following Yermak's dismissal in November, Arakhamia has dramatically increased his clout, with some analysts and lawmakers arguing that he is now the second most influential person in Ukraine.
However, Arakhamia's position became more precarious when NABU charged five lawmakers from his party in December with taking cash in exchange for parliamentary votes.
The same month, the bureau searched the premises of an Arakhamia aide, a law enforcement source told the Kyiv Independent.
But a lawmaker from Zelensky's party told the Kyiv Independent that some members of parliament looked to Kravchenko for political protection from NABU.
Asked whether Arakhamia is under investigation, SAPO chief Klymenko said in August that anti-corruption agencies were constrained in their investigations of lawmakers because they had to obtain the prosecutor general's approval.
Ukrainska Pravda also reported on Sept. 7 that Arakhamia was lobbying against Kravchenko's resignation. Arakhamia declined to comment on the report for the Kyiv Independent.
read also
What's next?
It is not clear who could replace Kravchenko as prosecutor general.
According to media reports, the candidacy of Serhii Ionushas, head of parliament's law enforcement committee, has been repeatedly considered for the post of prosecutor general since 2020.
"Serhii may well want to (become prosecutor general)," a lawmaker from Zelensky's party told the Kyiv Independent. "But it's complicated — who would take over his committee then?”
But anti-corruption activists believe that the only solution to the crisis is to select the next prosecutor general through a transparent contest with the participation of international experts.
"We keep going around in circles," Tetiana Shevchuk, a lawyer at the Anti-Corruption Action Center, an independent watchdog, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The problem with the Prosecutor General's Office lies with the prosecutor general, who essentially trades his political loyalty to the president for control over the law enforcement system and the financial benefits he derives from it. There is no other solution but to hold a transparent competition for the post."
A lawmaker from Zelensky's party said that "a competitive selection process is the better solution because it is systemic and institutional," and "with every scandal like this, the chances (of introducing a transparent competition) go up."
Many also believe the problems at the Prosecutor General's Office run far deeper than the personality of the person at its helm.
For critics, the latest corruption scandal is the clearest evidence yet that previous efforts to reform the body have failed.
"The case has highlighted the lack of proper vetting and selection of prosecutors, the absence of prosecutorial independence in handling cases, continued top-down micromanagement, and the lack of effective internal oversight — all things the reform was supposed to ensure," Shevchuk said.
Kravchenko's resignation also raises the question of whether the authorities will halt their assaults on NABU or launch a counterattack.
Some activists and lawmakers believe that a further attack on the anti-corruption institutions is imminent.
But Fesenko disagrees with this assessment.
Last year, during the authorities' attack on NABU and SAPO, "there was a sense of strength" at the President's Office, he said.
"The situation is completely different now," Fesenko added. "NABU does not see itself as weak. Zelensky, on the other hand, is significantly weakened. (The authorities) are on the defensive now; they are not in a position to attack."

IEA urges strategic gas reserves as supply shocks expose LNG market risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:35:16 UTC
00:35:16 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Governments should strengthen natural gas reserves and increase the flexibility of liquefied natural gas (LNG) markets to protect consumers against supply disruptions, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Wednesday.
In its report, Gas Reserve Mechanisms and Flexibility Options, the agency outlined measures countries could implement over the next five years as gas markets become more interconnected but increasingly vulnerable to geopolitical shocks.
The proposals include mandatory commercial storage obligations, government-controlled strategic reserves, LNG buffer stocks, joint reserves using existing infrastructure and cross-border stockholding arrangements.
The IEA also recommended examining pooled LNG purchase options and agreements allowing countries to access additional cargoes during emergencies.
The report follows two major gas-supply crises in five years. Reduced Russian pipeline deliveries to Europe after the start of the Ukraine war in 2022 caused record prices and reshaped global LNG trade. More recently, disruption to LNG shipments through the Strait of Hormuz due to the ongoing Iran war highlighted the vulnerability of import-dependent economies.
The IEA warned that competition for limited LNG cargoes during severe disruptions could cause extreme price volatility and significant economic damage without necessarily preventing physical shortages.
It said physical reserves, including underground storage, LNG tanks and floating storage, remained central to gas security. However, storage alone cannot address every disruption because countries differ in geography, infrastructure and import dependence.
More flexible LNG contracts, cargo swaps and commercial innovation could complement reserves by allowing available supplies to move more efficiently between markets, it added.
The recommendations are particularly relevant for Türkiye, which has expanded its underground storage and LNG import infrastructure while maintaining pipeline supplies from several countries.
Gas security will also be discussed at the LNG Producer-Consumer Conference, co-hosted by Japan’s Economy Ministry and the IEA on Friday.

Iran claims to have attacked 10 ships near strait of Hormuz after US strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:32:03 UTC
00:32:03 KST

Tehran has said it attacked 10 ships around the strait of Hormuz after the US sunk five Iranian tankers, as escalating strikes between the two countries sent the oil price above $100 a barrel for the first time since July.
The attacks were the sharpest flare-up of strikes in weeks, as the two sides struggled to break a deadlock in the six-month-long war. Fighting in recent weeks has largely revolved around who controls the strait of Hormuz, as Iran attempts to close off the waterway and Washington enforces a blockade of Iranian ports.
The strait is a critical route for global energy supplies, with up to 20% of the world’s oil and gas transiting it before the US-Iran war. The rising price of oil, above the psychologically significant $100 mark, is likely to raise inflation and the price of goods.
Stocks fell on Wall Street while rising fuel and food prices in the US will further frustrate the Trump administration, which faces a midterm election with an unpopular war and a cost-of-living crisis.
Among the vessels struck by Iran were two US vessels and eight oil tankers, the Iranian’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Wednesday.
The IRGC said the 10 vessels were “noncompliant” – a likely reference to ships that tried to traverse the waterway without its permission. At least one sailor was killed and another was missing.
The US denied that its vessels were hit, with US Central Command saying on social media that all “attempted attacks failed”.
A tanker in Iraqi waters carrying 2mi barrels of fuel oil was also struck by a drone, according to Iraqi officials. There were no reports of casualties among the crew and the Iraqi government said there were no reported oil leaks.
Iran said it also fired missiles at US bases in Jordan – 18 of which authorities said were intercepted while two fell in unpopulated areas.
The US had said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, publishing videos of ships on fire. The US military said the attacks were a response to Iran targeting a US navy warship twice in the previous two days.
Iranian state TV said the US strikes had followed a “complex intelligence and operational action at dawn” to seize a US underwater drone in the strait. The US said the seized craft was a “defective” older model that did not carry any sensitive data.
The back-and-forth strikes signalled an intensifying escalation between the two sides as Washington announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers if Iran targets its warships.
“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, told reporters.
Iran said it would also escalate its attacks, and that for every two or three tankers struck it would respond by hitting 20. The IRGC said it would also release maps of a new, much-larger area near the strait that it considers forbidden for ships to traverse, extending as far as the Gulf off Chabahar for the first time.
The conflict has also taken on an increasingly regional dimension as the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen traded strikes with Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis launched a wave of attacks on four cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, causing large fires at oil installations and wounding 73 people. The Houthis said dozens of people have been killed in Saudi airstrikes, something unconfirmed by Riyadh.
Fighting re-ignited between the two sides after the Houthis launched an offensive against the Saudi-backed government of Yemen in south Yemen last week, aimed at reaching the Red Sea.
The group is trying to enforce a Red Sea blockade against Saudi Arabia, announced in July. If enforced, it would cut off another route for the kingdom to export its oil.

Ceuta crisis: EU grants Spain €114 million in gesture of ‘solidarity’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:31:11 UTC
00:31:11 KST

The European Commission has approved funding to tackle the crisis in Ceuta, supporting border control, reception and returns, while Frontex, Europol and the EUAA also step up their assistance.
The European Commission has granted the Spanish government 114.7 million euros from its emergency aid fund to deal with the migration crisis that Ceuta has been facing since the end of July, in what the institution describes as an act of "solidarity" with Spain.
"This financial assistance comes on top of the Commission's immediate response from day one, when it offered Spain both financial and operational support," the Commission said in a statement. "The decision once again demonstrates the Commission's full solidarity with Spain in dealing with this difficult situation."
The funding comes from the Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund, which will provide 82.7 million euros, and from the Border Management and Visa Instrument, which will provide a further 32 million. The money will be used to reinforce border surveillance and protection and security infrastructure, with equipment such as thermal cameras, monitoring systems, buoys and underwater drones.
The aid will also make it possible to deploy additional staff and equipment, create facilities for screening migrants and support the return of those who are in Ceuta irregularly. It will also help to strengthen the city's reception capacity, including care for unaccompanied minors.
Brussels has also coordinated the mobilisation of support from European agencies. Frontex will maintain its joint operation Minerva and is ready to expand other operational plans in Spain in 2027, while Europol will continue to work with the Spanish security forces on investigations into migrant-smuggling networks.
For its part, the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) will provide support with interviews and interpretation. The Commission and the agencies will also set up a joint coordination group with the Spanish authorities, which will hold its first meeting this week.
Once the financing agreement has been signed, the Commission will have 30 days to pay up to 80% of the amount granted. The funds may also cover eligible actions carried out since the start of the emergency.

Olivia Rodrigo gives Palestinian fashion brand a lifeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:30:19 UTC
00:30:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Olivia Rodrigo gives Palestinian fashion brand a lifeline
American singer-songwriter and actress Olivia Rodrigo commissioned a custom-made dress from a Palestinian fashion label that was on the brink of shutting down as it struggled to operate under Israeli restrictions in the occupied West Bank.
Rodrigo turned to Nöl Collective, the Ramallah-based brand founded by Palestinian designer Yasmeen Mjalli, to create the dress for her inaugural Daisy Chain Fields Music Festival in California late last month.
The pale pink raw-silk minidress featured traditional Palestinian tatreez embroidery, with birds and flowers hand-stitched by Palestinian artisans in the occupied West Bank.
Mjalli described Rodrigo's commission as "divine intervention", saying it arrived as she was questioning whether Nöl Collective could continue operating.
"I was genuinely like, maybe we should stop, maybe this is our last effort. I was just so tired," she told Vogue Arabia.
In the same week Rodrigo made contact, a shipment of naturally dyed, handwoven wool that Nöl had ordered from India for its autumn collection was destroyed after being held for months by Israeli customs.
Mjalli then tried to travel to Jerusalem to find replacement fabric, but was turned back after the Israeli army closed roads out of Ramallah.
"We are unique in the sense that we have unfathomable restrictions in our movement and what we can do," she said.
With less than a week to make Rodrigo's dress, Mjalli instead sourced raw silk available in Ramallah before taking it to artisans in Bethlehem.
A journey from Ramallah to Bethlehem that would ordinarily take around 90 minutes took three hours because of Israeli checkpoints.
The dress passed through nine pairs of hands during production, including Palestinian embroiderers Um Musa and Um Mohammad, before another obstacle emerged: no local courier could get the finished garment to California in time.
Two strangers eventually volunteered to carry the dress in their luggage and hand-delivered it to Los Angeles.
Nöl Collective, founded in 2020, works with women's cooperatives, family-run sewing workshops and individual embroiderers across Palestine, incorporating traditional Palestinian craftsmanship into contemporary designs.
Mjalli said the situation has become even more difficult since Israel revoked work permits for Palestinian labourers following 7 October 2023, depriving households across the occupied West Bank of crucial income and pushing more women towards embroidery work.
For some families, she said, Nöl remains their only source of income.
"We keep going so that the community continues to thrive," Mjalli said.
The company operates amid an increasingly violent crackdown on Palestinians across the occupied West Bank, where Israeli military raids and settler attacks have intensified, while communities have faced forced expulsions and property demolitions. The escalating violence has prompted several Western countries to place sanctions on Israeli settlements.
Mjalli described Rodrigo wearing the Palestinian-made dress on such a prominent stage as a victory that went beyond fashion.
"Fashion is political no matter where you are," she said. "We're still here, we have not been forgotten."
She also said Rodrigo wearing Nöl Collective felt like a natural extension of the singer's political expression, adding: "Your political views as a punk rocker should include Palestine."
Rodrigo has also been outspoken over Israel's nearly three-year genocidal campaign in the Gaza Strip, which has killed more than 73,600 people, mostly civilians.
In a May interview on The New York Times' Popcast, Rodrigo was asked about using her platform to speak out politically, including on Gaza.
She said she made a conscious effort to stay informed but acknowledged that she was not an expert on geopolitics, describing her role as an artist as expressing honestly how events made her feel.
"I think it would just be disingenuous to be like, I don't feel heartbroken about what's going on in Gaza," Rodrigo said.
"As an artist, I feel like that's just what you do," she added, before saying she always felt she "could be doing more and saying more".

Indonesia’s wildfire emissions surge to world’s highest, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:30:06 UTC
00:30:06 KST

Indonesia’s wildfire emissions surge to world’s highest, data shows
The country is battling what authorities say is its most intense wildfire season in 11 years
Indonesia is facing a surge in emissions from wildfires burning through parched stretches of forest and peatland on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, with carbon dioxide readings currently the highest in the world, data has shown.
Fire emissions from Indonesia from September 1 to September 7 reached 19.7 million metric tons, overtaking Russia this week and making up more than a third of the global total, according to Fire Emissions Watch, a portal developed by the European Union’s Copernicus climate monitoring service, on Wednesday.
Indonesia is one of the world’s most fire-prone countries, but as “super-El Nino” weather conditions drive up temperatures and cause punishing droughts, the country is battling what authorities say is its most intense wildfire season in 11 years.
“We do expect to see some fires across the region at this time of year, but with El Nino, it clearly just gives a big enhancement to them,” said Mark Parrington, senior scientist at the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service in Bonn.
“It’s much drier, it’s hotter, and when there’s ignition, these fires burn in a far more extreme way.”
From September 1 to 7, fire emission intensity exceeded 1,500kg/sq km, more than 10 times the Russian level, with the highest concentrations in Kalimantan in Indonesia’s part of Borneo and eastern parts of Sumatra, Copernicus data showed on Wednesday.
Emissions were 273 per cent higher than the seasonal average, though still lower than the 21.7 million tons emitted in the same week of 2015, when Indonesia was battling similarly intense El Nino conditions.
Among the hardest hit areas has been the city of Pontianak in West Kalimantan, where the air quality index was 394 on Wednesday, according to Swiss air quality monitoring firm IQAir. A reading of 300 is considered hazardous.

SIA passenger recounts 20-hour delay after air traffic control glitch at major British airports

- Passengers faced long waits, lack of information, and limited food and water while travelling by bus, ferry, and coach to reach London.
- The glitch disrupted thousands of flights, causing 1,300 cancellations on Sept 8 and nearly 300 more on Sept 9 across British airports.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – Singaporean Aria Maish Nichani was supposed to land in London at 3.20pm on Sept 8 and settle into her new home for the next year as she pursues a master’s degree in curating at the Courtauld Institute of Art.
What she did not expect was for her journey from Singapore to London to include air, land and sea travel after a technical glitch affecting air traffic control services at major British airports extended her travel by more than 20 hours.
The 23-year-old was on one of two Singapore Airlines (SIA) flights that were diverted due to the technical glitch.
Two other SIA flights scheduled to depart London Heathrow for Singapore on Sept 8 were cancelled.
Aria’s flight, SQ308, which had 401 passengers and 29 crew members on board, was diverted to Paris’ Charles de Gaulle Airport in France, according to an SIA spokesperson.
From there, they were to take a ferry from Calais to Dover in England, before arriving in London, Aria told The Straits Times.
Recounting her experience, Aria said that she landed in Paris at 7pm on Sept 8.
She and the other passengers waited on board the aircraft for two hours before going through Paris immigration, she said.
At 12.30am on Sept 9, Aria finally boarded a bus that would take the passengers to the ferry terminal in Calais, a two-hour ride away.
But at the ferry terminal, they were told that there was no ferry booked for the passengers, Aria said.
So they had to wait at the terminal till a ferry arrived, she added.
The ferry, with the buses on board, finally left Calais at 10.30am and took 90 minutes to reach Dover.
Passengers of the flight disembarked at Dover in England before continuing their journey to London on the same bus for another two hours, Aria said.
The stress of the delays, long waits and uncertainty was compounded by the lack of information, she added.
“I’m just frustrated with the fact that we were left in the dark for so many hours throughout the whole ordeal,” Aria said.
“All this time with very little food and water provided,” she added.
In London, the bus dropped the passengers off at Victoria rail station. “We are just relieved we finally arrived, and safely too,” said Aria.
The other SIA flight that was diverted, SQ318, flew to Munich Airport in Germany and landed at 8.09pm local time. There were 203 passengers and 19 crew members on board.
Britain’s National Air Traffic Services said the issue had impacted its flight data processing system, resulting in thousands of flight disruptions across the country on Sept 8.
Travellers continued to face chaos at airports across Britain for a second day, with nearly 300 flights scrapped on Sept 9 due to the glitch.
This was in addition to the more than 1,300 cancellations to and from British airports on Sept 8.
The Straits Times has contacted SIA for more information.

US, Iran Trade Strikes On Shipping As Oil Prices Surge Above $100 A Barrel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:29:20 UTC
00:29:20 KST

Iran said it attacked vessels near the Strait of Hormuz on September 9 after the United States destroyed several Iranian oil tankers overnight, in a sharp escalation in the six-month war.
The tit-for-tat strikes led to a surge in global oil prices, with Brent crude reaching $100 per barrel for the first time since July.
Tehran also said it had fired ballistic missiles at a US base in Jordan. No casualties or damage were reported.
Iran and the United States have been engaged in tit-for-tat strikes in the past few weeks, in a move that observers say could reignite a full-blown war.
US President Donald Trump said on September 9 that the United States was not looking for a deal to end the war, although he added that negotiations could happen.
Trump also told reporters that he believes that the conflict will end “immediately” after the midterm elections in November because Iran “can't hold out any longer.”
Targeting Shipping
The US military said it sank five Iranian oil tankers overnight near Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub, calling it a response to Tehran firing missiles at a US Navy warship over the past two days.
Iran retaliated by firing 20 ballistic missiles toward Jordan, which said it intercepted 18 of them. Jordan said two of the missiles landed in unpopulated areas.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC), the elite branch of Iran’s armed forces, claimed that it also attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers, and 10 “noncompliant vessels” that were trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
A key artery for global energy supplies, the strategic waterway has been effectively closed by Tehran since the start of the war with the United States in February.
Earlier in the war, Iran established a shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz that hugged the Iranian coastline. It said any vessels using a US-backed route along Oman’s coast would be targeted.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which is affiliated with the British Navy, said on September 9 that “several” vessels in the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf were “subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region.”
Separately, the IRGC warned tanker crews in ports in Kuwait and Bahrain, both US allies, to evacuate, raising fears of further disruption around the Strait of Hormuz.
The escalation has already affected shipping: data from Kpler, a commodities and shipping analytics company, showed only six commercial vessels crossed the strait on September 8, well below the recent average.
Also on September 9, the IRGC for the first time added parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea to a new "prohibited zone" where vessels will be subject to “sanctions.”
US Warns Iran Will 'Lose Tankers'
Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the US attack on its oil tankers as “an overt threat to regional and international peace and security,” saying that they "increase the dangers of tensions in the region.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran would “lose tankers” every time it attempted to hit US ships.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers, and I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters on September 8 on a visit to Colombia.
Rubio's remarks came as Washington intensified its campaign to squeeze Iran economically. The United States announced new sanctions on September 8 targeting Iran's aviation sector and companies accused of helping Tehran obtain aircraft and sensitive technology.
On the same day, Iran's national currency, the rial, fell to a new low against major foreign currencies.
The United States has also imposed a naval blockade on Iranian vessels and ports, disrupting Iran’s oil exports, its key source of revenue.

Bangladesh measles deaths surpass 1,000 after vaccination drive falls short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:29:11 UTC
00:29:11 KST

Bangladesh measles deaths surpass 1,000 after vaccination drive falls short
Officials say a mass immunisation campaign missed millions of children as hospitals run out of beds.
At least 1,002 children have died from measles in Bangladesh, according to the country’s health officials, amid the world’s worst ongoing outbreak.
On Wednesday, health officials from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) also reported 187,484 measles infections since the outbreak began in March.
Recommended Stories
list of 2 items
- list 1 of 2US medical groups issue vaccine guidance, urge jabs for flu, COVID and RSV
- list 2 of 2Bangladesh protesters demand action over rising costs
Measles is a highly contagious disease that causes fever and a distinct rash, and has no specific treatment when caught. Severe cases can cause brain swelling and breathing problems.
However, it can be prevented with two doses of vaccine. Infants too young to be vaccinated disproportionately contract and spread the disease. Children under the age of five accounted for more than 80 percent of cases early in the outbreak.
‘Truly terrible situation’
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has said that the South Asian nation of 178 million is experiencing the largest outbreak of measles in the world.
Professor Mahmudur Rahman, former director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research in Dhaka, told the Reuters news agency that the situation was unprecedented in the country.
“To my knowledge, Bangladesh has never witnessed so many children dying from measles. Nor have we ever seen such a high number of patients in a single year. This is a truly terrible situation, and the saddest part is that the victims are children,” he said.
The WHO and UNICEF have linked the crisis to gaps in the nation’s immunisation programme that emerged in 2024 and 2025, during the political turmoil that followed the ousting of then-Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.
On Monday, Bangladeshi Health Minister Sardar Husain told parliament that changes to procurement policy in that period created a vaccine shortage.
Four million unvaccinated children
A nationwide emergency vaccination drive, launched in April, vaccinated 18 million children. But official figures show roughly four million were never reached.
“We couldn’t achieve herd immunity,” DGHS spokesman Zahid Raihan told the AFP news agency, saying that teams were still searching for children who had been missed.
“Measles cannot be eradicated and the aim was to reduce casualties. We will keep vaccinating our children,” he said.
The outbreak is straining hospitals that are simultaneously handling a surge in dengue fever. More than 45,000 people have been admitted for dengue, and Tuesday was a record day for both admissions and deaths from the disease.

Ukraine wants FIA to impose sanctions on Russian automobile federation: Report
Unknown

2026-09-09
15:28:26 UTC
00:28:26 KST

Burç Eruygur
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Ukraine urged the International Automobile Federation (FIA) to impose sanctions on its Russian counterpart.
Citing a statement by the Automobile Federation of Ukraine (FAU), BBC Sport reported Wednesday that the FAU said it is "outraged by the prolonged inaction of the global governing body."
"The FAU has already appealed to the FIA senate and FIA ethics committee, but has received no reaction or reply," said the FAU.
The report also noted a letter by FAU President Oleksandr Feldman addressed to FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem, in which, it said Feldman demanded that Ben Sulayem suspend Russia's FIA membership and re-impose "strict restrictions on Russian athletes' participation in international competitions."
"This is a dangerous precedent that paves the way for member organisations to disregard other provisions of the statutes and requirements of the rules, potentially leading to chaos and jeopardising the FIA's future as an institution," according to the letter.
Last month, FIA announced that it lifted restrictions on Russian and Belarusian motorsport participants, allowing them to compete with their national flags, symbols and anthems.
Ukrainian Youth and Sports Minister Matvii Bidnyi later that month said he appealed to FIA to reverse its decision.
“We call for this decision to be reversed,” Bidnyi said in a LinkedIn post, expressing that the reasons for the sanctions imposed after the start of the Russia-Ukraine war in February 2022 have not disappeared.
The FAU lodged an official complaint to the FIA Court of Appeal in late August, according to BBC Sport.
Commenting on the FIA’s decision in August, the Russian Automobile Federation expressed gratitude to the governing body for its “constructive” dialogue. “Sport and culture should remain above politics -- they are what unite nations. Justice has prevailed,” it said.
The developments follow the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) decision in July to provisionally lift a ban on the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC), saying its Executive Board had determined that the committee no longer included regional sports organizations in territories under the jurisdiction of Ukraine’s National Olympic Committee.
Ukraine, in response, said it had filed an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport challenging the IOC’s decision to provisionally lift the ROC’s suspension, arguing the governing body of the modern Olympic Games acted "prematurely" and without properly verifying whether the violations that led to the ROC's suspension in 2023 had been resolved.
The IOC recommended that Belarusian and Russian athletes be barred from international competitions days after the start of the Russia-Ukraine war.

‘Our desire to create is bigger than our fear’: How one Kyiv restaurant rebuilds, adapts and keeps going after 3 Russian attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:27:05 UTC
00:27:05 KST

‘Our desire to create is bigger than our fear’: How one Kyiv restaurant rebuilds, adapts and keeps going after 3 Russian attacks
Mykhailo plates the dishes in the Zavertailo kitchen before they are served to the guests in Kyiv, Ukraine on Sept. 8, 2026. (Danylo Antoniuk/ The Kyiv Independent)
It was never normal for Anna Zavertailo to shelter in her restaurant’s basement kitchen alongside her employees and diners as drones flew overhead. But after multiple attacks damaged her popular family-run businesses in Kyiv, safety has become the top priority.
Her restaurants-cum-bakeries, Zavertailo and Honey, which Anna runs with her husband, Stas, have been victims of three separate attacks in just over a year. But the couple has been selling carefully crafted cakes and pastries to foreigners and locals alike since 2014, and they refuse to let the strikes close down their business.
"Our desire to create is much bigger than our fear of Russia," Anna told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 8 over a poppy seed and cherry roll at the Zavertailo restaurant in the upscale Golden Gates neighborhood, next to St. Sophia’s Cathedral.
It’s the first day the restaurant has reopened and a handful of customers are sitting downstairs enjoying coffees and cakes. Just four days earlier, the restaurant’s floor-to-ceiling windows were blown out after a Russian jet-powered drone struck the security service (SBU) office next door.
The shock wave sent furniture flying, and glass shattered all over the restaurant as employees leaped into action and guided customers to the underground shelter in the kitchen. The couple weren’t in the restaurant at the time but heard the explosion from the British embassy down the road, where they had a visa appointment ahead of an award ceremony in London next month.
While none of their employees were injured, the attack still made the couple anxious. It was the second strike in four months, and they had just invested in a new Zavertailo location downtown. Now they would have to fork out for repair costs and close their most profitable location for several days.
read also
As Russia intensifies daytime drone attacks on Kyiv and civilian casualties rise, businesses like Zavertailo are adapting to a deadly new reality. The couple had dealt with overnight strikes before, when staff and customers were at home, but this was the first time an attack had happened during the day, when people were working and eating.
Each attack is a painful new learning experience for the couple. After the first one in August 2025, they stocked equipment such as industrial vacuum cleaners to suck up the shattered glass and plastic coverings to replace the broken windows. That way, they can clean up and reopen as fast as possible.
"We joke that, before long, we’ll be the top CEOs in crisis management. Every time we face a new level of crisis, we have to make a new set of decisions," Anna said.
Fortunately, the couple is lucky to have an amazing team that helps them, with management from all their branches working late into the night to clear up the debris on Sept. 4, Anna said. "We’re all in this together," she added, smiling.
The duo has little time to decompress, but they find energy in baking bread and washing plates — something to keep their hands busy, Anna said. But their minds are already focused on how to reopen and improve safety for their employees.
After the first strike, they introduced air alarm protocols for staff to go to the shelter, although that’s becoming harder in Kyiv as alarms drag on for hours. This time, they are looking for grants to buy expensive anti-blast film for their windows to protect them from shock waves.
They also set money aside to keep paying bills and salaries when they have to close locations or traffic dips. In total, the attacks have cost them $500,000 in both repair costs and lost income. For now, they are still profitable, but Anna says they are concentrating on "surviving" before they can think about "growing."
read also
Since 2024, their situation has worsened year by year, and Anna is terrified of the coming winter, which Ukraine, and particularly Kyiv, is underprepared for. In previous winters, the couple overcame lengthy blackouts with generators that kept them connected.
But this time around, Anna fears there will be a mass exodus from the city, and their customers, largely middle-class professionals and creatives, as well as foreigners, are the ones with the means to leave. The company can’t rely on passion alone.
"I am hysterical. I’m scared we won’t have enough guests to bring in the revenue we need," she said.
Their team is currently researching ways to preserve goods as Russia continues to target Ukraine’s food supply chains. Last month, attacks on supermarket logistics centers caused food shortages, depriving their bakers and chefs of chocolate and nuts. This winter, they worry key ingredients such as milk and butter could be in short supply.
With few government and international financial support programs available to Ukrainian restaurateurs, the Zavertailos rely on themselves to survive. Their customer base has been incredible, Anna said, with people buying bread, pastries, and other goods after attacks.
One option is opening a location in western Ukraine, where the attacks are less intense. But with cash flow at a low point, they would need to find an investor. For a business that has been entirely family-run for 12 years, finding a like-minded partner is not always easy, Anna said.
Even as Russia steps up its attacks, Anna says that they will remain in Ukraine. They know that they risk damage again, but they want to support the country economically and provide good jobs for their 350 employees. It’s about giving it your all to build a better future, even in the face of an existential threat, she said.
"We’re staying strong; we’re supporting our people. We want to fight and show how creative and adaptive we are," Anna said.
"We dream about a happy ending, but we understand that there might not be one."

In the Odrex doctors’ case, the court heard the defense’s objections concerning one of those accused of medical negligence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:26:23 EEST
00:26:23 KST

In the Odrex doctors’ case, the court heard the defense’s objections concerning one of those accused of medical negligence
Kyiv • UNN
The case of the Odrex doctors accused of negligence resulting in a patient’s death is ongoing in the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa.
A regular hearing in the case concerning Odrex clinic doctors Vitaliy Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska took place today at the Kyiv District Court of Odesa. The medics are accused of medical negligence which, according to the investigation, could have caused the death of businessman Adnan Kivan, UNN reports.
During today's court hearing, the defense of doctor Rusakov presented its objections to the prosecution's evidence. The court began hearing the defense's arguments at previous hearings, but at the latest one, held on September 4, Rusakov's lawyer filed a motion to recuse the judge. After consideration, the motion was denied, but this prolonged the court proceedings, as instead of examining the evidence, the court had to spend time on procedural matters.
The next court hearing is scheduled for tomorrow, September 10, and the court is expected to hear the objections of Maryna Bielotserkovska's defense.
The court is currently at one of the key stages of the proceedings – the examination of evidence. It is during this stage that the court must assess the medical documentation, the findings of forensic medical examinations, clinical protocols, and other materials on which the charges are based.
Rusakov and Bielotserkovska are accused under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – improper performance of professional duties by medical workers. According to the investigation, after the operation, the medics may have failed to prescribe Adnan Kivan the necessary antibacterial therapy and may have responded improperly to postoperative complications. According to the findings of the forensic medical examination, this could have led to the development of sepsis and the patient's death. The accused do not admit their guilt.
Actions of the defense and the time factor in the case of the Odrex doctors
The trial, which has already lasted more than seven months, has been accompanied by numerous attempts to delay the proceedings; in particular, hearings did not take place because of lawyers' nonappearance. It was repeatedly postponed because of procedural motions by the defense. The defendants' lawyers also filed motions to recuse judges, initiated a change of venue, and requested that the indictment be returned to the prosecutor. As a result, after the proceedings were transferred from the Primorsky District Court to the Kyiv District Court of Odesa, the preparatory proceedings had to be conducted again, and when the court finally moved on to consideration of the merits of the case, the defense lawyers began ignoring the hearings.
Doctor Rusakov is also actively pressuring the judge, in particular by publishing memes featuring his photograph. And when the court extended his suspension from his position at the Odrex clinic so that he could not communicate with witnesses, Rusakov appealed to his patients, urging them to complain to the High Council of Justice because they could not get an appointment with him. Large numbers of identical complaints may create psychological pressure on the judge, even if they subsequently prove unfounded. In such a case, the judge is forced to spend time explaining and responding to each appeal.
Lawyers interviewed by UNN did not rule out that the combination of such procedural actions could be a defense tactic aimed at having the case closed because the statute of limitations expires. In particular, Denys Neviadomskyi, president of the All-Ukrainian Association of Retired Judges, emphasized that every unjustified postponement of a trial brings the criminal proceedings closer to dismissal on the grounds that the statute of limitations has expired, which would make it impossible to establish justice in the case concerning Adnan Kivan's death.
The time factor plays a significant role in this case. Since Adnan Kivan died at the end of October 2024 and the charges were brought under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, the three-year statute of limitations prescribed for such cases expires in autumn 2027. By that time, the verdict must not only have been issued by the court of first instance but must also have entered into force.
Thus, the defense's constant procedural "maneuvers" may raise the question of whether a fair court decision will be issued or whether the case will be closed upon the expiry of the prescribed time limits.

FinTech company Activitis, which develops embedded financial solutions for businesses, is a potential buyer for Ukrainian private bank Bizbank, Forbes.ua reported.
If the deal goes through, it would be another M&A transaction in Ukraine’s banking sector in 2026, a sign of a busy market despite the war.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Antimonopoly Committee of Ukraine (AMCU) approved the acquisition of Bizbank by two unnamed Ukrainian citizens on Aug. 13. The buyers’ identities remain confidential.
Bizbank’s beneficial owners include Serhii Lahur, co-owner of the major fuel network WOG, alongside stakeholders of the former Continuum holding company. The bank serves retail and corporate clients.
Its revenues before tax totaled Hr.52.8 million ($1.23 million), and Hr.37.5 million ($872,100) after tax, placing it 36th in the system by both revenue and net profit. It also ranks 36th place by capital size, at Hr.789.2 million ($18.4 million), according to National Bank of Ukraine data for 2025.
Activitis reported Hr.809.5 million ($18.22 million) in revenue and Hr.143.4 million ($3.23 million) in net profit for the latest reporting period, according to the company’s financial statement on its website.
Both Bizbank and Activitis declined to comment on the potential deal to Forbes.ua.
National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) First Deputy Governor Sergiy Nikolaychuk has said that the 2026 M&A boom in Ukraine’s banking sector differs from the previous wave of foreign bank expansion in 2005-2008, when international lenders entered Ukraine bringing their own technologies and corporate governance systems. This time, he said, foreign investors are coming to Ukraine specifically for the technological expertise already developed within the country’s banking sector.

In January, Estonia’s fintech group Iute Group acquired Iute Bank, a bridge bank created from the assets of the failed RWS Bank – one of the few foreign entries into Ukraine’s banking market since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
The deal followed the National Bank’s declaration of RWS Bank as insolvent in November 2025 and its subsequent resolution through the Deposit Guarantee Fund’s bridge-bank mechanism.
Separately, French Crédit Agricole Ukraine announced on March 11 that it had signed an agreement to acquire up to a 100% stake in Bank Lviv. Historically a small regional lender, the western Ukraine-based bank has emerged as a key partner for international financial institutions (IFIs) since 2022, leveraging its safer location away from major hostilities to facilitate lower-risk transactions.

Israel Police nearly out of ammunition for elite marksman rifles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:25:49 UTC
00:25:49 KST

The Israel Police are running critically low on ammunition for ARAD 7 marksman rifles used by special and elite units, with only about 2,000 rounds left in storage.
Police are now seeking an urgent purchase of roughly 130,000 rounds, 65 times the amount currently remaining, after increased operational use sharply depleted supplies.
The shortage comes about two and a half years after police began equipping units with the rifles. Despite their use by specialized forces since then, the stockpile has now fallen to what officials describe as an unusually low level.
The situation is raising concerns over ammunition planning and readiness, particularly during a period of heightened security tension in which a sudden escalation, multiple simultaneous incidents or prolonged operations could quickly increase demand.
Police attribute the decline to what they described as a “change in professional doctrine” and greater ammunition use in the field, including in incidents involving people attempting to enter Israel illegally.
Marksman ammunition is used by forces that require greater accuracy during operational incidents, meaning a limited reserve could become a serious problem if police units are required to sustain intensive activity across several locations.
The Israel Police said in response: “For information security reasons, we do not provide details about operational methods and equipment.”

Tsahkna: Estonia and Ireland deepen cooperation in supporting Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:25:29 UTC
00:25:29 KST

According to Tsahkna, Ireland, as holder of the EU Presidency, has an important role in advancing Europe’s common decisions. “We consider it important to take robust action in supporting Ukraine and exerting pressure on Russia, including through additional economic sanctions, as well as in ensuring Europe’s defence and security,” Tsahkna said. Estonia also supports reaching agreement on the EU’s next long-term budget during Ireland’s Presidency.
Speaking about Ukraine, Tsahkna stressed that Europe must provide Ukraine with greater support and help the country move forward on its path towards accession to the European Union. “Ukraine’s future lies in the European Union, and EU membership is the best long-term security guarantee for Ukraine,” he said. The declaration of intent signed by Tsahkna and McEntee builds on existing Estonian-Irish development cooperation in Ukraine. Ireland’s €1 million contribution to ESTDEV’s ‘Education and Healthcare for Ukraine’ project will help improve rehabilitation and specialist medical care and train the specialists Ukraine needs.
On increasing pressure on Russia, Tsahkna stressed the need to tighten sanctions and make progress on using frozen Russian assets for the benefit of Ukraine. “Russia must pay for the damage it has caused. Europe must respond more forcefully to the increasing attacks and subversive activities,” he said.
According to Tsahkna, the international isolation of Russia and Belarus must also continue, including in the fields of culture and sport, and access to the European Union for combatants who have fought in Russia’s war must be restricted. “Aggression and war crimes must bring consequences,” Tsahkna said. Estonia called on Ireland to take the next step and join the agreement establishing the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression.
Speaking about European security, Tsahkna noted that Russia’s increasing attempts at sabotage and other subversive activities have not changed Estonia’s threat assessment. “Russia poses a long-term threat to European security, and strengthening Europe’s defence capabilities must remain our long-term priority,” he said.
According to Tsahkna, Estonia and Ireland are close partners with a similar understanding of the challenges facing Europe. “We have much in common, both in supporting Ukraine and in making Europe more secure,” he said.
The foreign ministers’ joint press conference is available to watch online.
Photos from the visit.

Messi to buy Spanish 2nd-tier club Eldense: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:22:58 UTC
00:22:58 KST

Halis Sünnetci
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Argentine football star Lionel Messi has reached an agreement in principle to acquire Spanish second-division club Eldense, Spanish daily Marca reported Tuesday.
The transaction could be formalized once the remaining legal and contractual procedures are completed, including a due diligence review of the club.
The deal will also require authorization from Spain’s High Council for Sports (CSD).
The agreement would see Messi acquire 100% of Eldense’s shares.
The 39-year-old former Barcelona forward currently plays for Major League Soccer side Inter Miami. He recently retired from international football after Argentina were beaten 1-0 by Spain in the 2026 FIFA World Cup final.
He has increasingly moved into football ownership in recent years, buying Spanish fifth-tier club UE Cornella in April and joining former Barcelona teammate Luis Suarez in Uruguay’s Deportivo LSM project.
Messi also became a co-owner of KRU Esports, founded by his former Argentina teammate Sergio Aguero, in 2023.
Eldense, based in Elda in Spain’s Alicante province, were founded in 1921 and have spent most of their history outside the top two divisions of Spanish football.
They returned to the second tier in 2023 for the first time since 1964 before being relegated in 2025 and earning promotion back this summer.
