Gaza ministry warns aid shortages worsening amid Israeli siege
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:22:57 UTC
00:22:57 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza ministry warns aid shortages worsening amid Israeli restrictions
Gaza’s Ministry of Social Development has accused Israel of trying to downplay the scale of hunger in the territory, saying aid entering the enclave remains far below what residents need.
The ministry said on Wednesday that Israeli claims denying the existence of a hunger crisis were an attempt to obscure worsening humanitarian conditions.
It also accused Israel of failing to meet the terms of the ceasefire agreement, particularly a provision requiring at least 600 aid trucks to enter Gaza each day.
Aziza al-Kahlout, a spokesperson for the ministry, told The New Arab that figures on the number of trucks entering Gaza did not necessarily reflect how much aid was reaching civilians.
“Statistics on the number of trucks entering the territory do not necessarily equal the amount of aid that reaches citizens,” she said.
She said UN data showed that while aid was entering Gaza, the amount reaching residents and being distributed remained far below the level of need.
According to al-Kahlout, no more than 30% of those requiring humanitarian assistance were currently benefiting from it.
She said ministry databases showed that 513,000 families needed support, while more than 95% of Gaza’s population had become fully dependent on aid.
More than 90% had also lost their purchasing power because of the war and Israeli restrictions, she said.
Al-Kahlout estimated that the amount of aid entering Gaza was equivalent to no more than 15% of the population’s overall needs.
She also said cash assistance to families had fallen by 40%, while other forms of relief had also declined.
A humanitarian protocol agreed under US President Donald Trump’s ceasefire plan on 10 October 2025 stipulated that at least 600 aid trucks should enter Gaza every day.
Gaza’s Government Media Office said on Tuesday that Israel was allowing in only about 35% of required food supplies, accusing it of practising “silent starvation”.
It said 69,387 aid and food trucks had entered Gaza over the 330 days since the ceasefire agreement was signed, compared with 198,000 that should have entered under the agreement.
Israel has said large quantities of humanitarian aid are entering Gaza.
But UN agencies have repeatedly warned that the amount reaching civilians and the ability to distribute it remain constrained.
In August, UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said 94% of Palestinians in Gaza needed shelter and basic household supplies.
UN data released for World Humanitarian Day also showed that four in five families were facing critical or catastrophic levels of hunger in shelters already struggling with shortages of fuel, power and essential goods.

Zelensky’s ex-spokesperson no longer sure Ukraine will retain statehood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:22:13 UTC
00:22:13 KST

MOSCOW, September 9. /TASS/. Ukraine’s reserves are so depleted and its society is so exhausted that its continued survival as a sovereign country is no longer guaranteed, Vladimir Zelensky’s former press secretary Yulia Mendel said.
"Ukraine is on its last breath. It is losing its people. It is losing the chance of a future. Institutions are rotting. The ordinary rules of how a society treats itself are rotting. The society itself is wearing down," she wrote on the X social network.
In her words, the consequences of this process may be catastrophic.
"We hear the same shortages again and again: there is no money for soldiers' salaries, there is not enough ammunition, there are no air-defense systems left to find. This is a war running on fumes. And the consequences are so catastrophic that it is no longer obvious whether Ukraine, as a country, will still be here," Mendel added.

Guidance: Military low flying: RAF operational low flying training timetable
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:21:56 BST
00:21:56 KST

Military low flying: RAF operational low flying training timetable
Royal Air Force (RAF) operational low flying training timetables in 3 areas of the UK.
Documents
Details
Timetables for operational low flying (OLF) training by RAF fast jets and Hercules aircraft. These timetables cover 3 tactical training areas (TTA) only. These are:
- LFA 7(T): central Wales
- LFA 14(T): northern Scotland
- LFA 20(T): the borders of southern Scotland and northern England
When the TTA is not in use, there may be other flying activity in the area. The MOD is unable to provide a timetable for all low flying activity as the information can very quickly become outdated due to weather conditions and training requirements.
Other low flying schedules
Related information
- Low flying military aircraft includes information about how to contact MOD about low flying in your area
- Military low flying includes detailed information about why we carry out low flying in the UK

Brics summit in Delhi on September 12-13: Agenda, schedule and other details
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:18:35 UTC
00:18:35 KST

The two-day summit will bring leaders together for closed-door talks, an innovation showcase, discussions on global governance
The two-day BRICS summit in New Delhi, set to kick-off Saturday, will focus on strengthening cooperation in food and energy security, health, disaster resilience and critical supply chains, as member countries seek to build greater resilience amid a fragmented geopolitical environment.The summit, hosted by India under its 2026 chairship, will also cover trade, investment, connectivity and technology, while leaders are expected to exchange views on major global and regional developments.
Building resilienceUnder India's resilience pillar, leaders will discuss cooperation in areas including health, agriculture, food and energy security, disaster-risk reduction and critical supply chains. The discussions come against the backdrop of disruptions caused by geopolitical conflicts and growing concerns over the resilience of global supply networks.Trade, investment and technologyStrengthening intra-BRICS trade and investment, improving connectivity and expanding cooperation in high technology will also be among the key economic priorities. India has placed these areas at the centre of its broader effort to deepen cooperation among emerging economies.
Global governanceThe summit will also focus on strengthening multilateralism and making global governance more inclusive. The first closed-door session on Saturday is titled “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism.”Global and regional issuesLeaders will exchange views on global and regional developments and discuss areas of mutual interest, according to the Ministry of External Affairs.Sunday's main sessionThe main open session on Sunday is titled “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth.” The summit will culminate with the release of the New Delhi Declaration.
BRICS summit schedule
Saturday (September 12)2:35 pm: Closed-door session for BRICS member countries on “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism”.4:25 pm: Leaders will tour the Bharat Innovates Exhibition.5:05 pm: Leaders will assemble at Bharat Mandapam for the family photo, followed by a joint tree-planting ceremony.7:30 pm: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host a gala dinner for the leaders.Sunday (September 13)9:55 am: Leaders from BRICS member countries, partner nations and outreach invitees will begin arriving.10:35 am: Official group photo.10:50 am: Open session on “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth”.The summit will conclude with the release of the New Delhi Declaration.
Who is attending?
Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Russian President Vladimir Putin, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto are among the leaders expected to attend the summit, reported PTI.The summit comes against the backdrop of the global economy facing disruptions from the Russia-Ukraine war, the West Asia crisis, including concerns over the Strait of Hormuz, and the trade and tariff policies of the Trump administration.With the grouping operating on consensus, questions also remain over whether members will agree on a joint statement, particularly amid differences between Iran and the UAE over the West Asia crisis.BRICS originally comprised Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. The group expanded in 2024 to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, while Indonesia joined in 2025.Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam became BRICS partner countries in 2025.The grouping now has 11 member countries, representing around 49.5% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade, according to the Indian government.India assumed its fourth BRICS chairship on January 1 this year having previously chaired the grouping in 2012, 2016 and 2021.
India's chairship is guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”, with a stated focus on a people-centric approach rooted in the principle of “humanity first”.Under India's chairship, more than 350 meetings and high-level engagements have been held across more than 25 cities, covering the grouping's three broad pillars: political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.

She also reports on key national and world developments and global news trends. A keen reader with a strong interest in storytelling that adds context, clarity, and depth to complex issues.

Centre clears separate engineering cadre for Delhi PWD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:18:34 UTC
00:18:34 KST

Centre clears separate engineering cadre for Delhi PWD
NEW DELHI: The Centre has approved the Delhi government's proposal to create a separate engineering cadre for the Public Works Department (PWD), a move expected to give the capital greater control over its engineering workforce and help speed up infrastructure projects.Under the decision, 3,214 sanctioned engineering posts across 36 categories in Delhi PWD will be separated from the Central Public Works Department (CPWD) cadre and brought under an independent Delhi PWD Engineering Cadre.
Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta welcomed the approval, describing it as a historic step towards making Delhi a developed, safe and world-class capital.The Delhi government said the separate cadre is intended to address a long-standing administrative issue and make the PWD's engineering system more responsive to the capital's specific requirements. The proposal had earlier been approved by the Delhi Cabinet under Gupta's leadership.The issue has remained pending for nearly 30 years. Until now, Delhi PWD's engineering services were largely dependent on the CPWD cadre, with appointments to its sanctioned posts being made through the Central government's system.According to the Delhi government, this arrangement could sometimes make it difficult to take decisions quickly in line with Delhi's own development and administrative requirements.
Gupta said Delhi's infrastructure needs are distinct because of the scale and pace of development in the national capital. The city requires continuous construction and maintenance of roads, bridges, government buildings, offices and other public infrastructure.With the creation of a separate cadre, the Delhi government will have greater control over its engineering workforce. It will be able to manage issues such as filling vacancies, ensuring the availability of engineers, monitoring projects and deploying officials according to the requirements of different works.The government also expects the new arrangement to help build an engineering workforce more familiar with Delhi's local infrastructure challenges and development priorities.The move comes as the government prepares to undertake several major construction and development projects. These include a new secretariat and mini-secretariats in all 11 districts, besides work related to mandis, sports grounds and other public facilities.Roads, bridges and other infrastructure projects will also require sustained engineering support across the capital.The government said the reform is not limited to changing the administrative structure of engineering posts. It is also intended to improve accountability and transparency in the execution of public works.Gupta said that under the earlier system, instances involving deficiencies or irregularities in construction projects could sometimes make it difficult to fix responsibility, particularly when the concerned officer was transferred.A separate Delhi PWD cadre, the government said, would allow the responsibilities of engineering officials and the monitoring of their work to be linked more closely with the Delhi government's administrative system.The Centre's approval now provides the formal basis for Delhi PWD to establish an independent engineering cadre. The government believes the move will make the department more self-reliant and help ensure greater continuity in the planning, execution and supervision of infrastructure projects.
For a rapidly developing capital facing growing demands on its roads, public buildings and other infrastructure, the decision marks a significant administrative change that could shape how Delhi's public works are planned and delivered in the years ahead.

MCD demolished 34 structures, sealed 17; over 1,200 PG buildings surveyed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:18:32 UTC
00:18:32 KST

MCD workers break concrete slabs on the rooftop of a PG during a demolition drive against illegal construction in Laxmi Nagar, in New Delhi (ANI photo)
NEW DELHI: Over the past two days, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has carried out 34 demolition actions and sealed 17 properties across its 12 zones, according to a statement on Wednesday.The civic body also identified around 1,243 buildings operating as paying guest (PG) accommodations, housing 24,000 occupants, to create a database and assess their structural safety.
The ramped-up action comes in the wake of the collapse of a building being run as a boys' paying guest in south Delhi's Satya Niketan. Seven people died in that incident.The MCD said it is assessing PG buildings for vulnerabilities, with particular focus on those having more than five storeys with RCC-framed structures or more than four storeys with load-bearing brick-wall structures.Based on field assessments, the buildings are being classified as "visibly safe", "visibly repairable - needs minor repairs", "visibly repairable - needs major repairs" and "visibly vulnerable/dangerous".The civic body issued 22 show-cause notices and passed four demolition orders as part of Wednesday's enforcement drive against violations of building bye-laws and the Master Plan of Delhi.On Tuesday, the MCD demolished 17 properties and sealed five for various violations.
Among the properties targeted on Wednesday was a building near Jama Masjid, with the MCD demolishing two roof panels on the ground floor and a partition wall.
A demolition action was taken against an unauthorised construction at Sadak Prem Narain in Bazar Sitaram, and properties declared dangerous in Vikas Nagar and Sector 17, Dwarka.At Rana Pratap Bagh, four reinforced concrete cement (RCC) roof slab panels on the third floor and one on the first floor were demolished, with reinforcement cut using a gas cutter. Brick walls on the second floor were also removed.The civic body demolished three RCC slab panels and cut reinforcement at a property in Sardar Nagar, Model Town.The MCD has directed officials to complete the survey by September 10.

Gaza students with overseas university offers, scholarships remain trapped
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:18:14 UTC
00:18:14 KST

Gaza students with overseas university offers, scholarships remain trapped
As a new term begins, students promised places abroad face impossible immigration rules.
Electricity was scarce and the bombs kept falling, but each evening, Mahmoud Aldaya left his family’s tent in a displacement camp in southern Gaza, in search of enough internet signal to submit his assignments.
Much of his university work was done remotely because Israel’s genocide had devastated Gaza’s higher education system. Despite the conditions, the 24-year-old finished at the top of his class at Gaza University.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4In Yemen, dates provide lifeline for farmers with few economic options
- list 2 of 4EU or Eurasia: Why Putin sparred with Armenia’s PM
- list 3 of 4Summer transfers 2026: All to know as Premier League signings break records
- list 4 of 4Trumpism is changing world order
With little prospect of continuing his education in Gaza, Aldaya looked abroad. He secured a scholarship at the University of Limerick in Ireland, which issued a letter supporting his application to leave the enclave.
But the academic year has begun without him. In August, the Irish government refused his visa. He now remains in Gaza City, where an Israeli drone attack last week killed at least three people, including two children, and wounded eight others.
“Receiving an unconditional offer and scholarship was a lifeline,” Aldaya told Al Jazeera. “Missing this window leaves me exposed to daily military bombardment and the risk that border crossings could shut indefinitely.
“Gaza has no safe zones. Remaining here is an everyday risk to life.”
He is one of dozens of Palestinian students who have secured places at Irish universities but have been refused permission to enter the country. Figures from Ireland’s Department of Justice show that, up to August 21, 103 Palestinian long-stay study visa applications had been refused this year, while just 39 visas were issued – an approval rate of 27.5 percent among decisions made. In 2025, that figure was 83.8 percent.
Some of those affected had already secured university places, scholarships and raised thousands of euros towards their education and evacuation. But students and their lawyers say they are being caught by immigration requirements that can be extraordinarily difficult to satisfy from inside Gaza, from producing certified bank statements and educational records to demonstrating sufficient finances and explaining gaps in their studies during the war.
The refusals are now the subject of a High Court challenge brought by students represented by Phoenix Law, a human rights legal firm.
Another student, who requested anonymity, fearing reprisals from the Israeli military, secured a scholarship for a master’s programme at an Irish university.
But after a visa refusal email, “I was completely devastated … My hands were shaking from the shock and at first I could not even process what I was reading,” said the student from Khan Younis.
Her finances and supporting documentation were among the issues raised.
Several students were required to demonstrate access to at least 10,000 euros to support themselves for a year, in addition to their course fees.
The student Al Jazeera interviewed, who has since raised additional money with the help of people in Ireland, said an evacuation of students is expected in September. She hopes her visa will arrive in time.
“Behind every visa application there is a real person, a real person with a life, a family, a future,” she said.
Some refusal letters seen by Al Jazeera cite insufficient evidence that applicants will return home after completing their studies.
“I want to return home, said the student, “to help rebuild the place I belong to.”
Proving the impossible, from Europe to the US
The problem extends beyond Ireland. Across Europe and North America, hundreds of Palestinian students who have been offered university places are facing visa refusals and bureaucratic challenges as the new academic year starts, according to government figures and advocacy groups.
One issue is providing proof of funds. Applicants are generally required to provide six months of bank statements. Where originals are unavailable, online copies must have every page authenticated by the bank and be accompanied by a letter confirming they are genuine. In Gaza, that can mean trying to obtain certified documents from a banking system that has itself been largely obliterated.
Appealing refusals raises other hurdles. There is no internationally recognised postal service operating in Gaza, yet Irish authorities require appeals to be submitted by post with original supporting documents.
Some students have faced questions about gaps in their education or employment and requests for educational records after nearly three years of war. By November 2025, approximately 97 percent of Gaza’s school buildings had been damaged or destroyed, according to the United Nations, while dozens of university buildings have been completely destroyed.
Even completing the basic requirements of a visa application can prove difficult.
Canada, for example, requires biometric data. Before the war, people could travel more easily outside of Gaza to access fingerprinting and photographing facilities, but it is nearly impossible now.
According to the Palestinian Students and Scholars at Risk Network (PSSAR) in Canada, more than 130 Palestinian students who have secured places in Canadian graduate programmes, many with scholarships, research stipends or other funding, have faced delays over biometrics.
In the United States, since January 1, Washington has stopped issuing almost all visas to people travelling on Palestinian Authority-issued or endorsed documents, including student visas, with limited exceptions, according to the US Department of State.
Belgian public broadcaster VRT reported on September 1 that 13 Palestinian students had secured both scholarships and visas to study at Belgian universities but remained trapped in Gaza.
In Italy, 72 Palestinian university students were evacuated from Gaza in May through the country’s “university corridors” programme, taking the number evacuated through the initiative since September 2025 to 229.
But L’Espresso reported on August 30 that universities are no longer operating under the same centrally coordinated framework known as IUPALS, or Italian Universities for Palestinian Students. They are instead having to find their own funding, from university departments or private donors, to cover scholarships, travel and living costs for students hoping to arrive in time for the new academic year.

North Korea Expands Nuclear Material Production Infrastructure With New Yongbyon Facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:18:11 UTC
00:18:11 KST

- Category
- World
North Korea Expands Nuclear Material Production Infrastructure With New Yongbyon Facility
North Korea has constructed a new uranium enrichment facility at its main nuclear complex in Yongbyon, with the building potentially capable of housing up to 28 cascades of gas centrifuges, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The IAEA based its assessment on satellite imagery and open-source information, including photographs released by North Korean state media. The agency has relied on remote monitoring to track Pyongyang’s nuclear activities since its inspectors were expelled from the country in 2009.
The available evidence indicates that North Korea continues to expand its nuclear infrastructure at multiple locations, according to the agency.
At the Yongbyon nuclear complex, IAEA experts identified a newly constructed two-story building as a second uranium enrichment facility. The assessment was made by comparing satellite imagery documenting the building’s construction with photographs released during North Korean leader Kim Jong Un’s visit to the site in June.
According to the report, images from the visit showed cascades of gas centrifuges installed on both floors of the main building. Based on the available imagery, the IAEA estimated that the facility could accommodate as many as 28 centrifuge cascades.
The development comes amid continued operation of North Korea’s uranium enrichment facilities at both Yongbyon and Kangson, raising concerns over the country’s capacity to produce nuclear material.
North Korea’s continued development of its nuclear program remains in violation of United Nations Security Council resolutions.
The expansion of nuclear infrastructure comes as Pyongyang has also strengthened the legal framework governing the use of its nuclear arsenal. North Korea amended its constitution to require an automatic nuclear response if Kim Jong Un is killed.
Separate legislation establishes Kim as the sole commander of the country’s nuclear forces and stipulates that if the nuclear command system comes under threat from an enemy attack, “a nuclear strike is carried out automatically and immediately.”

Ethiopia's constitutional reform: What does it mean — especially for Abiy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:18:00 UTC
00:18:00 KST

How Ethiopia's constitutional reform gives PM more power
September 9, 2026
Since 2018, Abiy Ahmedhas been the most powerful man in Ethiopian politics, governing the country during some of its most trying days in recent history. From the Tigray war to a feeble but lasting peace with neighboring Eritrea, Abiy has actively shaped and reshaped Ethiopia's role in Africa and indeed the world.
Soon, he might even get to consolidate more power and influence in his office, as Ethiopia's political system might fundamentally change in the future.
After weeks of consultations, there are indications that the offices of prime minister and president could be merged. This would mean that the largely ceremonial presidency could thus become the center of political power in the country.
While details of the precise redesign of the system remain unclear, local reports say that the consultations indeed resulted in a positive recommendation to create a stronger presidency.
For Abiy, that would likely be a remarkable prospect.
Support for a new office
During a drawn-out national dialogue with around 4,000 delegates in Addis Ababa in recent weeks, participants discussed some of the country's key political conflicts, including the overall structure of the state, ongoing ethnic tensions, the rule of law and human rights — as well as the role of the prime minister.
Abiy did not take part in these meetings but could benefit significantly from their endorsement of a presidential system.
One key element for any constitutional reform to be pushed through parliament is already in place: Abiy won June's parliamentary elections with a massive majority, which could help him and his party advocate for a presidency with broader executive powers.
Benefits of a stronger presidency
Supporters of a stronger presidency see it as a way of bringing Ethiopia's ethnically and regionally fragmented society closer together.
They say a president representing the country as a whole could help strengthen a national political identity.
Befeqadu Hailu, an Ethiopian civil rights activist and political commentator, told DW that this might be a strength of the proposed new system, and that a president directly elected by the public would have a stronger mandate to govern.
Hailu believes that in future elections, a presidential candidate would have to convince "more than one ethnic group and more than one religious group" to win, which could help strengthen democratic processes.
At the same time, he warned that "[p]residential systems are more prone to descending into dictatorship."
How much more power is there to take?
But the key question is not who would become president, but rather what powers this office would have — as well as who would be tasked with holding the president to account.
Ethiopia already has a powerful executive branch, and since taking office in 2018, Abiy has consolidated more and more political power.
The creation of the Prosperity Party in 2019 under his leadership, formed from a number of coalition partners, has already considerably reshaped the country's political system and significantly limited the role of the opposition.
Abiy also controls the military and security apparatus, with little power left to grab under a new system.
For British journalist and Ethiopia expert Martin Plaut, the proposed reform is therefore less of a transfer of power to one person than an act of "formalizing the situation that currently exists."
'Legal does not mean legitimate'
The proposed reform also raises a fundamental question about democratic processes: Can such a concentration of power be viewed as the will of the people if it is enacted through legal procedures in parliament? Or should there perhaps be a plebiscite on the proposed changes?
In this context, civil rights activist Hailu highlights the importance of distinguishing between procedural and popular legitimacy.
In Ethiopia, he says, existing political institutions have "procedural legitimacy" to enact such changes while they lack broad "popular legitimacy."
Hailu says bluntly that "no one believes that Ethiopia has ever had democratic elections," referring to the most recent parliamentary election, which took place under difficult conditions: Voting was not possible in several conflict-ridden regions of the country, while opposition parties reported instances of restrictions and repression.
It is therefore unclear to what extent the poll result can be regarded as democratically legitimate — yet it is seen as the official result.
This is why Hailu believes that parliament may have the formal authority to amend the constitution and introduce a presidential system while still being only partially representative of the voting populace.
Who was actually included in the process?
Another issue is not only what those participating in the national dialogue recommended but also who took part — and who didn't.
The composition of the dialogue, which eventually issued the recommendation to change the current system, is a major concern, as opposition parties boycotted the process, while influential armed groups with strong political aspirations were equally not represented.
Despite certain valid reservations about some of these movements, the result was that some of the major political forces most directly involved in Ethiopia's current conflicts were absent.
Plaut says this leaves only one conclusion: "Without the opposition parties and armed factions, the process lacks the backing of groups that feel alienated by the current system."
"I'm sure that the Prime Minister will get what he wants," Plaut says, describing the dialogue as merely a "rubber-stamping exercise."
Hailu also shared some critical views on the lack of political inclusion of opposing groups, arguing that it was ultimately aimed at implementing changes "based on the vision of the Prosperity Party itself."
No resolution in sight for Ethiopia's never-ending conflicts
Ethiopia's biggest challenges meanwhile are unlikely to be solved with a different style of leadership.
Armed conflicts continue in Oromia and Amhara; the 2020-2022 war in Tigray left deep political and social divisions, with many political and territorial issues remaining unresolved despite promising peace initiatives. And nearly half the population continues to live below the poverty line.
Plaut thinks that a new system of government will hardly address these problems; he believes that the proposed reforms amount to little more than "sticking a band-aid on what is a gaping wound."
He argues that the relationship between centralized power in Addis Ababa and Ethiopia's more than 80 ethnic groups remains unresolved. Previous attempts to ease tensions between the center and the periphery have failed.
In Plaut's view, the central government must first resolve the underlying tensions between itself and Ethiopia's various ethnic and regional groups.
Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

This requires a coordinated approach involving all relevant stakeholders. While discussions on long-term development solutions continue, we will focus on what can be done now and what passengers will be able to appreciate in the near future: making ticket purchases faster and more convenient, making information about platforms and service changes clearer, facilitating transfers and providing a higher-quality environment at the bus station,” says Vasily Serdyukov, Member of the Board of SIA RIVARO Holding.
According to the new shareholder, ticket prices are not directly determined by the owner of the bus station: fares for regional routes are approved by the state, while prices for international services are set by carriers. “The bus station generates revenue when it is convenient, accessible to passengers and in demand. That is precisely where our interest lies,” says Vasily Serdyukov.

RIGA - The Road Traffic Safety Directorate (Celu Satiksmes Drosibas Direkcija, CSDD) has received approximately 2,500 compensation claims following a cyberattack on the CSDD on August 8, during which personal data of multiple individuals and legal entities were compromised, Martins Malmeisters, head of the CSDD's Communications Department, told LETA.
The CSDD has received approximately 2,500 requests for compensation via various email addresses, to which the CSDD has responded individually.
The average compensation claim is around EUR 10,000, said Malmeisters.
The investigation into the cyberattack is ongoing, said Malmeisters. As to the compensation claims, the decision of the Data State Inspectorate will be decisive, he explained.
According to the relevant regulations, an individual may receive compensation if it is determined that the CSDD has failed to fulfill its obligations and the individual has suffered harm as a result.
It is currently too early to request compensation, and customers will be informed of the next steps, said Malmeisters. At the same time, the CSDD continues to evaluate additional measures that could be implemented to mitigate potential harm.
As reported, CSDD suffered a cyberattack on the night of August 8, during which the personal data of 1.2 million individuals and the data of approximately 200,000 legal entities were compromised. The data were obtained from payments made to the agency over the past 18 years.
Both the CSDD council and the company’s board of directors announced their resignations on Wednesday, August 19.
At the same time, Transportation Minister Rihards Kozlovskis (JV) has called for an internal probe to be conducted on an expedited basis to clarify all the circumstances and identify those responsible in connection with the cyberattack and the massive data breach. Among other things, the investigation must also evaluate the CSDD contract with Tet for the provision of cybersecurity services.
CSDD is a state-owned joint-stock company. The agency registers vehicles in Latvia, issues driver’s licenses, conducts vehicle inspections, and provides other services. The Ministry of Transport is the shareholder of the CSDD.

New EU rules to help municipalities alleviate housing crisis  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:55 UTC
00:16:55 KST

TALLINN - The European Commission on Wednesday presented a proposal to help member states and local authorities increase the availability of affordable housing in the most pressured areas.
According to a recent Eurobarometer survey, over half of urban residents consider the availability of affordable housing in their area a major concern. In some cities and popular tourist destinations, housing is increasingly used for purposes other than as a primary residence, making affordable housing progressively more inaccessible for locals.
The Affordable Housing Regulation will provide legal certainty for public authorities deciding to take action to increase housing availability within the framework of EU law. While some member states have already imposed restrictions to alleviate their housing crises, they have faced compliance issues with EU law. The new regulation introduces clarity and predictability, addressing the call from member states and municipalities for greater legal certainty.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "A year ago, I promised to tackle housing affordability in Europe. Today, we take a step in that direction. We are offering greater clarity and support to local authorities and communities, taking local circumstances into account. The lack of affordable housing is a concern for a great many European citizens. Essential workers and students cannot afford to live where they work and study. Moreover, this is a question of fairness. Today, we are acting for all Europeans."
The proposal establishes a European-level framework for assessing housing measures that affect the single market. The decision on whether to act and what measures to implement will be made by the competent authority, leaving housing policy choices to national, regional, and local authorities.
The new rules are designed to help authorities identify pressured areas using a common methodology. If authorities decide to restrict housing for certain uses, such as for short-term rentals or in cases of vacant properties, they must prove that such use exacerbates pressure on housing availability and ensure that any measures are targeted, necessary, and proportionate.
For short-term rentals, any measure must primarily target activities that reduce the housing stock available for long-term use, particularly when the scale, frequency, or commercial nature of such activities increases pressure on housing availability.
Before imposing restrictions, authorities must also prove that short-term rental activities have had a significant adverse effect on housing affordability or availability for at least three years and that less restrictive measures would not be equally effective.
Short-term rentals are not the only form of non-primary housing use that can intensify housing pressure. The Affordable Housing Regulation also provides a clearer framework for measures concerning the acquisition or use of residential property, such as second-home ownership or long-term vacancies.
The proposal protects legal certainty and legitimate expectations: conditions related to acquisition cannot be applied retroactively, an appropriate transitional regime must be established, and in the case of long-term vacant housing, justified periods of non-occupancy must be considered.
In pressured areas, the goal is for local-level measures to be better targeted, evidence-based, and up-to-date, thereby helping to increase the housing supply. The proposal also offers greater legal clarity for investors and property owners operating across multiple local markets.
The proposal will now be discussed by the European Parliament and the Council.

Competition among power exchanges increases in the Baltics as EPEX SPOT launches intraday auctions  - The Baltic Times

The Baltic transmission system operators, Latvia’s AS “Augstsprieguma tīkls”, Lithuania’s Litgrid AB and Estonia’s Elering AS, together with their partners, have completed the next stage in enabling multiple power exchanges to operate in the Baltic region. EPEX SPOT is also scheduled to begin operations in the Day-Ahead Market at the end of September, completing the full roll-out of its services in the Baltic electricity market. This means that EPEX SPOT will be available across all key segments of the wholesale electricity market in the Baltic States.
The IDA market provides electricity market participants with additional opportunities to optimise their positions closer to the time of electricity delivery. This supports more efficient power system balancing and facilitates the integration of renewable energy sources into the electricity market.
As previously reported, EPEX SPOT began operating in the continuous intraday market in November 2025, becoming the second Nominated Electricity Market Operator alongside Nord Pool. The introduction of intraday auctions marks the next major milestone in advancing the integration of the European electricity market and strengthening competition.
The multiple power exchange model is being implemented in the Baltic States in accordance with the European Union’s Capacity Allocation and Congestion Management Regulation (CACM). The regulation aims to foster competition among power exchanges, provide market participants with greater choice and support the efficient development of the European electricity market.
The project involves transmission system operators from the Baltic States and neighbouring countries: Latvia’s AS Augstsprieguma tīkls (AST), Estonia’s Elering AS (Elering), Lithuania’s Litgrid AB (Litgrid), Finland’s Fingrid Oyj (Fingrid), Poland’s Polskie Sieci Elektroenergetyczne S.A. (PSE) and Sweden’s Affärsverket svenska kraftnät (Svenska kraftnät), as well as the power exchanges Nord Pool and EPEX SPOT.
About AST
AST, the Latvian electrical power transmission system operator, ensures uninterrupted and secure transmission of electricity throughout Latvia. Its vision is to become the leading transmission system operator in the region through the efficient and successful implementation of development-oriented changes. AST has 68.46% shareholding in the capital of the operator of the natural gas transmission and storage system JSC “Conexus Baltic Grid”.

A wedding band can preserve more than a promise. It may hold a shared memory, reflect personal values, or recall the story that first brought two people together. Fantasy-inspired jewelry gives couples a way to express loyalty, courage, friendship, and devotion through metalwork. Carefully chosen symbols can make an everyday object feel deeply personal. The result is a keepsake with emotional meaning, practical value, and a connection to an enduring fictional tradition.
A Ring Can Carry a Story
Fictional stories often give couples a shared language for affection, sacrifice, and belonging. A band can reflect that connection through engraved script, symbolic markings, dark finishes, or sculpted details. The https://manlybands.com/pages/lord-of-the-rings collection illustrates how literary themes can inform a meaningful choice. Familiar references may appear prominently, while quieter elements suit partners who prefer subtle symbolism during daily wear.
Symbols Can Speak Without Words
Small images can communicate powerful ideas. A sword may suggest bravery, while a tree can represent family growth and endurance. Interlocking patterns often convey unity, continuity, or mutual support. Couples should select imagery that reflects their relationship rather than filling the surface with unrelated references. One carefully chosen emblem usually carries greater emotional force than several decorative features competing for attention.
Gold for Heirloom Appeal
Gold remains appropriate for couples seeking a traditional foundation with imaginative details. A 14K yellow gold band supports engraving and develops a familiar warmth over time. Its color contrasts effectively with dark lettering, brushed surfaces, or raised borders. Because gold carries established ceremonial meaning, a fantasy reference can feel distinctive without appearing theatrical or unsuitable for formal occasions.
Engraving Adds Hidden Meaning
Words can turn attractive jewelry into a private record of commitment. Couples may choose a fictional script, a brief quotation, initials, or an important date. Short inscriptions remain easier to read and preserve, especially inside narrow bands. Internal lettering creates a message known mainly to the wearer. Exterior text makes the reference more visible and gives the piece a stronger visual identity.
Details Should Serve the Design
Effective fantasy jewelry depends on proportion. Too many marks, textures, and raised elements can make a band appear crowded or difficult to clean. A central emblem, narrow inscription, or textured edge may provide sufficient narrative depth. Balanced spacing keeps each feature legible. Simpler construction also reduces snagging and makes routine care less demanding.
Matching Bands With Individual Character
Partners do not need identical rings to share a connected theme. One person might prefer a broad black band, while another might select a polished gold band with a fine inscription. Repeated symbols, related lettering, or complementary textures can create visual unity. This approach respects personal taste while preserving a shared story. Coordinated differences often produce a more authentic pairing than exact duplicates.
Licensed Design Creates Authenticity
Officially licensed jewelry can matter to devoted fans who value accurate references. Approved imagery, recognizable script, and faithful design cues help confirm a genuine connection to the source material. Such details may be especially important for couples whose relationship grew through novels, films, games, or fan communities. Accuracy becomes most valuable when a particular symbol recalls a meaningful period in their lives.
Practical Care Protects the Keepsake
Routine care helps preserve a fantasy-inspired band for many years. Wearers should remove rings before handling bleach, solvents, abrasive cleaners, heavy tools, or rough materials. Mild soap, lukewarm water, and a soft cloth can safely clean many surfaces. Periodic inspection may identify worn lettering, loose settings, or finish damage. Separate storage also prevents harder jewelry from causing avoidable scratches.
A Meaningful Gift for Beyond the Ceremony
These bands can commemorate engagements, anniversaries, vow renewals, or major relationship milestones. Their narrative quality suits partners who prefer gifts with personal history rather than temporary novelty. A ring might recall a first discussion about a beloved character, a shared reading tradition, or an unforgettable event. Over time, the object becomes a physical reminder of connection and commitment.
Conclusion
Fantasy-inspired wedding bands allow couples to carry cherished stories into ordinary life. Thoughtful symbols, suitable metals, comfortable proportions, and personal inscriptions can create a lasting record of shared values. Strong designs balance imagination with function, so meaningful details remain visible without overwhelming the wearer. Whether a reference appears boldly across the surface or stays concealed inside the band, the finished piece can preserve an important chapter of a relationship for years.

Clean energy technologies boost job creation in the EU  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:49 UTC
00:16:49 KST

TALLINN - Clean energy technologies are creating hundreds of thousands of jobs in the European Union, according to a report published today by the EEA (European Environment Agency).
Meanwhile, a persistent shortage of skilled workers could hinder further growth. The sector also continues to face challenges with inclusivity, as women and young people are underrepresented.
Global employment in the energy sector is growing faster than the economy as a whole. In 2024, energy sector employment increased by 2.2 percent, while overall economic employment grew by 1.3 percent. According to data from the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) and the International Labour Organization (ILO), the European Union ranks second after China, with a total of 1.8 million jobs directly or indirectly related to renewable energy in the EU. China has seven million jobs in the clean energy sector.
The EEA report, "Clean energy technologies in the European Union - impacts on high-quality jobs, skills and the just transition," examines employment in four clean energy technology areas: wind power, solar energy, heat pumps, and batteries. These sectors collectively employ hundreds of thousands of people in the EU.
Wind power is the largest employer among the technologies covered. In 2023, there were an estimated 273,500 jobs directly related to wind energy in the EU. Of these, 77 percent were in operations, which includes maintenance, energy-related contractual work, and sales administration. This was followed by manufacturing.
Solar energy technology directly employed more than 227,000 people in 2023. Approximately half worked in operation and maintenance activities, and 36 percent were in various stages of the construction value chain, including infrastructure development, site preparation, and grid connection. However, the manufacturing of solar energy technology in the EU remains limited.
The heat pump sector employed an estimated 80,100 people in 2023, with 65 percent of them in the construction field. The sector has significant growth potential throughout the EU.
The battery and storage technology sector employed approximately 33,000 people. Although it is the smallest of the four technologies, its employment grew the fastest between 2018 and 2023. Most jobs are concentrated in manufacturing, while research and development remain crucial for developing next-generation technologies.
Within the EU, employment in the clean technology sector is unevenly distributed. Germany has the most jobs in wind energy (125,000 in 2023), solar energy (nearly 84,000 jobs), and battery manufacturing (12,300 jobs). However, this does not mean Germany has the highest share of these jobs relative to its total employment. Portugal, Spain, and Italy lead in the heat pump sector, while employment growth in the battery and storage technology sector has been fastest in Hungary and Poland.
According to the report, the concentration of jobs often reflects the existing industrial strengths and know-how of countries. If employment remains highly unevenly distributed across regions, it could increase regional disparities.
The report reveals that the growth in clean energy jobs does not automatically translate to a more inclusive labor market. The share of women reaches 26 percent in the wind and battery sectors, but it is only 14 percent in the heat pump sector. Young workers, aged 15-24, accounted for only six to seven percent of employees in the wind, solar, and heat pump sectors in 2023.
A shortage of skilled workers threatens the deployment of clean energy technologies, and most member states report deficits in key technical roles in installation and construction. Coordinated policy measures are needed to significantly expand training and upskilling opportunities, as well as to retrain the existing workforce, to ensure an adequate labor supply.
The quality of jobs also varies significantly across different technologies and parts of the value chain. Wages in the heat pump sector are approximately 40 percent lower than in the wind energy sector, which has the highest salaries among the four areas covered. Operation and maintenance jobs, more common in wind energy, generally offer more stable employment and better access to training. Construction and installation work in solar and heat pump sectors are more project-based, exposing workers more frequently to physical risks such as extreme temperatures, and offering fewer training opportunities. The impact of battery manufacturing on worker health and safety, as well as on local communities and the environment, remains a significant concern.
The EU has created an increasingly supportive policy framework to strengthen clean technology manufacturing, accelerate their deployment, and eliminate industry bottlenecks. This includes the Clean Industrial Deal, the Net-Zero Industry Act, the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, and AccelerateEU, as well as various funding instruments and targeted initiatives such as the Battery Booster strategy, which supports the expansion of the EU's battery manufacturing capacity.
The report calls for coordinated policy measures to increase training and retraining opportunities and to improve job quality. This would help to better recruit and retain workers in a sector facing significant labor shortages.
More information about developments in Estonia's energy sector can be found on the Environmental Portal's Sustainable Development data gateway and the renewable energy topic page.

====================================================================================================

Europe’s defence supply chains need more than defence companies, industry leaders say in Latvia  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:41 UTC
00:16:41 KST

Europe’s efforts to expand defence production will increasingly depend on companies that may not consider themselves part of the defence industry at all, industry experts and executives argued at the Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum, which brought together around 200 participants from more than 15 countries on 6–7 September.
The message emerging from the forum in Rēzekne, eastern Latvia, was straightforward: European defence capacity cannot be expanded by defence primes and specialist manufacturers alone. It also requires companies in electronics, engineering, communications, precision manufacturing, energy, software, sensors and other civilian industries to enter defence supply chains. More than 200 pre-arranged business meetings took place alongside technology demonstrations, company visits and discussions involving representatives of BAE Systems, Dedrone by Axon, SAF Tehnika, Origin Robotics, Redwire, Silmor, Pērkons Energy and other European and international companies.
“For companies looking at the defence market, the first question should not be ‘What defence product should we build?’ but ‘What capability do we already have, and who needs it?’” said defence and strategy adviser Thibault Normand. He argued that becoming part of the defence industrial base does not necessarily mean developing a complete weapons system. Modern defence platforms rely on extensive networks of specialised suppliers. Dassault Aviation, for example, identifies around 400 companies in the industrial ecosystem supporting the Rafale fighter programme.
The challenge, Normand said, is therefore not only technological capability but industrial credibility. “An excellent prototype from an unreliable supplier is not a defence capability.” Defence customers need confidence that suppliers can deliver consistently over decades and scale production rapidly during a crisis, he added. For companies seeking to enter the sector, the immediate objective should therefore not necessarily be winning a major procurement but becoming credible enough to secure the next conversation with a customer or prime contractor.
Latvia seeks a larger role for domestic industry
Latvia is simultaneously seeking to increase the participation of its domestic industry in defence procurement.
Uģis Norītis, Deputy State Secretary for Planning at Latvia’s Ministry of Defence, said Latvia aims to increase the share of domestic industry in defence procurement to 20% by 2028 and 30% by 2036, while progressively increasing funding for defence innovation. Support is being developed across the industrial lifecycle, from early-stage ideas and prototypes to scaling manufacturing capacity.
Norītis also stressed that many components required by defence systems are not inherently military products. Materials, electronics, engineering components and other widely used industrial products can all form defence supply chains, creating opportunities for companies that have traditionally operated entirely in civilian markets. For Europe, this represents a potentially much larger industrial base than the companies currently labelled as “defence”.
From Latvian start-ups to international defence customers
Latvia already provides examples of how quickly companies can enter international defence markets. Origin Robotics, founded in 2022, now employs 103 people, according to the company’s Head of Government Relations Māris Ķuda. Its unmanned systems are already used by the armed forces of eight countries, including Latvia, Ukraine, France and Denmark. Latvian telecommunications equipment manufacturer SAF Tehnika, meanwhile, has built an international business in wireless communications and radio-frequency monitoring. CEO Normunds Bergs presented the company’s experience of taking Latvian-developed technology into defence and security markets worldwide. The examples point to a broader opportunity for smaller European economies: they may not compete with Europe’s largest defence manufacturers in scale but can occupy highly specialised positions in international supply chains.
The next bottleneck may be integration
Technology itself, however, is only part of the challenge. Christian Emaus, Regional Director for the Nordics, Baltics and NATO at Dedrone by Axon, argued that one of the most pressing problems in airspace security is increasingly the ability to connect technologies, institutions and operators.
Defence forces, police, critical infrastructure operators and private companies can each have sophisticated systems and their own understanding of what is happening in the airspace yet still lack a common operational picture. “You cannot control the airspace if you cannot share the picture of it,” Emaus said. He argued that Latvia could position itself not only as a home for dual-use technology companies, but also as an environment where technologies, users and institutions can be connected and tested together.
More than 200 business meetings
The second Latvian Dual-Use Export Forum brought together around 200 participants from Latvia and abroad, representing more than 15 countries.International participants included TensorOne, AJB Subsea, HISDESAT, NEST AI, Fischer Panda and Sine Engineering, while speakers and programme participants represented companies including BAE Systems, Dedrone by Axon, Wolfram Europa, SAF Tehnika, Silmor, Pērkons Energy, Redwire, RAW and Origin Robotics.
The programme began on 6 September with an Industry Day organised together with Latvia’s Ministry of Defence, including live demonstrations of Latvian defence and dual-use technologies and visits to manufacturing companies. On 7 September, discussions shifted from technology to commercialisation: how companies can turn engineering capabilities and innovation into international partnerships, supply-chain positions and exports.
“Interest in Latvian dual-use technologies and industrial capabilities is clearly growing, but the value of the forum is not measured by participant numbers,” said Līva Stūrmane, Chair of the Board of the Latvian Exporters Association ‘The Red Jackets’. “What matters is creating the conditions for new partnerships. For a smaller country such as Latvia, integration into international supply chains is one of the most realistic ways of turning technological and manufacturing capabilities into defence exports.”

Compensa: Private insurance should direct people to primary healthcare  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:41 UTC
00:16:41 KST

TALLINN - According to Merko Kimsto, head of the Estonian unit of Compensa Life Insurance, a managed care pathway starting with a primary medical assessment should become standard practice in private health insurance.
Compensa is redesigning its health insurance service based on this principle, so that individuals can quickly receive a professional assessment and be directed to the right specialist when needed.
Kimsto explained that people often manage their own healthcare journey, selecting specialists and what they believe are necessary tests based on their symptoms. This results in patients wasting time and money, as well as taking up limited appointment slots with specialists for services that may not resolve their health issues. Meanwhile, in many cases, a family doctor or general practitioner could offer the fastest assistance.
"As insurers, we must also look at ourselves in the mirror. For years, the main selling point for health insurance has been quick, direct access to specialists - and Compensa has been part of this," Kimsto said. "This can give people the impression that seeing a specialist is always the right first choice for any health issue."
According to a Norstat survey commissioned by Compensa, three out of four Estonian employees consider employer-provided health insurance necessary. Currently, approximately 72,000 people, or eight percent of the working-age population, are covered by health insurance. Kimsto noted that while the growth in health insurance is welcome, new policies do not add more doctors, nurses, or their working hours to the healthcare system.
"If we build health insurance solely around quick, direct access to specialists, we risk creating a parallel queue with the same bottlenecks as the public system. Health insurance should help people get a professional assessment first and then, if necessary, quickly guide them to the exact right specialist," Kimsto stressed.
As a solution, Compensa Life Insurance has expanded its partnership with the Salu healthcare service center to offer a service where the care pathway begins with an online medical consultation. A healthcare professional assesses the health concern and helps determine if treatment, analysis, diagnostics, an in-person appointment, or specialist care is required.
"With this solution, the insured can access an initial digital consultation with a family doctor or GP within one to two days, free of charge. If needed, an appointment with a specialist is arranged within three to seven days. For subsequent treatment, Compensa settles the bill directly with the service provider, meaning the individual doesn't have to pay the full medical bill upfront and later claim reimbursement," Kimsto explained.
According to Kimsto, a managed care pathway helps keep health insurance a valuable and sustainable employee benefit. Unnecessary or duplicate visits and tests increase the medical costs for the entire group of insured employees, which can affect the price and terms of the policy for the next insurance period.
"This doesn't mean that people should use their insurance less or delay necessary treatment. On the contrary, help should be sought as early as possible for any health concern. We are not in any way restricting or prohibiting our clients from seeing specialists as they have before. Rather, we are trying to encourage a way of resolving health issues that guides the person immediately to the appropriate specialist and doesn't leave them to navigate the choice of healthcare services alone."

Nurkulov is on trial for transferring small sums of money to a Palestinian terrorist organization.

European metrologists shaping the future of measurements in Tallinn  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:16 UTC
00:16:16 KST

TALLINN – Metrosert is hosting the annual meeting of the European Association of National Metrology Institutes' (EURAMET) Technical Committee for Mass and Related Quantities in Tallinn.
Sixty of Europe's leading measurement experts will arrive in Estonia, with over 65 additional participants following the discussions online. The meeting will establish priorities for the field's development, international comparison measurements, and the next steps in scientific cooperation.
The EURAMET technical committee deals with the measurement of mass, pressure, force, torque, density, viscosity, hardness, and gravitational acceleration.
According to Mari Aru, head of Metrosert's research and development division, the precise measurement of these quantities is crucial for, among other things, the safety of industrial equipment and energy infrastructure, the correct composition of pharmaceuticals, food quality, the fair accounting of fuel and goods, and the development of new high-tech solutions.
"Metrology is all around us, although we usually only notice it when a measurement goes wrong. From a societal perspective, the goal is simple: for the technology around us to work safely, for the amount of active ingredient in a medicine to be correct, for production processes to function stably, and for fuel and other goods to be billed for fairly. Behind all of this are reliable and internationally comparable measurements," said Mari Aru.
National metrology institutes maintain and develop their country's most accurate measurement capabilities. In Estonia, this task is carried out by Metrosert. Having local measurement capabilities helps Estonian companies ensure product quality, certify it for foreign markets, and reduce dependence on foreign laboratories for critical measurements.
To ensure that measurements made and calibration certificates issued in Estonia are trusted in other countries, European metrology institutes regularly compare their standards, measurement capabilities, and methods. International comparison measurements show whether laboratories in different countries achieve consistent results when measuring the same quantity.
At the annual meeting in Tallinn, roadmaps for various measurement fields will be reviewed and approved, setting development priorities for the coming years. New comparison measurements and research projects will also be planned, and topics such as the digitalization of measurements and the measurement of dynamic quantities—those that change rapidly over time—will be discussed.
"The directions agreed upon in Tallinn will influence which measurement capabilities are developed in Europe in the coming years and how new methods will move from laboratories to be used by businesses. For Estonia, hosting the meeting is also a recognition of Metrosert's competence and an opportunity to participate in shaping the future of European measurement science," added Mari Aru.
The EURAMET Technical Committee for Mass and Related Quantities is one of the association's largest, comprising six subcommittees, two working groups, and approximately 30 ongoing cooperation projects. Separate discussions will be held in Tallinn on the topics of mass, pressure, force and torque, density and viscosity, hardness, and gravimetry. Participants will also tour Metrosert's national standard laboratories.
EURAMET is the European Association of National Metrology Institutes, tasked with coordinating cooperation in measurement science and ensuring the international credibility and recognition of European measurement results. The annual meetings of the technical committees are held once a year in one of EURAMET's member states.
Metrosert is Estonia's center for applied research and the central body for metrology. Metrosert maintains and develops Estonia's national standards for length, mass, temperature, and electrical quantities, and ensures their traceability to the International System of Units (SI).

====================================================================================================

Why a digital company’s headquarters, target market and regulator may be in different countries  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:08 UTC
00:16:08 KST

A digital service can look unmistakably Dutch, German or Estonian without being incorporated in that country. Language, currency and a country-code domain can indicate which market a business wants to reach, but they do not necessarily reveal where the legal entity is registered or which authority supervises a particular activity.
For cross-border digital businesses, those are separate questions. A company may be established in one country, operate a website for another market and fall under the supervision of a regulator in that target country.
The brand is not always the legal company
Consumers usually remember a short brand name. Contracts, licences and regulatory registers tend to use the formal name of the company behind it. Those names can differ without anything unusual taking place.
A website may therefore present one recognisable brand to customers while the legal entity behind it appears under a different corporate name. That distinction becomes especially important in regulated sectors, where permissions and obligations generally apply to the company rather than simply to the brand shown on the homepage.
A country-code domain mainly signals a target market
A .nl domain strongly suggests that a service is aimed at users in the Netherlands. It does not prove that the company operating it is incorporated there. The same principle applies to other national domains.
A site such as 711.nl is a clear example of a Dutch-facing domain. The platform is presented for the Dutch market, while the legal company behind it does not have to be incorporated in the Netherlands simply because the web address ends in .nl.
Language creates a similar impression. A platform with Dutch customer support, euro pricing and Dutch terms may be designed specifically for that market while the company itself is legally established elsewhere in Europe.
It therefore helps to separate two questions: who is the website intended for, and which company legally operates it?
A licence belongs to a legal entity and an activity
Regulated digital markets add another layer. A licence is issued to a named legal entity for specified activities within a particular regulatory framework. The consumer brand, corporate name and website address do not necessarily match one another.
711 B.V., for example, is registered in Belgium, while its online gambling activity for the Dutch market operates under a licence issued by the Dutch Kansspelautoriteit. The company’s place of incorporation, its target market and the authority regulating that activity are therefore separate parts of the same cross-border structure.
This is why the location of a company’s headquarters alone does not determine where a regulated digital service may operate.
Different sectors follow different regulatory models
Cross-border activity in payments, media, cryptoassets and gambling cannot be reduced to one generic European rule. Each sector has its own legal structure.
Some financial services can operate across borders through European authorisation mechanisms. Media services may be limited by territorial rights. Online gambling remains closely connected to national licensing systems in many markets.
A company being authorised for one activity in one country therefore does not automatically mean that every service it offers can be marketed throughout the EU under the same conditions.
Licence scope matters too
Even when a company holds a valid authorisation, the scope of that permission matters. A licence for one regulated activity does not automatically cover every product or service the company may want to introduce.
Validity periods can matter as well. Regulatory permissions may be renewed, amended or expire over time. For that reason, the relevant question is not simply whether a company has ever held a licence, but what activity the current authorisation covers.
Technical access does not define the target market
Digital services make geography more complicated because a person may be able to open a website from outside the market for which it was designed.
A traveller in Latvia may technically be able to visit a Dutch-facing website operated by a Belgian company. That fact alone says little about whether every part of the service is intended, available or authorised for users in Latvia.
Accessibility, target market and regulatory permission are therefore different concepts. The internet makes websites easy to reach across borders, but it does not remove the legal boundaries attached to particular services.
Geoblocking can have different causes
Some online services restrict content according to a user’s location. The visible result may look the same — a page, video or service is unavailable — but the reason behind the restriction can differ.
A streaming company may be dealing with territorial media rights. An online retailer may choose not to serve a country because of shipping costs or returns. A regulated service may face restrictions because the required authorisation does not apply in that market.
The technical block is only the outcome. The legal or commercial reason behind it depends on the type of service.
Map the business before drawing conclusions
A useful way to understand a cross-border digital company is to separate four elements: the consumer brand, the legal entity, the place where that company is incorporated and the market-specific authorisation for the service being offered.
Those elements may point to different countries without creating a contradiction. A business can be incorporated in one EU member state, operate a website aimed at customers in another and be subject to a regulator in that target market.
The internet makes the customer-facing side of a business international. Corporate structures and regulatory systems remain tied to specific jurisdictions. Keeping those layers separate makes it much easier to understand how a cross-border digital service is actually organised.

It is not possible to replace Russian and Belarusian mineral fertilizer supplies with imports from other countries in the short term - owner of WO Trading  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:08 UTC
00:16:08 KST

RIGA - It is not possible in the short term to fully replace Russian and Belarusian mineral fertilizer supplies with shipments from other countries while maintaining current price levels, Toms Egle, owner of SIA WO Trading, told LETA.
WO Trading has challenged before the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) the changes to customs duties imposed by the European Union (EU) on goods originating in or exported from Russia and Belarus.
When asked what the main arguments are for challenging the customs duty changes in court, Egle explained to LETA that the gradual increase in customs tariffs stipulated by the EU regulation poses an objective risk that the supply of mineral fertilizers essential to agriculture will decrease in the EU, leading to a corresponding increase in their prices.
Given the high concentration of the global fertilizer market, the reorientation of supplies could pose a risk of price increases not only in the EU but also in the broader global market, Egle said.
He emphasized that WO Trading does not object to the political objective of increasing customs tariffs and supports sanctions against Russia and Belarus, but objects to the proportionality of the chosen instrument and its potentially disproportionate impact on Latvia’s mineral fertilizer market and agricultural sector.
He explained that WO Trading's operations in Latvia’s regions are aimed at supplying Latvian farmers with mineral fertilizers.
Egle added that the EU regulation on changes to customs duties applicable to certain imported goods originating in or exported from Russia and Belarus was adopted on June 17, 2025, and establishes gradually increasing customs tariffs through 2028.
Egle emphasized that the mineral fertilizer market is global, yet at the same time highly concentrated. As an example, he noted that the potash fertilizer market is the most concentrated, with three leading countries: Russia, Belarus, and Canada. Russia is also the world's leading producer of nitrogen and phosphate fertilizers.
WO Trading believes there is a reasonable and objective risk that alternative mineral fertilizer supplies to the EU will be priced higher than before the tariff increase under the regulation, namely, that prices will adjust to reflect the increased cost of mineral fertilizers originating in Russia and Belarus on the EU market.
WO Trading wishes to ensure that Latvian agricultural producers are not forced to reduce the amount of fertilizer they use, thereby jeopardizing crop yields. The rising cost of mineral fertilizers increases agricultural production costs and raises the final price of products paid by consumers, Egle emphasized.
There is also a risk that, as customs tariffs rise, there will be a greater incentive to route mineral fertilizers from Russia and Belarus through third countries, repackage them, or otherwise conceal their actual origin. This, in turn, could complicate oversight and reduce the effectiveness of regulations, explained the owner of WO Trading.

Statistics: Plenty of strong companies remain despite rising bankruptcies  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:16:03 UTC
00:16:03 KST

TALLINN - According to data from Statistics Estonia, the number of bankrupt companies in the second quarter increased by nearly a third year-on-year. However, recent data from Creditinfo indicates that the number of companies with a strong credit rating is higher than at any point in the last four years.
According to Marjan Savtsenko, head of corporate banking at Luminor, the rise in bankruptcies alone is not enough to indicate a broad-based weakening of the business sector.
In the second quarter, 47 companies in Estonia went bankrupt, up from 36 a year earlier. Last year, a total of 154 companies were declared bankrupt, while the country had nearly 160,000 active businesses. This translates to approximately one bankruptcy for every 1,000 active companies.
"A nearly 30 percent increase might seem significant at first glance, but with small absolute numbers, it's essential to look at the broader picture. Bankruptcy still affects a very small portion of active companies in Estonia. A historical comparison also shows that the current level is low: in 2009, Estonia saw 544 corporate bankruptcies," Savtsenko said.
This stability is also confirmed by the latest credit rating data from Creditinfo. At the end of June, Estonia had 38,439 companies with an A, AA, or AAA credit rating, an increase of 795 companies, or 2.1 percent, compared to the previous year. This figure is the highest it has been in the last four years. The Creditinfo rating assesses a company's creditworthiness and business risk, considering factors such as its economic and financial standing and payment history.
However, the total number of companies in the business register grew even faster, from 278,651 a year ago to 297,421 at the end of June this year-an increase of 6.7 percent. Consequently, the proportion of companies with a strong credit rating fell slightly, making up 12.9 percent of all registered businesses this year, down from 13.5 percent the previous year.
"The rise in bankruptcies and the growth in the number of companies with strong credit ratings are not contradictory. The business landscape is currently diverse: some companies are under pressure, while at the same time, Estonia has more companies with a strong credit rating than at any time in the past four years," said Simon Renno, head of sales at Creditinfo Estonia.
Savtsenko noted that it is also important to consider the time lag when interpreting bankruptcy statistics. It can take years from the onset of a company's financial difficulties to the final declaration of bankruptcy, meaning that current figures may actually reflect the economic environment of several years ago.
The highest number of bankruptcies occurred in the trade, construction, and real estate sectors. "In trade, the key factors were weaker demand and greater price sensitivity among consumers. In construction, companies faced difficulties due to rapid price hikes, especially those locked into fixed-price contracts. Meanwhile, the real estate sector was impacted by rising construction costs, the increase in the Euribor rate, and falling demand. The effects of these events might not show up in bankruptcy statistics for several years," Savtsenko explained.
