France's main far-right party has expelled a member who is a policeman after body cam footage of him making racist comments sparked outrage ahead of presidential elections it hopes to win next year.

How a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:15:00 EEST
00:15:00 KST

"Four of them couldn't walk": how a Special Operations Forces company commander evacuated a wounded soldier on foot, then went back for his comrade's body
Company commanders don't usually evacuate their soldiers personally. Their primary task is to direct their unit's actions from the command and observation post. But modern warfare has produced a rare breed of soldiers who are exceptions to the rule.
A few weeks ago, for instance, the whole of Ukraine witnessed how Vladyslav Polskyi, a company commander with the 475th Separate Assault Regiment (Code 9.2), personally evacuated two wounded soldiers.
When a video was released of Polskyi running over to them with no helmet or body armour, dragging them off a broken-down unmanned ground vehicle and loading them onto a pickup truck, it drew thousands of admiring comments. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later awarded the courageous company commander the title of Hero of Ukraine and the Order of the Gold Star.
"It was brave," Eighteen says of Polskyi's actions. Eighteen, a company commander in the 3rd Detachment of the 4th Special Operations Forces Regiment, says it is extremely rare for a company commander to take part in an evacuation personally.
Interestingly, however, at almost the same time as Vladyslav Polskyi was evacuating the two wounded soldiers, Eighteen also found himself in a situation where he could no longer stand back and direct the rescue of his men from afar.
Eighteen is 26 and has been at war since he was 19. He started out as a machine gunner with the 3rd Special Operations Forces Regiment, later serving as a marksman, sniper, squad commander and deputy group commander. He now commands a company in the 3rd Detachment of the 4th Special Operations Forces Ranger Regiment.
Recently one of his groups was on their way back from a mission when one soldier sustained a gunshot wound. Later, almost the whole group was hit by an improvised explosive device.
Four special forces soldiers were unable to walk independently, but ultimately all of them were evacuated.
Eighteen was, of course, far from the only hero in this successful rescue. The entire unit was involved in rescuing the group over the course of five days. The company commander is full of praise for the heroism and professionalism shown by all his comrades, from drone operators and medics to logistics personnel.
Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life) has decided to tell the story from the perspective of Eighteen – a commander who would normally have been directing the evacuation, but this time went in himself to bring his men out.
"If the company commander himself turns up, things are about to get interesting"
It all happened in August, when a group of special forces soldiers led by a commander with the alias Santa, serving with the 4th Special Operations Forces Ranger Regiment, was tasked with ambushing Russian troops along one of their routes.
The group infiltrated about 15 km into the area, where they succeeded in killing four Russians – they offered them the chance to surrender, but they refused. When the group received the order to withdraw, they moved into a forest to get some rest. But unbeknownst to them, danger was approaching.
"We were doing reconnaissance and spotted one of the enemy going into the forest where the guys were," Eighteen says. "He approached stealthily, and we didn't spot him until almost afterwards. We ordered the guys to clear the sector the enemy soldier had entered.
Just then one of our brothers-in-arms was shot and wounded. The group opened fire on the enemy and wounded him as well. We don't know what happened to him after that because the group was focused on evacuating our wounded brother-in-arms."
The bullets had hit a special forces soldier who goes by the alias Malyi (Little One): he had been shot in the abdomen and arm and several of his fingers had been blown off. He was given first aid. But then, as the group was leaving the wooded area, they triggered one of the improvised explosive devices that the grey zone is littered with.
By some miracle, Malyi wasn't hit by the blast – but now he wasn't the group's only casualty. Four other soldiers sustained severe leg injuries. One of them, Sava, died almost immediately after being dragged into cover.
Suddenly the group that had been evacuating one wounded soldier found itself having to evacuate almost half its members.
"The guys all had leg wounds," the company commander recalls. "There were two uninjured operators left in the group, plus one medic. They pulled everyone off the open ground and into the bushes so they could give them first aid, and they were treating the wounded, all of whom were now in a serious condition.
That was when I realised I had to go into the area and get my people out. Nobody could have imagined that out of a group of eight we'd end up with four seriously wounded men and one slightly wounded. Four of them couldn't walk."
Eighteen remained in contact with the group commander and watched everything unfold live. Heavyshot drones dropped everything that Santa's group would need for the rescue: additional stretchers and medical supplies.
"We understood that we couldn't leave the guys there. And time wasn't on their side – they'd already been in the area for about six days, and there were still around 13-14 km to cover during the evacuation. Everyone realised they wouldn't be able to get out on their own," he says.
Another group of special forces soldiers, which was on its way to a mission, was redirected to help the wounded. They evacuated one soldier, but the most seriously wounded man was still in the area.
Eighteen asked his commanding officer for permission to go in and retrieve him himself. He took a medic and two soldiers from his company with him. They managed to drive part of the way, but there was still around 15 km to walk.
They had to get to Malyi and carry him out without being spotted by Russian drones – and they did it.
"The most important things here are physical fitness and your knowledge. We got there as fast as we could," Eighteen recalls. "We picked up the most seriously wounded soldier. The medic immediately treated him, and since we had additional medication with us, we patched him up…
The main thing was that they realised we were now in the same situation as them. The group commander said when he heard over the radio that we were in the area, he said: 'If the company commander himself turns up, things are about to get interesting.'"
"There were moments when he lost heart. He said: 'You don't need to carry me anywhere'"
Early in the morning, the group led by Eighteen set off. The wounded soldier remained conscious throughout. The soldiers made their way through forests, over hummocks and through wooded areas torn apart by guided aerial bombs, and every time they had to make a dash for it, it was agony for Malyi.
"He was, shall we say, a bit cranky because of his wound. He'd been hit in the abdomen, so he was in a lot of pain, and it wasn't always easy to move him. Sometimes we had to run with him, carry him, or drag him," Eighteen recalls.
Drones dropped water, food and medicine for the soldiers. Time was another enemy, as Malyi was in urgent need of medical attention. The group would only allow the wounded man to rest occasionally, letting him sleep for an hour or two after taking painkillers.
"There were moments when he couldn't take it any more and lost heart. He'd say: 'I don't want to. You don't need to carry me anywhere.' But painkillers make all the difference. Obviously he was in a lot of pain. But he did well and held on.
Towards the end, when he realised there were only two or three kilometres to go, his attitude changed completely. We'd give him a cigarette and a swig of water from the bottle cap. And he started urging us on: 'Come on, let's get through here faster, let's not stop.' We were really surprised. We were exhausted by then and wanted to rest, and he was like: 'No, no, keep going,'" Eighteen says, smiling.
The journey with the wounded soldier took 15 hours. It wasn't until midnight that Malyi was handed over to the medics.
"It was a good thing we did the exfiltration so fast, because at the hospital we found out he didn't have much time left: his liver had been punctured," Eighteen says.
By this time, another group led by one of the battalion's senior sergeants was halfway there. Santa's group, whose members had been wounded, had also managed to make some progress, but they couldn't move very fast because the soldiers were exhausted. The wounded were moved out gradually: the tourniquets gave them a little leeway in terms of time.
"His family were very grateful that we brought his body back"
Eighteen's work wasn't over yet. As soon as Malyi had been handed over to the medics, the company commander decided they had to retrieve the body of the fallen soldier, Sava.
"He hadn't been with me all that long. He was a calm person – a really motivated, determined guy who wanted to get things done. He didn't have a wife or children, but he had a mother and a sister," the commander recalls.
To bring their brother-in-arms' body back, Eighteen, his two fellow soldiers and the medic set off once again into the area they had struggled so hard to get out of. In the course of rescuing the wounded and retrieving the fallen soldier's body, the group covered more than 50 km in total.
Sava was laid to rest in the city of Kryvyi Rih. He was 35.
"We've already buried him. His family were very grateful that we brought his body back," Eighteen says.
The rescue operation took five days. Everyone except Sava made it. Despite the severe injury to Malyi's arm, doctors managed to save it.
"The legs feed the wolf, as the saying goes. And in the Special Operations Forces, the wolf is us"
"We try to evacuate all our wounded," Eighteen says. Photo: 3rd Detachment of the 4th Special Operations Forces Ranger Regiment
During his seven years of service, Eighteen has fought on many of the hottest fronts: in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts.
He had to personally evacuate a comrade in 2023, when FPV drones were in use, but before enemy drones had begun to dominate the skies the way they do now.
A 23-year-old soldier in the group was seriously wounded: both his arms had been blown off and his legs were injured. Eighteen and the group quickly gave him first aid and handed him over for evacuation. Compared with the recent operation, it was a piece of cake. Evacuating soldiers is much more difficult now.
"Now the sky is completely controlled by drones – both ours and the enemy's. The hardest part is getting into an area and getting back out. When you're operating in the area, there's less chance of being wounded. We used to drive in, but now we have to go in on foot, carrying a huge amount of weight.
If you have a casualty, the entire mission comes to a halt. Everyone switches to getting the wounded soldier out. And if, as in our case, you have four people who can't walk, you have to deploy every resource you have.
That's what happened this time: everyone was involved. The UAV component was working, unmanned ground vehicles were delivering supplies, and the battalion- and regiment-level electronic warfare units were operating too, providing cover across the exposed areas we had to run through," the company commander recalls.
Although unmanned ground vehicles have come a long way, rescuing wounded soldiers from the most dangerous areas is still mostly up to their comrades, Eighteen explains.
Unmanned ground vehicles take on a significant share of the logistics, but where machines cannot cope, the human factor remains decisive.
"A person can squeeze through a narrow gap, make their way through bushes, or wait things out in the ruins of a building," Eighteen says. "An unmanned ground vehicle is much more vulnerable in those conditions: it can get stuck or simply be unable to get through. And the enemy usually monitors roads and bridges.
So when there's a wounded soldier in the area, you have to take the risk and carry him out yourself, because the enemy can just destroy an unmanned ground vehicle on difficult terrain. As the saying goes, the legs feed the wolf. And in the Special Operations Forces, the wolf is us. Our work depends on our legs."
When we ask Eighteen about the most memorable operations he has taken part in, he recalls Sievierodonetsk, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Velyka Novosilka. But he says the recent mission to rescue the group was particularly special to him. In his view, the most important thing for a commander is to value his people.
"We try to evacuate all our wounded. Of course there are some situations where the circumstances make that impossible," he says.
"We try to retrieve the fallen, too. Because people are our greatest asset now."
Olena Barsukova, Ukrainska Pravda.Life (Zhyttia)

09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said on Wednesday its team met Israeli authorities and toured a military detention facility as part of efforts to resume access to detainees held in Israel.
The ICRC said in a statement that the team held a technical meeting with detaining authorities, conducted an assessment and toured parts of the facility, but "neither met nor had direct contact with any detainees."
“This meeting is a step in the right direction towards resuming proper visits to detainees held in Israeli places of detention,” said Julien Lerisson, ICRC's head of delegation for Israel and the occupied territories.
Lerisson said the organization would continue discussing the arrangements for such visits with relevant authorities to enable their resumption.
The ICRC has been unable to access detainees held in Israeli detention facilities since October 2023.
It reiterated the need to be informed of the fate and whereabouts of all detainees and to be granted access to them.
Under international humanitarian law, detainees must be treated humanely, provided with acceptable conditions of detention and allowed to communicate with their families, the ICRC said.

Finding a path to peace: Nigeria’s long, faltering history of dialogue with Boko Haram
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:10:03 UTC
00:10:03 KST

Share & more
Mamman Nur, the senior cleric of Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), had tried to escape detention by his own comrades twice before – he knew this failed third attempt was likely his death sentence.
The influential ideologue had been a leading figure in Nigeria’s insurgent jihadist movement for more than two decades. He had been one of the closest aides to Boko Haram’s deceased founder, Mohammed Yusuf, was a key link to Islamic State-Central, and for a time was popularly thought of as ISWAP’s leader.
But the tall, charismatic teacher was now undone. He had been accused of secret contact with the Nigerian government through an initiative known as the “Swiss process”, which was exploring a path to dialogue and regarded Nur as a possible interlocutor. To ISWAP’s governing Shura council, this was treason.
With the blessing of IS-Central, Nur was detained while the council debated what to do. In September 2018, he was sentenced to death and publicly shot by the head of the amniya, ISWAP’s secret police.
Nur’s fate exposed the central problem facing any attempt to negotiate with Nigeria’s jihadists: Can a movement that treats dialogue as treason ever be persuaded to make peace? Nearly eight years later, a reported ceasefire between the government and Boko Haram suggests that, however tentatively, the answer may be changing.
Can you make peace with jihadists?
After 17 years of war and close to 350,000 indirect civilian deaths, the conflict in Nigeria’s northeast is stalemated. Yet behind the scenes there has been a long if faltering attempt by the Nigerian government to find a negotiated breakthrough to the jihadist insurgency.
The idea of negotiations with “Boko Haram” – officially Jama’at Ahl al Sunna li Da’wa wal Jihad (JAS) – and ISWAP, its offshoot and rival, sharply divides Nigeria. The government officially says there can be no talks with groups legally proscribed as terrorist organisations, even though a three-month ceasefire with JAS, agreed in June, seems to be holding.
The New Humanitarian has spoken to security officials, diplomats, mediators, and former jihadist fighters – protecting their anonymity so they could speak freely – to explore the potential of that dialogue process. Is there a path to a sustainable peace with extremist groups that reject the legitimacy of the Nigerian state, its secular constitution, and world view?
“Both sides believe a settlement is possible,” a diplomat with knowledge of the chronology of the dialogue process told The New Humanitarian. “For all parties, a non-kinetic [military] approach is intellectually acceptable.”
Military operations alone rarely resolves insurgencies. Political settlements, where they are possible, are more likely to produce lasting peace. But governments tend to exceptionalise jihadist groups and publicly shun the idea of dialogue with people typically characterised as irredeemably violent.
These groups’ perceived maximalist ideological demands are seen as obstacles to peace – the spiritual and sacred regarded as incompatible with the give and take of political bargaining.
Yet Islamist ideology is not monolithic. Extremist groups are political actors that shape and are shaped by their environments. Supposed “red lines” over political demands can also fade over time. In Egypt, Gama’a al Islamiya carried out armed attacks for two decades before it renounced violence and stood in elections in 2011. And more recently, in Syria, Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham transformed from an al-Qaeda franchise into the dominant force behind a transitional government.
However, the cell-like structures of jihadist groups, legal prohibitions, histories of distrust, and the difficulty of building domestic political consensus all weigh on the timing and incentives for peace talks. Negotiations demand patience, political will, and good intelligence networks, said the diplomat. Nigeria has struggled on all three fronts.
Successive governments have also avoided confronting the grievances driving the northeastern conflict or properly understanding their opponents. The traditional establishment approach has been to “settle” troublemakers, buying them off with money and positions. But JAS and ISWAP have been different: ideological foes not seeking a financial reward or patronage.
“Peace can be possible, but it needs trust and sincerity,” a former ISWAP commander who surrendered to the authorities last year, told The New Humanitarian. “The problem is that up until now, nobody has sat with [JAS/ISWAP] to understand them.
A close observer of the Nigerian conflict was far more sceptical. “The record shows that jihadist groups, like other insurgent groups, can engage in negotiations, at least preliminary or limited ones, when they are under pressure,” he noted. However, there are fewer examples of longer-term political solutions.
Talking about talks
The insurgency, which began in northeastern Maiduguri in 2009, was still growing when President Goodluck Jonathan was elected two years later. A southern Christian, his poll victory sparked riots in several predominantly Muslim northern cities in a controversy over whether he should have stood. For some in his administration it was proof of a conspiracy: that JAS was manufactured by aggrieved northern elites to undermine Jonathan’s rule.
In the early days of the conflict, mediation efforts were largely privately led. Former president Olusegun Obasanjo made the first attempt in 2011, followed by Sheikh Ibrahim Datti Ahmad, the respected president of the National Supreme Council of Sharia. Both ended almost as soon as they had begun – with each side blaming the other.
Demands by JAS were basic: the release of detained wives and colleagues, the rebuilding of homes and buildings destroyed by the security forces in Maiduguri, the payment of compensation to families of members killed, and the prosecution of the policemen responsible for the assassination of Yusuf, the movement’s founder. They have not included larger ideological goals.
As the conflict dramatically worsened – with bombings, kidnappings, attacks on towns, and the cold-blooded slaughter of civilians – Jonathan’s team seemed to struggle with a strategy. He was being urged by northern politicians to offer amnesty. He responded that his opponents were “ghosts” – although there were enough JAS detainees who could have served as conduits. Western governments, meanwhile, warned that there should be “no compromising with terrorism”.
With the intelligence service seemingly blindsided, a cottage industry quickly emerged of intermediaries claiming contact with JAS. Some may have been genuine, others were more fanciful – simply out to scam the government. JAS disowned all of them.
But the groundwork was being laid for a more strategic response. National Security Adviser Sambo Dasuki, in particular, was looking for an alternative approach. He hired psychologist Fatima Akilu to head a new outfit, the Behavioural Analysis and Strategic Communication unit, where she helped develop an ambitious countering violent extremism (CVE) framework.
Its significance was that it shifted thinking from a purely anti-terrorism strategy to one aimed at tackling the roots of radicalisation. It was recognised that JAS needed to be engaged rather than simply destroyed, with pathways to redemption created. Akilu’s work led to the creation of a series of defection and reintegration programmes, which arguably have had more success at reducing extremist ranks than battlefield action.
The professionals
In March 2014, a JAS unit stopped at a secondary school in Chibok, a small farming town in the northeast. It had come to steal food supplies and the school’s brickmaking machine, but on a whim the commander decided to kidnap the 276 schoolgirls they had managed to round up. The global reaction of outrage handed JAS new-found leverage, but it also kicked into gear a more professional approach to negotiations.
The Swiss government offered their “good offices” as neutral intermediaries between Dasuki, the domestic spy agency, the Department of State Services (DSS), and JAS. That evolved into what became known as the Dialogue Facilitation Team.
It comprised Swiss diplomat Pascal Holliger, Maiduguri lawyer Zannah Mustapha (who had helped arrange the Obasanjo visit), and a small core of people from the city who had links to JAS members. They all received negotiation training at an Alpine hotel on the shores of Lake Thun.
In August 2016, two years after the Chibok abduction, 21 exhausted teenagers were ushered towards Mustapha at a roadside rendezvous following the payment of a substantial ransom and the freeing of four detained senior JAS commanders. A second group of 82 Chibok students were freed in 2017. Over the years, some managed to escape on their own, but tragically in total more than 90 of the schoolgirls remain unaccounted for.
It had taken an incredible amount of painstaking work to put the initial release together – to find the right conduits to JAS leader Shekau, to win his trust, and to navigate Nigeria’s intense security inter-agency rivalries. The ambition was that the new opening would kickstart a broader dialogue process.
In February 2018, the formula was put to the test again, after ISWAP abducted more than 100 students from the Government Girls Science and Technical College in Dapchi, Yobe State. A month later, each one of the schoolgirls – bar the only Christian – were released. For Abuja, it was a step towards what it described at the time as a “wider cessation of hostility talks”.
Nur, ISWAP’s chief cleric, was behind the Dapchi release – a decision reinforced by IS-Central’s condemnation of the kidnapping. That reinforced an attitude he was key to a future dialogue. Although Nur was placed under US sanctions in 2015, he was not viewed by his comrades as a battlefield commander, and was not among the original “pioneers” – who together with Shekau – built JAS’s Sambisa Forest base.
He was on the negotiators' radar partly as a result of a then clandestine programme run by the DSS known as sulhu (peacemaking). The initiative targeted jihadist commanders, encouraging them to defect and stay in contact with their former comrades in the bush to persuade them to also cross over.
“Sulhu is more than a counter-insurgency strategy,” said a member of Nigeria’s security establishment. “The goal is for those contacts to reach [Lake Chad, the base for ISWAP and JAS]. The Swiss want to help negotiate a hudna (truce).”
Nur, though, had come under suspicion by ISWAP’s aminya over a computer he had requested from a courier based in northern Nigeria, and a small amount of money, The New Humanitarian was informed. Six months after the release of the Dapchi students, he was executed on Murfu island – one of the hundreds in the Lake Chad region.
The Swiss process
After taking office in 2015, President Muhammadu Buhari gave his blessing to negotiations and a “soft power” CVE approach, but insiders argue that it was never institutionalised. “For something as important as this, it needs a political home, taking official direction from the president who drives it,” said a former diplomat who served in Abuja.
Instead, the mediation organogram was a complicated one. Overall responsibility officially rested with the Office of the National Security Advisor. Day-to-day authority for running operations was under the DSS, and Borno State had its own initiatives. The military on the ground, however, weren’t always informed of operations, and that “caused problems”, two diplomatic sources confirmed.
Key to the overall strategy was the Swiss dialogue team, which had the mandate to try and find an entry point. Running parallel to their work was the British firm Inter Mediate, set up by Jonathan Powell, the UK’s chief negotiator on the Good Friday Agreement with the IRA that ended decades of violence in Northern Ireland. Inter Mediate was hired by the Nigerian government in 2012 in an advisory role, with a brief to help think through a negotiation process, the observer noted.
Inter Mediate wasn’t directly involved in dialogue outreach: that was left to a team known as the “intermediaries”, working with the UK firm, and linked to the government’s Norwegian-supported Fusion Centre for Dialogue and Peace Processes, a specialised military and security initiative.
The head of the fusion centre played a key political role, and the Swiss looked to blend their work with his intermediaries. But there were occasional frictions. “The bottom line was that the Swiss delivered, and the intermediaries didn’t – they didn’t have the buy-in from the guys in the lake,” said the Nigerian security official.
Much of Inter Mediate’s work was with the Borno State government’s "Borno Model” – an initiative aimed at demobilising and reintegrating former jihadist combatants. The strategy was linked to a broader Lake Chad Basin “soft power” approach backed by the World Bank, the UN Development Programme, and Western embassies.
Disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration
Borno’s demobilisation initiative was a version of the military’s Operation Safe Corridor – the direct descendant of Akilu’s CVE programme. But whereas OSC dealt only with low-level recruits, the Borno model included their families and tended to neglect both the deradicalisation and reintegration end of the work.
From its inception in 2021, it was caught up in a surge of defections. ISWAP had overrun Shekau’s Sambisa base, and he had committed suicide. JAS members refusing to accept ISWAP’s far stricter discipline – or who had had enough of the fierce fighting between the two groups – surrendered in droves.
The state government estimated that between 2021 and 2026, close to 350,000 people defected. The vast majority were women, children, and non-combatants who had been forcefully conscripted. The government lacked the resources to properly look after so many new arrivals, and it has largely failed as an advertisement for a better post-war life for combatants still in the bush.
Nevertheless, between 2022 and 2023 the Nigerian government felt it was on the brink of a series of ceasefires with JAS. The group, now led by Ibrahim Bakura Doro, was involved in intense fighting with ISWAP, while clashes with the military were declining. But the ceasefires “couldn’t be maintained”, said the security official.
What would a settlement look like?
For the past three months, a ceasefire does appear to have held between JAS and the government since the release in June of 360 people abducted from the village of Ngoshe in southern Borno – although the government has not commented on the reported truce. How sustainable it is, and whether it could develop into a broader agreement, is an open question.
“It could be just a temporary, tactical ceasefire that benefits both sides, but doesn’t really affect the trajectory of the war,” said conflict researcher Malik Samuel. “I don’t think it’s a step towards a sustainable peace settlement.”
One currently involved mediator acknowledged that a longer-term agreement was still a long way off. “The discussions are not yet into that,” he told The New Humanitarian. “Right now, it’s easier to talk about ceasefires, it’s all about the tactical.”
Akilu noted that so many more steps are needed before that point could be reached. “Do we actually have that many skilled negotiators? You need to build a skills set for peace – profilers, researchers, trauma specialists,” she explained. “There’s a whole series of steps needed before serious, long-term negotiations can start.”
There is also a political problem. There is a sharp regional divide in Nigeria over the idea of dialogue. Communities closest to the violence are more receptive to talks, but much of the rest of the country is extremely wary. “We have seen something similar with the negative reception to the issue of DDR (disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration),” said Samuel. Politicians and religious leaders have loudly condemned the alleged “coddling” of “terrorists”.
That prospect worries Akilu. “There has been no national strategic comms strategy to pave the way, to build consensus, to explain why we’re talking,” she noted. “We have a short four-year political cycle, and eyes are always on the next election [in January 2027]. For a government this is a hot potato, but it needs political will and buy-in to work.”
While JAS could perhaps be ultimately persuaded to accept a negotiated surrender, researchers suggest – with amnesty incentives, start-up grants for reintegration, and a more certain future promised for their families – ISWAP is a different proposition.
“We have communications with both groups,” said the mediator. “But JAS is easier to deal with. Bakura can hold a Shura meeting and make a decision. ISWAP needs greenlight approval from the ‘caliphate’ (IS-Central).”
Examples have been given of Pakistan’s tribal territories as a self-governing model that might apply to a Nigerian political settlement – few doubt that could work in a polarised multi-faith country where there are growing regional demands for secession. “Yes, it would be a challenge,” acknowledged the diplomat.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.

“Guess who covered more than 3,300 km and successfully hit the target,” the company wrote.
Later, Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces (SSO) confirmed their involvement in the attack.
“For the first time! Record defeat for the entire time of the war: SSO hit critical Russian plants 3,000 km away,” the report released Wednesday evening reads.

The Special Ops said that the facilities are critically important to Russia’s gas-condensate industry. The plants process significant volumes of gas condensate extracted from deposits in the Yamal region.
The Novy Urengoy condensate preparation plant has a design capacity of 19.5 million tons of raw materials per year, while the Purovsky gas-condensate processing plant processed 13.4 million tons of gas condensate in 2025.
“The SSO continue to successfully implement Ukraine’s long-range sanctions against Russia, reducing its ability to wage a war of aggression,” the report added.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also said in his morning address Thursday, Sept. 10 that Ukrainian forces had struck eight Russian infrastructure facilities “that are working for war” during the previous day. He listed a refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets region among the facilities hit.
“Russia continues its terror against Ukraine every day. And every day it receives a fair response. Thank you to every soldier, to everyone who ensures our long-range strikes and accuracy,” Zelensky added.
UAV threat reported in another oil region nearly 2,500 km from border
Drone threats were also issued Wednesday for the Khanty-Mansiysk Autonomous Okrug for the first time.
The region is about 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles) from the Ukrainian border and accounts for around 40% of Russia’s oil production. Residents were advised not to go outside, approach windows or leave safe locations until the warning was lifted.
Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsia, reported the temporary suspension of operations at six airports: Khanty-Mansiysk, Surgut, Sovetsky, Igrim, Nyagan and Urai.
Authorities also warned of disruptions to communications and mobile internet. Students attending second-shift classes at educational institutions were moved to remote learning.
A local teacher told NeMoskva outlet that the region initially introduced an “Unmanned Danger” warning, indicating the approach of drones toward the region. About an hour later, authorities issued the “Threat of UAV Attack” warning, indicating an imminent threat.
Before this, drones had not directly targeted cities and industrial facilities in the district. However, authorities declared a missile threat in the region for the first time on May 5.
The region is home to two major industrial facilities: Nyagangazpererabotka and the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant.
In summer 2026, Ukraine struck nearly all Russian refineries within range. Ukraine’s military said in July that the attacks had knocked 43% of Russia’s refining capacity offline, contributing to a nationwide fuel shortage and export restrictions.
Despite the loss of refining capacity, think tank analysis found Russia’s overall oil exports remained relatively stable between June and July, with higher crude exports and energy prices partly offsetting revenue losses.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has acknowledged the impact while arguing that, amid Russia’s fuel crisis, it is more “profitable to export crude oil than to process it domestically.”

Trump’s top six falsehoods about 9/11 as 25th anniversary nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:08:08 UTC
00:08:08 KST

1. Claiming the attacks made his building the tallest in downtown New YorkNot long after the attacks, Trump said in a telephone interview with a local news anchor that the destruction of the World Trade Center – previously New York City’s tallest building – meant his 40 Wall Street property was now the tallest in downtown Manhattan. “I mean, 40 Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan. And it was actually before the World Trade Center was the tallest,” Trump claimed. “And then when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second tallest. And now it’s the tallest.” It was not: 70 Pine Street, about a block away, held that distinction.
 2. Claiming he helped clean upTrump has repeatedly claimed to have assisted with the recovery from the World Trade Center’s collapse. “Everyone who helped clear the rubble, and I was there, and I watched, and I helped a little bit,” he said at a campaign stop in 2016. That comment was a rehash of one he made shortly after the attack, where he told a German broadcaster that “we’ll have a couple hundred people down here” helping with the cleanup. In 2019, PolitiFact interviewed a New York City fire department battalion chief who did not recall Trump sending any workers to the site.
 3. Lying about MuslimsWhen he first campaigned for the presidency in 2016, Trump repeated a story that “thousands and thousands” of Muslim Americans “were cheering” in Jersey City, New Jersey, on the day of the attacks in 2001. Despite many fact checks, no evidence has been discovered to back up this claim.
 4. Lying about Ilhan OmarIn September 2019, Trump retweeted a video that purported to show the Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar, a Muslim and the first Somali American to serve in the US Congress, dancing on the anniversary of the attacks, calling her: “The new face of the Democrat Party!” CBS News reported that Omar had been dancing at an event organized by the congressional Black caucus, which was not held on September 11.
 5. Claiming to have predicted the attacksIn his 2000 book, The America We Deserve, Trump mentioned the al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden as among “a bewildering series of smaller crises” faced by the US. At the time, Bin Laden was known to Americans because al-Qaida had in 1998 orchestrated the bombings of US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania. That didn’t stop Trump from in 2018 writing on X that the US “should have captured Osama Bin Laden long before we did”, adding: “I pointed him out in my book just BEFORE the attack on the World Trade Center.”
 6. Fumbling the facts on firefightersDuring a ceremony at the White House ellipse on Tuesday to honor emergency workers who responded to the attacks, Trump said that when he and a group of workers went to visit lower Manhattan shortly after the attacks, he was carried out by firefighters worried that the lower Manhattan skyscraper One Liberty Plaza – formerly known as the US Steel Building – would collapse. “Two firemen, big strong guys – and I’m not the smallest guy in the world – they grabbed me under the arm, said: ‘Got to get out of here.’ And they literally lifted me up,” the president claimed. “This is not easy to do – I’m big. They lifted me up and they started running with me. I said: ‘Fellas, I can run myself,’ but they were amazing. But they thought it was coming down. It didn’t come down.” PolitiFact notes that Trump has told a version of this story before, including in an interview with Fox News that aired earlier this week. It appears to be a stretch. While concerns about One Liberty Plaza’s stability did prompt the evacuation of at least one nearby building the day after the attack, there’s no evidence Trump was present, while his claim of bringing workers to the site is unsupported.

Palestinians increasingly favoring ‘peaceful negotiations’ over ‘armed resistance’ - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:08:07 UTC
00:08:07 KST

Palestinians are increasingly questioning the effectiveness of “armed resistance” in achieving their national ambitions, with only 13.3% now viewing violence as the most useful way to achieve those goals, according to a new poll conducted by the Jerusalem Media and Communications Center (JMCC) – founded in 1988 by Palestinian journalists and researchers – in cooperation with the Friedrich Ebert Foundation.
The survey, which collected responses from 1,200 Palestinians in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip between August 20 and 25, found that 15.7% of respondents in the West Bank and 9.7% in Gaza viewed “armed resistance” as the most effective way to achieve Palestinian national goals, a significant decline from 2023, when 37.1% of respondents said it was the most effective tool.
More than half of Palestinians (55.8%) now view the best approach to achieve their national goals to be peaceful negotiations, a significant increase from 2023, when only 28% said the same.
Demonstrating this shift in attitudes, the percentage of Palestinians who said they believed the October 7 attack served Palestinian national interests fell to 15.7% in August, down from 30.9% in September 2025 and 45% in September 2024.
A slight majority of Palestinians in the West Bank (50.1%) and a sizable number of Gazans (35.2%) said that Hamas’s invasions had hurt the national interests.
Support for a two-state solution to end the Israeli-Palestinian conflict has also grown compared to previous surveys. Nearly half of the respondents (47.9%) said they preferred two states over the alternatives, a significant jump from the 27.3% who answered the same in September 2023. Likewise, the percentage of those who would prefer to establish a single Palestinian state, removing Israel, declined to 18.6% from 24.7% in September 2023.
Only 28.8% of Palestinians in the West Bank expect the Palestinian Legislative Council elections to go ahead in November, while more than a third (35.5%) believe they will be postponed, and 22.4% expect the elections to be canceled altogether.
Most believe elections will happen at some point
Though most respondents appear to believe the elections will happen at some point, even if not on the date announced by Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, fewer than half (46.8%) said the process would improve the situation for Palestinians. A nearly equal portion of respondents (46.4%) said the elections would either worsen the situation or have no impact.
Trust in political parties remains relatively low, appearing to explain Palestinians’ pessimistic view of the elections. Only 55% said that they trusted an existing organization, with major camps notably seeing a decline in support over the past four years.
The percentage of respondents in the West Bank and Gaza who trusted Hamas fell from the 12% recorded in the July 2022 survey to only 6.7% in August. Likewise, trust in Fatah has declined from 28.8% to 22.3%.
The support Hamas amassed following the October 7 attack has since sharply declined, with 18.7% of respondents in the West Bank saying they trusted the Islamist group in October 2023, compared with only 4.5% in the latest poll conducted in August 2026.
Though several experts have suggested that Abbas is under pressure to postpone the elections over fears that Hamas could win a majority of seats, the poll found that Fatah remains more popular than Hamas.
Some 27.5% of respondents said they would vote for Fatah, including 23.5% in the West Bank and 33.4% in Gaza, while only 7.6% said they would vote for Hamas, including 5.6% in the West Bank and 10.5% in the Strip.
Public trust in Abbas remains low
If the poll is representative of Palestinian attitudes, Fatah could expect to emerge victorious in the elections, yet trust in Abbas remains low, at only 6.9%.
In direct contradiction with data gathered by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, JMCC’s poll found that trust in Marwan Barghouti stands at only 6.3%. Barghouti is currently serving five consecutive life sentences plus 40 years after being convicted by an Israeli court on charges including five counts of murder and attempted murder during the Second Intifada. He has long been considered a favorite for the Palestinian presidency.
Barghouti and his family have maintained that he was not involved in planning the attacks for which he was convicted, while he has expressed support for a two-state solution.
However, questions remain over the direction in which the imprisoned Fatah leader could take the PA from behind bars.
There is also growing support for Mohammed Dahlan, a former Fatah leader based in the UAE who has held talks with Hamas in recent months, while pushing for a more unified Palestinian leadership that includes all factions. Trust in Dahlan stood at only 2.7% in 2023 but has risen to 5.8% as of August.
His growing support comes after he helped facilitate millions of dollars in UAE aid to Gaza, which likely contributed to his increased standing among Palestinians.
Though the issue of settler violence has become increasingly discussed by international media, respondents prioritized the issue of Israelis living in the West Bank well below ending the war in Gaza (50.1%), improving the Palestinian economy (16.9%), rebuilding Gaza (13.4%), and achieving national unity (8.9%).
Only 7% said that confronting settlement activity should be the number one priority for Palestinians.
Though not the number one priority for those polled, 70.6% said that residents of West Bank villages do not receive sufficient support from Palestinian society when they are exposed to settler violence, and 77.9% said the PA specifically does not provide adequate support.
The Palestinian economy has struggled in recent years. Israel has withheld PA clearance revenues in response to its continued pay-for-slay policy for Palestinians convicted of carrying out attacks against Israel, and some 100,000 Palestinian workers lost access to jobs in Israel following Hamas’s October 7 attack.
Combined with the regional insecurity that has severely affected tourism, financial pressures have forced the PA to make significant cuts to public services, with schools operating only three days a week and civil servants receiving only a fraction of their salaries.
The financial crisis has led 39.6% of those polled to believe that the PA will collapse. And 58.1% said they believed that Israel was deliberately maintaining a weakened version of the PA.
Nearly a quarter (23%) said they believed that it would be better if the PA were dissolved, while 69.4% said it was important that it remain in place.

Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia is a test of new Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan pact - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:08:04 KST

The Iran-backed Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia this week. This has been deemed the first test of the new alliance that Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan initiated in August. The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, as it is being called, was formed to strengthen deterrence against any acts of aggression.
After its creation, a meeting in Turkey sought to form the framework for the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. The three countries then crafted the role of a permanent secretariat, which is supposed to be in Saudi Arabia.
“The move gives institutional shape to an alliance built around collective deterrence and regional responsibility. A mechanism for other countries to join the group was already underway, officials said,” Middle East Broadcasting Networks (MBN) reported on September 3.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan spoke about the importance of the new pact when he went to the Shanghai Cooperation Organization meeting in Kyrgyzstan, referring to “collective deterrence.”
Currently, people are wondering whether Pakistan or Turkey will respond to the Houthi attacks. Historically, both countries have been wary of any conflict with Iran. Unlike them, Saudi Arabia has been very critical of the Islamic Republic.
Turkish MFA condemns attack in the strongest terms
Saudi Arabia has, in fact, been fighting the Iran-backed Houthis since 2015. Over the past few months, the Houthi threat has increasingly worsened. Despite this, Riyadh apparently believes that Yemen’s troops can repel the Houthis.
On September 8, Turkey’s Foreign Affairs Ministry strongly condemned the Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia. Turkey also reaffirmed its support for the kingdom.
“These attacks undermine diplomatic efforts aimed at bringing the conflict in Yemen to an end through a lasting political solution,” the ministry said.
Turkey then called on the Houthis to cease their aggression. These statements, however, do not mean that Turkey plans to join Saudi Arabia in its fight against them.
Currently, Turkey has military assets near the area because it has been operating in Somalia. Notably, in late August, Turkey freed sailors from Somali pirates.
Pakistani PM condemns Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia
“Turkish and Somali forces have freed the MV LUTUF after pirates hijacked the vessel off the coast of Somalia. The 10-day operation killed 14 alleged pirates and destroyed four boats used by the attackers,” Deutsche Welle (DW) reported in late August.
Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said: “I condemn, in the strongest terms, the cowardly attack by Houthis targeting civilian and energy facilities in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, which have left many people wounded.”
He added that “Pakistan stands in unwavering solidarity with the Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, His Majesty King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, His Royal Highness Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and the brotherly people of Saudi Arabia.
The premier also noted that “such dastardly attacks threaten innocent lives as well as regional peace and security. We reaffirm our steadfast support for the kingdom’s sovereignty, security, and territorial integrity, and pray for the swift recovery of all who were injured.”
Turkiye Today reported: “Pakistan is likely to carry out airstrikes against Houthi forces in Yemen at Saudi Arabia’s request, according to Pakistani sources speaking to Turkiye Today. A source noted that the attacks may take place soon and will be made public shortly afterward.”
The report noted that “one of the military priorities for the Pakistani attacks would be to clear the Houthis from Saadah, along with other regions, according to one Pakistani source. However, a final decision on attacking Yemen’s Houthis has not been made.”
If the regional alliance acts against the Houthis, it will show that its pact has power.
This situation will likely be closely monitored by other countries, such as India, Israel, and Greece. This is due to the pact’s regional implications. The three countries may want to expand the pact beyond its initial premise. However, if they are unable to deter the Houthis, then their speeches about deterrence are rendered moot.

Israeli man sentenced to 13 years for killing Aysha Rabi in Jewish terror attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:07:53 UTC
00:07:53 KST

The Central District Court in Lod sentenced a man on Wednesday to 13 years in prison for killing Palestinian mother Aysha Rabi in a rare conviction for Jewish nationalist terror relating to a 2018 attack, concluding the trial stage of an unusually long and closely contested case.
The court also ordered the defendant to pay Rabi’s family NIS 258,000, the maximum compensation available under the law, and imposed an additional suspended prison term.
The defendant, whose identity remains barred from publication because he was a minor at the time, was 15 years and 10 months old when he carried out the attack.
On October 12, 2018, he positioned himself with two or three unidentified people on an embankment overlooking Route 60 near the West Bank settlement of Rehelim, the court found.
After identifying an approaching car by its Palestinian license plate, he threw a rock weighing approximately 2 kilograms through its windshield. The rock struck Rabi directly in the head as she sat beside her husband, Yacoub, and in front of their nine-year-old daughter.
Rabi, a resident of the Palestinian town of Bidya and a mother of nine, died from her wounds. The court found that the defendant acted from a nationalist motive, intending to harm the car’s occupants and disregarding the possibility that they could be killed.
In March, judges Michal Barak-Nevo and Michael Tamir found that the defendant had committed the offenses, while then-presiding judge Liora Brody voted to acquit him, contending that the very high standard of proof beyond any reasonable doubt had not been met.
Because the defendant was a minor at the time, the juvenile court first determined that he had committed the offenses without immediately entering a formal conviction. It formally convicted him on Wednesday as part of the sentencing decision.
He was convicted of manslaughter in circumstances amounting to an act of terrorism, aggravated stone-throwing at a vehicle, and intentionally damaging a vehicle, with all three offenses classified as terrorism-related.
Defendant originally accused of manslaughter, not murder
At the time of the indictment, the fact that the minor was accused not of murder but of manslaughter, and the filing of the indictment was delayed by several weeks, indicated that the path to any kind of conviction might be difficult.
Adi Keidar – a lawyer for the right-wing legal aid group Honenu – told The Jerusalem Post at the time that even the DNA evidence could be attacked in court.
A spokesman for Honenu said that there was no other evidence connecting the minor to the incident, and that the DNA evidence was weak compared to standard DNA evidence, as it was found on a moving object – the rock – as opposed to on a stationary object, such as a wall.
Honenu said this meant that the DNA could have come from a variety of sources, while the rock may have been moved.
In addition, the spokesman said the DNA was of a low resolution. In other words, while high-resolution DNA evidence can flag a specific person, in this case the evidence could point to a number of people.
The majority of the court disagreed with these arguments, resting principally on the defendant’s DNA, which was found on the rock recovered from inside the family’s car, while also citing the rejection of his alibi, statements they found untruthful, contradictions in later accounts, and his problematic conduct during questioning.
In August 2024, the Post learned that as part of the prosecutor’s case, extensive evidence had been presented to debunk the defense’s attack on the DNA evidence.
Defendant continues to deny involvement in the attack
Further, the Post learned that the prosecution was able to use a May 2019 decision by the Lod District Court regarding various issues in the case as something of a road map toward conviction.
Already in that decision, the court had ruled, in the context of debates about how long to keep the minor in detention of some sort, that the prosecution’s chances of conviction were extremely high because of the DNA evidence.
Despite the defense’s arguments, the prosecution presented evidence that the chances of the minor defendant just happening to have touched the rock randomly (vs using it as his killing weapon) are minuscule, given that the only DNA on the rock is Rabi’s, her husband who touched the rock after it hit her, and the minor defendant’s.
In May 2019, the court called such a theory to try to acquit the defendant-minor “blatantly and grossly unreasonable.”
Moreover, the prosecution has taken aim at the defendant’s alibi.
According to the prosecution, the Post understands, the minor’s alibi was completely unreliable because he refused to open his mouth not only throughout the time of his arrest and being interrogated by the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) from December 30, 2018, but even from October 15, 2018, when he was interviewed only as a third-party witness and not yet as a suspect.
The fact that the defendant would not speak even when he was not yet suspected of anything, the prosecution argued, drew much greater attention to his potential guilt and drew greater scrutiny to his alibi.
In other words, were he not worried about any criminal charges, what would he have had to lose by telling law enforcement that he was in a different place from where he would have needed to be to perpetrate the crime?
The Post learned that the prosecution noted that the defendant only produced an alibi once he knew what the final narrative of the prosecution against him would take place as the indictment was about to be filed.
The defendant continues to deny any involvement in the attack, although the sentencing summary said he expressed sorrow over Rabi’s death.
His family and the Honenu legal-aid organization said they would appeal both the conviction and sentence to the Supreme Court.
His lawyers, Ariel Atari and Keidar, called the conviction wrongful and said Brody’s detailed dissent gave them a “high chance” of persuading the Supreme Court to overturn the majority ruling and acquit him.
The court said the defendant’s age was the central consideration in his favor.
It also gave significant weight to the rehabilitation process he had undergone during the seven years since the attack, including treatment, his decision to live in a different environment, and the positive impression he made on the probation service.
The judges nevertheless described the attack as cruel, stressing that Rabi was killed in front of her husband and young daughter and that the rock could also have killed the other occupants or caused the driver to lose control of the car.
They also found that its nationalist character made the offense more serious and that attacks of this kind risked increasing violence between Israelis and Palestinians in the West Bank.
Yacoub told the official responsible for preparing the family’s victim-impact report that justice, for him, would have meant his wife continuing to live with her family while the defendant pursued his own life and studied at university.
“No sum of money can compensate the Rabi family for the loss of her life,” the court said.
The Central District Attorney’s Office said, “The court sent a clear and unequivocal message today, reflecting the severity of the defendant’s actions and the grave and tragic outcome of the attack, which claimed Aysha Rabi’s life.”
“This was an act of terrorism carried out for nationalist reasons against Rabi, a Palestinian woman traveling with her family.”
Prosecutors said that despite the defendant’s age at the time, the seriousness of the attack led them to seek a lengthy prison term, a position the court accepted.
“In our view, today’s sentence reflects the severity of – and the danger posed by – nationalist acts of terrorism of this kind,” they stated.
This would not be the only such case of Jewish terrorists facing justice for violence against Palestinians, with the 2014 murderer of Palestinian minor Muhammad Abu Khadir, Yoseph Chaim Ben-David, and the 2015 murderer of the Palestinian Dawabsheh family, Amiram Ben-Uliel, both sentenced to life.
In fact, one of the reasons that the Rabi case probably took longer is that the Shin Bet declined to use enhanced interrogation on the minor defendant after the agency’s use of such techniques on Ben-Uliel almost led to a mistrial.
Elor Azariah, Ben Deri, and other IDF soldiers have also been given prison time for killing Palestinians.

Grateful Dead Gathering brings mini-Woodstock to Arava oasis for three-day festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:07:48 UTC
00:07:48 KST

An oasis in the Arava will turn into a mini-Woodstock next weekend when the Grateful Dead Gathering takes over the Khan Gamalia at Ein Yahav for a three-day music festival, September 17-19 (Thursday-Saturday).
For over 15 years, on and off, Deadheads and fans of jam bands have gathered at the campsite to celebrate the music of the San Francisco band and the next-generation jam bands they spawned.
This year, along with finely curated DJ sets featuring the best, weirdest, and most esoteric of the San Francisco legends, there will be 10 live bands, including The Hardest Daze, one of Israel’s premier Dead tribute bands.
Another highlight is The Rusties, a tight, rocking tribute to Neil Young and his music.
The other bands offer original psychedelic music inspired by the more adventurous side of the Dead.
The festival will feature a kabalat Shabbat
Featuring a kabbalat Shabbat, a communal Shabbat dinner, and an inviting complex including a refreshing pool, the festival’s main attraction will be the hundreds of smiling, colorful Deadheads, both native Israelis and transplanted Americans.
Tickets can be purchased for all or any of the days, and the Shabbat-observant can stay on site until the end of Shabbat.

IAEA board draws a line under past Syrian nuclear activities, says outstanding questions resolved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:07:37 UTC
00:07:37 KST

The United Nations nuclear watchdog's 35-nation Board of Governors passed a resolution on Wednesday drawing a line under Syria's secret nuclear activities during the Assad regime, saying the new authorities had helped resolve all outstanding questions.
After Israel struck a site in the eastern province of Deir al-Zor in 2007 that it said was a secret nuclear reactor near completion, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) demanded Syria come clean on its nuclear activities, which it did not do.
The IAEA board declared Syria in breach of its non-proliferation obligations in 2011 and reported it to the UN Security Council. After the overthrow of Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024, Syria's new authorities pledged to work with the IAEA in helping clear up the past activities.
IAEA resolves outstanding issues with Syria
In a confidential report to member states last week, seen by Reuters, the IAEA said it had resolved all its questions about the outstanding issues originally reported to the board, and the resolution passed on Wednesday said Syria was no longer in non-compliance with its obligations.
"(The board) welcomes the transparency and cooperation of the Syrian Arab Republic, commends it for the actions taken in resolving its non-compliance," the resolution text submitted by Egypt, Jordan, Morocco and Saudi Arabia said.
The resolution was passed by consensus, meaning no state objected, diplomats at the closed-door meeting said.
The IAEA report confirmed it was "very likely" the bombed site was a nuclear reactor, and said fuel for it was made in Syria. The IAEA found around 73 metric tons of natural uranium metal in Syria, most of it in the form of fuel rods.
That material is now under IAEA oversight, and Syria has said it will stay in the country.

EU grants Spain $133M emergency aid over Ceuta border crossings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
15:05:23 UTC
00:05:23 KST

Melike Pala
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The European Commission on Wednesday announced €114.7 million ($133 million) in emergency assistance to Spain to help manage the situation in Ceuta following large-scale irregular border crossings on July 30-31.
The assistance will finance measures to strengthen border surveillance and protection, including thermal cameras, observation technology, floating buoy systems and underwater drones, as well as additional personnel and equipment, the commission said in a statement.
It will also support facilities for migrant screening, the return of people who remain illegally in Ceuta and reception capacity, including facilities for unaccompanied minors.
The European Commission said it coordinated additional operational assistance from the EU's border agency Frontex, law enforcement agency Europol and the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA).
Frontex is ready to extend its existing operational plans in Spain into 2027, ensuring the continued deployment of Frontex Standing Corps officers in Ceuta.
Additional Frontex assistance could include maritime assets, increased information exchange through Eurosur, support for returns and cooperation with Morocco, according to the bloc.
A joint core group comprising representatives of the EU Commission, EU agencies and relevant Spanish authorities will meet regularly to coordinate the emergency assistance and operational support.
The group's first meeting is scheduled to take place this week, alongside a second technical visit to Ceuta.
The bloc said the priority remains the swift return of people who remain illegally in Ceuta.
The mass crossings resulted in tens of thousands of people entering Ceuta from Morocco from July 30 to 31, according to Spanish government estimates.
Spanish authorities estimated that several thousand migrants remained in Ceuta after the initial crossings, although Vivas acknowledged that authorities still lacked a precise figure for the number who entered and those who remained.

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP's speech at Mansion House Defence and Security event
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:05:12 BST
00:05:12 KST

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP's speech at Mansion House Defence and Security event
Minister Pollard highlighting the importance of collaboration between government, industry and private finance, to strengthen UK deterrence and drive economic growth.
Lady Mayor, thank you very much for hosting this event today and good afternoon, everyone. It’s a real pleasure to be with you today.
Under this one roof we have many leaders and decision makers needed to spark that next generation of defence innovation that we need to keep our country safe and support our allies. So, thank you for giving up your valuable time to be here.
I’m honoured that I get to speak as warm up act to my friend, the Ukrainian Ambassador. I’ve spent a lot of time in Kyiv over the past two years in particular, and the courage of the Ukrainian people is something that we must honour not just in words but in the actual support that we provide for their frontline, for their nation, for the innovators and we do that by not just sending equipment to Ukraine but by partnering, innovating and developing new technologies together.
I know that there are people in this room whose work is not theoretical in that regard and you are making a big difference to our friends in Ukraine so thank you for what you do.
Now, we meet at a point where global geopolitics is more fragile, more disruptive and more changeable. And that means we need an entirely new system of warfighting and deterrence, which means more innovation and new approaches with new weapon systems that revolutionised the battlefield.
Certainly, the way that the United Kingdom would now fight is fundamentally different today than it was at the point when Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine only those four and a half years ago. We’re learning the lessons from Ukraine by supporting them, but that means changing the way that the United Kingdom operates.
Now, our most urgent mission right now is to transform Britain’s defence posture and turbocharge innovation. Many of the most critical advances in defence right now are coming from tech startups and tech scale-ups. Agile businesses which are seizing the opportunities on offer and driving change at speed. And so today our challenge is this: how can we get better at finding, funding and firing up the most creative minds and enterprise to get the best technology into the hands of our armed forces and those of our allies as fast as possible.
Now it was just over two years ago that this government took office and we inherited a defence programme which to be honest and to be frank was unfit to counter the dangers that we now face. We are moving towards warfighting readiness and in doing so we must discard the warm comfort blanket that we are used to in Britain, of polishing old things and pretending that that will protect us. If our technology and kit will not work in Ukraine, I do not want it in our armed forces. That is an opportunity for new technology, new thinking, new weapons to be brought to the fore. And in designing new technology, we need to design for the conflicts of today and the battles of tomorrow.
Now, our supply chains are critical to that. An industry that works in our supply chains know how painfully slow, wasteful and costly the procurement the MOD previously undertook was. We are changing that. I think it was especially true for those small businesses and scale-ups with amazing products who struggled sometimes to find the right buyer within the MOD.
Now since that time, we’ve produced a new blueprint for a completely different type of military and a different type of procurement. We published our Strategic Defence Review, Defence Industrial Strategy and Defence Investment Plan to build a more resilient and warfighting-ready military, backed by a world-class supply chain and we’re bringing industry into the heart of defence the fundamental enabler of everything that we are trying to achieve. To not only make our country more secure, but also more successful and prosperous, by creating high-quality defence jobs, skills and opportunities in every postcode.
I used to be incentivised by the MOD press office to say defence is an engine for growth in all my interviews, they used to be encouraging me to do it. With Andy Burnham in Downing Street I now say re-industrialisation, but the fundamental truth is there. Investment in defence creates good jobs. It provides opportunities in particular for our young people and we should be unafraid and unapologetic of saying that truth loudly. Defence spending is an engine for growth. It is a way of re-industrialising. It is a way of creating opportunity. It also keeps us safe.
Now to make our country more secure and more successful we need to create more high quality defence jobs, skills and opportunities. Now if we are to do that SMEs in particular, scale-ups, are really important. Within the MOD, we’ve reformed our system with a new National Armaments Director, Rupert Pearce, coming from a FTSE 100 company, bringing a new corporate approach and energy to the way that we procure.
We’ve established the Defence Office of Small Business growth to help remove those obstacles to entry, cut red tape, and roll out a 50% increase in spend from the MOD with medium and small-sized firms by Summer 2028. That’s moving an extra two and a half billion pounds into the pockets of SMEs by changing the way we procure, making it easier for small businesses to enter our supply chain.
We’ve published our SME Action Plan to set out what we will do so we can be held accountable for that change, and that supports start-ups, scale-ups, and other companies to be able to grow. And helping small firms navigate the routes to funding is something crucial if you want to get the best out of them. At a national level our Defence Office for Small Business Growth provides the guidance for those routes, removes duplication when we find it and clarifies the entry points where necessary.
At local levels I’m really pleased that the rollout of regional defence and security clusters have been so successful with more regions developing them, creating new regional routes to tailor support for businesses and bring together localised networks of major suppliers, devolved and local governments and importantly provide a forum for investors to meet them and support them as well.
Now, Ukraine has shown us the way to innovate at lightning speed because of the necessity of the war that they are fighting. And as we learn from Ukraine’s lead, defence must harness the resources that Britain possesses not just across tech and engineering sectors, but across finance, consulting and academia as well - to help create, inspire and deliver the change that we need. And finance is obviously key to our topic today.
Now, the government is already increasing defence spending. As a defence minister, of course, I would like more defence spending. But it’s not just from the taxpayer that there’s opportunities for investing in defence. It’s how you crowd in private capital, how you use the institutions, the networks, the structures of the City of London and the UK’s place at the heart of global financial trade, to bring more private capital into defence, creating more good jobs and more deterrence. Now, public investment will remain central to that mission as we increase our defence capabilities. But in a more dangerous world, we need to build more capacity now, rather than just wait for the increase in defence money that we know is coming over the next 10 years.
So that’s why the Defence Investment Plan sets out the priority areas that we will invest in both now, and later to provide the certainty for investors to understand what type of technologies, what areas of defence will the government invest in, where we also seek investment from the private sector.
And we need to work hard to make sure that Defence and our colleagues in the investment community speak the same language. Because I think, at the moment, there’s a risk that we sometimes speak past each other. And speaking the same language with the same necessary data will increase our ability to deliver.
Now, Britain has long prospered when government, industry and finance have worked together and our task today is not to reinvent the finance sectors, but a way of bringing us together to create that new partnership for today’s era.
Now, the prize is significant, not just stronger national defence and security, but a more innovative defence sector and a growing market that helps re-industrialise, but also an opportunity to export to our friends as well. Because it’s not just the United Kingdom that’s investing in defence. Our allies in NATO and further afield are doing the same.
Now, in the Defence Investment Plan, we announced a Defence Investment Unit because investors need a clearer interface with defence and defence needs financial expertise to turn priorities into market-facing propositions, speaking the same language.
Following the autumn budget this year, we will publish the Defence Finance Investment Strategy to set a clear framework for how government and responsible private capital can work together in support of security, resilience and growth. And in December, we will also hold a defence investment summit to turn strategy into delivery and bring together government, industry and investors to accelerate the flow of capital into priority defence capabilities.
Now, before I finish, I want to set out that this is not a theoretical game. This is happening right now and we need to make it easier for it to happen more frequently. In May, 13 British startups were awarded contracts of up to £4 million as part of the Defence Unicorn Fund programme. Kraken Technologies, as one of them, which manufactures maritime uncrewed surface vehicles, has since gone on to raise $175 million in a Series B funding round off the back of a $1 billion valuation. Green Jets is another British firm which has secured significant funding from capital. It was just one of three firms selected by the Ministry of Defence to develop a low-cost drone interceptor. Both Kraken and Green Jets received funding from the National Security Strategic Investment Fund and NATO Innovation Fund, while the British Business Bank also financed Kraken. And JET Connectivity, a small business which builds novel 5G and 6G communications tools was the only British firm to be admitted to the procedures NATO Diana mission track programme earlier this year from over three and a half thousand participants.
That was fantastic recognition of British innovation at its best, but I know it’s just the tip of the iceberg. There are so many other British, brilliant British companies that we need to be able to support as well.
Now, it is in these uncertain times that not only do friends stand together, which is why the support that we offer in Ukraine is long lasting, is serious and will not change no matter what threats Putin throws at us. It is also in these uncertain times that we need to make it easier to bring private capital and public investment together to create the new defence technologies that we need to keep our nation safe.
But let me finish with a final thought. Today we will not only get a clearer view of the potential on offer in the growing defence industry in the UK, and advice on how you can access more of that market. We also get a chance to keep Britain secure in a more dangerous world. Defence needs to be a national endeavour. A whole of society endeavour, a whole of government endeavour. It is the responsibility of the Ministry of Defence to lead that, but it is not the responsibility of the Ministry of Defence alone. To keep our nation safe, we need every part of society, every part of government and industry to step up to support that resilience, that innovation, and that drive to keep us all safe. Because as we can see from our friends in Ukraine, where deterrence fails, not only is it more and more expensive in treasure and lives and lost opportunity. It’s something that, as everyone here, we must take steps to avoid. That is why deterrence matters. That’s why increasing our deterrence matters with new technologies. But if deterrence fails, we must be ready to fight, and we must be ready to win. And all of you in this group can play a part in doing so.
Thank you for what you’re doing here today, and thank you Lady Mayor for bringing us all together.

The Moldovan military detected an "unmanned aerial vehicle" at 4:20 p.m. local time on Sept. 8, the Moldovan Defense Ministry said in a statement, identifying it as a "Shahed-type" drone that entered the country's airspace from the "direction of … Ukraine."

TEHRAN, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) said Wednesday that if any vessel enters the "restricted zone" to be announced by Iran in regional waters without coordination, it will be subject to the country's sanction measures.
"If a vessel enters this zone without coordination (with Iran), it will be subject to our sanction measures; meaning that if it seeks to use the Strait of Hormuz in the future, it will not be able to do so, and we will also refuse to provide it with port, insurance, and other required services," IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
He said the zone's exact coordinates will be announced in the future, adding that it will generally begin around Iran's southeastern port city of Chabahar and will include parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea as well as the routes that can lead to the Strait of Hormuz.
He described the Strait of Hormuz as the "strait of Iran's power," adding the country will use that power to respond to the "enemy's aggression" and force it to stop it.
Following U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran restricted passage through the Strait of Hormuz, while U.S. forces imposed a naval blockade targeting vessels traveling to or from Iranian ports and coastal areas.
Also on Wednesday, Iran's Foreign Ministry strongly condemned the U.S. Army's "aggressive" attack the night before against a number of Iranian oil tankers.
Expressing the condemnation in a statement, it said, "The U.S. military attack on Iranian commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman are considered to be in continuation of the U.S. government's military aggression, naval blockade and economic war against Iran, and in flagrant violation of the United Nations Charter and international law."
It called on the UN and the Security Council to take immediate actions against the "blatant violations" of international peace and security owing to "the U.S. aggressive actions against Iran."
The U.S. Central Command said in a Wednesday post on social media platform X that its forces had "destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers" on Tuesday night in response to the IRGC's targeting of "a U.S. Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days."
The IRGC announced in separate statements early Wednesday that its forces had targeted within the preceding hours four U.S. vessels, including two destroyers, and eight oil tankers in regional waters, as well as a U.S. air base in Jordan in retaliatory strikes. ■
