BLAGOVESHCHENSK, September 9. /TASS/. The Amur Region signed about 20 agreements, launched a project to build an international business center in Blagoveshchensk, and opened a new branch of the Warrior Center - during the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok, the regional government said.
"On the forum's sidelines, the region presented its investment potential, launched the construction of an international business center in Blagoveshchensk, and during the forum the Russian president opened the region's branch of the Warrior Center. The regional government has signed about 20 agreements," the government reported.
The Amur Region's delegation led by Governor Vasily Orlov arrived at the forum with a detailed list of projects and ready-made agreements. The agreements were signed with federal institutions, commercial companies and regional partners on infrastructures, construction, tourism, digital economy, and culture. A significant part of these agreements is the logical result of a long preparatory work that will become the basis for the projects' implementation in the coming years, the governor stressed.
The international business center's construction is a key item on the program aimed at building up Blagoveshchensk's status as a center for cross-border business cooperation, he continued. The new facility will host business missions, exhibitions, and negotiations with international counterparts.
The Russia-China agenda
During the forum, the governor participated in a meeting of the Russian-Chinese Intergovernmental Commission on Investment Cooperation led by Denis Manturov, Russia's First Deputy Prime Minister, and Ding Xuexiang, Deputy Premier of the State Council of the People's Republic of China. The meeting participants outlined three systemic directions for the commission's further work: constant monitoring and targeted support of projects, better awareness of the business community about investment opportunities, and the search for new forms of attracting financial resources to implement joint projects.
The interstate cooperation is becoming more practical, the governor said. "The agenda focused mostly on Russian-Chinese relations," he added. "The cities of Blagoveshchensk and Heihe are leaders in building interstate relations." the governor said. The support from Chinese counterparts confirms the interest in joint infrastructure and logistics projects that are important for the Amur Region's economy, the governor noted.
Key agreements
The signed agreements include documents signed with the Roscongress Foundation on the development of the Russian-Chinese Business Cooperation Competence Center, established in Blagoveshchensk in compliance with instructions from the president. This center will become a platform to support trade and investment initiatives, create expert and educational programs, and to follow-up projects with Chinese counterparts.
Two documents inked with DOM.RF are on the construction of a multifunctional community center on the Golden Mile and on the development in the region of "green" construction - technologies and standards aimed at cutting energy intensity and carbon footprint in the construction industry. An agreement with Vimpelcom is on development of the digital economy and telecom infrastructures to ensure easier access to the high-speed Internet and digital services in the region's remote areas.
Special attention is paid to social initiatives: an agreement with Russian Railways provides for tax benefits in exchange for the renovation of a summer camp for children and a sanatorium - to upgrade recreation infrastructures for the region's children. Another agreement was signed with the Soyuzmultfilm Animation Studio to create a themed space for family leisure, using characters from Soviet and Russian cartoons - to expand cultural and leisure opportunities in the region and to develop domestic tourism.
Tourism and cluster projects
The Amur Region signed a cooperation agreement with the Chukotka Autonomous Region in tourism. The document provides for joint routes, the exchange of experience in development of tourism infrastructures, and in promotion of Russian Arctic and Far Eastern destinations on a single platform. An agreement with Solovyevsky Mine is on a historical and cultural tourism cluster on Relochny Lane in Blagoveshchensk - the project will focus on preserving and presenting local history, attracting tourists and organizing related infrastructures.
Logistics and major infrastructure projects
When speaking at the forum's different sessions, the Amur Region's Governor Vasily Orlov focused on international logistics as a strategic direction in the region's development. Priority projects include building of the Dzhalinda (Russia) - Mohe (China) combined automobile and railway bridge that will lead to the road connecting the region with the Northern Sea Route. Such transport solutions will create new corridors for exports, will cut logistics costs and will open access to Arctic routes, the governor said.
Export expansion
During the forum, the governor had a meeting with a delegation from Belarus, where the parties discussed building up the trade, supplies of Amur agricultural products, supplies of Belarusian machinery, and the creation of joint ventures. The delegations paid special attention to humanitarian cooperation and knowledge exchange in the agro-industrial sector. These contacts may become a source for additional sites to sale agricultural products and to localize industrial production in the Amur Region.
Results
Based on results of the Eastern Economic Forum in 2026, the Amur Region has confirmed its status of a key Far Eastern region in attracting investments and developing international cooperation. The implementation of signed agreements and launched projects will create new jobs, improve the quality of life in the region, and will build up the region's position in the Far East's economic space. The governor noted that the regional team had completed the planned program and was ready to be working at the implementation stage.

A risk in a teacup: Researchers find link between very hot drinks and oesophageal cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:58:33 UTC
23:58:33 KST

The link between consuming very hot drinks and oesophageal cancer has been established by the world’s largest study into the subject yet.
Regularly drinking piping hot tea and coffee could triple the risk of developing oesophageal cancer — a cancer that's found in the gullet or food pipe, according to the world’s largest study to date that establishes a link between the two.
Hot drinks are some of the most widely consumed beverages across Europe, with Europeans reported to drink an average of 5.7kg of coffee per person each year in 2023.
While the health benefits of hot drinks have been widely studied, their potential cancer risks have remained unclear within Western populations, according to Oxford University researchers, who published their findings in the International Journal of Cancer.
Through a 14-year analysis of nearly a million middle-aged men and women based in the United Kingdom, those who have their drinks "very hot" — classified as 65 degrees Celsius or above by the International Agency for Research on Cancer — were found to face an almost three times higher risk of developing cancer of the food pipe or gullet than those who drink them “warm”.
The amount consumed also mattered, with six or more hot drinks per day increasing the risk.
“The study being so large definitely adds to the evidence that having hot and very hot drinks increases your risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma [a type of cancer that starts as a growth of cells on the skin],” Keren Papier, a nutritional epidemiologist at the University of Oxford's population health department and co-author of the study, told Euronews Health.
Most people drink coffee and tea at temperatures of between 50 and 60 degrees Celsius, although this can vary depending on region and preparation methods.
Even with the addition of milk, it’s advised to wait at least a few minutes before drinking.
“If a drink is uncomfortable to drink, letting it sit to cool down a bit to what you might expect to be warm or hot as opposed to very hot would be a good idea,” Papier said.
A rare cancer
Oesophageal cancer has two primary subtypes that describe where the cancer originates: squamous cell oesophageal cancer and adenocarcinoma.
It has a disproportionately higher incidence rate in the UK, listed as the 14th most common cancer in the country, according to Cancer Research UK. But the squamous cell oesophageal cancer subtype, which the study found links to, is still rare.
“The risk is a 1% lifetime risk of being diagnosed with this cancer in the UK,” Papier said. “But of course, drinking tea and coffee are things that are quite widely consumed, so if we can let the drink cool down a little bit, that would definitely be beneficial to help with preventing this cancer from occurring.”
Cancer Research also states that the main lifestyle risks for oesophageal cancer continue to be smoking and drinking, followed by obesity.
“The best thing beyond our study is to make sure that you cut your smoking and maybe avoiding alcohol helps a bit as well,” Papier said.
“It’s important to keep what we know generally about the risk factors of cancer across this cancer and other cancers, and not to forget that when thinking about prevention.”

Small Swiss firms asked to help expand wind power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:54:58 UTC
23:54:58 KST

Small Swiss firms asked to help expand wind power
Wind power has faced an uphill political battle in Switzerland. Now energy company Axpo wants to accelerate wind energy development with the help of small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs).
Private households are unlikely to buy a wind turbine, but for SMEs such an investment appears attractive.
Every wind power project begins with a wind measurement mast. One such mast is situated in Rossrüti, a meadow in the hilly countryside north-east of the town of Wil in canton St Gallen. Here, wind speed, wind direction, temperature and air pressure are measured.
+ Why do wind turbines windup so many emotions?
Existing data from Wind Atlas Switzerland, a federal database that measures wind speed and direction, was insufficient, according to Cédric Aubert, head of wind power at Axpo, which is planning to build a wind farm in this location.
“The topography is a crucial factor. That’s why we always have to take really precise measurements for every project,” he told Swiss public broadcaster SRF.
For the environmental impact assessment, Axpo must also monitor the activity of bats and birds. Axpo plans to erect three large wind turbines, which will generate enough electricity to power around 5,000 households, particularly in winter.
+ Alpine nimbyism freezes Swiss green energy dreams
Aubert says the measurements taken at the mast in Rossrüti have been promising so far. And, in principle, the site is ideal. “Because there is wind and because the electricity could be consumed locally,” Aubert said.
Energy security
Aubert hopes that, in addition to the surrounding local authorities, smaller companies from the region will also participate in the project. “Investing in wind power is ideal for SMEs because a wind farm has a lifespan of around 25 years,” he said.
“Anyone who invests in a wind farm can purchase electricity for this period at a fixed price. That means planning and supply security. You receive the electricity and are not exposed to the geopolitical situation or highly volatile electricity prices,” Aubert added.
Aubert is convinced that SMEs would be willing to pay a little extra for planning and supply security. Currently, a kilowatt-hour of wind power costs CHF0.02 to CHF0.03 ($0.025 to $0.037) more than the average price of electricity.
+ Read more: Switzerland needs energy, but what kind?
“In addition, electricity from wind turbines is renewable and clean. SMEs also need to consider their carbon footprint,” he said.
Axpo is in talks with various SMEs about potential investments. Aubert does not yet wish to name any specific companies. But one thing is clear to him: “If local industry gets involved, people will see this has a benefit – an economic one too – for the region. That would help with acceptance.”
The three wind turbines near Rossrüti could start generating electricity in 2031 at the earliest. Currently, only around 50 of these large turbines are in operation across Switzerland, producing well under 1% of the country’s electricity.
Similar to solar boom
According to the energy strategy, wind is set to contribute significantly more (7%) to the electricity mix by 2050. That sounds challenging, if not impossible. But Aubert is hoping for a similar development to that seen with solar energy.
“Fifteen years ago, solar power was also at 0.2%. Today, solar installations generate more than 14% of Switzerland’s electricity. Back then, everyone said it was impossible.”
However, this expansion is still far from certain. No fewer than two popular initiatives, which aim to severely restrict the construction of wind turbines, are expected to be put to a vote in 2027.
More
Two initiatives on wind turbine construction launched in Switzerland
The Wind AtlasExternal link measures wind direction and speed at various locations in Switzerland.
The planning tool from the Swiss Federal Office of Energy (SFOE) also highlights areas with particularly high wind potential.
For comparison, the Wind Atlas also displays a map of Switzerland showing the various federal interests in the area.
This map highlights, for example, building zones (with noise protection) or protected areas that would need to be taken into account when constructing a wind turbine.

Cut ties with MAGA to join – EU to bloc hopefuls
EU candidate countries should cut ties US President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement as they conflict with Brussels’ long-term interests, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos has said.
Speaking at a Centre for European Policy Studies event in Brussels on Tuesday, Kos warned that prospective members should not develop relations with outside powers that could pull them away from the EU.
”We should not risk our future members building dependencies on others that run counter to our long-term interest,” she said.
Kos singled out Trump’s political movement, saying the Brussels faces “pressure from the West, from the MAGA ideologists who try to persuade us that our European civilization is in decline, that our economy is in decline, and that we don’t have the right democracy.”
Her remarks come as the Trump administration has sought closer political and economic ties with nationalist and conservative forces in Europe. Kos also claimed that the EU is facing “adversaries” seeking to influence its enlargement process. “For the first time in history, we have adversaries in the enlargement process,” she said. Asked whom she meant, Kos replied: “Clearly, Russia is one of them.”
The comments come amid growing US economic engagement in the Western Balkans, where several countries are seeking EU membership. American-linked projects have been pursued in Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Albania, including a controversial resort development connected to Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
Kos has argued that enlargement should strengthen the EU amid growing geopolitical competition, saying last month that the process must adapt to a world in which “old alliances are fading and new ones emerging.”

Russia tells Trump ending US support for Ukraine could help end war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:53:13 UTC
23:53:13 KST

The United States must stop supporting Kyiv to help end Russia's war against Ukraine, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state broadcaster VGTRK on Sept. 9.
The remarks came a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone with U.S. President Donald Trump, as Washington intensifies efforts to revive peace negotiations.
"First and foremost... they should stop providing any assistance to Kyiv," Ushakov said, adding that Putin had outlined possible steps the U.S. could take to help end the war during the call.
While the U.S. has stopped committing direct financial and military aid to Ukraine, Kyiv's allies can still purchase U.S. weapons for Ukraine via a NATO mechanism. Washington also continues to share intelligence with Kyiv that helps Ukrainian forces strike targets inside Russia.
Ushakov's remarks follow visits by Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, to Moscow and, for the first time, Kyiv over the weekend as part of efforts to break the deadlock in peace talks.
People familiar with the talks told the Kyiv Independent that the envoys brought revised peace proposals, but no breakthrough was achieved as Putin appears intent on escalating Russia's war.
President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters after the Kyiv meeting that he expects "the war will continue" into the winter months despite the new peace push.
The most tangible outcome of the trip was an agreement between Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia to resume trilateral negotiations. Previous rounds of such talks produced little political progress but resulted in major humanitarian initiatives, including prisoner-of-war exchanges.
Ushakov said the Kremlin remains open to continuing negotiations in a U.S.-Russia-Ukraine format in the United Arab Emirates. Moscow considers Abu Dhabi, where several rounds of talks took place earlier this year, its preferred venue.
"We're talking about resuming the negotiation process with Ukraine that took place previously," Ushakov said. "We've also discussed this with our American colleagues, so it's possible that this process will resume in a trilateral format."
Putin told the U.S. envoys on Sept. 5 that he expects Russia to achieve its "goals" and that Moscow wants the so-called "root causes" of the war resolved.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv cede the partially occupied and strategically vital Donbas region in eastern Ukraine.
Ukraine has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front lines while stressing the need for Western-backed security guarantees to deter future potential Russian aggression.

En Europe, les datacenters devraient construire leurs installations d’énergie propre, selon Teresa Ribera
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:52:36 UTC
23:52:36 KST

En Europe, les datacenters devraient construire leurs installations d’énergie propre, selon Teresa Ribera
La hausse de la demande en électricité pour les besoins de l’IA risque d’entraîner une concurrence acharnée pour l’accès à l’énergie et de faire grimper les factures, a prévenu la commissaire européenne responsable de la transition écologique.
BRUXELLES — L’Union européenne devrait obliger les géants de la tech à investir dans l’approvisionnement en énergie propre afin de répondre aux besoins croissants en électricité de leurs centres de données, a estimé auprès de POLITICO la vice-présidente exécutive de la Commission européenne chargée de la Transition propre, juste et compétitive.
Teresa Ribera a averti que les infrastructures très gourmandes en électricité qui alimentent l’intelligence artificielle mettent de plus en plus à rude épreuve les réseaux électriques, entraînant une concurrence acharnée pour l’énergie et risquant de faire grimper les factures.
“Ça a été un choc, et ça se passe à un rythme effréné, a-t-elle retracé. En 2022, alors que nous cherchions à déterminer comment passer à une énergie entièrement électrique et propre, nous n’avions pas prévu une telle augmentation supplémentaire de la demande en électricité [...] et quelle que soit la rapidité avec laquelle nous planifions les réseaux et les nouvelles capacités d’énergie verte, la demande augmente à un rythme effréné. Cela crée donc certaines tensions.”
Advertisement
Selon l’Espagnole, les gouvernements ont trois options : ne rien faire et prendre le risque de voir s’aggraver les tensions économiques et sociales parce que “les prix ne cessent d’augmenter” en raison de la hausse de la demande ; imposer un moratoire sur la construction de centres de données, comme c’est le cas dans certaines régions des Etats-Unis ; ou obliger les opérateurs à produire leur propre énergie.
Selon elle, les géants de la tech ont les moyens d’envisager cette troisième option.
“Les entreprises à l’origine de cette activité [...] concentrent un pouvoir de marché et des capacités d’une ampleur sans précédent. On peut donc, pour parler sans détour, leur demander d’investir dans ce dont elles pourraient avoir besoin et de veiller à ce que cela évite de nouveaux conflits avec les populations locales”, a-t-elle défendu lors de l’interview.
Lorsqu’on lui a demandé si l’UE devrait obliger les Big Tech à financer eux-mêmes leur approvisionnement en énergie propre, Teresa Ribera a répondu : “Je pense que nous devrions le faire.”
Ces déclarations interviennent alors que la Commission continue de travailler à l’élaboration de nouvelles normes d’efficacité énergétique pour les datacenters. Le commissaire européen à l’Energie, Dan Jørgensen, avait insisté fin mai sur le fait que les entreprises souhaitant construire des centres de données en Europe devaient s’engager à respecter les objectifs climatiques et énergétiques du continent.
A l’inverse, le président de l’European Data Centre Association (EDCA), Lex Coors, s’est inscrit en faux en juin, déclarant à POLITICO que l’Europe devait donner la priorité à l’intelligence artificielle plutôt qu’à ses ambitions climatiques immédiates, sous peine de céder sa souveraineté technologique à la Chine.
Advertisement
Reste que les gouvernements européens se démènent aussi pour gérer la forte hausse de la demande énergétique des infrastructures d’IA et éviter une augmentation des émissions de gaz à effet de serre due à leur consommation d’énergie. A la fin de l’année dernière, l’Irlande a levé le moratoire sur les nouvelles constructions, à condition que les nouveaux datacenters disposent sur place de sources d’énergies renouvelables pour s’alimenter.
Teresa Ribera a évoqué un projet de décret dévoilé le mois dernier par le gouvernement espagnol, qui imposerait aux centres de données de s’approvisionner à hauteur de 80% en électricité provenant d’installations éoliennes et solaires récentes, soit via une production sur site, soit en signant des contrats d’achat d’électricité à long terme (PPA) issue exclusivement d’énergies renouvelables.
Mais elle a averti que ces PPA risquent de créer des tensions avec les autres consommateurs : “Si ces datacenters [...] signent des PPA avec des fournisseurs d’électricité, cette [énergie] constitue leur principale matière première et ils peuvent payer des prix plus élevés que ceux que notre industrie de base électro-intensive est en mesure de payer.”
Et l’Espagnole d’ajouter : “Le développement de nouvelles capacités de production d’électricité prend du temps. Cela pourrait donc avoir des répercussions non seulement en matière de durabilité, si cela [entraînait], par exemple, un retard dans la sortie progressive du charbon, mais aussi en matière de concurrence équitable ou de compétitivité pour nos industries lors de la production de biens.”
Compte tenu du développement rapide de l’IA et du nombre de centres de données cherchant à se raccorder au réseau en Europe, les autorités doivent agir rapidement pour mettre en place une réglementation, a plaidé Teresa Ribera.
“On parle de mois, a-t-elle souligné. On ne parle pas de décennies, et probablement même pas d’années.”
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

US-Israeli defense company to produce cruise missiles in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:52:19 UTC
23:52:19 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
US-Israeli defense company Covenant plans to begin producing long-range cruise missiles in the German state of Saxony next year, the company announced Wednesday.
Production of the Anthem cruise missile is expected to start near Leipzig in the first quarter of 2027, primarily serving European customers.
“In the first year, we will produce around 1,000 units and then ramp up to 5,000 units. That is our target for annual production,” said Covenant President Abigail Denburg.
Denburg said a production contract had already been signed for deliveries from Germany but declined to identify the buyer.
“This European customer will decide for itself when it wants to announce this,” she said.
Covenant said its German facility spans around 110,000 square feet (10,200 square meters) and will be supported by a European supply chain.
The company also opened a 105,000-square-foot factory in the US state of Texas to supply the American market and operates a smaller facility in northern Israel.
Designed for precision strikes against targets deep behind enemy lines, Anthem can carry a warhead weighing around 200 kilograms (441 pounds).
Although media reports have put its range at approximately 1,500 kilometers (932 miles), Covenant has not confirmed the figure.
The company said the missile would cost a six-figure amount, putting its unit price below $1 million and making it significantly cheaper than comparable long-range weapon systems.
Anthem has been flown more than 200 times since its maiden flight in August 2025, including multiple flight tests conducted with the US Army.
Most missile components are commercially available. Covenant has secured long-term agreem ents for other critical parts. The company said the production model was designed to enable rapid manufacturing in large quantities. 
Talks with German military
Covenant is also in talks with the German Armed Forces and the country’s military procurement agency, although the discussions have not been officially confirmed, according to German news agency DPA.
Founded in 2024 and headquartered in Washington, DC, Covenant has raised more than $250 million through three funding rounds.
Its investors include Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, Lux Capital, 8VC, Aleph, and Lightspeed.
The company has also appointed retired German Lt. Gen. Andreas Marlow as an adviser in Germany. Marlow previously served as deputy chief of the German Army and led the EU military training mission for Ukrainian forces beginning in 2022.
Covenant said it has secured $150 million in orders, including qualification, research and development, and production contracts.
The company’s expansion comes amid Israel’s genocide in the Gaza Strip. Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel has waged a genocidal war on Gaza that has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000, while 90% of the territory’s infrastructure has been destroyed, according to Palestinian authorities.

The agency said it continues to “provide education to thousands of Palestinian refugee children", despite the difficult conditions facing the sector.
UNRWA said it provided education to students affected by displacement and disruptions to schooling through temporary and alternative learning spaces, remote education and self-learning materials.
Around half of the students displaced from the Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps also returned to UNRWA schools.
Roland Friedrich, director of UNRWA affairs in the occupied West Bank, said the new school year offers thousands of Palestinian refugee children “renewed hope” after another year of displacement, violence and uncertainty.
In the occupied East Jerusalem, UNRWA said its six schools have remained forcibly closed by Israeli authorities since May 2025, affecting around 800 Palestinian refugee children.
The agency added that recent Israeli raids and measures at the Qalandia Training Centre threaten the continuity of its educational and training activities there.
UNRWA reaffirmed its commitment to providing education and creating opportunities for generations of Palestinian refugees, stressing that education is “a right for every child.”
In October 2024, the Israeli parliament passed two bills targeting UNRWA.
The first prohibits the agency from operating within the 1948 borders. The second bars Israeli officials from engaging with UNRWA in any capacity.
UNRWA was established by the UN General Assembly in 1949 and has since been a lifeline for millions of Palestinian refugees, providing humanitarian aid, education, healthcare, and essential services under challenging conditions.

Europe is playing a dangerous game with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:51:47 UTC
23:51:47 KST

Europe is playing a dangerous game with Russia
History doesn’t repeat itself, not even as farce, and thus the latest chapter in the centuries-long confrontation between Russia and Europe will look different from those that came before it.
Today, the German authorities are closing Russian cultural and diplomatic institutions on flimsy pretexts and Norway is seizing Russian research vessels – and while the methods are new, the underlying impulse is familiar. Europe has sought to constrain Russia’s independence since at least the late 15th century.
For now, however, European governments aren’t seeking direct military confrontation, but this should not be mistaken for pacifism in Berlin, Brussels, Paris, or London – nor should we take seriously their ritual declarations about dialogue and a new regional security architecture, given there are more practical reasons for their restraint.
First, Western Europe’s largest states lack the human and material resources for a war with Russia, and although their position is somewhat better when it comes to weapons, much of that capacity is already being directed toward Ukraine, whose population is being asked to make enormous sacrifices in pursuit of European objectives.
However, the European people show little appetite for these sacrifices, mainly because living standards haven’t deteriorated nearly enough to persuade ordinary Germans, Italians, French, and British people to march into a conflict with Russia. Nor should anyone place much faith in Poland or the rest of Eastern Europe because Warsaw’s increasingly belligerent rhetoric disguises a much weaker willingness to actually fight.
Second, the Europeans understand that their American patrons have no desire to become embroiled in a potentially fatal confrontation with Moscow. The supposed American nuclear umbrella over Europe has always contained an element of mythology, and the region’s leaders understood this even during the Cold War.
France’s development of an independent nuclear deterrent was itself an acknowledgement that Europe could not assume that the US would risk its own destruction on their behalf. Charles de Gaulle and his successors didn’t build this arsenal because they were confident of American guarantees.
Nobody in Europe, therefore, seriously believes that Russia can be easily defeated in a war, because if they did, the temptation to attempt it would be much greater.
Yet these rational calculations run up against a more subjective danger, and we shouldn’t overestimate the European elite’s instinct for self-preservation.
Unlike Russia or China, Western Europe has experienced no comparable replacement of its ruling elites over the past 150 years, meaning today’s political establishments are, in an important sense, descendants of those that led Europe into the First and Second World Wars.
Western European politicians, particularly German and British, have historically displayed a tendency towards adventurism. Indeed, George Kennan, an astute observer of political cultures, drew a revealing contrast in his 1946 Long Telegram where Russian foreign policy, he wrote, “is neither schematic nor adventurist” and “doesn’t take unnecessary risks,” but the same cannot always be said of Europe.
The US, for all its willingness to use military force, generally prefers overwhelming odds, which is why its habit is to attack when it is confident that the opponent can’t inflict unacceptable damage in return. This makes the Americans, in a certain sense, more predictable and therefore more amenable to diplomacy. Even at the height of American unipolar power, Washington harbored few illusions about what a direct war with Russia would entail.
Europe has a more troubling historical record and its powers have repeatedly created dangerous situations that ultimately escaped their control, with World War II as the supreme example. Napoleon’s invasion of Russia and Germany’s invasion more than a century later were also enormous gambles, courses of action that appeared reckless even to many contemporaries.
For the moment, Europe is conducting its struggle against Russia primarily through indirect means because it lacks the resources for something more ambitious and retains enough sound judgment to recognize the dangers of escalation – but it would be reckless for Moscow to assume this restraint will last forever.
With every new stage of confrontation, European governments are burning bridges that might have otherwise supported a more balanced system of coexistence. Seen in this context, Russia’s decision to close the Goethe Institutes isn’t merely a symmetrical response to German measures, but also makes sense in the long term.
Whether we like it or not, cultural and humanitarian cooperation has increasingly become an instrument of state policy, though exceptions remain. Russian and French museum professionals, for example, continue to work together on some projects, as do academics and cultural figures in other fields, but these relationships have become increasingly subordinate to the logic of soft power.
Even seemingly innocuous forms of international cooperation are now expected to serve national objectives, and this is regrettable – but it reflects the expansion of modern foreign policy far beyond traditional diplomacy. Governments can use funding and institutions to influence almost every sphere of international contact.
Russia isn’t entirely different in this respect. We too often judge educational and cultural cooperation by its political consequences, and governments and the public naturally ask why money should be spent on international projects if they produce no discernible benefit for the country that funds them.
But in Western countries, these demands are particularly pronounced, so institutions such as the Goethe-Institut cannot realistically be separated from Germany’s broader foreign-policy objectives, and German officials inevitably expect publicly supported cultural organizations to influence attitudes towards Germany and advance the country’s interests.
The result is paradoxical: The political burden placed upon cultural institutions eventually undermines the very value of the relationships they were created to foster.
Perhaps the erosion of these old forms of cooperation is therefore unavoidable and it may even prove necessary if future cultural and academic contacts are to become less dependent on the political climate in European capitals.
For now, however, Russia faces a more immediate problem, in which European leaders remain afraid of direct confrontation, yet their own decisions are steadily pulling them deeper into a spiral of confrontation.
Their caution is real, but history gives Russia little reason to assume that caution will always prevail over adventurism – and that requires vigilance from Moscow and the resolve to act accordingly.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

EU frontrunner Montenegro ready to help Ukraine with reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:51:06 UTC
23:51:06 KST

Montenegro does and can share best practices with Ukraine to help it advance the rule-of-law reforms required for EU membership, Montenegro's European Affairs Minister Maida Gorcevic told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 9.
The small Western Balkan country is on track to become the EU's newest member state. A draft accession treaty is being prepared, and Montenegro hopes to close all remaining negotiating chapters by the end of 2026.
Over in Kyiv, the parliament continues to block many of the reforms required for Ukraine to advance its own membership bid, potentially at the cost of billions of euros of financial aid from the EU and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
"Believe me, this is not an easy process at all," Gorcevic said during a breakfast meeting with journalists organized by the European Parliament's centrist Renew Europe political group.
In response to a question from the Kyiv Independent, Gorcevic described some of those reforms as variously "not easy," "not popular," and "not easy to understand."
EU legislation also has to be treated differently from other laws, Gorcevic explained. Amendments always require EU approval, and getting lawmakers to vote through rules without having the chance to amend them, she says, has been a tough sell.
"But the changes we are doing for the rule of law are not for Brussels... they are for our citizens," Gorcevic said.
That sentiment matched comments made by Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot when he visited Kyiv in August.
With Montenegro now in the closing stages of its EU integration process, it looks set to be the first country to join the bloc since Croatia in 2013.
Forging ahead with that process has led Montenegro to develop expertise on the rule of law in its membership process, which it is ready to share, Gorcevic said.
As an example, she mentioned that a dedicated rule of law team meets twice weekly with European Commission officials to go over the requirements in fine detail, a best practice set to be applied to all other candidate countries.
A Montenegrin diplomat showed the Kyiv Independent how that looked on their calendar. Three hours on Monday morning, another three hours on Thursday, surrounded by technical experts from three different departments of the European Commission.
Together, they go through the work to be done and the bills to be passed, "line by line."
"It's hard, but it gets the job done," that diplomat said.
Gorcevic also reminded that Montenegro has signed memoranda of cooperation with Ukraine, Moldova, and Albania, with a view to helping them advance.
The agreement with Ukraine, signed in March, foresees "the provision of expert support by public administration officials" to share practices in "rule of law, judicial reform, anti-corruption efforts, public administration reform, and economic criteria."
It also foresees regular meetings between EU negotiation teams, co-developing studies and projects, and organizing joint events to help advance European integration.
Gorcevic also noted that the information flow does not have to be one-way, adding that Montenegro "also learn(s) from other candidates."
Montenegro has closed 18 of the 33 negotiation chapters required to join the EU. It aims to close one more in September, and the rest by the end of December.
Ukraine has opened two of six "clusters," which contain seven of the 33 chapters. It expects to have all 33 opened by the end of 2026.

North Korean Elites and Regime Weakness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:51:00 UTC
23:51:00 KST

The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Jieun Baek – author of “Privileged but Powerless: How North Korean Elite Grievances Reveal the Regime’s Greatest Weakness” (Yale 2026) – is the 525th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Describe the key characteristics of North Korea’s elites.
North Korea officially rejects the idea that it has an elite class, yet it is one of the world’s most stratified societies. Its elites include Korean Workers’ Party cadres, intellectuals, senior military and security officials, and individuals personally close to Kim Jong Un. The traditional elite largely inherits status through favorable songbun [North Korea’s hierarchical classification system], family history, and proven political loyalty. A newer unofficial elite – the donju, or “masters of money” – derives influence from capital, markets, and connections.
These groups are not monolithic, but they share one defining characteristic: their positions help maintain the regime. In return, they may receive Pyongyang residency, superior housing and education, better food, prestigious employment and education, overseas opportunities, and access to luxury goods – European watches, imported cosmetics, pet poodles.
None of this is discreet. The regime stages elite reward deliberately. When the Kyongru-dong neighborhood opened, officials framed the new housing not as a public good but as the deserved inheritance of those whose loyalty had earned them “the best of civilization.”
Yet every privilege is conditional. Elites must continuously demonstrate political reliability, professional usefulness, and personal loyalty to Kim. And the most privileged are also the most closely watched: privilege and surveillance rise together.
Examine why North Korean elites are “privileged but powerless.”
North Korean elites possess influence, wealth, and access unimaginable to most citizens, but they lack the most basic power over their own lives. They cannot safely criticize policy, organize independently, protect their families from guilt by association, or know whether today’s privilege will survive tomorrow’s purge. Even the most senior officials can be demoted, imprisoned, or executed without due process, like Jang Song Thaek in 2013.
Their proximity to power actually creates additional danger. Elites face intense surveillance, mandatory ideological activity, extractive “loyalty” contributions, workplace rivalries, and constant evaluation. Thae Yong Ho, the most senior North Korean diplomat to defect in years, put it with characteristic economy: “The closer you are to the Sun, the higher the chances you will burn.” Several escapees told me middle-ranking posts felt safer than the apex.
They may supervise institutions or control substantial resources, but they cannot challenge the system that grants those privileges. As one elite escapee told me, they are “disposable slaves to Kim Jong Un.” They are powerful downward, toward those beneath them, but powerless upward, before the Leader.
Analyze the correlation between North Korean elite “feigned fealty” and the erosion of elite loyalty to Kim Jong Un’s regime.
North Korean public life is a carefully directed performance. Elites attend rallies, recite ideological texts, participate in self-criticism sessions, and display intense devotion. But visible obedience should not be mistaken for sincere belief.
One interviewee described this perfectly through an anecdote. Inspectors would arrive at his home in white gloves to check the portraits of the Kim leaders, hunting for a speck of dust that could bring serious consequences down on his family. He cleaned those portraits, he told me, not out of reverence but out of self-preservation.
As depicted in the table below, “Feigned fealty” describes that widening gap between low inward loyalty and high outward loyalty. Many elites perform devotion because doing so protects their careers, families, status, and lives. This is preference falsification under extreme coercion: everyone plays a role, while few can know what others truly believe.
The gap appears to be widening under Kim Jong Un. Elite defections have increased dramatically; younger elites prioritize money, business, foreign study, and opportunities for their children over service to the Party; and many privately favor economic reform and greater access to information. The regime’s elaborate demands for loyalty reveal not confidence, but anxiety. A system sustained by genuine conviction is resilient. One sustained by surveillance, rewards, and fear may look stable until a shock exposes how shallow its support has become.
Identify the five options for North Korean elites with grievances.
Aggrieved elites have five primary options.
First, they can maintain the status quo and do nothing. This is the least immediately dangerous and most rational choice, but it allows resentment and distrust to accumulate beneath the surface.
Second, they can defect and seek asylum abroad. Defection is an unequivocal rejection of the regime, but it carries extraordinary risks for escapees and their families.
Third, they can erode the regime’s monopoly over resources by building alternative power structures. Markets, private food production, solar energy, informal finance, tutoring, communications, housing, and healthcare can gradually reduce dependence on the state.
Fourth, they can engage in dissent – from coded criticism and hidden transcripts, to use James C. Scott’s concept, and subtle defiance to clandestine information sharing or organized resistance.
Fifth, they can push for democratization and systemic reform. This is the most ambitious and dangerous option because it requires trust, coordination, and first movers willing to confront enormous barriers to collective action.
Assess the role of North Korean elite grievances in revealing the regime’s greatest weakness and its implications for U.S., European, and Asian policymakers and geopolitical strategists.
The regime’s greatest strength and greatest weakness are the same: its dependence on elites. Elites are its architects, administrators, financiers, enforcers, and protectors. The broader population can be controlled through isolation and terror, but the regime must continuously manage elites through a delicate combination of privilege, surveillance, and coercion. If elite allegiance fractures, the system’s foundation begins to crack.
Policymakers should therefore look beyond missile tests and leadership imagery to study elite incentives, generational change, defections, market activity, information consumption, and signs of preference falsification. They should avoid assuming that elite dissatisfaction will automatically produce reform; North Korea’s barriers to trust and collective action remain formidable.
They should also avoid inadvertently improving the regime’s capacity to reward loyalty. Hard-currency access, prestige projects, and engagement channels the state can capture are redirected into patronage for insiders. Sanctions design and diplomatic sweeteners deserve to be tested against that standard.
The United States, Europe, South Korea, Japan, and other partners should expand secure access to outside information, combining radio and portable media with technologies that circumvent censorship. North Korean escapees should lead content creation so that it is credible, tailored, and safe for intended audiences. Governments should also protect escapees, strengthen pathways for asylum, document elite testimony, and support decentralized economic and information networks that reduce the state’s monopoly over daily life.
Finally, strategists must prepare for multiple futures, including gradual liberalization, elite-led reform, succession instability, or sudden internal shock. North Korea may appear immovable, but a regime that requires constant performances of loyalty is revealing its fear: that when people are finally free to choose, many of its most privileged citizens may choose something else.

Ajit Bharti moves Delhi High Court against trial court order denying anticipatory bail in SC/ST act case
NEW DELHI: Social media influencer and YouTuber Ajit Bharti has approached the Delhi high court seeking anticipatory bail in the SC/ST Act case registered against him over his comments concerning Chandrashekhar Azad Ravan, after a trial court denied him relief earlier this month.Bharti has challenged the September 7 order of a Delhi trial court which dismissed his anticipatory bail application.The trial court had declined Bharti's plea after holding that the material placed on record prima facie disclosed the ingredients of an offence under Section 3(1)(r) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.It had further held that the bar under Section 18 of the SC/ST Act applied and, consequently, precluded the grant of anticipatory bail."For the foregoing reasons, this Court finds that the ingredients of an offence under Section 3(1)(r) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 are prima facie disclosed on the material on record," the trial court had observed while dismissing the plea.Additional Sessions Judge Saurabh Partap Singh Laler of Patiala House Courts had passed the order on September 7 in connection with an FIR registered at North Avenue police station.
Ajit Bharti Bail Order.pdfThe case concerns statements allegedly made by Bharti during a programme aired on social media. The complainant had alleged that certain remarks made during the programme were casteist and derogatory towards members of the Scheduled Caste community.Bharti had sought protection from arrest, contending that the allegations did not make out an offence under the SC/ST Act. It was argued on his behalf that the remarks had to be considered in their overall context and that custodial interrogation was not required as the material forming the basis of the case was already available in the public domain.The State and the complainant had opposed his anticipatory bail application.After examining the FIR, transcript and other material placed before it, the trial court concluded that a prima facie case under Section 3(1)(r) of the SC/ST Act was made out and dismissed the application.
The court had, however, clarified that its observations were confined to the disposal of the anticipatory bail plea and should not be construed as an expression of opinion on the merits of the case.It had also made clear that the trial court dealing with the matter would not be influenced by any observations made in the bail order and that Bharti would remain free to seek appropriate remedies available under law if circumstances changed.

EU moves to curb Airbnb-style rentals to boost long-term housing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:48:50 UTC
23:48:50 KST

The EU has introduced a framework to support long-term rentals in tourist-heavy cities. Airbnb warns it creates regulatory uncertainty without improving long-term housing outcomes.
The EU has announced an affordable housing plan aimed at encouraging long-term rentals and making housing more accessible for Europeans.
Unveiled on Wednesday, the plan aims to create clarity and predictability in how rules are applied by local authorities, particularly in neighbourhoods popular with tourists where short-term rentals have displaced residents.
"Lack of affordable housing is a matter of concern for so many of our European citizens," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press statement. "Essential workers and students cannot afford to live where they serve and study. But most importantly, it is about fairness. Today, we are delivering for all Europeans."
While housing policy choices remain the preserve of national authorities, the new Commission plan aims to provide a common European framework of rules to guide implementation on the ground.
"The new rules are designed to help competent authorities identify 'areas under housing stress' using a common methodology," a Commission press release explains.
"Where authorities choose to restrict the use of housing, for instance for short-term rentals or vacant dwellings, they must show that this contributes to local housing pressures and ensure that any measures are targeted, necessary and proportionate."
Housing in Europe is getting worse
The latest data on access to accommodation across Europe are worrying, and have pushed the Commission to intervene.
Recent Eurobarometer data shows that 50 per cent of European city dwellers think that housing is an urgent problem they experience. House prices have skyrocketed faster than local incomes across most European capitals, rising 64.9% between 2015 and 2025 and rents 21.8%, according to EU data.
Even people who cannot afford to buy are facing rising rents, which consume 40% of household income, and middle-class families are also increasingly facing a reality where they can't afford to buy or rent, but also aren't eligible for social housing.
Many residents in cities like Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up, often forcing them to move.
Short-term rentals represent only 1.2% of the EU's total housing stock, but they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots. With too few homes being built where demand is strongest, Brussels estimates it needs more than 2 million new homes every year to fix the problem.
Airbnb, the largest worldwide platform for short-term rentals, has criticised the plan as not sufficiently clear.
"Airbnb shares the Commission's ambition to make housing more affordable. But as drafted, the Affordable Housing Act will not add a single home to the long term rental market, while adding regulatory uncertainty for hosts across European cities," the company wrote in a press statement after the Commission's announcement.
The plan must now be negotiated by the EU co-legislators before being approved.
Marta Pacheco contributed reporting.

The victims of the September 11 attacks will be remembered Wednesday evening at a ceremony in Jerusalem marking 25 years since the deadliest terror attack in U.S. history.
The annual commemoration will take place at the 9/11 Living Memorial in the Arazim Valley, in the foothills of Jerusalem, and will be broadcast live at 6 p.m. Israel time.
The memorial was established in 2009 by Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF) and Jewish National Fund-USA (JNF-USA). It is the only memorial outside the United States that includes the names of all 2,977 people killed in the September 11, 2001 attacks.
A piece of metal recovered from the ruins of the World Trade Center is incorporated into the base of the 30-foot bronze monument, which depicts an American flag rising in the shape of a flame.
This year’s ceremony, organized by KKL-JNF, JNF-USA and the U.S. Embassy in Israel, will include U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, actress Patricia Heaton and representatives of the two organizations, alongside relatives of victims and other guests.
Suri and Harvey Morgenstern, whose daughter Nancy was killed in the attacks, are also expected to attend.
The ceremony will include the laying of memorial wreaths and musical performances. Members of Art of Nova, including survivors of the October 7 Nova music festival massacre and a woman whose sister was killed there, will perform “Shir LaMa’alot,” alongside the Israel Police Orchestra and the Special in Uniform band.
In remarks prepared for the ceremony, Huckabee said the anniversary was a moment to remember “the 2,977 innocent lives taken and the families who have carried that loss.”
“Today’s memorial, at which the United States and Israel mourn together and stand together, is a testimony to our enduring solidarity and shared resolve to confront terrorism and protect innocent life,” he said.

Over 4,500 displaced in Sudan’s North Darfur, Blue Nile amid worsening insecurity: IOM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:46:39 UTC
23:46:39 KST

Adel Abdelrheem, Sahin Demir
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
More than 4,500 people were displaced in Sudan’s North Darfur and Blue Nile states amid deteriorating security conditions, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Wednesday.
In North Darfur, the UN agency said its displacement tracking teams estimated that around 1,275 people fled the villages of Gorbora and Wadi Arkawi in Um Baru locality between Sept. 3 and 6.
The displaced families moved to Karnoy locality in North Darfur, while some crossed the border into neighboring Chad.
The IOM said the situation remains “tense and highly volatile,” and that it continues to closely monitor developments.
Separately, the agency said around 3,315 people, equivalent to 663 families, were displaced in a single day from several villages in Geisan locality in southeastern Sudan’s Blue Nile state due to worsening insecurity.
The displacement was recorded on Sept. 7 from several villages, including Abu Shneina, Rabaa and Wadi Arab. The affected families moved to Wad al-Mahi locality within Blue Nile state.
The IOM said the latest displacement followed an earlier wave on Sept. 5.
On Sunday, the agency said another 1,690 people had been displaced from three villages in Blue Nile’s Kurmuk locality due to escalating violence.
Blue Nile has witnessed a military escalation in recent days amid attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), on several areas.
On Sept. 4, authorities in Kurmuk said the Sudanese army repelled an attack by the RSF and SPLM-N on the Al-Baraka area.
Since late June, villages in North Darfur’s Um Baru locality have also faced attacks blamed on the RSF, including raids on markets and the burning and looting of villages, according to Sudanese rights groups and organizations.
Sudan has been engulfed in a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

====================================================================================================

‘I fear the price could be high’: Inside the German state where the far-right surged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:45:01 UTC
23:45:01 KST

Asking residents in a city where a seismic political event has just taken place ‘How do you feel?’ demands chutzpah – this struck me as I walked around Magdeburg, Germany on Monday. The night before, the far-right populist, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin party Alternative für Deustchland (AfD) had landslide 44% win in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, sending shock waves to Berlin, across Germany and way beyond. Regardless of how people in the capital voted, it felt like a bit of an affront to probe. Given the radical plans of the victors, a party classified by domestic intelligence as “rightwing extremist”, that is what I wanted to know. But from the 21-year-old Guinean-German paramedic I met at the central bus station, collecting donations for a local hospice, to the elderly couple returning to their apartment after a stroll down the Elbe river, almost everyone I met opened up to me warmly.
Judith, 88, was initially reluctant to talk, but shared some of her life story. Her experience as an eight-year-old refugee, forced to leave Poland in 1946 and eventually ending up move with her family in Magdeburg, had shaped her outlook on life, her successful career as a project engineer – as well as her politics. The news that AfD had not only won the election, but by such a wide margin, was “heartbreaking”, she said.
Huy, from Vietnam, who runs a newsagents in the city centre, was also reticent, but laughed and rolled his eyes as he sold the last copy of that day’s local paper, Die Volksstimme, and pointed to the headline that read: “Landslide in Saxony-Anhalt”. Shaking his head, he said: “44%!” “I don’t want to think what it might mean … but maybe it will all be OK?” His question hung in the air.
A glance at the AfD’s manifesto, in particular its pledge for the first 100 days, focuses the mind. Top of the list: challenging Germany’s post-war memory culture (which it says stands in the way of national pride) – so, “more Bismarck, less Hitler”, as they put it. “From the first minute”, they say, the party will start the deportation of what it refers to as “irregular migrants”.
I met Franz-Josef, a 71-year-old retired mechanic and Green voter, on holiday from a small west German town. He called the election a “catastrophe”, particularly in the light of the country’s Nazi past.
Luisa, a 34-year-old bank teller told me she hopes “those who voted for the AfD thought about what they were doing”. It was one thing, she said, to “deliver a kick in the shins” to Berlin, over its failure to pull the German economy out of the doldrums. And maybe the AfD would fail to push through its promises in government. “But we cannot know, and I fear the price could be high.”
Fragrance of power
It remains unclear how precisely the AfD, led by charismatic former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, might take the reins of power in Saxony-Anhalt, if at all. He lacks an absolute majority by a whisker.
There have been rumblings for days – even prior to the election – of an AfD charm offensive to try to lure members of chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats, to make up the necessary numbers. The CDU denies any defections are expected.
Some AfD members have brazenly appropriated Ronald Reagan’s appeal to the Soviets to “tear down this wall”, from his 1987 speech in West Berlin. They are calling on mainstream parties to “tear down the firewall”, a reference to the Brandmauer, or refusal to ever coalesce with the AfD in an effort to prevent the far-right populists from coming to power. Yet an increasing number doubt that the firewall will hold much longer. Especially now that almost one in two of those who cast their votes on Sunday have opted for the party. Turnout at 78% was a record for the state.
Whatever the outcome, we can expect weeks, even months of wrangling. Expect stasis in the meantime on the federal government front, as we’re close to elections on 20 September in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, where the AfD is also expected to do well. Merz will be wary of doing anything that might drive more voters away. At the same time politicos in Berlin are debating how long he has in the job. In the Bundestag today, Merz accused the AfD of seeking “ethnic cleansing”.
No wonder Maryam, 16, whom I met as she returned from work experience at a retirement home, said she and her family were on edge. The Syrian teenager, whose father arrived in Germany in 2015, followed by her and her mother, told me she couldn’t stop thinking about what this vote might mean for her family. She wished, she said, for a return to the days of Angela Merkel, the German chancellor who welcomed in a million migrants including Maryam’s father, resentment over which turbo-charged support for the then-fledgling AfD.
Across the road, Doreen, a cleaner, who reluctantly admitted voting for the AfD, said: “What on Earth is there to thank Merkel for? It’s owing to her that we are in the state we’re in.” She recalled an attack near the Christmas market in the city centre in 2024, where six people were killed when a Saudi doctor drove a car into the crowd, an incident that helped fuel support for the AfD. “That attack is symbolic for a whole lot of misery, the decision to open our doors to strangers has brought us,” Doreen told me. “I say, good on the AfD for promising to clean up the mess.”
For such a small state, home to 2.1 million people, Saxony-Anhalt has managed to create a political maelstrom, the ramifications of which will be felt across Europe.

Torrential rains, winds from Hurricane Lowell leaves 30,000 without power

Torrential rains, winds from Hurricane Lowell leaves 30,000 without power
The Category 1 hurricane misses Kauai but causes widespread destruction, power outages and evacuations.
Catastrophic winds and torrential rains from Hurricane Lowell have pelted Hawaii’s western island of Kauai, knocking out power to at least 30,000 residents and ripping up tracts of beachside roads.
Vicious winds knocked down trees and left nearly 92 percent of Kauai Island Utility Cooperative (KIUC) residents without power by early Tuesday as the storm moved north into the open sea.
While the now-weakened Category 1 hurricane did not make landfall on Kauai, it blew down trees, power poles and lines, causing massive destruction from about 128 kilometres (80 miles) west of the island, according to the Hawaii County Civil Defense Agency.
With approximately 85mph (137km/h) wind gusts, the storm brought a deluge that flooded coastal roads and forced roughly 300 residents to evacuate.
The centre of the storm passed west of the islands in the overnight hours on Tuesday and receded further throughout the day, but dangerous surf from the remnants of the hurricane will impact the Southern California coast for several days given the intensity of the winds, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said.
Emergency officials are asking residents to conserve water and stay off the roads.
Hawaiian mayor Derek Kawakami said that there was “extensive damage” being reported on Tuesday.
“Everyone’s participation has gone from preparation to sheltering to staying off roads …. to now gathering data and information,” the mayor stated.
The Kauai County government urged locals to shelter in place to allow crews to assess damage, clear debris, and restore power and services safely.
Flooding and mudslides will continue to be a risk through the day, said Eric Blake of the National Hurricane Center.
The force of the sustained winds had decreased overall by early Tuesday, and the centre forecasts gradual weakening over the next few days.
In its latest advisory late Tuesday morning local time, the hurricane centre said Lowell had maximum sustained winds near 65mph with higher gusts and was moving north at 14mph.
Hurricane warnings for Kauai and the tiny island of Niihau, which has fewer than 100 permanent residents, were no longer in place by Tuesday morning local time. But high surf and deadly rip currents from the waning storm will continue to affect Hawaii’s exposed coasts for the next day or two.
A tropical storm warning was also lifted for Oahu, the state’s most populated island.

2 rescued after private plane makes emergency landing at sea off northeastern Türkiye

Ayfer Koçal, Selçuk Kılıç
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Two people were rescued after a private plane flying from Batumi, Georgia, to Türkiye's Ordu-Giresun Airport suffered an engine failure and made an emergency landing in the Black Sea off the northeastern province of Rize on Wednesday.
After developing the engine problem, the aircraft contacted the control tower at Rize-Artvin Airport seeking an emergency landing but was unable to reach the airport and ditched about 4 miles (6.4 kilometers) off the coast of Pazar district, according to local authorities.
Coast Guard teams were dispatched after receiving an emergency call and rescued the two people aboard.
The passengers, identified as Belgian nationals Vlasselaer Werner, 55, and Christian Peiffer, 69, were taken to Kackar State Hospital for checks. Both were in good condition and their lives were not in danger.
Rize Gov. Ihsan Selim Baydas said authorities were alerted after contact was established with the two-person aircraft.
"They could not approach the airport; they could not make it there. They had to land at sea. Our teams were immediately put on alert. Our Coast Guard teams reached the aircraft," he said.
"Two Belgian men, one aged 55 and the other 69, were rescued alive by our Coast Guard teams. They are in good condition, and their lives are not in danger. They were taken to hospital for checks," Baydas added.
Describing the incident as "an accident that could have been much worse," Baydas said there were no problems at the airport.
"There are no other findings at this point. The aircraft is floating on the surface, and our teams are recovering it. According to their own statements, they experienced an engine failure," he said.
The Pazar District Governor's Office described the aircraft as a training plane and confirmed that it contacted the Rize-Artvin Airport control tower after developing the engine problem.
"According to initial information, it was determined that the aircraft, which took off from Batumi, Georgia, contacted the control tower to land at Rize-Artvin Airport due to an engine malfunction and subsequently had to make an emergency landing at sea," it said.
Authorities are continuing their investigation into the incident.

Syutkin has published several books on the history of Russian and Soviet cuisine and hosted programs on national television and radio devoted to the history of food. In 2015, Syutkin represented Russia as an official ambassador at the World Expo in Milan.

Israelis can’t ‘do whatever they want in Thailand’ – Thai FM

Israelis can’t ‘do whatever they want in Thailand’ – Thai FM
Israel must do more to explain to its nationals how they are expected to behave in Thailand, according to remarks by Bangkok’s foreign minister, Sihasak Phuangketkeow.
Sihasak, who also serves as deputy prime minister, met Israeli Ambassador Alona Fisher-Kamm on Tuesday following a series of scandalous and potentially criminal incidents involving Israeli nationals that have stirred tensions in Thailand.
“Thailand is a country that welcomes tourists. But welcoming tourists does not mean that visitors, regardless of nationality, can do whatever they want in Thailand,” the minister told the press. “Visitors must understand and respect Thai culture and traditions,” just as Thai tourists must when traveling abroad.
Fisher-Kamm, who indicated ahead of the meeting that she wanted to raise concerns about growing hostility toward Israelis and Jews in Thailand, described the discussion with Sihasak as “good and open” and said it touched on “close cooperation in agriculture, labour, healthcare, and cybersecurity.”
Sihasak said he had requested that West Jerusalem be more engaged with tourists and residents of Thailand, which hosts large communities of Israeli citizens in Phangnga and Phuket, to ensure appropriate behavior.
Dual deportation case as Thailand tightens screws on troublemakers
Thailand, a country long known for tourist-oriented nightlife, is seeking to distance itself from its reputation as a destination for debauchery and attract other types of visitors, including families and people interested in ecotourism.
The policy shift coincides with changing attitudes toward foreigners among parts of the local population, particularly in cases where visitors are seen as disruptive to public order. The government has introduced several measures, including shorter visa terms and easier deportation procedures, aimed at dealing with troublemakers.
Last Friday, Israeli national Jacob Ohayon became the first foreigner to be expelled under the new deportation rules. A Thai court had sentenced him to a suspended 15-day jail term and imposed a fine over a dispute with the owners of Samui Exotic Park, a Thai woman and a French man.
The dispute stemmed from their flying a Palestinian flag, which Ohayon objected to in a manner that Thai authorities ruled violated local law. Among other things, the Israeli organized an online review-bombing campaign against their amusement venue in Ko Samui and issued personal threats.
The threats ultimately cost Ohayon his right to remain in Thailand, with Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, who also serves as interior minister, personally signing the deportation order. The French man, Kevin Dimino, was likewise expelled over his harassing and physically abusive behavior during the confrontation.
Sihasak cited the case, stressing that “anyone, regardless of nationality, who violates Thai law must face strict enforcement.” The foreign minister added that Bangkok values its good relations with Israel, where more than 60,000 Thai workers are currently employed.

The Ambassadori Aviation Village complex has officially opened in the Georgian settlement of Kachreti — a $15 million project combining an airfield, an aviation school, a service center and a gated cottage community for light-aircraft owners, UNN reports, citing "Georgia News."
Details
The complex occupies 16 hectares next to the Ambassadori Kachreti Golf Resort. Its key feature is villas with individual hangars: an owner's aircraft can be rolled out of the building directly onto the taxiway.
Up to 30 private-aircraft crews from various countries took part in the opening ceremony — they are participants in the international Private Pilot Expedition to Georgia 2026. They arrived in Georgia via the Luxembourg–Batumi–Kachreti route.
Prime Minister of Georgia Irakli Kobakhidze, speaking to the guests and foreign pilots, said it marked "the opening of a new page in the history of Georgian aviation."
The project was implemented by the Ambassador Group development company, owned by businessman Elguja Keburia, with state support and co-financing from the "Georgia Economic Development Corporation."
The "aviation address" infrastructure is designed for light and ultralight aircraft. In addition to the airfield, the complex includes an aviation academy, a service hub and residences for pilots.
In the future, the company plans to create a private air-transportation network between Georgia's regions.
The airfield in Kachreti is to become its first element. The next stage is said to be the Ambassadori Island Batumi artificial archipelago project in Batumi, where the construction of a runway is also planned.
According to the company's plans, this will eventually make it possible to organize private flights and air taxis between Kakheti and the Black Sea coast — from the Alazani Valley directly to the resorts of Adjara.
The opening of Aviation Village concluded with the signing of a memorandum of cooperation with the Georgian Aviation University and an air show over Kachreti.
