Swarming the battlefield: Elbit-FUSE reveals mass drone and robot armies as IDF plans new AI branch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:52:32 UTC
22:52:32 KST

The Jerusalem Post and a limited number of other media outlets on Wednesday visited the Elbit-FUSE facility for building mass-scale robot and drone armies.
The visit was timed to coincide with Elbit-FUSE’s unveiling of a range of new and updated products, enabling small numbers of human soldiers to direct dozens or even hundreds of robots and drones to perform defensive and offensive functions in large-scale swarms.
Imagine hundreds of drones combining with dozens of tank-style autonomous vehicles and smaller tactical bat-shaped, dog-shaped, and otherwise specialized robots to defend a border or take over an enemy urban neighborhood.
The drones provide air cover, the autonomous tank-style vehicles provide tactical firepower, and the smaller robots enter structures where the enemy forces are hiding to defeat them up close or neutralize their booby traps without a single soldier setting foot in the neighborhood.
This is the vision Elbit-FUSE presented on Wednesday. The company did not enter this arena in a vacuum. Ukraine announced in July that it had reached a production rate of 10 million small tactical drones per year and was looking to double that volume.
Drones, autonomous weaponry increasingly defining global warfare
China, the United States, and others are all starting to mass-produce drones and robots in astronomically larger quantities than in the past.
In line with these developments, IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir on Tuesday night announced that by Hanukkah (December), the IDF would have opened an entirely new branch to focus on robots, drones, and AI battle forces.
“Military forces are entering a new operational era in which combat effectiveness will increasingly depend not only on autonomous platforms themselves, but also on the ability to integrate and coordinate large numbers of autonomous systems within existing maneuver forces in real time,” Eyal Dahan, CEO of FUSE, said. FUSE is a recently developed Elbit unit focusing on these issues, having combined at least four other related entities into one.
“FUSE was established to deliver that capability today – combining autonomous platforms, operational AI, and scalable One2Many command capabilities into integrated operational solutions that can be rapidly deployed and integrated into modern combat formations,” Dahan explained.
Speaking at a private briefing on Wednesday, he explained that even mass swarms of robots and drones would not completely replace human soldiers.
Other Elbit officials clarified to the Post that, on defense, fewer human soldiers could be needed in general to manage the autonomous vehicle swarms.
In contrast, on attack, the officials explained that a larger number of soldiers could be required, depending on the mission.
As an ethical matter, Elbit officials said that humans would and must remain in the loop to sign off on targeting decisions and reduce collateral harm to civilians.
In that sense, the AI systems installed in Elbit’s myriad types of drones and robots, including extremely advanced sensors for distinguishing combatants from civilians, are still not the final line for approving an attack.
If an attack was in an area where few civilians and sensitive items were known to be in play, fewer human soldiers might need to be involved.
But if an attack was against a highly sensitive location or one where many civilians could be at risk if the strike was not precise, then more soldiers would be involved to analyze the situation, as currently occurs.
At the facility, the Post saw five different versions of the Firefox drone, with each version having different uses, abilities in day vs nighttime, and varying price ranges depending on whether a client-buyer seeks cheaper, less fancy machines or smarter, high-end ones.
Some drones might cost as little as $2,000, while others might be in the hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Large variety of machines in production
The Post also saw FPV drones; drones disguised as items in nature, something which has been previously reported on; machines with shorter and longer range capabilities; and machines with laser-guided capabilities
In another section of the facility, the Post witnessed multiple stages of drone and robot assembly.
Some Elbit-FUSE technicians were assembling single parts, such as cameras or wings; others were meeting to discuss ongoing technical issues; and others were assembling all of the many parts of a drone or a robot.
Many dozens of robots and drones were already assembled on shelves, and many others were secured in special wrapping material for delivery.
There were special rooms for simulating intense wind environments, as well as others for handling special laser-related issues.
These laser-related issues are important but not as complex as those in a different Elbit facility that the Post visited in June, which is at the heart of Elbit’s most complex laser production.
FUSE has 160 employees, with 110 at the main facility which the Post visited, of whom around 65% are engineers, with many others being programmers or having other special skills, all at just one subsidiary of Elbit’s much larger operations.
Dahan emphasized that having many engineers available was critical to constantly updating each product, noting that one drone had been updated four times in the last three years to stay on the cutting edge of developing technologies.
A major focus of the FUSE product launch was its One2Many operational capabilities, which are powered by a unified AI operating system enabling centralized coordination of autonomous swarms and distributed aerial and ground formations at scale.
FUSE said that at the core of the portfolio is Dominion-X, “an AI-powered unified operating system enabling One2Many operations in GNSS-denied environments, supported by advanced automatic target recognition (ATR) and homing capabilities.”
It added that “Dominion-X enables centralized real-time coordination and management of autonomous aerial and ground systems, including real-time mission data exchange between platforms and distributed operations across battlefield environments through a shared mission network.”
Designed for contested and GPS-denied environments, FUSE’s solutions “support resilient mission execution, distributed autonomous operations, and manned-unmanned teaming (MUM-T) alongside maneuvering forces and crewed platforms within existing military formations and command structures.”
FUSE said that it “delivers mature military-grade autonomous systems designed for scalable and resilient multi-domain operations, supported by Elbit Systems’ operational experience and high-volume manufacturing infrastructure.”
According to Dahan, FUSE’s solutions have accumulated more than 1,000,000 operational flight hours and over 100,000 autonomous ground operation hours, with thousands of platforms delivered worldwide.
Generally, FUSE’s products are focused on medium-to-longer range missions as opposed to competitors such as SpearUAV, an Israeli defense tech company based in Tel Aviv, which announced on Monday that it had close to 1,000 Viper 300 loitering munitions (LM) ready to deliver to customers around the world.
While Elbit-FUSE is focused first on Israel as a client, the US and many European countries remain strong customers.
Although there are large American and other foreign competitors in this field, Elbit-FUSE has shown that its products not only perform at a higher level product-to-product but also excel over many others in being able to connect the operations of swarms of products in the air and on the land simultaneously.
Dahan said that FUSE is also working on expanding into drone and robot swarm operations at sea.
It was previously reported that the Israeli navy has been operating autonomous sea vehicles in recent years, though it is unclear when operating swarms at sea will be ready to be rolled out.
Elbit Systems has already been among the Israeli companies developing such technologies, including its already publicized 12-meter Seagull autonomous surface vessel designed to patrol offshore infrastructure for up to four days. The Seagull “incorporates mine countermeasures (MCM), anti-submarine warfare (ASW), maritime security (MS), electronic warfare (EW), and other advanced systems and technologies.”

Israel can protect Sweida’s Druze without supporting Syria’s separation - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:52:29 UTC
22:52:29 KST

Sweida has become one of the most sensitive issues in the new Syria, not only because of violations suffered by Druze and Bedouin civilians, but also because of questions over the province’s future and its relationship with the Syrian state.
This raises an important question for Israel: if protecting Sweida’s Druze population is a genuine objective, is supporting separation or keeping the province outside state institutions really the best way to achieve it?
Or would a more realistic option be to encourage a political settlement inspired by the path taken by the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), whereby the Druze receive political guarantees, rights, and meaningful participation in state institutions without turning Sweida into a separate entity?
In my view, the second option is more realistic and safer.
Sweida is not the SDF, but its experience offers a lesson
The SDF fought Damascus for years, including in Aleppo and Sheikh Maqsoud, while tensions and clashes also occurred in Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, and elsewhere. Yet the conflict did not lead to an independent Kurdish state.
Instead, the SDF moved toward negotiations with Damascus over a formula guaranteeing Kurdish rights and participation within a united Syrian state, followed by arrangements for integration into state institutions.
The lesson is not that Sweida should copy the SDF. It is that conflict with the state does not make separation the only option.
The students’ crisis reveals the core of the problem
The case of Sweida’s students illustrates the crisis clearly.
After the disruption of examinations, the Syrian state took exceptional measures to ensure that students could sit their exams. It prepared examination centers, staff, and materials and made special arrangements for them.
But according to media reports, the so-called “National Guard”, affiliated with Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, prevented students from leaving Sweida to reach examination centers prepared by the Syrian state.
The question is simple: if the state prepared the examinations and provided the centers, who is preventing the students from reaching them?
Students should not become parties to a political conflict. When an armed force can prevent citizens from accessing state services, the issue becomes one of authority: who is responsible for providing basic services and protecting citizens’ rights?
Al-Hijri does not speak for all Druze
Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri has become one of the most prominent political voices in Sweida, but it would be wrong to treat him as the exclusive representative of Syrian Druze.
This matters to Israel because building long-term policy around one individual can lead to strategic miscalculations.
Reports concerning the detention, mistreatment, or killing of opponents and critics of al-Hijri also make independent investigations essential.
Al-Hijri’s past also matters
Israel should assess al-Hijri’s political record, rather than looking only at his current opposition to Damascus.
He has a history of political positions and relationships during the era of Bashar al-Assad, including positions that raised questions about his relationship or interaction with forces associated with various Iranian militias during different stages of the Syrian conflict.
If Israel is looking for a partner capable of producing stability in southern Syria, it should ask whether that person can build institutions capable of protecting the entire community, including those who disagree with him.
Violations do not make separation inevitable
The violations suffered by Druze and Bedouin civilians are unjustifiable and condemnable. Anyone who committed crimes against civilians should be held accountable, regardless of affiliation.
But justice does not require dividing Syria.
A state capable of investigating, prosecuting, and holding perpetrators accountable may provide stronger protection than local armed authorities operating outside a clear national judicial system.
Sweida therefore does not have to choose between submission to Damascus and separation from Syria. There is a third option: a genuine partnership within a united Syrian state.
Why should Israel think twice?
It is natural for Israel to view Sweida through a security lens and to care about protecting the Druze.
But this does not mean that supporting a separatist project is the best policy.
Israel can encourage a settlement between Sweida and Damascus that guarantees Druze rights rather than a permanent rupture.
If the Syrian state is responsible for security, services and the judiciary, while the people of Sweida participate in its institutions, clear arrangements can be established and monitored.
Keeping the province as a separate armed sphere of influence, by contrast, means continued uncertainty.
What if a Druze entity becomes a problem for Israel?
Even if establishing an independent Druze entity/state in southern Syria were possible, Israel should consider its long-term consequences.
Creating a political entity based on Druze identity would establish a new precedent in the region.
This raises a hypothetical question: what if the emergence of an independent Druze entity creates new identity dynamics among some of Israel’s Druze citizens?
This does not mean that Israel’s Druze citizens would seek separation or join such an entity. There is no basis for asserting that.
But an independent Druze entity across the border could, over time, open new debates about identity, belonging and relations between Druze communities across borders.
A state without recognition is not a guarantee of stability
There is also a practical question: who would recognize, finance, and protect an independent entity in Sweida?
A small entity without broad international recognition, surrounded by a complex regional environment and dependent on external support, could become a permanent zone of influence rather than a stable state.
Israel could ultimately face a new responsibility rather than more secure borders.
Damascus should put forward a political initiative
The Syrian government should build on the steps it has already taken (for example, students’ examinations) and make the people of Sweida see tangible benefits in remaining within the state.
What is needed now is a broader political initiative that includes holding accountable everyone who committed violations against civilians, ensuring a fair and transparent judiciary.
Sweida’s population needs to be included in state institutions and integrated into the state’s armed groups through clear and gradual arrangements, while ensuring the continuation of government services, particularly education and healthcare.
No settlement can succeed if an armed force remains capable of preventing state institutions from reaching citizens.
The SDF model offers Israel a third option
Israel does not have to choose between abandoning the Druze and supporting their separation from Syria.
It can encourage a third formula: Druze who are secure within Syria enjoy political representation and clear rights, while the Syrian state remains responsible for sovereignty and institutions.
Sweida can be part of the solution
The Druze do not need a new state to obtain their rights. Syria does not need to eliminate Sweida’s distinctiveness to preserve its unity. And Israel does not need an independent Druze entity to ensure the security of the south.
There is political space between these options: a united Syrian state, genuine Druze participation, justice for victims, and weapons organized under state institutions.
Protecting the Druze does not require dividing Syria, and preserving Syria’s unity must not mean ignoring Druze rights. If Israel genuinely wants to protect the Druze and contribute to the stability of its southern frontier, it should encourage this path rather than bet on continued division.
Stability in Sweida will not come from creating new borders, but from building a new relationship between Sweida and the Damascus government.
The writer is the Editor-in-Chief of Syria Focus.

Trump’s Iran war has left him without a clear path to victory - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:52:16 UTC
22:52:16 KST

US President Donald Trump keeps telling us he started the war with Iran so that the Islamic Republic “cannot have a nuclear weapon.” His energy secretary just gave the world reason to doubt his boss. Trump is unlikely to get what he called “the kind of deal that I feel is necessary.”
Energy Secretary Chris Wright told ABC News Sunday, “There may not be a nuclear agreement,” and the US will focus instead on “degrading their capacity to develop nuclear weapons.”
Sensing his humiliation, a dismissive Trump took to social media to say he “could not care less” if Iran makes a deal. He bounces back and forth between threatening to walk away and destroying the entire Iranian civilization.
Dealmaker Trump dramatically tore up the 2015 Iran nuclear pact (JCPOA) negotiated by the Obama administration, and said he could do better. He never really tried. There were limited but unproductive talks in his second term, with enough bombastic rhetoric going back and forth to destroy anyone’s hope.
Many believe the major flaw in the JCPOA from Trump’s standpoint was less its substance than the name most associated with it: Barack Obama. There is scant expectation that Trump could even get that deal today.
On March 25, 2025, Tulsi Gabbard, the director of national intelligence, told the Senate Intelligence Committee that America’s intelligence leaders “assess that Iran is not building a nuclear weapon, and Supreme Leader [Ayatollah Ali] Khamenei has not authorized the nuclear weapons program that he suspended in 2003.”
In Senate testimony a year later, she refused to say whether Iran posed any “imminent nuclear threat.” That’s not what Trump wanted to hear. “I don’t care what she said,” Trump told reporters. In his view, Iran was “very close” to having a nuclear bomb, PBS reported.
In private, Gabbard had advised against going to war and many of her arguments turned out to be spot on, according to leaked reports. Speaking truth to power apparently cost the intelligence chief her job; after weeks of rumors that Trump was planning to push her out, Gabbard resigned in May, citing her husband’s health.
Trump declared in June 2025 that US B-2s (stealth bombers) had “obliterated” Iran’s nuclear program. Apparently he oversold his achievement. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu convinced him that the job was unfinished, and they went back on February 28 this year.
Iran has taken a hell of a beating in a war Trump refuses to call a war but can’t find an exit. Iran’s navy, air force, and even much of its air defense system have been decimated, but the regime persists, as does much of its drone and proxy terror network.
The old leadership was killed on the first day, only to be replaced by even more hard-line rulers. The popular uprising Trump called for never materialized.
Iran causes global economic shock
Iran retaliated with its oil weapon, closing the Strait of Hormuz and shocking the global economy. Trump and his party are reeling.
The president has been promising that the resulting huge jump in gas and grocery prices will soon disappear, but no serious economist agrees. That terrifies Republican candidates in this fall’s midterm elections as they are being hammered by Democrats talking about “affordability.” Trump dismissed the talk of the high cost of living as just a “hoax” and a “con job” just before he flies off in Qatar Force One for a tournament at his Irish golf course.
Secretary Wright, who is also presiding over Trump’s takeover of major Venezuelan oil fields, told ABC News Sunday, “We are degrading [Iran’s] capacity to develop nuclear weapons and ultimately to deliver them, if they develop them.”
That’s a big and dangerous “if.” For decades prior to this war, Iranian leaders publicly swore off going for the bomb. US and Israeli intelligence largely agree, as Gabbard told the president and the Senate, Iran was enriching uranium to near-weapon levels but that it had not yet made the breakthrough decision. Now, the new leadership is said to be reconsidering that policy, pointing to North Korea, Pakistan, India and Israel, which went nuclear as deterrence insurance against hostile neighbors.
If you're picking winners and losers, Iran is a big loser just because of the military, economic and human damage that has been inflicted on it. But Trump cannot declare victory – despite doing so dozens of times – until Hormuz is open to the free and unfettered flow of shipping by all and there is an enforceable nuclear deal.
Trump may not be able to get either. His energy secretary said a deal “may await a next administration in Iran.” Thanks to the US and Israel, Iran got a new administration six months ago, and you know how that went.
Trump started an unnecessary war of choice without a clear operational plan or an endgame, without the support of Congress, the American people, or America’s allies.
Bombs are not the only things falling. The president’s approval rating has dropped to historic lows. Nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose his war and disapprove of the president’s handling of it. Four in five tell pollsters they blame the high and increasing cost of living on this war.
The president will try to stem the defection of disapproving Republicans when he speaks at this week’s mid-term convention in Dallas, but many Republican candidates won’t be there. They know their constituents are unhappy with how this war is hurting their pocketbooks, and candidates worry that on Election Day those folks may be staying home or pulling the wrong lever. The last thing they need is to be seen on television cheering Trump’s unpopular war.
The writer is a Washington-based journalist, consultant, lobbyist, and former legislative director at the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.

EU plan aims to help cities crack down on Airbnb, holiday rentals

EU plan aims to help cities crack down on Airbnb, holiday rentals
The European Commission’s Affordable Housing Act lays out conditions under which local authorities can limit short lets
European cities will gain more leeway to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb under new EU plans that aim to bring down housing costs in tourism hotspots.
The European Commission laid out conditions on Wednesday under which local authorities can limit short lets, under a proposal seeking to address Europe’s “housing crisis”.
“Short-term rentals are a part of the problem in many cities,” Dan Jorgensen, the 27-nation bloc’s housing commissioner, told a press conference in Brussels.
Though hugely popular with visitors, short-term lodgings are blamed by residents in many popular travel destinations for depriving locals of flats for long-term rental and pushing up prices – something holiday-let providers dispute.
Cities from New York to Tokyo and Barcelona have imposed or considered restrictions on tourist flats in recent years. But curbs have often been met with court challenges, resulting in legal uncertainty.
The commission’s Affordable Housing Act – which still has to be negotiated with lawmakers and EU countries – aims to provide cities with legal cover, clarifying when authorities can take action without falling foul of the bloc’s single market rules.

France’s record heatwave pushes champagne alcohol levels to historic high

France’s record heatwave pushes champagne alcohol levels to historic high
France’s record-breaking summer heat has forced champagne producers to contend with unusually high sugar levels in grapes, forcing authorities to allow alcohol content of up to 15 percent in the region’s sparkling wine for the first time. Champagne is usually capped at 13 percent.
Drinking this year's champagne might give you a heftier headache as France's record heatwaves are forcing some producers to up the alcohol levels, industry officials said Wednesday.
French authorities have allowed champagne houses to make their bubbly with alcohol content of up to 15 percent, a historic first for a wine usually limited to 13 percent.
Read moreFrench wine yields drop to new historic low after searing summer heat
Growers had to harvest exceptionally early this year as extreme heat sped sugar buildup – and hence natural alcohol production – in the grapes, according to the Comite Champagne industry association.
Nonetheless, "the crop already has all the hallmarks of producing great, perhaps even exceptional, wines", the group said in a statement.
Authorities have also allowed a temporary easing of strict rules for making several types of cheese after heatwaves scorched grazing pastures.
France is the world's second-largest wine producer after Italy, and this summer's heat and drought have deepened fears for many growers about how they will cope with climate change.
The 2026 harvest was the earliest ever recorded in the Champagne region, with the first grapes cut as early as August 6 and the harvest becoming widespread on August 17, two weeks earlier than in 2025, when it was already considered to be early, according to the association.
Read moreClimate crisis pushes French winemakers to bet on warmer future in Brittany and Normandy
Due to climate change, "this unusual harvest will probably become the norm in 10 to 15 years", said Maxime Toubart, the co-chairman of the Comite Champagne.
It "should prompt reflection on the champagne of tomorrow", he said.
Fellow co-chair David Chatillon said the relaxed alcohol content would concern just a small number of growers.
"The average after the harvest is below 12 percent," Chatillon said. "Not all winegrowers in Champagne will be above that level."
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

European Heritage Days 2026: protecting Europe’s heritage at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:48:48 UTC
22:48:48 KST

European Heritage Days 2026: protecting Europe’s heritage at risk
The 2026 European Heritage Days highlight how communities and EU-supported initiatives are protecting and adapting cultural heritage in response to climate change, societal shifts and other forms of threats, including conflict.
The EU strives to preserve cultural heritage under all circumstances, as reflected in the EU preparedness union strategy. Across Europe, communities are finding diverse ways to respond to these pressures with the support of the European Union.
Revive, resist, reimagine
Throughout September and October, the European Heritage Days 2026 invites people across Europe, under the theme “heritage at risk: revive, resist, reimagine” to discover how communities are protecting, restoring and reimagining their heritage for the future.
Protecting heritage from a changing climate
As climate change increases pressure on cultural sites and landscapes through extreme weather, flooding, fires and other natural hazards, protecting heritage also means finding ways to adapt. These challenges highlight how closely Europe’s natural and cultural heritage are connected.
Natura 2000, the EU’s network of protected areas, reflects this connection. In France’s Camargue, for example, protected wetlands and exceptional biodiversity – including one of Europe’s top breeding sites for greater flamingos – coexist with centuries-old traditions such as rice cultivation and salt production, both recognised through EU geographical indications.
EU-funded research is helping these landscapes adapt. The RescueME project, funded under Horizon Europe, works with communities in five European coastal areas – including Crete, Cinque Terre and Zadar – to develop solutions that strengthen the resilience of their cultural landscape in the face of climate change.
Giving old places a new purpose
Heritage can also become vulnerable when societal and economic changes leave historic buildings without their original function. Vacancy and neglect can gradually put their heritage value at risk. Adaptive reuse can help reverse this process, preserving the character of historic buildings while giving them new functions and keeping them part of community life.
In Rathfarnham, Ireland, the historic Castle Stables and Courtyards are being transformed into spaces for cultural, community and hospitality activities. Co-funded by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the THRIVE project shows how giving heritage a new purpose can contribute to its long-term preservation while creating new value for the local community.
Safeguarding heritage in times of conflict
Armed conflict and other types of threats can cause irreversible damage to heritage. Safeguarding it during and after armed conflicts requires both immediate protection and long-term commitment to restoration and recovery.
Europe’s recent history offers powerful examples. In Dubrovnik, Croatia, the Society of Friends of Dubrovnik Antiquities has worked for decades to safeguard the historic city, including during and after the conflicts of the 1990s. Its contribution was recognised with a 2024 European Heritage Award / Europa Nostra Award, supported by Creative Europe.
The Team Europe for Cultural Heritage in Ukraine supports 89 initiatives from EU countries and the European Commission to safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage from the impacts of Russia’s war of aggression – from emergency protection and recording damage to cultural sites and digitally preserving endangered heritage, to training heritage professionals and supporting restoration.

When war takes away the classroom, can children ever catch up?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:48:35 UTC
22:48:35 KST

Attacks on education have surged worldwide. Education Above All Foundation's Dr Maleiha Malik says keeping children learning is possible, but conflict-caused damage cannot be undone easily.
For millions of children living through conflict, war can mean months or even years away from the classroom.
From Ukraine to Sudan and Gaza, schools have been damaged or closed and education systems disrupted.
As the world marks the International Day to Protect Education from Attack on 9 September, the latest Education Under Attack report says at least 8,566 attacks on education and incidents involving the military use of schools and universities were recorded in 2024 and 2025.
That represents an increase of more than 40% compared with the previous reporting period, with at least 10,600 students, teachers, professors and other education personnel harmed.
For Education Above All Foundation Executive Director Dr Maleiha Malik, the numbers point to consequences that can follow children long after the fighting stops.
“The impact of that is devastating,” Dr Malik told Euronews.
Dr Malik said the damage goes beyond school buildings, affecting entire education systems and potentially feeding “long-term poverty and cycles of violence”.
‘We can't compensate for the damage’
One of the biggest questions is what happens to children who have already missed months or years of education.
Dr Malik says accelerated learning programmes and technology can help close some of those gaps, but there are limits to what can be recovered.
“We can have some accelerated learning, they can catch up, but I don't want to give the impression that there is any way we can compensate for the damage that conflict causes. We can't.”
According to her, the COVID-19 pandemic showed both the cost of disrupted education and how learning can continue when children cannot physically be in a classroom.
“During COVID we were able to look at new technologies, ways of delivering learning outside the traditional paradigm of a school building,” Dr Malik said.
But catching up academically is only part of the challenge.
“Even before we think about knowledge gaps, learning gaps, we have to think about that child as a whole,” she said, stressing the need to address trauma and the emotional impact of conflict.
‘An alarming red line’
Malik also pointed to the sharp rise in attacks on education.
“A 40% increase isn't just a small increase, it's a surge,” she said.
Citing a recent UN report on children and armed conflict, Malik pointed to the role of government forces in attacks on schools as one of the most concerning developments.
“I think the really alarming red line we've crossed this year is that government forces have crossed the line and are willing to use extreme state violence to attack schools, to attack education.”
“We haven't seen it to this level,” Dr Malik added, highlighting what she described as a greater willingness by states to risk attacking civilian targets and infrastructure.
Conflict closer to home
Dr Malik said the impact of regional conflict is also being felt by children in Qatar and other Gulf countries.
She said children have had to become familiar with rocket fire and interceptions, sudden school closures, airports shutting down, and flights being grounded.
“Clearly, that is a kind of constant interference, constant stress, anxiety for children,” she said, adding that it can have psychosocial and emotional effects on children, parents and teachers.
For parents trying to explain what is happening, Dr Malik recommended being honest without unnecessarily alarming children and using age-appropriate language.
International law is meant to protect schools and civilians during war. But as attacks on education rise, Dr Malik said the international system is falling short.
“You can't help but reach that conclusion,” she said. “I think there's a huge failure in terms of the international community.”
She argued that the answer is not to abandon international institutions, but to strengthen them.
“I'm more determined than ever and would call for a strengthening of our commitment to multilateralism as a way of bringing about peace rather than war," Dr Malik concluded.

Will it kill off humanity? Computer scientists and politicians wrestle with risks of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:46:44 UTC
22:46:44 KST

Does artificial superintelligence really pose a risk greater than nuclear weapons? Is there a significant chance of “a Chornobyl-sized catastrophe”. Might there even be a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” in the next decade?
These warnings were issued over the past 48 hours on both sides of the Atlantic about the potential impact of a technology that most people still think of as a more talkative search engine.
Some of the threats were raised in the UK as MPs and peers began to wrestle with the danger of AI outperforming human capabilities. The nuclear warnings came from Des Browne, a former defence secretary, and Prof Stuart Russell, an eminent Berkeley computer scientist.
Beatrice Fihn, who won the 2017 Nobel peace prize for leading the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, told parliamentarians: “It is not the first time we’re confronted with abilities that could end up killing us all.”
The session on Monday was convened by Control AI, a lobbying group pushing for international regulation of the technology. It is backing a bill tabled in parliament this week by the Labour MP Alex Sobel and aimed at banning the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI).
On Tuesday night, a senior employee at Anthropic admitted he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade and warned that his AI company did not have a plan to ensure ASI was aligned, meaning it did no harm. Predictions for when ASI might be reached vary from several years to more than a decade.
Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, posted the comment after Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at the San Francisco company and previously at OpenAI, resigned, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”. He said they were “gambling with our lives”.
Coxon said the risks at Anthropic were well understood but they were “locked in a race to get there first”. In a glimmer of hope, he added that he was optimistic about the potential for coordination between US labs on pacing their progress in the race.
Anthropic has been approached for comment on the issue. OpenAI pointed to a statement from its chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, who said last week: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.”
The push for wider coordination to control ASI was at the heart of events at Westminster this week. According to the Financial Times, government officials voiced concern that Anthropic had declined to submit its latest model – Mythos 5.1 – to the UK’s AI Security Institute for pre-release testing.
Only a few US organisations have had access to Mythos 5.1, the Cabinet Office confirmed. A spokesperson added: “The AI Security Institute continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic.”
The Labour MP Darren Jones has written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the heads of the UN and the OECD calling for a “multinational treaty for the regulated and safe development of superintelligence – not a ban on innovation or scientific endeavour but a safety-first approach to the rapid development of this technology”.
Citing Coxon’s resignation, Jones added: “The debate ranges from the end of humanity to claims of ‘marketing hype’. Either way, governments must now step in.”
On the other side of the Atlantic, Bernie Sanders ratcheted up his AI safety campaign this week by again calling on Congress to regulate the technology. He pointed to polling suggesting that 81% of Americans believed their politicians should take action.
The independent senator for Vermont said: “We can’t allow a handful of greedy people to play God and determine the future of humanity – our economy, environment, democracy, privacy and more – without public input.”
ControlAI is funded by Jaan Tallinn, the multi-billionaire founder of Skype who calls himself an “anti-extinctionist”. He has dedicated part of his fortune to campaigning for AI safety and says some senior AI executives would be happy for humanity to be wiped out.
Despite being an early investor in Anthropic and Google DeepMind, two of the leading AI labs, Tallinn estimates that 10-15% of AI employees believe the technology will be a worthy successor to humanity.
He said in an interview earlier this summer: “A fairly known AI researcher said to me ‘Jaan, don’t worry about this. Humans are a disposable species’. From what I understand he was fine with becoming extinct.”
Tallinn’s lobby group ran the session for MPs and peers at Westminster on Monday and urged them to back measures to curb the most powerful AI models. On every chair was a copy of the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: The Case Against Superintelligent AI.
The politicians heard from Russell, who made the Chornobyl warning and said: “The other possibility is a much larger catastrophe, in which humanity loses control irreversibly. But we have no say over whether we continue to exist.”
Browne said that when he was defence secretary he thought nuclear war was the most likely threat facing humanity. Now he believed “a superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale”.
Other contributors were more cautious. Dr Andrew Rogoyski, of the Surrey Institute for People-Centred AI, said: “In reality, these systems are nowhere near as versatile as humans, let alone humans acting collectively. I suspect we’re heading towards ‘the great disappointment’ where advanced AI turns out to be too expensive and not useful enough to continue in its current form.”
David Barber, director of Sofair, a state-backed AI research lab combining academics from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and UCL, said he was worried about people “throwing the baby out with the bathwater”.
“AI is not going to go away,” he said. “It’s incredibly useful, whether or not you allow it in a fully unconstrained way to access the internet and various systems that’s potentially problematic. We may need to learn how to better control these things. There are vulnerabilities in the software frameworks that need to be patched. But that’s doable.
“What we need as a country is to get to grips with the duality that is both an incredibly important and useful technology, and at the same time, it’s something that needs to be carefully thought about and carefully controlled.”
Sandra Wachter, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute, said she did not believe in “Terminator scenarios” but that AI posed real threats including its environmental impact, spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs.
“These problems are real and urgent and need addressing now,” she said. “Terminator scenarios are a big distraction from real issues.”
Gary Marcus, an AI industry commentator and academic, said: “There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not.
“It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive. So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lack of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten us where we are, with intense mistrust all around.”

Russia Begins Denying Foreign Passports to Men as Mobilization Fears Grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:44:14 UTC
22:44:14 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Begins Denying Foreign Passports to Men as Mobilization Fears Grow
Russian men subject to military registration have begun reporting refusals and delays in obtaining international passports, with some applicants told that restrictions imposed by military enlistment offices prevent them from leaving the country.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Moscow Times on September 9, one such case involved a 25-year-old Russian man named Konstantin, who applied for an international passport through Russia’s Gosuslugi state services portal.
Two weeks later, he received a notification saying that his application had been rejected because a military enlistment office had temporarily restricted his right to leave Russia.
Konstantin told the Russian conscription-rights organization School of the Conscript that he had last visited a military enlistment office while in the 10th grade and had received no subsequent notifications.
Other Russian men have reported similar problems. A Moscow resident told the outlet Mozhem Obyasnit that his passport application had been rejected because of his military-liable status. He said two acquaintances who were also subject to military registration had encountered the same issue.
Another applicant said his passport application, submitted in June, was later marked as suspended, forcing him to apply again and search for an available appointment at a government services center in another city. Russian travel-related online communities have also reported delays lasting more than a month.
Mikhail Liberov, a lawyer with School of the Conscript, said that a refusal to issue a passport is unlawful if a person has not been formally called up for military service and no conscription commission has issued a decision concerning them.
“An exit ban imposed for failing to appear in response to a military summons does not, by itself, provide grounds for refusing to issue a foreign passport. This should be appealed. The military enlistment office may explain it as a technical error, as such cases have occurred before,” Liberov said, according to The Moscow Times.
The reports come amid renewed speculation over whether Russia could expand military recruitment following the September State Duma elections.
The Economist previously reported, citing Kremlin-linked sources, that Russian authorities could seek another 300,000 to 400,000 people for the war against Ukraine without formally announcing a new mobilization campaign. Russia’s 2022 mobilization decree, under which approximately 300,000 people were called up, remains in force.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has rejected reports that another mobilization could be required, calling them “nonsense” and an “information attack.” “There is currently no scenario that would require mobilization. This is simply a deliberate information operation,” Putin said.
A day earlier, a 24-year-old Russian reservist was prevented from leaving the country after a military enlistment office imposed a temporary travel restriction through Russia’s electronic military registry. The man only learned about the ban during passport control in Krasnodar.

Military police have found multiple weapons hidden near a primary school in Overassel following last week’s gun attack on a property in the Gelderland village, which resulted in the murder of one man and serious injury on two police officers.
Investigations have been ongoing since the attack, with 35 people arrested – all but two of whom are being held for murder or manslaughter – and extensive searches in the surrounding areas. It is suspected the attack was part of a feud over cocaine dealing linked with a resident of the village, who has been targetted before.
Police would not say how many weapons were found near the school or other details. In the day after the attack, dozens of men – who were seen heavily armed on CCTV footage – were caught hiding in the countryside, on the motorways and near rail stations as they fled the scene.
After the events unfolded, a video surfaced on social media of masked men holding automatic weapons and reading out a threat message to Jan G. Jr., the Overassel resident linked to the attack. They said he owed a “Belgian friend” 1,283 kilograms of “goods” and had to return it within 12 hours or they would kill his family.
They spoke in a heavy Spanish accent and said the goods had never left Spain as they were supposed to.
On Tuesday, Spanish police intercepted a shipment of exactly 1,283 kilograms of cocaine in a transport truck carrying coconuts. It is not yet clear whether the two cases are connected.
The shock of the attack on Overassel pushed justice minister David van Weel to warn that “unprecedented” violence is occurring due to international drugs smuggling, though he dismissed the idea of the Netherlands becoming a so-called “narco state”.
Reports of gunshots in nearby Nijmegen on Monday night drew in heavily armed police, who closed off several streets before determining no shots were fired. A relative of Jan G. Jr, who lives in the city, was moved for his own protection.

Special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the Russian and Ukrainian capitals on Saturday and Sunday, respectively, for talks with the leaderships of both countries.  
Ties with Hungary
Peskov also spoke about recent developments in Russian-Hungarian ties, saying Budapest's expulsion of Russian diplomats will negatively impact bilateral relations.

Russia Is Helping Supercharge North Korea’s Military Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:39:00 UTC
22:39:00 KST

Russia’s expanding military partnership with North Korea has become one of the most significant proliferation risks of the Ukraine war. Since Pyongyang began actively supporting Russia’s campaign, Moscow is believed to have transferred sensitive technologies such as naval reactors for nuclear‑powered submarines, air defense systems, and other advanced capabilities in exchange for North Korean weapons and troops. Russia has already provided drone technology to Pyongyang, and the rapid evolution of Russian battlefield innovations now raises concerns that North Korea could, in time, gain access to far more sophisticated systems, including new versions of autonomous AI–enabled and jet–powered drones.
In a war that began as an artillery‑heavy conflict, drone usage and tactics have evolved rapidly. One of the most consequential developments is Russia’s experimentation with autonomously controlled AI‑enabled drones. Earlier iterations required a human operator to confirm targets, with AI used primarily to counter radio‑jamming and ensure the drone reached its destination. In recent months, however, Russia has begun allowing onboard AI systems to make independent strike decisions. This shift toward autonomous targeting represents a significant technological leap and raises concerns that North Korea, already receiving Russian drone technology, could eventually gain access to these more advanced capabilities.
As with much of the evolution of technology in the Ukraine war, Russia’s has equipped its autonomous AI drones with off-the-shelf technology, specifically commercial grade Nvidia Jetson Orin computers designed to create AI-enabled devices. Using such tools, Russia is training the drone AI to identify specific targets such as gas stations.
Russia has also begun modifying drones with jet powered engines. Jet powered drones are more expensive than the propellor powered models that have been heavily utilized during the war, but they are also more difficult to shoot down. The Geran-5, a Russian version of the Shahed drone, also has a China connection: Its 200 kilogram-thrust turbojet engines are believed to have Chinese origins.
North Korean Drone Cooperation With Russia
Since becoming active in the war against Ukraine, North Korea has transferred over 15 million artillery shells and provided Russia with an estimated 15,000 troops. Reports suggest that Moscow agreed to provide drone technology to Pyongyang in exchange for the troop deployment, but North Korea’s decision to provide Russia with cluster bombs for its suicide drones was likely also a factor.
The partnership that has developed between Russia and North Korea has allowed Pyongyang to rapidly advance its drone development program. Prior to the Ukraine war, North Korea only possessed outdated reconnaissance drone technology despite development efforts dating back at least to the early 2010s, including initial efforts to develop a strike drone based on U.S. technology. The war in Ukraine, however, has allowed Pyongyang to not only undertake rapid technological advances in its drone technology but to also gain battlefield experience in utilizing them.
When Russian President Vladimir Putin met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in September 2023, Russia provided North Korea with four suicide drones and one reconnaissance drone. More significantly, Russia is believed to have transferred the technology behind Iran’s Shahed-136 drone, the template for Russian drone advances, to North Korea, as well as equipment to enable production.
North Korea has also unveiled its Geumseong series tactical attack drones, which closely resemble Russia’s Lancet‑3 loitering munition and Israel’s HERO‑30, a similarity that strongly suggests additional technology transfers from Moscow. Pyongyang claims the Geumseong series is already AI–enabled, a capability it has not previously demonstrated. Given North Korea’s limited domestic experience with autonomous guidance systems and Russia’s active development of AI‑driven loitering munitions, this initial integration of AI was almost certainly achieved with Russian assistance.
Pyongyang has additionally benefited from its partnership with Russia beyond the transfer of technology. Unconfirmed reports suggest that North Korean laborers were being recruited through the Jihyang Technology Trading Company to support production of Shahed/Geran drones at Russia’s Yelabuga drone production facility in Tartistan. The North Korean workers were expected to assist in production and handle secondary and itinerary assembly, practical skills that would over time enhance North Korea’s own ability to produce drones.
North Korean troops have also gained practical tactical experience in drone warfare on the battlefield. North Korean tactics quickly evolved during their deployment to Russia to the realities of drone warfare. This includes the deployment of troops in smaller groups to evade enemy drones and adoption of tactics in long-range strike missions.
Pyongyang’s participation in the war is also giving it access to real world data on the success of North Korean drones and ballistic missiles against Western defensive systems, and access to Russian operational tactics for electronic warfare. Taken together the knowledge gained from North Korea’s combat experience will enhance its ability to utilize drones and evade defensive systems.
Will North Korea Produce AI-Enabled or Jet-Powered Drones?
In 2025, the General Staff Department ordered the North Korean military to integrate AI into both manned and unmanned systems, including drones. With AI integration part of North Korea’s weapons development policy, advances in the field from Russia are likely to be adopted in time.
The Jetson Orin computers in Russian drones are commercial grade parts and had circuit boards printed with “Made in China.” Russia is likely procuring them from illicit Chinese supply chains; North Korea will be able to as well. The kits are also relatively cheap. Some versions cost less than $300.
Given the battlefield experience that North Korea has gained in Russia using drones and the technology cooperation between the two, including initial usage of AI, it would seem only a matter of time before Pyongyang integrated autonomous AI strike drones into its arsenal. This will enhance its ability to hit targets in the South, including civilian infrastructure, and overwhelm traditional missile defense systems over time.
Jet powered drones would require North Korea to make modifications to its production lines that go beyond those needed for AI adoption or other iterative advances drone technology from the war. While Pyongyang could likely acquire the engines from China or develop its own version, doing so would raise the cost of its drones but not to an extent that it would be prohibitive using off-the-shelf technology.
Strategic Challenges for the United States and South Korea
As Russia continues to push the boundaries of drone technology, we should expect those innovations to make their way to North Korea with implications for security on the Korean Peninsula. Notably, South Korea’s own drone technology, especially drone interceptors, is still in an early stage of development.
In the current conflict, the use of drones in combination with traditional ballistic missiles has overwhelmed missile defense systems with sustained attacks. Drones are both cheaper and more easily produced than ballistic missile interceptors. They also have rendered tanks useless and hindered the advance of ground troops. Because these systems are highly mobile and easy to hide, they are difficult for even militaries with air superiority to eliminate, as the Iran-U.S. war has demonstrated.
Autonomous targeting drones and jet-powered drones will provide North Korea with increasingly capable asymmetric tools to counter the United States and South Korea during a conflict. While they will not provide North Korea with a decisive advantage, they will complicate allied operations and increase the cost to civilian infrastructure and military systems that will be required to win a conflict.
This shift to cheaper, more mobile, and increasingly autonomous systems is a trend that will reshape conflict for the foreseeable future and one that the United States and South Korea must adapt to more quickly.

On September 8, the U.S. Treasury Department announced new sanctions aimed at grounding Iranian airlines, as part of the Trump administration’s “Operation Economic Outcast.” The sanctions hit 36 entities, including cargo service providers and general sales agents based in Turkiye, Kazakhstan, and Malaysia.
The Trump administration’s war against Iran has stretched into its seventh month. Although the U.S. government claims to be in control of the vital Strait of Hormuz, traffic remains low. Reuters reported that six commodity vessels passed through the strait on September 8, “down from nine a day earlier and below the 10-day average of about 12.” In 2025, before the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, more than 100 commodity vessels passed through the strait each day on average.
In late August the Treasury Department announced an “economic D-Day.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent explained: “In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third countries. Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran’s financial connections around the globe. Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”
The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 8 designated 27 Iranian commercial airlines “for operating in the aviation sector of the Iranian economy.”
In addition, OFAC took aim at a number of companies tied to Mahan Air, a privately owned Iranian airline. It was first sanctioned back in 2011 for providing “financial, material, and technological support to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force (IRGC-QF).” The Treasury Department at the time alleged that Mahan Air secretly ferried IRGC operatives, weapons, and funds.
In 2020, OFAC designated two UAE-based companies, Parthia Cargo and Delta Parts Supply FZC, “for their material support of Iranian airline Mahan Air.” At the time, the Treasury Department outlined how the sanctioned companies helped Mahan Air “sustain its fleet of Western-manufactured aircraft.” The Treasury Department alleged that Mahan Air transported “terrorists and lethal cargo to Syria” and also “ Iranian technicians and technical equipment to Venezuela…”
In its latest round of sanctions, the Treasury Department designated several UAE-based companies it claims were involved in the transfer of three B-777 aircraft to Mahan Air.
The sanctions also designated a pair of Turkiye-based companies – S Sistem Lojistik Hizmetler Anonim Sirketi and Mes Cargo Transportation Tourism and Foreign Trade Limited Company – for coordinating shipments and serving as a general sales agent for Mahan Air. Similarly, Malaysia-based Icargo SDN BHD and Kazakhstan-based Tour Invest LLC were designated for acting as general sales agents for Mahan Air.

Kuwait to terminate contracts of 7,000 foreign teachers

Breadcrumb
Kuwait to terminate contracts of 7,000 foreign teachers amid staffing overhaul
Kuwait is set to terminate the contracts of more than 7,000 foreign teachers as part of a drive to address staffing surpluses across the country's education system.
The Ministry of Education has begun the first phase of the plan, covering around 7,019 male and female teachers from Arab and other nationalities, according to local media reports.
Termination notices have begun being sent through Kuwait's government Sahel app under the heading "Contract Termination Notice".
The move follows a study that identified a surplus of around 33,268 teachers across a number of subjects where staffing levels exceed schools' requirements.
The first phase will affect 1,551 male teachers and 5,468 female teachers, with physical education and Islamic education among the subjects facing staffing surpluses.
Kuwaiti authorities expect the measures to save around 42 million Kuwaiti dinars ($137 million) annually in salaries, while maintaining employees' rights in accordance with existing regulations.
The country's education workforce comprises around 91,761 teachers, of whom 70.6% are Kuwaiti nationals.
Gulf nationals and stateless residents account for around 10.1%, while teachers from other Arab and foreign nationalities make up around 19.3%.
Kuwait has a population of around 5.31 million, with expatriates accounting for roughly 70% and Kuwaiti citizens around 30%.
Are 7,000 Egyptian teachers being dismissed?
The announcement comes amid reports in Egyptian and Saudi media claiming that Kuwait had terminated the contracts of 7,000 Egyptian teachers.
However, the official figures cited in the report do not support that claim.
The 7,019 figure covers teachers of various Arab and other nationalities, and there are no recent official figures specifying how many Egyptians are included in the first round of terminations.
Egyptians have traditionally made up a significant proportion of Kuwait's expatriate Arab teaching workforce.
Figures from 2025 put the number of Egyptian teachers working in private schools at around 6,527, while older reports estimated that more than 20,000 Egyptians worked across Kuwait's public and private education sectors at certain points.
Egyptian teachers have also been disproportionately affected by previous localisation drives, accounting for more than 82% of teachers affected by one such decision in 2023, according to the report.
The move comes against a much broader push over the past two years to reshape who has access to Kuwaiti citizenship, public-sector jobs and state benefits.
Kuwait has stripped tens of thousands of people of citizenship, while nationality laws have been repeatedly amended. In 2025 alone, nearly 50,000 people reportedly had their Kuwaiti nationality removed.

China reiterates its One China principle on Taiwan over UN resolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:37:51 UTC
22:37:51 KST

Beijing reaffirmed its One-China principle following a renewed dispute over the interpretation of a UN resolution that defined lawful representation of China at the world's foremost intergovernmental body.
Beijing reiterated on Tuesday that “Taiwan has never been a country and will never be a country,” in a fresh exchange in the ongoing dispute over a United Nations General Assembly resolution.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning accused what Beijing refers to as Lai Ching-te authorities of distorting Resolution 2758 and showcasing again what she called “their separatist nature for Taiwan independence." Mao insisted that the UN resolution reaffirms the One-China principle.
Previously, Lai said that China was contorting UNGA Resolution 2758 and that Taiwan is a "sovereign independent nation".
“Lai Ching-te authorities' rhetoric will not change the historical and legal fact that the two sides of the Taiwan Strait belong to one and the same China, nor will it undermine the international community's steadfast commitment to one China,” the spokesperson said.
Mao said that in Beijing’s view, the resolution “resolved once and for all the question of the whole of China including Taiwan at the United Nations" as, she stated, there is no such thing as "two Chinas" or "one China, one Taiwan".
Beijing also accused the Taiwan Democratic Progressive Party of what it called their “new two-state theory”, with Chen Binhua, spokesperson of Taiwan Affairs Office of the State Council, saying that “the one-China principle is a basic norm of international relations”.
The UN resolution from 1971 recognised the People’s Republic of China as the only legitimate representative of China at the United Nations, expelling “the representatives of Chiang Kai-shek” — or the then-Kuomintang regime — from the world’s top intergovernmental organisation.
The resolution said nothing about Taiwan's sovereignty or political status.
According to Beijing, more than 180 UN member states support the One China principle.
Most major powers, including the US, the EU, the UK, Japan, India and Australia, maintain a "one China policy" under which they recognise the PRC as the government of China and acknowledge but do not explicitly endorse Beijing's claim over Taiwan.

Nigeria, Boko Haram reportedly reach secret three-month ceasefire

Nigeria, Boko Haram reportedly reach secret three-month ceasefire
The reported truce follows the release of 360 villagers abducted during a Boko Haram attack in northeastern Nigeria.
The Nigerian government has been involved in a secret ceasefire with Boko Haram for the past three months, according to an investigation by The New Humanitarian, in a development that could mark a rare pause in years of fighting in northeastern Nigeria.
The reported truce began in June after negotiations that secured the release of 360 civilians abducted from Ngoshe village, in the foothills of the Mandara Mountains near Nigeria’s border with Cameroon, The New Humanitarian reported.
Three people with contacts among Boko Haram members, including some senior figures, independently told the organisation that the ceasefire had been in effect since June and was likely to be extended for another 40 days.
Two of the sources said attacks had stopped in communities around Ngoshe, which have repeatedly been targeted by the armed group.
Truce followed mass abduction
The 360 villagers were abducted in March during a Boko Haram attack on a nearby army base, according to The New Humanitarian.
The negotiations that led to their release reportedly included a payment of five billion naira ($3.7m) by the Nigerian government.
The alleged payment has become controversial in Nigeria, with the government denying that it paid a ransom.
The New Humanitarian said it contacted government, defence and army spokespeople to verify the reported ceasefire but received no response before publication.
Al Jazeera has not been able to independently verify the reported ceasefire or the alleged payment.
The reported agreement does not include Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), a rival armed group that operates in northeastern Nigeria and the wider Lake Chad region.
Fighting between Boko Haram and ISWAP has continued, according to The New Humanitarian.
Government publicly rejects talks
The reported ceasefire comes despite the Nigerian government’s public rejection of negotiations with Boko Haram, which is designated as a “terrorist organisation” by the Nigerian authorities.
President Bola Tinubu has instead focused on expanding the military’s capacity to fight armed groups. In July, he announced plans to recruit 30,000 additional personnel and create four new army divisions.
Behind the scenes, however, there have been repeated attempts to establish dialogue with Boko Haram, according to The New Humanitarian, citing security officials, diplomats and mediators familiar with previous efforts.
Those efforts have included ceasefire arrangements that eventually collapsed.
Conflict researcher Malik Samuel told The New Humanitarian that the latest reported agreement should not necessarily be interpreted as the beginning of a lasting peace process.
“It could be just a temporary, tactical ceasefire that benefits both sides, but doesn’t really affect the trajectory of the war,” Samuel said.
The current arrangement could also allow Boko Haram to strengthen its position, with two sources warning that the group could use the pause to move equipment into the Mandara Mountains, The New Humanitarian reported.
Boko Haram has carried out attacks and kidnappings in northeastern Nigeria and neighbouring countries around the Lake Chad region since 2009. The group has since fractured into several factions, while ISWAP operates as a separate and rival armed group.

More than 1,000 children dead in Bangladesh measles crisis
The South Asian nation of 170 million has recorded 1,002 deaths and 187,484 infections among children since March
The death toll from measles in Bangladesh topped 1,000 children since March, health officials said on Wednesday, admitting that failures in a vaccination drive could have fuelled the outbreak.
The South Asian nation of 170 million has recorded 1,002 deaths and 187,484 infections among children, making this year’s outbreak the country’s deadliest in decades, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Measles is highly contagious, spreading through coughs and sneezes, and has no specific treatment once caught.
Complications can include brain swelling and severe breathing problems. Although anyone can catch the disease, young children are particularly vulnerable.
The disease has kept spreading in Bangladesh even as health authorities rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak.
DGHS spokesman Zahid Raihan said more than 18 million children had been vaccinated so far, and teams were searching for those who had missed inoculations.

IAEA board draws a line under past Syrian nuclear activities

IAEA board draws a line under past Syrian nuclear activities
VIENNA, Sept 9 - The U.N. nuclear watchdog's 35-nation Board of Governors passed a resolution on Wednesday drawing a line under Syria's secret nuclear activities during the Assad family's rule, saying the new authorities had helped resolve all outstanding questions.
After Israel bombed a site in the eastern province of Deir al-Zor in 2007 that it said was a secret nuclear reactor near completion, the International Atomic Energy Agency demanded Syria come clean on its nuclear activities, which it did not do.
The IAEA board declared Syria in breach of its non-proliferation obligations in 2011 and reported it to the U.N. Security Council. After the overthrow of Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024, Syria's new authorities pledged to work with the IAEA in helping clear up the past activities.
In a confidential report to member states last week, seen by Reuters, the IAEA said it had resolved all its questions about the outstanding issues originally reported to the board, and the resolution passed on Wednesday said Syria was no longer in non-compliance with its obligations.
"(The board) welcomes the transparency and cooperation of the Syrian Arab Republic, commends it for the actions taken in resolving its non-compliance," the resolution text submitted by Egypt, Jordan, Morocco and Saudi Arabia said.
The resolution was passed by consensus, meaning no state objected, diplomats at the closed-door meeting said.
The IAEA report confirmed it was "very likely" the bombed site was a nuclear reactor, and said fuel for it was made in Syria. The IAEA found around 73 metric tons of natural uranium metal in Syria, most of it in the form of fuel rods.
That material is now under IAEA oversight, and Syria has said it will stay in the country. REUTERS

Syria no longer under IAEA probe

Breadcrumb
Syria no longer under UN nuclear watchdog IAEA probe
The UN nuclear watchdog's board of governors on Wednesday decided to close a long-time probe against Syria launched under ousted leader Bashar al-Assad after the country's new authorities led agency exports to key nuclear sites.
Inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) last month visited two sites, one in Deir al-Zour and a second in an undisclosed location identified to them by Syrian authorities. IAEA head Rafael Grossi said on Monday that a near-complete nuclear reactor found in Deir al-Zour and built secretly during the rule of al-Assad would have been able to produce material to make nuclear weapons.
The IAEA board "adopted by consensus" a text stating that a 2011 resolution finding Syria in non-compliance with its obligations was "terminated", noting the current government's cooperation, two diplomats told AFP.
The resolution, seen by AFP, was submitted by Egypt, Jordan, Morocco and Saudi Arabia and "encourages Syria to continue its cooperation with the agency, including the excavation work at the Deir al-Zour site".
It also "requests the director general to update the board, as appropriate, on the outcomes of ongoing activities of the agency" in Syria.
'Clandestine' activities
Assad was toppled in December 2024 and the current Islamist government came to power.
Grossi said on Monday that it was "obvious that the previous government was pursuing a number of clandestine" activities.
Besides the reactor under construction at the Deir Ezzor site, the IAEA found a fuel fabrication plant where nuclear fuel for the reactor was manufactured, and a location where nuclear fuel as well as uranium scrap and waste were stored.
In a confidential report seen by AFP last week, the IAEA said it found around 73 tonnes of natural uranium metal.
Grossi has praised Damascus's "courageous decision" to report the undisclosed site.
The UN atomic watchdog had declared in 2011 that the location was "very likely" to host a nuclear reactor, adding that its information suggested it was being built with North Korean assistance.
Last month, Grossi visited the site in Deir al-Zour in the east, which has been shut for 18 years.
In 2018, Israel admitted carrying out a top-secret air raid on the site 11 years earlier.
In 2008, less than a year after the strike, US officials accused Syria of having sought to build a secret nuclear reactor and acknowledged that Israel had destroyed it in the raid.
Israel also has an undeclared nuclear arsenal.
Robert Kelley, a former director of IAEA inspections and now an associate fellow of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, told AFP following the IAEA report that there was "no evidence of any weapons programme" in Syria.
Instead the aim before the site was destroyed may have been to produce plutonium for North Korea, possibly to sell to a third party, he added.

Drone Nets Appear on Roads Near Chornobyl
Unknown

2026-09-09
13:31:32 UTC
22:31:32 KST

Anti-drone nets have appeared over roads leading toward Chornobyl in the Kyiv Oblast as Ukraine reinforces an area used by Russian troops during the opening stage of the full-scale invasion, according to a report published Wednesday, Sept. 9.
The barriers were documented by Ukrainian outlet Telegraf, which said they formed broader defensive preparations near Ukraine’s border with Belarus.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Similar structures have been previously used along roads in frontline regions to protect military vehicles, civilian transport, and pedestrians from Russian first-person-view (FPV) drones.
The nets are stretched between tall metal poles, creating covered sections for those on the road. An approaching drone can become entangled in the barrier or detonate before reaching its intended target.
They can be effective against both kamikaze drones and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) carrying explosives intended to be dropped from above. Nets can also obstruct reconnaissance drones used to identify targets and adjust artillery fire along logistics routes.
The report did not identify which Ukrainian authority was installing the barriers or disclose their precise locations.
Why Chornobyl?
The Chornobyl Exclusion Zone lies close to Ukraine’s border with Belarus, where Russian forces entered northern Ukraine in February 2022.
Russian troops occupied parts of the zone, seized the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, and used the surrounding territory during their unsuccessful advance toward Kyiv. They withdrew from northern Ukraine weeks later.
71% of Ukrainians Say They Are Happy Despite Russia’s War, Poll Shows
Telegraf, citing German newspaper Der Spiegel, reported that Ukraine had also established checkpoints, dug trenches, and defensive pits, along with constructed fortified positions across parts of the exclusion zone.
The reinforcements come amid Ukrainian intelligence reports that Russia’s political leadership instructed its military to prepare several possible plans for operations toward Kyiv and Chernihiv.
As Kyiv Post previously reported, Deputy Head of the Presidential Office Pavlo Palisa said the information had been verified through several intelligence sources.
However, Palisa stressed that the existence of contingency plans did not mean that another offensive was imminent. Ukraine had not observed Russia forming the strike force necessary to attack Kyiv or Chernihiv, he said.
Palisa added that the Ukrainian General Staff had already prepared defensive and counteraction plans.
Similarly, in August, Deputy Chief of Ukraine’s Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR) Maj. Gen. Vadym Skibitsky said that there were no current signs Russia had assembled the forces required for another northern offensive.
“Theoretically, yes, but in practice there are no conditions or indicators showing that they are ready for this operation,” Skibitsky said.
He warned, however, that Russia could potentially form a new strike group by February 2027 if the Kremlin launched another mobilization campaign following its parliamentary elections.
Nets cannot stop Shahed drones
The road barriers are intended primarily to counter relatively small FPV drones flying at low altitudes. They would not provide meaningful protection against larger Shahed-type attack drones carrying heavier warheads.
Russian drones have repeatedly flown close to the Belarusian border and the Chornobyl nature reserve while approaching Kyiv and other targets in northern Ukraine.
Some FPV drones are controlled using conventional radio signals or mobile networks, which can potentially be disrupted by electronic warfare. Russia has also expanded its use of fiber-optic drones, which remain connected to their operators by a cable and cannot be disabled through conventional signal jamming.
Therefore, physical barriers such as nets provide an additional layer of protection, particularly along roads and logistics routes where electronic warfare alone may be insufficient.
