By Bikash Koley, Vice President, Google Global Infrastructure.
Google is deepening its commitment to Finland with a €13 billion investment in digital infrastructure, clean energy, and local partnerships. This investment will support thousands of jobs and help fund regional environmental projects across the country.
Since we converted a former paper mill in Hamina into a data center 15 years ago, Finland has been a vital hub for Google. Today, we’re deepening that commitment with a €13 billion investment in digital infrastructure, clean energy projects and economic partnerships across Finland over the next two years, to help meet growing demand for Google’s core services — such as Search, Maps, and Gemini — that people and businesses rely on every day.
Powering growth and local jobs
Throughout our 15-year history in Hamina, we have supported more than 40 social and community organizations in Hamina while pioneering environmental initiatives such as a seawater-based cooling system and offsite heat recovery distribution to local homes and businesses. From 2023 to 2025 alone, Google’s presence in Hamina supported an ecosystem of more than 600 Finnish suppliers across construction, operations, and network fiber that has created a multiplier effect for the economy. The Hamina data center currently supports a variety of jobs, from computer technicians, to electrical and mechanical engineers, to security staff, to catering, to facilities management, and more.
Today’s announcement, our largest single investment in Europe, will provide a significant boost to the Finnish economy. During the initial construction phase in 2027 and 2028, over 37,000 jobs nationwide will be supported and will contribute €3.6 billion annually to Finland’s GDP. Once fully operational, the new facilities will support thousands of permanent jobs, ranging from engineers to security and catering staff.
We’re also investing €31 million into local communities In Hamina, Kajaani, Muhos, and Vaala over the next four years to support education and economic growth. This includes teaming up with local colleges to offer AI upskilling programs for more than 4,400 workers and creating new training opportunities for 100 Finnish students for future data center careers.
Investing in clean energy and nature
As we grow, we are partnering on a portfolio of solutions that are aligned with our commitments to keep energy affordable for consumers and invest in clean energy. We’re taking steps to further support Finland’s grid by signing a 22-year agreement to support the life extension of the Loviisa nuclear power plant, adding new onshore wind capacity, and contracting for a new 94-megawatt battery system to help stabilize prices during cold, windless periods.
Finally, we want to support the local environment. We’re funding projects to regenerate native forests and wetlands near our sites, and building accessible recreational trails, public saunas, and fishing piers for the community to enjoy.
We’re excited to build the next chapter of digital innovation, right here in Finland.

Buildings Department files 259 charges over work at fire-ravaged Hong Kong estate
Charges against two firms, four individuals relate to alleged use of substandard materials and failure to properly supervise repairs
Hong Kong’s Buildings Department has filed 259 charges against two companies and four individuals over repair works at the inferno-ravaged Wang Fuk Court, after investigations found non-fire-retardant materials were used and safety obligations were not met.
The department said on Wednesday that the charges included allegedly permitting or authorising to be used in the carrying out of building works materials which are defective or did not comply with the provisions of the Buildings Ordinance, as well as failing to properly supervise repair works, among other offences.
The two companies charged are the project’s consulting firm, Will Power Architects, and main contractor, Prestige Construction & Engineering.

In June, both firms, the four individuals and three others were charged by police and the Independent Commission Against Corruption with offences including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, money laundering, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.
The Labour Department also laid 25 charges on Wednesday against related parties – the contractor, the project consultant and an individual – under the Factories and Industrial Undertakings Ordinance, in connection with the deaths of five contractors’ staff during the fire.
A Buildings Department spokesman said the department and the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit “spared no effort in conducting investigations into the major repair works at the estate” following the Wang Fuk Court blaze.

Mahmood Farooqui on Storytelling, Survival and the Human Cost of Imprisonment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:30:14 UTC
22:30:14 KST

Mahmood Farooqui is an acclaimed writer and performer known for reviving Dastangoi, the lost art of Urdu storytelling. He has received the Ramnath Goenka Award for Besieged: Voices From Delhi-1857. He has been visiting fellow at the University of Michigan and University of California, Berkeley. Mahmood has co-directed Peepli Live and produced The Great Shamsuddin Family. In this conversation, he discusses 'The Tihar Players'. Excerpts from the interview:
Q: Let's start with the art of storytelling. A: When I began work on reviving this or studying about it, I had never seen anyone perform Dastangoi because the last Dastango passed away in 1928. I was very blessed to have the scholarship and the guidance of the great Shamsur Rahman Faruqi, one of the greatest writers, novelists, critics and poets that modern Urdu, or indeed modern India, has produced. But he had also never seen somebody perform. So when we tried to put up the first show, we had the stories, but we had nothing to emulate or no model. So it was really our intuition... that put together the first modern show...
And of course, the stories themselves were phenomenal. You know, the story, the fantasies of tricksters and sorcerers, nothing of that kind of imagination and fertility and fecundity has been written anywhere in the world, as far as I know... And then, of course, I started writing my own stories, I started doing workshops. So today, 21 years later, we have. Now the word 'dastan' is back in the currency of our usage in a huge way... We live in a multicultural society. We live in a multilingual society. So any text that I approach, whether I'm working on the Mahabharata or the Ramayana,... many writers in different languages, many literatures have worked on those things. So whenever we present the Mahabharata, people are startled that there are so many versions of the Gita in Urdu or the Mahabharata in Urdu or in Persian, there are so many poems to odes to Lord Krishna, similarly for Ramayana. It's all our legacy. The world of Sanskrit, the world of Persian, the world of Urdu, the world of medieval Hindi. And we bring all that together in the spoken word... Q: When you were in Tihar prison, you put together a motley crowd of amateur actors, many of them illiterate, and you had nothing, and yet you brought this about. Let's talk about that. A: I had to do something which in prison terms in India is called mashakkat — rigorous imprisonment. So I went to the education ward and I proposed that I should set up a theatre class... You might think, what is the point of this? You know, my case is more important. I'm very tortured, as everybody in prison is. You know, everybody is suffering. Everybody has got a plethora of problems because there are court cases to deal with, there are families to deal with. There are problems inside prison. There is food, there is medical health. So amongst all those problems and preoccupations, if somebody's saying, come and do theatre with me, it seems a little odd... And then people started getting into it with workshops. When I started, you know, getting them to play out scenes from their own life, from their prison life, then they started enjoying the catharsis... I would consider myself immensely blessed and fortunate that I could see them grow as actors grow in confidence. And it did wonders to their own self esteem. Many of them have benefited from it. Now they're outside, they're working, whether as instructors, public speakers or you know, photographers. And also it did wonders to the atmosphere inside prison because a prison is a very coercive space... We were fighting not so much to be artists, but to restore our own humanity and to find dignity which came to us on stage, which came to us as performers when we saw the gleam in people's eyes, when we saw that for moments when we were doing the Ram Leela, people forgot about everything that was troubling them and they were lost in it. Q: How does the language of the performance shift? A: I took a Premchand Munshi called 'Nasha' which we improvised completely. It was a device play. So we brought in a lot of prison lingo...When we did 'Charandas Chor', I tried to retain as much as possible the Chhattisgarhi dialect there because when that dialect was understood by people in Edinburgh, why wouldn't people in Delhi understand it? When I did Molière, I lampoon prison doctors inside... I coined a song about paracetamol. You're dying, you get paracetamol... All the capital and social and cultural capital that I had accumulated outside was of zilch value inside... Nothing really mattered because we had all been reduced to the bare bones of being a human being where we were all being shoved and abused, not just by authoritarian orders or officers, but also inmates. Because always, everywhere, there is a chain of violence that comes from top down, and then you replicate it, then you bully others in turn. When you are stripped of everything that you know, everything that makes your identity, how do you form your identity and where do you stand? How do you say that you know who you are? And I was lucky that my drama class began to believe in me. They began to respect me. They formed a core around me, and I was able to find a place in prison without money, without clout, which is not a mean gift, you know... And when I lived there, I realised people may have committed acts which are illegal, which are maybe reprehensible... Every day they know their families are suffering... There is disgrace, there is suffering, there is deprivation. Sometimes their children have to leave school, sometimes they have to change addresses. Their families sometimes travel hours and upon hours to just come and meet them. So a person's conduct outside does not mean that a person has ceased to be a human being. And second, we send people to prison as punishment. So once a person is inside prison, the person has been punished because a person has been confined. A person has been deprived of their family, of food, of comfort, of a phone, of hugging their children, of hugging their dog, sitting on their chair, having a morning chai. So many everyday things and textures they've already been deprived of when they are inside prison.
The law and rules and regulations also follow them inside prison. So people are sent to prison as punishment. But within prison also, they are being punished. Their mulakat might be taken away. Where they are staying might be shifted. Their court cases are inflicting suffering on them. So there is an infinite everyday addition of suffering and punishment and retribution that a person inside is already going through. Regardless of what is happening with their trial, they are suffering humiliation, they are suffering loss of respect, they are suffering insults, they are suffering loss of food, loss of romance, loss of women, loss of hope, loss of time, loss of opportunity. So when you are inside, you're already suffering regardless of the outcome of the case.

Winter work shows it really pays to be a smart mountain chickadee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Winter work shows it really pays to be a smart mountain chickadee
A multidecade study of wild chickadees shows how smart they need to be to survive
A mountain chickadee waking up in the Sierra Nevada range on a snowy morning has no time to dawdle.
Weighing about as much as a pencil, it needs to find stashed pine nuts within minutes or succumb to the howling winds and subzero temperatures. But fortunately, these tiny songbirds are master memorizers, says behavioral ecologist Ai Ana Richmond. A given chickadee knows exactly where it hid each of the hundred thousand seeds it stored for winter.
Richmond, of the University of Nevada, Reno, and her UNR colleagues trek year-round to the Sierras to study this remarkable ability — by snowmobile when necessary. Much work looking at animal cognition is done in the lab. But the site where this team is working — Sagehen Creek Field Station, about 16 kilometers north of Truckee, Calif. — hosts one of the longest running studies of animal cognition in the wild. Automated technology operating there annually tests the memory of up to 250 birds. These and other long-term data are revealing the role of memory in survival, reproduction and other life history traits, insights that are difficult and often impossible to get in a lab.
The need to be — and stay — smart affects every aspect of the birds’ lives. “Since we understand how important these memory abilities are to chickadees, we can ask all sorts of questions” about what affects those abilities and how those abilities alter the birds’ reproductive success, says UNR behavioral ecologist Katherine Johnson.
Surviving harsh winters takes some serious bird brains
Vladimir Pravosudov, a behavioral ecologist at UNR, founded the chickadee study to get a more realistic understanding of why animals need good memories. His interest in avian cognition dates to his days as an undergraduate in Russia, where he studied seed storing in tits that live above the Arctic Circle. He started working with mountain chickadees (Poecili gambeli) in 1999.
Called a’ni ki in the Shoshone Indigenous Goshiute dialect, these birds ferret out single-seed stashes from tree crevices “in brutal conditions,” often with more than four meters of snow on the ground, Richmond says.
About two-thirds never make it through their first winter, the team’s work showed. Those that do can survive a decade or more. The smartest live the longest, the researchers reported in Science in 2024. Now the team is studying the consequences of such long lives.
These discoveries were made possible because in 2013, Pravosudov and his colleagues developed arrays of eight feeders that enable testing of spatial memory in the wild.
Open sesame seed
The team’s bird feeders rely on the same technology as key cards that let guests into only their own hotel room. The feeders can be programmed to open only when a specific banded bird visits it. The birds wear microchips on their legs. Programmed computers in each battery-powered feeder control an individual bird’s access to the feeder and precisely record the timing of each bird’s visits.
Each winter, the researchers allow the birds to get used to the feeders, then test how quickly each one learns which feeder feeds them. That test is a measure of the birds’ spatial memory. After several days, the researchers change which feeder is available to each bird and record how quickly the birds learn to go to the new feeder — a measure of cognitive flexibility. They combine these results with other data on genetics, reproduction, nesting and mating habits and long-term survival.
It’s “a very clever experimental setup,” says Lauryn Benedict, an animal behaviorist at the University of Northern Colorado in Greeley, who isn’t involved in the work.
Keeping those feeders operating and observing the birds in person sometimes requires Herculean effort. Behind her snowmobile, Richmond pulls a sturdy storage tub — built for Canadian ice fishers — filled with birdseed, computer boards, batteries, shovels, other tools and spare parts, extra layers of wool sweaters, a thermos of hot tea and a chainsaw in case downed trees obstruct her 30-kilometer round trip. “On rough days, it’s rather fun in a strange way to strip down to your T-shirt and shovel your snowmobile free,” Richmond says.
Memory experiments are seeding results
The effort is worth it, as the arrays have boosted the group’s ability to understand what the birds are capable of and what’s driving their smarts.
For example, the group has determined that genetics can explain about 80 percent of cognitive differences among these birds. Richmond wondered whether the mix of microbes in the gut might also influence how smart they are. So she examined the makeup of bacteria in droppings collected from 41 birds while at their feeders. She and her colleagues identified the microbes and examined their DNA to see what by-products they produce.
Birds with the best spatial memory had more of the bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids, Richmond reported in July at the annual meeting of the Animal Behavior Society in Cincinnati. A few studies from other labs have suggested these fatty acids may be good for brain health. Thus, it could be that the makeup of the gut bacteria — with some birds having more beneficial microbes — could help explain the nongenetic component of the birds’ cognitive abilities, she says. Next, she hopes to track whether these so-called microbiomes are stable over time. That work should help confirm their contribution to how good the birds’ memories are. “If the microbiome is very critical to memory then technically it shouldn’t be changing,” Pravosudov says.
Some researchers are cautious about this linkage. “There’s a lot of hype about what [it is] about the microbiome [that] can improve cognition, but no clear connections yet,” says Anya Parks, an evolutionary psychologist at George Washington University in Washington, D.C., who studies cognition in dogs. “So, it’s really valuable for there to be comparative research [in different species] to further what we know about the gut-brain relationship.”
Most animals, humans in particular, show memory decline as they age. Hence the saying, “You can’t teach an old dog new tricks.” But that adage doesn’t apply to old chickadees, Johnson reported, also at the Animal Behavior Society meeting. She’d developed an interest in bird smarts as an undergraduate but nearly decided not to pursue animal cognition research because so much of it takes place in controlled laboratory conditions. When she learned about Pravosudov’s work, “my heart leapt.” For this project, she analyzed cognition tests given to 804 chickadees through the years, with some going back a decade. There is no decline, she found: “Our old birds are sharp!”
Johnson’s result “just blew my mind,” says Meenakshi Vengarai, a neuroecologist at the University of Kentucky in Lexington who studies cognition in honeybees.
The work could have relevance beyond chickadees. “Finding the cause for this result in birds could certainly be advantageous for other species including humans,” says Preston Foerder, a comparative psychologist at the University of Detroit Mercy. It may lead to ways to prevent this decline in other animals, he says.
Chickadees’ smarts impact their mating game
More broadly, others working on this cognition project have been looking at connections between cognition and mating success. Carrie Branch, now a behavioral ecologist at Western University in London, Canada, analyzed which males successfully cheated on their lifetime mates. The smarter males sire plenty of young with their usual mates. But they also attract other females and produce more young outside their usual family than less smart males, Branch, Pravosudov and colleagues reported June 16 in eLife.
Moreover, the analysis revealed that these females are choosing to cheat with partners that are smarter than their permanent mates. These “matings may provide females the opportunity to obtain ‘good genes’ that they may not obtain [otherwise],” says Branch.
How the female knows a male is smarter is unclear. These males sing more during the day, the team reported May 20 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, so that’s a possible cue, Pravosudov says. There could be other factors, such as how shiny the male’s feathers are, that attract these females, so the team is looking into that as well.
Overall, he’s trying to take a very integrative approach to the chickadees. “We’re not just looking at one behavior,” he says. “All of these components are part of the same puzzle and it would be really nice to understand all of them.”
At 65, Pravosudov plans to keep studying these birds as long as he’s physically able. “I just love being in the field,” he says. “I get all my ideas by watching birds in the wild.”

How the US post-9/11 overreaction built today's illiberal world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:28:53 UTC
22:28:53 KST

Breadcrumb
How the US post-9/11 overreaction built today's illiberal world
There are events that happen within history, and there are events that change its direction. The attacks of 11 September 2001 unquestionably belonged to the latter.
Twenty-five years ago, Al-Qaeda's attacks on New York and Washington killed almost 3,000 people, traumatised the US and produced images that became instantly seared into global consciousness.
But 9/11 was more than an atrocity. It altered the course of an era.
Barely a decade after the collapse of the Soviet Union, the US stood as the world's sole superpower and liberal democracy appeared to have no serious ideological rival. Francis Fukuyama's famous declaration of the "end of history" captured the extraordinary confidence of the age.
Liberal democracy, globalisation and an international system supposedly governed by universal rules appeared not merely ascendant, but inevitable.
Then the planes hit.
A quarter of a century later, that world seems almost unrecognisable. Liberal democracy is in retreat, the far right is ascendant across much of the West, most notably in the US, Russia is waging a war of territorial conquest in Europe, and the international rules supposedly restraining state power appear increasingly conditional.
This week provided another remarkable marker of how far we have travelled. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, its greatest electoral result to date, bringing a party once considered beyond the limits of respectable German politics tantalisingly close to governing a German state.
None of this can be solely blamed on 9/11. But nor can the world of 2026 be understood without examining what the US and its allies did in response to it.
The Global War on Terror (GWOT) transformed more than US foreign policy. It changed the relationship between security and liberty and helped normalise the idea that extraordinary threats demanded extraordinary powers.
The Patriot Act vastly expanded surveillance. Guantanamo Bay became a legal black hole in which alleged "enemy combatants" could be detained indefinitely without charge. The CIA abducted suspects and transferred them through an extraordinary rendition programme to states where torture was routine. The invasion of Iraq showed that even the world's leading liberal democracy was willing to bypass the international order it claimed to defend.
The Bush administration was not pursuing an explicitly illiberal project. Quite the opposite: it believed US power could protect and ultimately spread liberal democracy.
But it pursued liberal ends using profoundly illiberal means.
That distinction matters. Donald Trump is not simply George W. Bush with the mask removed, nor did the Patriot Act somehow inevitably produce the AfD. But the GWOT created a political world in which exceptional measures became increasingly normal and showed how easily restraints on state power could be discarded once "security" was invoked.
I have previously called what followed the "procession of illiberalism": ideas and machinery created for the War on Terror being taken up and repurposed by movements with very different, explicitly illiberal goals.
The Western front
Orban's Hungary became perhaps the clearest European example.
During his 16 years in power, Orban openly set about building what he called an "illiberal state". His governments expanded Hungary's counterterrorism apparatus while increasingly depicting Muslim migrants as an existential threat to Hungary and Christian Europe.
The terrorist became the extremist; the extremist became the Muslim migrant; those helping migrants became accomplices; and eventually multiculturalism, LGBT rights, liberal civil society and "globalism" itself were portrayed as threats to the survival of the nation.
Orban may have lost power this year, but the politics he helped pioneer travelled far beyond Hungary.
The AfD's victory in Saxony-Anhalt cannot be reduced to this history. Economic stagnation, anger at Germany's established parties and the particular history of eastern Germany all matter.
But today's European far right operates on political terrain profoundly shaped by the post-9/11 era. Borders become front lines and migration becomes invasion. Muslims are treated as a civilisational danger, while multicultural liberal democracy itself is presented as something weakening the nation from within.
In Trump's US, the process has become almost absurdly literal.
Guantanamo, perhaps the ultimate physical symbol of the GWOT's suspension of normal rules, has been repurposed for the detention of migrants. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), itself created by the Bush administration during the War on Terror, has become the frontline institution of Trump's mass-deportation programme.
The machinery and language built to confront foreign terrorists have turned inwards.
The targets have changed, but the logic is familiar. Identify an existential enemy, strip away normal protections and invoke security to justify extraordinary state power.
The War on Terror never left the Middle East
If the GWOT has turned inward in the West, in the Middle East its original logic never really disappeared.
Israel's genocidal war on Gaza made this explicit. Israeli leaders repeatedly invoked 9/11 and presented the war as part of the same civilisational struggle against terrorism. Benjamin Netanyahu described 7 October as Israel's own 9/11 and compared Israeli military action beyond its borders to what the US did after the attacks.
The comparison is revealing.
Once again, an appalling terrorist attack became the justification for an overriding security imperative. Once again, exceptional violence was presented as necessary because the threat was existential. And once again, international law was treated as secondary to the state's claimed need to destroy its enemy.
The results in Gaza have been catastrophic - the enclave devastated, tens of thousands of Palestinians killed and most of its population displaced, while the US supplied the military and diplomatic support that allows the genocide to continue.
Gaza is not simply another version of the GWOT. But the political logic is recognisable. Terrorism becomes more than a crime or military threat. It becomes a condition under which normal restraints can be suspended - even one under which genocide can be justified in the language of security.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has revived another defining feature of the post-9/11 era, namely the crime of preventive war.
In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran amid under the guise of negotiations over its nuclear programme, wiping out its entire leadership, bombing civilian targets, most deplorably a girls school, and civil infrastructure. The war has since spread across the region, with Iran attacking US bases and neighbouring pro-US Arab states and fighting engulfing the economically vital Strait of Hormuz.
Once again, the language is strikingly familiar - nuclear danger, terrorism, national survival and a threat that cannot be allowed to materialise.
This was one of the central ideas behind the GWOT, namely that waiting for a threat to become imminent could itself be too dangerous.
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the War on Terror has therefore taken two different paths. In the West, its security politics have increasingly been redirected from terrorists towards migrants and other supposed internal enemies. In the Middle East, many of its original assumptions about preventive war, existential threats and exceptional violence remain alive.
When the rules stop being universal
Vladimir Putin shows how the same era also helped weaken the international order from another direction.
Putin initially enthusiastically embraced the GWOT. Russia was already waging a brutal war in Chechnya when 9/11 occurred, and he rapidly recast Moscow's campaign as another front in the global struggle against terrorism. Bush, in turn, described Putin as a partner in that struggle.
But by Putin's 2007 Munich Security Conference speech, Russia was openly attacking the US-led order and accusing Washington of violating international law.
The War on Terror had given Putin both an opportunity and, later, an alibi. Russia borrowed its language of existential security while pointing to Iraq and US exceptionalism as proof that the liberal international order was hypocritical.
That does not mean Iraq justifies Russia's invasion of Ukraine. It does mean the US weakened the very principles needed to condemn such aggression consistently.
Gaza has deepened that crisis further. When Western governments invoke sovereignty, international law and civilian protection in Ukraine while giving Israel the means to devastate Gaza, the damage goes beyond charges of hypocrisy.
If the rules depend on who is breaking them and against whom, they stop being universal rules at all.
Before 9/11, the US emerged from the Cold War claiming to lead a liberal world order grounded, however imperfectly, in international law, human rights and democratic government.
The GWOT did not destroy that order. It fractured it.
Its deeper tragedy is that the Bush administration believed US power could be used not simply to defeat terrorism, but to preserve and spread liberal democracy. Torture, rendition, indefinite detention and illegal war were justified by supposedly liberal ends.
Twenty-five years later, even the ends have changed.
The ascendant illiberals of our age do not promise to improve the liberal order. They promise to replace it: universalism with ethno-nationalism, international law with raw sovereign power, multiculturalism with civilisational identity, and the restraints of liberal democracy with the permanent demands of "security".
Nor is this solely the work of those who openly seek liberalism's destruction. As during the GWOT, the rise of illiberalism has also been made easier by governments that defend international law selectively, tolerate its violation by allies and then wonder why appeals to the "rules-based order" carry less and less weight.
Modern illiberalism would almost certainly have emerged without 9/11. But the response to those attacks hastened its rise, furnished it with powerful political tools and helped knock the world off its liberal democratic axis.
Perhaps the most enduring legacy of 9/11 and the War on Terror is therefore neither Afghanistan nor Iraq, but the spread of its central proposition: when the threat is grave enough, the rules no longer apply.
Twenty-five years after the towers fell, the state of exception has escaped the emergency that created it.
The enemies have multiplied, the exceptions are becoming the rule, and the world that once proclaimed the inevitable triumph of liberal democracy increasingly resembles an age of monsters.
Sam Hamad is a writer and History PhD student at the University of Glasgow, focusing on totalitarian ideologies.

Ukraine Presents Components of Shershen Air Defense System
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:28:12 UTC
22:28:12 KST

Ukraine presented components of the multicaliber Shershen air defense system at the MSPO 2026 international exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
Militarnyi’s correspondent reported this.
The international consortium of companies Shershen Group, which is developing an air defense system for Ukraine, presented a command post, launcher and target-tracking radar station.
This modular system can use both Soviet-made missiles such as the R-60, R-73 and R-27, and Western AIM-9 and AIM-132 missiles.
A mock-up of the Ukrainian-made R-120 missile, which is currently under development, was also displayed on the launcher.
The system consists of a target-tracking station, a combat control post, and up to four launchers.
Regarding the surveillance radar station, a company representative said that any radar can be integrated into the system. It can also use information from the Oreanda or Virazh-Planchet mobile automated command-and-control systems for the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ aviation and air defense forces and assets.
The system can also operate with the Krechet system, through which it can receive information from other radars and air target detection sources.
The multi-caliber Shershen air defense system project was first presented in February 2026 at the World Defense Show 2026 defense exhibition in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.
At the exhibition in Poland, the system’s components were displayed for the first time, including the command post with workstations for the commander and operator.
The system’s engagement range and altitude depend on the specific missile type it uses.
For example, when using R-27ET1 missiles with infrared homing seekers, which are used on India’s Samar-2 air defense system, the stated engagement range against an aerial target is up to 20 kilometers.

Trump attributes state election win of Germany’s far-right to immigration
- US President Donald Trump credited Germany’s far-right AfD party's state election win in Saxony-Anhalt to "horrible" immigration rules hurting the country.
- AfD's leader promises swift deportations of illegal immigrants, reflecting policies similar to Trump's, marking a major setback for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservatives.
- German officials rejected Trump's interference in domestic politics; a planned Merkel-Trump phone call was postponed, highlighting tensions amid differing US-Germany views on key issues.
AI generated
WASHINGTON/BERLIN - US President Donald Trump attributed the win of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in a state election to immigration rules and regulations that he cast as “horrible”.
The AfD, bolstered by public angst over the scale of mass immigration, surged into first place on Sept 6 in the election in Saxony-Anhalt, the first time a far-right party has come within reach of power at the state level since World War II.
Trump has long accused various European countries including Germany of losing control of their borders, following a large influx of migrants and asylum seekers, especially from the Middle East and Afghanistan, over the past decade.
"Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night. They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sept 8.
The AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund, who hopes to become the new premier of Saxony-Anhalt after the Sept 6 election, has promised “deportations (of illegal immigrants) from the first minute” in an echo of Trump’s own policies.
The AfD’s victory also represents one of the biggest setbacks for Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives since they returned to power at the national level in Germany more than a year ago.
When asked about the Saxony-Anhalt election on Sept 9, Merz’s chief spokesperson, Stefan Kornelius, declined to comment directly on Trump’s social media post.
But he added that Merz has indicated in the past that interventions or comments from abroad on domestic German politics, particularly elections, are “out of the question” for the chancellor.
At the same regular press conference, Kornelius said the government had postponed a planned phone call between Merz and Trump on the upcoming 25th anniversary of the Sept 11 attacks in the US.
“The German side postponed this call today. A new date has not yet been set,” he said, declining to give a reason for the postponement.
The US and Germany have traditionally been close allies, but their relationship has been put to the test since Trump’s return to office, with differing views on a host of topics, including tariffs, the US-Israeli war on Iran, and support for Ukraine.
Kornelius said Germany remains ready to stand up for the values that define and unite the two countries. “These are freedom, democracy and respect,” he said. REUTERS

Swiss business federation chief warns Switzerland is losing competitiveness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

22:27:33 KST

Swiss business federation chief warns Switzerland is losing competitiveness
Christoph Mäder, the outgoing chair of economiesuisse, the Swiss Business Federation, has warned that Switzerland is losing ground to rival economies when it comes to competitiveness.
He said the Swiss government has shown little appetite for measures to strengthen the country’s business environment.
+ Swiss business federation sets priorities amid global tensions
Many people in Switzerland now take it for granted that the country will “almost automatically” rank among the world’s most competitive economies, Mäder said in an interview published in TA Media newspapers on Wednesday.
Mäder is stepping down this month and will be succeeded by Silvan Wildhaber at the helm of the business umbrella organisation.
He warned that such complacency was dangerous. “Countries such as Ireland and Denmark are making significant gains. We need to measure ourselves against Europe’s top performers, not just our immediate neighbours.”
+ Head of Swiss business federation criticises government
Mäder said Switzerland faces a backlog of overdue reforms. “Yet the government has shown no sign that it is willing to tackle these challenges with the urgency they require,” he said. One example is pension reform. He described the decision not even to discuss the retirement age as part of the next AHV reform package as “irresponsible, to put it mildly”.
On immigration, Mäder argued that Switzerland should address what he sees as the root cause of the issue. He said asylum seekers are driving much of the public unease over immigration. Although asylum-related migration accounts for only a small share of overall immigration, he said it attracts a disproportionate amount of attention.
He acknowledged, however, that labour migration to Switzerland had reached a critical level in recent years. “But this type of immigration is likely to ease anyway if our competitiveness continues to weaken. I wouldn’t be surprised if demand for newcomers began to fall,” he said.

Türkiye’s airports welcome 167.5M passengers in 8 months

2026-09-09
13:26:49 UTC
22:26:49 KST

Seda Tolmaç
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Turkish airports handled some 167.5 million passengers in the first eight months of the year, according to the State Airports Authority General Directorate (DHMI) on Wednesday.
Abdulkadir Uraloglu, Turkish transport and infrastructure minister, stated that passenger traffic increased by 2.8% by the end of August this year compared to the same period last year, including direct transit passengers.  
Aircraft movements in January-August totaled 1.6 million, including overflights, with 667,653 on domestic routes and 611,588 on international destinations.
Cargo traffic reached nearly 4 million metric tons, 654,295 tons of which were carried on domestic destinations and nearly 3.6 million metric tons were transported on international routes.
IGA Istanbul Airport served 56.6 million passengers aboard a total of 52,468 flights in the first eight months of the year, while recording 365,487 aircraft movements. Uraloglu noted that 11.9 million of the total passenger count flew on domestic routes and 44.7 million traveled on international destinations during this period.
The airport served nearly 8.6 million passengers in August alone, 1.8 million of which were on domestic and 6.7 million were on international routes.
Sabiha Gokcen Airport, Istanbul’s Asian air hub, carried 33.1 million passengers in January-August aboard a total of 188,833 flights, 84,077 of which were on domestic routes and 104,756 were on international destinations. Some 15.2 million passengers flew on domestic destinations and 17.9 million on international routes, the minister said.
Istanbul Ataturk Airport served some 17,903 aircraft over the eight-month period, while handling 2,594 in August alone.
Meanwhile, the number of passengers served at airports in tourism hubs reached a total of 41.6 million in January-August, while the total number of flights hit 277,435 over the same period.
In August, some 28.8 million passengers were served, while a total of 255,970 aircraft took off and landed at passenger and eco-friendly airports, including overflights, with domestic destinations accounting for 97,625 and international routes making up 106,231 — the total number of international flights surged 1.5% month-on-month.
“Türkiye’s airports with the highest passenger capacities, specifically the IGA Istanbul Airport and Antalya Airport, served 81.7 million passengers in just eight months, exceeding twice the number of passengers served across the country in 2002,” he said.

Ukraine's digitalization team has returned from a working trip during which it held a series of important meetings with international donors, Big Tech representatives and venture funds. The main goal of the trip was to attract additional investment and resources for the country's continued transformation, the development of products like Diia, Mriya and Diia City, and the rollout of artificial intelligence, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said.
"It's important to use my contacts around the world to bring additional funding into Ukraine, to keep doing this, and, conversely, to scale up everything that's already been done so nothing stops," Fedorov said in a statement on his Telegram channel.
He also said the team had secured resources that will allow the creation, in Kyiv, of the largest venture fund in the Defense Tech sector, which will invest in both military startups and established companies.
"We have three key priorities. The first is sensorization and robotization of the front line, to protect our soldiers' lives and speed up front-line robotization as much as possible. The second is jet interceptors, cheap missiles and other means to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds and missiles - and we know the scale of the threat today. Just this morning, a Shahed hit a residential building in Kyiv. The goal is to accelerate solving this problem. And the third is cheap strike missiles, eventually with AI. We need to have a response to every enemy attack, and to have our own system built that's capable of responding at scale," the former minister said.
He said the Defense Tech Fund will be launched "soon."
"I'll be inviting both startups and experts to join it and work within the fund," Fedorov added.
He also said an analytical center is planned for launch.
"Over the past 7-8 months, we've found the key to the Russians: how to find their vulnerabilities, how to strike and seize the initiative in the air and on the ground. The goal is to use our experience to be able to forecast the war's next steps and proactively generate solutions to seize the initiative. So there will be an announcement about this soon too," he said.
He stressed that the main task today is finding solutions that will allow Ukraine to win the war for independence, end the war, and do so through innovation, technology and asymmetry.
"So everything I've done up to now, we're continuing to do with our team. And I hope this gives hope to someone who has it, or restores hope to someone starting to lose it. Everyone in their own place, regardless of status, wherever we are - we keep fighting," Fedorov concluded.
It was reported on August 28 that former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov had become an advisor to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto.
In addition, Fedorov announced on September 1 the creation of a defense technology company.
"Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir, will become its first lead investor," Fedorov said.
He said the company's goal is to use the experience and expertise he gained during the technological transformation of Ukraine's defense sector to create new technologies with global potential.

Russia launches online marketplace selling counter-UAV systems and other equipment
Russian state-owned corporation Rostec has launched the industrial marketplace PCAT.ru, with counter-UAV systems among its most sought-after products.
Source: Rostec
Details: The platform allows businesses to present their products and production capabilities, find ready-made solutions and establish production chains for specific projects.
According to Rostec, PCAT.ru currently brings together more than 180 companies and research organisations. The platform offers over 1,250 ready-made products and 370 production capabilities.
The Russian state corporation claims that more than 23,000 users access the platform every day, while 60% of enquiries come from corporations and large businesses.
In addition to counter-UAV systems, Rostec listed all-terrain vehicles, as well as aerostatic and aerodynamic systems, among the most sought-after products on PCAT.ru.
The platform has been integrated with the Bank of Technologies and a Moscow service for finding alternative suppliers. Rostec also said that companies in Krasnodar Krai and Tver, Tula and Ryazan oblasts had gained access to federal cooperation through PCAT.ru.
The platform is operated by the Rosel holding company, which is part of Rostec.
Shortly after announcing the launch of PCAT.ru, Rostec reported a cyberattack on the platform that made it unavailable. The corporation said it is working to resume the site's operation.
Background: Earlier, it was reported that Russia's Roy.Market service is being relaunched as a full-fledged marketplace for the needs of Russian armed forces. The platform includes components for drones, among other products, and its catalogue is planned to expand to more than 10,000 items by 2027.

Czech Prime Minister’s former companies still in EU focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:25:09 UTC
22:25:09 KST

The European Commission announced on the 8th of September that the European Union has suspended the payment of some subsidies to the Czech Agrofert group, which was previously owned by Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš but is now under the management of a trust fund, Reuters reports.
Babiš set up the trust fund in December 2025 to avoid a conflict of interest after returning to the post of prime minister. Giving up his business interests was a prerequisite for Babiš to lead the government.
The EC has indicated that the politician has not sufficiently severed ties with the agricultural conglomerate, and its spokesman said that the EC believes that the Czech Prime Minister is in a situation of potential conflict of interest in relation to the management of cohesion policy and agricultural funds, and the trust fund created by Babiš does not sufficiently eliminate the situation.
Agrofert brings together hundreds of companies in the agricultural, chemical and other sectors, and has so far received millions of euros from EU subsidy funds for farmers, as well as other types of support. An EC spokesman said
the EU decision to suspend payments does not apply to payments that are automatically granted to farmers.
Agrofert is the largest Czech agricultural group, managing about 130,000 hectares of land. Babiš shrugged off the EU decision. He said he no longer owns Agrofert, never will, and he does not benefit from it.
The Czech agricultural support manager SZIF announced on the 7th of September that the EC had suspended payments of three million euros. Agrofert, which is also one of the largest fertilizer producers in Europe, said it had met all the requirements.

From prototype to export markets: LIAA opens autumn applications for the business incubation programme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:23:43 UTC
22:23:43 KST

From 9 to 24 September, the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) invites young companies to apply for its Business Incubation Programme. Participants can receive financial support covering up to 70% of business development costs, as well as consultations with experts and mentors, training, networking opportunities and access to LIAA co-working spaces throughout Latvia.
The programme is intended for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises registered in Latvia that have been operating for no more than five years and are developing innovative, technological, export-ready or creative-industry products and services. Companies developing dual-use products may also apply, as can businesses in other eligible sectors with export or innovation potential.
“In the first years of a company’s operations, the ability to test its business model quickly, improve its product and reach its first customers is crucial. The Business Incubation Programme brings together funding, expert knowledge, mentors’ experience and business contacts in one place. This helps transform a good idea into a competitive product and prepares the company for its next stage of growth, including expansion beyond Latvia. We encourage entrepreneurs who have already developed their product to at least the minimum viable product stage and are ready to work purposefully on its further development to apply,” emphasises LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.
Results Achieved by the Programme
There are currently 359 companies participating in the Business Incubation Programme throughout Latvia. During this year’s spring intake, 83 new participants joined the programme: 41 innovative companies and 42 export-ready companies, including 14 creative-industry businesses and five dual-use companies. Since the programme began, its participants have received €7.96 million in support.
Funding and Knowledge for Business Growth
Participants in the Business Incubation Programme can receive grants covering 70% of eligible costs:
- up to €10,000 for the purchase of services;
- up to €8,000 for the purchase of equipment;
- up to €5,000 for the purchase of raw materials.
Companies that meet the criteria for an innovative enterprise can also receive a grant of up to €10,000 to cover employee remuneration costs, as well as funding of up to €20,000 for prototyping, technology development and the purchase of specialised services.
In addition to funding, programme participants can receive individual consultations with experts and mentors from Latvia and abroad. The programme offers training and seminars on business modelling, marketing, product development, financial planning, attracting investment and other matters relevant to business growth. Participants also have access to networking and experience-sharing events, as well as LIAA co-working spaces.
Companies Must Have Developed at Least a Product Prototype
Companies may apply to the programme if their product, service or technology has reached at least the minimum viable product, or MVP, stage. An innovative product must have reached at least Technology Readiness Level 4 (TRL 4), while an export-ready or conventional product must have reached at least Business Idea Maturity Readiness Level 5 (BIMRL 5). A company’s outstanding tax debt may not exceed €1,000 on the application date.
Support Available Throughout Latvia
Applications are accepted on a regional basis through 20 LIAA representative offices across Latvia, as well as through the Creative Industries and Technology representative offices in Riga. LIAA’s regional offices are located in Jūrmala, Tukums, Valmiera, Cēsis, Smiltene, Madona, Gulbene, Alūksne, Sigulda, Liepāja, Saldus, Ventspils, Kuldīga, Talsi, Jelgava, Bauska, Ogre, Jēkabpils, Rēzekne and Daugavpils.
Creative-industry companies may apply either through the Creative Industries representative office in Riga or through their nearest LIAA regional office. Innovative companies based in Riga may apply through the Technology representative office in Riga.
Applications Open Until 24 September
Applications can be submitted through the liaa.business.gov.lv platform from 8:30 a.m. on 9 September until 11:59 p.m. on 24 September. Before preparing an application, entrepreneurs are encouraged to contact their nearest LIAA representative office for advice on the programme’s conditions, the most suitable form of support and the required documents. LIAA recommends not postponing submission until the final day of the application period.
Business incubation support is provided under the Innovative Business Development Programme for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises, co-financed by the European Regional Development Fund and the Latvian state budget.

Why we're still looking for dark matter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:23:00 UTC
22:23:00 KST

Why we're still looking for dark matter
September 9, 2026
On September 1, 2026, scientists at a dark matter detector called LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) reported they had observed an event, a particle interaction, that they were unable to explain.
The team, based in South Dakota in the United States, said the event resembled what they think a dark matter particle should produce when it collides with liquid xenon, one of a range of materials used for detecting dark matter.
They stopped short of calling it the discovery, or proof of dark matter, that many in the field have been hunting for almost 100 years.
The term "dark matter" was coined by physicist Fritz Zwicky in 1933 as a means to describe unseen matter that would explain fast-moving galaxies.
The LUX-ZEPLIN observation came just days after the release of the second season of Dark Matter, a sci-fi thriller starring Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly. Both events pushed the term "dark matter" back into people's minds.
Here's what you need to know, with the science separated from the series.
What is dark matter in simple terms?
Dark matter is often described as an "invisible" substance. But it may be better described as "transparent" because it can be seen, or detected, by the gravitational attraction it exerts.
That said, it neither emits nor reflects light and has never been observed directly. So, in that sense, it is invisible.
Is it true that 95% of the universe is invisible?
Yes, roughly.
Ordinary matter — everything that can be seen or touched — accounts for about 5% of the universe.
Dark matter accounts for about 27%, and dark energy, a separate force linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe, about 68%. Together they account for about 95%.
A different figure of 85% is dark matter's share of matter alone.
But does dark matter really exist?
The strongest evidence that dark matter exists comes from the so-called Bullet Cluster, which formed when two galaxy clusters collided. The collision produced hot gas clouds that interacted. This interaction revealed mass in the gas clouds that distributed differently from the gas. Researchers said that mass could be dark matter.
How do scientists search for dark matter on Earth?
Scientists use detectors like the LUX-ZEPLIN that passively wait for interactions between naturally occurring particles and detect radiation.
They tend to be buried deep underground, where the surrounding rock blocks cosmic radiation that would otherwise distort signals.
They are built from materials chosen for their very low levels of trace radioactivity, so a genuine detection is not lost in background noise.
The LUX-ZEPLIN detector specifically works by watching for a faint flash of light and pulse of electric charge released when a passing particle strikes a liquid xenon particle. Liquid xenon, a noble gas, has good properties for detecting radiation.
What is dark matter made of?
These are leading candidate particles:
WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles, are the longest-standing theory. They are heavy and interact only rarely with ordinary matter.
Axions, which are lighter and behave more coherently than WIMPs. A team at Kyoto University, Japan, say data from Earth's magnetic field could be used to search for axions.
What does dark matter do to humans?
Dark matter passes through the body constantly without measurable effect. Billions of candidate particles cross through a person every second but only about 10 strike a nucleus in the body over a year.
The resulting radiation exposure is far lower than what people receive from radon or cosmic rays.
Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

Braga celebrates African heritage over two days with music, film and debates

22:22:52 KST

The festival celebrates African heritage, between the "culture we inherit" and the "reality we build". It takes place on 11 and 12 September in Braga.
The performance by the Cesária Évora Orchestra on Saturday, 12th, is the highlight of the Paraíso festival, which celebrates African culture over two days in the city of Braga.
Made up of musicians who accompanied the "Barefoot Diva" in live performances and studio recordings at the height of the Cape Verdean singer's career, including Teófilo Chantre, composer of many of the songs sung by Cesária Évora, the orchestra backs the voices of Elida Almeida, Lucibela and Ceuzany, regarded as among the greatest voices of Cape Verde. The concert, a tribute to the singer who died in 2011 and is considered one of Cabo Verde's greatest ever symbols, will take place at Theatro Circo at 21:30.
The festival's theme is "Past and Future in Afro-descendence" and it features music, gastronomy, cinema and debates at various venues around the northern city. In addition to Theatro Circo, Paraíso also takes in the Centésima Página bookshop and the gnration venue (source in Portuguese), where on Friday, 11th, the film "Si Destino" by Vanessa Fernandes will be screened, followed by a debate between the director and academic Ana Cristina Pereira, also known as Kitty Furtado, one of the festival's curators.
On Saturday, the same venue will host a debate with the authors of the project "Anti-racist Handbook for the Arts and Education", with contributions from Dori Nigro, Melissa Rodrigues and Raquel Lima, from União Negra das Artes. The presentation of this project, which will soon take shape as a book, forms part of the centenary of the birth of Amílcar Cabral, a central figure in the struggle for the independence of Guinea-Bissau and Cabo Verde.
"At a time when it is important to look at what preceded us in order to be able to project what lies ahead, we propose to debate ways of existing between the heritage we receive and the realities we build collectively", say the organisers of the event, which forms part of the programme of activities marking the 30th anniversary of the CPLP.

Ukrainian vehicle license plates — what types there are and what the letters and numbers mean
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:22:44 EEST
22:22:44 KST

Ukrainian vehicle license plates — what types there are and what the letters and numbers mean
Kyiv • UNN
There are 15 types of license plates for different vehicles in Ukraine. We explain the meaning of the colors, letters, and numbers on them.
Vehicle registration plates of Ukraine are identification plates attached in designated places on motor vehicles (except trams and trolleybuses) and trailers, and intended to register vehicles with an authorized body of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Today, there are 15 types of license plates in Ukraine. UNN explains which types of license plates exist in Ukraine and what the letters and numbers on them mean.
"Standard" license plates
State registration license plates are issued for all vehicles when they are registered for the first time or re-registered in Ukraine. Service centers of the Ministry of Internal Affairs issue both standard elongated state registration plates, which make up the majority on Ukraine's roads, and plates for vehicles with a non-standard mounting space—so-called "American" plates—which are rectangular and closer to a square in shape than standard plates.
Depending on their type, the plates must contain information about administrative and territorial affiliation, the serial number and series, as well as symbols indicating state affiliation.
A "standard license plate" has a white background with black letters and numbers. It is used for all types of automobiles.
White plates may also have green numbers and letters. Such license plates are issued for electric cars that do not have an internal combustion engine.
License plates for taxis and route buses
Buses and taxis registered in the Unified State Register of Legal Entities and Individual Entrepreneurs as means of conducting business activities involving the carriage of passengers by road are issued yellow license plates, with the letters and numbers shown in black.
However, yellow plates may also have green letters and numbers. They are issued for taxis and route buses equipped with an electric motor.
Departmental plates
Black plates with white symbols are the standard format for the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Military license plates have a standard format:
-  four digits; 
-  a letter; 
-  an additional digit or index. 
The first digits are the internal registration number of the equipment in the military accounting system. The letter series makes it possible to determine the type or purpose of the vehicle.
Letters: А, В, Е, К, Н, Р, С, Т—main combat and transport equipment, including passenger cars, trucks, buses, and tractors; І, М, О, Х—trailers and semi-trailers; А1, А2—vehicles of headquarters and command; А3, А4, А5—communications, medical evacuation, reconnaissance, and special forces equipment.
License plates for vehicles of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine have a white background with black letters and numbers. Until 2020, SBGS vehicles had license plates with a black background and the letter Ю, which specifically denoted the SBGS.
Currently, SBGS license plates have a white background with black letters and numbers. The plate also displays the SBGS emblem in the form of a straight-sided equilateral cross with diverging green ends and yellow stripes. At the center of the emblem is an image of the Sign of the Princely State of Volodymyr the Great in gold (yellow) on a blue field, surrounded by a wreath of yellow oak leaves.
License plates for vehicles of the Operational Rescue Service of Civil Protection (DSNS) have a white background with black letters and numbers, and must also bear the emblem of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine.
The letters at the beginning of the plate indicate administrative and territorial affiliation, the numbers are the serial number, and the letter Е with the emblem indicates affiliation with the Operational Rescue Service of Civil Protection.
The National Guard of Ukraine uses white plates with black letters and numbers.
The letters at the beginning of the plate indicate administrative and territorial affiliation, the numbers are the serial number, and the letter G with the NGU emblem indicates affiliation with the National Guard.
The Security Service of Ukraine also uses white license plates with black letters and numbers, where the letters at the beginning of the plate indicate administrative and territorial affiliation, the numbers are the serial number, and the letter С with the emblem indicates affiliation with the SBU.
Vehicles of the National Police of Ukraine have license plates with a blue background, with the letters and numbers shown in white.
At the beginning of the plate, there is a digit indicating the code of the administrative-territorial affiliation, followed by the National Police emblem, while the digits indicate the serial number.
It should be noted that, since August 31, three “phantom patrols” have begun operating in Kyiv and the Kyiv region.
The “phantoms” have regular license plates—with a white background and black letters and numbers.
In April this year, Ukraine introduced a new model of diplomatic license plates, which are now olive-colored.
The structure of a diplomatic license plate includes: the first three digits indicate the code of the diplomatic institution (embassy/mission of an international organization), while the next three indicate the vehicle’s individual serial number.
Ukraine introduced new diplomatic license plates08.04.26, 17:21 • 4301 view
Red license plates
Temporary license plates, also known as transit plates, are red plastic plates used on vehicles that have not completed the registration process. They have a standard format: 4 digits and 2 letters.
Since 2020, transit plates have been issued only for new vehicles sold through car dealerships or dealers, as well as when deregistering used vehicles for subsequent export abroad.
Under current legislation, the owner of a new car is required to register it within 10 days of purchase. Registration is carried out at a territorial service center of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, regardless of the owner’s place of residence or place of registration.
If a vehicle is purchased from a commercial organization, the owner may be issued license plates for one-time trips (red in color). They are needed so that the car owner can use the vehicle to visit a service center of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and register it with the state.
License plates for one-time trips are issued for a period of two months. If the owner has not registered the car within 10 days or the validity period of the red plates has expired, the vehicle should not be used on public roads. Operating an unregistered vehicle may constitute grounds for an administrative fine.
Driving a vehicle that has not been registered or re-registered in accordance with the established procedure is punishable by a fine of 850 hryvnias.
What the letters on license plates mean
The letters on license plates that indicate the region are written in Cyrillic, and only those with Latin equivalents are used. This means that on car license plates you can encounter only the letters А, В, Е, I, К, М, Н, О, Р, С, Т and Х.
The letters on car license plates can also indicate where a person completed the purchase and registration of the vehicle—at a service center of the Ministry of Internal Affairs or online, for example, through Diia.
If this was done online, they will be issued a license plate with the letters DI and PD, while those who completed the purchase\sale transaction through the electronic account in the Ministry of Internal Affairs system will be issued a plate with the letter combinations ЕD and DC.

Zheng Baoguo (3rd R) poses for a group photo with colleagues in Luozhuangzi Town of Jizhou District in Tianjin, north China, on Sept. 3, 2026.
The Sangyuan campus of Hongshuizhuang Central Primary School is located at the foot of the Yanshan Mountains in Jizhou District. The small rural school has just 28 students and serves three neighboring villages. It allows local children to attend classes close to home rather than travel nearly 10 kilometers to the town's central primary school.
Zheng Baoguo, 56 and a native of Jizhou District, has worked at the school for more than 20 years. After graduating from a secondary normal school in 1989, he became a rural teacher. He has long believed that education is a key to a brighter future for children in mountainous areas.
In 2003, Zheng became the first principal of the Sangyuan campus. Although he later had an opportunity to work in an urban school, he chose to stay and continue his career in his hometown. More than two decades later, Zheng still teaches classes himself despite serving as principal, and he always creates a relaxed and cheerful atmosphere for his students.
"A teacher can change a child's life. As a teacher, I must live up to families' trust," Zheng said, "As long as the school remains open, I will keep doing my best to ensure that children in these mountain villages have access to education close to home." (Xinhua/Li Ran)

Across China: Int'l experts immerse in Shenzhen's dynamic practices of Chinese modernization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:22:00 CST
22:22:00 KST

International tourists visit an exhibition showcasing Shenzhen's latest sci-tech feats on the 116th floor of the Ping An Finance Center in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Sept. 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Yang Shenshen)
SHENZHEN, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- When Zoon Ahmed Khan, a research fellow at Tsinghua University, tried out an exoskeleton robot in Shenzhen, she reflected on the southern Chinese economic and tech hub's astonishing transformation over the past decades -- a development trajectory that few could have foreseen.
"A great number of the technologies we experience today, and the innovations I have encountered throughout China, target real-life difficulties," said the Pakistani scholar during a field trip as part of an international symposium on Monday. "The products are not only showcasing Shenzhen's achievements but, more importantly, inspiring visitors."
The delegation, consisting of international experts, scholars and guests, toured various sites across Shenzhen, to observe how modern technology and cultural heritage converge in this dynamic metropolis.
On the 116th floor of the Ping An Finance Center, the world's highest glass-floor cantilevered observation deck, the delegation visited an exhibition showcasing the city's latest sci-tech feats, such as DJI drones, Tencent AI office solutions, HONOR's embodied robots and Hypershell exoskeleton robots.
Rami Khalil, an Armenian expert at Sichuan International Studies University, said he was impressed by China's domestically designed Hualong One nuclear reactor.
"Green energy is a very essential part of Chinese culture. Instead of dominating nature, Chinese philosophy advocates integration," he said.
At the Eyes of the Greater Bay Area, the world's largest physical book mall, which commenced operations in September last year, Nathan Bonar, a research fellow at the Institute for Postmodern Development of China, purchased a book and a calligraphy copybook about Ci poetry of the Song Dynasty (960-1279).
"I really like the way it's set up. It's not just for purchasing books, but a space for people to actually read, enjoy themselves and interact with one another," said the book lover with a collection of more than 4,000 books.
While Shenzhen is often associated with technology, its achievements are deeply rooted in culture. "I'm encouraged by seeing people who know how to use technology to make their lives better and more enjoyable, so that they can sit down and read poetry," he added.
"China is deeply rooted in its own culture and civilization. Reading links people to knowledge, and this pursuit of knowledge also paves the way for modernity," said Fouzia Amin, a research fellow at the Understanding China Forum in Pakistan.
In Nantou Ancient Town, which boasts a history of nearly 1,700 years, cafes, specialty restaurants and art galleries line the ancient alleyways. For Bruno Guigue, a research fellow at France's University of Reunion, the town showcases that traditional culture and modern technology are fully compatible.
"Chinese people can develop humanoid robots while keeping their cultural roots. This is quite fascinating to me," said Guigue. "Shenzhen was once a tiny fishing village and has grown into a metropolis with innovation hubs and financial centers. It embodies a new China."
Gustavo Sabino Vaca Narvaja, former Argentine ambassador to China and director of the Center for Sinology Studies at the University of Buenos Aires, said the "Shenzhen Moment" represents a new stage of productivity brought by rapid technological progress and the integration of tradition and modernity that generates fresh innovation.
"China's growth and technological development have been achieved without losing its own identity, which constitutes a valuable asset for modernization," said the former diplomat. "That is also why I believe it offers opportunities for the Global South." ■

Namibia calls for green financing to drive industrialization, job creation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:21:59 CST
22:21:59 KST

WINDHOEK, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Namibia on Wednesday called for innovative green financing to support industrialization, job creation and expanded electricity access as the country seeks to meet its development targets by 2030.
Speaking at the opening of the Second International Conference on Finance and Sustainable Business in Windhoek, Minister of Industries, Mines and Energy Modestus Amutse said green finance should go beyond funding environmentally friendly projects and help build the country's productive capacity.
Under Namibia's Sixth National Development Plan (NDP6), the country aims to achieve an economic growth rate of at least 7 percent and an employment rate of 75 percent by 2030. It also seeks to increase manufacturing's contribution to gross domestic product from 10.6 percent to 18 percent and raise electricity access from 59.3 percent to 70 percent.
Amutse said achieving those targets would require a range of financing instruments, including grants, concessional and blended finance, guarantees and patient capital, tailored to projects at different stages of development.
"A just transition cannot end where creditworthiness ends," he said, calling for financing models that can also reach rural households, informal businesses and other underserved groups.
Amutse said Namibia should also derive greater value from its critical mineral resources through domestic processing and beneficiation rather than remaining primarily a supplier of raw materials to global markets.
Developing mineral value chains would require coordinated investment in electricity, water, logistics, laboratories and specialized skills, as well as closer cooperation among authorities responsible for mining, energy, water, industrial policy and finance, he said.
He added that emerging sectors including green hydrogen, renewable energy and petroleum should contribute to skills development, infrastructure and broader economic diversification.
The two-day conference, hosted by the Namibia University of Science and Technology, brings together researchers, policymakers, industry experts and other stakeholders to discuss green finance and sustainable business models. ■

South Africa secures first access to China for cherry exports
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:21:48 CST
22:21:48 KST

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- South Africa has secured access to China for its cherry exports for the first time, in a deal that could spur investment and create jobs in the domestic industry, the Department of Agriculture announced on Tuesday.
According to a statement from the department, Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp and Sun Meijun, head of China's General Administration of Customs, signed a protocol opening the Chinese market to South African cherries at the ninth Sanitary and Phytosanitary Ministerial Meeting in Beijing on Tuesday.
The department said the agreement could bring "huge economic benefits" for South Africa, with China being the world's number one importer of cherries. China imported about 586,900 tons of cherries in 2025, valued at 3.3 billion U.S. dollars, according to the statement.
In the statement, Aucamp praised China's role in advancing two-way agricultural trade and thanked it for speeding up South Africa's requests for market access.
"We truly appreciate China's efforts to speed up our market access requests for South African agriculture products," Aucamp was quoted as saying. "This achievement is record-breaking as it is the first time that two market access protocols have been signed with China within a year."
The opening of the Chinese market is expected to stimulate investment in cherry production and create about 600 new jobs, in line with the government's priorities of inclusive economic growth and job creation, the department said.
The agreement forms part of efforts to broaden agricultural trade between South Africa and China under a framework that provides zero-tariff market access to Chinese markets, according to the statement.
Aucamp added that negotiations to secure access for South African blueberries were at an advanced stage. China has submitted a draft protocol for blueberry imports, and South Africa aims to finalize the agreement before the end of the year, the statement said. ■

Sun was also deprived of his qualification as a delegate to the 20th CPC National Congress.

Thailand's industrial confidence slips in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
21:21:39 CST
22:21:39 KST

BANGKOK, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's industrial sentiment dropped in August, dragged down by concerns over high production costs, weak purchasing power, and heavy rainfall and flooding in several areas, data showed on Wednesday.
The Thai industrial sentiment index dipped to 89.7 last month from 90.0 in July, as key components of the index deteriorated, led by higher operating costs and weaker orders, sales and output, according to the Federation of Thai Industries (FTI).
The decline was attributed to intense rainfall and flooding affecting production, logistics, and agricultural raw materials, while elevated energy and petrochemical feedstock prices continued to pressure manufacturing sectors, said Pimjai Leeissaranukul, chairperson of the FTI.
Pimjai said industrial operators also faced constraints from limited access to credit, weakening domestic purchasing power, notably in the automotive market, alongside intense competition from low-priced imported goods, particularly among small businesses.
Despite the softer reading, exports of technology and electronics products continued to expand on strong global demand for artificial intelligence applications. The food industry also expanded further in line with global demand, especially for processed foods and pet food, she told a news conference.
Based on a survey of 1,330 entrepreneurs across 48 industry groups conducted by the FTI, concerns heightened in several areas, especially the global economy, energy prices, and the domestic economy. Meanwhile, worries about government policy and access to credit declined.
The index forecast for the next three months stood at 97.0 in the August survey, up from 96.1 a month earlier, supported by government measures aimed at boosting investment and higher seasonal spending during the year-end festivities.
Additionally, economic stimulus programs in the final quarter of 2026, together with initiatives promoting the energy transition, are expected to be key drivers of increased fund circulation and support for broader economic activity.
However, the Middle East conflict continues to threaten production sites, raw material supply chains, and energy price stability. At the same time, Super El Nino-related weather volatility could disrupt agricultural output, raw material supplies, and industrial operations.
The group urged the government to promote local content in foreign direct investment projects by tying incentives to Thai business development, helping local suppliers upgrade and integrate into foreign supply chains. ■
