22:02:20 KST

The economy built around AI has continued to boom even as experts and leaders work to hammer out the technology's execution problem and debate the guardrails that should be put around it. Demand for AI chips remains strong, as Nvidia holds its top spot in TIME and Statista’s 2026 statistical ranking of the World’s Best Companies, highlighting top performing companies around the globe based on evaluations of employee satisfaction, revenue growth, and sustainability transparency. But new companies are also entering the scene as the AI boom reaches down the supply chain.
Companies like Wistron (no. 16), Lenovo (no. 51) and Zurich Insurance Group (no. 70) are new additions to the 2026 list. Major Nvidia supplier Wistron reports that the demand for its AI servers continues to exceed supply. The Taiwan-based manufacturing company recently opened a plant in Texas to ramp up production. Chinese computer company Lenovo, known for being a maker of devices like PCs, smartphones and tablets, saw annual profits rise to record sales driven by the newer AI server part of their business. And the wave of growing demand for physical infrastructure to support AI has created an opportunity for firms like Zurich Insurance Group to cash in on selling more data center construction-related insurance. Zurich plans to expand its dedicated insurance and risk management solution for large-scale data center projects soon into Europe and Latin America. S&P Global puts total insurable values for each data center at up to $30 billion per location.
Beyond AI, European defense technology companies are seeing cashflow as a result of European NATO allies committing in 2025 to spend a projected €800 billion on defense readiness by 2030. “The increased defense spending in Europe is actually one of the largest demand signals we have seen in generations,” says Hugues Lavandier, senior partner in McKinsey’s Aerospace & Defense Practice. A good portion of that spending is still going outside of Europe, but Lavandier “won't be surprised that we increasingly see more of that spend going to Europe for sovereignty reasons.” The war in Ukraine among other recent geopolitical tensions has shown Europe that the art of war fighting and the equipment needed is also changing. “The share of that money being spent on equipment is actually going up,” Lavandier says, especially on new technologies like drones and unmanned vehicles, and addressing technical challenges like navigation, electronic warfare, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance.
Traditional companies in the space like French defense electronics maker Thales (no. 22; up from no. 224 in 2025) and Italian defense and aerospace company Leonardo (no. 25; up from a no. 126 in 2025) are seeing uptick in orders. At the same time, “non-traditional players are entering into the field, especially as suppliers,” Lavandier says. “In particular, a number of automotive players have entered into the fray…sometimes even selling plants, making capacity available.” Thales, for example, recently announced a sovereign drone partnership with French carmaker Renault (no. 42). A number of new startups are also taking this opportunity to translate the investment into innovations, sometimes as standalone products or in partnership with other companies, similar to Anduril’s ventures in the U.S. For example, German drone-maker Quantum Systems, which is currently supplying armed forces in Ukraine, announced significant investment from German telecomm giant Deutsche Telekom (no. 7), which owns the T-mobile brand, and also announced a new partnership with Rheinmetall (no. 287) to co-create an anti-drone shield.

Meet Nazym Kyzaibay, Kazakhstan’s first female world boxing champion and Olympic bronze medallist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Nazym Kyzaibay recounts her rise from a young boxer to Central Asia’s first female three-time world boxing champion and an Olympic bronze medallist.
Nazym Kyzaibay is one of Central Asia’s leading athletes and a pioneering figure in women’s boxing in Kazakhstan.
She is a three-time world champion and a bronze medallist at the Paris 2024 Olympics. In 2026, she continues to compete internationally and has already won a World Cup stage in China.
But her journey began at a time when women’s boxing in Kazakhstan was only starting to grow.
She began her sporting career in rhythmic gymnastics, but in 2008 Kyzaibay chose boxing instead. As one of the first female boxers of her generation to make the national team, she was part of a group of athletes who helped lay the foundation for women’s boxing in Kazakhstan.
“My first competition was the Kazakhstan Championships in Almaty. I had four fights there and won the national title for the first time,” said Nazym Kyzaibay.
After winning her first national title, Kyzaibay began competing internationally.
“My first World Championship was in the junior category. I was already part of the women’s national team, but I was still very young,” she added.
“In 2011, the championship was held in Turkey, where I won bronze. Then, in 2012, I competed in the senior category in China and won another bronze medal.”
Her first breakthrough came in 2014. At the World Championships in Jeju, South Korea, Kyzaibay won a gold medal, becoming the first Kazakh woman to win a world boxing title. Two years later, she won the title again at the World Championships in Astana.
In 2024, she made her Olympic debut in Paris. She reached the semi-finals, where she lost to China’s Wu Yu. Nazym Kyzaibay took bronze, marking a historic achievement for women’s boxing in Central Asia.
Her Olympic medal was not the end of her career.
In 2025, Kyzaibay returned to the top of world boxing. At the World Championships in Serbia, she won her third world title.
Looking beyond the ring
Nazym Kyzaibay is not planning to leave competitive boxing yet. Her main goal is still Olympic gold.
“Kazakhstan does not have an Olympic gold medal in women’s boxing or a gold medal at the Asian Games yet. Winning gold is the dream of all of us on the national team,” she said.
She is also thinking about what comes after her boxing career. She says she would like to become a coach.
“I have spent so many years in boxing and gained a lot of experience. I want to share it with other athletes, especially young boxers, and help create new champions

More than EUR 21 million will go toward upgrading Dnipro's public electric transport fleet, under which the city will purchase five new trams and 15 low-floor trolleybuses, Ukraine's Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport reported Wednesday.
The purchase is being carried out under a program implemented jointly by the Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport and the Ministry of Finance.
The first five trams have already been manufactured in Dnipro by the Ukrainian producer Tatra-Yug. The new vehicles will operate, among other routes, along the city's first barrier-free route.
"Upgrading city transport has a direct impact on people's daily quality of life. In Dnipro, thanks to cooperation with the European Investment Bank, the city is getting modern low-floor trams and trolleybuses that will run on key routes, including along the first barrier-free route," said Mykola Kalashnyk, Ukraine's minister for restoration, infrastructure and transport.
He stressed that the project also supports Ukrainian manufacturing: the new trams are being built in Dnipro with up to 70% localization, and more than 100 Ukrainian enterprises are involved in the production chain.
Three more trams and maintenance equipment are planned for purchase in the next phase.
In 2026-2027, Dnipro will also receive 15 "Dnipro T-203" trolleybuses with autonomous drive capability. Once the project is complete, the share of modern low-floor trolleybuses in the city will rise to 65%.

Iceland premier calls Trump’s map ‘absurd,’ rejects sovereignty jokes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:00:22 UTC
22:00:22 KST

Melike Pala
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir on Tuesday condemned a map shared by US President Donald Trump that depicted several countries, including Iceland, as part of the US.
“In my view, the undertone of what we are seeing here is absurd,” Frostadottir said at a news conference, according to Icelandic broadcaster RUV.
"There is nothing funny or normal about making jokes about the sovereignty of states, especially today, when sovereignty cannot be taken for granted," she said, describing Trump's social media post as an "insult.”
The map showed the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean covered by the American flag, with the entire area labeled “United States of America.”
Frostadottir said the US ambassador to Iceland had been summoned to the Foreign Ministry over the post to “make it absolutely clear that, from our perspective, this was completely unacceptable.”
“No one else can decide or bargain over our independence or sovereignty. We do that on our own terms,” she added.
Iceland's Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir also reiterated Iceland's support for Greenland and said Reykjavik would continue to stand with its people.
At the same time, she said Iceland wanted to maintain cooperation with the US in areas including trade and defense.
Frostadottir said Iceland had not experienced problems in its direct relations with the US but agreed that Trump's post should not be dismissed as insignificant.

Beijing boosts Taiwan-facing firepower with brigade-level 155mm howitzer deployment
Upgrade for Eastern Theatre Command’s 71st Group Army streamlines PLA’s firepower across land and sea as US artillery programmes lag
Beijing has reinforced its military firepower facing the Taiwan Strait by deploying more 155mm PLZ-05 self-propelled howitzers, according to state media reports.
This marked the first time the PLZ-05 had been assigned at the brigade level. The powerful artillery system was originally operated at the group-army level as a long-range suppression weapon.
“For us, receiving 155mm self-propelled howitzers for the first time has significantly improved our overall combat effectiveness,” brigade officer Sun Xialong said.
Painted in brown desert camouflage, the batch of tracked howitzers appeared to have been relocated from the Western Theatre Command, which has instead received lighter, wheeled PCL-181 155mm self-propelled howitzers better suited to the plateau and mountainous terrain it covers.

Elbit Systems unveils new brand for its autonomous combat drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:00:06 UTC
22:00:06 KST

- Elbit Systems unveiled FUSE, a new portfolio uniting its autonomous drone and ground vehicle systems under software called Dominion-X.
- The technologies have logged more than 1 million flight hours and are already in service with customers in Israel, the United States and Europe.
Elbit Systems has introduced FUSE, a new business line bringing together the Israeli defense contractor’s autonomous drone and ground vehicle systems under one portfolio, the company announced September 9 in Rosh HaAyin, Israel.
FUSE centers on software called Dominion-X, which lets a single operator control multiple autonomous aircraft and ground vehicles at once, a setup Elbit calls “One2Many.” The system is built to work in GPS-denied environments, using automatic target recognition to help unmanned systems identify and track targets without relying on satellite navigation that can be jammed. Elbit first unveiled Dominion-X in February 2025, and the software has since reached Technology Readiness Level 9, the U.S. government’s top maturity rating, meaning it has been proven in real operational use rather than only in testing.
The portfolio includes several previously announced products now grouped under FUSE. Among them are the Pirani-X loitering munition drones for ambush and strike missions, ground and air robots designed to fight alongside armored vehicles, and a family of backpack-portable reconnaissance drones called X-intra, THOR and Magni-X. Elbit also folded in systems built for urban combat against fortified positions and for automated border surveillance with minimal staffing.
“Military forces are entering a new operational era in which combat effectiveness will increasingly depend not only on autonomous platforms themselves, but on the ability to integrate and coordinate large numbers of autonomous systems within existing maneuver forces in real time,” said Eyal Dahan, CEO of FUSE. “FUSE was established to deliver that capability today, combining autonomous platforms, operational AI and scalable One2Many command capabilities into integrated operational solutions that can be rapidly deployed and integrated into modern combat formations.”
Elbit says the technologies behind FUSE have logged more than 1 million flight hours in the air and over 100,000 hours of ground operation, with thousands of drones and hundreds of unmanned ground vehicles already delivered to customers. The company says FUSE systems are currently in service with military customers in Israel, the United States and Europe, though it did not name specific units, countries, or contracts.
Elbit has built earlier versions of this concept before. The company’s Legion-X program, which combines autonomous drones with the ROOK unmanned ground vehicle, has been demonstrated for missions including reconnaissance, urban warfare and casualty evacuation. FUSE appears to extend that approach into a formal product line spanning both air and ground systems.

====================================================================================================

Farage is clearly struggling – I saw that for myself. But his legacy will be a poison that runs deep | Andy Beckett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

For much of the time since Nigel Farage resumed the Reform UK leadership two long years ago, his party has been an island of relative stability in the increasingly rough sea of British politics. While other parties plunged queasily in the polls, messily purged dissidents, argued publicly about their direction and changed leaders, Farage dominated Reform UK and gave impregnably self-assured interviews. The party’s popularity moved steadily upwards, comfortably above that of all the others.
It is a paradox that a new party with wildly expectant members, not many experienced politicians and few properly worked-out policies became the pole around which the country’s political debate revolved, and yet this seemed to do no harm to Reform’s chances of winning the next general election. As with rising rightwing populist parties across the world, Reform’s tendency to make it up as it went along appeared to be not a weakness but, for many voters, much of its appeal.
That seems less the case now. Amid multiple, worsening funding scandals, and with the party openly divided about how to respond to them, this year Reform has lost about a quarter of its support and its poll lead over Labour. There are internal mutterings about the attention-seeking and leadership ambitions of its home affairs spokesperson, the relentlessly abrasive Zia Yusuf, and its Treasury spokesperson, the slippery former Tory Robert Jenrick.
Meanwhile, Farage himself, who at 62 is two decades older than them, and has been active in politics for more than 40 years, may be finally losing his composure. Interviewed by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg last weekend, after months of largely and uncharacteristically avoiding journalists, he switched between anger at his enemies, claims to victimhood and unconvincing insouciance: eyes bulging with fury one moment, head bobbing with forced laughter the next. Even by the feverish standards of modern British politics, it was a strange, almost manic performance.
What might happen to Reform and our wider politics if the party’s troubles continue and deepen? The answers may be less reassuring than Reform’s enemies like to think. While the diminishing likelihood of a Reform government is welcome, the party’s crisis could change Reform, and the forces massing further to the right of it – both in parliament and on the streets – in unpredictable and dangerous ways.
At the party’s conference last week, the mood felt brittle and volatile. Whereas speakers insisted that Reform was still a “government in waiting”, and banners, lanyards and speeches relentlessly hyped its potential “first 100 days”, the delegates I spoke to were worried about the party’s slide in the polls and general election chances, Andy Burnham’s assured start as prime minister, and the growing pressure Farage was under. After his speech was repeatedly interrupted by hecklers from the green group Climate Resistance, I overheard two delegates, mild-looking, middle-aged men in suits, discussing the protest. “It’s got to stop,” said one. The other said: “Smash ’em in the face!”
Another Reform reaction to the party’s difficulties has been to announce ever more extreme, dramatic policies, such as deporting foreign prisoners, possibly to the infamously brutal jails of El Salvador, and deploying the Royal Navy and Royal Marines to intercept and take all small boat migrants back to France, in “the biggest military operation in the English Channel since the second world war”. In his conference speech, Yusuf described “Operation Fortress” with lingering detail, while huge images of a military helicopter and warship were projected on to the set behind him, and a storm of applause came from the packed hall. Perhaps the potential for such authoritarian political theatre and performatively aggressive policy was always there in Reform, but both feel much more central to its activities now.
“All parliamentary recesses will be cancelled,” declared Farage in his speech. “Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, six days a week, until we pass the necessary legislation.” Nothing would be allowed to obstruct “the will of the people” – even though, with modern election turnouts low and half a dozen parties now competing seriously across the country, a Reform victory might represent the will of only a fifth of voters, or less.
This year, with the party losing the electoral initiative, new movements have appeared on the anti-migrant right: the even more hardline Restore Britain, and Patriot Platform, the black-clad blockaders of Dover and Portsmouth. Though Farage has criticised both groups, the latter for wearing balaclavas at their protests, the boundaries between Reform and these rivals are not as firm as he would like more mainstream rightwing Britons – whose support Reform badly needs – to think. Restore and Reform’s rhetoric and policies can be hard to distinguish, while on Monday, Yusuf visited Portsmouth and spoke amicably with Patriot Platform’s organiser, Daniel Thomas, a convicted attempted kidnapper.
Thomas told Yusuf he was upset by Farage’s criticism, and that the protests were not meant to intimidate, but that he still considered Farage a “hero” for his campaigning against the small boats. “You have done really well,” said Thomas. “A lot of people support you.” “Thank you,” said Yusuf, who listened to him at length, nodding respectfully. Then Yusuf replied: “I will take that message – you’ve got my word … take that back to him [Farage].”
The encounter suggested that Reform’s problems may create new alliances and opportunities for the hard right, reshaping but not weakening anti-migrant politics. While the Conservative shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, condemned the Portsmouth violence, he added: “People are genuinely angry at the government’s failure to stop the boats.” Even Labour dares not challenge the legitimacy of what the policing minister, Sarah Jones, called on Monday “the frustration we see in our communities today” about the boats. Just as Reform’s rise made both Labour and the Tories more nationalist and socially conservative, there is a danger that its decline, temporary or otherwise, could continue that process, as they compete for its former supporters.
If you’re opposed to Reform’s policies, and especially if you might become one of their victims, then its setbacks this year may be a relief. But that relief will only be partial while its ideas and claims remain so thoroughly embedded across politics and the media, and in many people’s everyday conversations and thinking. One day, Farage will retire, but what he represents will be even harder to stop.
- 
  Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

New study reveals how depression twists our perception of fairness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

People experiencing symptoms of depression often view social situations differently than others. A recent study found that individuals with depressive symptoms are more likely to perceive unfair financial offers as fair, but only if they consider themselves to have a high social standing. The research was published in the journal PLOS One.
Depression involves more than just a persistently low mood or a loss of interest in daily activities. It frequently brings about cognitive distortions, which are biased ways of thinking that negatively alter how a person perceives themselves and the world around them. These mental filters can change how someone evaluates risk, assesses their personal value, and judges the intentions of others in everyday social exchanges.
Researchers often use a behavioral economics task called the Ultimatum Game to study how people process fairness. In a typical version of this game, one person is given a sum of money and proposes how to divide it with a second person. The second person then decides whether to accept or reject the offer.
If the responder accepts the deal, both players keep their respective shares of the money. If they reject the offer, the money is forfeited, and neither player receives anything.
From a purely logical standpoint, a responder should accept any offer greater than zero, since walking away with a small amount of money is better than walking away with nothing. However, human behavior rarely follows strict economic logic.
Typically, people will reject highly uneven splits, such as an offer where the proposer keeps 90 percent of the money and offers only 10 percent to the responder. Participants are often willing to sacrifice their own financial gain to punish the other player for violating social norms of fairness.
This behavior, known as altruistic punishment, relies heavily on a person’s emotional state and their cognitive ability to recognize a situation as inequitable. Studies show that facing an unfair offer triggers negative emotions and activates brain regions associated with conflict and disgust.
Psychology researcher Yin Hanmo of Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia and a team of colleagues wanted to understand exactly how depression influences these decisions. Previous studies on depression and the Ultimatum Game have yielded conflicting results. Some research indicates that depressed individuals reject more offers due to heightened negative emotions, while other studies show they reject fewer offers.
The researchers suspected that a person’s subjective socioeconomic status might explain the discrepancy. Subjective socioeconomic status refers to how an individual views their own rank in society, regardless of their actual income or education level.
To test this idea, Hanmo and the research team recruited 274 university students in China and Malaysia. The participants completed a standardized questionnaire designed to measure the frequency of depressive symptoms over the past week, such as feeling sad, experiencing restless sleep, or struggling to get going.
The students also completed a widely used assessment to gauge their subjective socioeconomic status. They looked at an image of a 10-rung ladder representing where people stand in society. The top rungs represented people with the most money, most education, and best jobs. Participants selected the rung that best matched their own perceived position.
Next, the participants played a modified, paper-based version of the Ultimatum Game. They received a list of 18 proposed monetary splits from anonymous partners. Some of the offers were equal, splitting the money evenly down the middle, while other offers were highly skewed in favor of the proposer.
For each proposed split, the participants had to choose whether to accept or reject the deal. They also rated the perceived fairness of each offer on a scale from one to seven, with one being very unfair and seven being very fair.
The researchers found that depressive symptoms alone did not directly dictate how often a participant rejected an uneven offer. Instead, the effects of depression depended heavily on a participant’s self-reported social standing.
Among individuals who ranked themselves high on the social ladder, having higher levels of depression was associated with viewing unequal offers as more fair. Because these individuals perceived the bad deals as relatively fair, they were subsequently less likely to reject them.
This pattern did not appear among participants who placed themselves lower on the social ladder. For these individuals, experiencing depressive symptoms did not alter their perception of unequal offers. Consequently, their likelihood of rejecting a bad deal remained unchanged regardless of their depression levels.
The researchers suggest that differing baseline expectations may drive this divergence. People who feel they have a high social status generally expect to be treated equitably and with respect. When they face a highly unequal financial offer, the gap between their expectations and reality creates psychological friction.
The authors propose that individuals with both high social standing and depressive symptoms might subconsciously cope with this friction by rationalizing the bad offer. By mentally reframing the unequal split as acceptable, they can avoid the emotional distress of acknowledging unfair treatment. This cognitive reappraisal acts as a defense mechanism, reducing immediate discomfort but ultimately leading to skewed financial decisions.
In contrast, people who view themselves as lower on the social ladder may frequently encounter systemic disadvantages and social inequality. Because they do not expect strict equity in the same way, an unequal offer does not trigger the same intense psychological conflict. As a result, depression does not force them to artificially adjust their perception of fairness to cope with the situation.
The current study focused on university students experiencing varying levels of depressive symptoms, rather than patients clinically diagnosed with a major depressive disorder. Studies involving clinical populations have occasionally found that severe depression leads to higher rejection rates in the Ultimatum Game. The regulatory mental strategies that cause people to rationalize bad offers might break down as depressive symptoms become more severe, leaving patients overly sensitive to unfairness.
Additionally, the researchers measured subjective social standing rather than objective financial metrics like household income or accumulated wealth. Because university students typically share similar educational environments and do not yet have established careers, their sense of social status might function differently than it would in older adults in the workforce.
Future studies will need to test whether objective income levels produce similar effects on financial decision-making. Researchers also hope to measure participants’ baseline expectations of fairness directly to confirm whether expectation violations drive these behavioral shifts.
The study, “Subjective socioeconomic status moderates depression’s impact on fairness perception in the ultimatum game: A moderated mediation model,” was authored by Yin Hanmo, Rozainee Khairudin, Shi Yixin, Zhang Xi, Chen Xinyu, Syakirien Yusoff, and Nasrudin Subhi.

Israel’s grip on American politics is finally being questioned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The only good thing that has come out of the Iran war is that it is OK to say that Israel dragged us into a (stupid, hateful) war, and that Israel and its lobby work against the American people’s interest.
Kamala Harris says so. Trump “got pulled into it [the war with Iran] by Bibi Netanyahu, let’s be clear about that”,” she said this spring.
So does Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan. Israel is “taking us to a war we don’t need to fight.”
The facts are out there. The New York Times exposed Netanyuahu’s presence in the White House situation room in the weeks before Israel launched the illegal war. And Joe Kent resigned as Trump’s counterterrorism director saying that Israeli officials packaged intelligence for Trump officials.
So Israel helped convince Trump to go to war, with disastrous consequences for the world and civilian life.
Two questions arise from this awful revelation. How long has this been going on? And why does Israel and its lobby have such power? The answers are, A long time, and, Money in politics.
How far back does Israeli influence in American politics go?
As to the history, we are at last entering an era where the mainstream is investigating Israel’s sway over foreign policy. The public and even Democratic Party leaders are (finally) so angry over Israel’s slaughter and persecution of Palestinians that they are willing to hear the facts of Israel’s nullification of American policy.
New York Magazine and the New Yorker have investigated the Biden administration’s supplication to Israel in 2023-2024 as it perpetrated a genocide in Gaza—blatant violations of law that surely played a role in Kamala Harris’s ignominious defeat (and that have damaged the reputations of Biden, Tony Blinken and Samantha Power).
Israel tried to drag us into war with Iran back in the Obama administration, Hillary Clinton now confesses.
“When I was secretary [of state] it was a constant theme by Netanyahu and his then government, the then Defense Minister Ehud Barak, the former prime minister. It was relentless. It was a constant push,” Clinton told David Remnick at the 92d Street Y. “He would basically say, “You need to support us in attacking Iran.”
(Yes, reread Jeffrey Goldberg’s 2010 piece in the Atlantic promoting an American attack on Iran because he believed as “a near-certainty” that Israel was about to act alone. Bullshit.)
And what about the Iraq war?
Twenty years ago Walt and Mearsheimer wrote that the Israel lobby pushed the Iraq war against U.S. interests, and they were denounced and censored. Jeffrey Goldberg smeared the scholars at the Center for Jewish History, saying, “Jews start all wars.” But a new book, “Israel’s Lobby: America in the Grip of a Foreign Power,” by Eli Clifton and Ian Lustick echoes that assertion, and it’s being promoted by the Nation.
The best thing Rahm Emanuel has done in his apparent presidential run is say there has been zero accountability for the Iraq war. “You had an Iraq war that was built on a lie. Thousands of people lost their lives and are maimed for life. We spent a trillion dollars, and everybody accountable for that lie never faced one day of either career or professional justice,” he said on CNN.
The failure of anyone to pay a price for advocating that calamity is a big reason behind the institutional breakdown in our society. The center does not hold– because the center authored a massive blunder that killed hundreds of thousands. And the Best and the Brightest have carried on being the Best and the Brightest.
Netanyahu and AIPAC both pushed the Iraq war, and many influential Americans pushed it for Israel. Tom Friedman said he wanted to “smash” something in the Arab world because of suicide bombings in TelAviv.
Jerrold Nadler said the neocons had the delusion of rearranging the Middle East for peace in Israel. Joe Klein said the same. Tom Friedman also said if you’d have put 25 neocons on a desert island the war would never have happened.
Let’s go back further. Our support for Israel was a factor in Al Qaeda’s decision to attack the United States on September 11. Osama bin Laden and some suicide bombers said that the Israeli occupation of Palestine angered them. But you were not allowed to say so publicly. Pro-Israel voices did all they could to censor that view, including in the official 9/11 report, which all but dismissed the idea.
The Israel lobby destroyed the two-state solution. Again and again it twisted our leaders’ arms to make sure that Israel could continue the war crime of moving civilians into occupied territory (the settlements) without any consequences. George W. Bush overlooked the colonization of Jerusalem at the urging of the late Sheldon Adelson. Obama began his administration stating that settlements must end, but soon reneged on that promise under the pressure of Netanyahu and the lobby.
Obama got the clear political message that presidents who took on Israel – Jimmy Carter and George H.W. Bush – didn’t get a second term. (Even Tom Friedman agrees with me on that point.)
Let’s keep going back. It is arguable that our policy on Israel may have resulted in the murder of Robert F. Kennedy in 1968 (a new book by the eminent scholar Michael Fischbach says so) and there are journalists on the internet who say that John Kennedy was killed because he tried to stop Israel from getting nuclear power (I don’t find this argument convincing, but LBJ’s flipflop on nukes is a significant undertold story).
Most importantly, State Department officials warned in 1947-48 that establishing a Jewish state in the Middle East would create regional unrest for generations. They were right. And though it is true that Arab states said they would recognize Israel 50 years later, if a Palestinian state was established, what took the U.S. 11 minutes in Israel’s case – recognizing a state – has forever eluded Palestinians, even as their families are bombed mercilessly and they are forced off their lands.
Has support for Israel finally become toxic?
On to Question two. Why has the U.S. gone against its own people’s interest to support Israel endlessly?
No doubt there are many reasons. The shadow of the Holocaust gave an enormous historical moment to the U.N.’s decision to resolve the “Jewish Question” in Europe by setting up a Jewish state. Liberal American political culture continues to carry that historical burden. There is also the realpolitik idea that Israel was an important ally in geopolitical struggles. But that claim has evaporated. Israel is today distracting the U.S. from its goal of pivoting to Asia/Chinese strategy, as Eli Clifton said on a Nation podcast.
The chief reason for nullification of the U.S.’s own policy is factional influence, the Israel lobby, using the lever of money. Truman got into office thanks to the generous donation of pro-Israel donors, according to historians, and the lobby pushed him to overcome his opposition to a religious state. Obama credited his political rise in Chicago to a “cabal” of generous liberal Zionists. And Netanyahu forced Obama’s collapse on settlements in 2011-12 by deploying the “leadership of the American Jewish community”, who in turn used the lever of big donors, Obama’s top foreign policy aide said.
Trump destroyed the Iran deal and moved the embassy to Jerusalem in all-but-frank deference to his biggest donor, Adelson.
Biden and Harris ignored a genocide for the same reason. The weight of the Jewish community’s contributions to Democratic campaigns is “gigantic” and “shocking,” as a J Street panel stated in 2016—and that redounds to the strength of the Israel lobby. One of the first places a congressional candidate goes to raise money is the Jewish community, Stephanie Schriock of Emily’s List reported at that event. “But before you went to the Jewish community, you had a conversation with the lead AIPAC person in your state and they made it clear that you needed a paper on Israel.”
The key fact about Israel lobby contributions is that they’re not party-loyal. They are up for grabs. There are always “threats that the money could go elsewhere,” as Clifton stated on the Nation broadcast. The lobby abandoned George H.W. Bush for Clinton in the ‘92 presidential election because Clinton ran to Bush’s right on settlements. Haley Stevens just spent a staggering $60 million in the Democratic primary she lost to Abdul el-Sayed in Michigan, and at least half that money was from pro-Israel donors—and there is now fear among Democrats that Michigan Jews will abandon the party for the Republican candidate in the general election because of Israel.
That’s why Biden and Harris said nothing about a genocide in 2023 and 2024. They feared that the lobby money would go to the other side.
Those days are ending. A genocide and an illegal war foisted on the U.S. have exposed Israel’s political reach, and made Israel a pariah nation. AIPAC is such a dirty word in politics that even El-Sayed’s Republican opponent is said to have sought distance from the lobby. Over 100 Democratic congresspeople seek an end to U.S. aid to the apartheid state, and heroes like Zohran Mamdani have demonstrated that you can win powerful office while insisting on BDS (boycott divestment and sanctions targeting war crimes).
Most critically, the Jewish community is fracturing. (Yes I know, I’ve predicted this forever). A privileged, educated liberal cohort in American life is at last ashamed of Israel’s conduct and examining our community’s organizational role in forcing U.S. political obeisance to war crimes.
Yes, it’s about time. And generations of Palestinians have paid the price.

A Stealth Startup Thinks It Just Hacked the Memory Shortage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

An ambitious chip startup that has spent more than seven years quietly trying to redesign the architecture for computer memory has just come out of stealth mode and believes its new approach can help ease the global memory-chip shortage—provided it can produce its technology at scale.
Kepler Computing, a San Jose, California–based startup founded in 2018 by a team of physicists and computer scientists, says it has developed a new architecture for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) that directly addresses some of the chip supply bottlenecks that are constraining the computing market.
While chipmakers typically rely on expensive extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUV) to shrink the transistors on a chip, thereby packing more technology into the same amount of space, Kepler claims that its “3D stacking” approach and a proprietary new material allow it to increase density without relying on EUV at all—and it can work with existing semiconductor fabrication plants.
Kepler says it has made similar gains for the high-speed cache memory typically used in CPUs, GPUs, and XPUs. This so-called SRAM sits within the core of a chip die in order to cut down on data transfer times. HBM, by contrast, uses stacks of DRAM, which is a separate memory component of chips.
The company has raised $468 million in funding over the past few years from big-name backers. This includes GlobalFoundries, Intel Capital, AMD Ventures, the British investment fund Baillie Gifford, and Bill Gates, through his private Gates Frontier fund. In July, the US Department of Commerce committed to give Kepler up to $245 million to “develop in the US a new class of high-performance AI memory technology, enabled by innovative 3D and ferroelectric technologies.”
For now, much of Kepler’s testing is happening in Singapore, which is where GlobalFoundries—a manufacturing partner and investor of $50 million—has a facility. Over the past two years Kepler has been building out what it refers to as “mini fabs,” where it produces its memory chips in conjunction with Global Foundries’ 28-nanometer chips. (It has also been running tests in GlobalFoundries’ facilities in Burlington, Vermont.)
Kepler and its investors say the startup’s new approach to building memory chips couldn’t come at a better time. The global memory chip shortage has reaffirmed at least two realities about the market: Building new fabs is hugely expensive and painstaking, and the demands around certain kinds of memory tend to be cyclical. In a data-center-driven, AI-crazed world, HBM has become the memory du jour.
Some of the world’s leading memory makers, including SK Hynix and Micron, have been racing to build multibillion-dollar fabs in order to meet demand, wagering that even by the time those facilities are operational, the industry will still be looking for high-bandwidth memory.
“For a long time our thinking was that we’d work on SRAM first and then follow up with DRAM and HBM,” says Debo Olaosebikan, a Kepler Computing cofounder and its chief executive officer. “But with the launch of ChatGPT [in 2022] and the explosion of demand for an HBM alternative, we started working on our HBM road map. Now we’re making SRAM and HBM in parallel.”
“We didn’t go in thinking that this would be a replacement for DRAM or a replacement for SRAM,” says Srini Ananth, managing director at Intel Capital. “We figured the market would dictate that, and now you’re seeing a demand for both.”
In bypassing ultraviolet lithography, Kepler is one of a few tech startups working to avoid one of the major bottlenecks in semiconductor manufacturing. The startup claims it can produce SRAM that achieves the same density as 2-nanometer or 3-nanometer chips without having to invest in EUV.
“Kepler’s approach is at the sweet spot of our strategy,” says Ed Kaste, senior vice president of GlobalFoundries’ CMOS business. “It’s a new materials system, with multigenerational scaling potential, without having to build entirely new systems in the fab or invest in very expensive lithography equipment.”
Material Impact
Kepler’s overarching pitch is that the accelerated computing market shouldn’t have to wait for brand-new memory fabs to be built in order to meet demand. Instead, new approaches to building memory within existing fabs can increase supply.
Their approach is twofold. In terms of improving HBM, Kepler says it has developed a novel 3D-manufacturing technique that fits more memory chips within a fixed footprint. The core compute can then sit closer to the memory, so the data travel between the two uses less energy. Their ultimate goal is to move data around in HBM with the amount of energy that’s comparable to SRAM, all while keeping HBM’s large capacity.
Kepler also says it has improved the density of SRAM using ferroelectrics, which can read and write data at lower voltages than the mechanisms typically used to process and store data in semiconductors. The startup did this by developing a new, low-voltage, composite material that works with this ferroelectric approach.
Sasi Manipatruni, a Kepler cofounder and its chief technology officer, says the Kepler team went through 35 iterations of composites before they landed on a material class that they thought would make memory chips easier and cheaper to make.
“Once we found a way to solve the physics problem—as in the physical limitations for HBM—we came up with a material innovation that helps with the amount of memory you can have between chips,” he says.
In its early build-outs with GlobalFoundries, Kepler says it was able to convert a fab into a “next-generation” fab in just eight months, compared to a typical 24-month timeframe.
“Out goal is to take the fabs and architectures already built, and push them to the limits of physics,” Olaosebikan says.
Basically Kepler is betting that any additional costs that come from new materials or retooling existing fabs would far outweigh the $20 billion to $40 billion it costs to build new ones and outfit them with equipment worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
Waiting to Scale
Kepler Computing still has a long road ahead before it reaches full-scale production—assuming it gets there. To date, the company has run its technology on around 2,000 wafers. The startup says it’s planning to ship its first samples of HBM chips later this year, ramp up production out of Singapore next year, and start chip production in the US in 2028.
Kaste, the GlobalFoundries executive, says he’s confident that the “fundamental breakthroughs have happened. What remains is getting good results on thousands of wafers and millions of devices.”
He points out that one of the challenges with a material system like the one Kepler is using is that it includes iron in its composite. “Iron is a tough contaminant to introduce into a production facility. So Kepler’s solution has to run on dedicated equipment, or be fully encapsulated so that it can’t escape,” he says.
“The art is in keeping that material really well isolated through our production flow,” Kaste says.
Olaosebikan wouldn’t confirm the specific elements of the company’s composite material. “What I can say is, we’re using a small number of materials, and some of them aren’t what you’d typically find in mainstream ferroelectrics,” he says.
Kepler Computing isn’t the only startup looking to upend the semiconductor industry. Late last year, a well-funded startup called Substrate also made waves for its new approach to lithography, which uses nanoparticles to etch details onto advanced chips. Some industry analysts were skeptical of the startup’s ambitions, noting that it would be extremely difficult for Substrate to produce a large number of chips “that meet incredibly stringent specifications, on time and on budget,” as reported in Bloomberg.
Scale is a common challenge when attempting to innovate semiconductor manufacturing, whether with new processes, materials, or some combination of both. “The question is how to overcome all the limitations of contamination, different materials, and different tooling, in such a way that the resulting innovation can be used at scale and is worth the cost,” says Austin Lyons, a chip analyst for Creative Strategies, who was not briefed on Kepler’s innovation.
Proving out a new method for memory is one thing; meeting the historic demand for it will be another altogether.

Albania, Hong Kong and Egypt tipped as the trending destinations to watch in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

New data predicts which destinations are tipped to take off in 2027, with major sporting events and a spectacular solar eclipse also set to shape where travellers choose to go next year.
Are you already dreaming of trips in 2027, but aren’t sure where to go? New data has revealed the top trending destinations for the upcoming year, and it makes for interesting reading.
Statistics from Advantage Travel Partnership, a UK-based consortium of independent travel businesses, have tipped Albania as the destination to watch for 2027, thanks in part to its stunning beaches and solid value for money.
Further afield, the data showed that Hong Kong, Egypt and Vietnam are likely to be popular next year, too.
The findings show that the busy sporting calendar will have a significant influence on travel in 2027, with the Ryder Cup in Ireland, the FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil, and the Men’s Rugby World Cup in Australia set to drive bookings.
The solar eclipse in North Africa and Spain is also attracting plenty of interest from astronomy-loving travellers.
Summer 2026 booking trends
The travel body’s data also looked at trends from this year, which could well influence 2027’s patterns.
For British travellers, Spain came out on top in summer 2026, with Tenerife, Mallorca and the Costa Blanca revealed as the most popular short-haul destinations. Lanzarote, the Costa del Sol and Antalya in Türkiye were also popular options for shorter-haul trips.
In terms of long-haul travel, New York, Orlando, Jamaica and Thailand topped the charts of the most booked destinations.
Due to the conflict in the Middle East, travellers who would originally have visited that region opted instead for trips to the USA, the Caribbean and the Far East. The USA saw a further boom in visitors thanks to World Cup fever.
While family holiday bookings dipped around Easter, likely because of the conflict, they were up some 5% in the summer and in the October school break, too.
Touring holidays gain popularity
The data showed that touring holidays – trips where you travel along a planned route through a region or country, moving from place to place to see multiple destinations rather than staying in just one spot – were a major area of growth from 2025 to 2026.
South Africa, Kenya and Japan have been particularly popular as long-haul destinations as travellers hunt for experiences centred around wildlife, culture and exploration.
Closer to home, Italy, France and Spain were seen to be leading the short-haul touring market.
“Touring has been a real growth story for us in 2026. People are looking beyond a traditional fly-and-flop holiday and increasingly want to see and experience a destination properly,” John Sullivan, Commercial Director at Advantage, said.
For next year, he tipped China, Indonesia and South America as destinations to watch.
In 2025, China eased entry restrictions for citizens from 74 countries – including many European nations – who can now enter the country for up to 30 days without a visa.
That move, Sullivan said, will help to “shine the light on the incredible cuisine, culture and nature of the expansive country”.

"The longer Moscow sees hesitation, the more it will try. The task is to change that calculation," the foreign minister concluded.

AfD election victory in Saxony-Anhalt warning, not turning point for Germany – expert
Pavel Havlíček, a research fellow at the Association for International Affairs (Prague), said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
The expert urged against talking about “catastrophic scenarios” for Germany and called for taking into account the specific circumstances of the country’s eastern regions.
“The strong performance of populist and far-right forces is linked to local problems, including depopulation, economic difficulties, and demographic challenges,” Havlíček said.
He added that this was a warning sign for the central government and major political parties, particularly the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), whose support has seen a noticeable decline.
“However, Germany’s parliamentary system remains considerably more stable. The main area of risk at present is the regional (state-level) jurisdiction over the media, education, and security services, where regional authorities have significant influence,” the analyst explained.
As reported, elections to the state parliament (Landtag) were held in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. The far-right AfD won 44.4% of the vote, securing 39 of the 83 seats and significantly outperforming the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which lost substantial support and received 17.2%.
Despite its victory, the AfD failed to secure the absolute majority needed to form a government on its own.

Trump hails AfD win in Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt
U.S. President Donald Trump has congratulated Alternative for Germany (AfD) Tuesday for its landslide victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right party won nearly 44 percent of the votes on Sunday.
“Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, Politico reported. “They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly.” He concluded his message with a German variant of his Make America Great Again acronym, “MGGA!!!”
It is unusual for a sitting U.S. president to comment on German state elections, however the Trump administration has cultivated close ties with the AfD. U.S. Vice President JD Vance met the party’s co-leader Alice Weidel at the Munich Security Conference in February 2025 and criticized Germany’s “firewall” against the party. AfD officials visited the White House later that year, and senior Trump allies and administration figures have repeatedly backed the party.
Despite these extensive ties, AfD leaders have sought to distance themselves from the Trump administration over concerns that the U.S. president’s unpopularity in Germany could turn into an electoral liability.
AfD scored a historic victory in Saxony-Anhalt’s state election on Sept. 6, winning 43.8 percent of the vote — more than twice its 2021 result. It grants the party 39 of the 83 seats in the state parliament, leaving it three seats short of an outright majority and raising the prospect of Germany’s first far-right state government since World War II.
The right-wing party advocates a sharply restrictive immigration policy, alongside a nationalist and socially conservative agenda. It also opposes further military support for Ukraine, calls for an end to sanctions on Russia and closer ties with Moscow.
Trump’s praise has already sparked a backlash in Berlin. Dirk Wiese, the chief whip in the Bundestag of the center-left Social Democratic Party — the coalition partners of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, said Trump’s comments were “not acceptable.” He added: “I don’t think we can put up with that, at least as the federal government.”

Why the South Korea-US Alliance Needs the Dark Eagle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:58:00 UTC
21:58:00 KST

Rumors about the United States potentially deploying its Multi-Domain Task Force (MDTF) and the “Dark Eagle” hypersonic weapon to the Korean Peninsula are sparking predictable anxieties. Given the fierce economic and political backlash South Korea endured after hosting the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system in 2016, it is easy to see why critics are sounding the alarm. They argue that bringing in offensive hypersonic missiles will simply turn South Korea into a pawn in the broader China-U.S. rivalry.
But focusing strictly on China’s anxieties and possible reaction misses a far more urgent reality: South Korea faces an existential, rapidly accelerating threat from North Korea’s evolving military capabilities.
War is no longer just fought on land, at sea, or in the air; it spills over into space, cyberspace, and the electromagnetic spectrum. The MDTF is built for this new reality. The task force is not just another conventional weapon to park on a base. It is a theater-level tool designed to blind an adversary’s radars, sever their communications, and seize control of the battlefield almost instantly.
The star of the MDTF is the Dark Eagle. According to the U.S. Army, this hypersonic glide vehicle boasts a range of over 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles). What makes it genuinely disruptive is not just its speed – exceeding Mach 15 – but its unpredictability. Unlike traditional ballistic missiles that follow a standard, trackable arch, the Dark Eagle skims the upper atmosphere at altitudes of 30 to 50 kilometers. By flying this low and fast, it slips beneath the sightlines of ground-based early warning radars and easily bypasses legacy air defense systems.
For the Korean Peninsula, this technology rewrites the rules of deterrence. Over the past few years, North Korea has aggressively shifted toward solid-fuel ballistic missiles and mobile launchers. This means Pyongyang can roll a missile out of a tunnel and fire it in roughly 10 to 15 minutes. Older weapons, like Tomahawk cruise missiles, simply fly too slowly to eliminate these targets before they launch.
The Dark Eagle solves this timing crisis. If stationed in South Korea, it could obliterate command bunkers in Pyongyang or missile sites across the country in minutes. Even if launched from bases in Guam or Japan, the weapon would reach its target in roughly 10 minutes. This speed fundamentally shifts the strategic calculus. Knowing that a U.S. hypersonic weapon can strike the origin point of an attack almost instantly guts the logic of a surprise launch. It renders North Korea’s deeply buried nuclear bunkers highly vulnerable, serving as a visceral deterrent against miscalculation by leadership in Pyongyang.
Naturally, positioning an offensive weapon like a hypersonic missile in Northeast Asia is going to ruffle feathers. If THAAD was a shield, the Dark Eagle is undoubtedly a spear. But Seoul cannot afford to abandon the precise, asymmetric deterrence that modern weapons provide simply because of diplomatic friction with China.
Furthermore, the deployment of the MDTF would offer a strategic benefit: silencing the recurring political chatter in Washington about drawing down U.S. Forces Korea (USFK). Committing a flagship, next-generation asset to the peninsula would be ironclad proof that the United States is willing to project its most advanced military capabilities to defend South Korea.
The conversation needs to move past the rigid binary of either unconditionally hosting the MDTF forever or rejecting it out of sheer geopolitical panic. Washington and Seoul need a strategy that bolsters defense while managing diplomatic fallout. Instead of rushing into a permanent deployment, the two nations should establish a joint working group of experts and military officials to map out the logistics and political implications.
A smart first step would be a limited, rotational deployment of the MDTF during upcoming combined military exercises. This would allow both militaries to test how the Dark Eagle integrates into existing defense networks without the permanence that triggers regional crises. A phased, transparent approach buys Seoul the time it needs to build public consensus while offering diplomatic space to reassure neighbors that the weapon is meant to stabilize the region, not upend it.
Ultimately, the debate over the Dark Eagle is about much more than a single weapon system. It is a crucial test of how the U.S.-South Korea alliance is adapting to the unpredictable, multidomain threats of the 21st century. It is time approach the situation with strategic clarity, ensuring both the strength of the alliance and lasting peace on the Korean Peninsula.

US Patriot Batteries Go Into “Machine-Gun Mode” Against Iranian Ballistic Missile Attack, Video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:57:12 UTC
21:57:12 KST

- Category
- World
US Patriot Batteries Go Into “Machine-Gun Mode” Against Iranian Ballistic Missile Attack, Video
US-operated Patriot batteries may have fired roughly 60 interceptor missiles to counter an Iranian barrage of just 20 ballistic missiles over Jordan, highlighting the enormous ammunition demands involved in defending against sustained ballistic attacks, Defense Express reported on September 9.
Iran struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan overnight, a facility used by US forces. Jordanian authorities said air defenses intercepted 18 of 20 incoming ballistic missiles, while two fell before reaching their intended targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage from the attack, however, provides an unusually revealing look at how intensely Patriot batteries were operating during the engagement.
Defense Express estimated from available videos that approximately 60 Patriot interceptors may have been launched during the defense. Claims circulating online that as many as 100 were fired appear exaggerated, the outlet noted.
Even the lower estimate would mean roughly three interceptors launched for every Iranian ballistic missile in the salvo, although the exact number of Patriot missiles fired has not been officially confirmed.
Defense Express described several Patriot batteries as effectively operating in a “machine-gun” mode as they attempted to defeat the incoming missiles.
Video from the attack also appears to show Iran using ballistic missiles carrying cluster submunitions, adding another layer of difficulty to the interception effort.
The scale of Patriot expenditure is particularly notable because the systems protecting the area are believed to be operated by US forces rather than Jordanian crews.
Jordan has never publicly declared Patriot systems as part of its own inventory. The United States, however, has deployed Patriot batteries in the country when necessary to defend US facilities and support Jordanian airspace protection.
That distinction matters, Defense Express noted.
Previous cases of unusually high Patriot interceptor consumption against Iranian ballistic attacks could potentially be explained by limited experience among foreign operators.
US air-defense personnel have already spent more than six months responding to repeated Iranian ballistic missile attacks against American military installations since the beginning of Operation Epic Fury on February 28.
The crews therefore have substantial practical experience with this particular threat environment.
If the estimate of roughly 60 Patriot interceptors is accurate, the September 9 engagement illustrates that high missile consumption may be an inherent feature of defending against modern ballistic salvos rather than simply a consequence of inexperienced operators.
For Ukraine, which relies heavily on Patriot to stop Russian ballistic missiles, the episode also underscores a familiar problem: successful air defense can consume enormous quantities of some of the world’s most expensive and difficult-to-produce interceptors in a matter of minutes.
As Defense Express noted, the question is therefore not only whether Patriot can stop ballistic missiles, but how many interceptors must be available when a sustained barrage arrives.
Earlier, reports emerged that US forces may have used as many as 96 to 128 PAC-3 interceptor missiles in a single night while defending military bases in Jordan from an Iranian ballistic missile attack—potentially consuming up to 17% of estimated US stocks.

Cambodia's floating schools hit by rising fuel costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:57:00 UTC

Cambodia's floating schools hit by rising fuel costs
September 9, 2026
Every morning, 12-year-old Soksan Set faces a journey most children his age never have to think about. Outside his home, there is no road, only water.
Soksan lives in Prek Toal, a floating community on Tonle Sap, Southeast Asia's largest freshwater lake where boats are the main means of transport. A Grade 4 student at the local primary school, he travels several kilometers on water to attend class and sometimes helps younger children along the way.
But increasingly, the biggest obstacle between Soksan and his classroom is not distance. It is fuel. His family, like many others in the commune, depends on fishing for their livelihood. When fuel prices rise, they are forced to make difficult choices.
"When gasoline prices go up, we don't have enough money to take our children to school regularly," said Soksan's father, 41-year-old Set Soeum. "We don't catch enough fish, and we need around three liters (0.8 gallons) of gasoline a day to travel long distances for fishing. Because of this, Soksan often has to miss school."
For families living on the water, rising fuel costs can quickly become a barrier to education.
Why rising fuel costs hit Cambodia's poor the hardest
Cambodia relies heavily on imported fuel, leaving households exposed to global price shocks and regional supply disruptions. The 2026 Iran war has driven up energy costs, making transport to remote communities more expensive. Around Tonle Sap, this has hit students and their families.
Gasoline prices rose 45% and diesel prices more than 70% in March, the largest single-month increase since 2008, according to the World Bank.
Gasoline currently costs 5,700 riel ($1.41, €1.21) per liter, up 26.7% from 4,500 riel a year ago, according to Global Petrol Prices.
Although Cambodia does not depend directly on the Strait of Hormuz for most of its fuel imports, it is exposed to higher global oil prices and supply disruptions affecting regional suppliers. Cambodia imports all of its petroleum products and has no domestic refining capacity.
For Soksan's family, the pressure is felt both on the fishing boat and the school boat. Some days, they borrow money to buy gasoline. On other days, they cut back on food, clothing or school supplies.
"Five students collect money to buy gasoline, sometimes just one liter at a time," Soksan said. When they cannot afford even that, they row themselves. "We row the boat ourselves. It can take up to an hour, but we still try to go to school," he noted.
On the Tonle Sap, 12-year-old Siyien Ly walks more than 30 minutes to school during the dry season. When flooding makes the roads impassable, she relies on an aid-supported school boat. Some of her classmates have stopped attending, because their families cannot afford the cost of transport.
"Even though fuel prices are rising, we still keep trying to come to school because education is important for our future," Siyien said.
Siyien's family of six has four children in school. Her mother, Kunthea Chin, now sells sugarcane juice after Siyien's father developed serious hearing problems following a water-related accident.
Kunthea said that her daily income has fallen by around half from about $20 to around $10 while the cost of supplies has risen. The family spends around $150 a month on fuel, which they need for both the children's transport and her business.
Taking risks to reach the classroom
Families also try to reduce costs by traveling together and sharing fuel expenses. Some have returned to traditional rowing boats. But saving money can come at the cost of safety.
When several children share a small boat, it can become crowded. During storms and heavy rain, parents worry about their children's safety on the water.
"My mother worries when too many students ride together," Siyien said.
Remote schools also depend on boats to transport teachers, textbooks, classroom materials, food and maintenance supplies. Higher fuel prices can therefore increase the cost of delivering education itself.
"For children living in floating and remote communities, access to education depends not only on having a school, but also on being able to reach it," said Samphors Vorn, country director of Action Education in Cambodia.
"When fuel prices rise, the cost of that journey rises with them. For families already living with very limited incomes, this can turn transportation into a barrier to attendance and, ultimately, to a child's right to education."
The Cambodian government has introduced measures to cushion consumers from international fuel-price increases, including fuel discounts, tax reductions and zero customs duties on fuel imports.
But subsidies at the pump cannot fully shield families whose incomes remain low and unpredictable.
Climate and economic shocks deepen education woes
In 2025, DW reported from the region on how climate change was disrupting children's education. Rising and falling water levels, extreme weather and the dangers of traveling by boat were making it harder for children in floating communities to reach school.
The challenges have since deepened.
Today, 14-year-old Nary is no longer in the classroom. She has been unable to return because of persistent headaches following health complications linked to suspected long-term meningitis.
Her younger sister, 11-year-old Naren, continues to attend Grade 2. She relies on a school boat and pays around 12 cents for the return journey.
For their family, even small costs matter. Their father, Tit Sarin, earns around $7.50 a day from traditional fishing. But traveling farther across the lake to find fish can require about six liters of fuel, costing roughly $6.60.
"When we cannot afford fuel, we have to find other work," he said.
The family then works as day laborers, picking chilies for as little as 25 cents per kilogram. For families like Nary's, climate change and rising fuel costs are now a double burden.
Nary hopes to return to learning. Her father is saving to buy a boat dedicated to shuttling his children to school and back home.

Ukraine’s Intel Hacks Russia’s Institute Behind Yars, Bulava, Iskander-M and Oreshnik Missiles

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Intel Hacks Russia’s Institute Behind Yars, Bulava, Iskander-M and Oreshnik Missiles
Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) has breached the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology (MIT), Russia's chief designer of intercontinental ballistic missiles, and identified 2,648 of its employees who it links to the killing of Ukrainians.
The operation was announced in a statement on HUR's official Telegram channel on September 9. The agency described a unique cyberspace operation inside Russia through which its specialists obtained an array of data on the corporation's structure, leadership, and current and prospective developments.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to HUR, engineers at the institute's facilities in Moscow and other Russian regions produce the drawings, software, engines, and control units for several of Russia's core strategic systems:
- the Yars (RS-24) intercontinental ballistic missile, a central component of Russia's nuclear forces;
- the mobile Topol-M (RT-2PM2) intercontinental missile system;
- the Bulava (R-30), a three-stage missile designed for submarines;
- the Iskander-M operational-tactical missile complex;
- the Kedr, also known as the Oreshnik, Russia's newest hypersonic ballistic system.
HUR added that the institute also develops satellite communications for the Russian army, including a system for rapidly deploying military satellites into low orbit to provide Russian forces with a resilient, protected command-and-control network.
The agency noted work on the Start-1M conversion launch vehicle, which could let Moscow deploy low-orbit satellite constellations for optical-electronic and radar reconnaissance, alongside a scalable space platform designated Typoryad.
The Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology is at the center of Russia's strategic missile industry, with subordinate enterprises including the Prozhektor design bureau, the Vympel machine-building plant, the Votkinsk Plant, and the Iskra enterprise.
Among the people identified, HUR named the corporation's director general, reserve Lieutenant General Sergey Ponomarev, along with his deputies Yuri Kirillov, Yuri Solomonov, Andrey Bashirov, Artyom Khrebin, and Sergey Solonichkin.
HUR stated that the material would be used to weaken Russia's capacity to wage its war against Ukraine and to hold those tied to war crimes accountable.
The corporation has surfaced before as the endpoint of sanctioned supply chains. Computer-controlled machine tools traced through Chinese intermediaries—including controllers built by Germany's Siemens and Heidenhain and Japan's Fanuc—reached the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology despite export bans intended to deny Moscow access to the technology.
Roughly 70% of the CNC machines operating in Russia are imported, and as much as 80% of that equipment goes to the military.
The machinery has sharpened the accuracy and lethality of missiles such as the nuclear-capable Oreshnik, first fired at Ukraine on November 21, 2024.

Wes Streeting praises Wargame docudrama for highlighting UK defence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:55:55 UTC
21:55:55 KST

A docudrama depicting a Russian attack on a Britain led by an unlikely pairing of Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon has been praised by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, for writing “my spending review submission”.
The Wargame, due to be broadcast on Sky this month, features a string of former politicians advised by ex-securocrats, grappling with an unusually powerful Moscow, while highlighting limitations in the British military.
It features Gove, who was a Conservative minister for more than a decade, as prime minister – a job he unsuccessfully ran for in 2016 – and Sturgeon, the former first minister and leader of the Scottish National party, as his deputy, in a mock Downing Street Cobra emergency situation room.
Labour figures involved in the production include the former Scotland secretary Jim Murphy as foreign secretary, as well as Harriet Harman and the peer Ayesha Hazarika, who plays the role of director of communications in the embattled team.
After a preview screening at the National Gallery in central London, with many of the former politicians present, Streeting quipped: “On behalf of the association of UK defence secretaries, thank you for my spending review submission.”
Though the war depicted was of “a low likelihood, albeit high impact”, Streeting said he anticipated the show would stimulate public debate on defence spending, currently planned to rise by about £30bn by 2035.
Streeting said The Wargame would “play a role in making people think about where they would put defence in the order of priorities as voters”, though he added that wildfires, floods and other natural disasters should also prompt the public to think how they would be able to cope in a crisis.
The scale of the cash increase, pushed for by the US president Donald Trump but signed up to by the UK and other Nato allies, is such that it would require taxes or borrowing to be raised, or substantial cuts from other government spending after the next election.
The five-part programme is a spin-off from a Sky News podcast presented by the journalist Deborah Haynes, who has helped to develop the television show. “We want our country to understand better what the threat is, what credible defence is”, she said.
Producers said a series of incidents involving Russian sabotage in the UK and Europe had made the programme more relevant. During filming in mid-June, a Russian frigate south of the Isle of Wight unexpectedly fired warning shots near an approaching pleasure yacht in the Channel, terrifying a British couple onboard.
Gove – who was a minister between 2010 and 2024 – said it had come as a surprise to him how limited Britain’s missile defence capability was during filming, an issue highlighted in the show. “For anyone watching, they will think: ‘WTF. How did we get into that situation?’” It was, he said, “quite sobering” for somebody who had been in government for as long as he had, though he had not been a defence minister.
A succession of cuts to defence spending made by Conservative and Labour governments from the end of the cold war until the early part of the decade have reduced defence investment and left the navy struggling to deploy warships and submarines.
Since then, there has been a growing consensus across the centre of British politics for increased defence spending. Though Russia remains fully engaged in its war in Ukraine, Moscow retains the ability to conduct cyber, sabotage and disinformation operations in the UK.
Sturgeon said the programme could help dispel “the optimism bias that this won’t happen”. Gove said: “I never thought I would say this, but I agree 100% with Nicola”.
- 
  The Wargame airs on Sky One from 21 September

Five inburgering exam myths, tested against real exams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:55:34 UTC
21:55:34 KST

Partner content
Five inburgering exam myths, tested against real exams
A lot of people preparing for the inburgeringsexamen run into advice: “pick the longest answer”, “choose B if you are stuck”, “expect it to get harder as you go up a level”. Most of it is passed on in good faith. Almost none of it has ever been checked. Inburgeringscursus.nl coded 881 questions from 35 official exam sets – three years of the Staatsexamen NT2 plus the DUO practice exams.
Here are the myths that came up most often:
“Pick the answer with words you recognise from the text”
 This is the most repeated piece of exam advice there is and it does not hold up against the data. We checked it on 288 reading questions. In four of them there was exactly one option that shared words with the text. The rest of the time it pointed at two or three answers at once.
The reason is simple once you see it. The most common wrong answer quotes the text accurately and then answers a different question. Both the right answer and the wrong ones borrow words from the passage, roughly 86% against 95%. A feature that shows up in nearly every option cannot tell them apart.
“Answer B is more often correct”
 This one looked real. Across 176 items B came up more often than chance and it held up under statistical checking. So we tested it on all the available exams and there it landed at 31.7%. That is what guessing gets you.
Even if it had been true, it would not have helped. Answering B every time scores between 10 and 19 points across the six exams we measured. The pass mark is 24. It does not pass a single one. So when in doubt, choosing “B” is not the safe bet.
“The exam gets steadily harder from A2 to B1 to B2”
 Half true. The half that is wrong matters if you are planning your study time.
 A2 really is a different exam from B1. But B1 and B2 do not separate cleanly. The individual exams overlap, and the gap between them is relatively small.
There are two groups here, not three steps on a ladder. Moving from B1 to B2 is a smaller jump than the label suggests. Moving from A2 to B1 is the real one.
“The reading exam is the same task from start to finish”
 Not true, and this is the most useful thing we found. It applies to the Staatsexamen NT2 at B1 and B2 level.
Above every reading text sits one line of instruction. Five of them say roughly the same thing: “Answer the question”. The last one says something different: “read the question first, then find the answer in the text”.
That line appeared on the final text of every exam we looked at, 34 items out of 34, across six exams at B1 and B2. And there the answer sits almost word for word in the text 47% of the time. Everywhere else it is 9%. The exam board is telling you to stop reading and start searching.
One warning. It is not the easy section. Half-correct answers appear twice as often there, 24% against 12%. In 13 of those 34 items the information you need sits in two separate articles. The difficulty moves from understanding to locating. Searching faster without checking is how you walk into it.
“KNM is mostly about Dutch customs and etiquette”
 Not really. KNM covers eight themes across 40 questions, and they are nowhere near equal in size. Work and income runs to eight or nine questions. Institutions get seven. Together they are about 40% of the exam. Manners and education get three each.
This held across all official practice exams. It tells you where to start, not where to stop. Those two themes leave 60% elsewhere, and the pass mark is well above that.
Why we counted all this
 Patterns like these are only useful if you can practise them. That is what Inburgeringscursus.nl is for: an online course for the inburgeringsexamen and the Staatsexamen NT2. The platform is built on this research so you practice exactly what the real exams ask of you.
It covers all five parts at A2, B1 and B2. It starts with theory on what each part asks, then you move on to practice questions that follow the real patterns and finally the mock exams. These mock exams are timed and marked on the official criteria. The practice never runs out either. You generate new questions yourself whenever you want them, on exactly the points you keep getting wrong. This way you can practise until you know you are ready instead of hoping you are.
