France co-hosts major space summit with Germany despite US firms' withdrawals and Merz absence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:53:55 UTC
20:53:55 KST

France is co-hosting a major space summit with Germany this week, as Europe finds itself at a strategic crossroads.
Astronauts, heads of state, as well as major economic players in the space industry united in Paris on Wednesday for the international space summit, co-hosted by France and Germany, at Paris’ Grand Palais.
On Wednesday afternoon, French President Emmanuel Macron announced that more than 50 projects are expected to be signed over the course of the two-day event, stressing the need to "strengthen the European and space research", but also to deepen partnerships with other countries around the world.
Alongside Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, he also welcomed the European Space Agency’s (ESA) next private astronaut mission, PAM-6, to the International Space Station (ISS), scheduled for 2027 — which will mark the first ever journey to space by a Greek astronaut, Adrianos Golemis.
Taking to X Wednesday evening, he also hailed a major deal signed between Amazon Leo and Arianespace, stating that “Amazon Leo is renewing its trust in Arianespace with 6 additional launches, 24 in total."
Ahead of the summit, several US companies reportedly withdrew from the event, due to pressure from Washington over support for "EU policy positions."
Challenging US dominance
Despite this, the summit comes at a strategic crossroads for the European space industry, described by President Emmanuel Macron as an opportunity to "bring Europeans together around a common ambition" and develop a "shared vision of Europe's place on the map of global space powers by 2035" when he announced the event in October 2025.
According to the Elysée, the summit will focus on international space cooperation and strengthening space security. In recent years, Europe has increasingly sought to challenge US dominance of the global space market: developing its own homegrown rockets and increasing funding for space at both a state and bloc-wide level.
Europe has historically invested 0.07% of GDP into space programmes, compared with 0.24% by the US.
But 2025 marked a turning point, as the European Space Agency (ESA) approved a record-breaking €22.3 billion budget for its three-year funding cycle (2026–2028) in November, with €35 billion for space for security and defence.
Lunar mining has also emerged as a potential avenue for securing clean-energy resources and critical raw materials, as Europe works to move away from Chinese and Russian dependencies.
Divergence between France and Germany
Nearly a year after Macron announced the summit, it encountered some bumps in the road before the event had even begun. Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz confirmed on Friday that he would not attend the summit due to domestic commitments, with defence minister Boris Pistorius and space minister Dorothee Bär set to go in his place.
Behind the scenes, France and Germany have faced a number of disagreements over space and defence projects, ditching the Future Combat Air System (FCAS) project in June 2026, after years of disagreements.
Macron has consistently stressed the importance of building up Europe's strategic autonomy, backing programs like Ariane 6, rather than relying on US providers such as Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
Meanwhile, Germany has expressed a greater willingness to rely on lower-cost US alternatives, such as SpaceX. On Saturday, German startup Isar Aerospace launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from mainland Europe, marking a major turning point in Europe's quest to secure independent access to space. Merz described the launch as “the beginning of a new era.”
US companies withdraw from event
A number of US companies also withdrew from the event, after a White House official reportedly warned them that their attendance "could look like tacit support for EU policy positions," Politico reported.
A spokesperson for France's Ministry of Higher Education and Research, which oversees national space policy, told the AFP news agency that SpaceX, Blue Origin, Stoke Space, and Starcloud had withdrawn from the event, stating "it’s hard not to link it to the rumours of pressure in the press.”
Speaking to Euronews, Hermann Ludwig Moeller, Director of the European Space Policy Institute described France as a "driving force" in Europe's space sector, providing "strong political support" to the industry, stressing that the "relevance of space is only increasing."
"It is increasingly becoming a war fighting domain, while at the same time it has become evident also to the general public that conflict has become hybrid in nature, for instance through attacks on critical infrastructures in transport, energy, digital. This is where space can provide increased resilience."
Moeller stressed the role that space technologies such as satellite navigation have in terms of both civilian and military usage.
"While they are essential to everyday life, the war in Ukraine has also highlighted their strategic importance in modern warfare", he said.
Kyiv's reliance on Musk's Starlink following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has underlined the strategic importance of space services during wartime — that the satellite network provides resilient internet connectivity even when infrastructure is damaged or destroyed.
This reality also pushed Europe to develop its own independent satellite networks, notably the secure internet constellation known as IRIS².

Israel in numbers: National population hits 10.305m., new CBS data shows ahead of Rosh Hashanah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:53:47 UTC
20:53:47 KST

Israel’s population stands at an estimated 10.305 million ahead of Rosh Hashanah, after growing by approximately 124,000 people over the past year, the Central Bureau of Statistics said on Wednesday.
The figures were released as part of the CBS’s annual “Israel in Numbers” report ahead of Rosh Hashanah, which compiles data covering population, health, education, employment, housing, the economy, transportation, agriculture, the environment, and other aspects of Israeli life.
According to the CBS figures, the annual population growth rate was 1.2%. Of the country’s residents, about 7.828 million are Jews and others, representing 78.3% of the Israeli population, while approximately 2.173 million are Arabs, or 21.7%. Another 304,000 residents are foreign nationals.
The figures show that approximately 182,000 babies were born over the past year, while around 50,000 people died. At the same time, Israel recorded a negative international migration balance, with roughly 8,000 people deducted from the Israeli population through migration.
Around 24,000 new immigrants arrived in Israel over this period, along with some 4,000 people through family reunification. Approximately 21,000 Israelis who had previously emigrated returned to the country, while some 57,000 Israelis left after being classified as having emigrated abroad, according to the CBS.
Israel’s migration rate has risen sharply since 2023. A Tel Aviv University study published in August, based on CBS data, found that a total of 268,930 Israelis left Israel in 2023 (86,509), 2024 (91,499), and 2025 (90,922). For comparison, the study showed that during the same period in 2013, 2014, and 2015, only 83,219 citizens left Israel.
The bureau uses a specific methodology for determining when a person is classified as an emigrant, and noted in the report that its population data are provisional and are based on the 2022 census, with changes made to the method for calculating Israelis living abroad and the addition of the foreign population.
At the end of 2025, Israel’s total population was estimated at 10.203 million, including 9.916 million Israelis and 286,700 foreign residents. During 2025, 20,900 new immigrants arrived, down from 31,100 in 2024, while 69,500 Israelis were recorded as leaving and 18,800 as returning under the CBS’s annual migration methodology.
A separate Aliyah and Integration Ministry report released in June said that more than 22,500 new immigrants moved to Israel in 2025, with increased immigration from several Western countries despite the security challenges of recent years.
Israel also remains home to nearly half of the world’s Jewish population. As of January 1, 2026, there were an estimated 15.9 million Jews worldwide, approximately 46% of whom lived in Israel, according to the CBS.
Israel's fertility remains far above OECD average
The bureau’s annual figures also highlighted Israel’s relatively high fertility rate. A total of 183,678 live births were recorded in the relevant annual data, with the total fertility rate standing at 2.88 children per woman, compared with an OECD average of 1.41.
There were more than three million private households in Israel, with an average of 3.17 people per household, compared with approximately 2.5 across OECD countries. Some 53,025 couples married in 2024 and 16,499 divorced.
Life expectancy remained high by international standards. Israeli men had a life expectancy of 81.4 years and women 85.9 years, according to the latest figures. CBS international comparisons placed Israeli men seventh among OECD countries and women eighth based on the comparable 2024 data. This continues a pattern in which Israeli life expectancy ranks among the highest in the OECD.
The labor market remained tight, with 4.577 million people participating in the labor force and the unemployment rate standing at 2.9%. The employment rate among Israelis aged 15 and over was 60.9%, including 63.6% among men and 58.2% among women.
Housing data presented a mixed picture. The housing price index fell 1%, and the index for new-home prices declined 2.8%, while average rent rose 4.3%. The average home price stood at approximately NIS 2.33 million, while average monthly rent reached NIS 4,919.

Kernel, EBRD commit EUR 1 mln to Ukrainian workforce, recovery programs
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:53:37 EEST
20:53:37 KST

Kernel agricultural holding and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) have signed a EUR 1 million grant agreement to develop the company's human capital programs.
According to the agricultural holding's press service, the funding will be used to train young technical specialists and create a barrier-free work environment. The partnership is based on the shared belief of Kernel and the EBRD that investment in people is a necessary condition for Ukraine's recovery and that these steps need to be taken now, with a long-term perspective in mind, the statement said.
"For us, partnering with the EBRD is about much more than financing — it reflects a shared commitment to long-term development. An international financial institution of this calibre has entrusted Kernel with implementing strategic social projects during wartime. Together, we are demonstrating that Ukrainian business can operate according to the highest international standards of transparency while investing in vocational education and workplace inclusion where these investments are needed most," the press service quoted Kernel HR Director Natalia Teriakhina as saying.
"The EBRD supports projects that help Ukrainian businesses build resilience while investing in the country's future. Our partnership with Kernel demonstrates how the private sector can take a leading role in rebuilding Ukraine's human capital. Investments in accessibility and inclusive technical education create new opportunities for people, strengthen business resilience, and demonstrate the maturity of Ukrainian companies to future international investors," the press service quoted Sonia Jordan-Kirwan, Director for Gender and Economic Inclusion at EBRD, as saying.
The project's first area of focus will be the creation of modern training laboratories at four vocational and technical colleges in Ukraine: in Odesa, Poltava, Kropyvnytsky and Starokostiantyniv. They will train skilled tradespeople whose expertise is critically important today for the agricultural sector, industry and renewable energy: electricians, production automation specialists and other technical specialists.
The laboratories will be equipped with modern industrial equipment, enabling students to gain practical, hands-on experience aligned with current industry requirements. Over the next five years, the programme is expected to train approximately 600 qualified young professionals, helping address Ukraine's growing workforce shortage and supporting regional economic recovery.
The second area of the grant programme provides for the modernization of Kernel's production facilities in accordance with international principles of accessibility and universal design.
The company is implementing all solutions in cooperation with veterans to ensure that they meet the actual needs of people returning to civilian employment. This work is part of a comprehensive veteran support program covering workplace adaptation, as well as physical and psychological reintegration.
"The agreement marks a new stage in the long-standing partnership between Kernel and the EBRD, reinforcing their shared commitment to human capital development and Ukraine's long-term recovery," the agricultural holding said.
The initiative is being implemented under the EBRD's Human Capital Investment Incentive (HCII) grant program, launched in 2024 to support Ukrainian companies in addressing war-related workforce challenges. The program provides co-financing for investments aimed at creating employment opportunities, developing professional skills and improving access to workplace infrastructure. Donor support for the EBRD-Kernel cooperation is provided by the TaiwanBusiness-EBRD Technical Cooperation Fund.
Kernel is the world's largest producer and exporter of sunflower oil, Ukraine's largest grain exporter, an operator of an extensive network of logistics assets, and a leading producer of grains and oilseeds in Ukraine. It is one of Ukraine's largest producers and sellers of bottled oil. The company grows agricultural crops and markets them.
In the first nine months of fiscal 2026 (from July 1, 2025), Kernel reduced net profit by 5% to $208 million, while revenue increased by 0.4% to $3.092 billion and EBITDA rose by 1% to $403 million.

Russia says it hopes US-mediated talks with Ukraine will resume soon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:53:36 UTC
20:53:36 KST

Russia hopes that US-mediated peace talks on ending the war in Ukraine will resume soon, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Wednesday.
No such talks between Russia and Ukraine have taken place since February, but US President Donald Trump sent his negotiators to Moscow and then Kyiv at the weekend in a bid to relaunch the stalled process.
Peskov was responding to a comment by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that it may be possible to draw up a roadmap to restart talks and work towards an acceptable outcome for both sides.
A huge gulf remains between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the 4-1/2-year war, with Kyiv rejecting Moscow's demands that it give up more territory.
Peskov said Moscow would not publicly discuss any specifics of a potential settlement, but there was a "confirmed political will" to resume talks.
"We hope that these negotiations will resume in the foreseeable future, and we remain in contact with our American counterparts," he said, a day after Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone.
Prisoner exchange a 'constant item' on agenda, Peskov says
Peskov added that the issue of exchanging prisoners between Russia and the US was "a constant item on the agenda," including between the two presidents. He noted that Russia had released one American prisoner, Robert Gilman, at Trump's request last month.
The two countries have traded prisoners at several points in the past few years.
The biggest such deal was in August 2024, when Russia got back eight prisoners held in the West, including a member of its FSB security service convicted of murder in Germany.
In exchange, 16 people were released from Russian and Belarusian jails. Among those freed by Moscow were prominent Russian dissidents and three US citizens, including Wall Street Journal correspondent Evan Gershkovich.

Still, he commands support from his ruling Serbian Progressive Party, which on Saturday nominated him to run for prime minister in the upcoming elections. It is unclear if Vucic will resign from his position as president before the parliamentary elections or after.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" Hubinger said.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Wednesday that he is a “proud British Jew” but disagrees with the UK's chief rabbi over criticism of government measures targeting illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Speaking to the BBC, Miliband said the UK had to “call out” settlement expansion in the West Bank before it was “too late” to save the two-state solution.
The prospect of a Palestinian state alongside Israel is “being destroyed by the facts on the ground,” he added.  
Speaking to Sky News, Miliband said the continued expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank amounts to “the oppression of the Palestinian people” and that the government is not “willing to stand by in the face of that.”
Israel on Tuesday ordered the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem and imposed an entry ban on 11 British lawmakers after Miliband announced measures targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The UK measures include a ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements, sanctions on companies and individuals facilitating settlement expansion and additional sanctions on extremist Israeli occupiers accused of supporting or inciting violence against Palestinians. 
"I regret what the Israeli government has announced, but I'm proud of what we did yesterday, and it was the right thing to do," Miliband said.
He acknowledged that the closure of the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem would be “damaging” to links with the Palestinian Authority but said: “We weighed up the costs and the benefits in advance of this. And we did something very important.” 
The measures drew both praise and criticism from Britain's Jewish community. 
Ephraim Mirvis, the UK's chief rabbi, called it a “dark day for British Jews.” 
In a statement on US social media platform X, Mirvis claimed the move amounted to “little more than a political flag bearing a mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric, and those who harbour a dangerous obsession with the Jewish state.”
However, several British Jewish organizations condemned occupier violence in the West Bank and welcomed the government's announcement.

Station Narva draws record 5,766 visitors for 10th edition
The weekend's Station Narva festival attracted nearly 6,000 visitors, a record figure in the decade the event has been running.
The music and city festival, held from Thursday, September 3 to Sunday, September 6, brought 5,766 visitors, and founder and director Helen Sildna said attendance confirms that Station Narva has found a place in the hearts of its audience.
"The city of Narva and the people of Ida-Viru County have embraced us. It brings our team heartfelt joy to see such different people spending time together at the festival – from young people to seniors, from across Estonia and Europe. That is exactly our wish and aim: to create a cultural event that brings people together and unites, motivates and encourages them. We are already starting work today on the tenth Station Narva," Sildna said.
Culture Minister Heidy Purga (Reform), who opened the festival's music program, said Station Narva is evidence of how music brings people together and opens the city to new perspectives.
"You may leave here with a new favorite song, a new friendship or a reason to return to Narva. What moved me most this year was Skoone's concert and meeting local young people, whose energy and desire to connect their creativity with their hometown and Station Narva show that this festival has a future in Narva that is very much its own and very much needed," Purga said.
Musical headliners included British trip‑hop pioneer and Station Narva regular Tricky, Icelandic electronic pop act GusGus and Estonian artists spanning several generations and genres, among them folk‑pop band Sadu, veteran punk act Propeller and Narva native and 2023 Eurovision representative Alika, who was also celebrating her birthday.
Concerts mainly took place at the Narva Museum inside the historic Hermann Castle, and at the Ro‑Ro club.
Free daytime concerts featured actor and solo artist Mihkel Kuusk as well as other local and Estonian acts, art installations and more.
Next year's Station Narva is the 10th edition and is set to run over the same weekend, September 2‑5, 2027.

German chancellor accuses far-right AfD party of seeking ‘ethnic cleansing’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:50:28 UTC
20:50:28 KST

Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has accused the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) of seeking “ethnic cleansing” with its “remigration” drive, after the nativist party’s seismic weekend victory in a state election.
In his first public confrontation with the AfD since Sunday’s shock outcome in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz said at a raucous parliamentary debate that the far-right party would take an axe to one of the pillars of the German economy with a racist campaign of mass deportations.
“The term ‘remigration’ is nothing but a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” he said on Wednesday to applause from the other parties in the Bundestag lower house.
In a fiery speech addressed to the AfD parliamentary group, which repeatedly interrupted him with loud taunts and heckling, Merz said millions of working immigrants were crucial to German society.
“If those working in Germany have to leave the country again because you are championing ‘remigration’,” Merz said, “then the skilled trades in Germany will no longer be able to function: not a single care home will remain open, not a single hospital in Germany will remain operational, and not a single restaurant in Germany will be able to stay in business.”
He said the AfD’s rhetoric, which propelled it to the strongest showing for a far-right party in a German state since the Nazi period, “is precisely what is dividing our society so deeply”.
The AfD has repeatedly called for large-scale expulsions of irregular migrants, a policy that would face stiff challenges under German law.
In the election, the party rode an international wave of populism, nationalism and discontent with mainstream parties, underscored overnight by congratulations from Donald Trump.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, the US president hailed the AfD’s “really big night” in Saxony-Anhalt. “They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly,” Trump wrote.
Merz responded by cancelling a planned phone call with Trump on Wednesday. A spokesperson for the chancellor declined to explain but noted that Merz had always objected “in general terms” to “interfering in or commenting on the domestic political situation, particularly regarding elections”.
Support for Merz, a conservative Christian Democrat, has plummeted in the 16 months since he took office at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats, amid disappointment over slow progress on economic growth and the cost of living.
He has adopted a hard line on border policy in a faltering effort to win back AfD supporters, and acknowledged Germany still had “problems in the area of migration”.
“We still have many people in Germany who should not have permanent residency. This is consensus in the [ruling] coalition, that we need to deport more people,” he said on Wednesday.
“But we make a careful distinction between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, and who are welcome here, and those who do not have permanent residency in Germany and who must leave our country. Unlike you [the AfD], we take great care to make this distinction.”
The AfD won nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt but fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is seeking potential supporters among the other parties to elect him as state premier.
Merz, who has acknowledged his unpopularity played a role in the halving of support for his party in the state, tried to put a brave face on the rout. “Fifty-six percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt didn’t vote for you,” he told the AfD.
He accused Siegmund, whose party is classed as rightwing extremist by domestic intelligence, of “electoral fraud” by already breaking a campaign promise not to seek to govern the state if he failed to win an absolute majority.
“And you won’t manage that in Germany either [at the federal level],” Merz told the AfD co-leader Alice Weidel. “Nowhere in Germany will you get a majority. You are and remain a destructive force.”
Merz also attacked the AfD for its opposition to military assistance for Ukraine, and accused it of making common cause with Russia, which Berlin has alleged is mounting a sabotage and disinformation campaign on its soil.
He said that despite “clear evidence” a failed drone bomb attack at Leipzig airport last month “had been planned in Russia for months and was specifically directed against Germany”, the AfD had remained silent on it.
Earlier, Weidel had savoured her party’s resounding election victory from the podium, saying the CDU had been “pulverised” and calling it a referendum on Merz’s leadership.
Attacking the government’s migration policy and blaming it for crime and other security problems, Weidel said: “Your time is up. The public want a change in policy, and they will get it,” reiterating her party’s aim to form a federal government in the foreseeable future.
Polls show Merz’s fractious coalition would not have a majority in a general election, though the next national vote is not due until 2029. The AfD is polling in first place at 28% to 29%, with the wind at its back before another two state polls this month, in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

INNOPROM. India opens in New Delhi ahead of BRICS summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:50:15 UTC
20:50:15 KST

INNOPROM. India opens in New Delhi ahead of BRICS summit
The first edition of the International Industrial Trade Fair INNOPROM. India opened on September 9 at the Bharat Mandapam exhibition complex in New Delhi, bringing together more than 130 Russian and Indian companies.
The event, taking place in Pavilion No. 1, is being held ahead of the 18th BRICS Summit. It is organized by the Russian Ministry of Industry and Trade and India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The operators are Formika Event LLC on the Russian side and the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) on the Indian side.
Organizers said the Russian and Indian national sections were given equal exhibition space. The Russian side features some of the country’s largest state corporations and industrial firms, including Rostec, Rosatom, Roscosmos, United Aircraft Corporation, United Engine Corporation, Sber, Natsproektstroy, Transmashholding, RUSAL, PhosAgro, the Center for Research and Development in Advanced Technologies, A7, and Arnest.
Regional group stands from Moscow, Tatarstan, Krasnodar Krai, and the Chelyabinsk Region are also part of the exhibition, along with companies taking part in a business mission organized by the Russian Export Center. The Russia National Centre has a separate stand displaying traditional Russian folk arts and crafts.
India’s section includes major companies and institutions from sectors such as metallurgy, mining, digital technology, transport engineering, textiles, energy, and oil and gas. Among the participants are MECON, Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL), NMDC, MOIL, Central Electronics Ltd., RVNL, Titagarh Rail Systems, Tata Power, ITC Group, KABIL, Shatei Engineering, and Bansal Spinning Mills.
A notable part of the fair is the focus on cultural showcases. Organizers have set aside special demonstration areas for traditional Russian and Indian arts and crafts, where local producers are holding master classes for visitors.
Business matchmaking is also a major theme of the fair. The Russian Export Center and the Confederation of Indian Industry have created networking zones at the venue to help companies identify suppliers and customers and to discuss potential joint projects.
“INNOPROM provides an important platform for bringing together representatives of industry, technology providers, investors, and government institutions from India and Russia to explore new opportunities for cooperation,” said Vishnu Sharma, Deputy Director General for Corporate Affairs and Marketing at the National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC).
He added that India is developing “world-class industrial smart cities” and said platforms such as INNOPROM support direct engagement with Russian and other international firms, while helping them enter the Indian market and expand their presence there.
According to Sharma, such cooperation could help turn the growing economic relationship between the two countries into “tangible investments, manufacturing localization, technology partnerships, and the creation of new industrial ecosystems in India.”
The trade fair’s business program is running on September 9 and 10, with discussions focused on expanding Russian-Indian trade, economic and industrial ties. Participants are expected to address potential cooperation in industry and high-tech fields, as well as new business opportunities.
The central event will be the main plenary session on September 10, titled “Enhancing Russian-Indian Trade and Industrial Partnership: Towards Greater Self-Reliance.” It is set to feature Russian Industry and Trade Minister Anton Alikhanov and Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal.
Officials from both delegations are also expected to tour the exhibition on the second and third days of the fair.

have opened to visitors on Rome's central Oppian Hill after a
dig and restoration that Rome Mayor Roberto Gualtieri said "has
enabled us to return a wonderful space to the city".

to certain areas and artifacts of exceptional value.

Rome's history. The restoration of the Painted City and the

also speaks to the extraordinary nature of a city where any

to light and enrich our knowledge of the past," said Mayor
Gualtieri.

ongoing effort to care for and highlight the Capital's
millennia-old history. "We are aware that Rome is adding a major
highlight to its wonders," Gualtieri emphasized, explaining that
the two large decorative features are of particular significance
"in terms of both artistic beauty and historical and documentary
importance."
Claudio Parisi Presicce, the Capitoline Superintendent for
Cultural Heritage, described the area's complex historical
layering.

others date them to a later phase—though still prior to the
construction of the baths. The Baths of Trajan, designed by
Apollodorus of Damascus and inaugurated on June 22, 109 AD,
covered an area of approximately 60,000 square meters.

Trajan's Baths open to visitors on Rome's Oppian Hill
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
13:48:27 CEST
20:48:27 KST

The ruins of Emperor Trajan's Baths have opened to visitors on Rome's central Oppian Hill after a dig and restoration that Rome Mayor Roberto Gualtieri said "has enabled us to return a wonderful space to the city".
The site features the biggest mosaic ever discovered in Rome and a huge fresco illustrating buildings according to rules of perspective which would only be rediscovered 700 years later by Renaissance masters including Florentine master builder Filippo Brunelleschi.
    The new museum space was unveiled Tuesday in the heart of the Oppian Hill, situated between the exedra of Trajan's Baths and the underground gallery housing the "Painted City" and the "Great Mosaic". 
    The restoration and enhancement project—carried out under the PNRR-Caput Mundi initiative—was unveiled in the presence of Gualtieri and the Capitoline Superintendent for Cultural Heritage, Claudio Parisi Presicce. 
    The project allows the public, for the first time, full access to certain areas and artifacts of exceptional value. 
    "With this project, we are returning a wonderful site in the heart of the Oppian Hill to the city and finally making it accessible, while recovering and showcasing unique traces of Rome's history. The restoration of the Painted City and the Great Mosaic, alongside new discoveries from the excavations, also speaks to the extraordinary nature of a city where any intervention on its heritage can bring new fragments of history to light and enrich our knowledge of the past," said Mayor Gualtieri. 
    For the mayor, this represents "an important new piece" in the ongoing effort to care for and highlight the Capital's millennia-old history. "We are aware that Rome is adding a major highlight to its wonders," Gualtieri emphasized, explaining that the two large decorative features are of particular significance "in terms of both artistic beauty and historical and documentary importance." Claudio Parisi Presicce, the Capitoline Superintendent for Cultural Heritage, described the area's complex historical layering. 
    "Since 1871, this has been a protected monumental area—a decision made by the city immediately after it was proclaimed the capital," he explained, highlighting how this specific status allowed the archaeological layers to be preserved. 
    "Here, we have a sequence of particularly interesting monuments." Subsurface investigations, begun in the area of the ancient Papal Powder Magazine, led to the discovery of an underground gallery and the remains of structures predating the Baths of Trajan. According to Parisi Presicce, some scholars believe these remains may be linked to the Domus Aurea, while others date them to a later phase—though still prior to the construction of the baths. The Baths of Trajan, designed by Apollodorus of Damascus and inaugurated on June 22, 109 AD, covered an area of approximately 60,000 square meters. 
    "The bath complex was an innovative model," the superintendent explained, because alongside spaces dedicated to physical care, it included a vast system of porticoes, areas for walking and sports, and spaces dedicated to culture. 
    Among these was the large southwestern exedra—measuring about 30 meters in diameter—where numerous niches may have housed cabinets for documents and books. 
    "The restoration project envisions using these spaces for contemporary events, conferences, and concerts, ensuring the area is fully utilized," Parisi Presicce added. 
    Two exceptional decorative features within the underground gallery have been restored: La Città Dipinta (The Painted City)—a fresco covering approximately ten square meters and dating back to the 1st century AD—and the Grande Mosaico (Great Mosaic), a monumental wall decoration arranged in multiple registers. 
    The project also involved improvements to visitor routes, including a new walkway, a reception area and bookshop, a space dedicated to fistulae (ancient lead water pipes), new green areas, lighting, tiered seating, and educational displays. 
    "The research is ongoing," concluded Parisi Presicce, explaining that excavations will continue to see what else the site might yield. 
    A trial opening to the public will take place on Saturday, September 12, and Sunday, September 13, featuring free guided tours in Italian that require a reservation. 
    From October 2, tours will run from Friday to Sunday, with six daily time slots—at 10:00, 11:00, 12:00, 13:00, 14:00, and 15:00—and a maximum of 15 participants per slot.

Republican midterm convention 2026: What to know about Trump’s Dallas event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:48:03 UTC
20:48:03 KST

Republican midterm convention 2026: What to know about Trump’s Dallas event
Unorthodox event seeks to mobilise midterm Republican voters, even as Trump approval rating tanks.
Why are Republicans hosting a midterm convention?
The United States Republican Party – and its talisman President Donald Trump – is descending on Dallas, Texas, to host a rare convention before the midterm elections in November.
Usually reserved for presidential election cycles, Trump’s call to hold the high-cost event before the November 3 midterm vote has underscored both the president’s unorthodox campaign style and the urgency of the political moment for his Republican Party.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3‘A rally like none other’: Trump unveils 2026 Republican midterm convention
- list 2 of 3All the big elections to look out for in 2026
- list 3 of 3Democrat Kamala Harris teases 2028 presidential bid, following Trump loss
Trump’s approval rating has tanked in the lead-up to the midterm vote, with polls pointing to a panoply of factors, most notably the US-Israel war on Iran and its knock-on economic effects for US consumers.
The lack of enthusiasm threatens what are already considered long-shot odds in the Republicans’ effort to hold on to control of the House of Representatives. Shifting public opinion has also put control of the Senate increasingly in play, although Democrats still face an uphill battle to pull off an upset.
A loss of control in either chamber would serve as a major check on Trump’s authority in the final two years of his second term.
But not all Republicans have bought into Trump and the party’s claims that the convention will spur voter turnout.
Several, particularly those in the tightest races, have kept the event at arm’s length amid concerns that associating with the president could only further mobilise his detractors.
Here’s what to know:
When and where is the Republican midterm convention?
The convention will be hosted at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on Wednesday, September 9 and Thursday, September 10.
The event is expected to run from 3pm to 9pm Central Time (20:00 to 02:00 GMT) on both days.
Trump is scheduled to speak on both nights, including a Wednesday address and the convention’s closing keynote on Thursday from 8pm to 9pm Central Time (01:00 to 02:00 GMT on Friday).
US Vice President JD Vance will close out night one with a speech.
Is this a typical political convention?
Not at all.
The Republican National Committee (RNC), the party’s official organising body, has billed the Dallas midterm convention as a “first in American political history”.
Both Democratic and Republican national conventions have historically capped the primary season before a presidential election. The emphasis has historically been on the presidential nomination process during the largely ceremonial events.
During those conventions, so-called “delegates” from every state pledge their votes for a candidate based on the primary election outcome from their home state.
A candidate who secures the required majority of delegates formally becomes the party’s presidential nominee at the convention.
Parties also typically hold several smaller meetings surrounding the event to establish and release the party’s official platform.
Why are Republicans holding a midterm convention in 2026?
To start with, there will be no nominating process – presidential or otherwise – during the event, as there is no presidential election in 2026.
Instead, the convention has taken the shape of a supercharged campaign rally and fundraiser.
It has been pitched as an opportunity to introduce candidates in punishing races to potential donors and to give a clear, if Trump-dominated, party message as the races enter their final stretch.
The RNC has promised “a primetime showcase for President Trump’s success, candidates, and causes that have propelled the 2026 midterms to unprecedented focus”.
What’s on the schedule?
There will be quite a lot. The official programme lists “53 items and speakers” on night one, followed by 56 more on night two.
The first night will focus on issues including tax cuts, healthcare affordability, immigration, border policy, trade and domestic manufacturing.
The second night will focus more on affordability and families, including policies related to taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security.
The subject areas hew closely to Trump’s wider political messaging.
The official programme gives relatively little attention to several other subjects. The US-Israel war with Iran and Trump’s aggressive tariff policy receive scant mention.
Who else is speaking?
Trump and Vance are the convention’s marquee speakers, but an array of prominent Republicans and candidates are expected to feature across the two-day programme.
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is likely to get a healthy amount of stage time. Paxton is running for Senate against Democrat James Talarico, whose early lead in polling has raised alarm bells for Republicans. A Democrat has not won statewide office in Texas since 1994.
“We’re going to have a lot of speakers, and the ones we want to focus on will be obviously Ken Paxton,” Trump told reporters last week. “We gotta get him elected.”
The race is particularly personal for Trump, who endorsed MAGA-aligned Paxton over Republican Senator John Cornyn, a four-term incumbent seen by many as the surest challenger for Talarico.
Will Trump’s convention help Republicans in the midterms?
It remains to be seen whether the convention will help to turn out voters in a meaningful way.
Trump has proven a canny campaigner in the past, leveraging his eye for television spectacle to build support and turn out low-propensity voters. But several factors could limit the impact.
Trump’s Thursday night speech conflicts with the opening games of the National Football League (NFL) season. The event also runs up against several memorial events for the September 11, 2001 attacks throughout the week.
Some Republican officials have also reportedly criticised the hasty announcement of the event, which Trump called for in late June, raising questions over whether organisers will indeed be able to achieve the spectacle envisioned.
For his part, Trump enters the convention with his approval rating continuing to tank, hovering at a 38 percent average in major polls. Several of the most recent polls, including a Reuters-Ipsos poll and a Financial Times-Focaldata poll conducted in late August, reflected only a 33 percent approval.
Trump entered office in January 2025 sitting at about 52 percent approval.
Why are some Republicans skipping?
To be sure, several Republicans in key races have said they will attend the convention.
They include former Congressman Mike Rogers, who is running against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for an open Senate seat in Michigan; Ohio Senator Jon Husted, who is facing an unnerving challenge from former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown; and Georgia Congressman Mike Collins, who is seeking to unseat Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff.
Others have been wary.
Trump’s policies in his second term have cast a long shadow, leaving many candidates calculating whether attendance could backfire and instead energise voters opposed to Trump.
Democratic primary turnout in several key states – including Michigan, Wisconsin, Texas and Georgia – has soared this year, while Republican turnout has remained steady but unextraordinary, as reported by The Associated Press news agency. That has been a worrying sign for Republicans.
Maine Senator Susan Collins, a Republican incumbent seen as vulnerable in her race against Democrat Troy Jackson, has been among those who have said they will not attend.
Several candidates in key House races have pointed to prior commitments.
Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks told The Bulwark she preferred to spend her time in her home district in Iowa, where she faces a challenge from Democrat Christina Bohannan.
“Because I have a district that I have to be in and take care of, so I’ll be in my district,” she explained about her decision.
Miller-Meeks eked out a victory over Bohannan in 2024, winning by a margin of just 0.1 percent.
Are Democrats countering?
Several left-leaning groups are organising protests.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has announced that four Democratic lawmakers will travel to Dallas for counterprogramming during the Republican convention.
However, the cash-strapped Democratic National Committee (DNC) has avoided holding its own midterm convention.
The committee went into debt in the wake of the 2024 presidential election, even putting up its Washington, DC-based headquarters as collateral for a $15m loan, the NOTUS news site reported in July.
The RNC has not yet released a final price tag for its convention.

Faster walking may lower early death risk: Australian study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:43:57 CST
20:43:57 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Taking fewer daily steps at a faster pace may substantially lower the risk of early death by up to 43 percent, new research finds.
The study analyzed movement data from over 64,000 middle-aged participants in the UK Biobank who wore activity trackers for seven consecutive days between 2013 and 2015 to monitor the number and intensity of daily steps taken, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's Monash University.
Published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, the research found that walking at a brisker pace may be the sweet spot for those with sedentary lifestyles.
The findings could help people who struggle to increase their daily step count due to lack of time, disability or environmental restraints, said lead author Professor Emmanuel Stamatakis from the Monash School of Psychological Sciences.
"We found that the risk (of early death) was substantially lower among those achieving a higher stepping pace but fewer than 5,000 daily steps," Stamatakis said, adding the risk was also significantly reduced among those taking 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps at a slower pace.
The findings did not support the popular theory that everyone must take at least 10,000 steps a day to get fit, researchers said, adding that "every step counts" and how people take those steps can also matter. ■

Mainland welcomes growing discussion in Taiwan on "one country, two systems": spokesperson
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:43:55 CST
20:43:55 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese mainland welcomed growing discussion in Taiwan about national reunification and a proposed "one country, two systems" framework for the island, a spokesperson said Wednesday.
Chen Binhua, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, was responding to a question about a Taiwan scholar who had published three consecutive articles on social media discussing the proposed framework.
"It is normal to have different opinions and debates between people on the mainland and Taiwan in the process," Chen said.
"We believe more of our compatriots in Taiwan will break free from the ideological constraints and 'information cocoons' created by the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities, and increasingly recognize the advantages of the 'one country, two systems' and the inclusiveness of the Taiwan solution it offers," he said.
The Taiwan question is left by a full-blown civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. In 1949, the remnants of the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China (PRC) was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation, though the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed.
Peaceful reunification under "one country, two systems" is the best approach to achieving national reunification, Chen said.
"The specific form of implementation of 'one country, two systems' in Taiwan will fully take into consideration the realities in Taiwan, fully absorb the opinions and suggestions of people from all sectors on both sides of the Strait, and fully safeguard the interests and sentiments of Taiwan compatriots," he said.
While discussions about reunification grow in Taiwan society, the DPP authorities continue to challenge the one-China principle. Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te has recently again argued that United Nations General Assembly Resolution 2758 was not related to Taiwan.
Chen said such attempts would only bring humiliation upon Lai and the DPP authorities and were bound to fail.
No matter what they do, Chen said, they cannot alter the legal and factual reality that Taiwan is part of China, undermine the international community's adherence to the one-China principle, or halt the historical trend toward national reunification.
The U.N. General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758 in 1971 by an overwhelming majority, clarifying that the PRC government is the sole legal government representing the whole of China. This resolution, from the perspective of international law, completely eliminated possibilities of "two Chinas" or "Taiwan independence." ■

Dutch inland waterway freight falls nearly 19 pct in August amid drought
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:43:38 CST
20:43:38 KST

THE HAGUE, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Dutch inland waterway vessels carried 21.8 million tonnes of freight in August 2026, down 18.8 percent compared to the same month last year and the lowest volume recorded for August in the past 15 years, Statistics Netherlands (CBS) reported Wednesday.
"In the summer of 2026, inland waterway transport was severely affected by drought. Water levels in rivers dropped, meaning that vessels could carry less weight." CBS said in a statement.
The decline in freight volumes was particularly pronounced in cross-border transport. In August 2026, imports by inland waterway were 20.2 percent lower than a year earlier, while exports fell by 22.2 percent, according to CBS.
Freight transport by inland waterway declined to and from almost all countries. Germany, one of the Netherlands' most important trading partners, recorded the sharpest drop. The volume of goods transported to Germany fell by 2 million tonnes, or 39.7 percent, while freight arriving in the Netherlands from Germany fell by 1 million tonnes, or 49.5 percent.
The decline did not reflect reduced shipping activity. In fact, the number of voyages increased by 3.4 percent in August. However, vessels carried an average of 1,299 tonnes per voyage, compared with around 1,500 tonnes in August in most other years since 2012.
The Netherlands has been facing a prolonged drought, putting increasing pressure on efforts to retain and distribute freshwater, the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management said on Aug. 11, 2026. ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:43:29 CST
20:43:29 KST

CAIRO, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Belarusian performance "Zhenya + Tanya = Love" won the Best Performance award at the 33rd Cairo International Festival for Experimental Theatre (CIFET), which concluded Tuesday evening with an awards ceremony at the Cairo Opera House.
The work, a contemporary theatrical adaptation of Alexander Pushkin's classic verse novel "Eugene Onegin," blends classical text with movement, laughter and dance to explore youthful idealism, unrequited love, missed opportunities and misunderstandings.
Tunisia's Taher Issa Ben Larbi won Best Director for "Show Off," a drama that blends cinematic elements with fashion to critique consumerism, commercial dominance, and art's role in contemporary crises.
The Best Actor award was shared by Aleksei Titkov of Russia for "Poor Liza" and Amir Dridi of Tunisia for "Show Off." "Poor Liza," based on Nikolay Karamzin's well-known story, follows the tragic first love between a peasant girl and a young nobleman.
Held from Sept. 1 to 8, the 33rd CIFET featured 19 theatrical performances, including 15 works from 13 countries in the official competition, as well as 14 intellectual and research sessions and seven theatre workshops.
Established in 1988 by Egypt's Ministry of Culture, CIFET is one of the Arab world's longest-running international festivals for experimental theatre and a key platform for theatrical exchange. ■

China recognizes 11 new occupations as new industries create fresh roles
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
19:43:24 CST
20:43:24 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- China on Wednesday officially recognized 11 new occupations and 23 new specialties under existing occupations, reflecting evolving labor demand driven by technological advances, industrial upgrading and shifting consumer needs.
The new occupations, released by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security and other government departments, include shore-based ship management engineering technicians, embodied intelligence robot technicians and sports data analysts.
Authorities also revised information concerning six existing occupations or specialties, including agricultural product brokers.
The recognition of the new occupations and specialties will help promote employment and entrepreneurship, offer workers more diverse career paths and better match talent supply with job demand.
Five of the newly recognized occupations are classified as digital occupations and three as green occupations, bringing the respective totals in China to 113 and 142.
A ministry official said China is expected to face a sizable shortage of workers with digital skills for some time, adding that the recognition of the new occupations would spur training and open up broad employment prospects.
The latest additions also highlight the continued expansion of modern services.
Some of these new occupations focus on business development and industrial upgrading, including corporate sustainability planners, airport obstacle-clearance inspectors, and artificial intelligence (AI) agent developers. Others respond more directly to people's demand for higher-quality services, including incense-making artisans, smart furniture assembly and commissioning workers, and fresh-cut flower processing workers.
More modern service occupations are expected to emerge amid the increasing specialization and upgrading of producer services and improvements in the quality, diversity and convenience of consumer services, the official said.
New specialties under existing occupations include community workers, low-altitude logistics operators and age-friendly renovation designers.
Since 2019, China has released eight batches of 121 new occupations.
Of these new occupations, 60 percent were service-related, while professional and technical occupations and manufacturing-related occupations each accounted for 17 percent.
By industry, 43 percent of the new occupations were in modern services, while 34 percent were in advanced manufacturing.
The ministry said it will formulate national standards for the new occupations to guide vocational education, skills training and talent assessment.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) period, China aims to explore new employment space in the digital economy, green economy and silver economy. ■

BELGRADE, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic on Wednesday signed a decree dissolving parliament and called snap parliamentary elections for Oct. 25.
Vucic made the announcement in a televised address at noon, saying the decision was aimed at easing prolonged political tensions and giving voters a clear say on the country's future. "We need election results that will clearly determine and demonstrate the will of the citizens, where, in what direction, and on what path Serbia is heading," he said.
As president, Vucic said, he had always been guided by "the vital state interests of the Republic of Serbia and the interests of the citizens of Serbia." He said the timing of the election would allow Serbia to prepare for Expo 2027, which will open in Belgrade on May next year, as well as for the country's future development. "We will have enough time to prepare for the Expo and for everything that lies ahead," he said.
Vucic urged political parties and voters to take part in the 45-day campaign in a peaceful and dignified manner, respect differing political views, and respect the choices made by voters. "It is important to respect different political opinions, the right to freedom of assembly, and public expression," he said. He expressed confidence that the Serbian people would "choose the right path into the future."
Serbian Prime Minister Djuro Macut formally proposed that the government ask the president to dissolve the National Assembly and call parliamentary elections following an extraordinary government session on Monday.
At a session of the Main Board of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) on Sept. 5, the party unanimously nominated Vucic as the lead candidate on its parliamentary election list and as its candidate for prime minister. ■

Pavel Havlíček, a research fellow at the Association for International Affairs (Prague), expressed this view in comments to Ukrinform.

EU court rejects Hungary's lawsuit over frozen Russian assets - Reuters
Kyiv • UNN
The EU Court rejected Hungary's lawsuit against the use of windfall profits from frozen Russian assets for military support to Ukraine. Budapest has repeatedly challenged the financing mechanism.
The General Court of the European Union rejected Hungary’s lawsuit against the EU decision to use windfall profits from the frozen assets of Russia’s central bank for the needs of Ukraine’s Defense Forces. The decision was made on Wednesday, September 9, Reuters reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
The EU General Court-the bloc’s second-highest judicial body-stated that it was not authorized to hear the case. Hungary had sought to challenge the European Union’s decision to direct windfall profits from frozen Russian assets toward military support for Ukraine, but the court dismissed the lawsuit.
Additionally
This is not Hungary’s first attempt to challenge the mechanism for financing Ukraine using frozen Russian assets. Budapest had already filed a lawsuit with the EU court against the Council of the EU’s decision to direct nearly all proceeds from the taxation of profits from frozen assets through the European Peace Facility, which compensates member states for the costs of military assistance to Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
Recall
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar stated that Budapest opposes an accelerated process for any candidate country to join the European Union. Accordingly, this also applies to Ukraine.
At the same time, the Hungarian authorities, led by Prime Minister Peter Magyar, condemned Russia’s aggression and supported Ukraine’s sovereignty.

====================================================================================================

Lords warn funding doubts threaten Poland defence pact
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:41:59 BST
20:41:59 KST

Uncertainty over Britain’s defence spending plans is raising questions over how the UK will fund commitments made under its new defence and security treaty with Poland, a House of Lords committee has warned.
The International Agreements Committee said the UK-Poland Defence and Security Partnership represented an important strengthening of relations with a major NATO ally, but warned that a lack of clarity over future defence funding could undermine implementation of some of its commitments.
The treaty was signed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in May 2026 and was described at the time as “the biggest step forward in our defence and security relationship with Poland in a generation”.
It commits Britain and Poland to closer cooperation across defence and security, including ambitions to become joint European leaders in the development and manufacture of the next generation of missiles.
In its report published on Wednesday, the committee said it was “concerned about how the Treaty’s commitments on security and defence will be funded in light of the UK’s defence spending plans”.
It warned that uncertainty over funding may “not only undermine the UK’s reputation as a key partner in security and defence at a time of geopolitical uncertainty, but also limit the UK’s ability to respond to increasing challenges from hybrid threats”.
The committee nevertheless welcomed the treaty as an important step in strengthening bilateral relations with Poland, particularly against the background of Russia’s war against Ukraine and the wider deterioration in European security.
It also welcomed recognition of Poland’s “crucial” role in the Euro-Atlantic security architecture and backed measures to deepen cooperation on hybrid threats and defence industry activity.
The agreement extends beyond traditional military cooperation into areas including national security, economic resilience, energy and climate security.
Questions over detail and mutual defence
Despite supporting the overall direction of the treaty, the committee concluded that many of its provisions were expressed in high-level terms and lacked sufficient detail on how they would be delivered.
It also questioned whether the treaty’s mutual defence provisions created substantial new commitments beyond the obligations Britain and Poland already have to one another as members of NATO.
Lord Johnson, Chair of the International Agreements Committee, said: “As this Treaty recognises, Poland is a crucial ally for the UK and plays a vital role within the NATO alliance. We welcome the strengthening of UK-Poland cooperation under this Treaty, particularly in tackling hybrid threats and strengthening defence industry cooperation, though we also found that much of the Treaty is rather general in nature and lacking in substance.”
He added: “We are concerned, however, about how this Treaty’s commitments on security and defence will be funded in light of the UK’s defence spending plans. Many of the Treaty’s commitments are laudable, but without adequate funding it is unclear how they will be implemented. We would welcome further clarity on this from the Government.”
The committee has also asked ministers to clarify the practical significance of the treaty’s mutual defence provisions.
Lord Johnson said: “We have also asked the Government to clarify whether the Treaty’s mutual defence provisions are meaningful, given that the UK and Poland are already committed to defend each other under NATO.”

====================================================================================================

‘Their boat was sinking’: RNLI vows to keep rescuing asylum seekers despite attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:41:52 UTC
20:41:52 KST

Three police forces on the south coast of England are working to protect lifeboat volunteers, staff and buildings from rightwing activists who blame the Royal National Lifeboat Institution for helping asylum seekers to land on the British coast.
Dozens of Dorset police officers were posted outside the charity’s headquarters in Poole on Wednesday evening as about 50 people gathered to protest against the RNLI’s involvement in the small boats crisis.
Hampshire police were patrolling RNLI sites amid fears that people and assets may be targeted, while the Sussex force was investigating “offensive and threatening” remarks made on social media.
The RNLI has vowed to continue to rescue asylum seekers in the Channel despite attacks from rightwing activists after its involvement in a rescue on Sunday in which a dinghy carrying asylum seekers was brought into Portsmouth.
RNLI bosses said workers had been subjected to online and physical abuse and there had been “baseless” rumours circulating that the charity had housed asylum seekers or moved them to secret locations after helping them to shore.
The charity emphasised that responding to small boats was only a tiny percentage of its work and updated its webpage explaining its work in the Channel, which includes powerful testimonies from volunteers involved in the operations.
The protest outside the RNLI’s headquarters was attended by groups including the Poole Patriots and Hampshire Resistance.
Protest leaders handed out rape alarms to women, claiming they were at risk from men brought into the UK by the RNLI, and called for people to stop donating to the charity.
Mandy Ward, a member of Hampshire Resistance, claimed the RNLI was being compromised by its work with small boats in the Channel. “They are acting as a taxi service to people who are not in distress at all,” she said.
Another protester, Marianne, said she had been donating to the RNLI for decades but had cancelled her subscription. “It breaks my heart to do that but I’m disgusted that the government is using the RNLI like this. It’s not what the RNLI is there to do.”
Steve, a former soldier, said: “I’m urging people to stop funding them. It’s a shame – we need the lifeboats but we must stop this invasion.”
Images of some RNLI crew members who were apparently involved in the operation on Sunday have been published on social media with the accusation that they were complicit in an “invasion” of the UK.
Sussex police said: “We are aware of offensive and threatening commentary towards RNLI volunteers circulating on social media. We are proactively supporting our partners in the RNLI regarding the safety of their staff and volunteers.
“Investigations are ongoing to establish if there are any criminal offences in the social media content.”
An RNLI staff member in Poole, who asked not to be named, said security had been stepped up.
“I think it’s fair to say that lots of people who work and volunteer for the RNLI are feeling nervous at the moment,” they said. “Most people who work here believe in what the RNLI stands for and it’s upsetting to see our work attacked by a few people.”
A second staffer said: “There’s also been lots of support and promises of donations from people who want to make the point that they think we are doing the right thing.”
Peter Sparkes, the RNLI chief executive, said that for more than 200 years the RNLI had rescued people without judgment, fear or favour.
“Yet [staff and volunteers] and their families are being threatened by those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard,” he said. “Their action, in contrast, is wholly unacceptable in a civilised society.”
Sparkes said rumours that the RNLI housed asylum seekers on its premises, or that there were RNLI missions to move migrants to secret locations were “completely baseless and untrue”.
The charity said RNLI lifeboats launched 9,058 times in 2025 but only 109 of those call-outs were to small boats in the Channel, representing 1.2% of its rescue work.
It said almost 95% of those who crossed the Channel in small boats last year were picked up by the UK Border Force.
One of the testimonies on the RNLI’s small boats webpage came from Dan, a volunteer helm at Walmer lifeboat station in Kent.
He said: “One thing I would like people to understand is that these people genuinely need our help.”
Speaking about one rescue in the Channel, he said: “We launched to an overcrowded, unseaworthy small boat that was taking on water. One family was so scared. They were screaming. Their boat was sinking in front of their eyes. It was a horrible, horrible situation.
“We managed to rescue that family. We stopped them from drowning. There was a little girl on the boat. She looked me straight in the eye and said: ‘I love you, thank you.’
“As a father, that went straight to my heart. That rescue cemented in my head that what we are doing as an organisation is exactly the right thing.”
Paula, a volunteer lifeboat crew member at Dover, described another Channel rescue: “When I arrived on scene, it was a shock. There were people in the water, some disappearing under the water.
“There was this man holding on to the edge of the boat. He had no strength left. I leant over, lay on my front and I grabbed his arms, and he had no strength to hold me. I looked into his face and his eyes were wide, his face was grey. He was so scared.
“I just knew that if I let him go, he wouldn’t be there. I also knew that there was absolutely no way I was going to let him go. I held on to him and I called for help from my colleagues, and together we pulled him to safety.”
The charity said it responded to small boats in the Channel when HM Coastguard reported that people might be in danger at sea.
It continued: “International maritime law outlines that any vessel that becomes aware of people in distress at sea must take all reasonable measures to assist. All small boats crossing the Channel are classed as being in distress.
“The RNLI is one of several declared search and rescue capability providers and, under long-established procedures, RNLI volunteer crews respond to anyone at risk of drowning, regardless of who they are or how they came to be in difficulty.
“The men, women and children who find themselves in distress and sinking in one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes are no exception. Our crews will go to their aid today when tasked, just like generations of lifeboat crews have done before them, in wartime and peace.”
The charity rejected the accusation that it was a “taxi service” for asylum seekers.
“We are not. HM Coastguard coordinates maritime search and rescue operations around the UK. Our lifeboat crews are tasked to assist people who are in difficulty, both in the Channel and around the coast of the UK.
“RNLI crews launch to the rescue, doing everything they can to save lives, without any thought to where the people they rescue are travelling from, nor their migrant status.”
The febrile atmosphere on the south coast was illustrated when rightwing activists arrived at a hotel in Portsmouth on Tuesday believing that asylum seekers were being housed there, only to find they were a cricket team from Pakistan.
