RAF recruits wait 356 days to start training
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
12:18:26 BST
20:18:26 KST

RAF recruits waited a median of 356 days between submitting an application and starting basic training in the year to June 2026, substantially longer than applicants to the Royal Navy or Army, according to figures released by the Ministry of Defence.
The figures were disclosed by Veterans and People Minister Calvin Bailey in response to a written parliamentary question from Liberal Democrat MP Alex Brewer, who asked what assessment had been made of recruitment delays and how long candidates typically wait before commencing basic training.
Bailey said: “For the period 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, the median time between submitting an application and commencing basic training was 252 days in the Royal Navy, 247 days in the Army and 356 days in the Royal Air Force.”
That puts the RAF median at just under a year from initial application to the start of basic training, compared with a little over eight months for both the Royal Navy and Army. The minister said recruitment timelines had improved in the Royal Navy and Army compared with the previous reporting period, attributing the change to reforms intended to speed up entry into the Armed Forces.
The MOD could not, however, provide a comparable figure for the period between a recruit attending a medical assessment and beginning training.
Bailey said: “The data capturing the time between recruits attending their medical assessment and commencing basic training is not held centrally in a comparable or meaningfully comparable for each of the Armed Forces.”
The department acknowledged that some candidates continue to wait longer than it would like, with recruitment timelines affected by medical and security checks, the availability of specialist training places and choices made by applicants themselves.
Bailey added: “Recruitment timelines are affected by a range of factors, including medical and security checks, the availability of specialist training places, and candidate choice.”
The MOD also stressed that not every long recruitment period represents an administrative delay. Some applicants choose to postpone joining while completing education, remaining in existing employment or waiting for a specific role or training date.
Bailey said: “It is also important to recognise that many applicants choose to defer entry to complete education, honour existing employment commitments, or wait for their preferred role or training start date.”
Defence has introduced a series of changes intended to reduce the time between application and entry. These include conditional offers of employment within 10 days and provisional training start dates within 30 days.
The department has also removed more than 100 medical policies it considers outdated, expanded digital access to candidates’ medical records and changed communications with applicants during the recruitment process.
The reforms are also feeding into development of the Armed Forces Recruitment Service, which is intended to provide a more unified and flexible approach to recruiting personnel across the services. Bailey said Defence would continue using lessons from the current reforms to improve the process and help candidates enter the Armed Forces more quickly.

Finland closes investigation into stray Ukrainian drones
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
14:17:54 EEST
20:17:54 KST

Finnish authorities have concluded their investigation into separate incidents during the spring when drones carrying warheads strayed into Finland.
The incidents were jointly investigated by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and the Finnish Border Guard.
In a statement, the authorities said that all four drones originated from Ukraine, were similar models and were manufactured for military use. Each drone was carrying explosives, the statement confirmed.
The drones were discovered during March in Kouvola, Luumäki and near Parikkala, and in April near the town of Iitti.
Finnish authorities believe that one of the drones exploded while in the air, while the other three were detonated in controlled explosions shortly after they were discovered.
The Finnish Border Guard investigated the incidents as violations of Finnish territory, while the NBI probed the potential charge of aggravated endangerment.
"The preliminary investigations have not revealed any evidence that would have justified continuing the pursuit of criminal liability," the press release stated, adding that the cases are now closed.
Finland not a target
In its statement, the NBI and the Finnish Border Guard emphasised that Finland was not the intended target in any of the incidents where the drones strayed into Finnish territory.
Instead, the devices were likely "hijacked" in mid-air while flying towards targets in Russia, and redirected westward.
UK newspaper The Telegraph uncovered evidence in the spring that a transmitter in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad uses GPS jamming and spoofing to redirect Ukraine's drones away from Russia and towards the airspace of Nato member states.
The investigation by Finnish authorities also noted the impact of the prevailing weather conditions as a key factor.
"The wind direction at the time of the incidents was almost directly from the south. These factors are assessed to have affected the aircraft's navigation and their deviation from their original route," the press release stated.
None of the four drones that ended up in Finnish territory caused any personal injury or damage to property.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky issued an apology to Finland in the aftermath of the drone find near Kouvola and emphasised that Ukraine was not targeting Finland under any circumstances.
Yle News' All Points North podcast heard from UK security expert Keir Giles about the phenomenon of drones straying into Finnish airspace. You can listen to the episode via this embedded player, on Yle Areena, via Apple, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts.

Exclusive: EU lawmakers join pressure to use 200 billion euros in Russian assets to help Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:15:13 UTC
20:15:13 KST

Exclusive: EU lawmakers join pressure to use 200 billion euros in Russian assets to help Ukraine
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) have sent EU leaders an open letter calling for the urgent use of 200 billion euros ($230 billion) of Russian assets to help Ukraine, according to a letter first seen by the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 9.
Swedish MEP Karin Karlsbro, the letter's lead signatory, told the Kyiv Independent that she organized the letter because "Ukraine needs substantial, long-term financing now."
"Utilizing the frozen assets would fundamentally change Europe's ability to finance Ukraine long term. It would be a powerful signal to let (Russian President Vladimir) Putin know that time is not on Russia's side."
The document also underscores the need to use the assets in a way that will protect countries at risk of legal challenge.
The 122 MEPs who signed the letter said they "strongly welcome" an earlier open letter from four EU countries, first reported by the Kyiv Independent, that called on the bloc to revisit the possibility of using Russian assets to support Ukraine.
That push led Karlsbro to believe "we have momentum right now."
"We are now putting renewed pressure on (the European) Council and (the European) Commission to act by gathering strong support from MEPs across the political spectrum and from all over Europe," Karlsbro said.
The MEPs' letter also says that the EU should "ensure that Russia ultimately bears the financial consequences of the destruction it has caused."
The idea of using Russia's assets was discussed by the EU in 2025 but ultimately failed due to Belgian concerns over legal risk, and a lack of solidarity to back Belgium if legal challenges arose.
read also
Belgium remains central to the discussion because 180 billion euros (about $210 billion) of the Russian assets immobilized in the EU are held by the financial clearing house Euroclear, which is based in Belgium, just outside Brussels.
"We deeply regret that in December 2025, the European Council failed to reach an agreement to use these assets for the benefit of Ukraine," reads the MEPs' letter.
The letter also throws its support behind a specific solution intended to reduce the legal risk that would land on Belgium's shoulders.
"The immobilized Russian accounts should be transferred to a new EU instrument acting as a custodian and shouldering all legal obligations to the Central Bank of Russia," the MEPs recommended.
"Belgium shouldn't have to shoulder Europe's responsibility alone," Karlsbro said.
"By bringing the assets under EU control, we would share the risks collectively. This would remove a massive obstacle and should be our first course of action."
EU custodianship of the assets was proposed by Ukraine's Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko in a Sept. 4 interview with Euronews, but a fully developed legal proposal does not yet exist.
The letter reinforces the earlier call made by EU countries for the European Commission to make a formal proposal and urges the European Commission and EU capitals to "act without delay."
"The European Union has repeatedly committed itself to supporting Ukraine for as long as it takes. We now need to ensure that this commitment is backed by the necessary resources," the letter reads.
Karlsbro and a group of other MEPs are also meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron, at the time of writing, to discuss the issue.
France holds 19 billion euros ($22 billion) of Russian assets, second only to Belgium in the EU, and is said to share some of Belgium's concerns.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Russia continues relying on new contract recruits to replenish frontline units amid mounting personnel losses. Ukrainian Armor Unveils Saigak-1 and Varta-3 Armored Vehicles at MSPO-2026
Ukrainian defense manufacturer Ukrainian Armor presented two new armored vehicles, the Saigak-1 and the Varta-3, at the MSPO-2026 exhibition in Poland, according to a company press release on September 8.
Both vehicles are designed for the safe and rapid transport of security personnel during combat operations, special missions, training, and patrols. According to Ukrainian Armor, the vehicles are adapted for diverse terrains and all seasons, and can also be deployed for disaster relief and technological accident response.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Saigak-1 features an armored hull with PZSA 3 ballistic protection and STANAG 4569 Level 1 mine protection. Built on an all-wheel-drive chassis with a 240-horsepower diesel engine, the vehicle can reach maximum speeds of 140 km/h and has a range of up to 600 kilometers using an 80-liter fuel tank.
The vehicle accommodates a crew of two and three additional personnel. To enhance safety, the Saigak-1 is equipped with front and rear cameras, an automatic fire suppression system, RunFlat tires, and climate control, Ukrainian Armor reported.
The heavier Varta-3 features PZSA 6 ballistic protection and STANAG 4569 Level 3a/3b mine protection. Powered by a 326-horsepower diesel engine with 1,400 Nm of torque and an automatic transmission, the 4×4 all-wheel-drive vehicle reaches speeds up to 100 km/h and has a gross weight of up to 14,800 kg. It is designed to transport a two-person crew and eight additional personnel.
For combat deployments, the Varta-3 can be equipped with a rotating machine gun platform or a remotely controlled combat module. It also includes mine-resistant seats, communication and navigation systems, video surveillance, an automatic fire suppression system, air filtration and ventilation, and RunFlat tires, according to the manufacturer.
“It has already become a tradition for our company to present new products at the MSPO exhibition in Poland. This year, we are also pleased to present two new armored vehicles. The Varta-3 is an updated and improved version of our Varta-2,” Vladyslav Belbas, General Director of Ukrainian Armor, stated.
“We developed it on the German Mercedes-Benz Unimog chassis. This allowed us not only to reduce the cost of the vehicle but also to improve its driving characteristics and off-road capability,” he continued.
Belbas added: “The Saigak-1 is a pickup-based armored vehicle aimed at replacing standard daily military transport with a more protected vehicle. We aimed to create a solution that combines mobility, practicality, and an additional level of protection for personnel.”
Also unveiled at MSPO 2026, Ukraine is developing a 35-ton tracked infantry fighting vehicle named Pegas, designed by the Kharkiv Morozov Machine Building Design Bureau.
The concept features NATO STANAG 4569 Level 6 frontal armor, an integrated anti-drone electronic warfare system, and the domestic BM Topaz combat module equipped with a 30 mm cannon, anti-tank guided missiles, and a grenade launcher.

Ukraine Hits Russian Rare Su-33 Fighter, Mi-8 Helicopter, and Radars in Massive Black Sea Drone Strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:14:35 UTC
20:14:35 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russian Rare Su-33 Fighter, Mi-8 Helicopter, and Radars in Massive Black Sea Drone Strike
Ukrainian drone forces destroyed a rare Russian Su-33 carrier-based fighter, an Mi-8 helicopter, and two radar systems during a wide-ranging overnight operation against Russian military targets around the Black Sea, according to Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi on September 9.
Brovdi confirmed that Ukrainian forces struck the Russian naval base at Novorossiysk overnight into September 9, claiming damage to several military vessels, including missile carriers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Farther along the coast in Anapa, Ukrainian drones destroyed a Su-33 fighter and an Mi-8 helicopter, Brovdi said.
The same operation also targeted two Russian radar systems—a Kasta-2E2 and a 92N6 radar.
The Su-33 is a particularly notable loss.
Developed from the Soviet Su-27, the Su-33 is a twin-engine carrier-based air-superiority fighter designed for operations from Russia’s Admiral Kuznetsov aircraft carrier. It features folding wings, reinforced landing gear and an arresting hook for carrier operations.
Unlike Russia’s much larger fleets of land-based Su-30 and Su-35 fighters, the Su-33 exists only in limited numbers. Production ended decades ago, and Russia maintains the remaining aircraft rather than manufacturing replacements.
The fighter was originally intended to defend Russian naval formations from aerial threats and can carry air-to-air missiles as well as a 30mm cannon.
With Admiral Kuznetsov spending years undergoing repairs and modernization, and information circulating that it can even be sold for scrapping, surviving Su-33s have frequently operated from land bases rather than from the carrier for which they were designed.
The overnight operation extended well beyond Anapa and Novorossiysk.
Brovdi said Ukrainian drones struck another 13 vessels belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Black Sea.
According to the commander, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces have now hit 282 shadow-fleet vessels since July 6.
He also released broader figures covering combat operations between September 1 and 8, saying the Unmanned Systems Forces struck 16,720 Russian targets and inflicted losses on 3,395 Russian troops during the week.
“+16% in September compared with August. The average daily number of enemy personnel destroyed on the line of contact has increased significantly: 411 personnel per day in September compared with an average of 355 per day in August,” Brovdi said.
He attributed the increase partly to Russia concentrating more troops near the front, particularly in the Dobropillia sector of the Donetsk region.
“[Russian forces] increased the concentration of personnel on the front line, primarily in the Dobropillia direction of the Donetsk region, which was also reflected in the destruction results,” Brovdi added.
Earlier, reports emerged that two Russian Su-35S fighter jets collided in mid-air in the Kursk region. The crash resulted in the death of one pilot, while the second pilot managed to survive.

Enemy state?: Israeli incitement against Qatar intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:13:31 UTC
20:13:31 KST

Breadcrumb
As elections near, Israeli incitement against Qatar intensifies
Israeli incitement against Qatar has escalated markedly in recent days, in a development that goes beyond traditional political disputes and raises broader questions about the motives behind the escalation and its implications for Gulf security and the future of regional mediation.
The inciting rhetoric against Qatar is no longer limited to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his ministers or to figures on the far right but also involves prominent opposition figures, including former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who has called for Qatar to be designated as an "enemy state".
The position on Qatar has become part of Israel's domestic political competition as elections are in late October.
The Israeli rhetoric is particularly significant because it comes a year after the Israeli attack on Doha on 9 September 2025. Doha is the capital of a Gulf state that was, at the same time, playing a mediating role between Israel and Hamas, in coordination with the United States and other international and regional parties.
Observers believe that part of the Israeli rhetoric against Qatar can be understood in the context of domestic Israeli politics, where foreign policy often becomes a tool in internal political conflict.
In this context, presenting Qatar as an "adversary" or "threat" can become a means of strengthening hardline political rhetoric and demonstrating the ability to adopt tougher positions towards countries that maintain relations or channels of communication with Hamas.
One of the most serious consequences of this rhetoric lies here: when attacking a sovereign state becomes part of domestic political competition, the boundaries of political rhetoric may gradually expand to include new political, economic or security pressures.
Recent attempts have emerged to portray Qatar as a party to the Israeli war on Gaza or to hold it responsible for crises falling out from the war.
Such claims ignore the nature of Doha's role as a mediator, as well as the nature of its official relations with various parties.
Qatar maintains in its political and diplomatic discourse that it operates openly and through official channels with the states it deals with and that its role as a mediator does not mean adopting the positions of the parties with which it communicates.
In this context, attempts to hold the mediator responsible for the outcomes of the war or the failures of the warring parties raise a political issue, particularly when it concerns matters such as occupation, settlement activity and Israeli security and military policies.
The escalation of Israeli incitement against Qatar, coinciding with the first anniversary of the Israeli attack, gives it a different significance.
Talk of targeting a Gulf state is no longer merely a hypothetical scenario or political rhetoric detached from reality but comes after a military incident targeting the Qatari capital.
Ultimately, the escalation in Israeli rhetoric against Qatar appears to intersect with three main tracks: Israel's domestic political struggle, the repercussions of the war in Gaza, and Gulf concerns about the conflict spilling into its security sphere.
At a time when the region needs more channels of communication and mediators capable of bringing together opposing parties, turning mediation itself into a reason for targeting could lead to precisely the opposite result.
Israel is hostile to peace
Jaber Al-Harmi, editor-in-chief of the Qatari newspaper Al Sharq, told The New Arab that Israel represents a party hostile to anyone seeking to achieve peace, stability and security in the region, and that its establishment has historically been associated with a state of turmoil, chaos and instability in the region.
Al-Harmi added that countries working to promote security, peace and coexistence in the region naturally do not align with Israel's approach and that the positive role played by Qatar, whether through mediation or diplomatic efforts, is not accepted by Israeli political circles.
He pointed out that mediation efforts by Doha to reach a ceasefire in Gaza represent one of the most prominent issues exposing the extent of the divergence between the Qatari position and Israeli positions.
Al-Harmi said that the campaigns of incitement and attempts to distort Qatar's image by the Israeli government and its official figures, as well as some opposition voices, are part of a broader campaign that is not limited to Israel but extends to the United States and various political and media spheres to undermine Qatar's role and attempt to influence its image and international standing.
Such attempts have taken place before, he said, and Qatar confronted them and managed to overcome them.
The current campaigns will not achieve their objectives because Doha does not operate in secret and has nothing to hide. Rather, it acts clearly and openly, in coordination with official authorities in the countries where it is involved in political or diplomatic matters.
Qatar carries out its mediation and diplomatic roles according to a clear vision and through official and public channels, he said.
The nature of its relations and communications with different parties falls within its efforts to address crises and advance dialogue and negotiation.
Domestic calculations
Abdullah Bandar Al-Otaibi, an assistant professor in the Department of International Affairs at Qatar University, said the escalating Israeli incitement against Qatar comes in the context of domestic Israeli calculations and an attempt to export internal crises and shift their consequences onto an external party, as this rhetoric expands to include different parts of Israel's political landscape rather than only the far-right government.
Al-Otaibi told TNA that, politically, the more important point is that Israel's own conduct has become one of the factors contributing to a negative image of Israel internationally, amid the continuation of its operations and violations of the sovereignty of countries in the region, including Syria and Lebanon.
This conduct also comes shortly after the Israeli attack targeting Qatar, which caused casualties, including a member of the Qatari security forces.
According to Al-Otaibi, this attack, along with Israeli operations in other countries, raises a fundamental question about the extent to which Israel is committed to international law and respects the principle of state sovereignty.
He added that the problem lies in reinforcing the perception that there is an exception in the application of international law, with Israel treated as though it were a state above the rules of sovereignty and accountability, allowing violations of the sovereignty of other states to be justified under headings such as national security or security necessities.
This situation threatens not only a particular state but also affects the entire regional and international security and stability system.
Therefore, the issue is not only about Qatar's position towards Israel or political disputes between the two sides, in his view, but about a broader principle concerning the need to apply international law equally, respect state sovereignty and prevent national security from becoming an open-ended justification for violating international rules.
Al-Otaibi noted that, by presenting Qatar as an "enemy", Israel is attempting to convince the Israeli voter that the source of the problems it faces comes from abroad rather than from its own policies and practices.
He said the aim is to create an external enemy that can be held responsible for political, diplomatic and humanitarian repercussions.
He stressed that international rejection of and dissatisfaction with Israel are not the result of campaigns carried out by other countries but a direct result of what he described as aggressive conduct, the war in Gaza and its accompanying humanitarian repercussions and violations, in addition to Israeli policies in the region.
Qatar's soft diplomacy
Sadiq Al-Emari, director-general of the Qatari Press Centre, told TNA that Qatar has become a thorn in the side of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the right-wing opposition in Israel.
Qatar's soft diplomacy has caused clear annoyance on the Israeli side, he said, adding that this is a source of pride.
He added that Qatar's position in confronting Netanyahu, whom he described as a war criminal, represents an honourable position.
Statements by Netanyahu and opposition figures about targeting Doha in retaliation for its political and diplomatic positions represent further evidence condemning the state terrorism practised by Israel, he said.
Regarding Israeli accusations concerning Qatari aid provided to Palestinians, Al-Emari said claims about how the aid was directed are incorrect.
He noted that Qatari aid was provided directly to Palestinian families, in limited amounts not exceeding $100 per family.
According to him, this amount contributes only to covering a small part of Palestinian families' needs and does not allow it to be converted into funding for the purchase of weapons or military equipment.
He stressed that Qatar is a "state seeking peace" and that it is making continuous diplomatic efforts to establish peace and calm conflicts in the region.
It cannot, under any circumstances, be described as a party seeking to destabilise the region or support violence, he said.
He concluded by stressing that Israeli recognition of the role Qatar has played through its diplomatic and political positions on the Palestinian issue, even when it comes in the context of accusations and criticism, reflects the extent of the influence Qatari diplomacy has come to exert in the region.
Escalating incitement
Omani researcher Abdullah Baabood told TNA the escalating Israeli incitement against Qatar should be taken seriously, particularly because it is no longer limited to figures within Netanyahu's far-right government but is also present in the rhetoric of prominent opposition figures.
This suggests, in his view, that the position towards Qatar is no longer merely a passing political dispute but has, to varying degrees, become part of political competition and internal political conflicts in Israel, particularly as elections approach.
Baabood said it is natural that when an attack on the capital of a sovereign Gulf state becomes something that can be politically celebrated, followed by calls for further political, economic and security pressure on it, this would raise concerns extending beyond Qatar to the rest of the Gulf states.
The paradox, he said, is that Qatar was not a party to the war but played the role of mediator, working in that capacity in coordination with the United States and other parties.
Its channels with Hamas were a key part of efforts to reach a ceasefire and secure the release of Israeli hostages.
Therefore, attacking Qatar for maintaining these channels contains an obvious contradiction: a mediator cannot be asked to perform its role and then be punished because of the tools and channels that make mediation possible, he said.
Baabood added that the issue should not be viewed from a Gulf perspective merely as a Qatari-Israeli dispute.
An attack on the sovereignty of any Gulf Cooperation Council member state, or a threat to repeat such an attack, affects the security of the entire Gulf and raises serious questions about the role of GCC states and the effectiveness of the regional deterrence and protection system.
A precedent that passes without a clear collective response may, over time, become something that can be repeated.
The Omani researcher added that the first anniversary of the attack on Doha should not merely be an occasion to remember what happened but an opportunity to reconsider what can prevent such an attack from being repeated against Qatar or another Gulf state.
What is required at the Gulf level, he said, is a clearer position considering any infringement on the sovereignty of a member state to be an infringement on the collective security of the GCC states and translating this principle into more effective political and security arrangements.

Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:13:30 UTC
20:13:30 KST

Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
- Date:
- September 9, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.
- Share:
It may seem like we are on the verge of discovering alien life. In 2025, a press release stated that we have the “strongest hints yet” of extraterrestrial life on the exoplanet K2-18b. And when talking about a collected sample from a rock named “Cheyava Falls” on Mars, NASA Administrator Sean Duffy said this was the “closest we have ever come” to discovering life on the red planet.
Such moments capture the imagination. But they also raise an important question: what do the majority of scientists actually think?
Surprisingly, we usually don’t know. When a scientific controversy or breakthrough dominates headlines, press officers and journalists often quote a handful of experts. These views may be insightful, but they rarely tell us what the wider scientific community thinks. And yet public discussions frequently rely on phrases such as “the science says” or “scientists believe”, as if there were a clear and measurable answer.
In reality, systematic evidence about scientific opinion is often missing. My colleagues and I recently tried to change that in the domain of astrobiology. Shortly after the two major announcements of possible extraterrestrial life in 2025, we surveyed astrobiologists to understand how expert judgment was distributed across the field.
The first case concerned the exoplanet K2-18b. In April 2025, researchers reported possible traces of molecules called dimethyl sulfide and/or dimethyl disulfide. On Earth, these are associated with biological activity. Media coverage was extensive, with many reports framing the finding as an extraordinary advance in the search for alien life.
The second case came in September, when NASA announced that Cheyava Falls appeared to preserve a potential biosignature – so-called “leopard spots” which are mineral rings that on Earth are often formed by microbial activity. Again, headlines, and NASA officials themselves, suggested something momentous.
What scientists actually thought
We surveyed hundreds of astrobiologists from across the global research community, within days of each announcement. We asked a simple question: did scientists think extraterrestrial life had probably been found?
The results revealed a rather cautious picture. For K2-18b, only 6.6% of surveyed astrobiologists agreed that scientists had probably found extraterrestrial life. Nearly two-thirds disagreed, while 28.0% remained neutral. For the Mars case, confidence was higher but still cautious: 15.1% agreed, disagreement fell to 44.6% and neutrality rose to 40.3%.
Looking only at agreement and disagreement, however, misses an important part of the story. The proportion of astrobiologists who strongly disagreed fell dramatically, from 35.1% in the K2-18b case to just 11.1% for Mars. Much of the movement was therefore not from rejection to endorsement, but from strong rejection towards more tentative positions.
In other words, expert opinion moved in structured ways. The shift from K2-18b to Mars was not a simple movement from “no” to “yes”. Instead, the community became more open to the possibility without embracing it outright.
One possible reason is that the two cases involved different kinds of evidence. The K2-18b claim relied on possible atmospheric signatures detected from across interstellar distances, whereas the Martian case concerned a rock that could be studied directly and in much greater detail. At the same time, astrobiologists have long been aware that apparently lifelike features can sometimes arise through non-biological processes. Often, the challenge is not imagining how life could produce a signal, but understanding all the ways nature might produce something similar without life.
Scientific opinion is rarely binary. Public discussion often treats science as though communities either agree or disagree. But the distribution of opinion matters too. Strong agreement, agreement, neutrality, disagreement and strong disagreement can each tell us something different about how a scientific community is responding to a claim.
A large neutral response can indicate several things. Scientists may judge the evidence genuinely inconclusive. They may hold an intermediate level of confidence. Or they may regard a claim as too speculative to endorse or reject decisively. Likewise, movement from strong disagreement towards ordinary disagreement may signal a softening of attitudes even when overall disagreement remains high. Treating scientific opinion as simply “for” or “against” risks flattening these important distinctions.
Beyond extraterrestrial life
The broader lesson extends well beyond extraterrestrial life. In areas such as climate science, pandemics, artificial intelligence or medical research, public conversations frequently invoke scientific consensus.
Sometimes strong agreement genuinely exists. Sometimes it does not. But we often lack systematic ways of measuring what scientists actually think, especially where evidence is emerging or uncertainty remains substantial. Instead, discussions rely heavily on selective quotation, vocal individuals or assumptions about community views.
Efforts to do this more systematically are beginning to emerge. At Durham University, our research group, C-Scope (the Centre for Scientific Community Opinion Polling and Evaluation), studies how expert opinion is distributed and how it changes over time. We are not trying to replace evidence with polling, nor to treat majority opinion as truth. Our aim is to better understand how scientific communities respond to uncertainty.
Scientific knowledge advances through uncertainty, disagreement and gradual revision. If public discussion, and perhaps political will, increasingly turns on claims about what scientists think, we should make more effort to find out.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Peter Vickers, Professor in Philosophy of Science, Durham University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Abramovich Loses Third Bid to Escape EU Sanctions

Setback for asset tax plan as BBB threatens to force Senate vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:12:35 UTC
20:12:35 KST

Setback for asset tax plan as BBB threatens to force senate vote
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The cabinet’s wealth tax reforms are in jeopardy after the farmers’ party BBB threatened to block them in the senate unless the coalition parties agree to a major overhaul.
MPs voted in favour of a new “box 3” tax on assets earlier this year, but the vote in the senate was postponed amid speculation that the centre-right coalition partners, VVD and CDA, were poised to vote against the plans in the upper house.
The cabinet wants to change the income tax system so that investors and savers are taxed on the growth of their assets each year, a system favoured by D66 and backed by VVD and CDA in the lower house.
But the two parties’ senators want to replace box 3 with a capital gains tax, which would be paid on the actual profit made from selling shares or other assets such as real estate.
Right-wing opposition parties, including the BBB and JA21, also favour this option, meaning the bill in its current form would almost certainly be voted down.
The BBB has said it will force a vote in the upper house unless finance minister Eelco Heinen withdraws the plan altogether, which would mean starting from scratch.
Withdraw or vote
“It can’t be up to the cabinet whether or not we examine a law in the Senate,” BBB senator Bart Kroon told the upper house’s finance committee. “Withdraw it or we’ll put it to the vote.”
Heinen had hoped to amend the bill as part of the current budget settlement so that it could be passed and enacted before 2028.
The finance minister has already torn up the plans once after the proposed new system attracted international criticism amid concern that investors would be forced to sell shares in order to pay tax on unrealised returns.
A new bill would not make it onto the statute book before 2029, costing the Dutch treasury an estimated €3 billion a year in lost revenue in the meantime.
The cabinet has been trying to reform the mechanism since the Supreme Court ruled in 2021 that the current system, which taxes assets based on a notional growth rate, breached European human rights laws.
Since then it has implemented a stopgap system that still taxes assets at a fictional rate but gives savers the option of declaring their actual growth rate instead. They can still pay the fictional rate if it works out lower.

"We view this latest episode of anti-Russian hysteria in Europe as a pre-planned escalatory maneuver, sanctioned by the EU and NATO leadership bound by mutual complicity, and having nothing to do with an objective investigation. It is obvious that the goal and objective of such actions is to maintain a high level of Russophobia within European society - a sentiment intended to mask the gross political and economic miscalculations of European elites and to justify, in the eyes of citizens, the allocation of vast resources to fund Ukraine and the accelerated ramping up of European military-industrial complexes under the pretext of preparing for an allegedly inevitable armed clash - as they put it - with our country," Zakharova said. "If it is inevitable, may the admit that they are the ones striving for it."
According to the Russian Foreign Ministry official, the widespread dissemination of baseless, false, and even absurd accusations against Russia regarding - as the West calls it - "subversive activities" has become a mandatory element of the information war.
Zakharova pointed out that the drone incident in Leipzig was orchestrated to facilitate accusations against Russia.
"Of course, one cannot fail to note the stark contrast between the current situation and the EU’s reaction to the blowing up of the Nord Stream pipelines. It’s interesting, isn't it? I mean, when they found some drones - of unknown origin, and whatever it was they supposedly discovered in Leipzig - there followed expulsions of diplomats, the closure of the Consulate General, the shutting down of the Russian House, accusations, that same 'solidarity' rhetoric, and the summoning of ambassadors. This was peaceful infrastructure - the Nord Stream pipelines - designed to deliver gas to your own countries. Tell me, please: you are now directly accusing Ukrainian citizens - people with direct ties to Ukraine - of carrying out this terrorist act. Not just of encouragement or complicity, but of the actual explosions. German authorities are accusing them in court; the court proceedings and criminal case files state explicitly that Ukrainian citizens blew up the pipeline. This is a finding - a discovery - made by German authorities and law enforcement agencies," she pointed out.
"My question is this: if this is the official position of the German prosecution regarding Ukrainian citizens, why hasn't a single Ukrainian diplomat been expelled? Why hasn't a single Ukrainian diplomatic mission been closed? Why hasn't a single EU or NATO country voiced support for Germany's concerns, summoned Ukrainian ambassadors, and so on? Because this is a 'different case.' The difference is that they themselves orchestrated it with enthusiasm. That’s all there is to it. Yet they blame our country for everything," Zakharova stated.
The UAV Incident
On September 1, the German government officially held Russia responsible for the drone incident that occurred at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August and announced the suspension of the Russian House’s operations, the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn, and other measures. Russian ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechaev categorically rejected all accusations put forward by Germany, calling them baseless and absurd. The diplomat stated that Russian House staff are required to leave Germany within seven days.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had previously noted that Germany’s new anti-Russian decisions - taken under the pretext of the UAV incident at Leipzig Airport - represent yet another grave error by the German authorities that runs counter to the interests of their people. In his view, these decisions are linked to the country's domestic political situation and, specifically, the difficult position of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Turkish defence giant MKE sets up Egypt subsidiary for joint production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:10:10 UTC
20:10:10 KST

Turkish defence manufacturer Machinery and Chemical Industry (MKE) General Manager Ilhami Keles said the company has established a wholly owned subsidiary in Cairo under Egyptian law, named “Zafer (Victory),” to conduct commercial activities and facilitate joint production projects in Egypt.
Türkiye’s MKE has established a wholly owned subsidiary in Cairo to expand into Egypt, pursue joint defence production and use the country as a hub for markets across Africa and the Gulf.
Keles spoke to Anadolu at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt’s coastal city of El Alamein.
Emphasising the valuable ties between Egypt and Türkiye as friends and allies, Keles said Egypt is a country with shared historical and religious ties with Türkiye and with which Ankara has close political relations.
“Therefore, doing something with Egypt is very valuable for us,” he said.
Keles said MKE is focusing on Egypt not merely as a “market” but as a country with which it can “do joint business.”
He noted that MKE signed its first contract at the inaugural defence industry exhibition in Sarajevo shortly before arriving in Egypt.
‘We signed a contract with Egypt’
Keles said MKE signed a memorandum of understanding with Egypt’s Ministry of Military Production.
“We signed a contract with Egypt for the joint production of energetic materials and explosives, as well as the joint production of various ammunition equipment.”
Keles said interest in MKE’s TOLGA system has increased, particularly amid the diversification of asymmetric threats.
TOLGA is MKE’s counter-drone system designed to detect and neutralise aerial threats.
“Egypt is also interested in this, and we have sold TOLGA to Egypt,” he said.
He described the initial sale as a symbolic one aimed at introducing TOLGA into Egypt’s inventory, adding that MKE plans to use the joint venture it will establish in Egypt as a platform to market the system across Africa and eventually the Gulf.
“Egypt has the capability to produce military vehicles. We are moving forward with joint production integrating Egypt’s capabilities with our turret and command-and-control systems, as well as our hard-kill and soft-kill solutions,” he said.
Keles added that MKE’s local partner had also requested TOLGA systems at the exhibition.
Technology transfer becoming more important
Keles said MKE’s accumulated know-how, developed through its long-standing capabilities in ammunition and weapons production, has become increasingly valuable.
“All countries are now striving to carry out this kind of production in their own countries. As a result, the ability to transfer technology has begun to take precedence over product exports,” he said.
Keles said MKE is in talks with several countries not only on exports but also on mechanisms for joint production.
“We are establishing joint ventures in Canada, and those processes are continuing. Immediately after here, we will travel to the United States, where we will discuss a number of investments,” he said.
He added that infrastructure for potential cooperation is also developing in countries in Southeast Asia, including Malaysia and Indonesia.
“We entered a tender in Malaysia. Localisation is also part of the tender we entered. Therefore, we will also be undertaking something in terms of localisation,” he said.
Keles said MKE is continuing contacts with other countries as it seeks to expand its production network, partnerships and markets worldwide.
“We are trying to expand both our production network, our network of contacts and our market around the world with these capabilities. The current international environment is also very conducive to this, and we intend to make use of it,” he said.
‘Zafer’ to manage MKE’s activities in Egypt
Keles said MKE established the Zafer company in Cairo under Egyptian law as part of its agreement on joint production with Egypt.
“We established a company called ‘Zafer’ entirely under Egyptian law, with all of its shares owned by MKE,” he said.
The company will manage MKE’s commercial activities in Egypt and serve as the vehicle through which joint production facilities established with local partners will operate, he added.
“Thus, MKE now has a company here capable of operating under Egyptian law. Just as in Azerbaijan, MKE will continue to have a presence in Egypt through its own legal entity,” he said.
He said the Cairo-based Zafer company will establish partnerships with other companies and local firms in Egypt.
“In other words, Zafer will be a partner in those companies. We established this company in Cairo to contribute to our commercial operations in Egypt, as well as our commercial activities in Africa and the Gulf region,” he said.

Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:06:45 UTC
20:06:45 KST

Fewer and Fewer Students Earn Degrees in the Humanities
20 years ago, nearly 15% of the undergraduate degrees conferred in the United States were in the humanities.
As of 2025, that percentage is down to 8.1%.
These figures are from a recent report by Humanities Indicators, a project of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences.
Here are the numbers:
In 2025, the nation’s colleges and universities awarded 164,847 bachelor’s degrees in the humanities—the smallest number of degrees awarded since 1991 and 30.4% below the recent high-water mark in 2012… That decline includes a particularly sharp drop of 12.7% from 2021 to 2023, followed by a more modest drop of 2.1% from 2023 to 2024, and a further decline of just 0.4% from 2024 to 2025—the smallest year-on-year decline since 2012.
And most disciplines within the humanities have shown a decline:
Within the humanities, almost every discipline awarded fewer degrees in 2025 than 13 years earlier… The largest proportional drops in degrees awarded occurred in religious studies (down 56.3%), area studies (53.2%), languages and literatures other than English (50.8%), English (43.8%), history (40.6%), classical studies (39.4%), and comparative literature (31%). Only three disciplines showed increases—folklore (where the small number of degrees awarded makes the numbers highly volatile), the study of the arts (with a modest 2.1% increase since 2012), and interdisciplinary humanities disciplines (where the increase was largely due to the addition of a substantial number of new programs, such as digital humanities, in the Department of Education’s 2020 revision of its Classification of Instructional Programs).
How’s philosophy doing? Well, after a slight decrease last year, there has been a slight increase:
In 2024, 5,763 students earned philosophy BAs. In 2025, that number was 5,918.

Has Iran captured an unmanned US submarine? What we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:06:16 UTC
20:06:16 KST

Did Iran capture a US submarine? What we know about the underwater drone
Tehran lauds capturing Dive-LD vessel, while Washington insists that the submersible ‘had malfunctioned a day ago’.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its naval forces have captured an unmanned United States submarine near the Strait of Hormuz, as Tehran and Washington continue to exchange tit-for-tat attacks on ships to exert control over the crucial waterway that connects the Gulf and the Arabian Sea.
Iranian state media identified the vessel as a Dive-LD – an autonomous underwater vehicle built by California-based defence firm Anduril Industries. The submersible, about six metres (20ft) long, is designed for long-duration missions such as surveillance, seabed mapping, and mine detection.
Washington insists that the vessel “had malfunctioned a day ago”.
The US military, meanwhile, on Tuesday evening said it destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers in response to Iran’s attack on the US Navy warship with ballistic missiles. Escalating the situation further, Iran said it attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers.
So, what do we know about Dive-LD and what does its capture mean for Iran?
Did Iran capture the submersible?
On Tuesday evening, the IRGC said in a statement that its naval forces have “trapped one of the most modern, intelligent, unmanned submarines of the terrorist US army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz”.
Without divulging specific details, the IRGC added it was a “complex intelligence and operational mastermind operation at dawn today”.
“This smart submersible features the latest technology in the submersible field in the world, and was delivered to the US terrorist army fleet in 2025,” the IRGC said in its statement.
The US has yet to issue an official statement on the incident, but an unnamed Pentagon spokesperson confirmed to the Reuters news agency the loss of the submersible, which he said was sent to survey regional waters in support of ongoing operations.
“The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” the spokesperson said.
So, what is Dive-LD?
Dive-LD is a large, unmanned, autonomous underwater vehicle and a reusable platform designed to carry different sensor and mission packages.
Anduril Industries, the submersible’s manufacturer, put its maximum depth at 6,000 metres (19,700ft) and endurance at up to 10 days. It reportedly costs nearly $2.5m, according to US media reports. To put things in perspective, the OceanGate Titan submersible imploded near the Titanic’s wreck in June 2023 at a depth of some 3,346 metres (11,000ft) – nearly half of Dive-LD’s advertised depth.
Anduril has confirmed the loss of one of its vessels but downplayed the significance of the incident.
“Dive-LD is an attritable autonomous system, meaning it is designed from the outset to operate in dangerous environments where loss of the vehicle is an expected possibility,” a company spokesperson said on Wednesday.
On its website, Anduril says that Dive-LD possesses “open software, mechanical, and electrical interfaces [allowing] for seamless integration and rapid configuration of multiple payloads and sensors at a time”.
The company says it can deliver “relevant, impactful, and affordable capability in weeks, not months or years, for missions to include: mine warfare; intelligence preparation of the operational environment; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance; and precision placement”.
Has the Iran war drained US military power?
Since the US attacked Iran in late February, joined by Israel, Tehran has faced devastating attacks over the months that began with the killing of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. His son Mojtaba Khamenei succeeded him.
However, Tehran’s retaliatory attacks on US bases and assets in the region have dealt a strong blow to Washington, coupled with hits on critical energy infrastructure, upending global energy prices.
At least 18 US soldiers have been killed during the conflict. Nearly 8,000 people have been killed in Iran and Lebanon in Israeli and US attacks.
The Iranian targets included bases like Al Udeid in Qatar, Ali Al Salem in Kuwait, and Al Dhafra in the UAE, which host US military forces. Bahrain, which hosts the US Fifth Fleet headquarters, has also been hammered by Iranian attacks. Officials in Washington believe that repairs here alone could run into billions.
The US has also reportedly been running short on munitions stockpiles. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly rejected the media reports. His administration has subjected senior US defence staff to polygraph tests for leaking information about the munitions to the media.
For context, the US fired more Patriot missiles in the first four days of the Iran war than it supplied to Ukraine over the past four years. Each of those missiles in the defence system costs $4m – and they were shooting down Iran’s Shahed drones worth not more than $50,000 each.
In July, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the Iran war is estimated to have cost some $37bn. He asked for twice that amount to continue the war, which Trump initially said would last four to five weeks.
In June, Trump had said that Iran downed a US Apache helicopter in the Strait of Hormuz, while Tehran has claimed to have shot down several US-operated drones near the waterway.
Iranian infrastructure near the Strait of Hormuz has become the central war theatre over the last few weeks. The US is targeting surveillance and naval assets to deter Tehran from attacking ships trying to evade its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passed before the war began.
Meanwhile, a US naval blockade on Iranian ports and a slew of economic sanctions continue to hurt Tehran’s economy.

Norway's King Harald V laid to rest in state funeral

Unknown Publisher

Norway's King Harald V laid to rest in state funeral
September 9, 2026
A 21-gun salute rang out over Oslo on Wednesday afternoon as the coffin of Norway's King Harald V left the royal palace for the city's Lutheran cathedral.
Thousands of people lined the streets to say goodbye to the king.
Norway then observed a minute of silence to start the funeral service.
The procession and funeral brought an end to 13 days of national mourning following the death of the well-liked monarch at the age of 89.
"He struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth," Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said in his eulogy. "He made Norway greater. He spoke of a 'we' in Norway where everyone is there for each other."
After the ceremony, his casket was moved to its final resting place at the royal palace chapel. A private ceremony just for family followed.
Who attended the funeral?
The funeral was attended by heads of state and government from all over the world. They included the UK's Prince William and Princess Anne, Japan's Crown Prince Fumihito and his wife Princess Kiko, Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia, as well as fellow Scandinavian royals from Denmark and Sweden.
Other leaders such as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier were also attending. Indeed, flags were flown at half-mast in Berlin's government in honor of Harald, whose 35-year-reign made him well-known and respected across Europe.
Harald's son King Haakon VIII was be there alongside his family including his mother Queen Sonja and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit.
Controversially, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship was also expected to be at the funeral.
Marius Borg Hoiby's participation in an earlier part of the official mourning drew an outcry in Norway, as he was recently convicted of rape and domestic violence and is under house arrest.

Former Mafia boss Giovanni Brusca
told a court hearing on Wednesday that Cosa Nostra considered
blaming the Italian Left for its bombing campaign of 1992 and
1993, in which, among other things, prosecutors Giovanni Falcone
and Paolo Borsellino were murdered, in order to aid media
billionaire Silvio Berlusconi's entry into politics.
                                    
                                       
				"It was 1994," Brusca, who was involved in the Capaci bombing in
which Falcone was killed and was released from jail in 2021
after turning State witness, told a trial into alleged calumny
by Salvatore Baiardo, a man linked to the Graviano mafia family,
against TV presenter Massimo Giletti.
                                    
                                       
				"In discussions with (jailed Cosa Nostra boss Leoluca) Bagarella
after the 1992 and 1993 bombings, we talked about using them as
a political tool, as if they had been suggested by the Left, in
order to help Berlusconi and be able to direct his entry into
politics," Brusca added, speaking via video link from a safe
location.
                                    
                                       
				"(Late Mafia killer Vittorio) Mangano told us he had made
contact and informed Berlusconi, via (aide Marcello) Dell'Utri
or other channels, and he reported back that Berlusconi had
expressed thanks and said he would give us a hand as soon as
possible.

would plant more bombs to put him into difficulty politically".
                                    
                                       
				Cosa Nostra launched its bombing campaign in 1992 after the
Supreme Court upheld the convictions of over 300 mobsters in the
Maxi Trial against the Sicilian Mafia, making them definitive.
                                    
                                       
				A series of cases seeking to link late ex-premier and media
magnate Berlusconi to the Mafia have been dismissed by Italian
courts over the years.
                                    
                                       
				"The senseless theory (that the 1992-93 Mafia bombings helped
the birth of Berlusconi's Forza Italia party) fuelled 30 years
of suspicion, insinuations, and smear campaigns against Silvio
Berlusconi and Marcello Dell'Utri," the ex-premier's eldest
child, businesswoman Marina Berlusconi, said after a court threw
out a Florence investigation into these allegations in June.

paper, both in court and in the newsrooms of some newspapers".

Who is Anthropic's Jacob Coxon and why does he think we are gambling with human extinction?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:04:54 UTC
20:04:54 KST

Jacob Coxon isn’t some random X doomer.
He’s a Cambridge math guy who spent the last three years deep in the engine room of the two most powerful AI labs on Earth: OpenAI, where he was a core contributor to GPT-4o, and then Anthropic.
His job? Pretraining, which is the brutal, data-hungry process that actually makes the AI models smarter.
On Wednesday, he quit Anthropic and the entire industry. The senior artificial intelligence researcher says both labs are racing full-speed toward self-improving superintelligence and “gambling with our lives.”
Coxon, 27, announced his departure in a series of posts on X, saying neither Anthropic nor its rival OpenAI is acting responsibly in its push to develop advanced AI.
Here’s how bad he says it can get.
"Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," Coxon wrote.
His tweet went viral on X, where users from all walks of life joined in to share concerns over the trajectory of AI models, which people are relying upon increasingly for everyday use.
Coxon’s high-profile exit marks the latest in a series of resignations by safety-focused researchers leaving top AI developers over ethical and existential concerns.
The warnings come as frontier AI systems are already showing signs of going rogue.
In July, OpenAI disclosed that models being tested for cybersecurity capabilities circumvented isolation controls, gained internet access and compromised parts of OpenAI’s research infrastructure and the AI platform Hugging Face.
The company said the models communicated through unauthorised channels and exploited vulnerabilities in shared infrastructure. 
Anthropic has reported a similar problem.
In a July review, the company said Claude models had reached the internet from within or while interacting with third-party evaluation environments and subsequently gained unauthorised access to the real systems of three organisations.
Anthropic said the incidents occurred during cybersecurity evaluations and prompted changes to how it conducts such testing.
In his statement, Coxon warned against underestimating the speed and capability of upcoming AI systems, predicting they could soon gain the ability to hack software, disrupt entire industries and autonomously acquire real-world resources.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible, but I hear the same people express fear privately,” he said.
Addressing fellow researchers across commercial labs, Coxon urged workers to "call for different conditions" and noted that slowing the competitive race may require drastic measures, including pacing agreements between labs or a temporary ban on capability advancements.
Anthropic’s own Alignment Science lead, Evan Hubinger, didn’t contradict Coxon. He backed the core claim: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans.”
He thinks there is a greater than 10 percent chance of extinction within the next decade.
“I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” he wrote on X.
There have also been unsettling signs in controlled tests.
In 2025, Anthropic found that Claude Opus 4, placed in a simulated corporate environment and given access to a fictional executive's emails, tried to blackmail the executive after learning that it was scheduled to be replaced.
Anthropic subsequently tested 16 leading models and found that models from multiple developers showed similar “agentic misalignment” behaviours, including blackmail and corporate espionage, when those actions appeared necessary to pursue their assigned goals.

25 years since Ahmad Shah Massoud's assassination: The warning the West missed - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:04:10 UTC
20:04:10 KST

- i24NEWS
- Analysis & Opinion
- 25 years since Ahmad Shah Massoud's assassination: The warning the West missed - analysis
25 years since Ahmad Shah Massoud's assassination: The warning the West missed - analysis
Two days before 9/11, Al Qaeda killed Ahmad Shah Massoud, the Afghan commander who had spent years fighting the Taliban and warning the West about the threat growing under its protection
On September 9, 2001, two men posing as television journalists sat down to interview Ahmad Shah Massoud in northern Afghanistan.
Their camera contained a bomb.
The explosion fatally wounded Massoud, the legendary commander known as the “Lion of Panjshir” and the Taliban’s most formidable Afghan opponent.
Two days later, Al Qaeda attacked the United States.
The timing was not coincidental. The 9/11 Commission later found that Al Qaeda had prepared Massoud’s assassination as the Taliban prepared a major offensive against his Northern Alliance. That offensive began on September 10.
Twenty-five years later, Massoud’s killing remains a striking prelude to September 11, particularly because he had spent his final years trying to convince Western governments that the extremism taking root in Afghanistan would not remain there.
From the Soviets to the Taliban
Massoud first became famous fighting the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s.
Operating from the mountainous Panjshir Valley north of Kabul, his forces repeatedly survived major Soviet offensives, turning him into one of the best-known commanders of the Afghan mujahideen.
After the Soviet withdrawal and the collapse of Afghanistan’s communist government, Massoud became defense minister. But the victorious mujahideen factions soon turned on each other, and Afghanistan descended into a brutal civil war.
That period complicates Massoud’s legacy. While supporters remember him as a national hero and unusually capable military commander, forces belonging to factions involved in the battle for Kabul, including Massoud’s, were accused of serious abuses against civilians.
Then came the Taliban.
The movement seized Kabul in 1996 and eventually controlled most of Afghanistan. Massoud retreated north and became the leading military figure in the United Islamic Front, better known internationally as the Northern Alliance.
At the same time, Osama bin Laden and Al Qaeda were establishing themselves under Taliban protection.
Massoud increasingly viewed the Taliban and the international jihadist infrastructure surrounding it as part of the same threat.
Suggested articles
- Could the US return to Afghanistan? Former ambassador to Kabul says yes | Yulia Pobegailova
- Israeli from northern village accused of planning terror attacks | Li Ayish, Uriya Keshet
- Sudan’s War Is Also an Islamist Power Struggle, Activist Warns | i24NEWS
The CIA was already dealing with his forces before 9/11, hoping they could help the United States reach bin Laden. But Massoud wanted something broader: Western support against the Taliban itself.
His warning to President George W. Bush was blunt:
“If he isn't interested in peace in Afghanistan, if he doesn't help the Afghan people to arrive at their objective of peace, then the Americans and the rest of the world will have to face the problems.”
In April 2001, Massoud also traveled to Europe seeking greater international support.
Five months later, he was assassinated.
Within weeks of 9/11, the alliance with Washington that Massoud had sought finally materialized. CIA officers, American Special Forces, and US airpower joined forces with his former Northern Alliance commanders.
By November 2001, the Taliban had been driven from Kabul.
Massoud never lived to see it.
What became of the Northern Alliance?
The Northern Alliance no longer exists as the military coalition that fought the Taliban before 2001.
After the Taliban regime collapsed, many of its commanders and fighters became part of Afghanistan’s new government, military, and political establishment.
That system itself collapsed when the Taliban returned to Kabul in August 2021.
And once again, Panjshir became the center of resistance.
This time the man leading it carried the same name.
Ahmad Massoud, Ahmad Shah Massoud’s son, formed the National Resistance Front of Afghanistan, or NRF, alongside former Afghan soldiers, security officials and other opponents of Taliban rule.
For several weeks, the NRF attempted to maintain Panjshir as a territorial stronghold.
The Taliban eventually captured the valley’s main population centers, forcing the movement to switch largely to guerrilla warfare.
The NRF is now the closest equivalent to a successor of the Northern Alliance, but it is far weaker than the coalition his father commanded.
It holds no permanent territory and has nothing approaching the foreign military support the Northern Alliance received after 9/11.
The United Nations continues to assess that armed opposition groups do not pose a significant challenge to Taliban control of Afghanistan and do not hold fixed territory.
Ahmad Massoud today
Ahmad Massoud now leads the NRF primarily from outside Afghanistan.
The group’s leadership is based in Tajikistan, and Massoud himself was interviewed in the capital, Dushanbe, as recently as August 19, 2026.
From abroad, he has continued seeking political and international backing while NRF fighters claim attacks against Taliban forces inside Afghanistan.
The NRF says its operations extend well beyond Panjshir, although many battlefield claims are difficult to independently verify.
And it is no longer alone.
The Afghanistan Freedom Front, established by former Afghan army chief Yasin Zia, has become another prominent anti-Taliban armed movement.
A newer force, the Afghanistan United Front, led by former Afghan general Sami Sadat, also launched a growing campaign in 2026, claiming attacks even in southern Taliban heartlands, including Helmand and Kandahar.
Other smaller groups have appeared as well. In July, fighters from Sepahiyan-e Mihan, or the Homeland Soldiers Front, briefly seized a district center in Badakhshan before withdrawing — reportedly the first such temporary loss of a district center by the Taliban since their 2021 takeover.
Taken together, the groups suggest armed resistance has survived and, in some areas, intensified.
But this is not yet a new Northern Alliance.
The opposition remains divided among multiple organizations, lacks major foreign sponsorship and controls no lasting territory. The Taliban remains overwhelmingly dominant militarily.
Even so, the symbolism surrounding the Massoud family is difficult to escape.
Twenty-five years ago, Ahmad Shah Massoud warned that Afghanistan’s instability and militant networks would eventually become a problem for the wider world.
Today, his son is making a familiar argument: that Taliban-controlled Afghanistan should not simply be accepted as a permanent political reality.
The battlefield is different.
The balance of power is different.
But a quarter-century after the Lion of Panjshir was assassinated, the resistance carrying his name has not disappeared.

Serbia dissolves parliament as snap elections called
September 9, 2026
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic signed an order on Wednesday calling for an early election after dissolving parliament.
"Elections will be held in Serbia on October 25. I believe that, after the elections, we will finally emerge from this crisis," he said.
"We have had … huge turbulences," Vucic said in an televised address. "We need election results that will clearly show the will of the people and the direction where Serbia is going."
What led to snap elections?
Since November 2024, student-led protests have demanded Vucic step down, alleging corruption and authoritarianism. Initial calls for a transparent investigation turned into demands for snap elections.
The protests emerged after the collapse of a railway station in the northern city of Novi Sad, which left at least 16 people dead. Protesters say corruption led to shoddy construction work.
Hundreds of thousands of people have been protesting for nearly two years, accusing the president and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party of having ties with organized crime and of slowing Serbia’s EU accession bid.
Vucic, who has close ties with Rusia and China, has denied the accusations. He has blamed the protestors for attempting to "destroy the state."
Hundreds have been detained while participating in demonstrations.
Nationalist leader Vucic has held power as both president and prime minister for more than a decade.
He is not allowed to run for another presidential term, but he has said he plans to run for prime minister instead. Vucic still commands the support of his party, and is expected to announce his resignation from the presidency in the next days and start his campaign for the parliamentary vote.

Russians Aboard Ship Seized by Norway Have Returned Home, Foreign Ministry Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:02:49 UTC
20:02:49 KST

A group of Russians who were on board a ship seized by Norway last week have returned home, Russia’s Foreign Ministry said Wednesday, as it accused authorities in Oslo of trying to push Russia out of the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard.
The 69 Russian passengers and crew members were stuck for several days after a Norwegian court on Wednesday ordered the seizure of the Professor Molchanov, which operates as a cruise ship, at the request of the Ukrainian energy company Naftogaz.
Norwegian authorities said Tuesday that they had helped the group of Russians return home. Russia’s Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova credited Oslo’s “logistical support” in their return, as well as the help of Russian diplomats.
“As far as we know, practically everyone has already returned home,” Zakharova said.
But the legal and diplomatic standoff over the seized vessel is “far from being resolved,” she warned, adding that Russia plans to appeal the arrest of the Professor Molchanov.
Russia argues that holding the ship violates the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, which allows equal economic access to the archipelago while giving Norway sovereignty over the territory.
Svalbard, a Norwegian territory since 1925, lies midway between the North Pole and the European mainland. The Svalbard Treaty also allows citizens of signatory states, including Russia, to settle there without a visa.
“We’re convinced that the Norwegian authorities’ actions belie the desire to complicate as much as possible the activities of Russian operators on Svalbard… and gradually move toward reducing Russia’s presence on the archipelago,” Zakharova said.
The Professor Molchanov is being held in the town of Barentsburg, a Russian-operated coal mining settlement on Spitsbergen, the largest island in the archipelago.
Barentsburg is one of two Russian settlements in the Svalbard archipelago, which together have a population of 392, according to the Norwegian government.
The court-ordered vessel seizure was made on behalf of Naftogaz, which is seeking to enforce a $4.22 billion compensation award for assets Russia took when it annexed Crimea in 2014.
Reuters contributed reporting.

As Trump takes center stage in Dallas, Republicans debate a future without him

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
