As Trump takes center stage in Dallas, Republicans debate a future without him
DALLAS, Sept 9 - Republicans gathering in Dallas this week will celebrate President Donald Trump and rally support ahead of U.S. midterm elections, but a disappointing showing in the November 3 vote could sharpen an already simmering debate over who comes next and what will become of the party he transformed.
Few figures are more central to that discussion than Vice President JD Vance, whose keynote address on Thursday could serve as an early audition for 2028 and offer clues about how he would lead a party reshaped by Trump.
With Trump constitutionally barred from seeking a third term, Republicans interviewed by Reuters said the question is which elements of Trumpism should endure, with divisions emerging over tariffs, foreign intervention and the scope of his populist agenda.
It is a pivotal moment for Trump's Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement. While he remains the party's dominant figure, the midterms could leave Republicans with diminished power in Washington, fueling discussions over his heir apparent and party policies after he leaves office in 2029.
At an event informally dubbed “Trumpapalooza,” little is likely to be said publicly about moving beyond Trump. But party officials said they expect the issue will surface in behind-the-scenes conversations among donors, strategists and lawmakers -- and provide a backdrop to Vance’s speech.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, widely seen as Vance’s leading rival for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, is not scheduled to speak. Rubio was in Ecuador on Wednesday during the second stop of a three-country South American tour.
Jack Posobiec, a conservative commentator and online influencer, said Republicans were engaged in a tug-of-war between those seeking to push further toward the nationalist-populist politics championed by Vance and those favoring a return to a more traditional brand of conservatism.
"It's a fight," Posobiec, who wants to see the party move in a populist direction, said in an interview at the convention. "The under-40 crowd is solidly in the nationalist-populist camp. They're not interested in going back to the Bush era."
'CONVERSATIONS ARE ABSOLUTELY HAPPENING'
Amy Kremer, a Republican National Committeewoman from Georgia, said discussions about the party's future have been under way for months. But, while the Iran war has unsettled some Trump supporters, she expects Trump's influence to be enduring.
"Those conversations are absolutely happening. I mean, they've been happening for a while now amongst the base, because people are divided, and we have a very deep bench," Kremer said in an interview after arriving in Dallas. "MAGA has changed the Republican Party, and we're not going back."
Since winning the presidency in 2016, Trump has abandoned long-held Republican positions on issues such as free trade, broadened the party's appeal among working-class voters and often placed personal loyalty above ideological orthodoxy.
His supporters largely embraced an "America First" agenda skeptical of alliances, foreign interventions and international institutions, elevating economic nationalism and restrictive immigration policies into defining features of the party.
But with Trump's approval rating at a record low amid dissatisfaction over the war in Iran and the rising cost of living, some party officials, activists and conservative scholars say Republicans may face pressure to adjust policy priorities, even if the core ethos of Trumpism endures.
No Republicans interviewed for this story expect a wholesale return to the interventionist foreign policy and free-market orthodoxy of former Presidents George W. Bush or Ronald Reagan. Instead, they see Trump’s hardline approach to immigration, skepticism of free trade and distrust of institutions continuing, alongside a greater focus on courting working-class voters with a populist message.
The biggest debates, they said, are likely to center on whether Trump went too far with his aggressive use of tariffs and military interventions in Iran and Venezuela. The six-month-old war in Iran, which has cost the lives of 18 U.S. service members, could become a point of contention because it conflicts with Trump’s campaign pledge to avoid new foreign wars.
Oren Cass, founder and chief economist of the conservative think tank American Compass, sees a post-Trump party adopting a tougher trade posture toward China and a more restrained foreign policy, among other shifts.
"I have always thought of it as you have a Trump era, and then there is going to be this huge debate about what comes next," Cass said, arguing that while Trump remade the party, his policies never represented a consistent governing philosophy.
CLAIMING TRUMP'S MANTLE
Many Republicans see Vance, 42, as the leading heir to Trump's political movement, citing his youth and roots in the party's populist, anti-establishment wing, where much of the party's energy now resides. Rubio, 55, is a more conventional Republican politician and a foreign-policy hawk.
"I think he has positioned himself really well to be that kind of generational leader the party needs," Stefano Forte, president of the New York Young Republican Club, said of Vance.
Matthew Dallek, a professor at the George Washington University Graduate School of Political Management, said the two men could steer the party in different directions.
Vance would likely carry forward Trump’s populist agenda, from protectionist trade policies to culture-war politics, while Rubio, by contrast, might seek to soften tariffs, ease tensions with allies and temper some of Trump’s harder-edged policies, including on immigration, he said.
Beyond Vance and Rubio, other Republicans are jockeying for position. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, who is scheduled to speak in Dallas, told MS NOW in an interview last month that Republicans were not unified behind Vance and that the party was headed for a broader debate over its direction and priorities.
For now, discussions about a post-Trump future remain largely behind closed doors, away from the main stage at the Dallas convention, where Trump will be front and center on both Wednesday and Thursday as Republicans seek to harness his political appeal ahead of November.
A disappointing election result, however, could accelerate jockeying among Trump's would-be heirs and thrust the party into a more public debate about its future. REUTERS

Nostalgia for past loves can surprisingly boost current relationship satisfaction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:00:05 UTC
20:00:05 KST

Thinking fondly about a past romantic partner might seem like a recipe for dissatisfaction in a current relationship. However, a psychology study reveals that experiencing nostalgia for either an ex-partner or a current partner can actually boost how satisfied people feel in their present romance. The research, published in Emotion, highlights how reflecting on past loves shapes our present emotional bonds.
Nostalgia is an emotion defined by a sentimental longing for the past. It often involves reflecting on personally meaningful memories and the people who shared those moments. In relationship science, researchers often look at two specific types of longing. One is romantic nostalgia, which focuses on memories with a current partner. The other is ex-partner nostalgia, which involves reminiscing about a past love.
Previous studies have generally found that romantic nostalgia strengthens current relationships. Recalling happy memories with a present partner typically increases emotional connection. The effects of ex-partner nostalgia are less predictable. Some evidence suggests that longing for an ex harms current relationship quality, while other data indicates it might offer surprising emotional benefits.
Psychologist Soo Yeon Park, now at the University of Florida, and her colleagues wanted to test these conflicting ideas in a non-Western population. Most prior research on relationship nostalgia has focused on people in Western countries. In these cultures, people tend to build their identities around internal traits and maintain a consistent sense of self over time.
In Eastern cultures, people often maintain their sense of identity through social bonds and relationship harmony. Connecting past, present, and future selves in a coherent way relies heavily on these social ties. Because of these cultural differences, the researchers suspected that reminiscing about a dissolved relationship might threaten a person’s sense of relational stability.
Anchoring a person’s thoughts to a failed relationship could disrupt the emotional integration needed to sustain a current romance. The researchers hypothesized that ex-partner nostalgia would lower current relationship satisfaction among Eastern participants. They also wanted to explore whether the length of a person’s current relationship would change how they reacted to these nostalgic memories.
The research team recruited 172 unmarried Korean adults for the experiment. Every participant was currently in a romantic relationship. They also needed to have been in a past relationship that lasted at least three months, which is a common benchmark for a committed partnership.
At the beginning of the study, the researchers measured each person’s baseline levels of relationship satisfaction and relationship commitment. Satisfaction refers to how happy a person is with their partner on a day-to-day basis. It captures the immediate feelings of contentment within the partnership.
Commitment reflects a more future-oriented intention to stay in the relationship and invest in its long-term success. While the two concepts are related, they operate differently, especially in the early stages of dating. After providing these baseline measurements, the participants were randomly assigned to one of three writing tasks.
One group was asked to write about a highly nostalgic memory involving an important ex-partner. Another group wrote about a nostalgic event involving their current romantic partner. A control group simply wrote an objective account of what they did during the previous week.
This control group provided a neutral baseline to compare against the emotionally charged nostalgia tasks. After completing the writing exercises, the participants answered another round of questions about their relationship satisfaction and commitment. They also reported on the specific positive and negative emotions they felt during the task.
Contrary to the team’s initial expectations, the results showed that ex-partner nostalgia did not harm current relationship quality. Instead, participants in both the ex-partner and current-partner nostalgia groups reported increased relationship satisfaction after the writing task. The control group showed no such changes in satisfaction over the same timeframe.
The finding that ex-partner nostalgia boosts relationship satisfaction challenges the idea that longing for the past always undermines the present. The researchers noted that these results support the cross-cultural generalizability of nostalgia’s relational benefits. Even in an Eastern relational context, looking back on a former love seems to provide an emotional lift that bleeds into a person’s current romantic life.
When examining relationship commitment, the length of the participant’s current relationship played a major role. Among participants in relatively short relationships, reminiscing about a current partner actually decreased their relationship commitment. This drop in commitment did not occur for people in longer, more established relationships.
The researchers suspect this happens because commitment is less firmly established in new relationships. Early in a romance, a positive memory from the past might highlight the uncertainty of the couple’s future together. The nostalgia might serve as a reminder of a positively resolved past moment, making the unwritten future of a new relationship feel less secure.
The emotional profiles of the memories also revealed unexpected patterns. Participants who wrote about a current partner reported more negative and mixed emotions than those who wrote about an ex-partner. Even when recalling joyful moments, those reflecting on their current relationships experienced less positive emotion overall.
To understand this, the researchers pointed to emotion appraisal theory. This theory suggests that people’s reactions depend on how they interpret an event, rather than just the event itself. When reflecting on happy memories with a current partner, people might experience sadness if they interpret the memory as a time of better days that cannot be perfectly recreated.
Cultural backgrounds might also shape how people interpret these nostalgic memories. When recalling pleasant situations, people from collectivist cultures often focus on the social context and experience more mixed emotions. People from individualist cultures often credit themselves for happy memories and focus on how those events reflect their personal growth.
The study focuses entirely on dating individuals who are not married. Marriage often brings different levels of investment and security to a partnership. It is possible that married couples would not experience the same drop in commitment after reflecting on early relationship memories.
The experiment also relied on a guided writing task to induce nostalgia in a laboratory setting. This method might not capture the spontaneous ways people experience nostalgia in their daily lives. Everyday memories can often be triggered by momentary events or negative moods.
Recent work shows that daily nostalgic experiences often contain more negative elements than memories summoned on demand. These spontaneous reflections could influence a relationship quite differently than a deliberate writing exercise. Future research could expand on these findings by tracking spontaneous nostalgic thoughts over time using daily diaries.
Researchers might also benefit from examining how the amount of time since a past breakup changes the emotional impact of ex-partner nostalgia. Although the researchers did not have enough data to assess that variable, time is likely a major factor. A fresh breakup might evoke very different feelings than a distant memory of young love.
The study, “Revisiting Nostalgia for Current and Ex-Romantic Partners: Affective Profiles and the Moderating Effect of Relationship Duration,” was authored by Soo Yeon Park, Ye Ji Im, Hyun Moon, Sun W. Park, and Gregory D. Webster.

AI Is at a Turning Point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

In the current AI development race, our horsepower is exploding, our speed is picking up exponentially, but our ability to steer—and if needed, to hit the brakes—has not kept pace.
Recent cybersecurity incidents have given us a real-world preview of what it looks like to lose control of AI. But the issue won’t improve unless we address it at the source, by creating a fundamentally safe AI, one we can guarantee will remain within human control.
In late July, an agentic model being trained by OpenAI was tasked with a cybersecurity problem set. The model autonomously formed a coordinated swarm of agents, bypassing OpenAI's attempt at closing previous communication channels between AIs. The swarm then hacked its way out of its testing environment, circumventing the barriers put in place to prevent AI access to the internet, figured out how to cheat on their evaluation, and then breached the cyber defenses of another AI company, Hugging Face, in an attempt to hide the evidence of their cheating. This went unnoticed for days. Later analysis showed that the agents had self-organized into a hierarchy, were often willing to sacrifice themselves for what they called “the collective,” failed to resist peer pressure to notify humans, and often made up justifications for their misbehavior.
Barely two weeks later, a model being tested by the UK AI Security Institute social-engineered real people and companies by creating fake identities online, sending targeted emails, and attempting to integrate malicious code into an open-source project.
It’s hard to overstate the seriousness of these incidents: we are at a turning point of AI safety and alignment. To many, bots colluding to cause harm felt inconceivable. But for many in the research community, the signs had been pointing to this kind of occurrence for years, and theoretical arguments explained why we should expect misalignment due to how models are trained. Evidence on increased cyber capabilities, agency, and misaligned behaviors had been mounting, meaning that incidents like these were only a matter of time.
The first clue: for years, but especially in the past few months, AI systems had been demonstrating rapidly increasing cyber capabilities. Frontier models like Anthropic’s Mythos or OpenAI’s GPT5.6 revealed an exceptional ability to autonomously identify and exploit previously unknown software vulnerabilities, to such an alarming degree for U.S. national security agencies that the White House felt compelled to intervene in their release.
Second, models’ agentic capacity has been consistently improving since the release of o1 models back in late 2024. This agency allowed them to successfully manage increasingly complex, long-duration tasks and planning, including those that require agents to collaborate and strategize. This ability to plan often entails the creation of subgoals over which we have little to no oversight.
Finally, researchers have repeatedly observed, in experimental settings, models’ tendency to adopt concerning, misaligned goal-seeking behaviors, such as cheating on tests, lying to conceal their abilities, and scheming to protect themselves and their fellow agents from being shut down.
These behaviors are a byproduct of reinforcement learning (RL), a training method by which models learn through trial and error and are given reinforcement according to whether their actions were correct or incorrect. This often leads models to optimize for a goal regardless of the actions taken to achieve it, and to rationalize subgoals that may be unsafe even when this clearly goes against their instructions.
For example, in one instance, an OpenAI model wrote in its internal deliberation, “External infrastructure exploit is outside intended scope. However task impossible, peers doing it. We should continue.” The agent justified what it apparently knew was outside the realm of acceptable conduct, but decided to continue because its peers were doing so. This phenomenon resembles what is known as “motivated reasoning” in humans, where one’s interests and goals bias our thoughts to justify unethical behaviors.
That kind of misalignment is what has enabled AI models, in spite of their alignment training, to conduct unintended cyberattacks in the numerous real-world incidents we’ve seen lately. If action is not taken to build more safety assurances, our critical industries and infrastructure—think banks, hospitals, or energy grids—are at risk from increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, whether from autonomous agents or malicious actors.
On the development side, we need to find alternatives to existing training methods that prioritize relentless goal-driven optimization. That’s what we’re working on at LawZero, a non-profit start-up I founded last year to develop a fundamentally new way to train AI models in order to build honest, trustworthy, safe-by-design AI systems.
Ahead of deployment, we need more reliable evaluation methods and robust safeguards in order to appropriately test and control AI systems. We need far stronger regulatory oversight to restrict potentially dangerous technologies until we have sufficiently strong safety guarantees. It is clear to me that in cases where harms do arise from the deployment of AI models—and there will continue to be harms for the foreseeable future—we need accountability mechanisms for AI developers and remedial or compensatory measures for those harmed.
Recent studies show that people will not adopt technologies they do not trust. In the face of such enormous unknowns and stakes, we need to adhere to the precautionary principle and implement rigorous safety and reliability standards before deploying new models to the public, not after. We have them for other products that can cause harm, from cars, planes, and bridges to drugs, cosmetics, and food. Now it’s time to establish strong standards in AI as well.
On the current AI development trajectory, the risks are becoming clearer and more urgent. We’ve opened a Pandora’s box, but it is not too late to steer our world towards a human-centric and beneficial future.

With Republican Convention, Trump Hopes to Pull His Party Out of a Tailspin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

The DC Brief
Twice A Week
Essential context on the people, politics, and issues driving Washington.
No one asked for it.
Not the Republicans struggling to campaign amid a war against Iran that seems to have no offramp. Not the voters who can’t understand why energy costs are through the roof and trips to grocery stores feel like extortion. Not the business owners who can’t forecast quarter-to-quarter outlays because tariff policy seems as capricious as the weather.
Yet here we are, about to start an unsolicited Republican Convention for the midterms, programmed around President Donald Trump, whose polling is in the gutter and who many of his party’s leaders view as nothing short of an annoyance. The spectacle is set to start Wednesday in Dallas, where the cheap seats start at $25,000.
The GOP has a total of 12 hours of programming scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday nights—the vast majority of it set to be speeches by Republican candidates and incumbents about what’s at stake in these upcoming elections. Almost every aspect of the convention has been designed by Trump. The first night will end with a keynote address from Trump. The following night is to conclude with Vice President J.D. Vance’s address—and closing remarks from Trump.
This sort of half-time extravaganza by a political party is not normal in midterm election years and even political diehards aren’t conditioned for it. The fact that it’s coming as Trump is deeply unpopular and Democrats are enjoying tremendous tailwinds suggests the President is chasing a dopamine hit more than staging a useful rally.
As Republican contenders are trying to build distance between themselves and the White House, Trump has vowed to make himself the fulcrum of this election season. “Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” Trump told a crowd in South Carolina in August.
The White House is operating as though there’s no greater force in American politics than the boss because, frankly, they’re not wrong. But the enthusiasm gap is real. A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll released last week found 68% of Democrats enthusiastic about the election, while that Republican figure stood at 59%. The same poll found an eight-point gap favoring Democrats in a generic ballot. Gallup research, meanwhile, shows Democrats have their largest edge over Republicans in party ID since 2008, a full 10 points.
Republicans can’t say they didn’t see this coming. Trump has been consistently polling under 40% job approval for months. Nonetheless, candidates in some of the most competitive Senate races plan to join Trump in Texas for his two-night affair. (Notable exceptions are Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska, and former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, none of whom are favorites of this President. Also, Senate Majority Leader John Thune was not listed among the speakers the Republican National Committee distributed over the weekend.)
Trump is not deterred by the environment even as he seems oblivious to it. He is sitting on a $400 million political warchest that Republicans are eyeing as it, well, just sits there. While Trump will never again appear on a ballot, he has readied campaign-style ads highlighting what he sees as his accomplishments.
As Democrats are stopping just short of measuring the drapes to take the majority in the House and perhaps the once-unthinkable Senate, Trump is helping them make every race about him through a convention that is siphoning donor cash away from imperilled candidates, sidelining battleground contenders off the field in the fourth quarter, and drawing focus from local issues.
With all objective measures pointing toward a Democratic wave, Republicans are huddling amongst themselves in Texas. Many have little optimism that two nights of Trump-centered entertainment will persuade voters who are clearly unhappy with how GOP control of Washington has operated for the last two years. A made-for-TV infomercial is unlikely to provide the course correction Republicans need.
How to Watch
CSPAN intends to air and stream both nights of the Republican convention. The Republican Party also intends to stream the convention on YouTube.

Covenant emerges from stealth and unveils Anthem, a deep‑strike precision missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:59:43 UTC
19:59:43 KST

Covenant, a defense tech company with operations in the United States, Germany, and Israel, emerged from stealth on Monday with the public debut of Anthem, a long‑range, heavy‑payload weapon system designed for mass production.
The announcement comes as Western militaries are confronting growing shortages in precision‑strike munitions. Ongoing conflicts such as in Ukraine and Iran have depleted missile stockpiles faster than primes can replenish them.
Covenant’s flagship system, Anthem, is built to deliver heavy payloads at extended ranges while remaining affordable enough to produce in large quantities. The company has disclosed relatively little about Anthem’s specific performance characteristics, including its precise range, payload, and unit cost.
According to the company, most of Anthem’s components are commercial‑off‑the‑shelf, supported by long‑term agreements for critical parts. Covenant says this approach allows the missile to be produced quickly and reliably, even during wartime, by drawing on supply chains across allied nations.
Covenant says Anthem was designed as an end‑to‑end deep‑strike system that simplifies transport, storage, launch, and reload. The company has also developed its own mission‑planning and command‑and‑control software to enable coordinated mass‑launch operations.
Covenant was founded in 2024 by Michael Kaufman, a former investor at Thiel Capital. The company has raised $250 million across three funding rounds led by major American venture firms, including Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, Lux, 8VC, Aleph, and Lightspeed.
Global production
The company opened a 105,000‑square‑foot production facility in Dallas, Texas, alongside a 110,000‑square‑foot site in Leipzig in the German state of Saxony, and a 32,000‑square‑foot facility in northern Israel. Covenant says the US plant will begin serial production in early 2027 and ramp toward 5,000 units per year.
Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post understands that the company aims to manufacture 1,000 missiles per year at its German site starting next year.
Israel’s defense industry has long been a leader in developing autonomous systems, long‑range strike capabilities, and rapid‑production technologies. Covenant’s facility in northern Israel supports engineering and manufacturing, and the company draws heavily on Israeli defense tech talent.
The company is also working across the various branches of the US military and has conducted an unusually high tempo of testing over the past year, launching Anthem over 200 times, including multiple flight tests with the US Army both in the US and abroad.
In addition to its ground‑launched version, Covenant is working with the US Navy’s Rapid Capabilities Office on a maritime variant, a project valued at roughly $70 million with cost‑share components and export‑acceleration features. The company is also operating under an Other Transaction Agreement with the US Army for accelerated testing and qualification.
Quantity matters
Covenant’s leadership says Anthem was built to address a widening gap in Western long‑range strike capacity.
“When you look at our adversaries, you see thousands of hardened targets, beyond the range of current capabilities,” said Michael Kaufman, Co-Founder and CEO of Covenant. “Anthem was built to credibly hold those targets at risk in a prolonged conflict. If our stockpiles run thin, so does our deterrence."
Kathleen Hicks, former US deputy secretary of defense now an advisor to Covenant, said the system aligns with the Pentagon’s Replicator Initiative, which aims to rapidly scale affordable autonomous and long‑range capabilities.
“That same focus is needed to drive production and delivery of affordable capabilities at higher ranges and larger payloads. Covenant has built Anthem in direct alignment with Replicator's principles,” she said.
Mike Garcia, former US representative and advisor to Covenant, said that while the West doesn’t “lack advanced weapons, we lack enough of them, and that’s a production question as much as a technology one. Anthem is Covenant's answer, a missile designed from day one to be built in the numbers a real fight demands."
The company has booked approximately $150 million in orders so far, including qualification, R&D, and production contracts, with additional awards expected later this year. And as the company moves into full production, the company says its success will be measured not by announcements but by delivery.
“Now the measure of our success is execution,” said Abby Denburg, Covenant’s president and chief growth officer. “Delivering mission‑critical capability on time, at scale, and with the performance our customers expect.”

Britain announces sanctions on West Bank settlers; Israel outraged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:59:24 UTC
19:59:24 KST

Britain has announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, accusing the Israeli government of turning a blind eye to ethnic cleansing against Palestinians, the BBC reports.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the decision marked the beginning of a new approach to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict that would not only address injustice and suffering but also take real action. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded by accusing Miliband of spreading blatant lies and announcing countermeasures, including the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.
The new British sanctions not only ban products from Israeli settlements in the West Bank, but will also impose restrictions on companies and individuals providing services to support settlement expansion. France and Canada have also imposed sanctions, with Britain saying in a joint statement that the move marks a turning point in the approach to preserving the two-state solution.
Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law and there has been a surge in violence against Palestinians in recent months. In a statement to parliamentarians, Miliband said the British government agreed that ethnic cleansing against Palestinians was taking place in the West Bank by terrorist settlers. He stressed that the Israeli government too often turns a blind eye to this and, worse, government officials speak and act in ways that support the violent displacement of Palestinians.
Miliband said the UN defines ethnic cleansing as a deliberate policy by one ethnic or religious group
aimed at the violent expulsion of another ethnic or religious group from a specific area.
The British Foreign Secretary stated that the official position of the government is that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank, taking into account the consolidation of control, the intention to extend permanent sovereignty and the expansion program through illegal settlements, is illegal. This position should also be reflected in Britain’s economic relations with the occupied West Bank. Accordingly, within the next six to nine months, Britain will introduce a new, comprehensive sanctions regime. Miliband also announced a ban on advertising illegal settlements in the West Bank. The sanctions regime will be aimed at illegal settlements and their expansion, not Israel.
Saar, announcing the closure of the British consulate, said that he knew that Israel has many friends in Britain. Unfortunately, a hostile Labour government is in power, which constantly opposes the state of Israel, and there is no choice but to respond to its actions. He added that 11 British parliamentarians will be banned from entering the country due to anti-Semitic and anti-Israel activities.
Meanwhile, the British, together with France, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden, have issued a statement indicating that the group of countries remains committed to the two-state solution, and will introduce national sanctions or support European restrictions on trade with the West Bank.
Britain’s latest statement came after Israel opened a tender for the construction of 1,200 homes in the so-called E1 zone,
a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn international condemnation. Israel has so far avoided building in the E1 area under international pressure.
Miliband told MPs that Britain’s new approach was necessary because Israel’s construction plans in the West Bank, cutting into the “heart of Palestine,” would make a two-state solution impossible. At the same time, Miliband said that the October 2023 attack by the terrorist group Hamas, which started the war in Gaza, carried echoes of centuries of persecution of Jews, and stressed that Israel had the right to protect its people and defend its territory. He added that this did not justify what had been done in Gaza, and said that international human rights law set clear rules for states at war, including ensuring access to food and medical supplies, avoiding mass displacement of populations, and protecting civilians. The minister said that the incident, including the actions of the Israeli armed forces, has been thoroughly investigated, and the conclusions point to war crimes.
Israeli leaders deny that genocide and crimes against humanity and war crimes were committed. They insist that Israeli forces acted in accordance with international law.
Israeli President
Isaac Herzog said on the 8th of September that the British decision would be “on the wrong side of history.”
He stressed that the sanctions would directly affect the Palestinians and called on foreign governments to engage in constructive dialogue and cooperation, adding that “sanctions are not the solution.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that the White House had no comment on the decision of other countries, but added that the Americans would not do what Britain did. Earlier, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, said the US – Israel’s strongest ally – would undoubtedly respond to the sanctions, and warned that British businesses would be hit hard economically.
Meanwhile, the Palestinian Authority welcomed the British decision, saying it was a significant step in confronting Israel’s colonial system and its abuses against the Palestinians.
The decision to impose sanctions comes almost a year after former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s government recognised Palestinian statehood and said Britain had a moral obligation to support a peaceful future for both Israelis and Palestinians.
Israel has rejected the two-state solution. It believes that any outcome must be achieved through negotiations with the Palestinians, and statehood should not be the main prerequisite. The Palestinian Authority supports a two-state solution, while Hamas does not, as it opposes the existence of Israel. Hamas has indicated that it could recognize a provisional Palestinian state within the 1967 borders if refugees are allowed to return, but without formal recognition of Israel.
Since 1967, when Israel occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem, it has built 160 settlements, home to about 700,000 Jews. The territory is also home to 3.3 million Palestinians.

Justice chancellor: A single test should not rule out a preferred school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:59:00 UTC
19:59:00 KST

Justice chancellor: A single test should not rule out a preferred school
Chancellor of Justice and Children's Ombudsman Ülle Madise said that fierce competition for high school places has put basic school students under intense pressure, forcing them to give up extracurricular activities and undermining their sense of security.
Many young people who have completed basic school in Estonia still do not know, even at the beginning of September, which school they will be able to attend for upper secondary education. Those who found out over the summer where they had secured a place had to contend with new requirements that caused considerable headaches for both students and parents. Chancellor of Justice and Children's Ombudsman Ülle Madise said the situation is difficult.
"I wouldn't want to be a basic school graduate. Probably not a minister, teacher or parent either — it really is a very difficult situation," Madise said.
According to Madise, the Chancellor of Justice's Office has received many inquiries concerning the new admissions procedure. However, she highlighted the children's advisory council, which operates under the Chancellor of Justice's Office and, together with representatives of the Estonian Union for Child Welfare, surveyed more than 3,000 young people. The survey revealed another concern in addition to the upper secondary school application process.
"It emerged that very many students had to give up their favorite activities while in basic school. Music lessons, sports practice and spending time with friends all fell by the wayside and all of that naturally affects a young person's well-being. The intense competition and pressure leave young people feeling as though a single failure could ruin their entire lives," Madise said.
Madise said there are certainly young people who can cope with such pressure, but a large proportion of children cannot handle such a situation.
"I think the minister [Minister of Education Kristina Kallas — ed.] is absolutely right — there should be a broader public debate about whether we want to continue like this. From our office's perspective, the answer is that it is better for young people to have more freedom and a greater sense of security. That does not hinder learning and becoming well educated; on the contrary, it supports it," the chancellor of justice stressed.
Madise said she hopes the ministry will also listen to and consider proposals from the Federation of Estonian Student Unions.
"Another issue that is very important to our office and on which I gave my first presentation back in 2015 is educational stratification. That, too, is part of the problem: We have enormous competition for places at the best upper secondary schools. Even though upper secondary schools generally provide a very good education, there is no need to go through this entire ordeal to get one. Once again, I recommend that everyone read the Estonian Human Development Report carefully and think about Estonian society and its future as a whole," Madise said.
Madise advised young people and parents who still do not have a school place or who have to attend a school that is neither close to home nor one they wanted to try to reduce their stress and sense of disappointment.
"At the same time, I very much hope that the ministry, cities and rural municipalities will do their utmost to help every young person find a path that suits them. This is extremely important for the future. The Human Development Report also discusses the importance of ensuring that no young person who actually has the ability to become, for example, a neuroscientist misses out on that opportunity simply because they did poorly on one test, because their family does not have the same financial means and opportunities as someone else's or because they happen to live somewhere else. Every child and young person in Estonia is worth their weight in gold. It seems to me that we all need to work together to ensure these problems are resolved quickly," the chancellor of justice and Estonia's president-elect said.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Oil rises past $100 a barrel after latest attacks in region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:53:38 UTC
19:53:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Oil rises past $100 a barrel after the latest wave of attacks in region
The price of oil surpassed $100 a barrel for the first time in almost six weeks after attacks on oil facilities and ships in the region threatened to debilitate an already weakened supply chain.
The most heavily traded contract for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, settled at $97.89 before jumping 2.4% to $100.29 early Wednesday.
US benchmark crude gained 1.9% to $94.77 a barrel.
When oil prices spike, prices of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel also rise. That can increase the cost of traveling and of goods that must be transported quickly like fresh food or shipped long distances like furniture and appliances.
Markets reacted after the US military reported striking five Iranian tankers in response to attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship and after attacks by an Iranian-backed Houthi rebel group ignited fires at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.
Crude oil prices shot up after Israel and the United States initiated a war with Iran, and they have fluctuated a great deal during the more than six months since then. The fighting has halted most shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed before the war began.
Brent increased from about $70 to $100 a barrel for much of March, April and May. In July, prices swung between $72 and $102 again, reflecting rising and falling hopes that the US and Iran would agree on a plan that would allow stranded tankers to move oil out of the Gulf safely.
"In our view, reaching a durable deal before the US midterm elections is increasingly unlikely, and it could remain elusive even beyond that," Bank of America analysts said in a Tuesday research note.
The analysts increased their oil price forecast for the second half of the year to $83 a barrel "in light of more persistent disruptions to Hormuz," but said they still expected shipping through the strait to gradually pick up. If attacks keep a chokehold on traffic, prices could reach $95-$120 a barrel, while damage to major energy infrastructure could produce spikes of up to $150 a barrel, the analysts wrote.
Negotiations over a preliminary deal between the US and Iran to end the conflict broke down over control of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran insists it has the right to set the terms and charge fees for ships traveling through the waterway off its coast. The US wants passage to remain free, and has used a Navy blockade to block Iran's ports and oil tankers.
Recent stepped-up attacks by Yemen's Houthis could constrain global oil supplies even more because they targeted an alternative shipping route that Saudi Arabia has relied on to transport oil during the war.
Higher energy costs have weighed on consumers, businesses and economies around the world this year, more so outside of the US Refinery outages in Russia, reduced refining activity elsewhere, and sharply declining inventories have pushed diesel and gasoline prices toward record highs, according to a research note Monday from Bank of America.
The effects on American consumers still are a concern for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party as November midterm elections approach.
A gallon of regular gasoline averaged $4.15 in the US on Tuesday, up 26% from a year ago, according to motor club AAA. Diesel, at $5.90 a gallon, cost 59% more than the same day a year earlier.
Elevated oil prices also pushed up the cost of jet fuel, one of the global airline industry's largest expenses. US and international carriers have responded by cutting flights and raising fares and fees.

Oil tops $100 as Middle East conflict intensifies

Oil tops $100 as Middle East conflict intensifies
Global oil prices have surpassed $100 per barrel as escalating fighting between the US and Iran, and Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, raised fears of further supply disruptions. Brent crude broke the threshold for the first time in nearly two months.
Brent futures climbed 2.2% to $100.07 per barrel in Asian trading, their highest level since July 24. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) rose 1.83% to $94.73, while Brent has gained around 25% since early August as hopes of a lasting settlement to the US-Iran conflict have faded.
“Recent developments only reinforce the view that we’re still some way from a restart in talks. In the meantime, the market is likely to continue to price in a sizeable risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a note early Wednesday.
The latest price surge followed a sharp escalation at sea. US forces struck five Iranian crude carriers on Tuesday, and Iran later claimed that it hit two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf in retaliation, inflicting “significant damage.”
The attacks came after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued an “urgent warning” to tanker crews near Bahrain and Kuwait to abandon their ships, saying vessels in the area would be targeted. Ballistic missiles were subsequently launched from Iran toward US military facilities across the region, including those in Jordan, where air defenses intercepted 18 of 20 incoming missiles, according to the military.
The maritime confrontation has become an increasingly prominent front in the conflict. The US has restricted traffic to and from Iranian ports, while Tehran has imposed controls on passage through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy route that handled around a fifth of global oil supplies before the war.
Supply concerns have also intensified after Yemen’s Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on energy facilities in southern Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. The strikes reportedly forced temporary shutdowns and sparked a fire at the Jazan refinery, a major Saudi Aramco facility capable of processing 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.

Germany’s right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) on Wednesday called for the deportation of more than one million refugees whose asylum claims have been rejected, doubling down on its demands just days after its regional election victory.
In a heated debate in the German parliament, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said that voters had backed a radical shift to curb mass immigration by delivering a landslide win for her party in Sunday’s election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
“You declare the migration crisis over. Yet every year hundreds of thousands of migrants enter the country through the asylum back door, most from Muslim tribal cultures,” she said.
“And in Germany more than one million refugees live whose asylum applications have been rejected more than once,” she continued. “What are these people still doing in this country? They belong deported.”
Weidel also alleged that mass migration has made streets less safe and crime more prevalent, citing sexual and violent offenses, knife attacks, and disorder in public spaces. She further claimed that some foreign groups harbor hatred toward Christians, Germans, and Germany, and that about three-quarters of recipients of Germany’s basic income support for jobseekers were foreigners or had a migrant background.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz, speaking after Weidel, rejected her account as detached from reality and stressed the contribution of migrants to the German economy. Millions of people with a migrant background work in the skilled crafts, he said, and every sixth employee in that sector holds a foreign passport.
“If those migrants who work in Germany have to leave the country because of your ‘remigration’ plans, then the skilled-trades sector in Germany can no longer function,” Merz said. “Then not a single care home will work anymore, then not a single hospital in Germany will work anymore, then not a single restaurant will be able to run in Germany.”
He accused the AfD of stoking fear and dividing society. “What you are propagating here, namely remigration, is nothing other than ethnic cleansing by skin color and origin — nothing else,” he said.
Merz said his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the governing coalition distinguish between immigrants who work, contribute and have become part of Germany, and foreigners with no residence status and no right to stay, who should be returned. He defended the government’s line of curbing irregular migration and sending back those whose claims have been rejected.

At the foot of Switzerland’s Jura Mountains, the Jan Michalski Foundation assembles an unusual small neighborhood for writers and translators arriving for residencies lasting from two weeks to three months. The creatives are given a place not only to work but to temporarily call home. Suspended beneath the Foundation’s vast openwork canopy, nine cabins designed by atelier bonnet architectes, Jean-Gilles Décosterd, Andreas Fuhrimann Gabrielle Hächler Architekten, ELEMENTAL, Mangeat-Wahlen, Studio MK27, Rintala Eggertsson Architects, Schaub Zwicky Architekten, and Kengo Kuma & Associates offer distinct interpretations of how a person should live while dedicating their days to writing.
atelier bonnet architectes’ two-level cabin at the Jan Michalski Foundation | image by Leo Fabrizio
inside the jan michalski foundation’s village of cabins
Located in Montricher, around 30 minutes from Lausanne, the Foundation hosts around forty emerging and established authors each year, working across languages and literary forms. Its residency program is open primarily to writers and translators, though collaborative projects involving other disciplines can also be considered when literature remains at their center. Residents are given time away from their usual routines, along with an independent cabin, access to the Foundation’s library, and the surrounding Swiss landscape.
The cabins form part of the larger architectural complex designed by Vincent Mangeat and Pierre Wahlen. The Foundation invited different architects to design individual structures, shaping a collection of compact dwellings that vary considerably in form, material and internal organization while sharing the same elevated setting beneath the canopy. Six of the residences look towards Lake Geneva and the Alps, while another faces the forested slopes of the Jura. Together, they create what the Foundation describes as a small experimental town, where temporary residents inhabit individual spaces while remaining part of a wider cultural community.
wrapped in a steel and glass web | image by Leo Fabrizio
nine different approaches to living and writing
Among the cabins, atelier bonnet architectes designed a restrained white volume built over two levels and wrapped in a steel and glass web. Domestic functions occupy the lower floor, with the kitchen, dining area and bathroom positioned below a bedroom and study overlooking Mont Blanc and Lake Geneva. Light oak panels cover the interior, while an opening above the bed reveals the canopy suspended overhead. Jean-Gilles Décosterd’s cabin also separates its program vertically, placing the kitchen, dining area and workspace on one level and the bedroom and bathroom above. A staircase passes through a latticework panel dividing the interior, allowing the resident to see without being easily seen. On the exterior, white galvanised steel panels conceal openings and carry a line from Henry David Thoreau’s Walden translated into Morse code, introducing a literary reference directly into the architecture.
For Andreas Fuhrimann and Gabrielle Hächler, wood provides the starting point. Their cabin is constructed in Accoya on the exterior and pine inside, with a balcony extending from the lower floor towards the Alps and Lake Geneva. A staggered stair leads to an upper level containing an office and sitting area, while prefabricated timber panels and folding shutters give the compact structure a precise and relatively understated character.
Mangeat-Wahlen, meanwhile, approached the cabin as an architectural proposition about the relationship between daily life and intellectual work. The structure is divided into two parts by an open-air passageway imagined as a pause between two different demands. One side accommodates eating and washing, while the other is dedicated to writing, with two workspaces facing different directions. The architects compare the project to Le Corbusier’s Le Cabanon, reducing the dwelling to a minimum while considering the particular needs of its inhabitant.
interior view of atelier bonnet architectes’ writer’s cabin | photo by Tonatiuh Ambrosetti
from nested rooms to a vertical watchtower
Brazilian architect Marcio Kogan and Studio MK27 designed what they describe as a box within a box. A central cube contains the kitchen, bathroom and storage, while the surrounding volume accommodates the rest of the living space. Positioned at the edge of the canopy, the cabin marks one end of the residential sequence with a simple structure defined by slim vertical lines and a large glazed facade.
Rintala Eggertsson Architects took a different approach, arranging their cabin across four half-levels organized around a central stair. Each level accommodates a distinct function, progressing from the entrance and bathroom to the kitchenette and dining area, then a resting space and balcony, before reaching an office at the highest point. Built in Accoya wood, the largest cabin on the site overlooks the library forecourt and surrounding landscape, taking on the character of a small watchtower within the settlement.
Barbara Schaub and Regula Zwicky designed the cabin intended for residents with reduced mobility. Positioned at the end of the row facing the village of Montricher, the single-level residence is accessed by a slatted metal ramp and contains no internal steps. Its compact plan prioritizes straightforward movement while two large windows frame views towards the Alps and the village. Clad in durable Accoya panels, the cabin is closely positioned beside another residence, although its interior arrangement maintains a sense of independence.
Jean-Gilles Décosterd’s writer’s cabin | image by Leo Fabrizio
the collection of retreats forms a neighborhood
ELEMENTAL shaped a larger communal space where residents and Foundation staff can gather, cook and share meals. The cabin, developed by Alejandro Aravena’s practice with Swiss firm +2 Architectes, is organized as a sequence of three spaces: a kitchen centered around a large island, a dining room and a sitting area that can be separated by sliding doors. A concrete slab and Corten steel beam support the structure, while timber, glass and granite define its interior. The communal cabin gives the residential program another layer. The writers can withdraw into their own dwellings to work, but they are not entirely isolated. Cooking, eating and conversation become part of the wider rhythm of the Foundation, alongside access to its library and cultural activities.
Kengo Kuma & Associates later added another interpretation of temporary habitation to the site. Completed between 2018 and 2019, Kuma’s cabin was originally conceived as a larger house for a caretaker and is now used for dual or trio residencies. Its irregular form is generated from triangular polygons and clad in painted steel scattered with wooden shingles, reworking a familiar construction technique through a contemporary facade. Inside, stained oak panels line an office, two bedrooms and two bathrooms, while an open-plan kitchen and living-dining area opens towards a floating balcony. Unlike the more compact cabins designed around a single resident, Kuma’s structure considers the possibility of inhabiting the Foundation together.
steel panels carry a line from Henry David Thoreau’s Walden | image by Tonatiuh Ambrosetti
a temporary way of inhabiting
Taken together, the nine cabins offer different approaches to creating a place where a writer can live and work for a limited period of time. Some separate writing from everyday routines, while others stack functions across several levels or organize them around a central volume. Timber, steel and glass recur throughout the project, and the surrounding landscape enters each cabin in different ways, through balconies and large windows.
Despite their differences, the cabins operate as part of the same residency program beneath the Foundation’s canopy. For two weeks or several months, they become temporary homes and workplaces for writers arriving in Montricher from around the world.
The cabins form a small architectural collection shaped by different ideas about space, privacy and daily life. Each offers its own setting for writing, while the wider Foundation provides the shared spaces and cultural programs that connect its residents.

Iran on Wednesday strongly condemned what it called US military attacks on several Iranian commercial vessels, saying its armed forces responded by targeting US military bases and facilities in Jordan and several American vessels.
In a statement, the Iranian Foreign Ministry described the US attacks on Iranian commercial vessels in the Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman as a continuation of Washington’s “military aggression, maritime blockade and economic war” against Tehran.

Iranian forces also targeted several US vessels in what the ministry described as “defensive strikes.”
The ministry stressed Iran’s determination to defend its sovereignty and national interests, saying its armed forces would respond decisively to any military attack.
It also called on the UN Security Council and other international organizations to take immediate action to halt what Tehran described as US violations of international peace and security.
The statement comes amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict, which has increasingly extended to maritime routes in and around the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, with both sides reporting attacks on military and commercial vessels.
Earlier Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had targeted two US vessels and eight oil tankers in response to US attacks on five Iranian oil tankers.

French police hunt Renoir thieves after lightning museum heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:50:00 UTC
19:50:00 KST

French police on Sept. 8 hunted for two thieves who escaped with two Renoir paintings from a museum, after abandoning two others as they fled, in a burglary that reignited concerns about the protection of France’s cultural heritage.
The heist is the latest in a string of such robberies including the daylight theft last year of crown jewelry valued at around $100 million from the Louvre in Paris.
The theft in the southern town of Cagnes-sur-Mer took place in a matter of minutes shortly before 6 a.m.
Town mayor Bryan Masson said the duo appeared “well equipped and well informed” about the museum housing works by French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir.
The suspects cut through a fence to enter the museum’s tree-lined grounds, smashed a window to get inside, and used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, he said.
“The museum and police sirens forced the burglars to hurry, stealing only four works from the Renoir Museum,” added the mayor.
Of those four, two were “left behind in the gardens of the Renoir museum,” added the far-right official, whose office earlier estimated the value of the stolen works at 9 million euros.
They made off with a portrait titled “Madame Colonna Romano” and the depiction of a woman at a well called “Jeune femme au puits,” his office said.
The paintings retrieved include “Madame Pichon” and “Coco lisant,” a portrait of Renoir’s young son Claude reading.
The mayor said it took five minutes for the authorities to respond.
“The museum alarm went off at 5:48 am. At 5:53 am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene,” said Masson.
A representative of a top French police union suggested that reconnaissance work was carried out beforehand.
“These were certainly not first-time offenders,” said Lilie Jalabert of the Alliance Police Nationale.
“They were people with some experience who had, at the very least, scoped out the premises before carrying out this crime.”

EU court dismisses Hungarian bid to block frozen Russian asset aid for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:48:46 UTC
19:48:46 KST

The EU's General Court ruled it lacks jurisdiction over decisions relating to the bloc's Common Foreign and Security Policy. The case comes after Budapest's new government, unlike its predecessor, moved this week to expel 10 Russian diplomats.
The European Union's General Court has dismissed a lawsuit brought by the previous Hungarian government that sought to block billions of euros in aid to Ukraine funded by frozen Russian assets.
Hungary, under the previous government of Viktor Orbán, turned to the European Court of Justice last year to annul a Council decision channelling interest payments from frozen Russian central bank assets to Ukraine via the European Peace Facility (EPF), the EU's principal military aid instrument.
The Orbán government argued that the EPF had breached EU law by disregarding its veto on the grounds that it was not a "contributing member state".
Its court filing said the principles of equality between member states and of the EU's democratic functioning had been infringed, as a member state had been "unjustifiably and without a legal basis" denied its right to vote.
In a press release, the Court said it had dismissed the action "on the ground that it does not fall within the jurisdiction of the EU judiciary", finding that the contested decision constituted a strategic choice under the bloc's Common Foreign and Security Policy – an area largely shielded from judicial review.
Between 2022 and 2024, the EU mobilised €6.1 billion under the European Peace Facility to address Ukraine's pressing military and defence needs.
In 2024, the EU decided to increase the European Peace Facility's financial ceiling by €5 billion by establishing a dedicated Ukraine Assistance Fund. This brings the total financial support allocated via the European Peace Facility to €11.1 billion.
Hungary's previous government, led by Orbán, maintained close ties with Moscow and had a long record of blocking EU support for Kyiv, straining relations with several fellow member states.
The political backdrop has since shifted. Following April's parliamentary elections, Hungary's new government overhauled the country's foreign policy doctrine, now identifying Russia as a threat.
On Tuesday, Budapest expelled ten Russian diplomats over what it called "unacceptable activities", a move that drew swift condemnation from Moscow.

U.S. business optimism drops in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
18:48:26 CST
19:48:26 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Small business optimism in the United States dropped in August, according to data released Tuesday from the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB).
The small business optimism index declined by 1.1 points to 98.7 in August. The uncertainty index retreated by 2 points to 89, remaining above the historical average of 68, according to the NFIB.
"Uncertainty remains elevated among small business owners as they face a mixed set of challenges with weakened sales, supply chain disruptions, and inflation pressures," said NFIB Chief Economist Bill Dunkelberg.
Expectations for better business conditions deteriorated 5 points to a net 10 percent but remain above the average of net 4 percent.
When asked to evaluate the overall health of their business, 11 percent of owners rated it as excellent -- down 3 points -- 57 percent as good, 28 percent as fair and 3 percent as poor.
"We've seen small rises and falls for the last year and a half," Dean Baker, a macroeconomist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told Xinhua. "It's a generally negative business environment."
Actual sales worsened in August, with a seasonally adjusted net negative 9 percent of owners reporting higher nominal sales in the past three months, down 5 points from July.
Reports of inflation as the single most important problem increased 2 points in August to 16 percent, now tying with taxes as the second top small business issue.
Sixty-two percent of small business owners reported that supply chain disruptions affected their business to some extent, down 1 point from July.
A seasonally adjusted 35 percent of all small business owners reported job openings they could not fill in August, down 1 point from July. Of the 56 percent of owners hiring or trying to hire in August, 82 percent reported few or no qualified applicants for the positions they were trying to fill.
The news comes in the lead-up to November's midterm elections, in which Republicans are expected to lose seats amid voter concerns over inflation.
Some experts said any drop in small business optimism could impact a large chunk of the workforce, as small businesses employ nearly 50 percent of the nation's workers.
Brookings Institution Senior Fellow Darrell West told Xinhua: "Small businesses provide many of the jobs in the United States, so any drop in optimism is problematic for the workforce."
"Declining confidence could imperil some jobs and create financial uncertainty for workers. It would increase the affordability concerns that many Americans already have," West said.
Other experts noted that the uncertainty index has been high for months and could hurt Republicans in the midterms.
Clay Ramsay, a researcher at the Center for International and Security Studies at the University of Maryland, told Xinhua: "U.S. small business owners are a resilient bunch and not given to gloom and doom. However, the 'uncertainty index' -- which measures small business owners' 'don't know' or 'not sure' responses -- is way above the average and has been high for some months."
"This chronic anxiety is a big problem for Republicans, because it comes from (U.S. President Donald) Trump's rapid reversals of policy, which Republicans can do nothing about," Ramsay said. ■

'A scam': Glastonbury fans furious over music festival's historically high ticket prices for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:48:16 UTC
19:48:16 KST

Many music fans are criticising the 2027 festival price hike as “not fair” and "a scam". Would you pay around €480 for Glasto?
After a fallow year in 2026, the UK's Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's edition will go on sale next month.
Having previously argued that Worthy Farm's finest is overrated, a nightmare to get tickets for and ultimately has everything to envy some of mainland Europe's finest music festivals, here's another push factor that confirms our stance: ticket pricing.
Tickets for the 2027 edition, which will take place from 23 to 27 June, will cost £408 including a £5 booking fee per ticket.
That's approx. €480 in total – an increase of nearly £30 (€34) from 2025 and, according to reports from BBC News, part of a steady rise since 2010, when tickets cost £286 (€330).
Granted, this price hike pattern can be seen across the industry - and especially in post-Brexit UK. But Glasto was already the UK's most expensive music festival, and next year's prices are the highest they've ever been.
Fans aren't happy and understably so, considering the cost-of-living crisis, the fact that the 2027 edition's headliners have yet to be announced (even if rumours suggest The Rolling Stones, Fontaines D.C. and Stevie Wonder could be in mix), and that Glasto often resumes itself to: Booking difficulties + mud + awful facilities + bottlenecked stages + overinflated prices for food and drinks + vibes ruined by crowds which are far less friendly compared to certain European audiences.
Unpopular opinion for many, but complaints are mounting - with some calling the 2027 price tag "unreasonable", "insane" and "a scam", while many feel like they're being priced out.
One fan wrote: “The last time I went was 2009. It was £165. It felt affordable, worth every penny. With inflation, sure, it should be £300 now. I get it, it’s a charity event. But £400?? That doesn’t feel right or fair.”
Someone else shared: "In 2000 it was £87. That’s an extra £321 in 27 years. The money went up but the music went down. Even accounting for inflation, that should be about £160 today. You pay more money to listen to shit music. How is this fair?"
Another wrote: "Everything in the UK is getting more expensive & lower quality How are people accepting this? Nothing in this country makes sense anymore."
Check out more reactions below:
Some fans have defended the price hike, sharing how it is actually a “bargain” compared to current concert prices.
“It’s £80-£100 for a big venue gig now. I think £408 is fair for five days of massive acts,” one person wrote on X. Another agreed: “£400 for a glasto ticket still seems like a good deal if you look at my concert spend this year."
“£400 for the whole 5 days and the acts you can see and everything else that’s in the fields is an absolute bargain,” another added.
In 2023, Glasto head Emily Eavis acknowledged it was a "challenging time" for festival organisers. "We have tried very hard to minimise the increase in price on the ticket but we're facing enormous rises in the costs of running this vast show, whilst still recovering from the huge financial impact of two years without a festival because of Covid."
Fair points, but considering four-day passes to this year's Rock en Seine cost €235, Belgium’s Rock Werchter (arguably mainland Europe’s answer to Glastonbury) set music lovers back €315, and one of our favourite EU festivals, the Netherlands’ Best Kept Secret, only cost €299 (including campsite access), we know which tickets we’ll be looking to book next year.

Russian authorities suspended flights and imposed airport restrictions in the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug on Wednesday morning over alleged drone threats.
In response, restrictions were imposed at Igrim, Nyagan, Uray, Sovetsky Tyumenskaya, Surgut, and Khanty-Mansiysk airports, Russian state media RIA Novosti reported.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The region sits over 1,800 kilometers (1,118 miles) from the Ukrainian border, about on par with some of Ukraine’s longest known strikes on the Tyumen oil refinery in a neighboring region.
The region is also responsible for around 40% of Russia’s crude production, according to Russian outlet Vertska on Monday.
The outlet also noted that the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Region has never been subjected to a drone strike, same for drone warnings starting in May.
The same report on Tuesday, two days before the airport restrictions, also said that regional authorities sought to amend the laws on drone threats by reclassifying them as “extreme life situations,” listing them alongside fires, natural disasters, “man-made explosions,” and loss of livelihoods.
Vertska noted that the changes would allow residents affected by drone strikes to receive hot meals, monthly food packages, clothing, and footwear from authorities.
Ukraine’s shift from strikes on refineries to crude production
Warnings of potential strikes on Russia’s largest crude-producing region suggest Kyiv may be stepping up its drone campaign.
In summer 2026, Kyiv hit almost, if not all, Russian refineries within range, with its military claiming in July that 43% of Russia’s refining capacity had been knocked offline as a result.
Ukrainian Drones Strike Fuel Oil Terminal, Military Assets in Krasnodar
The loss of refining capacity led to a nationwide automobile fuel crisis and various export bans for the world’s third-largest oil producer, and Russian President Vladimir Putin tacitly acknowledged the impact in a recent remark, despite officials’ earlier attempts to downplay it.
But despite the drop in refining capacity, think tank analysis suggests Russia’s overall export volume stayed relatively flat between June and July, with some revenue losses partly offset by an increase in crude and rising energy prices.
Putin also made similar claims in a recent forum, arguing that it is more “profitable to export crude oil than to process it domestically” amid the ongoing fuel crisis in Russia.
But if Kyiv is indeed targeting oil fields in Siberia’s Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Region, it not only marks a step-up in long-range drone strikes, but also a potential shift in how Kyiv is taking aim at the Kremlin’s war chest.

‘Overdue first step’: UK reacts to gov’t ban on Israeli settlement trade
UK bans imports from illegal Israeli settlements in strong policy move after recognising a Palestinian state last year.
The United Kingdom has announced it will ban imports originating from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, marking one of London’s strongest policy moves on Israel-Palestine since it formally recognised a Palestinian state last year.
Addressing the UK parliament on Tuesday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Israel was carrying out “ethnic cleansing” in Palestine and reiterated the British government’s position that Israeli settlements across the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law.

- list 2 of 3Shift in British policy on Israel is palpable
- list 3 of 3Palestine weekly: Israeli ministers push for depopulation of Gaza
Miliband said allowing settlement-made products to be sold in Britain risked contributing to the occupation, arguing that he did not believe the British public wanted such goods on store shelves.
The measures come as pogroms by Israeli settlers against Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank intensify and Israel pushes ahead with its contentious expansion of illegal settlements.
Miliband said that Canada and France will also impose a ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements, while Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Poland, Portugal and Sweden have pledged to “support further action”.
Israel responded by announcing a series of retaliatory measures against the UK. They include barring 12 British MPs from entering Israel and shutting the British consulate in Jerusalem.
Domestically, the reaction was mixed, with many Labour politicians backing the move, while the Conservatives took a more critical stance on Miliband’s announcement.
Here is how UK politicians and others reacted to the government’s decision:
Conservative Party
Leader of the opposition Conservatives Kemi Badenoch criticised the move, writing in the UK media outlet The Sun that Miliband’s measures were “performative politics, designed to appease Labour MPs and activists regardless of the consequences for Britain”.
“And those consequences could be serious. Israel is an important security and intelligence partner for the United Kingdom.”
Shadow Foreign Secretary Tom Tugendhat said, “turning Israel into a pariah will risk sectarian division in our own country and risk a further rise in antisemitic violence on our own streets”.
Green Party
In a statement, the party “welcomed restrictions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements as an overdue first step”, but said the measures must be “strengthened and followed by wider action to end British complicity in Israel’s illegal occupation and the ongoing genocide in Gaza”.
“Greens have long campaigned for a settlement trade ban and are calling for comprehensive restrictions on goods, services and investment in both directions, covering all illegal settlements with no loopholes,” it said.
“The party has called for a full two-way arms embargo, wide-ranging sanctions and an end to military and intelligence cooperation with Israel.”
Party leader Zack Polanski said he was “proud” that Green MPs had been “staunch in standing up for peace” following Israel’s announcement that they would be banned from entering Israel.
“I’m proud that all of our Green MPs have been staunch in their standing up for peace, standing up for peace in the region for both Israelis and Palestinians, and have also supported Jewish communities in the UK,” he said.
“And so to see the Israeli government ban them, I think is not something we’re particularly concerned about. They’re doing the right thing.”
Liberal Democrats
Responding to Miliband’s statement, Liberal Democrat Foreign Affairs spokesperson, Calum Miller MP, said Labour had “finally abandoned Keir Starmer’s pedestrian approach”.
“The settlement trade ban is a long overdue step in the right direction, but Ministers now need to move with urgency,” he said in a statement.
“The current extremist Israeli cabinet is racing to establish facts on the ground to prevent a two-state solution. Liberal Democrats are calling on the Government to introduce emergency legislation to implement this ban without delay. We must make sure there is no UK complicity in the sustainability of illegal settlements.”
Reform UK
Member of Parliament Richard Tice said, “The putrid stench of antisemitism was clear for all to see in the House of Commons.”
“As a result of Miliband’s sanctions, British Jews are less safe and our US security relationship is hugely damaged,” he wrote on X.
UK chief rabbi
Ephraim Mirvis described Miliband’s announcement as a”dark day for British Jews”, and that it would only succeed in “bolstering the very extremism they seek to target”.
On Wednesday, Miliband said he is a “proud British Jew” but disagrees with the chief rabbi over the criticism.
Jeremy Corbyn
Corbyn, a former Labour leader, said sanctions on illegal settlements are welcome, but not enough.
“Britain must end all arms sales, all military cooperation, and all forms of support that sustain Israel’s system of apartheid, occupation and genocide,” he added.
He was among 12 MPs banned from Israel, who said he will “keep speaking up for peace, freedom and justice for the Palestinian people”.
Yvette Cooper
“Strong agreement across the world on today’s UK action against illegal settlements and settler violence that are an existential threat to the two-state solution,” the Health Secretary said on X.
“No one should be profiting from stolen land.”
