Search and rescue efforts are under way for eight people, including five journalists, who went missing after travelling to the area around Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau island to cover a volcanic eruption, authorities have said.
Al Amrad, head of the Search and Rescue Office in Indonesia’s Banten province, said in a statement that contact had been lost with a speedboat carrying five photojournalists, two crew members and a guide.
Amrad said one of the journalists had sent a message to relatives saying they had reached waters around Anak Krakatau, adding that it was the last communication received from the group.
Search and rescue teams in the area have not yet been able to establish contact with the group or determine their location, he said.
Those reported missing include journalists working for Indonesia’s state news agency Antara, Merdeka and iNews, as well as Firdaus Wajidi, a freelance cameraman working for Anadolu.
Volcanic eruption disrupted air traffic
Meanwhile, although the intense eruptions at Anak Krakatau have subsided, volcanic activity on the island continues.
An eruption occurred at Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau volcano on September 6, sending volcanic ash up to 6,000 metres over Java and as high as 15,000 metres over Sumatra.
Flights were cancelled at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in the capital Jakarta after volcanic ash spread across western parts of the country.
More than 2,300 domestic and international flights were cancelled nationwide following the eruption, leaving around 340,000 passengers stranded at seven airports.
Authorities later determined that conditions were safe for aviation, and Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and Halim Perdanakusuma Airport, along with three other airports where flights had been suspended following the eruption, resumed operations.

German far right’s ‘remigration’ plans amount to ethnic cleansing, says Merz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:38:56 UTC
19:38:56 KST

BERLIN — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Wednesday that plans put forward by the far-right Alternative for Germany for a tough migration crackdown would devastate the German economy.
“’Remigration’ is nothing more than a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin color,” Merz said during a speech in the Bundestag, in his sharpest attack yet on the surging AfD after a dismal election defeat for his center-right Christian Democratic Union.
“One in six workers in the skilled trades holds a foreign passport. If those who work in Germany are forced to leave the country again because you’re championing ‘remigration’, then the skilled trades in Germany will no longer be able to function. Then not a single nursing home would remain open, and not a single hospital in Germany would continue to operate. Then not a single restaurant could stay in business in Germany. That would be the result of your immigration policy,” he added.
“Remigration” is a far-right concept that can range from deporting people without legal status to the mass removal of immigrants and their descendants. The AfD had dedicated an entire chapter to “immigration and remigration” in its election program for Saxony-Anhalt.
Its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund — who is also the state’s potential next premier — attended a 2023 meeting at which party figures and far-right extremists discussed “remigration plans” that included the mass deportation of “non-assimilated” German citizens and sparked nationwide protests.
Merz’s comments constitute the harshest condemnation yet of the AfD’s policies and come as the chancellor himself is facing mounting questions over his ability to lead Germany’s weakened coalition government. His dismal approval ratings helped fuel the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday — and contributed to his party losing more than half of its support.
Following the election, Merz and his CDU are searching for a new narrative in their fight against the far right. The AfD, now the most popular party in national polls, has vowed to destroy Merz’s conservatives and seize power nationwide after the next national election, scheduled for 2029.
“You have failed to understand the message that voters in Saxony-Anhalt sent you last Sunday,” said AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel, who spoke before Merz in the Bundestag. “That doesn’t really matter anyway, because your time is up. The people want a change in policy, and they will get it. In the next election, the people will give the AfD — that is, us, the Alternative for Germany — a clear mandate to govern.”

Merz also attacked the AfD over its Russia-friendly positions, accusing the party of ignoring the threat facing Germany.

Teens charged in hate‑fueled arson attacks on ethnic-owned Tallinn food businesses

Unknown Publisher

Teens charged in hate‑fueled arson attacks on ethnic-owned Tallinn food businesses
A 16-year-old boy has been charged with multiple arson and assaults motivated by extremist views, with a 19-year-old also charged over a hammer attack.
The 16-year-old is charged with systematically setting fire, with the use of accelerants, to cars and restaurants, reportedly owned by people of color, and causing over €82,000 in damages, the prosecutor's office said.
The prosecutor says evidence points toward the youth holding extremist views, including on Islam and on immigration, and the people and businesses targeted were maingly from the Bangladeshi, Pakistani and Nigerian communities.
According to the indictment, the teenager repeatedly set fire to cars belonging to ethnic minority people, and also set fire to a kebab kiosk on Akadeemia tee in Mustamäe and a restaurant serving Indian food on nearby Rahumäe tee. He allegedly used lighter fluid or bottles filled with gasoline to do so. At the time of the restaurant fire, a person was inside the building when he set fire to it, meaning a threat to life and well-being.
The acts were not limited to attacks on property. In June, the 16‑year‑old and a 19‑year‑old followed a victim and attacked him using a hammer. The prosecutor's office charged both men with attempted assault causing life‑threatening bodily harm.
"The acts which the young man is accused of were well thought out, planned and committed within a relatively short period of time," said Prosecutor Rita Siniväli. "The evidence collected indicates that his actions were influenced by extremist views, including anti‑Islamic, anti‑Muslim and anti‑immigration narratives."
She added that the young man's views were "expressed in actions directed against specific people and groups. The victims are mainly citizens of Bangladesh, Pakistan and Nigeria who have lived and worked in Estonia for a lengthy time."
Siniväli called it important to see the implications of how the actions can evolve. "A person can hold very extreme or unacceptable views for others. However, a line is drawn where hostile attitudes begin to manifest in crimes directed against other people or their property. In this criminal case, the young man's hostile attitudes did not remain in just thoughts or words, but based on the evidence collected, they manifested themselves in arson and violence and became increasingly dangerous over time."
Vadim Kuperštein, head of the Crimes Against Persons Department of the Northern Prefecture Criminal Bureau, said the cases seemed distinct at first glance but were unifited by the similar circle of victims. "The young people made a conscious effort to avoid being identified and learned to cover their tracks," he said. "Despite this, the police saw commonalities between the cases, identified the young men, and arrested them in June."
According to Kuperštein, neither young man has expressed any remorse. "This is a clear sign that the young men did not act out of momentary emotions, but had specific motives and goals that they were trying to achieve."
He urged parents to be vigilant about the content young people consume. "It is important to react early. The longer a young person is exposed to such information, the more extreme views and beliefs can become entrenched, and it will be much more difficult to change the situation later."
Both young men are currently in custody.

Ebola virus spreads to new DRC health zone, WHO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:35:25 UTC
19:35:25 KST

The number of health zones affected by Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has risen to 61 across six provinces after the virus spread to the Kayna Health Zone in North Kivu province, the World Health Organization’s Africa office said in a situation report late on Tuesday.
At least 6,686 cases, including 3,226 deaths, have been recorded since the outbreak began in mid-May, according to the report.
WHO said the epidemiological pattern of the Bundibugyo virus strain outbreak was becoming increasingly heterogeneous, with transmission trends diverging across affected provinces and health zones.
“The trends reinforce an increasingly heterogeneous epidemic, with declining transmission in some areas occurring alongside intensification and continued geographic spread elsewhere,” the report said.
The affected provinces are Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and Tshopo.
Ituri remains the main focus of the outbreak, while substantial transmission continues in North Kivu and Haut-Uele and new areas continue to be affected.
WHO also highlighted the rising proportion of deaths occurring within communities.
Between August 31 and September 6, the proportion of confirmed deaths occurring in communities reached 75 percent, up from 56.6 percent two weeks earlier.
The report said persistently high community mortality could reflect several barriers, including delays in detection, notification and transfers to treatment facilities, limited recognition of the illness, transport and geographical challenges, and a lack of community trust.
“This divergence is concerning, as the increase in community deaths alongside the continued decline in treatment facilities deaths indicates that the earlier reduction in overall mortality has not been sustained,” it said.
The government of DRC and health partners last week launched a revised 180-day multisectoral response plan worth $1.3 billion aimed at breaking chains of transmission.
The plan calls for a major expansion of epidemiological surveillance, contact tracing, community engagement, risk communication and logistical capacity, as well as preparedness measures in at-risk provinces.

Srebrenica, Ratko Mladic and what his war crimes tell us about the Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:34:21 UTC
19:34:21 KST

The death of Ratko Mladic, the infamous Bosnian Serb general and convicted war criminal, marks the end of one of the darkest chapters in history.
Yet, his death does not close the window of pain and suffering for thousands of Bosniaks – many of them survivors, some others family members of those killed by the Butcher of Bosnia.
And most of all, Mladic’s death brings into sharp focus the sufferings of Palestinians and the war crimes committed by the state of Israel over the past three years. And the inaction of a world which refuses to see the genocide unfolding right before its eyes.
To understand Mladic - he died in The Hague at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence for his war crimes – we must look back to July 1995, when he led a group of Bosnian Serb soldiers into the town of Srebrenica with the intent to clear it of the non-Serb population.
According to findings by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), upon entering the town, he declared, “we give this town to Serb people as a gift,” by which he meant to forcibly remove the Bosniaks and Croats from the country.
Later, in the presence of international media, he emphasised the need to eliminate Bosnia’s non-Serb populace, either temporarily or permanently.
Mladic was not just a monstrous general but the chief architect of ethnic cleansing in Bosnia, convicted of many crimes, including genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes.
As commander of Bosnian Serb forces, he ordered the siege of UN-declared safe Bosniak areas (Bihac, Gorazde, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Sarajevo), held UN soldiers hostage and blocked the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.
He also masterminded the systematic torture and execution of Bosniaks and Croats in concentration camps such as Omarska, Manjaca, Keretem, and Trnopolje.
Mladic’s role in orchestrating the Srebrenica genocide, in which at least 8,372 Bosniak men and boys were separated from their families, transported, and killed by the Bosnian Serb army, is well documented and was affirmed by both the ICTY and the United Nations.
Despite extensive court proceedings, ICTY findings, and testimonies of survivor witnesses detailing and proving his primary role in the genocide, Mladic remained at large for nearly 16 years, moving to different locations within Serbia.
Eventually, he was detained in northern Serbia, indicted by the international tribunal, and transferred to The Hague. The court found him guilty of at least 11 charges, including two counts for genocide.
But he pleaded guilty to none and brazenly denied the genocide in Srebrenica.
Wounds that never healed
Mladic’s case has been one of the most significant cases before the ICTY.
It raises serious questions about the functioning and capacity of the legal systems, particularly the ICTY and the International Criminal Court (ICC).
What exposes the global judicial system is the fact that the fate of thousands of people who disappeared during war is still unknown.
Hence, the gap between the legal system and survivors’ lived experiences persists, although his capture and trial have marked a major success for the tribunal.
Some survivors of the Bosnian War and relatives of victims of Srebrenica have expressed that they found solace in Mladić’s death, while it hardly mattered to others, as it reawakens their traumatic memories of the war.
Women who endured the worst atrocities, particularly sexual abuse, are still dealing with long-term psychological effects, negatively influencing their lives today.
According to studies, many survivors are still suffering from panic attacks, nightmares, and persistent anxiety because of reliving their traumatic experiences.
A study shows that at least 57 percent of women in Bosnia who have suffered sexual violence during the war continue to meet clinical criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and are struggling to reconcile with the past events even after decades.
Sexual violence is often employed as a weapon of war, used by perpetrators to take revenge and to punish, terrorise, and humiliate their victims.
In the Bosnian context, such violence was not confined to women and young girls, but young boys and elderly men were also among the worst sufferers, subject to the worst forms of sexual violence.
Many survivors contend that Mladic’s death cannot compensate for the scale of loss and suffering he has orchestrated and therefore offers them no relief.
Lessons for the world
While justice does not necessitate death for each wrongful death, it does demand an end to hatred and an apology, something that is not observed in the case of any convicted war criminal, many of whom instead exhibit deep resentment toward victims.
More than 30 years after the end of the Bosnian war, survivors are still waiting for justice and accountability.
Their experiences and trauma are influenced by both the past events and present situations, especially the denial of genocide.
The rhetoric of genocide denial is so prevalent in the Balkans that it is frequently combined with toxic narratives, such as negationism, revisionism, and triumphalism.
Such narratives get reinforced when convicted war criminals such as Ratko Mladic, whose aim was to create ethnically pure Serbia by eradicating Muslims and Croats, are awarded and glorified.
The horrific atrocities unfolding before our eyes in Gaza bear many similarities to those that occurred in Srebrenica over thirty years ago.
From bombing civilian infrastructure and using rape as a tool of war to blocking humanitarian aid convoys, every single incident is recurring.
Yet, the international community, including the European Union and the United States, stand by in silence and inaction.
In stark reality, what enables the loss of human lives is both the inaction and the injustice of those who can prevent such brutalities.
Thus, the lessons learned from the earlier experiences must not be forgotten or remain confined to history books, commemoration events, or memorial sites; they must instead serve a purpose to stop genocides from happening anywhere on Earth.
The world must act now to uphold international law and human rights and hold perpetrators accountable for their crimes. It will help break the cycle of impunity and vengeance.

Durban Conference 25 years on. Mandi Mudarikwa: “It’s up to us all to build the kind of world we want to live in”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:34:00 UTC
19:34:00 KST

The third UN Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance in 2001 was a watershed moment for millions across the world. Seven thousand people representing governments and civil society from 170 countries gathered in Durban, South Africa. Led by countries in the Global South, the Durban Conference challenged the idea that human rights is a Western concept, recognized the historical roots of contemporary forms of racism and called on States to repair the lasting consequences of colonialism and slavery. While the US and Israel withdrew from the Conference, the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action were adopted, both of which became foundational documents for the global fight against racism. But with racism still very much alive, we spoke with activists about their struggles and hopes.
My name is Mandi Mudarikwa and I’m a human rights strategic litigator at Amnesty International. My legal career has been about using law and the courts as instruments of justice, accountability, and the advancement and enjoyment of human rights.
Human rights are a promise and a commitment. The promise of equality, freedom of speech, privacy and access to, among others, health and education as well as the commitment to make these rights a reality. Too often, however, these are promises that remain as words on paper. In this context, my work seeks to use strategic and precedent-setting litigation to challenge systemic injustice, shape progressive jurisprudence, and advance human rights standards across diverse legal systems.
Moments of hope
When I think about how far we have come, and all the work that has been done to not only reject but confront racial discrimination, the legacies of colonialism, slavery, and apartheid, I also think of systems that once, in some places, still define people as superior or inferior based on the colour of their skin, their race, ethnicity, descent or national origin, denying their humanity and their rights. But alongside that history, I also think of the moments of hope, solidarity and unity that show us what is possible when we come together in unity to challenge injustice and human rights violations.
 
Despite those efforts contributing, unfortunately those in power have not done enough to dismantle the structures and systems that enable racism, discrimination and xenophobia. Committing to a world that is substantively equal and fair for everyone does not, by itself, undo historic injustices and transform our societies. The adoption of the promise of equality was not enough to undo the systemic underfunding and under-resourcing that resulted from decades of state-sanctioned discrimination. 
We can see this, for example, in schools in many countries that predominantly serve racialized communities. Many continue to be underfunded and under-resourced reflecting inequalities that were not erased simply because discriminatory policies were formally abandoned or condemned. The promise of substantive equality and fairness, therefore, has not yet translated into true substantive equality or the enjoyment of human rights for all.
Dehumanization
Even further, we are witnessing the promise of substantive equality being intentionally challenged and undermined, including through people feeling increasingly emboldened to speak openly about others as inferior simply based on their race, their nationality or their background. Dehumanizing language and ideas have gained momentum and with them, the willingness to openly question whether everyone is truly entitled to the same human rights.
We have witnessed people adopting a zero-sum approach to human rights as though one person’s rights or one group’s progress must come at the expense of another’s. Progress towards racial equality is framed not as expanding rights for everyone, but as chipping away the rights of others. It’s a dangerous way of thinking that intentionally pits people against one another. Instead of recognizing equality as a principle that strengthens the human rights and dignity of everyone, it turns human rights into a competition.
And that is when you begin to see how difficult it is going to be to really leave racism, discrimination and xenophobia in the past. We are not only struggling to dismantle the systems and inequalities that these ideologies created, we are also confronting efforts to revive and legitimize the very ideas that underpin them.
The Durban Declaration
The Durban Declaration came about in response to a conversation about the need for more protections and more concrete and transformative action.  
 
In that moment in 2001, there was almost a global recognition of the need to do away with racism, discrimination and xenophobia because of their impact on access and enjoyment of human rights.  
For me, one of the most important things about both the Declaration and the Programme of Action is that they go beyond condemnation. They provide a plan for action, a commitment to confront the structures, systems and inequalities that allow racism and discrimination to persist.
What we need now is for states to use this plan of action to take clear, concrete actions and turn the promises into reality, to remember why they were made, to defend the progress we have achieved, and to build a world that is fundamentally different from the one we had before.
Strategic litigation
Strategic litigation can be a powerful tool to drive change, and the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action provides an important framework for strategic litigation because it gives us a clear set of principles for challenging racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related forms of intolerance. It helps translate international commitments into arguments for accountability, equality and access to rights at the national level.
We saw this in a case whereby Amnesty International intervened in Canada earlier this year where an asylum seeker woman was excluded from access to free childcare, and without childcare, she was unable to work. We supported the case when it went before the Supreme Court of Canada, which ruled that excluding asylum seekers was discriminatory and unconstitutional. It’s a powerful example of how the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action can inform concrete legal change.
But a ruling is only the beginning because strategic litigation does not end when a Court issues its decision. Its real impact depends on implementation. Progress takes time, and one decision on its own may not transform a system. But when combined with others and with advocacy, organizing and other strategies for change, each victory can build on the last and contribute to lasting systemic change. Accordingly, if fully implemented, this decision has the potential to dismantle the compounded effects of the intersection of racism, discrimination, and xenophobia.
My message to young people?
Never forget that we are not equal until we are all equal. Importantly, equality does not happen by chance, nor through passive hope, it requires deliberate action. It calls on each of us to challenge, confront, and dismantle systems upon which inequality and discrimination thrive. So, onwards and forwards: together, with purpose and courage, turning our commitment to substantive equality into meaningful action and creating the world we want to live in; a world where everyone is valued, respected, and substantively equal.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday denounced the far-right AfD’s call for mass “remigration,” calling it “ethnic cleansing by skin color and origin.”
His comments came in a heated parliamentary exchange with Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel, three days after the party scored a crushing election victory over Merz's center-right CDU in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The chancellor took aim at AfD's demand for mass deportations of rejected asylum-seekers and people arriving via irregular channels.
"The word 'remigration' is nothing other than a synonym for ethnic cleansing," Merz said about the AfD's flagship policy.
"Remigration is nothing other than ethnic cleansing by skin color and origin," he added to howls of protest from AfD deputies in the Bundestag.
The AfD took almost 44% of the vote in Sunday's election, against 17% for the CDU.
The AfD, which fell three seats short of an absolute majority, said it was now in talks with other groups and MPs in an effort to form a state government.
The rise of the AfD has unnerved many who feel Germany has a special responsibility to atone for its Nazi past.
Weidel took to the lectern first, declaring that the days of Merz's coalition "are over."
People wanted "a change of course in politics at last, and they don't want 'business as usual,'" she said.
She also denounced the government's immigration policy, saying it had made Germany unsafe.
"German citizens have to live with the daily consequences of mass migration," she said.
"With knife violence every day, attacks on trains and in stations, with run-down and threatening cityscapes."
Hitting back, Merz said the AfD's immigration policy would massively impact the labor market.
"Not a single care home could work operate, not a single hospital, not a single restaurant," he said.
Merz also accused the Moscow-friendly AfD of contributing to what he said were Russian efforts to "destabilize" Germany, following a foiled drone attack at Leipzig airport last month Berlin blamed on Russia.
"There has been nothing from you, Mrs. Weidel, on what happened on Aug. 4 at Leipzig airport," he said. "You are part of the problem we have here in Germany."

"We aren't on a football pitch here; save that for the weekend," she said.
"If this kind of behavior happens again, I will have you thrown out."

Finland completes work on 200km fence along border with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:33:47 UTC
19:33:47 KST

Helsinki says the fence will help protect NATO's longest border as concerns grow over Russian hybrid activity and the potential use of migration to exert pressure on the country.
Finland completed a 200-kilometre security fence along its border with Russia, strengthening NATO’s longest frontier with a country's accused of intensified hybrid attacks on Europe.
The project was launched after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine transformed Finland’s security environment and prompted the country to abandon decades of military non-alignment and join NATO in April 2023.
Later that year, more than 1,300 migrants without visas arrived at Finland’s eastern border. Helsinki accused Moscow of “hybrid warfare” by orchestrating the movement of third-country nationals towards the frontier, a charge the Kremlin denied.
Finland shut its land border with Russia in late 2023. Apart from a brief reopening of two crossings that December, the frontier has remained closed ever since.
“Today, it is calm but tense, and we really don't know about tomorrow,” Interior Minister Mari Rantanen told reporters on Monday at a media event near the Nuijamaa border crossing in south-eastern Finland.
“It can change really rapidly and that is why we need to be very prepared.”
The 4.5-metre-high fence has been built in sections and is equipped with cameras and sensors.
It covers 200 kilometres of Finland’s 1,340-kilometre frontier with Russia, with most of the barrier concentrated in the southeast.
“This is one part of our border security and it is helping us for surveillance, but also keeping people out of Finnish territory if needed,” Rantanen said.
The new fence cost €356 million, with an estimated €2-3 million in annual maintenance costs, according to Finnish border authorities.
Despite rapid advances in drone technology, a physical barrier was still “viewed as the best solution for crowd control,” Border Guard project manager Erkki Matilainen said.
Rantanen said the fence could be extended further and called for greater EU financial support for countries along the bloc’s eastern frontier.
“What we particularly need is EU funding for eastern member states so that projects like this can be financed,” she said.
Last week, Helsinki proposed extending its Border Security Act until the end of 2028.
The legislation allows Finland, under exceptional circumstances, to restrict the reception of asylum applications in limited areas of the border when its sovereignty or national security is deemed to be under threat.
The law has proved controversial, with legal experts warning that it risks breaching Finland’s international human rights obligations and EU law.
Similar barriers have been built elsewhere along NATO and the EU’s eastern flank, as countries bordering Russia and Belarus strengthen their frontiers.

Center Party head: Snap elections a realistic possibility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:33:00 UTC
19:33:00 KST

Center Party head: Snap elections a realistic possibility
The replacement of ministers just six months before general elections, along with crises in several sectors, is a clear sign that Estonia needs a snap election, Center leader Mihhail Kõlvart told ERR.
Kõlvart said the current government reshuffle, which will see Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur and Energy and Environment Minister Andres Sutt, both of the Reform Party, leave their posts, shows there is nothing left to save in the current governing coalition, not even through a reshuffle.
"It seems to me that the situation within the Reform Party itself is probably not particularly stable at the moment either," Kõlvart said. "If ministers decide not to continue in politics, then they don't see a future. Nor do they see a future for their own party."
Given the coalition's low approval ratings and the scandal in the defense sector, Kõlvart said the reasonable course of action would be to hold a snap election.
"If we look at the situation pragmatically — insofar as politicians are capable of looking at a situation pragmatically at all — we can see crises in key sectors," he said, pointing to defense, education and healthcare, as well as the need for a new political leader for the energy sector.
"Every sector needs a new approach and a fresh start," Kõlvart said.
He added that Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's departure alone is not enough.
"In my view, the responsibility today is primarily political and extends beyond a single minister. The systemic disorder is not solely a problem of the Ministry of Defense," Kõlvart said.
With public trust in both the government and the Riigikogu at a record low, Kõlvart argued that a snap election is the only way out of the current political crisis.
"The sooner the better, even if it is just three or four months earlier rather than seven months from now," he said. "Then these issues can be addressed systematically, rather than having new ministers come in and spend their time campaigning for the election."
Although the Social Democrats have said they do not support a snap election, Kõlvart said holding one remains a realistic possibility because Estonia currently has a minority government and the opposition has more votes in the Riigikogu than the governing coalition.
"It comes down to political choices," he said. "We have also seen that politicians, including the Social Democrats, can change their minds and quite quickly."
Kõlvart said the Center Party's aim is to demonstrate that there is a genuine need for an early election. He also rejected the argument that there would be insufficient time for proper political debate.
"It seems to me that the argument that a snap election should not be held because we wouldn't have time to organize a debate is not entirely sincere," he said.
Kõlvart argued that voters can already distinguish between parties that genuinely want political change and those that would prefer to wait until the scheduled election in the hope of improving their polling numbers.
"Today, society can judge who genuinely wants change and who says quite openly that because our poll numbers aren't high enough and our competitors' numbers are high, we should wait another six months for the situation to change so that we can win more seats in the Riigikogu," he said.
Turning to the upcoming Riigikogu election, Kõlvart said no one can predict what will happen when voters go to the polls in March. Like every other party, he said, the Center Party's goal is to enter government, while its current level of support also gives it reason to hope it could win the election.
As for potential coalition partners, Kõlvart said governing with the Reform Party could largely be ruled out.
"The Reform Party has had plenty of time to put its vision into practice and show what it can achieve in the economy and in defense," Kõlvart said. "In our view, the Reform Party has failed to deliver. Therefore, our goal would be a coalition in which the Reform Party would not participate for the next four years."

Swiss and French train stations named among best in Europe – with Germany free-falling down rankings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:30:42 UTC
19:30:42 KST

The latest European Railway Station Index ranks the top 60 busiest railway stations in Europe – and there are clear winners and losers.
The latest edition of the European Railway Station Index is out now – and the best major hub on the continent is Switzerland’s Zürich Hbf.
Issued by the Consumer Choice Center, the new ranking evaluated 60 of Europe’s busiest railway stations looking at the percentage of services which are delayed and the average wait time.
It also took into account factors such as the number of in-station services, accessibility options, whether or not the station has free wifi, national and local railway coverage and ticket types.
Switzerland “continues to set the standard for reliability”, with a national punctuality rate of 94.1%. Zürich Hbf came in first place overall, with just 4% of its train services delayed, while Bern Hbf was joint fifth with a delay percentage of 1.8%. Although ranked 14th overall, the most punctual trains departed from Luzern Hbf, which had just 0.3% of its services delayed.
On the flip side, Germany’s performance “continued to deteriorate” compared to previous editions.
Of the bottom 30 stations, 15 are in Germany, and the highest ranked station from the country is Berlin Hbf in 18th, where 61.1% of services are delayed and the average wait time is 20 minutes.
Europe-wide, the average delay rate is 29% – in Germany, it is 49.4%. Similarly, the average wait time on the continent is 8.06 minutes, versus 14.74 minutes in Germany.
Polish stations on the rise
For 2026, 10 new stations joined the ranking thanks to increased passenger numbers.
Two of the top five best performers among these newbies come from Poland: Kraków Główny in first place (ninth overall), and Poznań Główny in third (13th overall).
Consumer Choice Center note that Kraków’s main station boasts direct routes to Warsaw, Zakopane, Łódź, Gdańsk and Katowice domestically, as well as top destinations like Berlin,
Munich, Vienna and Prague elsewhere on the continent.
Kraków Główny is also fully integrated with the Galeria Krakowska shopping centre, giving travellers access to plenty of shops and restaurants. Praise was also lavished on the station for having integrated bus and tram services, written and verbal station announcements, and a first-class lounge.
Looking ahead, Consumer Choice Center points to the ongoing modernisation of the network with a plan for an additional 4,700km of new track “ultimately promises to transform Polish rail into one of the most modern rail networks in Europe”.
Time for a rail escape to Poland, anyone?

Alibaba sends AI ‘digital employees’ to work in rival apps from ByteDance, Tencent

Alibaba sends AI ‘digital employees’ to work in rival apps from ByteDance, Tencent
QoderWake tool now lets users create assistants that can function within office communication platforms from rivals, as well as Alibaba’s
The latest version of the QoderWake tool, launched by Alibaba Cloud on Tuesday, allowed users to generate fully functioning workers using a single-line description of the required role, the company said. These digital workers could then be put to work within any of China’s three major workplace communication platforms: Alibaba’s DingTalk, ByteDance’s Feishu and Tencent’s WeCom.
QoderWake’s digital workers could “operate seamlessly” within the three workplace platforms, autonomously absorbing context from shared documents, calendars and group chats, Alibaba said on Tuesday.
The move reflects how domestic tech giants are aggressively pivoting their costly AI models towards lucrative business-facing applications capable of executing complex enterprise workflows. Meanwhile, they are open to incorporating rival products at the application layer, shifting away from their traditional “walled-garden” approach.
Beyond customised roles, QoderWake also had 10 ready-to-use roles, including product manager, data analyst, user interface designer and front- and back-end developer, the company said. These roles had been fine-tuned using data from top-tier industry teams, allowing them to undertake real-world tasks without requiring additional training, it added.
Since its initial release in April, QoderWake had deployed nearly 100,000 digital employees, executing around 2 million tasks across real-world enterprise scenarios over the past three months, the company said.

MS NOW Wants to Turn Its Viewers Into a Fandom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Even if you’re a casual consumer of MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, you know the names: anchors like Chris Hayes, Stephanie Ruhle, and yes, the one and only Rachel Maddow. The network has built a stable of talent who’ve amassed a massive number of casual viewers, plenty of fans … and more than a few obsessives.
Now, the network’s president, Rebecca Kutler, is looking to build that entire audience into something more akin to a fandom—turning casual viewers and fanatics alike, whether on TV or online, into paying members of an MS NOW media universe.
To do it, she’s launching an ambitious subscription program, called the MS NOW Membership, designed to connect MS NOW consumers much more directly to the Hayeses and Maddows of the world. Sure, plenty of news providers now offer subscriptions, WIRED included (and by the way, you can subscribe here). But what struck me about Kutler and Co.’s efforts was both their methodical approach—they surveyed 18,000 people before landing on a final offering—and their resolute focus on MS NOW’s deep bench of talent as the locus of their paid program. In a world where influencers are the new newscasters, and linear TV is in an inevitable decline, MS NOW is diving directly into the breach: applying the influencer playbook to build a sustainable business that’s future-proofed … at least until the next great audience pivot.
I caught up with Kutler at WIRED’s New York studios, just days before MS NOW’s subscription launch. We talked about turning TV talent into fandom magnets, beating Fox, and whether media consolidation is actually good news for the network.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
KATIE DRUMMOND: Rebecca, thank you so much for being here today. Start by telling me when you joined MSNBC. What’s the timeline?
REBECCA KUTLER: I think it was right before the midterms in 2022. I had grown up at CNN. I spent more than 20 years there. I left earlier in 2022, and some folks that I knew and really respected reached out from then MSNBC, and they talked about one of those jobs that has a lot of running room and is a little ambiguous, but in the best way. I thought, “Yeah, let's check it out.” I started at MSNBC, now MS NOW, running their digital businesses, basically all their nonlinear businesses.
It gave me a real opportunity to learn the place, but also think about what are the missed opportunities that we could take advantage of in the next few years.
At some point in your tenure, you took on the whole thing.
Yes.
What were those big challenges that you identified when you looked at the whole portfolio and thought to yourself, “What are we going to do here?”
One of the things that immediately struck me when I came over was the fandom.
I had worked in other newsrooms. I have friends who work in other newsrooms. I love the news and love what we do, but I had never worked at a place where the audience really sees themselves as fans, with a deep connection to talent.
When I joined MS, it was also at the same time Jen Psaki joined, and we had known each other a little from a previous life. So we went out into the field together and did a few pretty straightforward field reporting pieces. And I've walked through airports over my career with a lot of different anchors and newspeople, but I’ve never had the experience of walking through with Jen and seeing the [attention she got]. That's why she was a great fit for MS. She’s someone people were behind and were rooting for, and had a deep connection with.
When you think about Rachel Maddow and how she lands. You’re very close to this industry. If you talk to anyone in publishing and ask them where they would ideally like to debut their book, I think most of them would say The Rachel Maddow Show. There’s a reason for that: The audience loyalty and engagement with Rachel has been proven over decades.
It’s funny, when she shares a WIRED story on social media, the traffic to that story and the engagement on her social media around WIRED is crazy. I can tell you firsthand looking at the analytics, you can feel it.
I want to ask you more about talent in a minute, but that brings me to this Membership program you're launching. I'm going to read from the press release, which I very rarely do. You will offer “new opportunities for members to interact directly with the brand’s trusted journalists, exclusive community features to engage with each other, a new roster of contributors and experts, original creator content, new verticals that explore how news and politics impacts everyday life, and 24/7 access to livestreams and television programming.”
In layman’s terms, if someone’s a MS NOW viewer, they watch it on TV sometimes, they see it on social media, what should they expect from this? What are they getting that they’re not already getting by having cable TV?
I want to answer your question directly, but I just don’t want to assume your audience is the MS NOW audience. So if you'll allow me 30 seconds …
Give us your best pitch.
We launched as a new brand about a year ago. People traditionally see us as this cable channel, and that's great. We have a huge cable audience. We're actually right now the number two most-watched basic cable channel.
Who's number one?
Fox.
I see. OK. We might talk more about that later.
But that’s just one piece of our business. We have, right now, a digital business before we even launch what we're launching this week, that has more uniques than places like Axios, Politico, The Atlantic. People spend more time with us digitally than places like the Washington Post and NPR.
And on YouTube, we have been quite efficient at building out our presence in that space. We get more clicks on YouTube than ABC News, NBC News, and CBS News combined.
I say all of that to say we are starting from a position of strength. What we are excited about, and why we're launching this product, is all those digital things I just mentioned, we don't have a way to catch all those people if they’re not going to be watching cable.
Got it.
It’s taking our current superfans who watch us on linear and giving them more. So what are they going to get? They're going to get direct access to our talent. Seven days a week at noon and at 6:00 pm, if you are a member of the MS NOW community, you can hop on and directly interact with one of our anchors or one of our reporters.
On Monday it’s going to be Rachel Maddow, and then you go through the week. You're going to hear from Michael Steele, you’re going to hear from Jen Psaki, you're going to hear from Reverend Al Sharpton. You’re going to hear from the people that you know and love from watching them on MS NOW and have the opportunity to ask them your question directly, and not just interact with our talent, but also interact with each other.
When we started this process around a year and a half ago, we didn’t just sit in a conference room and think, “Hmm, let’s make another commodity news app.” Because let's be honest, a lot of that already exists. What we did was actually start from a place of product research. We went out to 18,000 people. We did surveys, we did in-person interviews, and we spent time taking that research and getting to where we are this week.
What I most want people to know is, what you see this week will look vastly different six months from now and a year from now if we're doing our jobs right. What we need to do is build and learn and test and add investment and expand where we need to, but not really think that we’re going to get it all right on day one, but give ourselves that latitude.
Is the goal to pull linear viewers onto digital, or is it to better engage the digital audience, or both?
It's both. All those people consuming us on YouTube, on digital, on social, in audio, 90 percent of those people do not regularly consume us on linear television. So a big function of this product is to say, “Hey, you’re watching YouTube videos all the time of Lawrence O'Donnell. Maybe you’re not someone who's going to be a cable subscriber. But can you come join our community in another capacity? Can we create a product that entices you to be part of an MS NOW community, even if you're someone who's reluctant to become a cable customer?”
I would say that, for the average person, if you ask them, “Fox News, MS NOW, who do those networks reach?” I would say Fox News reaches Republicans, and that’s who has it on TV, that's who’s going to that website. I would say MS NOW reaches progressives, Democrats, left-leaning people. Is that a stated goal for you, or do you want that tent to be bigger?
Is the audience for MS NOW different from the audience for Fox? Of course it is. There's probably a small amount of overlap, but not a lot, and that's OK.
For example, when I think forward to election night, I gotta say, I think there’s nowhere I'd rather hang out on election night than at our table with Rachel and Nicolle [Wallace] and Lawrence and Chris [Hayes] and Michael [Steele] and everyone.
What we try to do is be smart, respect our audience, and be a fun place, and a place where, again, Michael Steele is a big part of our election night. He was chairman of the Republican National Committee.
Right.
We have a broad range of views, but I think they all fall under that pro-democracy banner.
Are you competitive? Do you want to beat Fox? Do you want to see that number one?
Look, I am a pretty competitive person. I just see who our competition is as wider than that typical cable landscape.
I want to build a great product right now and have a large membership community, and I want to make sure that we are competing on every battleground.
That is yes, absolutely on cable, yes on digital, yes on YouTube, yes in audio. I think that because of the life that this brand lived under previous ownership, there were times when our wings were clipped a little from a business perspective, and that wasn't—if I was sitting in the seats of the leadership team at NBC, I might have made the same decisions.
When you’re working for the very large, very successful companies that NBCUniversal and Comcast are, they need to look at the whole company and figure out where best to invest their dollars. So what they did makes sense for them. But now we're lucky to be a part of Versant, and Versant has several pieces of their portfolio that generate a lot of cash.
What is Versant, for those who may not know?
Versant is the spinoff, so a spinout, of NBCUniversal. For folks that weren't following along day by day, around a year ago, NBCUniversal spun out a series of businesses. Those include what is now MS NOW, CNBC, brands like E!—you know, Live from the Red Carpet—and then golf.
We are now part of a company that is incentivized to invest the money that we earn as MS NOW back into MS NOW. We're just no longer part of a company that has to invest in theme parks and other things that, for that company, made a lot of sense.
I don’t think it’s a secret that cable news audiences are declining, and I’m going to ask this in the bluntest possible way: That’s an older audience, so what do you do when they die?
I am not blind to the long-term challenges. That’s why we are investing in digital. But do I think the cable business right now for MS NOW is quite healthy? I do.
Our average viewer watches nine hours a week.
That is a lot of MS NOW.
Do I wake up in a panic in the middle of the night? No. Do I know there are long-term challenges? Yes.
What do you wake up at night worrying about? Working in media and journalism is hard. It's a hard business, and these are really difficult transformations to try to undertake, and to undertake successfully. What's the hardest part of this for you right now?
What I wake up angsty about sometimes is I know we have this guest or that guest coming up, but how can we upgrade? How can we make it better? What is the better question? What is the better way in?
I might be old-school when I say this, but I think content always wins. Every single race.
I want to ask more about talent. You do have some real fandom magnets. I think one of the biggest challenges in publishing today, especially on digital, is that it is so noisy. There is so much competition. It’s not just news, but it’s everything on someone's Instagram feed. How do you encourage your journalists, your talent, to break through that in a digital context?
I'll just pick on Chris Hayes for a minute here. Because there’s almost no time that I talk to Chris Hayes that I don’t then hang up the phone or walk out of his office and think to myself, “That guy’s brain is huge.”
I think that’s the answer to the question of how do you break through? Every brand and every place in the media has to figure out what their breakthrough is. Look, there's people who want to break through by showing cat videos all day. People want to break through by writing outrageous headlines that aren’t really based in facts.
Yes.
Where I want MS NOW to break through is being brainiacs, is coming to the table with something that is intellectually interesting, that is showing me something or teaching me something or adding value to a news story in a way I hadn’t thought about it before, of drawing on their experience, decades of experience working in the room, being in the room where it happened.
What has the experience been like of transitioning some of the more TV-comfortable talent that you have, who are accustomed to doing a cable news show, and saying to them, “Now you do these interactive sessions with our audience, now you do TikTok, now you participate in these other parts of the ecosystem”?
One of my rules is: don’t do anything that feels weird for you. What I mean by that is, if you in your own life don’t use TikTok, I don’t recommend trying to become a TikToker. It’s going to land weird. We’ve seen it. So what I have encouraged our shows, our hosts, everyone in the MS NOW family, to do is don’t try to be everywhere. Don’t try to be everything.
I mean, a great example, Symone Sanders [Townsend] is fantastic at TikTok and Instagram because she grew up in those spaces and knows those audiences. That might not be the same for Lawrence O’Donnell. Lawrence O’Donnell is a huge hit on YouTube.
What has Trump 2.0 been like over there? Have you seen an audience bump? Have you seen fatigue? The challenge with the story of Trump 2.0 is that there are a thousand stories a day. How are you thinking about reaching your audience in a way that can grab them and hold them?
What I want our audience to know is that we are who we are, and we’re proud of who we are, and you can come to us on any platform at any time and trust that you are getting our best reporting and our best analysis without fear.
We haven’t talked about it yet, but as part of the spinoff, we had to build our own newsroom. What we tried to do is build our newsroom knowing the moment. We’re not trying to be commodity news. We’re trying to build an absolutely kickass DC newsroom, and I think we’ve done that.
MS NOW is one of the very few media brands in growth mode right now. It's impressive.
I'm curious about your take on the possibility of a merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, which would place CNN and CBS News under one owner. Would that consolidation be good for you? Does this help you even if the broader implications can be troubling?
In a functioning healthy democracy, you need a very healthy free and fair press. So I am rooting for better, stronger newsrooms. I worked most of my career at CNN, and while they might be technically a competitor or rival now, the world is a better place with a stronger CNN.

Ukraine Unveils RK-2PZ Surface-to-Air Missile Based on Barrier Anti-Tank Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:28:21 UTC
19:28:21 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Unveils RK-2PZ Surface-to-Air Missile Based on Barrier Anti-Tank Missile
Ukraine’s state defense conglomerate Ukroboronprom has unveiled a new anti-aircraft missile designed for upgraded Strela-10 surface-to-air missile systems and the new Desna air defense system, Militarnyi reported from the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland on September 8.
The new RK-2PZ surface-to-air missile was developed on the basis of the Barrier anti-tank guided missile, itself a modification of the R-2 missile family.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The RK-2PZ has a caliber of 130 mm and carries a 6.1-kilogram warhead. The missile itself weighs 28.9 kilograms, while its total weight in the launch container reaches 47 kilograms.
After receiving target designation, the operator selects a target for automatic tracking using a control panel and either the television or thermal imaging channel of the system’s optical targeting station.
Once launched from its container, the missile is guided toward the target using a laser guidance system. As it approaches, a proximity sensor is activated to initiate the high-explosive fragmentation warhead. In the event of a direct hit, a contact sensor triggers the warhead.
The RK-2PZ is intended for use with upgraded Strela-10 air defense systems, also known as Ryf. The modernized system retains the original Strela-10’s MT-LB tracked chassis, launcher rotation mechanism, and operator station.
The Ryf underwent its first live-fire tests in December 2021.
The missile is also intended for the new Desna air defense system. Unlike the upgraded Strela-10 platform, Desna is a newly developed launcher module for RK-2PZ missiles that will be mounted on a chassis that has not yet been publicly demonstrated.
According to Militarnyi, detailed performance specifications for both the RK-2PZ missile and the Desna air defense system have not been publicly disclosed.
During the exhibition, Ukraine has also revealed the launcher for its Koral surface-to-air missile for the first time, showcasing an upgraded system intended to engage both conventional aerial threats and ballistic targets.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Ukraine Revives Osa Air Defense Systems With New Domestically Made RK-19 Missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:27:56 UTC
19:27:56 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Revives Osa Air Defense Systems With New Domestically Made RK-19 Missile
Ukraine has developed a new domestically produced surface-to-air missile designed to replace Soviet 9M33-series interceptors used by the Osa-AKM short-range air defense system.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 8, the RK-19 missile was displayed at Ukraine’s defense industry stand during the MSPO defense exhibition in Poland, where its intended role and key technical specifications were disclosed publicly.
The RK-19 can engage aerial targets at ranges of up to 10 kilometers and altitudes of up to 5 kilometers. Its maximum flight speed is listed at 600 meters per second, exceeding the roughly 500-meter-per-second maximum speed of the Soviet 9M33M3 missile it is intended to replace.
Like the original Osa ammunition, the Ukrainian missile uses radio-command guidance. The RK-19 carries a 14.3-kilogram warhead, while the missile and its launch container have a combined weight of 163 kilograms. The container measures 3,255 mm in length, 320 mm in width, and 303 mm in height.
The missile was first shown publicly in April 2026 during a video address by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy marking Ukraine’s Gunsmith Day. At the time, its specific launch platform had not been officially detailed.
The latest presentation confirms that the RK-19 was developed as a replacement for the Soviet-made 9M33 family used by the Osa-AKM, potentially allowing Ukraine to keep the existing air defense systems operational without relying on dwindling stocks of Soviet missiles.
The Osa-AKM is a mobile, short-range surface-to-air missile system designed to protect troops and infrastructure from aircraft and cruise missiles. Each combat vehicle carries six 9M33M3 missiles and can engage targets at ranges of up to 10 kilometers and altitudes of up to 5 kilometers.
Ukraine has operated Osa systems extensively during Russia’s full-scale invasion, including against Russian drones and cruise missiles. However, stocks of compatible Soviet-produced interceptors have declined during the war, limiting the intensity with which the systems can be employed.
Earlier, Ukraine unveiled the launcher for its domestically developed Koral surface-to-air missile, a significantly redesigned interceptor intended to engage both conventional aerial threats and ballistic targets. The latest version weighs about 450 kilograms, carries a 36-kilogram warhead, and uses inertial navigation, radio-command correction, and an active radar seeker.

Russia Bleeds 1.5 Million Troops in Ukraine—100 Times the Soviet Toll in Afghanistan
Russia’s military personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine have surpassed 1.5 million killed and wounded, according to figures released by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 9.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The General Staff said Russian forces lost another 1,480 personnel on September 8, bringing Ukraine’s estimate of total Russian personnel losses since February 2022 to 1,500,870.
“This is the largest loss in a single war suffered by the Russian army since World War II,” the General Staff said, adding that the figure exceeds the combined losses of the Soviet and Russian armies in all wars and armed conflicts of the second half of the 20th and early 21st centuries.
“This is 100 times greater than the Soviet Union’s losses in Afghanistan over 10 years,” the General Staff said. Ukraine’s military also said the estimated losses are 125 times higher than the officially acknowledged Russian losses in the First and Second Chechen wars.
The 1.5 million figure represents cumulative battlefield personnel losses reported by Ukraine and includes both Russian troops killed and wounded. Moscow does not publish comprehensive figures that can be directly compared with Ukraine’s running estimate, and the total cannot be independently verified in real time.
Ukraine has published daily estimates of Russian personnel and equipment losses throughout the full-scale invasion, updating its figures as new battlefield information becomes available.
Meanwhile, Russia is preparing to mobilize up to 600,000 additional troops through 2027, according to Ukrainian military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko. He said Moscow is currently able primarily to replace battlefield losses, while additional manpower would be needed to expand offensive operations in Ukraine.

Russia’s military spending hits a record 44% of its budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:27:05 UTC
19:27:05 KST

- Russia's military spending hit a record 44% of federal budget outlays in the first half of 2026, economist Janis Kluge calculated from Finance Ministry data.
- Classified spending, mostly military-related, already exceeded 8.4 trillion rubles after six months against a full-year budget target of 11.6 trillion rubles.
Russia spent a record 44% of its federal budget on the military in the first half of 2026, according to calculations published by Janis Kluge, a research fellow at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, based on data from Russia’s Finance Ministry.
Direct military spending totaled 10.7 trillion rubles, about $125 billion at current exchange rates, for the first six months of the year, Kluge found, a 30% increase over the same period in 2025. That spending equaled 10.5% of Russia’s gross domestic product for the first half of the year and 57.3% of federal budget revenue, meaning more than half of every ruble the government collected in taxes and other income went toward the war.
Kluge’s data shows classified spending, budget lines the Kremlin does not disclose in detail, driving much of the increase. Russia’s 2026 budget law set a full-year target of 11.6 trillion rubles for classified spending, but the government had already spent more than 8.4 trillion rubles on those hidden categories after just six months, putting the full year on pace to blow well past its own budgeted figure. Russian budget documents indicate that roughly 85% of classified spending goes to military needs, based on figures Kluge has cited from earlier quarters this year.
The military’s share of the federal budget has climbed steadily since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. Kluge’s tracker, which compares the first half of each year going back to 2018, shows military spending at 24.5% of federal budget outlays in the first half of that pre-war year, dropping to around 20% in 2020 and 2021, then rising sharply to 29.6% in the first half of 2023, 36.6% in 2024, and 39.3% in 2025 before reaching the current 43.8% figure for 2026. Open, publicly itemized military spending has held relatively steady over that same stretch, hovering between roughly 11% and 15% of the budget each year.
Nearly all of the growth has come from the classified category, which has gone from a modest supplement to open spending before the war to now making up close to two-thirds of the total military budget.
Total direct budgetary military spending since the start of the full-scale invasion now stands at 57.1 trillion rubles, or roughly $666 billion, according to Kluge’s calculations. That figure covers only formal federal budget line items and does not include off-budget costs such as regional government spending on recruitment bonuses and compensation payments to the families of killed and wounded soldiers, costs Kluge has tracked separately in other analyses of Russia’s regional budgets.
The first quarter of 2026 alone saw military spending reach 5.9 trillion rubles, itself a record at the time and up 30% from the first quarter of 2025, driven largely by a 43% jump in classified spending during that period compared with a year earlier. Kluge has since raised a technical question about the scale of that first-quarter jump, noting that Russian federal spending patterns showed unusually low classified outlays at the end of 2025 and that December 2025 budget spending overall fell sharply from a year earlier.
That pattern, he has suggested, could mean the Finance Ministry deferred some spending originally planned for 2025 into 2026, in part to avoid missing the deficit target the government had publicly committed to for last year.
The spending surge has come as Russia’s oil and gas revenue, historically the backbone of its federal budget, has weakened. Kluge’s first-quarter data showed oil and gas revenue falling 45% year over year, a decline tied to Western sanctions on Russian energy exports and a stronger ruble that reduces the ruble value of oil sold in dollars.
Non-oil and gas revenue rose about 7% over the same period, but not enough to offset the shortfall, leaving military spending equivalent to roughly two-thirds of total federal budget revenue in the first quarter, by Kluge’s calculation. Bloomberg has separately reported that Russian finance officials have privately told President Vladimir Putin that current war spending levels are becoming unaffordable.
Kluge’s calculations rely on published Russian Finance Ministry budget execution data, which the ministry continues to release on a regular schedule even as it withholds detail on how classified funds are ultimately spent. He has cautioned that spending patterns typically ease in the second and third quarters of the year compared with the first, meaning the full-year share of GDP devoted to the military could land lower than a straight-line projection from Q1 alone would suggest, even as the absolute ruble totals keep setting records.

North Macedonia ready to share EU accession experience with Ukraine - minister
Timcho Mucunski, North Macedonia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, made these remarks in an interview with Ukrinform.
First and foremost, he expressed his conviction that EU accession should not be accompanied by intimidation or the practice of unilateral concessions.
“Since our country gained independence [here], there has never been any doubt that we were and remain unwavering in our aspirations to build a modern Euro-Atlantic society. In this regard, most often at the request of external forces, we have made various concessions,” Mucunski noted.
For instance, North Macedonia changed its country’s name and flag and amended its Constitution several times.
“We will continue to move steadfastly toward full membership, as we believe we deserve it. At the same time, we will not allow intimidation and the practice of bilateral agreements to continue during the EU accession process,” added Mucunski, referring to Bulgaria’s demands that North Macedonia recognize the Bulgarian national minority at the constitutional level.
The minister noted that Ukraine and North Macedonia are united by a shared aspiration to join the EU.
He added that during its time as a candidate country, Skopje has achieved truly “excellent results in implementing European reforms,” which it is ready to share with Ukraine.
During his visit to Kyiv, Mucunski held talks with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. “We discussed the exchange of experience gained in various fields, particularly in agriculture—for example, regarding the harmonization of national legislation with that of the European Union. Thus, our bilateral discussions focus on joint work and joint efforts toward the process of both our countries’ accession to the EU,” the North Macedonian minister emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, last year Ukraine and the Republic of North Macedonia signed a memorandum of cooperation in the field of European integration.

EU reiterates Israeli settlements illegal under intl' law, calls them obstacle to 2-state solution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:26:04 UTC
19:26:04 KST

Melike Pala
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The European Union reiterated its longstanding position that Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories are illegal under international law, saying they constitute an obstacle to peace and the viability of a two-state solution.
"We take note of the announcement of eight member states – together with the UK, Canada, Iceland and Norway – to impose national restrictions on trade with illegal settlements," Anouar El Anouni, the EU Commission spokesman for foreign affairs, told Anadolu.
"The EU's longstanding position is clear: settlements are illegal under international law. They constitute an obstacle to peace and to the viability of the two-state solution," he added.
The bloc considers Israeli settlements established in the occupied Palestinian territory after June 1967 to be illegal, he said.
"Goods originating from Israeli settlements in territories that came under Israeli administration since June 1967 are not entitled to benefit from any preferential tariff treatment," El Anouni noted.
His remarks came after 11 European countries — France, the UK, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden — as well as Canada announced their intention to impose national restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements.
The countries also said they would support European restrictions on such trade.
In a joint declaration, the countries said the situation in the occupied West Bank is "rapidly deteriorating," citing unprecedented levels of occupiers' violence and continued settlement expansion.
"We firmly oppose any action resulting in the annexation of Palestinian land and the forced displacement of Palestinian populations," they said.
The countries called on Israel to immediately halt the expansion of settlements and civilian administrative powers in the occupied West Bank.
They also urged accountability for occupiers responsible for violence and called for investigations into allegations involving Israeli forces.
Growing calls to EU
There are growing calls in Europe for the EU to go beyond measures targeting settlement goods and take broader action in its trade relations with Israel.
Several European governments, lawmakers, and civil society groups have called on the EU to suspend or restrict trade arrangements with Israel, arguing that the bloc should use its economic relationship with Israel as leverage to address settlement expansion and the treatment of Palestinians.
The calls have also focused on the EU-Israel Association Agreement, which provides the framework for bilateral trade relations and grants preferential treatment to certain goods.
Supporters of stronger measures have argued that the agreement should be reviewed or suspended in response to Israel's policies in the occupied Palestinian territory and the wider conflict.
However, EU-wide trade measures require agreement among member states, and divisions between EU countries have so far complicated efforts to adopt a common position.
While the EU has not yet imposed a general import ban on products originating from illegal Israeli settlements, it excludes such products from trade preferences under the EU-Israel Association Agreement and continues to assess options for broader trade measures.

Ben Shelton defeated defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in five sets to reach the US Open semifinals in the latest-finishing match in tournament history.
The eighth seed beat Alcaraz 6-7 (5-7), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (10-7) in 4 hours and 28 minutes at Arthur Ashe Stadium. The match ended at 3:33 a.m. local time (0733 GMT), setting a record for the latest finish in US Open history.
Shelton will face fellow American Frances Tiafoe in the semifinals.
Tiafoe produced a remarkable comeback against compatriot Alex Michelsen in the day’s other men's quarterfinal, recovering from two sets down to win 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (10-6) after 4 hours and 39 minutes.
Michelsen served for the match in the third set before Tiafoe fought back to reach his third US Open semifinal.
In the women's draw, defending champion Aryna Sabalenka survived a stern test from Czech Linda Noskova, winning 7-6 (7-1), 3-6, 7-6 (10-7).
American Jessica Pegula also came from behind to beat compatriot Emma Navarro 3-6, 6-4, 6-3, setting up a semifinal against Sabalenka.
The remaining men's and women's quarterfinals will be played on Wednesday.
In the women's singles, China's Zheng Qinwen will face Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina, while American Coco Gauff takes on Mirra Andreeva.
The men's draw will see Russia's Karen Khachanov face Belgium's Alexander Blockx, while top seed Alexander Zverev of Germany meets Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp.

BERLIN, September 9. /TASS/. Alice Weidel, co-chair of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has sharply criticized the German government's energy policy under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, calling for the resumption of Russian gas supplies amid low domestic storage levels.
"You decided to forgo cost-effective pipeline gas from Russia. You allowed the Nord Stream pipeline to be blown up right under your noses without uttering a word or lifting a finger," Weidel said during a Bundestag debate, addressing Merz. "Instead of laying the groundwork to resume supplies via the surviving pipeline branches in the future, you continue to reward the alleged organizers of the terrorist attack in Kiev with billions in payments at Germany's expense – in case you haven't noticed yet."
She warned that Germany's gas reserves are at a record low.
"Therefore, gas injection must be the top priority. If the winter is cold, we face the prospect of purchasing gas at astronomical, market-inflating prices or facing consumption rationing that would deal a final, devastating blow to our economy and private households," the politician emphasized, adding that the German Chancellor is "leading the country toward a catastrophic supply crisis this winter."
"We must put an end to the failed energy transition and embark on a return to nuclear power. The key word here is the sustainability of our energy supply. That is precisely why we also need cheap natural gas from Russia, and we will work toward this for the sake of the German economy," the AfD co-chair stated.
At the same time, she called for a radical reduction in development aid and global climate protection spending. "With a total development aid budget of 26 billion euros, Germany is ahead of even the United States. This money is available for the entire world, but not for our own citizens. We must significantly limit payments to the EU. Almost a billion flows to Brussels every week, yet only a small fraction returns," Weidel noted, highlighting the need to reduce the state apparatus and the public sector.
Earlier, the DPA news agency, citing data from the Association of Gas Storage Operators, reported that Germany's gas storage facilities could be completely depleted as early as the beginning of February 2027 if the upcoming winter proves cold.

'We know who lives here' — German foreign minister floats giving Kyiv data on Ukrainian men eligible for conscription
Berlin could share information about draft-age Ukrainian men in Germany with Kyiv so Ukraine can contact them about potential military conscription, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said in an interview with Bild on Sept. 8.
Wadephul floated the idea during the interview and agreed with CSU leader Markus Soder, who demanded that Ukrainian military-age men currently in Germany return to Ukraine.
"We know who lives here. Who receives social benefits, who is registered with local authorities, who holds residence status," Wadephul told Bild.
Germany could send this data to Kyiv, so Ukrainian authorities could contact the men about their conscription, said Wadephul. At the same time, the process of men returning to Ukraine should happen "without coercion," Wadephul said in the interview.
As the fifth year of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine goes on, mobilization has become one of the most contentious domestic issues in Ukraine.
Ukraine's military faces a growing need to replenish fighting units, build reserves, and allow existing soldiers to rotate off the front line. As Ukraine steps up its mobilization efforts, draft offices are often accused of forced conscription without compliance with fundamental civil rights and ill-treatment of conscripts.
Wadephul's comments came hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky said Germany is 'ready to provide' additional supplies of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, on Sept. 8.
"In addition to PAC-2 interceptor missiles, Germany will further step up its continuous provision of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to provide greater quantities to Ukraine," German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said on Sept. 8, also committing to deliver additional IRIS-T air defense systems to Ukraine.

John Malkovich bails on Israel performance following backlash
Unknown

2026-09-09
