France 'will reject extremism' and Le Pen in presidential election, Haddad says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:45:47 UTC
18:45:47 KST

Polls suggest far-right veteran Marine Le Pen is on course to become France’s next president, though the race remains in its early stages. But EU minister Haddad says voters will reject her.
French minister for European Affairs, Benjamin Haddad, told Euronews he's "quite confident" the French electorate will reject extremism and won't elect a far-right candidate to replace President Emmanuel Macron in next year's election.
His comments come days after an Elabe poll for BFMTV/La Tribune Dimanche showed Le Pen dwarfing all other candidates, predicting her to win between 34% and 35.5% of first-round votes.
Le Pen was cleared to stand in July despite an appeals court upholding an embezzlement conviction against her.
"We still have a long way to go before the election, but I'm quite confident that the French, like they've done so many, many times, will refuse extremism," Haddad said on Euronews' interview programme 12 Minutes With.
"The French people have repeatedly said no to extremism, to euroscepticism, and populism," he said.
He said next spring's 2027 election will be "a tough one, like every election," but added that he "never trusts the polls," arguing that they have been wrong in the past.
"When I personally started supporting Emmanuel Macron in 2016, he was far, far behind in the polls," said Haddad, who belongs to Macron's party, Renaissance (formerly La République En Marche!).
Ahead of the 2017 elections, Macron rose from third position in the polls after he declared his candidacy in November 2016, to briefly poll ahead of Le Pen weeks ahead of the elections.
He gained 24% of the vote in the first round in April 2017, then won the presidency in the second round with 66% of the vote, in contrast with Le Pen's 34%. This margin narrowed significantly in the second round of the 2022 elections, when Macron beat Le Pen with 59% of the vote to her 41%.
French are 'deeply European'
Haddad said the French are "deeply European" and will ultimately reject Le Pen.
"The French are proud of the role that their country is playing on the European stage," he said.
"Marine Le Pen, for a long time, has been the candidate of 'Frexit'," he said, referring to the demand by some on the fringes of French politics, who called for France to leave the EU and the eurozone.
The prospect of France leaving the EU was a strong component in Le Pen's 2012 and 2017 manifestos. At present, she still maintains a staunchly eurosceptic stance, pledging to cut back on Europe's contributions to the bloc and calling for the scrapping of norms, but no longer explicitly advocates for a referendum on France's membership of the EU.
"She's been the candidate [standing for] leaving the eurozone. She was the candidate of the alliance with Vladimir Putin," Haddad said.
"She's trying to make people forget about all of this and sometimes even says that it never happened, even though we know her stance on the European Union for a long time."
Despite his conviction that the French public will vote against Le Pen, Haddad warned politicians from other parties should approach the rise of the far-right and populism "with a lot of humility."
"Our first responsibility is to continue to deliver on results. All the issues that we're discussing, from migration and security, from competitiveness, prosperity, from defending the security of Europeans against foreign threats, we have to continue to deliver on this, Haddad explained.
He went on to say that continuing to "campaign, to meet the French, to listen to voters, and to respond" is also central in this mission.
Uniting around one candidate?
The linchpin to his proposal to beat the far-right will perhaps be the most challenging of all to attain, given the fragmented nature of the race with eight months to go until the first round of elections.
"We need to unify around a candidate, because right now we have a lot of talent in the centre, but we have a fragmented political offer," Haddad said.
Around 30 figures have already expressed their ambition to run. Two of those considered likely candidates are Macron’s former prime ministers: centrist Gabriel Attal (Renaissance) and centre-right figure Édouard Philippe (Horizons), while conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau (Les Républicains) is one of the president's former ministers.
On the hard-left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon (La France Insoumise) is vying to be president, while other candidates running on the left include Marine Tondelier (the Greens) and MEP Raphaël Glucksmann (Place Publique).
"I think by the end of the year we will have one candidate that can rally the centre and the centre-right and then we will make a case." Some candidates have suggested they would consider partaking in a primary.
Extremism 'not the answer to uncertainties'
Still, Le Pen remains the front-runner in the polls. In 2024, her party won the European Parliamentary elections in France with more than twice the number of votes of Macron’s party, pushing the president to call a snap election at the time.
Haddad conceded that global uncertainties fuel populism's popularity, pointing to the fact that many of the certainties people had before "are crumbling."
"Trade is being weaponised as a tool of pressure. You see China's subsidised overcapacities coming to our markets and destabilising our industries. Our traditional alliances are being questioned; there's the war of Russian aggression on our continent," he explained.
"When you have these uncertainties, and the pillars on which we built our European Union and our transatlantic alliance are questioned, this very often paves the way for radical answers," Haddad added, noting that he doesn't believe those answers are right,
"I don't think that in a world where you have the pressure from China, from the US, the threat coming from Russia, we would be stronger going it alone. I don't think we'd be stronger looking inwards."
The first round of the French presidential election will take place on 18 April 2027, while the second will be held on 2 May 2027 if no candidate wins a majority of votes.

Conspiracy theories can provide answers, but not peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

Conspiracy theories can provide answers but not peace
September 9, 2026
Psychology is not an exact science. That may irk a few researchers in the field. But it is important to mention upfront: Researching the psychology of conspiracy theories — why people are drawn to believing them and the effect they have on those people — is a complicated field of research, and conclusions are difficult to derive.
That is due, in part, to one of the basic problems with psychology, whether it's in treatment or in research, and that is that it relies on people's self-awareness.
If we take the example of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, some people continue to maintain it was "inside job," orchestrated by a secretive and powerful club of evil doers in the US government, intent on controlling citizens' lives by fear. And that may be true. But it may also be true that you, as a believer in such a theory, have always felt powerful people — your parents or teachers — have controlled and curtailed your agency in life. You may even have a false memory of how the terrorist attacks evolved on that day in 2001. Then, if someone asked you, "What really happened?", could you really say it for sure? I couldn't.
Self-report data are an issue in conspiracy research
Whether as patients or participants in a study, we may be asked to "self-report" — to look inside ourselves and express how we feel and why.
Self-reporting is an established way of measuring conspiracies, said Neil Dagnall, a professor of psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University, in an interview with DW.
But self-report data are "not perfect," he added.
They can be difficult data to handle because each judgment a person makes about themselves is relative, inherently subjective and open to outside influence and bias. People's answers can change from day-to-day, especially when they involve emotions or feelings about mental state, depending on a multitude of events and experiences in our lives. In addition, there is no common scale.
Say, for example, you and a friend were asked, "Are you happy?" You may both say "yes," but your reasons for doing so may be completely different and be subject to different variables. The same goes for a question like, "Do you believe in conspiracy theories?"
"The judgment I'm making is a relative one. What's my norm? Am I comparing it to my friends who don't believe in conspiracies, or am I in a group of people who do believe in conspiracies? We're always making relative judgments about our psychological propensities," said Dagnall. 
Which suggests we're unlikely to ever get a definitive answer. Self-report data suggest correlations, not causation.
In a study on conspiratorial beliefs and well-being, which Dagnall co-authored and published in May 2026, "self-report data" was specifically highlighted as a limitation.
This makes it very difficult to assess whether "conspiracy belief" or "conspiracy ideation" is good or bad for people and their sense of well-being. Especially as people who seek and believe in conspiracy theories often start out with a skewed view of reality.
Observing behavior can offer clues
There are ways of "triangulating" self-report data, as the authors of the study put it, to get a more reliable, objective reading of a person's emotional or psychological state.
For example, psychologists use behavioral observations, like measuring heart rate variability or Galvanic Skin Responses such as the electrical conductance of a person's skin, which is affected by sweating under stress. You can also retest participants' self-reported data, and therefore its reliability, by asking the same questions at different points in time.
But there is another factor that complicates research into the psychology of conspiracy theories, and that is that they, and people who believe in them, are more common than we like to think or admit (even when we believe them ourselves).
"The idea that people who believe in conspiracies in general populations are remarkable or different is not true," said Dagnall.
The truth: 'conspiracies theories are common'
Most of us, at some point in our lives, are bound to see something strange or stressful in society and question whether we, as individuals or as a member of a group, accept the accepted truth of how that thing or event came about. It can be a healthy sign of a questioning mind.
There are positive examples of conspiracy theories that happened to kickstart investigations that then revealed the horrible truth of government corruption.
Take Partygate during the COVID pandemic in the United Kingdom or — the mother of all conspiracies — Watergate during the Nixon Administration in the United States.
And there are other conspiracy theories, such as the one that nobody has ever landed on the moon, which you can either take seriously or laugh about.
It all comes down to "the degree to which we engage in conspiracies generally, and the extent to which they interfere and disrupt our everyday lives," said Dagnall.
For Dagnall, who doesn't believe in the 1969 moon landing, it doesn't seem to disrupt his daily life — at least, that is what he self-reported to DW.
But for some people, conspiracy theories are disruptive and can lead to a sustained sense of dissatisfaction.
"Ample studies suggest that exposure to conspiracy theories or belief in them might lead to more negative emotions, heightened anxiety or even paranoid thoughts," said Zuzanna Molenda, a researcher at the Polish Academy of Sciences and lead-author of a 2023 study on emotion dysregulation and belief in conspiracy theories.
Some people may be primed to more readily believe in conspiracy theories because they generally struggle to deal with psychological threat and distress. When they then seek answers in conspiracy theories, their pre-existing negative psychology may be enhanced.
"If anything, the available evidence suggests that rather than help people manage difficult emotions, conspiracy beliefs may be accompanied by or contribute to further distress," wrote Molenda in an email to DW.
No long-term benefit from conspiracy belief
There may be some psychological benefit to conspiracy theories, said Molenda, but only in the short term.
"Conspiracy beliefs can provide people with a sense of explanation and understanding when events feel uncertain or difficult to make sense of. For some people, they might also be a source of entertainment and fun. For others, they can provide a sense of belonging and connection with others who share the same beliefs, and they can be an important part of social identity," Molenda said.
But these potential benefits do not necessarily translate into better well-being in the longer term, said Molenda.
In the end, we're all searching for meaning and purpose in life. If we find a satisfactory answer, it gives us something that psychologists call presense — a direction in life, and that is good.
But if your search only leads to more uncertainty, more anxiety and more doubt in your purpose in life, then that's bad.
"And people who believe in conspiracies are asking questions but not getting answers," said Dagnall.
Edited by: Kristie Pladson

Police step up campaign to stop illegal fireworks at New Year

Unknown Publisher

Police step up campaign to stop illegal fireworks at New Year
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch police say they will take a “zero tolerance” approach to illegal New Year fireworks in the first year after a ban was imposed on most types of rockets and firecrackers.
A nationwide crackdown was launched after the ban came into force on August 1, including monitoring border crossings and checking vehicles that have been used in the past to import illegal firerworks.
“One of the conditions for introducing the fireworks ban was an extensive enforcement plan,” Ko Minderhoud, national fireworks co-ordinator for the Dutch police force, told the Telegraaf.
“We have a larger team than ever ready to go and we are starting earlier.”
MPs voted to ban all fireworks apart from the lightest category, F1, which includes sparklers and Roman candles, last year following a long campaign by doctors and emergency service workers.
The annual fireworks bonanza on December 31 is the busiest night of the year for police, ambulance and fire services.
Attacks on first responders in recent years prompted centre-right parties such as VVD and CDA to change their position and accept the need for a ban, even though many voters see New Year fireworks as a national tradition.
30% have fireworks stashed
The task facing the police is a daunting one. A survey by RTL found that nearly 30% of people who regularly set off fireworks said they still have some left over from before the ban, but just 4% are willing to hand them in.
View this post on Instagram
Just seven people turned up on the first day of an amnesty in Terneuzen on September 1 to take advantage of an offer to dispose of their fireworks anonymously without risking a fine.
The amnesty runs until October 9, with police buses touring the country to collect fireworks that are no longer permitted such as rockets and fountains.
Minderhoud said the illegal fireworks trade has been taken over in recent years by criminal gangs and increasingly resembles the drugs trade. “It’s become a sideline for classic organised criminals, because there’s a lot of money to be made,” he said.
“We see armed men transporting container loads. It was a different story a few years ago.”
He urged consumers to play their part by not buying illegal fireworks at New Year. “Set a good example and abide by the law,” he said.
“It’s also very dangerous. Look at the recent incidents at football matches. If you buy fireworks despite the ban, you’re getting involved in a murky world with very dangerous stuff.”

Pakistan faces new frontier against attacks: Balochistan’s Pashtun areas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:44:10 UTC
18:44:10 KST

Pakistan faces new frontier against attacks: Balochistan’s Pashtun areas
A surge in attacks in Balochistan’s Pashtun-majority districts is raising questions about a widening rebellion.
Islamabad, Pakistan — Violence has surged since June across Balochistan’s Pashtun-majority districts, areas which had largely escaped the fighting that has engulfed much of Pakistan’s southwestern province.
Balochistan is Pakistan’s largest province by area, resource-rich but its least developed, bordering Afghanistan and Iran.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4How will Pakistan deal with the unrest in Balochistan?
- list 2 of 4Why peace remains elusive in Pakistan’s troubled Balochistan
- list 3 of 4At least nine police officers killed in southwestern Pakistan attack
- list 4 of 4Pakistan military says 42 killed in fighter attacks in Balochistan
While Baloch nationalist rebels have waged an armed rebellion against the state there for two decades, the Pashtun-majority districts had, until recently, remained largely outside that conflict.
That pattern has now changed.
On September 1, security forces said they had repelled an attack, claimed by the Pakistan Taliban (known by the acronym TTP), on a customs facility at a major intersection, Ziarat Cross, in the Pashtun-dominated Pishin district, 100km northeast of Balochistan’s capital Quetta. Several armed fighters and six security and customs personnel were killed.
Three days later, security forces said they had killed 26 more fighters from the group in a separate operation in Shaban, on the outskirts of Quetta, another Pashtun-populated area.
It was during the same period, on September 3, that gunmen ambushed a paramilitary convoy returning from Ziarat district, situated more than 100 kilometres (62 miles) east of Quetta. A police officer, speaking to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity, said more than a dozen paramilitary personnel were killed.
The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), the most prominent armed separatist group, claimed responsibility for the attack, but the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the Pakistani military’s media wing, has not officially acknowledged the attack.
Al Jazeera sent seven questions to Pakistan’s military media wing about the security situation in Balochistan, including a query about the September 3 ambush, but received no response.
Al Jazeera also sought comment from Babar Yousafzai, an official in the Balochistan home department, who did not respond.
Balochistan overtakes Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Data from multiple Pakistani monitoring organisations tracking violence shows that Balochistan has this year overtaken neighbouring Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as the country’s most violent province.
The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based think tank, publishes monthly and weekly assessments of violence across the country.
According to its data, Balochistan has been Pakistan’s most affected province through most of 2026, with the gap over Khyber Pakhtunkhwa widening sharply from July. PICSS called July “the deadliest month of 2026” nationally and said the security situation had deteriorated most sharply in Balochistan.
Its weekly review for the first week of that month recorded 25 attacks and 102 deaths in Balochistan alone, pointing to “increasing TTP activity in northern districts” as a contributing factor.
The TTP, formed in 2007, is separate from the Afghan Taliban, though they fought together against United States-led forces in Afghanistan. The TTP has also hosted Afghan fighters in Pakistan.
In August, PICSS recorded security forces killing 115 fighters in Balochistan, compared with 56 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and 32 in the merged tribal districts, giving the province the highest toll of the three regions.
The military’s own moves suggest it is treating the shift seriously.
Faisal Naseer, until recently the director-general for counterintelligence at Inter Services Intelligence — Pakistan’s main spy agency — was appointed national coordinator of the National Counter Terrorism Authority (NACTA) on September 4. The following day, Naseer was in Quetta when Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir visited Quetta Garrison, where he was given a detailed briefing on measures aimed at maintaining “peace and stability” across Balochistan.
“The field marshal reaffirmed that the peace, prosperity and well-being of the people of Balochistan remained central to the efforts of the state,” ISPR said.
On September 6, Naseer also met Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti and other political leaders to discuss the overall law and order situation and a coordinated strategy for establishing peace.
Bugti, speaking in the Balochistan Assembly over the weekend, said it was “deeply disturbing” that people and security personnel were “being killed on a daily basis”.
A belt largely spared
Until this June, one part of Balochistan had remained largely outside the violence.
Open-source tracking by the Durand Dispatch, a Pakistan-focused security monitor, shows that 11 Pashtun-majority districts – Zhob, Sherani, Qila Saifullah, Loralai, Musakhail, Duki, Barkhan, Pishin, Qila Abdullah, Ziarat and Harnai – recorded not a single attack by an armed group between January and May.
That changed the following month. On June 10, gunmen on motorbikes attacked police installations across four of these districts. Pashtun-majority districts have recorded at least 13 attacks by armed groups since then, including the killing of 27 police personnel guarding a dam project near Ziarat in July. The June attack was claimed by the BLA, while the TTP and Baloch groups claimed the different July attacks.
The July killings of police personnel, in particular, drew sharp public reaction. Families of the dead and Pashtun nationalist parties held a three-day sit-in in Quetta, accusing the government of leaving trapped officers without reinforcements.
Rafiullah Kakar, a Balochistan-focused policy analyst, told Al Jazeera the pattern “represents a relatively new and significant development”.
“The group’s [BLA’s] willingness and apparent ability to strike beyond its traditional areas of operation indicate an expanding geographical reach,” he said. “It also raises questions about whether there is some degree of tactical coordination or cooperation of the BLA with the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan [TTP].”
Iftikhar Firdous, a security analyst and cofounder of The Khorasan Diary, an independent research and media portal that tracks regional conflicts, told Al Jazeera the TTP had been building outreach in Balochistan since 2019, “initially ideologically focused literature in the Balochi language”.
“The TTP chief, Noor Wali Mehsud, had expressed the desire publicly to create an alliance with the ‘Sarmachars’,” he said, using the Balochi language word for armed fighters.
He pointed to how the N-50 national highway connects Balochistan’s Pashtun-dominated districts of Zhob and Ziarat, via regional capital Quetta, with South Waziristan, the birthplace of the TTP, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.
A trade corridor under strain
Then there is the corridor that carries much of Balochistan’s trade with Iran and domestically with Karachi. Businesses along it say they are being squeezed hard.
Haji Amin Sumalani, a chief executive member of the Balochistan Goods Trucks Owner Association, told Al Jazeera that the N-40, the major road connecting the border town of Taftan to Quetta, and the N-25, which connects Quetta to Karachi, the country’s largest city, had been “effectively unusable” for four months.
“Our drivers are in fear and not willing to travel on these highways due to the imminent threat of attack by armed militants who often set our goods transport trucks on fire,” he said.
More than 100 trucks had been set alight during that period, he said, causing losses of hundreds of millions of rupees, or at least hundreds of thousands of dollars. Two drivers had also been killed.
Muhammad Ayoub Miryani, president of the Quetta Chamber of Commerce, told Al Jazeera that roughly 90 percent of the chamber’s business had stopped.
“Every trader is losing crores of rupees,” he said. A crore is 10 million rupees, worth about $36,000 at current exchange rates.
What comes next
Questions remain over why Balochistan’s Pashtun belt is clearly the latest front in Pakistan’s battle against armed groups, and what this means for the government’s response.
Imtiaz Baloch, a Quetta-based independent researcher tracking security with a focus on Balochistan, told Al Jazeera that armed groups were trying “to extend their operations beyond their traditional strongholds and target strategic transportation corridors that carry both military and economic importance”.
He said the routes through northern Balochistan had, unlike highways elsewhere in the province, “largely remained operational and have proven difficult for insurgent groups to gain any success similar to others”, which is precisely what makes the corridor an attractive target now.
Rahim Nasar, another Quetta-based security and political analyst, pointed to how the Pakistani military had carried out major military campaigns against the TTP in January and February in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.
Since those campaigns, “most of those fighters migrated here,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Their resurgence began after April, and by June, they had confirmed their strategic positions and significantly ramped up attacks,” Nasar added.
Still, he said he was unsure about active collusion between the TTP and the BLA, two ideologically divergent groups. Rather, he said, “whoever finds access to an area strikes there”.
Baloch, meanwhile, cautioned against reading the shift as the result of a single trigger.
“Insurgency in Balochistan should be understood as an evolving conflict shaped by cumulative grievances and strategic calculations rather than a single catalyst,” he said.
Kakar, too, argued that parts of the Pashtun belt were already experiencing political and economic discontent, including protests over border closures and restrictions affecting cross-border livelihoods.
An expansion of armed groups into these areas risks making that worse.
“This could deepen existing grievances against the state, particularly if communities perceive themselves as simultaneously bearing the economic costs of tighter security measures and the consequences of deteriorating security,” he said.

Human rights organisations condemn 'racist murder' of Manipuri singer Chongtham Vikram in Delhi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:43:35 UTC
18:43:35 KST

The groups called for support, protection and compensation for Vikram's family and urged authorities to protect them from intimidation, harassment or further victimisation.
NEW DELHI: A group of civil society and human rights organisations has condemned the death of Manipuri music teacher and singer Chongtham Vikram, who was allegedly killed by a mob in Delhi on Monday. The group called for a thorough probe into the possible racial motive behind the attack.The joint statement was issued after a meeting of the Manipur Students’ Association Delhi (MSAD), Manipur International Youth Centre (MIYC), People’s Progressive Alliance Manipur (PPAM), Karwan-e-Mohabbat (KeM), North East India Support Centre and Helpline (NEISCH) and Human Rights Alert (HRA) on September 8 at the Centre for Equity Studies in Sarvodaya Enclave, New Delhi.
The groups said Vikram's murder should not be treated as an isolated criminal incident. They said it must be examined in the wider context of racial prejudice and violence faced by people from Northeast India.The statement said an FIR, numbered 0296, has been registered at Sunlight Colony police station under Sections 103(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.Section 103(2) deals with murder committed by a group of five or more people acting together on grounds including race, caste, community, sex, place of birth, language or personal belief.
Section 3(5) provides for joint liability when several people commit a criminal act in furtherance of a common intention.The organisations said the police investigation so far appeared inadequate to address what they described as a broader pattern of racist crimes against people from the Northeast.They also pointed to the recommendations of the MP Bezbaruah Committee, which was set up by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs and submitted its report in 2014. The committee had recommended measures to tackle discrimination, violence and the vulnerabilities faced by people from Northeast India.The groups said most of those recommendations, including a proposal to specifically criminalise racist acts, remain unimplemented.They also highlighted the absence of a comprehensive legal framework dealing specifically with racial discrimination. The statement noted that Article 15 of the Constitution prohibits discrimination on several grounds but does not expressly list colour, descent, national origin or ethnic origin.The organisations further cited recommendations issued by the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) on August 25, 2026. They urged the Centre to adopt comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation with a clear definition of racial discrimination, covering both direct and intersecting forms of discrimination in public and private spheres.The groups demanded an impartial and transparent investigation into Vikram's death, including an evidence-based examination of any racial motive.They also called for all those responsible to be identified and prosecuted, including anyone who may have participated in, facilitated or encouraged the attack.The organisations urged authorities to ensure that the case is not investigated merely as an ordinary criminal offence without considering its alleged racial dimensions.
They also sought immediate measures to prevent further racist violence against people from Northeast India, along with institutional mechanisms to tackle racial discrimination and hate-based violence.The groups called for support, protection and compensation for Vikram's family and urged authorities to protect them from intimidation, harassment or further victimisation.The statement said, "Justice for Chongtham Vikram is not merely a demand for accountability for one murder. It is a demand for dignity, equality, security, and the fundamental right to live free from racial violence for all people from Northeast India."The meeting ended with a two-minute silence in memory of Vikram and in solidarity with his bereaved family.
Vijaya Srivastava is a journalist and feature writer whose expertise lies in covering human-centred developments. Her stories explore how policy, technology, economic shifts and social change influence people's everyday lives. Her work also focuses on bringing depth, context and a human perspective to complex issues.
Her reports primarily cover society, healthcare, safety, public policy and emerging trends, alongside other political developments.

Germany could help Ukraine with finding fighting-age men, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:43:32 UTC
18:43:32 KST

In an interview with Paul Ronzheimer, Johann Wadephul said Berlin could share its data on Ukrainian men with German residency permits. | Ralf Hirschberger/AFP via Getty Images
The German government could help Kyiv with bringing men of military age who reside in the country back to Ukraine, said Foreign Affairs Minister Johann Wadephul.
In an interview with Paul Ronzheimer of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network released Wednesday, Wadephul said Berlin could share its data on Ukrainian men with German residency permits.
“We know who lives here. For example, who receives social benefits or who is registered here,” said Wadephul. On the basis of this data, these men could “be contacted by the Ukrainian government and called upon.” The whole process, however, should run “without coercion,” added the minister.
Advertisement
Approximately 1 million Ukrainian refugees obtained a temporary residence permit in Germany following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, including around 450,000 men, according to official 2025 data.
Ukraine has been under martial law since February 2022, prohibiting men aged 25 to 60 who are eligible for military service from leaving the country. Approximately 1.17 million adult Ukrainian men are currently benefiting from temporary protection across the EU, and their presence abroad has been a matter of discussion between Kyiv, Brussels and EU capitals.
German Chancellor Freidrich Merz urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in November 2025 to curb the flow of young men leaving Ukraine. And in April this year, Zelenskyy said in a press conference alongside Merz that the return of men of fighting age was “a matter of fairness.”
In July, the EU banned men of fighting age from its refugee scheme in response to “the evolving military needs of Ukraine.” The ban only covers new applicants, and not men already residing in the EU.

In central Warsaw, a Polish man beat a Ukrainian tourist and was placed under arrest
Kyiv • UNN
The 33-year-old Polish man struck a 20-year-old Ukrainian at a crossing, causing him to lose consciousness. The court remanded the attacker in custody for three months.
In central Warsaw, a Polish man attacked a 20-year-old Ukrainian for no reason. The victim lost consciousness and fell to the ground. The entire incident was captured by a surveillance camera: the attacker was detained just a few minutes later, reports the Warsaw District Police Department, according to UNN.
Details
According to the investigation, the man attacked a 20-year-old Ukrainian citizen at a pedestrian crossing. The attacker punched him in the head. The blow was so powerful that the victim briefly lost consciousness. Passersby provided him with assistance.
The perpetrator turned out to be a 33-year-old Polish citizen. He was charged, and his conduct was classified as a hooligan offense. The court ruled that the suspect would spend the next three months in custody.
It was also established that during questioning, the man did not give a reason for his behavior. In the past, he had convictions for similar crimes, namely: he had attacked an elderly woman in a similar manner, for which he served a prison sentence.
His victim at the time was an 86-year-old woman, whom he kicked twice in the back, causing her to fall and sustain head injuries. Several days later, he threatened to kill another random woman. He was quickly located and detained by police officers from the city center. Ultimately, the court sentenced him to nearly a year in prison
In this case, based on the evidence collected, the 33-year-old man was charged with creating a direct danger of loss of life or serious harm to a person's health, as well as causing an injury to a bodily organ that lasted no longer than 7 days. The victim's testimony indicates that he had never seen the attacker before and had come to Poland as a tourist for several days.
The court granted the motion of the Warsaw prosecutor's office, imposing pretrial detention on the suspect for a period of three months. The suspect's conduct was classified as a hooligan offense. In such a case, the court may impose a more severe punishment.

AIPAC, Netanyahu and Israel take center stage in New Hampshire Democratic primaries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:42:23 UTC
18:42:23 KST

One night of primaries in New Hampshire offered Democrats two nearly opposite pictures of their changing relationship with Israel. In the more important race, the Senate primary, Chris Pappas, a moderate congressman with a clear pro-Israel record, defeated a progressive challenger who made Israel and allegations of genocide a central part of her campaign. Hours later, in the race for the House seat Pappas himself is vacating, Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of one of the state’s most powerful political families, cruised to victory after making an anti-AIPAC campaign one of her most prominent weapons.
Pappas, 46, quickly won the Democratic Senate primary with about 63% of the vote, securing a place in one of the most important races of the November midterms. He will face Republican John Sununu, a former senator and the son and brother of two former governors, in a contest that could prove significant in the fight for control of the Senate. Democrats must hold the seat of retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen — Stefany's mother — and Republicans have already identified New Hampshire as one of their best opportunities.
But Pappas is not just another moderate Democrat with a long résumé. If he wins in November, he will be the first openly gay man to serve in the U.S. Senate. He also comes from a family that holds another, far less stately American distinction: His grandfather, Charlie Pappas, is credited with inventing the chicken tender in 1974, the fried chicken strip that has since become a national institution. The Pappas family still owns the Puritan Backroom restaurant, a pilgrimage site for politicians visiting New Hampshire, where Pappas also celebrated his victory. The claim that the family invented the tender is difficult to prove, but Manchester, New Hampshire, has already officially declared itself the “Chicken Tender Capital of the World.”
His connection to the Shaheen family also completes an almost perfect political circle. In 1996, when he was a 16-year-old high school student, Pappas volunteered on Jeanne Shaheen’s first campaign for governor. Since then, he has passed through nearly every possible stage of local politics, from the state Legislature to a powerful executive council, before being elected to Congress in 2018. Now, 30 years after handing out campaign literature for her, he is the candidate seeking to replace her in the Senate.
For Jerusalem, Pappas has long been considered part of the more Israel-friendly wing of the Democratic Party. AIPAC supported him in previous House races and he was among the Democrats who voted to condemn Palestinian American Rep. Rashida Tlaib over her use of the phrase “from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free.” He supports Israel’s right to defend itself and a two-state solution. But the current primary highlighted just how much the atmosphere inside the party has changed. In recent months, Pappas has distanced himself from Israel’s right-wing government, saying Netanyahu “has to go” and is not a reliable U.S. partner. He also voted present on a proposal to completely eliminate $3.3 billion in aid to Israel and pledged that in the Senate he would support restrictions on shipments of heavy bombs and certain military equipment.
That was not enough for his opponent, Dr. Karishma Manzur, a medical scientist and member of the local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, the faction that has produced figures such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Manzur accused Israel of “genocide” and claimed Netanyahu controls nearly 90% of Congress and the White House. She called Pappas “AIPAC’s emissary” and accused him of “getting paid” by the lobby in exchange for his votes. Billboards attacking his ties to AIPAC were even put up in his hometown.
Manzur managed to narrow the polling gap in recent weeks and ride the same anti-establishment wave that has carried other progressive candidates this year. But on Election Day, it became clear that the establishment is still alive. Pappas had the backing of Kamala Harris, Elizabeth Warren and Mark Kelly and, above all, a nearly absurd financial advantage: He had raised more than $15 million through the end of August, compared with less than $500,000 for Manzur.
'Choose a fighter, not a family name'
That same night, however, a few miles away, the family name was working in an entirely different direction. Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of the retiring senator, was on her way to a narrow primary victory for the House seat Pappas is leaving behind. Her main rival, Maura Sullivan, a former Marine officer who served in Iraq and a former senior Obama administration official, tried to turn the political dynasty into a liability. In a campaign ad, she urged voters to “choose a fighter, not a fancy family name” and accused Shaheen of feeling entitled to the seat. Sullivan had already tried to win the same seat in 2018, when Pappas was the one who defeated her in the primary.
The “nepo baby” label attached to Shaheen Jr. also has a numerical basis. Nearly $740,000 raised by her campaign came from donors who had previously contributed to her mother. At least one major donor said the senator herself contacted him and asked him to support her daughter. Her father, Billy Shaheen, is also a longtime Democratic establishment figure in New Hampshire who has managed local campaigns for presidential candidates including Jimmy Carter, Al Gore and John Kerry over the years.
But Stefany Shaheen has a story of her own. She served on the Portsmouth City Council and chaired its police commission, founded a digital health company and has spent years working on diabetes issues after her eldest daughter was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes at age 8 and nearly died. She is the mother of four, is a graduate of programs at MIT and Harvard and wrote a bestselling book about her family’s experience with the disease. Her campaign focused on health care and support for universal health insurance, but in recent weeks Israel and AIPAC took on a more prominent role.
Shaheen repeatedly attacked Sullivan over donations from people who had also contributed to AIPAC and aired an ad portraying her as “funded” by the pro-Israel lobby “aligned with Netanyahu.” Her campaign showed an image of Netanyahu alongside the declaration: “Let’s show them New Hampshire’s not for sale.” Sullivan, for her part, insisted that AIPAC itself had neither donated to nor supported her.
Shaheen sought to fend off accusations of antisemitism by securing the support of J Street, the liberal pro-Israel lobby considered an ideological rival of AIPAC, as well as pointing to her Jewish supporters. She is a staunch supporter of ending U.S. military aid to Israel and pledged to vote for any proposal to do so. She still describes Israel as an “our strongest ally in the Middle East,” recognizes its right to exist alongside a two-state solution, but on aid and the pro-Israel lobby she is clearly to the left of Democrats of her mother’s generation.
Thus, while Pappas demonstrated that a Democrat with a pro-Israel record can still easily defeat a rival who built a significant part of her campaign around attacks on Israel and AIPAC, in the neighboring race the daughter of the senator he is seeking to replace found that one way to prove to voters that she is more than just “the daughter of” is to attack AIPAC and oppose military aid to Israel. The two results do not tell the same story, but they once again demonstrate where the Democratic Party stands in 2026: Israel is no longer a foreign policy issue that candidates can skip over in a primary. It has become a political test in which candidates are expected to choose a clear side.

Gaps in measles shot leave Bangladesh with world's worst outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:42:00 UTC
18:42:00 KST

Once close to eliminating measles, Bangladesh is facing its worst outbreak on record, with 999 suspected and confirmed deaths reported since March as hospitals struggle to cope with a surge of sick children.
The prolonged outbreak, despite a nationwide emergency vaccination campaign launched in April, follows disruption to routine immunization in 2024 and 2025, experts said, when the country was going through political turmoil after a deadly uprising against then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.
Bangladesh is currently experiencing the biggest measles outbreak in the world, according to a list on the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website.
Health officials and experts said missed vaccinations and vaccine supply problems as a result of the political upheaval had left children vulnerable, particularly infants under nine months who are too young to get routine vaccinations, helping fuel transmission across age groups.
Since the outbreak emerged in March, Bangladesh has recorded more than 166,000 suspected measles cases, including 19,835 laboratory-confirmed infections, according to Health Ministry data.
The outbreak has been linked to 999 deaths, including 100 confirmed measles fatalities, while more than 146,000 suspected patients have been hospitalized.
Experts blamed the outbreak on weak program oversight, insufficient monitoring and procurement policy changes under the interim government that replaced Hasina, disrupting vaccine availability and leaving many children unprotected against the highly infectious disease.
Health Minister Sardar Md. Sakhawat Husain told parliament Monday the procurement changes triggered a vaccine shortage, while the 2024 postponement of a vaccination program and the cancellation of a nationwide measles-rubella campaign the following year left more children vulnerable to infection.
The World Health Organization, UNICEF and other health agencies have also pointed to the disruption to immunization schedules. Under-5s accounted for about 80% of cases during the early stages of the disease's spread.
The outbreak follows years of progress toward measles elimination. Bangladesh maintained high measles vaccination coverage for much of the past decade, with rates staying at or above the 95% level recommended by the WHO for most of the period, apart from a dip during the COVID-19 pandemic.
"Bangladesh missed its measles elimination target because of vaccination gaps in 2024 and 2025," said professor Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and former director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research.
"To my knowledge, Bangladesh has never witnessed so many children dying from measles. Nor have we ever seen such a high number of patients in a single year. This is a truly terrible situation, and the saddest part is that the victims are children," he said.
Rahman said closing immunity gaps, increasing vaccination coverage and stepping up public awareness were immediate priorities to contain the outbreak.
Hospitals are struggling to cope with the surge in measles cases at a time when growing numbers of dengue patients are putting additional pressure on an already overstretched health care system.
More than 45,000 people have been admitted to hospital for dengue this year, according to health ministry data. On Tuesday, dengue deaths rose to nine, while admissions climbed to 1,571, both daily highs for the year.
"Patients are pouring in, and it is very difficult to accommodate everyone," said Dr. Nanda Dulal Saha, acting director of the state-run Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital in Dhaka, adding the hospital currently had 60 beds for measles patients, but many were being treated on the floor.
Saha said a shortage of pediatric saline, which can help alleviate the symptoms of measles, was complicating the situation.
The hospital, designed for 1,350 patients, is currently caring for more than 2,350, he said.
For families, the outbreak has meant weeks of uncertainty, repeated hospital visits and mounting costs.
Nasima Begum, 35, a house help, said her 13-month-old son contracted measles nearly two months ago. After failing to secure a bed at four hospitals, he was finally admitted and discharged 10 days later, but continues to suffer recurring fever and has yet to fully recover.
Begum said her son missed his vaccination because he was sick. When they returned to the vaccination center later, they were told the vaccine was unavailable. Unlike her youngest son, her four older children had received their routine vaccinations.
Mohammad Ripon, a factory worker, said his 8-month-old daughter developed a rash and other measles-like symptoms days after being discharged from hospital, forcing the family to seek treatment at multiple facilities before turning to a dedicated measles hospital for answers.
"We are just hopping around from one hospital to another," Ripon said. "We are not getting the correct information at all."
Bangladesh's emergency measles-rubella vaccination campaign targeted about 18 million children aged six months to under five years. More than 19.7 million children have since been vaccinated, according to Health Ministry data, but experts said stronger routine immunization and catch-up campaigns were still needed.
The twin health crises of measles and mosquito-borne dengue, a debilitating illness linked to warmer temperatures and urbanization, underscore the challenge facing Bangladesh's health system in maintaining routine services while responding to preventable infectious diseases.
Although measles is one of the world's most contagious diseases and typically causes fever and a tell-tale rash, it can be prevented with two doses of vaccine.
"We are poor and cannot afford treatment. I only pray that my son recovers," Begum said. "I don't want any other mother to see her child suffer or die from this disease."

AI generated
LONDON – The British government will require technology companies such as Apple and Google to stop children from taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their phones and tablets, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has told the House of Commons.
Nandy said the government would introduce legislation “as soon as we can”, but declined to give a precise timetable.
The government gave Apple and Alphabet-owned Google a three-month deadline in June to introduce such measures voluntarily. Although both firms scan sensitive content for young users, neither comprehensively block the taking or sending of nude selfies.
Nandy praised Apple’s rollout of age checks earlier in 2026 on its operating system. She called commitments by the iPhone-maker and Google “a step in the right direction”, but said they were ultimately insufficient.
“For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from some of the worst harms,” Nandy said. “And to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace that we need it to, while harm is being done now.”
A spokesman for Google said the company was “pleased to have made progress”, and that it was “fully committed” to working with lawmakers, app developers and safety experts on ways to keep children safe.
An Apple spokesman said the company in 2021 added a feature that prevents children from viewing or sharing photos or videos that contain nudity, and it now includes support for some third-party apps.
“We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen Communication Safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe,” the representative said.
Britain has strict online child safety protections, although the current rules mostly apply to services and platforms rather than devices. Pushing Apple and Google to introduce stronger, proactive nudity detection at the device level is a significant expansion, intended to stop children from creating and sharing intimate images of themselves online.
While child safety organisations have welcomed the prospective new laws, there are questions around privacy and technical feasibility. Currently, Apple and Google’s measures involve detecting nudity in an image that has already been taken.
Nandy said some questions needed to be ironed out, such as what devices the new rules would apply to.
She said the government would reassess legislation if the companies introduce the restrictions before a Bill is passed.
“Children cannot face more delays, so the government must act swiftly and ensure these measures are enshrined in law at the earliest opportunity,” said Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children.
In the Commons chamber, the Conservative Party’s Shadow Secretary of State Rebecca Paul also praised the announcement as a “a huge practical step, which has the potential to prevent immeasurable harm”, but added that details on the legislation remained vague.
Privacy campaign group Big Brother Watch said online that protecting children is a “noble goal”, but criticised what it described as digital ID checks and surveillance software.
The restrictions will not apply to adults who have passed age verification.
Britain is on track to bring its social media ban for under-16s, announced earlier in the summer, into force by spring 2027, Nandy said. BLOOMBERG

Estonia might remove companies that miss reporting deadlines from Business Register
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:36:00 UTC
18:36:00 KST

Estonia might remove companies that miss reporting deadlines from Business Register
Nearly 67,000 Estonian companies have yet to file their annual reports, but officials say those that are only a few months late are not at immediate risk of being removed from the Business Register.
The deadline for filing annual reports was June 30. All companies, large and small, as well as foundations and nonprofit organizations, are required to file a report every year. Companies that had no economic activity must also file a report.
As of Tuesday, nearly 67,000 companies had failed to file their annual reports, accounting for 24 percent of those required to do so.
The Business Register is administered by the registration department of Tartu County Court. According to the court, both larger and smaller companies have encountered problems. Larger organizations may have difficulties with audits, while smaller ones simply forget or wait for a warning, Tartu County Court spokesperson Siim Saavik said.
Business owners often tell the court that they did not receive a warning or that the court never sent one to the organization. "In the digital world, there is a record of such actions. The warning was indeed sent, but amid the hectic pace of life, it went unnoticed. Organizations should check whether their contact information is up to date and whether they are able to receive notifications," Saavik said.
Three years ago, at the beginning of 2023, a law took effect giving the registrar greater powers to bring late filers into compliance. For example, late filers can be fined repeatedly, with fines of up to €3,200.
Risk of being struck from the register
The law allows companies that have failed to file their annual reports to be removed from the Business Register three months after the filing deadline. That three-month period expires October 1.
Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta explained that this does not mean all companies that have failed to file their reports will be removed from the register on October 1. Tartu County Court also confirmed that companies whose reports are only a couple of months overdue are not at risk of being removed. Companies whose reports have been overdue for longer and that have previously received a warning of removal may face being struck from the register.
Pakosta stressed that companies cannot be removed if they have outstanding debts to individuals or the Tax and Customs Board or if they are involved in ongoing court proceedings.
Pakosta said the state has made several changes aimed at improving compliance with reporting requirements.
"There have been several changes, so there isn't really a clear timeline we can lay out. By now, the approach is one that places more responsibility on the market itself. If an annual report has not been filed, the state has the right to impose sanctions, but it is not required to do so. For example, it can issue a fine or remove a legal entity from the register. But again, it is not required to do so," Pakosta said.
Pakosta said companies that fail to file their reports make themselves appear unreliable, meaning it is also in their own interests to meet the deadlines.
"Filing a report late actually affects a company's ability to operate in the market or in society. That's certainly the case for a potential partner deciding whether to buy something from the company or enter into a contract with it. If its annual report isn't available, that's a major risk. The purpose of making annual reports public is precisely so that market participants know who they should do business with and who they shouldn't," Pakosta added.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

ECB to hike rates again due to inflationary pressures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:35:30 UTC
18:35:30 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu, Emirhan Yilmaz and Emir Yildirim
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
The European Central Bank (ECB) is gearing up for its second rate hike of the year amid inflationary pressures, mostly due to energy prices, while all eyes are turned to the bank’s projections and its president Christine Lagarde’s upcoming statements.
Oil prices once again reached $100 a barrel due to the ongoing Middle East conflict, while natural gas prices in Europe rose to levels higher than those of 2023.
The eurozone’s annual inflation rose to its highest level in the past three years at 3.3% in August due to the rapid rise in energy prices.
Peter Vanden Houte, chief economist at the ING Group, told Anadolu that the bank is expected to raise its deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% due to the eurozone economy’s resilience and that high energy prices pushed inflation back up above 3%.
Houte stated that core and services inflation have yet to signal broader concerns as the ongoing pressures remain largely energy-driven, which could prevent the ECB from adopting an overly hawkish stance at its upcoming conference.
“We expect the ECB’s new projections to contain only modest upward revisions to growth and inflation forecasts,” he said. “Although financial markets are pricing in further rate increases later this year, we are a bit more cautious.”
Houte noted that the bank might adopt a wait-and-see stance after this month’s rate hike.
“Only if the Middle-East conflict drags on, potentially pushing energy prices even higher, the ECB might consider hiking rates again in December,” he added.
Bill Diviney, head of macro research and senior eurozone economist at ABN AMRO, told Anadolu that the bank’s updated macroeconomic forecasts and Lagarde’s remarks will draw attention from the markets, as the ECB’s 2027 inflation forecast is expected to see an upward revision.
“Lagarde will likely be pressed on the prospect of future moves given that markets are pricing in nearly two more hikes after September’s move, but while we expect hawkish rhetoric around inflation, she is likely to reiterate the ECB’s meeting-by-meeting approach,” he said.
Alain Durree, head of European macro research at Natixis, stated that Lagarde might adopt a neutral tone in the near future to keep all options on the table while avoiding signaling a prolonged rate-hiking cycle.
Durree noted that the ECB would not pause rate hikes until the end of 2027.
“First, a resolution of the Middle East conflicts by early January should ease energy prices. Second, softening labor market conditions by then will limit the risk of second-round effects,” he said.
“Third, the projected appreciation of the euro will further dampen both headline and core inflation,” he added, noting that these three main factors could support the bank’s likelihood to continue rate hikes despite a complex economic balance after September.
Marco Wagner, senior economist at Commerzbank, told Anadolu that the bank’s trajectory after this month’s rate hike is “less certain.”
“Investors in the futures markets expect two more rate hikes by the middle of next year; however, we consider it more likely that key interest rates will remain unchanged in the coming months,” he said.

Emre Aytekin and Emir Yildirim
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Aktif Bank became the first Turkish bank to participate in China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) in a newly signed deal at the China International Fair for Investment and Trade (CIFIT).
The system facilitates global payments and settlements to be made in Chinese yuan while eliminating the time and cost differences that traditional multi-currency conversions require, which is expected to benefit Turkish small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) alongside large corporations, the bank’s general manager told Anadolu.
Aysegul Adaca Ogan, speaking on the sidelines of the event, stated that the relatively young platform was developed by the People’s Bank of China (PBoC) and has grown over the past five years with foreign banks participating in the scheme, serving over 1,800 banks.
She noted that yuan-denominated payments via CIPS rose to 28% of China’s foreign trade volume totaling $6 trillion over the past five years, while the trade volume between Türkiye and China rose from $25 billion to $50 billion over the same period.
“With rising yuan payments in Chinese foreign trade and the growing demand for yuan payment systems in Türkiye, joining this platform has been a viable opportunity for us,” she said.
Ogan stated that Aktif Bank will open its digital banking platform to enable SMEs to make payments through CIPS.
“We have over 1,300 banks worldwide, and we want to expand our corridor to include regions like China after Europe and the Americas, after closely monitoring opportunities in the Chinese market,” she said.
“We’re the only Turkish bank at the fair’s pavilion and our presence here today is an important step in our long-term strategy,” she added.

KONGSBERG adds U.S. radar to its top-selling gun system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:33:16 UTC
18:33:16 KST

- KONGSBERG has integrated Echodyne's MESA radar into its PROTECTOR RS4 and RS6 remote weapon stations to counter drones.
- The PROTECTOR family is the world's most widely fielded remote weapon station, with more than 25,000 units delivered to over 31 countries.
Norwegian defense company KONGSBERG has selected a radar built by U.S. firm Echodyne to help its remote weapon systems detect and shoot down drones, the companies announced September 9.
KONGSBERG has integrated Echodyne’s MESA radar into its PROTECTOR RS4 and RS6 remote weapon stations, turning the widely used gun mounts into counter-drone systems capable of tracking and engaging small unmanned aircraft. The PROTECTOR family is the most widely fielded remote weapon station in the world, with more than 25,000 units delivered to over 31 countries and more than 8 million hours of combat use, including in Ukraine. The stations let troops fire machine guns, grenade launchers or larger weapons from inside a vehicle, using cameras and sensors instead of exposing a gunner.
Echodyne’s MESA radar is a solid-state, electronically steered radar built to be smaller and lighter than traditional radar systems with similar performance, a design meant to let it fit on vehicles and stationary mounts without adding significant weight or power draw. The radar feeds range, speed, bearing and other tracking data to the weapon station’s fire-control system, which the companies say helps the gun hold a stable lock on fast, small drones that are difficult for older sensors to track.
“Integrating MESA radar gives the PROTECTOR family the precise, stable and persistent tracks needed to cue the fire-control system, sustain target lock and act decisively against fast-moving, low-signature drone threats,” said Eben Frankenberg, CEO of Echodyne. “Just as important, MESA delivers that performance in a compact, software-defined package that can scale across a large installed base and adapt as the threat evolves.”
The radar becomes especially useful when PROTECTOR systems fire programmable airburst rounds, ammunition set to detonate near a target rather than on direct impact. Precise tracking of a drone’s speed and distance helps the system time the round’s detonation to catch the target in its flight path. The radar can also work alongside other sensors on the battlefield, receiving a target track from a separate radar or spotting system and refining it for the weapon station to use.
Echodyne and KONGSBERG have spent several years testing the radar-equipped system together before this announcement, the companies said, and plan to keep working on other uses for the radar across KONGSBERG’s broader product line. Beyond the PROTECTOR integrations already announced, the companies did not specify which additional systems they are exploring or provide a timeline.
Echodyne has previously supplied radar for counter-drone work with the Australian Defence Force and other security applications, but this marks its selection for KONGSBERG’s PROTECTOR line specifically. The two companies are exhibiting the system this week at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland, which runs through September 11.

hurt by trees and branches brought down by the violent wind and
torrential rain.

1950.

normal.

droughts, supercharged storms and flooding more frequent and
more intense.

causing global heating, the main driver is the burning of fossil

The Fairphone (Gen 6+) Review: Finally in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Finally available in the US! Repairable with long-term software support. Five-year warranty. Good performance. Daylong battery life. Distraction-free mode. Expandable storage. Capable cameras.
TIRED
Feels very plasticky. Not supported on Verizon, with caveats on other carriers. Not waterproof. Cameras still don’t match the competition.
It’s time to vote with your wallet.
The US has long had fewer smartphone options than the rest of the world. The Apple-and-Samsung duopoly, supported largely by carriers—where people buy most smartphones—has made it hard for other phone brands to break through. It’s partly why the Dutch manufacturer Fairphone hasn’t sold its repairable, ethically made smartphone in the US in its 13-year existence—until now.
Fairphone finally made it across the pond with a new model, the Fairphone (Gen. 6+). If you’ve complained about the lack of repairable smartphones, the inability to self-replace a battery, or even the idea of a more ethically manufactured phone, the Fairphone should be on your list (if it’s time to upgrade).
I’ve been using this $650 Android handset for several weeks, and it’s pretty good.
Fairer Phone
There isn’t much of a difference between the Fairphone (Gen. 6) I reviewed last year and the (Gen. 6+). The phone comes in a new cobalt blue color to commemorate people who work in the cobalt mines (a crucial component in smartphones) and the Fair Cobalt Alliance, a nonprofit cofounded by Fairphone.
Chiefly, the Fairphone has a slightly more souped-up processor—the Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4—alongside 12 GB of RAM. That last part is important, as many of the new software features in our smartphones, specifically those powered by artificial intelligence, demand a lot of memory; the 12 gigs here should give the Fairphone a longer shelf life in being able to take advantage of those capabilities.
Performance has been plenty satisfactory, whether I was using Google Maps to navigate, doomscrolling through Instagram Reels, or playing PokémonGo while waiting for a doctor’s appointment. My benchmarks show the tiniest of performance bumps over the processor in the Gen 6. You may see a slight stutter here and there, but it barely affects day-to-day use. The software is also more polished this time around; I haven’t run into notable bugs, which I can’t say for last year’s model.
I don’t mind the look of the new Fairphone—the blue and the yellow-accented button is a fun combo—but it does have a very plasticky feel. You might like Fairphone’s accessory system, which lets you replace part of the backplate with accessories like a wallet or phone grip by removing two screws (you can use the included screwdriver). I haven’t bothered, as it feels a little clunky; I don’t want these items permanently on the back, and unscrewing them is a hassle. Hopefully, Fairphone can move to a MagSafe-like system in the future.
The 6.3-inch AMOLED, 120-Hz screen is more than adequate. It’s colorful, sharp, and bright enough to read in sunlight. Fairphone’s adaptive brightness mode can be a little aggressive, so I often manually adjusted the brightness slider, but I don’t have much else to complain about.
Battery life from the 4,415-mAh cell isn’t impressive, but it won’t have you running to a wall outlet all the time either. I typically ended most days with around 20 percent by bedtime; that’s with around five to six hours of screen-on time. It’s a shame there’s no wireless charging, but that’s a nice-to-have not necessarily a deal-breaker. Oddly, the phone doesn’t come with a USB-C cable (the lack of a charging block is standard across phones these days), but the idea is that you probably have one lying around in a drawer. Less e-waste!
The dual-camera system, powered by a 50-MP main and a 13-MP ultrawide, is solid. No, Fairphone can’t really compete with the big tech giants like Google, Apple, and Samsung on this front. Low-light scenes suffer the most, with details lost in shadows—stay very still to avoid a blurry image. Photos from the 32-MP selfie camera can also look a little soft. Still, it’s not so poor that you won’t use it. You’ll get perfectly adequate results, but if you rely heavily on your smartphone’s camera for video and photos, you may want to look elsewhere.
Photograph: Julian Chokkattu
Main camera
Fairphone doesn’t meddle too much with the base Android 16 software, except for Fairphone Moments, which is tied to the yellow switch on the right edge of the phone. Flick the switch and the phone’s interface goes minimal, only offering access to a handful of apps. You can create your own Moments—up to five apps—to help you focus on the task at hand. For example, if you’re driving, you can flick the switch and have it only let you access Google Maps, Spotify, and Phone. It’s a neat system, though its practicality completely depends on your willpower to use it.
I’d have liked to see Fairphone win some brownie points with a headphone jack, but alas. You’ll at least appreciate the microSD card slot to expand on the already generous 256 GB of internal storage (unusual at this price). You might even prefer the capacitive fingerprint sensor baked into the side power button, rather than the under-display fingerprint sensor in most Android phones.
Long-Lasting
People are holding onto their phones for longer. But manufacturers can do several things to make it easier. Software and security updates are crucial, and thankfully, Fairphone promises seven years of updates through 2033. It also comes with a five-year warranty, virtually unheard of for a phone.
A big part of the Fairphone is repairability (iFixit gave it a 10/10 score). With the included screwdriver, you can remove that same backplate mentioned earlier to access the battery. Fairphone has instructions on its website for accessing the 11 other components you can replace, from the speakers and display to the USB-C port. Fairphone will sell these parts through 2033, and they’re cheap, too! Replacing the display, for example, will cost just $90. (You can also access most of this information in the preinstalled My Fairphone app.)
There are some caveats. The Fairphone (Gen. 6+) only has an IP55 dust- and water-resistance rating, meaning it’ll be fine in the rain, but a drop in the pool may wreck it. That’s the trade-off for having such easy access to the device’s internals for repairs.
And while the Gen. 6+ works on T-Mobile and AT&T, it doesn’t support Verizon (which includes all the smaller MVNOs that rely on Verizon’s network, like Visible). Fairphone’s website has a chart showing carrier compatibility, and you’ll see that some MVNOs on AT&T’s network are only partially supported, like Boost Mobile and Cricket. Other limitations include the lack of millimeter-wave 5G or missing eSIM support on T-Mobile. For what it’s worth, I’ve used it with an eSIM on Google Fi—the phone dips to 4G more often than other phones, but it hasn’t been a big issue for me. Your mileage may vary.
Can you find better specs for the money? Sure. The Pixel 10a will easily give you a better camera system. For $50 more, the new Samsung Galaxy S26 FE delivers flagship-grade performance and a telephoto camera. But you’ll also be out of pocket if you drop either phone and need a screen replacement. The Fairphone doesn’t have that problem, and you’ll have a little more peace of mind that your phone was made sustainably, with fair wages paid out to folks in the supply chain. The Fairphone (Gen. 6+) proves you no longer have to make massive compromises just to take a stand.

Russian sources warn Ukraine’s drone war has entered a new sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:29:07 UTC
18:29:07 KST

- Russian sources describe a pattern of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian-linked assets expanding from the Black Sea into the Caspian and Baltic seas and now the Mediterranean.
- Ukraine's SBU has publicly claimed only one of three cited Mediterranean strikes, the December 2025 attack on the tanker Qendil.
A Russian military-affiliated Telegram channel has raised alarm that Ukraine’s reach at sea now extends beyond the Black Sea into the Mediterranean, framing a string of drone strikes on Russian-linked vessels there as part of a wider pattern that has already put Russian military and commercial assets at risk across three separate seas.
Ukraine’s drone campaign against Russian naval and shipping targets started in the Black Sea, where a senior U.S. defense official said last year that Ukrainian forces had destroyed or damaged at least 32 medium to large Russian naval vessels, forcing much of Russia’s fleet to relocate away from Crimea. Kyiv has since extended that campaign into the Caspian Sea, over 1,000 km from Ukrainian territory. Ukraine’s military intelligence claimed its first Caspian strike in November 2024, damaging the missile ships Tatarstan and Dagestan at the port of Kaspiysk in Russia’s Dagestan region. Ukrainian forces have hit Caspian targets repeatedly since, including three Lukoil offshore drilling platforms in January 2026 and an FSB border patrol boat in May 2026, with Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces publicly claiming responsibility for each strike.
Ukraine has also struck Russian assets in the Baltic Sea. In May 2026, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian drones hit the Baltic port of Primorsk, setting it on fire, and struck an oil tanker, a Karakurt-class missile ship and a patrol boat. Kyiv also blew up the Russian Baltic Fleet corvette Boyky at Kronstadt Naval Base. Ukrainian or suspected Ukrainian drones later crossed into NATO airspace over the Baltic states and Finland that same spring, according to open-source tracking, during the wider campaign against Russian oil export infrastructure at ports including Primorsk and Ust-Luga.
Against that backdrop, the Mediterranean now appears to be the newest theater. Ukraine’s SBU security service publicly claimed responsibility for a December 2025 drone strike on the Qendil, an Oman-flagged crude oil tanker tied to Russia’s sanctioned shadow fleet, more than 2,000 km from Ukraine. The SBU said its Alpha special unit used aerial drones to critically damage the empty tanker, and Reuters confirmed the vessel shown in strike footage matched the Qendil using file imagery.
Two more Mediterranean incidents remain unconfirmed by Ukraine. In March 2026, the Russian-flagged LNG tanker Arctic Metagaz caught fire and sank between Libya and Malta while carrying gas from the Russian port of Murmansk. Russia’s Transport Ministry blamed Ukrainian naval drones and called the strike an act of terrorism; Libyan port authorities confirmed the vessel suffered explosions and a fire before sinking, and all 30 crew members were rescued.
Ukraine did not respond to the allegation. In the most recent incident, on September 6, 2026, Russian opposition journalist Alexander Nevzorov published footage he said showed the sanctioned, Russian-flagged cargo ship Lady Mariia struck 12 times by drones while carrying Iranian weapons and armored vehicles toward Russia. Neither the strike’s origin nor the cargo claim has been independently verified.

Kozinoğlu’s grave in Istanbul’s Ümraniye district is expected to be opened in the coming days. Tissue samples taken from the grave will undergo toxicological and chemical analyses.
Investigators will also examine whether Kozinoğlu was given any medication other than those he was prescribed while in prison.
Kozinoğlu was arrested in 2011 as part of the Ergenekon investigation. The Ergenekon trial was later found to have been based on fabricated evidence and allegations made by FETÖ, who sought to purge military officers by accusing them of plotting a coup.
Kozinoğlu died in prison on Nov. 12, 2011, during the eighth month of his detention, shortly before he was scheduled to testify in the case.
His death was officially attributed to a heart attack. However, questions were raised over whether he had received timely and adequate medical attention, while allegations that he may have been poisoned also fueled controversy surrounding his death.
The case file also contained conflicting accounts from prison guards and medical personnel regarding the circumstances under which Kozinoğlu was transferred from the prison to hospital.
The investigation into his death was recently reopened after the Justice Ministry established a special unit to examine unresolved cases that have attracted significant public attention.
As part of the renewed investigation, security camera footage showing how long it took for an emergency alarm to be noticed on the night Kozinoğlu fell ill is being re-examined, along with an email reportedly sent to his lawyer after his death.
One of the key areas of focus in the reopened investigation is an allegation that Kozinoğlu had requested Coraspin, a blood-thinning medication and vitamin pills shortly before his death, but that the vitamin medication was not subjected to a detailed toxicological and chemical analysis during the autopsy.
The case file also includes an email reportedly sent to Kozinoğlu’s lawyer after his death, which allegedly claimed that his death was not caused by a heart attack.
