EU member states have once again failed to advance Ukraine’s accession process amid continued resistance from Hungary.
At a meeting of the Council's Working Party on Enlargement and Countries Negotiating Accession to the EU (COELA) on Tuesday, Hungary's representative maintained the veto first introduced last week, which consisted of opening a new negotiating cluster with Ukraine covering the internal market and competition policy.
Hungary opposed the opening, despite support from a large number of member states and the European Commission.
Hungary did not extend its veto to Moldova, whose accession process is being handled jointly with Ukraine's, clearing the way for cluster three to open on that front. However, other member states are reluctant to decouple the two candidate countries, whose accession tracks remain formally linked.
Budapest is conditioning further progress on Ukraine's EU bid on the implementation of pledged guarantees for the rights of Ukraine's Hungarian minority — a position it made explicit last week, when it vetoed the opening of the two clusters.
Hungarian and Ukrainian officials held talks over the summer on the rights of the Hungarian-speaking minority, during which Kyiv committed to safeguarding its educational, cultural and linguistic rights. Budapest is now pressing for those commitments to be put into practice.
In a statement on Monday, Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said progress had been made on this front, noting that work had begun on drafting new education legislation.
Earlier, Hungary had approved the opening of two negotiating chapters with Ukraine, covering fundamental rights and external relations.
The move underscores a shift in Budapest's approach to Ukraine's EU ambitions. Whereas the previous government under Viktor Orbán categorically blocked any progress on Kyiv's membership bid, the new government led by Péter Magyar has shown greater flexibility — while still opposing any fast-tracked accession.

Israel to open embassy in Slovenia as relations thaw
LJUBLJANA, Sept 9 - Israel will open its first embassy in Slovenia on Wednesday in a turnaround in relations between the countries after populist Janez Jansa formed a centre-right government this year.
The rapprochement comes as Israel faces growing diplomatic isolation elsewhere over its West Bank policies, including import bans by Britain, France and Canada on products from Israeli settlements.
"This is the first resident embassy in Slovenia, it is indeed a historic day," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said at a news conference with his Slovenian counterpart Tone Kajzer.

A delegation of Israeli businessmen will also attend an economic forum later in the day which is expected to result in new investment, Kajzer said.
"After a long period of less intensive political contacts, it is time to shift cooperation between Slovenia and Israel into a higher gear," he told reporters.
However, there was some opposition to the move in Slovenia.
The liberal Freedom Movement of former Prime Minister Robert Golob, joined by the Left party, on Wednesday submitted to parliament a proposal for impeachment of Jansa, primarily over his government's foreign policy which they said was exclusively in the interest of Israel.
Protests against the opening of the embassy are scheduled on Wednesday evening by student movements, a left-wing political opposition party and pro-Palestinian groups.
It marks a change in approach Slovenia, a tiny Alpine country which is a European Union and NATO military alliance member. Under the previous liberal government, it was one of a few European countries to recognise a Palestinian state.
Slovenia was also among the first EU countries to ban imports from the West Bank and entry for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his two hardline ministers, decisions that were quickly revoked by the new government. REUTERS

Geneva vs Zurich: which is the better safe haven?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:01:23 UTC
18:01:23 KST

Geneva vs Zurich: which is the better safe haven?
At a time of global unrest, Switzerland’s two big cities are seeing an influx of arrivals. But with significantly contrasting lifestyles, choosing between them is a challenge.
Switzerland’s reputation for stability is longstanding. Within weeks of the first military strikes in the Middle East earlier this year, Knight Frank reported a sharp rise in short-term letting demand in the country, demonstrating the appeal, in particular, of the country’s two principal lakefront cities as safe havens.
    
        External Content    
    
        
    
The new arrivals continue a well-established trend of recent international buyers in Switzerland. Between 2011 and 2024, net migration to Geneva rose 86 per cent. Zurich’s lower growth over the same period, 5 per cent, masks the significantly higher numbers heading there, almost 16,000 in 2024 compared with Geneva’s 9,000.
“Current global challenges and conflicts mean we’re seeing plenty of movement to countries considered safe havens, and that includes Switzerland, a country that has always remained fiercely politically neutral,” says Alex Koch de Gooreynd, partner in Knight Frank’s residential team. “Add in the strong Swiss franc, their very low interest rates, a world-class education system and the Alpine beauty and you get a snapshot of the reasons for its enduring popularity. You might not come to these Swiss cities for a party lifestyle — that’s what St Moritz or Verbier are for — but if you want personal safety for you and your family, with an outdoor lifestyle, where you won’t be taxed excessively, Switzerland ticks the boxes.”
Against this backdrop, Geneva and Zurich are remarkably different, says Koch de Gooreynd: “Geneva is French-speaking, a diplomatic centre with the UN headquarters and numerous trading companies. Zurich is much larger, German-speaking and the banking capital.” However, he adds that the single biggest difference for many contemplating a move is tax. “Geneva has the forfait fiscal, a lump-sum taxation option [an alternative to income tax] and Zurich does not. This allows non-Swiss residents in Geneva, who are not working in Switzerland, to be taxed based on their living expenses rather than on worldwide income and assets.”
More
New arrivals make do with the dregs of the Zurich’s housing market
Income tax in Switzerland is charged at federal, canton and municipal level. That’s one reason why the scenic lakeside town of Zug, 23km south of Zurich, attracts a disproportionately large number of wealthy relocators. Those accustomed to the bright lights of New York, Dubai or London might find it alarmingly staid, yet Zug has one of Switzerland’s lowest tax rates.
Federal rates are capped at 11.5 per cent while each of the country’s 26 cantons (districts) can set their own rates. Total income tax rates vary from around 22 per cent in Zug canton up to 43 per cent at their highest in Geneva canton. The forfait fiscal option is on offer in 21 cantons.
To add more complexity for would-be relocators, Switzerland also has strict rules governing foreign property ownership. “In general, with just a handful of exceptions, only Swiss citizens or residents are permitted to buy residential property, making residency pathways critical for international buyers,” says Colin Woolcock of Geneva Homes, an associate of Property Vision International in Geneva. “Broadly, there are two structures: standard residency tied to employment in Switzerland and the forfait fiscal. In Geneva, those relocating under the forfait fiscal are mostly buying homes north of £10mn.”
Woolcock, a former international banker from South America who has lived in Geneva for 28 years, says there’s “friendly competition” between the two cities: “Zurich is three times our size, wealthier and the business centre of Switzerland. In Geneva, we play in smaller leagues. We are more relaxed. Zurich is more structured. We’re in the middle of Europe, everything works, you’re close to the mountains, and living on Lake Geneva the quality of life is outstanding. It might not be hip enough for 20 to 30-year-olds,” he laughs, “but it is for everyone else, it’s a great place.”
British-born Russell Collins, chief executive of real estate at Andermatt Swiss Alps, and his wife Anna moved to Küsnacht, 30 minutes outside Zurich, six years ago. Their children, aged eight and six, attend an international school and Collins commutes 50 minutes daily to Andermatt.
More
Housing shortages – what works and what doesn’t
“Zurich combines the feel of a global financial centre with the atmosphere of a village,” he says. “In summer, it’s a usual pre- or post-work ritual for office workers to head down to a badi [public bathing spot] dotted around the lake for a swim. As a family, we regularly go after school.”
“For us, Zurich offered somewhere with real character where we’ve never felt we had to choose between career and quality of life,” he adds.
Zurich’s proximity to snow-sure Andermatt makes it ideal for winter weekend ski trips but overall, Geneva would probably be a more usual choice for avid skiers, says Koch de Gooreynd. “You’re close to wonderful ski resorts, Villars and Verbier among them, and the French Alps are nearby too, Chamonix and Megève,” he says. “This does mean, however, that Geneva is quieter at weekends as people head to the mountains. Overall, Zurich is arguably buzzier than Geneva. There’s certainly more going on in the evenings and more people around at weekends.”
Geneva is where the International Baccalaureate programme was first introduced in the 1960s and both cities have an illustrious roster of prestigious international schools. Both cities also have well-connected international airports, Zurich taking first place for the range of destinations on offer and a more seamless travel experience. But, curiously, Geneva has a wider spread of international residents: more than 41 per cent hold foreign citizenship, observes Costas Dambassinas from Engel & Völkers Private Office, Geneva.
The city is the more expensive property market in absolute terms according to Knight Frank, while Zurich has recorded stronger growth. Top prices in Geneva are around SFr26,895 a square metre (£24,582), an increase of 19 per cent over the past five years, and in Zurich are SFr25,527 (£23,338), a 27 per cent increase over the same period.
Frustratingly for international relocators, there’s a shortage of available quality properties for rent and sale in both cities. “Zurich’s main limitation is scarcity; prime homes in the best lakeside locations rarely come to market and price high,” says Claude Ginesta, chief executive of Ginesta Immobilien. “The city is under pressure from population growth, expat flows and housing shortages.” Data from property consultants Wüest Partner for the first quarter of 2026 shows Zurich as the most expensive of the two for apartments.
More
Renters who land a publicly owned flat in Zurich hit the jackpot
Prices vary significantly by neighbourhood. Cologny tops the prime locations in Geneva, a sought-after commune on the left bank of the lake, well away from the planes, trains and automobile noises that can affect parts of the right bank. “The majority of sales over SFr10mn in Geneva are done in Cologny and in nearby Collonge-Bellerive,” says Koch de Gooreynd. “The equivalents in Zurich are west-facing Zollikon and Küsnacht on the so-called Gold Coast, where available stock is severely limited.”
Tax and neighbourhood niceties aside, at the end of the day, “the Geneva-versus-Zurich decision is usually about choosing between two different versions of international Switzerland: Geneva’s global diplomatic network and Zurich as an economic and financial hub,” says Niki Thomet, managing partner at Engel & Völkers Zurich.
It’s a largely self-selecting decision, generally driven by work and economics. “Those who want the biggest business opportunities, who travel frequently across Europe and work in banking, tech or corporate HQ functions choose Zurich,” Thomet says. “Those who work in diplomacy or commodities trading, who prefer French culture and want a highly international social circle choose Geneva.”
Recent clients deliberating between the two cities include a UN executive relocating from Washington DC, who chose Geneva for its professional network, diplomatic ecosystem and concentration of international organisations, and a tech founder moving from Berlin who opted for Zurich because of the city’s venture capital community, the talent pipeline at ETH University (a world-leading centre for science and technology) and the city’s growing innovation landscape. A London-based banker, eyeing up Geneva for its private banking heritage and Zurich for its scale and career options, settled on Zurich for the opportunities it offered his partner and for its schools.
If neither Geneva nor Zurich hit the spot, where else might Swiss-bound international relocators look?
“Lucerne is a fun city, 45 minutes by train from Zurich with a decent tax regime,” says Koch de Gooreynd. “Outside of Geneva, look at Lausanne, a student town with plenty going on, though you’ll need to be fit to handle the hills. And Lugano comes up more and more in conversations. You’re further from the ski slopes but it combines an Italian lifestyle with Swiss efficiency,” he says.
“People are often accused of moving to Switzerland simply to avoid paying tax, but that’s not necessarily so. It has a good tax regime to encourage people to come, but it is the personal safety and the lifestyle that are the main motivators.”

Senate starts examining ruling majority's bill for new election system
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
11:01:00 CEST
18:01:00 KST

The floor of the Senate on Wednesday started the second reading of a bill presented by the parties of Premier Giorgia Meloni's ruling coalition to bring in a new election law. 
    The bill would see the current system, a mix of first-past-the-post and proportional representation, replaced with a proportional-representation system with bonus seats for the coalition that obtains the most votes, as long as it reaches a threshold of 42%, to ensure it has a working majority in parliament. 
    If no coalition reaches the threshold, or the votes for the Lower House and the Senate produce different results, a purely proportional system is used. 
    The coalitions would have to name their candidate to be premier before the election. 
    There had been talk of lowering the bonus threshold to 41% although this was ruled out during a meeting of 'sherpas' from the ruling majority's parties on Wednesday and the hypothesis of holding a run-off vote was ditched too. 
    There are some other issues have still yet to be definitively decided within the ruling coalition, including the question of whether the contribution of small parties who get just 1% or 2% of the vote should be counted when it comes to calculating if a coalition has reached the threshold. 
    The opposition has cried foul about the drive to overhaul the electoral system, saying the ruling alliance us changing it because it fears losing the general election set to take place next year and wants to minimize the chances of this happening. 
    They have said, among other things, that the envisioned system of bonus seats is unconstitutional. 
    The examination of the bill started with opposition parties illustration four objections presented to the bill. 
    They were dismissed. 
    The Upper House is set to hold its final vote on the bill by September 15 and the bill will move to the floor of the Lower House on September 28 for its third reading in parliament.

Both Omar and Farooq Abdullah stood in attention as full version of Vande Mataram played
NEW DELHI: The Congress has urged its allies to “stand with us” in singing a shorter version of Vande Mataram, after all six stanzas of the national song were played at an event attended by Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah and his father, Farooq Abdullah, the top two leaders of Congress ally National Conference (NC).Congress general secretary (organisation) KC Venugopal argued that the full version of Vande Mataram “sits uneasily with the syncretic and pluralist ethos that our freedom fighters envisioned and nurtured for India.”“For us, the considered judgment of Mahatma Gandhi, Pandit Nehru, Sardar Patel, Subhash Chandra Bose, Rajendra Prasad, Acharya Narendra Dev, Maulana Azad, Sarojini Naidu and J.B. Kripalani — shaped in no small part by the counsel of Gurudev Rabindranath Tagore — remains paramount,” Venugopal said on X.
“With respect and humility, we would like our allies to honour the wisdom and judgment of our freedom fighters, and stand with us in singing only the version of this beautiful and historic song that they adopted,” he added.The Alappuzha MP maintained that the Congress' decision to sing only the first two stanzas was made “deliberately” to prevent the song from being “communalised." He was referring to the Congress’ 1937 resolution recommending that only the first two stanzas of the national song be sung to “maintain communal harmony."
In July, the BJP-led Centre enacted the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, 2026, granting Vande Mataram statutory protection on par with the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana. The law mandates the singing of the full version at official events and provides for imprisonment of up to three years, a fine, or both for anyone found guilty of “insulting” the song.On August 15, Vande Mataram was played for the first time at the official Independence Day ceremony. It was played in full before and after Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s address to the nation from the ramparts of the Red Fort in Delhi.Accused of "minority appeasement" by the ruling BJP, the Congress has stood its ground, repeatedly invoking the 1937 resolution to justify singing only the first two stanzas.

Historic Istanbul bathhouses hit real estate market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:00:22 UTC
18:00:22 KST

(AA Photo)
Dozens of centuries-old Turkish baths in Istanbul are hitting the real estate market as multiplying heirs clash over operations despite surging tourist demand.
The city houses 1,500 to 2,000 active bathhouses, but inheritance disputes and a lack of operators force many historical venues to close, the Chamber of Istanbul Bath, Sanitary Bath, Hot Spring, Sauna and Massage Parlor Operators Head Tahsin Kalyon said.
“The increase in hamams for sale stems from heirs failing to reach an agreement as the number of fractional owners multiplies,” Kalyon said.
Istanbul records nearly 200 historic bathhouses, mostly located in Fatih’s Suriçi district, featuring traditional domes and unique acoustics. Road construction and neglect destroyed several others, leaving 20 to 25 historical venues registered with the chamber alongside about 150 modern facilities.
Corporate baths register directly with the Chamber of Commerce, making the tradesmen chamber the organization with the fastest declining membership, Kalyon said. Three to five partners often form companies to run hotel spas, bypassing the tradesmen chamber.
Customer numbers steadily increase at both venues, driven by location, size and architecture. Traditional baths draw Russians, Germans, Britons, Greeks, Egyptians and Saudis, with Chinese and Korean tourists recently showing interest.
“Customers come to rest, get a scrub and massage, sweat in the sauna and swim,” Kalyon said. “Locals prefer them for the healing they cannot find at home.”
After the 1453 conquest, Turkish baths expanded rapidly throughout the region. Combining unique architecture with physical cleansing, these social hubs remain a vital part of Türkiye’s cultural tourism.

Caught between US and Iran, South Korea weighs Hormuz role
Seoul is sending a fact-finding mission to the UAE as it balances Washington’s security requests with warnings of Iranian retaliation
The South Korean team left for the United Arab Emirates over the weekend and was reportedly assessing operational conditions for a potential deployment.
Seoul’s Ministry of National Defence maintained that the mission “is not being conducted on the premise that an actual deployment would take place” and denied reports that Washington had requested troop deployments by November.

The UAE hosts military forces and support facilities operated by the US and other allied countries. If approved, South Korean forces are expected to use a UAE base as their main operating hub.

‘I am seen as a Marmite figure’: Margaret Hodge on political battles, victories, errors – and regrets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:00:05 UTC
18:00:05 KST

Margaret Hodge doesn’t do small talk. “So, how d’you think Andy’s doing?” is her opening gambit. “Not too bad, huh? I think he’s had a really good start.” It’s classic Hodge – sufficiently curious to ask the question about the new Labour prime minister, and assertive enough to provide the answer before you get yours out. “Yep. Fantastic empathy. But then he’s got to deliver. I think the budget is going to be the key moment. And we’ve also got these awful global challenges and Iran and Hormuz. God, it’s a mess. Ugh. Hahahaha!” She hoots with laughter at the horror of it all.
She says she was against ousting Keir Starmer. “I thought we were doing so badly that what we really needed was a complete change in what we were about, what our ambitions were, where we were going, what our priorities were and how we were going to have a message of hope. I thought it was about much more than Keir at that point. I thought changing leaders was like rearranging deckchairs on the Titanic. I think I was wrong, right?”
Hodge has seen it all. Decade-long leader of Islington council when it was regarded as part of the “loony left”; Labour moderate and Blair-Brown loyalist throughout the years in power; scrapper extraordinaire who has taken on the BNP as MP for Barking, antisemitism in Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour and tax-avoiding tech companies as the formidable chair of the cross-party public accounts committee (PAC).
Now, in the week of her 82nd birthday, Hodge is publishing a memoir, Battleaxe. “I’m reclaiming the term. It shouldn’t be a term of derision. It’s a strong woman.” Who came up with the title? “If I’m absolutely honest, it was my agent. My children don’t like it, but lots of people do.”
Does she really feel like a battleaxe? “People do say: ‘Oh, you don’t want to take on Margaret.’” She stares me down, fiercely proud, big brown eyes aglint. “Can I tell you what I think about myself? I listen and reflect, but when I’ve made up my mind I’m quite strong and determined.” She reminds me of the great football manager Brian Clough, who said: “If I had an argument with a player, we would sit down for 20 minutes, talk about it, and then decide I was right.”
We are at her London home, where she lives alone. It’s every bit as immaculate and stylish as she is. “Don’t look in the garden,” she says. “It’s such a mess – I’ve been away for six weeks.” Her gardening tools are at the ready by the door. The walls are covered in lovely paintings. There are busts of her husband (the high court judge Henry Hodge, who specialised in immigration and died aged 65 in 2009) and her father (Hans Oppenheimer, who co-founded Coutinho, Caro & Co, a steel trading firm that became the multinational Stemcor). On the main wall in the living room is a gorgeous splash of abstract colour by Gillian Ayres. “I love it because it’s painted in big bold strokes and is really optimistic.” You could say much the same of Hodge.
She’s had a fascinating life. Her Jewish parents fled Germany to escape the Nazis, and she was born in Egypt. After a window was broken at her father’s business in 1948 during the first Arab-Israeli war, he took the hint. This time the family fled to Kent in England. Although they were atheists, the family’s only friends were other Jewish refugees.
On Christmas Day in 1954, when Hodge was 10, her mother died of stomach cancer. Shortly afterwards, it was decided that as the brightest child in her class, she should skip a year. So within months she had lost her mother and her peer group. She was devastated, and became increasingly unruly. Oppenheimer didn’t know what to do with her and sent her away to boarding school in Oxford, which she hated. In 1966 she graduated from the London School of Economics with a third-class honours degree in economics.
She worked in corporate market research for seven years, and did a stint as an unqualified teacher. In 1968 she married Andrew Watson, an economist with whom she had two children. She joined the Labour party in 1973, and won a seat on Islington council in the same year. A friend had told her that getting involved in local politics would keep her sane while raising a family. She was, and remains, driven by two desires – to equalise life chances and fight racism.
By 1975, she was chair of the council’s housing committee, with Henry Hodge, then a solicitor, as her deputy. In 1978, she divorced Watson and married Hodge. They went on to have two daughters. In 1982, she became leader of the council. Opponents nicknamed her Enver Hodge, a play on Enver Hoxha, the brutal communist dictator who ruled Stalinist Albania.
Hodge admits she was pretty hardline. “I don’t hold back. Henry always used to try to restrain me.” Can she give an example? “We did a walkout on Michael Heseltine because he did a conference on inner-city regeneration and he was chopping all our funding. I thought it was such hypocrisy.”
Why did Henry object to the walkout? “He said it was a daft thing to do. It was gesture politics. And in that era we were seen as engaging in too much gesture politics.” She pauses. “But,” she barks, “having said that, he was incredibly supportive.”
She gives another example of her gesture politics. “I refused to meet Margaret Thatcher. But she did do these awful things.”
I’m fully aware of the things she did, I say, but wasn’t it … She finishes the sentence for me. “It was stupid. It was stupid. I wouldn’t do it today, but isn’t that interesting to learn that of yourself and how you’ve changed? And it fitted with the time. She was taking on local government and the unions. She was destroying what Andy’s now going to try to recreate.”
She says that pre-Thatcher, she had so much power as a council leader, and the Iron Lady gradually stripped it away – rate-capping, grant cutting, privatisations, the abolition of the Greater London Council. “It was a terrible transformation. We did hate her. She was a Marmite figure, wasn’t she? You loved her or you hated her.”
That’s funny, I say: Marmite is how you describe yourself in Battleaxe. “Yep. Ha! This is true. I am controversial. I am seen as a Marmite figure, too. Why is that? Why is that?” And for once she doesn’t answer her own question.
Has she been surprised by her career? “Yes. As a school kid, I never thought I’d be anybody. I thought I’d be a mum. I’d lost my mother and it made me think the only thing I want to be in life is a mum. So I feel surprised by the extent of my experience and opportunities.” There’s another thing that has surprised her – this time, not so positive. “I never thought I would become a hate figure in the way that I became sometimes.”
What does she consider her greatest achievement? “BNP,” she says instantly. “It has to be the BNP, doesn’t it?” In 2006, the neo-Nazi party won 12 of the 51 seats on Barking and Dagenham council. It looked as if it could go on to win the 2010 council election and that the BNP leader Nick Griffin could oust Hodge as MP in the general election.
Labour had committed the cardinal sin of taking the electorate for granted, Hodge says. What’s more, it was terrified of talking about migration. Meanwhile, her constituency had become unrecognisable to many. “It went from 98% white to under 50% in a generation, which is massive. If your community or my community changed liked that in a generation, we would feel unsettled. At best, unsettled. Kids in the street change, neighbours change, food in the shops changes.”
Hodge discovered her constituents were furious because they believed they were being ignored and that migrants were being prioritised for social housing. She proposed that weighting be given to people’s links to the community rather than housing being based purely on immediate need, which eventually happened.
Many fellow Labour MPs criticised her. Keith Vaz said she “appears to want to be the Alf Garnett of Islington”, while Alan Johnson accused her of pandering to the BNP. “He said that on Question Time. He was going for the deputy leadership,” Hodge says. Did they have a point? “No. I never ever caved in to the racism. Ever. Ever!”
In 2010 Labour wiped out the BNP and she trounced Griffin by 18,000 votes. How did that feel? “Very mixed because it was just under a year since Henry had died. There was a lot of ‘why is Henry not here?’ in it. But I also felt fantastic. Jubilant. If I hadn’t changed the way I’d operated politically, and knocked on doors, I think we would have had a BNP council and a BNP MP. It took me four years of work – it wasn’t just a quick three weeks before the election.”
She talks about the echoes today with Reform. “We lost control of immigration so I think what Shabana [Mahmood] is doing is really important. Now you don’t have massive delays in dealing with asylum seeker applications. People who come here have to abide by our rules, and if they don’t, they lose the right to be here. If they commit a criminal offence they should lose the right to be here.”
Really? Surely our rules are that you serve a sentence for a crime, then come out and get on with your life? I point out that many refugees are deported for minor crimes. “That changes once you’ve got your British citizenship,” she says. But under new Labour legislation, you could wait 20 years for that. “No, I agree,” she says. “I have problems with a 20-year wait.”
What was tougher, fighting the BNP or antisemitism? “The BNP was a much easier fight in an odd way. It was much clearer.” Why? “Because antisemitism was in the Labour party. It was horrible. Antisemitism is the worst of all the battles I have fought. I hated it. I absolutely hated it. It was miserable. I hated the abuse. I hated walking into rooms and thinking: ‘God, who’s for me and who’s against me in this room?’” Abuse on social media included: “The only support she deserves is a handrail to climb the gallows”.
Was she surprised when in 2018 she ended up calling Corbyn … Again she finishes the sentence for me. “An antisemite? Was I surprised at myself? No, that’s the battleaxe in me, isn’t it?” She had told two fellow MPs that she had planned to do it beforehand. So, I ask, was there a theatrical element to it? “I didn’t do it publicly. These two lads wanted me to say it to him on the frontbench. I said, ‘I’m not going to do that – I’ll catch him on his way out [of the House of Commons chamber]’, which is what I did.”
The 2022 report by Martin Forde KC into the toxic culture in the Labour party concluded that antisemitism was weaponised by the left and the right of the party. “I was anti-Corbyn; but no, I never used it as a weapon,” Hodge says. Does she agree in general that it was weaponised on both sides? “Yes, probably. I think there was some weaponising.”
If she saw Corbyn now, what would she say to him? “He doesn’t talk to me. Haha! He passes me by. Haha! Ignores me.” She chuckles with satisfaction. The Labour party asked her to apologise to Corbyn, but she told it where to go. After the party dropped its investigation in August 2018, she told Sky News: “On the day that I heard that they were going to discipline me and possibly suspend me, it felt almost like … what did it feel like to be a Jew in Germany in the 30s?”
Was this when she felt most hated in politics? “Yep.” Has it left scars? “It’s still there. But it’s a joy now to be in the Labour party. When Keir became leader, he single-mindedly tackled antisemitism. I hadn’t expected that and I appreciate it. But it’s a part of my life, so it doesn’t disappear.” Now she says it took Corbyn to help her rediscover her identity. “It’s brought me back to feeling an empathy with who I am – a Jewish immigrant refugee.”
What is her biggest regret in politics? She immediately cites the sexual abuse scandal in Islington children’s homes when she was leader of the council. “I just don’t think any of us thought paedophiles were operating out of children’s homes. It was unconscionable. Now it’s unconscionable today to think that we didn’t realise it. That’s probably caused me more political problems than anything.” She had just been made the UK’s first children’s minister when the scandal became headline news again decades later in 2003. She offered her resignation to Tony Blair, who refused it.
But many people knew it was going on and told you so? “We went through each allegation, and I had all the officers there and they denied any of this was happening. Remember, back then kids in care were called naughty. Today that is unconscionable, isn’t it? I’d listened to all the officers, but I didn’t talk to the kids, and that’s a regret.”
What was even more unconscionable is that she tried to close down an investigation by BBC Radio 4’s Today programme and called Demetrious Panton, a child abuse survivor, an “extremely disturbed person”. She squirms when I mention it. “That was a terrible error. Terrible error.” Why did you do that? “I was advised. Everyone was ringing me up saying the Today programme was digging around and I thought: ‘How the hell can I stop this?’ That was an appalling bit of advice. But in the end I took responsibility. I did it.” Hodge was forced to issue an unreserved public apology in the high court, she paid Panton’s legal costs, and was ordered to pay him £30,000, which included a £10,000 donation to a charity of his choice.
But in the end Hodge, who now sits in the Lords, will be remembered more for exposing corruption than for covering it up. Although she never achieved high office as an MP, she became a political rock star as chair of the PAC between 2010 and 2015. She was convinced it was going to be a dull job when she took it on, yet it proved anything but. The cross-party committee tasked with assessing the value for money of government projects became a must-watch as corporate executives and senior civil servants were held to account for dodging taxes, playing fast and loose with public money, failing to answer questions or simply being rude.
Hodge proved herself a fearless one-woman grilling machine. Google’s Matt Brittin (now director general of the BBC) was well and truly Hodged when she threw the company motto back in his face, saying: “You are a company that says you ‘do no evil’. And I think that you do do evil.” After a session challenging BBC execs over excessive severance payoffs, she concluded it was “a very unedifying experience watching seven people at the top of the BBC dancing on the head of a pin to try and avoid responsibility”.
In 2024, she was made the UK’s official anti-corruption champion, a fiscal Wonder Woman fighting dirty money, offshore tax dodgers and economic crime. On her kitchen table today is a tax file she tells me I mustn’t look at on pain of death. For all of Hodge’s warmth, I tell her she can be terrifying. “Why?” Well, I’ve seen you in action on the PAC, I say.
Again, Hodge hoots with happy laughter. That’s the battleaxe, she says. Then she half-whispers, almost conspiratorially: “I’m always surprised when people say: ‘God, you don’t cross Margaret.’” But I’m not so sure she is.
Battleaxe by Dame Margaret Hodge is out on 10 September, published by HarperCollins (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

‘One day the Taliban will need women to be educated’: three sisters on being forced back to Afghanistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:00:05 UTC
18:00:05 KST

It was a warm summer afternoon on 15 August 2021 when the Taliban entered Kabul and changed the lives of millions. Shallah*, then 16, watched the news at home on the Afghan TV channel Tolo news. She ran crying to the garden, to tell her mother that Afghanistan had fallen.
Her younger sister, Fatimah*, then 11, was at her cousin’s house, where her aunt told her the news. At the time, she says, she did not understand what a takeover meant, or who the Taliban were. Her elder sister, Maahi*, then 22, was well aware of the consequences and remembers her hands shaking at work as she read the news on her phone, on Facebook pages of Afghan news.
At that point the three sisters were living thousands of kilometres away in Qom, a city in central Iran, their family having left Afghanistan six years earlier because of the growing violence and a desire for the girls to grow up in peace. But the family had entered the country illegally and knew they could be arrested or deported at any time.
At first the older sisters tried to convince themselves that if the worst happened, maybe things would not be so bad for women and girls under the Taliban. Perhaps, they thought, these Taliban were different from the ones of the late 1990s, who had implemented a systematic denial of women’s rights that gave rise to the concept of gender apartheid. Twenty years had passed, and the Taliban was now making reassuring promises of women’s rights and girls’ education.
But inside Afghanistan, others were not so sure. Millions have fled to Pakistan and Iran over the past decade, with the numbers accelerating after the Taliban takeover. By the end of last year, there were an estimated 1.4 million undocumented Afghans living illegally in Iran, alongside a further 3 million living there with visas, residency permits or legal refugee status.
Mass deportations from both countries over the past year have seen more than 1 million people forced back to life under the Taliban, with about 400,000 Afghans deported from Iran since the start of the year.
The three sisters were born in Iran, but their parents brought them back to Afghanistan in about 2010 to allow Maahi and her brother to study. At the time, Iran did not allow undocumented Afghan children to remain in education past primary school.
Maahi remembers the strange feelings she had – a mix of happiness to come back home but fearful of leaving the only life she had known until then. At 11 years old, she did not yet understand the war between the US-led coalition and the Taliban.
By 2017, the ongoing war and attacks on civilians convinced her parents to leave again for Iran, to keep their children safe. Maahi was in her last year of high school, and wanted to study to become a journalist. She admired two Afghan journalists: Yama Siawash, who has since been assassinated, and Farahnaz Forotan, who now lives in exile.
The Iranian authorities had relaxed their policy regarding Afghan refugees’ access to schools and published an edict allowing them, even if undocumented, to study in Iran until the end of high school.
Maahi was overjoyed, until she realised that the authorities had put an age limit on this: she was 21 by then, as it had taken her two years to get the educational papers allowing her to study, but only Afghans below the age of 20 could study in Iranian schools. She was forced to start work to support her parents while her younger sisters went to school.
But studying for the first time at a school in Iran, Fatimah, the youngest sister, then five, says she was shocked by the treatment of Afghan children. “When we took our exams, Iranian students always got higher grades than Afghan students, and the principal would find any excuse to criticise the Afghans’ uniforms, never the Iranians’,” she says.
“Because we were undocumented, if we did something that the principal did not like, they threatened to expel us, saying they could drop us from school as they wished,” she says.
Shallah also joined an Iranian school and was a bright student, but this did not stop her from being insulted, including being called “afghani” – the name of the currency – instead of Afghan. She cried at the bus stop and hid the harassment from her parents.
She says she finished top of her class at the age of 12 and was meant to receive a prize. But when she stood up in front of the school and the official realised she was Afghan, the school principal said there had been a mistake, and instead gave the prize to the second-best student, an Iranian girl.
Shallah was among the last Afghan girls to benefit from the edict allowing Afghans to go to school. Fatimah was still in grade 8 (aged 14) when the edict expired in 2025. As she was about to start a new semester, she says the principal came to their class and informed them that only Iranians and documented Afghans would be allowed to register to continue.
The end of the edict last year coincided with a wave of anti-Afghan xenophobia and Iranian authorities’ accusations that Afghans had helped Israel in its attacks against the country.
The authorities intensified arrests and deportations and in May this year, their father was detained while at work. When Maahi and their mother went to look for him at the police station, they were arrested too, with the whole family later deported.
The sisters and their family have now settled in Herat, the city closest to the Iranian border in western Afghanistan. But any earlier hopes Maahi had for a more tolerant Taliban movement have long faded away. Women and girls have been barred from nearly every aspect of public life: schools, universities, most jobs and even parks.
The sisters say they now mostly stay at home, fearful of the Taliban “morality police” and its crackdown on what they deem inappropriate clothing. At least two people, including a boy, were killed by security forces in Herat province in June after protests over the arrests of women accused of violating dress code.
Despite the ban on schooling, the three girls do manage to attend unofficial private classes. The family are using their savings to pay the monthly fees of 2,500 afghani (£28) for the three sisters. It cannot award them diplomas, but the sisters say it keeps them focused on a future in which they might be able to resume their studies.
Maahi, the eldest sister, studies German, and says she hopes she can one day finish high school and emigrate there.
“I am not one to wait for what the future will bring me,” she says. “I am one to make my future by chasing opportunities.”
Shallah, the only one of the sisters who finished high school, says she is considering applying to an overseas university, with the hope of bringing her family with her. “For now, going to these classes [at the academy] gives me a little hope to go to university one day. Without this hope, my life would have ended by now.”
The youngest sister, Fatimah, recently sent her school certificates to the Iranian authorities to ask for help to return, but has had no response. She says she still hopes things will change in Afghanistan.
“I believe that one day, the Taliban will need the women to be educated. They will need women doctors to treat the sick and pregnant women of their family. So they will have no choice but to allow us to study eventually.”
* Names have been changed to protect their identities

Artist Aapo Pukk: Köler made Estonian portrait art great
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Artist Aapo Pukk: Köler made Estonian portrait art great
This March marked 200 years since the birth of Estonian painter Johann Köler. Artist Aapo Pukk honored the anniversary by painting actor Ivo Reinok — dressed as Köler — in the ERR morning show studio.
The choice was no coincidence: Köler is Reinok's distant relative. Pukk admitted that painting in Köler's manner is quite a challenge, but he did not attempt a direct copy.
"I try to chase what Köler might have been thinking, what the journey was, why he did things the way he did. If we take the attitude — why an artist does something — then you can place that in any style or era. Through this, I want to teach what remains constant through time. To rely on those things."
As an artist, Köler was, according to Pukk, a true master. "With a good education, and his career was exceptionally successful: he moved within the tsar's family, and for Estonians it is important that he came from Estonia, was in Estonia, left Estonia, made Estonia and portrait art great, and returned to Estonia. Before him, the masters were not from Estonia — they were Baltic‑German artists — and after him, art became a bit more emotional and individualistic," he explained.
As a characteristic feature of Köler's work, he highlighted its illustrative quality. "He comes with a solid foundation. When you look at his drawings or the preparations for his paintings, people say it's a sketch, but in reality it is made with a very firm line, as if a machine today had drawn it. He simply had such strong, good education and a fantastically good eye," Pukk described.

Senate starts examining ruling majority's bill for new election system
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
10:59:46 CEST
17:59:46 KST

The floor of the Senate on Wednesday started the second reading of a bill presented by the parties of Premier Giorgia Meloni's ruling coalition to bring in a new election law. 
    The bill would see the current system, a mix of first-past-the-post and proportional representation, replaced with a proportional-representation system with bonus seats for the coalition that obtains the most votes, as long as it reaches a certain threshold, to ensure it has a working majority in parliament. 
    The bill currently puts the threshold at 42% although this and several other issues have still yet to be definitively decided within the ruling coalition. 
    If no coalition reaches the threshold, or the votes for the Lower House and the Senate produce different results, a purely proportional system is used. 
    The opposition has cried foul about the drive to overhaul the electoral system, saying the ruling alliance us changing it because it fears losing the general election set to take place next year and wants to minimize the chances of this happening. 
    They have said, among other things, that the envisioned system of bonus seats is unconstitutional. 
    The examination of the bill started with opposition parties illustration four objections presented to the bill. 
    The Upper House is set to hold its final vote on the bill by September 15.

Person dies in fire at Swiss commercial building
One person died in a fire at a commercial building in the Swiss canton of Solothurn on Tuesday.
According to police, the building was completely destroyed. Damage is estimated at several hundred thousand Swiss francs.
The body was found inside the building of fruit and vegetable wholesaler Siragusa in Bellach, Solothurn cantonal police said. Investigations are ongoing to establish the person’s identity, as well as the cause of death and the fire.
The fire at the company’s premises was reported shortly after 10:30am. Fire, ambulance and police crews were dispatched immediately. By the time they arrived, the property was already engulfed in flames, police said.
According to authorities, the full extent of the damage to the company building has yet to be assessed, but it is likely to run to several hundred thousand Swiss francs. Several vehicles were also damaged and the facade of the neighbouring discount supermarket suffered damage from the fire.

What does it mean to say that an artwork contains a mistake? Putting aside the obvious case where…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:59:10 UTC
17:59:10 KST

What does it mean to say that an artwork contains a mistake? Putting aside the obvious case where the artist declares some part to be a mistake, is it even possible for an artwork to be wrong?
When we say something is wrong, it is because it doesn’t reach the standard or norm that we’ve applied to it. We feel it falls short in some way that it shouldn’t. This kind of judgment makes sense when we’re examining something where an error could cause harm. We want to minimize the harm done to ourselves and others so we enforce our norms in an attempt to ensure this happens.
But strictly speaking, an artwork cannot harm anyone. Whatever mistake we see is only a deviation from our own sensibility, from the judgments we would have made if we had been the artist. An artwork is necessarily the creation of a particular individual (or group of individuals). Its form and content are an expression of the artist that comes directly from their unique judgments.

Finland buys over 100 mobile mortar systems from Patria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:57:19 UTC
17:57:19 KST

- Finland has ordered more than 100 Patria TREMOS mortar systems, with an option for hundreds more, and deliveries run through 2028.
- The Finnish Army, which calls the system the 120 KRH M3, received a smaller pre-series batch of TREMOS units in 2025 before this larger order.
Finland has agreed to buy more than 100 Patria TREMOS mortar systems, with an option for hundreds more, defense manufacturer Patria announced.
Deliveries under the serial production contract begin this year and will continue through 2028, Patria said. The Finnish Army designates the system the 120 KRH M3. Finland already received a smaller pre-series batch of TREMOS systems in 2025 ahead of the new order.
TREMOS is a mobile mounting system that lets an existing 120 mm or 81 mm mortar barrel and breech be installed on a wheeled or tracked vehicle instead of towed or carried by hand. Patria developed the system with the Finnish Army and the Finnish Defence Forces Logistics Command, first unveiling it in October 2024. Because it reuses existing barrels, ammunition and firing tables rather than requiring a new weapon altogether, the system is meant to simplify training and logistics for a military that already operates mortars.
The system’s recoil technology absorbs the shock of firing without needing separate ground support legs, which Patria says lets crews open fire within 60 seconds of arriving at a position and drive away immediately after firing their last round. It weighs about 2,800 kg (6,170 pounds), fires 12 to 15 rounds a minute, and can hit targets more than 7 km (4.3 miles) away depending on ammunition. The integration module can be mounted on 4×4, 6×6, 8×8 or light tracked vehicles and can be moved between different vehicles.
“Patria TREMOS is a unique and innovative mortar concept developed to meet the mobility requirements of modern warfare,” said Mikko Leino, executive vice president of Patria’s Defence and Weapon Systems business area. “We expect strong international market potential for the system and are proud to have reached this milestone together with the Finnish Defence Forces, whose collaboration has been excellent throughout the development process. Having Finland as the launch customer is an important milestone for our weapon system business and creates a strong basis for future success.”
Patria will build the systems at its Finnish production facilities, drawing on a supply network of dozens of companies. The company estimates the contract will generate around 130 person-years of work.

The European Commission has approved the pilot project “Summers of Europe”, an initiative of Bulgarian MEP Hristo Petrov for international summer educational camps for children living in poverty. The project envisages the creation of a European network of free summer camps for vulnerable children. The aim is to give them access to sports, culture, education, creative activities, and opportunities to interact with peers from other EU member states, BTA reported.
The initiative is part of efforts to ensure equal access for vulnerable children to extracurricular activities, including sports, culture and leisure. The project has a proposed budget of EUR 1.45 million.
“This is a success for me, but much more than that, it is a success for our country, because we are showing that Bulgaria can put an important social issue on the European agenda and turn it into a real instrument”, MEP Hristo Petrov said.

Oil prices continue to increase, Brent exceeds $100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
08:55:10 UTC
17:55:10 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
09 September 2026•Update: 09 September 2026
Oil prices rose 2.2% on Wednesday, with Brent crude futures exceeding $100 a barrel as the US-Iran tensions continue to affect energy markets.
The international benchmark climbed above $100 a barrel as of 0730GMT.
The price of West Texas Intermediate (WTI) also rose 1.5% to $94.5 per barrel.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday its naval forces targeted two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf, claiming the attacks inflicted heavy damage on the vessels.
In a statement, the IRGC said the strikes were “carried out in response to US aggression, including an attack on five Iranian oil tankers in the Persian Gulf.”
The IRGC did not identify the US vessels or oil tankers it said were targeted, nor did it provide details on when the attacks took place.
The statement also said Iranian naval forces had targeted 10 other vessels that “attempted to enter a restricted and unsafe area of the Strait of Hormuz,” claiming they were acting with the “encouragement and support of the US military.”
The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding in June, mediated by Pakistan and Qatar, outlining steps toward ending hostilities, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing economic restrictions.
The two sides have since accused each other of failing to implement commitments under the memorandum, while military tensions have continued alongside disputes over sanctions and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

China ranks 2nd in global trade in services brand value: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:54:44 CST
17:54:44 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- China ranks second globally with 21 brands in the world's 100 most valuable trade in services brands, with a combined worth of 876.8 billion U.S. dollars, a British consultancy report showed Wednesday.
The ranking, titled Trade in Services 100 2026, was released by Brand Finance, a leading brand valuation consultancy, as the 2026 China International Fair for Trade in Services got underway in Beijing.
The world's 100 most valuable trade in services brands are worth 4.6 trillion U.S. dollars in 2026, the report said, adding that Chinese brands accounted for 19.08 percent, trailing only the United States.
China's trade in services maintained steady growth in the first seven months of 2026, as the export of travel and transport services drove more than half of the overall export expansion, commerce ministry data showed.
The country's services trade totaled nearly 4.45 trillion yuan (about 655.8 billion U.S. dollars) during the period, up 8.3 percent year on year, the data showed.
Digital platforms, financial networks, professional services and travel brands are transforming intangible capabilities into cross-border value, the report noted. "Trade in services is one of the principal mechanisms through which intangible assets are converted into economic value across borders," it said.
Alex Haigh, managing director of Brand Finance Asia Pacific, said by leveraging the synergies of digital platforms, communications networks and large financial institutions, Chinese trade in services brands are rising rapidly, reflecting a new trend of extending "Made in China" to "China services" and "China brands."
China has intensified policy efforts to boost service sector development. The outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) and this year's government work report both made specific arrangements for this sector.
In April, the State Council issued a guideline on advancing the expansion and quality upgrading of the sector. According to the guideline, China aims to make marked progress in high-quality service sector development by 2030, with the total scale of the sector exceeding 100 trillion yuan by then, while more competitive and influential "China services" brands will be cultivated. ■

Unknown Publisher

16:54:40 CST

ISLAMABAD, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Pakistani security forces killed 11 terrorists in two intelligence-based operations in the country's southwest Balochistan province, the military said on Wednesday.
The operations were conducted in Kharan and Washuk districts on Sept. 6 and 7 following reports about the presence of terrorists, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the media wing of the Pakistani military, said in a statement.
Eight terrorists were killed after security forces intercepted them while they were attempting to establish a roadblock and disrupt traffic in Kharan district on Sept. 6, the ISPR said.
In a separate operation in Washuk district on Sept. 7, security forces raided a terrorist hideout and killed three of them following an intense exchange of fire, it added.
Security forces also recovered 2.9 tonnes of explosives allegedly intended for the preparation of improvised explosive devices, according to the statement.
Sanitization operations were underway in the areas to eliminate any remaining militants, the ISPR said. ■

U.S.-Canada trade tensions escalate as Trump tightens tariffs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:54:34 CST
17:54:34 KST

NEW YORK/OTTAWA, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Trade tensions between the United States and Canada escalated Tuesday as U.S. President Donald Trump announced new import bans and tariff adjustments on Canadian products.
Trump signed five proclamations under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, banning imports of certain Canadian alcoholic beverages, dairy and other products previously subject to 50-percent tariffs. The import bans will take effect on Sept. 29.
The measures also revise the scope of tariffs announced on July 20, removing products including rock salt and cement while adding others such as all-terrain vehicles and additional dairy products. The changes will take effect on Sept. 15.
The Section 338 tariffs apply to covered Canadian goods regardless of whether they qualify for preferential treatment under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, and are imposed in addition to tariffs under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
Earlier Tuesday, Trump also directed the U.S. Trade Representative and the General Services Administration (GSA) to remove 50 billion U.S. dollars worth of Canadian-origin products from the GSA's Multiple Award Schedules.
Canada is assessing the latest U.S. measures, Canadian minister responsible for Canada-U.S. trade Dominic LeBlanc said Tuesday, stressing that the government's priority remains protecting Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the country would focus on building strength at home and diversifying partnerships abroad. His government's plans include developing new ports, mines and major energy infrastructure, as well as pursuing more than 20 new trade and defense agreements across five continents.
Trump imposed 50-percent tariffs on about 20 billion U.S. dollars worth of Canadian goods on Aug. 22, prompting Canada to retaliate with tariffs on an equivalent value of U.S. imports, which took effect Tuesday.
The Canadian government is scheduled to hold a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alberta, on Sept. 10-11 to review policy plans and receive analysis from experts in economics and international affairs. ■

HAVANA, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Cuba on Tuesday denounced the U.S. restrictions on fuel imports on power generation on the island.
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said on X that "100 million (U.S.) dollars, an amount similar to the much-touted humanitarian aid offered by the U.S. government, equals only the fuel Cuba needs for limited electricity generation for two weeks."
Rodriguez said the U.S. energy and fuel blockade prevents Cuba from importing fuel oil and diesel for generators used in distributed power generation, which would help reduce blackouts. He said it also hampers the purchase of solar panels and batteries for new photovoltaic parks.
"If they allowed fuel tankers to enter, electricity generation would improve greatly," Rodriguez said, adding that the restrictions are part of what he called "a coldly calculated design" that collectively punishes the Cuban people.
Cuba will present a report to the United Nations (UN) General Assembly on Oct. 27 and 28 to support its draft resolution calling for an end to the U.S. economic, commercial and financial blockade against Cuba.
The report said U.S. sanctions caused 8.08 billion dollars in damages to Cuba at current prices from March 1, 2025, to Feb. 28, 2026, the highest amount recorded so far.
According to the document, the U.S. president's Jan. 29 executive order imposed a fuel blockade that blocks supplies, including those already paid for, through the threat of sanctions and intimidation of companies that own fuel tankers.
The measures also target shipping companies and prevent them from transporting parts and components for Cuba's thermoelectric power plants, some of which have been operating for more than 40 years.
According to Cuba, the energy siege, together with other measures that have sharply intensified the blockade, constitutes an act of genocide and collective punishment against the Cuban population, as well as a violation of international law, international human rights law and international humanitarian law. ■

Researchers develop crater-based AI system for lunar navigation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:54:22 CST
17:54:22 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have developed a crater-based artificial intelligence (AI) navigation system to help spacecraft determine their position during long-duration lunar mapping missions.
Researchers from Adelaide University's Australian Institute for Machine Learning (AIML) and the Andy Thomas Center for Space Resources developed STELLA (Spacecraft craTer-basEd Localization for Lunar mApping), bringing landmark-based navigation to the Moon, according to a university statement released Wednesday.
"Our system helps a spacecraft detect the craters it sees through its camera, match them with the craters on the lunar map, and use that information to determine its position," said Chee-Kheng Chng from AIML, co-lead author of the study published in the journal Astrodynamics.
Researchers tested the system on a comprehensive and realistic synthetic dataset of more than 15,000 images emulating a year-long lunar orbit under a range of conditions, including challenging lighting and different viewing angles.
STELLA consistently achieved meter-level position accuracy and sub-degree altitude accuracy in most scenarios, the researchers said, adding the system could provide a baseline for further development of vision-based navigation solutions for long-duration orbital missions.
"Because it's not possible to put people in space easily or cheaply, there needs to be a way to find information before you go, and that's where AI comes in," said study co-lead author Sofia McLeod from AIML.
With global interest in lunar exploration growing, accurate location data will be increasingly important, particularly for missions searching for resources such as water on the Moon, McLeod said. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: "China Buffer" stabilizes world economy amid tensions, crisis
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-09
16:54:05 CST
17:54:05 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- With ship flows through the Hormuz Strait having largely collapsed during the latest Middle East tensions, China has emerged as a stabilizing force for energy prices by sharply cutting its oil purchases, thereby easing pressure on the global market.
Data released by China's customs authority on Tuesday showed that China imported 320.9 million tonnes of crude oil in the first eight months of the year, down 14.6 percent year on year.
From February to May, China slashed its crude oil imports by nearly 40 percent, or 4.6 million barrels per day, "helping significantly to ease wider pressures in the global market," read a commentary published on the official website of the International Energy Agency.
This is made possible partly because of the large inventories and lower refinery runs in China. Moreover, China has become less dependent on oil as by 2025, renewable energy accounted for about 60 percent of the country's total installed power generation capacity. The rapid adoption of electric vehicles has also reduced its reliance on oil.
China's energy resilience and how it cushions the global market against disruptions offer a revealing lens through which to view its broader economic role. Rather than creating the so-called "China Shock," a narrative that frames China's industrial might as a force that puts pressure on competitors, the Chinese economy has demonstrated both its readiness and capability to contribute to the world as a shock absorber.
At multiple critical junctures, China has acted as a buffer against major risks and shocks facing the global economy.
In the 2008 global financial crisis, while much of the developed world fell into recession, China's swift stimulus package not only stabilized its own economy but also sustained demand for commodities and intermediate goods from dozens of trading partners, helping arrest a deeper global downturn.
During the COVID-19-induced economic contraction, China was the first major economy to register positive annual growth, and its early resumption of manufacturing production provided critical supplies of medical equipment, electronics and daily necessities to pandemic-stricken regions worldwide.
China's role as a supply-side stabilizer has since become even more evident. In recent years, as the global economy has struggled with sluggish growth and elevated inflation, China's high-quality, efficient and cost-competitive products have enriched global supply, lowered living costs and helped ease inflationary pressures across the world.
Backed by its comprehensive industrial system, China has maintained steady growth in foreign trade while effectively cushioning the impact of rising global costs and supply-chain disruptions, thereby helping ease international inflationary pressures, noted Hsia Hua Sheng, associate professor of finance at Getulio Vargas Foundation's Sao Paulo School of Business Administration.
This has benefited both advanced and emerging economies while strengthening market confidence in global production networks, he added.
The role has become particularly visible in the clean energy sector. Through technological innovation and intense market competition, China has built the world's largest and most integrated supply chains for the new energy industry.
Over the past decade, the global average cost of electricity from wind and solar power has fallen by more than 60 percent and 80 percent, respectively. Chinese solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and electric vehicles have made the energy transition more affordable for developing economies, helping them tackle the impact of climate change.
This cushioning effect has benefited millions of households across the world. During Europe's recent heatwave, Chinese air conditioners became a hot commodity as European consumers rushed to keep cool. Behind that surge was China's ability to respond quickly to demand gaps, relying on its efficient and innovative supply chains.
Such gains are not confined to consumers, but also extend upstream into production. For many developing economies, imports from China, including machinery, equipment and industrial components, are critical inputs that help local firms cut costs, raise efficiency, expand capacity and connect more deeply with global markets, cushioning them against disruptions in supply chains and the effects of rising trade protectionism.
As the world's largest manufacturing country, China has built extensive, well-integrated production capacity across a wide range of industrial goods, intermediate products and consumer goods, allowing producers around the world to access key equipment, components and intermediate goods at lower cost and with greater efficiency, noted Geng Nan, a researcher with the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.
A 2025 World Bank working paper found that imports of intermediate goods from China helped boost productivity, capacity utilization and manufacturing employment in Ethiopia, with particularly strong employment gains in labor-intensive industries.
As a market-side buffer, China's demand provides an important outlet for producers around the globe, particularly when protectionism elsewhere is narrowing access to major markets.
Its continued opening up, including the zero-tariff treatment extended from May to imports from all 53 African countries with which China has diplomatic relations, offers developing economies greater access to one of the world's largest consumer markets and serves as another source of support for global trade.
In August, China's imports expanded by 21.7 percent, with growth exceeding that of exports for a sixth successive month. As China moves to expand domestic consumption and pursue more balanced trade, its vast market is expected to create growing demand for commodities, intermediate goods, advanced equipment, consumer products and services.
Seen in this light, China's contribution to the global economy goes beyond traditional output expansion, encompassing multiple roles as a growth engine, a major source of demand, a key supply hub, a driver of green development and a platform for cooperation, noted Gong Liutang, a professor at the Guanghua School of Management of Peking University. ■
